Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Abhidhammapiṭake

In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka

Vibhaṅga-mūlaṭīkā

Root Commentary on the Vibhaṅga

1. Khandhavibhaṅgo

1. The Analysis of the Aggregates

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Suttanta Section

Catusaccadasoti [M 0.0001][V 0.0001] cattāri saccāni samāhaṭāni catusaccaṃ, catusaccaṃ passīti catusaccadaso. Satipi sāvakānaṃ paccekabuddhānañca catusaccadassanabhāve anaññapubbakattā bhagavato catusaccadassanassa tattha ca sabbaññutāya dasabalesu ca vasībhāvassa pattito parasantānesu ca pasāritabhāvena supākaṭattā bhagavāva visesena “catusaccadaso”ti thomanaṃ arahatīti[V 0.0002]. Nāthatīti nātho, veneyyānaṃ hitasukhaṃ āsīsati pattheti, parasantānagataṃ vā kilesabyasanaṃ upatāpeti, “sādhu, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kālena kālaṃ attasampattiṃ paccavekkhitā”tiādinā (a. ni. 8.7) vā taṃ taṃ hitapaṭipattiṃ yācatīti attho. Paramena cittissariyena samannāgato, sabbasatte vā guṇehi īsati abhibhavatīti paramissaro bhagavā “nātho”ti vuccati. “Saddhamme gāravaṃ katvā karissāmī”ti sotabbabhāve kāraṇaṃ vatvā puna savane niyojento āha “taṃ suṇātha samāhitā”ti. “Porāṇaṭṭhakathānayaṃ vigāhitvā karissāmī”ti vā etena sakkaccasavane ca kāraṇaṃ vatvā tattha niyojento āha “saddhamme gāravaṃ katvā taṃ suṇāthā”ti.

As to 'seer of the four truths' (catusaccadaso): the four truths brought together are 'the four truths' (catusaccaṃ); one who sees the four truths is a 'seer of the four truths.' Although disciples and paccekabuddhas also possess the vision of the four truths, it is the Blessed One in particular who deserves the praise 'seer of the four truths.' This is because his vision of the four truths was not preceded by another, because he attained omniscience therein and mastery over the ten powers, and because it is well-proclaimed as being extended into the mental continuums of others. One who protects is a 'protector' (nātha). This means one who wishes for and desires the welfare and happiness of those to be trained; or one who torments the defilements and afflictions that have arisen in the mental continuums of others; or one who requests that very beneficial practice, as in: 'Good, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should from time to time reflect on his own attainment.' The Blessed One is called 'protector' because he is a supreme lord, possessing supreme mastery of mind, or because he exercises authority over and surpasses all beings with his qualities. Having stated the reason for being worthy of being heard—'Having paid reverence to the good Dhamma, I will compose [this]'—he then urges them to listen, saying: 'Listen to it with concentration.' Or, having by this—'Having plunged into the method of the ancient commentaries, I will compose [this]'—stated the reason for careful listening, he urges them to it, saying: 'Having paid reverence to the good Dhamma, listen to it'.

Ettha [M 0.0002] ca “catusaccadaso”ti vacanaṃ thomanameva catuppabhedāya desanāya samānagaṇanadassanaguṇena, “aṭṭhārasahi buddhadhammehi upeto”ti ca aṭṭhārasappabhedāya desanāya samānagaṇanaguṇehīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathāvuttena vā niratisayena catusaccadassanena bhagavā catudhā dhammasaṅgaṇiṃ desetuṃ samattho ahosi, aṭṭhārasabuddhadhammasamannāgamena aṭṭhārasadhā vibhaṅganti yathāvuttadesanāsamatthatāsampādakaguṇanidassanametaṃ “catusaccadaso upeto buddhadhammehi aṭṭhārasahī”ti. Tena yathāvuttāya desanāya sabbaññubhāsitattā aviparītataṃ dassento tattha satte uggahādīsu niyojeti, niṭṭhānagamanañca attano vāyāmaṃ dassento aṭṭhakathāsavane ca ādaraṃ uppādayati, yathāvuttaguṇarahitena asabbaññunā desetuṃ asakkuṇeyyataṃ dhammasaṅgaṇīvibhaṅgappakaraṇānaṃ dassento tattha tadaṭṭhakathāya ca sātisayaṃ gāravaṃ janayati, buddhādīnañca ratanānaṃ sammāsambuddhatādiguṇe vibhāveti.

Here, the statement 'seer of the four truths' is simply a praise by means of the quality of showing a number equal to the teaching with its four divisions; and it should be seen that 'endowed with the eighteen qualities of a Buddha' is by means of the qualities of a number equal to the teaching with its eighteen divisions. Or, by means of the unsurpassed vision of the four truths as described, the Blessed One was able to teach the Dhammasaṅgaṇī in four ways; and by being endowed with the eighteen qualities of a Buddha, he was able to teach the Vibhaṅga in eighteen ways. This statement, 'seer of the four truths, endowed with the eighteen qualities of a Buddha,' is an indication of the qualities that accomplish the ability for the teaching as described. Thereby, by showing that the teaching as described is not distorted because it was spoken by the Omniscient One, he directs beings to learning it and so on. By showing his own effort in bringing it to completion, he generates keen interest in listening to the commentary. By showing the inability of one who is not omniscient and lacks the aforesaid qualities to teach the treatises of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and the Vibhaṅga, he generates exceptional reverence for them and for their commentaries. And he clarifies the qualities of the jewels beginning with the Buddha, such as the quality of perfect self-enlightenment.

Tattha cattāri saccāni pākaṭāneva, aṭṭhārasa pana buddhadhammā evaṃ veditabbā – “atītaṃse buddhassa bhagavato appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ, anāgataṃse…pe… paccuppannaṃse…pe… imehi tīhi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ ñāṇānuparivattaṃ, sabbaṃ vacīkammaṃ…pe. … sabbaṃ manokammaṃ…pe… imehi chahi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato natthi chandassa hāni, natthi dhammadesanāya, natthi vīriyassa, natthi samādhissa, natthi paññāya, natthi vimuttiyā hāni. Imehi dvādasahi dhammehi samannāgatassa buddhassa bhagavato natthi davā, natthi ravā, natthi aphuṭaṃ, natthi vegāyitattaṃ, natthi abyāvaṭamano, natthi appaṭisaṅkhānupekkhā”ti.

Herein, the four truths are evident enough, but the eighteen qualities of a Buddha should be understood thus: 'The Buddha, the Blessed One's, knowledge of the past is unimpeded; …of the future…; …of the present…. For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these three qualities, all bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows upon knowledge; all verbal action…; all mental action…. For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these six qualities, there is no decline in aspiration, no decline in teaching the Dhamma, no decline in energy, no decline in concentration, no decline in wisdom, no decline in liberation. For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these twelve qualities, there is no playfulness, no rashness, nothing unpervaded by knowledge, no hastiness, no pointless arising of thought, no unreflecting equanimity.'

Tattha [V 0.0003] natthi davāti khiḍḍādhippāyena kiriyā natthi. Natthi ravāti sahasā kiriyā natthi. Natthi aphuṭanti ñāṇena aphusitaṃ natthi. Natthi vegāyitattanti turitakiriyā natthi. Natthi abyāvaṭamanoti niratthako cittasamudācāro natthi. Natthi appaṭisaṅkhānupekkhāti aññāṇupekkhā natthi. Katthaci pana “natthi dhammadesanāya hānī”ti alikhitvā “natthi chandassa hāni, natthi vīriyassa, natthi sattiyā”ti likhanti.

Herein, 'there is no playfulness' means there is no action with playful intent. 'There is no rashness' means there is no impetuous action. 'There is nothing unpervaded' means nothing is untouched by knowledge. 'There is no hastiness' means there is no hurried action. 'There is no unoccupied mind' means there is no useless mental activity. 'There is no unreflecting equanimity' means there is no ignorant equanimity. In some places, however, instead of writing 'there is no decline in teaching the Dhamma,' they write: 'there is no decline in aspiration, no decline in energy, no decline in mindfulness.'

1. Dhammasaṅgahe dhamme kusalādike tikadukehi saṅgahetvā te eva dhamme suttante khandhādivasena vutte vibhajituṃ vibhaṅgappakaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha [M 0.0003] saṅkhepena vuttānaṃ khandhādīnaṃ vibhajanaṃ vibhaṅgo. So so vibhaṅgo pakato adhikato yassā pāḷiyā, sā “vibhaṅgappakaraṇa”nti vuccati. Adhikatoti ca vattabbabhāvena pariggahitoti attho. Tattha vibhaṅgappakaraṇassa ādibhūte khandhavibhaṅge “pañcakkhandhā rūpakkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho”ti idaṃ suttantabhājanīyaṃ nāma. Nanu na ettakameva suttantabhājanīyanti? Saccaṃ, iti-saddena pana ādi-saddatthajotakena pakāratthajotakena vā sabbaṃ suttantabhājanīyaṃ saṅgahetvā viññāṇakkhandhoti evamādi evaṃpakāraṃ vā idaṃ suttantabhājanīyanti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā ekadesena samudāyaṃ nidasseti pabbatasamuddādinidassako viya. Tattha nibbānavajjānaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ saṅgāhakattā sabbasaṅgāhakehi ca āyatanādīhi appakatarapadattā khandhānaṃ khandhavibhaṅgo ādimhi vutto.

1. The treatise Vibhaṅga was taught in order to analyze those same dhammas that were collected in the Dhammasaṅgaha by triads and dyads such as the wholesome, and that are spoken of in the Suttas in terms of the aggregates and so on. Therein, 'analysis' (vibhaṅga) is the analyzing of the aggregates, etc., that were stated in brief. Whatever Pāḷi text in which that analysis is made the topic and made primary is called the 'Vibhaṅga treatise.' And 'made primary' means 'grasped as what is to be spoken of.' Therein, in the Analysis of the Aggregates, which is at the beginning of the Vibhaṅga treatise, this passage 'the five aggregates: the aggregate of form… the aggregate of consciousness' is called the Suttanta Analysis. But isn't the Suttanta Analysis more than just this? True, but it should be understood that by the word 'iti' (thus), which indicates the meaning of 'etc.' or indicates manner, the entire Suttanta Analysis is included, meaning 'this Suttanta Analysis is "the aggregate of consciousness," and so on' or 'is of this kind.' Or, it indicates the whole by way of a part, like one indicating a mountain or an ocean. Therein, the Analysis of the Aggregates is stated at the beginning because the aggregates are inclusive of all dhammas apart from Nibbāna, and because the aggregates have fewer terms than the bases and other all-inclusive categories.

Na tato heṭṭhāti rūpādīnaṃ vedayitādisabhāvattābhāvā yasmiṃ sabhāve atītādayo rāsī katvā vattabbā, tassa ruppanādito aññassābhāvā ca heṭṭhā gaṇanesu saṅkhatadhammānaṃ aniṭṭhānaṃ sāvasesabhāvaṃ, na heṭṭhā gaṇanamattābhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Chaṭṭhassa pana khandhassa abhāvā “na uddha”nti āha. Na hi savibhāgadhammehi nissaṭassa atītādibhāvarahitassa ekassa nibbānassa rāsaṭṭho atthīti. “Rāsimhī”ti saddatthasahitaṃ khandha-saddassa visayaṃ dasseti. “Guṇe paṇṇattiyaṃ ruḷhiya”nti visayameva khandha-saddassa dasseti, na saddatthaṃ. Lokiyalokuttarabhedañhi sīlādiguṇaṃ nippadesena gahetvā pavattamāno khandha-saddo sīlādiguṇavisiṭṭhaṃ rāsaṭṭhaṃ dīpetīti. Keci pana “guṇaṭṭho ettha khandhaṭṭho”ti vadanti. Dārukkhandhoti ettha pana na khandha-saddo paññatti-saddassa atthe vattati, tādise pana puthulāyate dārumhi dārukkhandhoti paññatti hotīti paññattiyaṃ nipatatīti vuttaṃ. Tathā ekasmimpi viññāṇe [V 0.0004] pavatto viññāṇakkhandhoti khandha-saddo na ruḷhī-saddassa atthaṃ vadati, samudāye pana niruḷho khandha-saddo tadekadese pavattamāno tāya eva ruḷhiyā pavattatīti khandha-saddo ruḷhiyaṃ nipatatīti vuttaṃ.

'Not below that' is said with reference to the fact that in enumerations of fewer than five, conditioned phenomena are left with a remainder, not with reference to the mere absence of enumeration below. This is because form, etc., do not have the nature of being a feeler, etc., and because there is no nature other than that which begins with being afflicted, etc., in which past and other states can be spoken of as massed together. But because there is no sixth aggregate, he said 'not above.' For there is no meaning of 'heap' for the one Nibbāna, which is released from things with parts and is devoid of past states, etc. The phrase 'in a heap' shows the domain of the word 'aggregate' together with its literal meaning. The phrase 'in qualities, in designation, in usage' shows only the domain of the word 'aggregate,' not its literal meaning. For the word 'aggregate,' occurring with reference to qualities such as virtue without remainder, whether divided into worldly and supramundane, indicates the meaning of 'heap' as distinguished by qualities such as virtue. Some, however, say: 'Here the meaning of aggregate is the meaning of quality.' But in 'a log of wood,' the word 'aggregate' does not function in the sense of the word 'designation'; rather, for such a thick and long piece of wood, the designation 'log of wood' arises, so it is said to 'fall within designation.' Similarly, the word 'aggregate' in 'aggregate of consciousness,' though occurring for a single consciousness, does not express the meaning of the word 'usage'; rather, the word 'aggregate,' established in the sense of a collection, when occurring for a single part of that, occurs by that very same usage, so it is said to 'fall within usage.'

Rāsito guṇatoti sabbattha nissakkavacanaṃ visayasseva khandha-saddappavattiyā kāraṇabhāvaṃ sandhāya katanti veditabbaṃ. “Rāsito”ti imamatthaṃ saddatthavasenapi [M 0.0004] niyametvā dassetuṃ “ayañhi khandhaṭṭho nāma piṇḍaṭṭho”tiādimāha. Koṭṭhāsaṭṭhe khandhaṭṭhe chaṭṭhenapi khandhena bhavitabbaṃ. Nibbānampi hi chaṭṭho koṭṭhāsoti. Tasmā “khandhaṭṭho nāma rāsaṭṭho”ti yuttaṃ. Yesaṃ vā atītādivasena bhedo atthi, tesaṃ ruppanādilakkhaṇavasena taṃtaṃkoṭṭhāsatā vuccatīti bhedarahitassa nibbānassa koṭṭhāsaṭṭhena ca khandhabhāvo na vuttoti veditabbo.

The unreserved statement everywhere, 'From heap, from quality,' should be understood as made with reference to the object itself being the cause for the application of the word 'aggregate.' In order to show this meaning of 'from a heap' by defining it also by way of its literal meaning, he said: 'For this meaning of aggregate is the meaning of a mass.' If the meaning of aggregate were 'portion,' there would have to be a sixth aggregate, for Nibbāna too is a sixth portion. Therefore, it is proper that 'the meaning of aggregate is the meaning of heap.' Or, for those things that have distinctions by way of past, etc., their state as this or that portion is spoken of by way of characteristics such as 'being afflicted.' Therefore, it should be understood that for Nibbāna, which is without distinctions, the state of being an aggregate is not spoken of with the meaning of 'portion'.

Ettāvatāti uddesamattenāti attho. Cattāro ca mahābhūtā…pe… rūpanti evaṃ vibhatto. Katthāti ce? Ekādasasu okāsesu. Iti-saddena nidassanatthena sabbo vibhajananayo dassito. Idañca vibhajanaṃ oḷārikādīsu cakkhāyatanantiādivibhajanañca yathāsambhavaṃ ekādasasu okāsesu yojetabbaṃ, evaṃ vedanākkhandhādīsupi. Viññāṇakkhandho pana ekādasokāsesu purime okāsapañcake “cakkhuviññāṇaṃ…pe… manoviññāṇa”nti chaviññāṇakāyavisesena vibhatto, na tattha manodhātu manoviññāṇadhātūti vibhajanaṃ atthi. Taṃ pana dvayaṃ manoviññāṇanti vuttanti imamatthaṃ dassetuṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “manodhātu manoviññāṇadhātū”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'By this much' (`ettāvatā`) means by way of a summary statement. 'The four great elements… form' is thus analyzed. If it is asked, 'Where?' In the eleven instances. By the word 'thus' (`iti`), which serves as an illustration, the entire method of analysis is shown. This analysis, and the analysis of the eye-base, etc., into gross and subtle, etc., should be applied to the eleven instances as is appropriate. Similarly for the aggregates of feeling, etc. The aggregate of consciousness, however, is analyzed in the first five of the eleven instances with the distinction of the six bodies of consciousness, as 'eye-consciousness… mind-consciousness.' There, the analysis into mind-element and mind-consciousness-element does not exist. To show the meaning that those two are called 'mind-consciousness,' it should be understood that it is stated in the commentary: 'mind-element and mind-consciousness-element.'

Evaṃ pāḷinayena pañcasu khandhesu dhammaparicchedaṃ dassetvā puna aññena pakārena dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādimāha. Etthāti etasmiṃ khandhaniddese.

Having thus shown the determination of phenomena in the five aggregates according to the canonical method, in order to show it in another way, he said, 'Furthermore' (`apica`), etc. 'Here' (`ettha`) means in this exposition of the aggregates.

1. Rūpakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Form

2. Yaṃ kiñcīti ettha yanti sāmaññena aniyamanidassanaṃ, kiñcīti pakārantarabhedaṃ āmasitvā aniyamanidassanaṃ. Ubhayenapi atītaṃ vā…pe… santike vā appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā yādisaṃ vā tādisaṃ vā yaṃ kiñcīti napuṃsakaniddesārahaṃ sabbaṃ byāpetvā saṅgaṇhātīti aññesupi [V 0.0005] napuṃsakaniddesārahesu pasaṅgaṃ disvā tassa adhippetatthaṃ aticca pavattito atippasaṅgassa niyamanatthaṃ “rūpa”nti āha. Yaṃkiñcīti sanipātaṃ yaṃ-saddaṃ kiṃ-saddañca aniyamekatthadīpanavasena ekaṃ padanti gahetvā “padadvayenapī”ti vuttaṃ.

2. In the phrase 'whatever' (`yaṃ kiñci`), 'yaṃ' is an indefinite indication of generality; 'kiñci' is an indefinite indication that touches upon the distinction of other kinds. By both together, it encompasses and includes everything suitable for neuter designation—whether past… or near, whether small or large, of whatever kind it may be. Seeing the over-application to other things also suitable for neuter designation, in order to restrict the over-application that proceeds by exceeding its intended meaning, he said 'form' (`rūpa`). Taking the combination 'yaṃkiñci'—the word 'yaṃ' and the word 'kiṃ'—as a single term because it illuminates a single indefinite meaning, it is said, 'by the two words' (`padadvayenāpi`).

Kiñca, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ vadethāti tumhepi rūpaṃ rūpanti vadetha, taṃ kena kāraṇena vadethāti attho, atha vā kena kāraṇena rūpaṃ, taṃ kāraṇaṃ [M 0.0005] vadethāti attho. Athetesu bhikkhūsu tuṇhībhūtesu bhagavā āha “ruppatīti kho”tiādi.

'And what, bhikkhus, do you call form?' The meaning is: 'You too call form "form"; for what reason do you say so?' Or the meaning is: 'For what reason is it form? State that reason.' Then, when those bhikkhus remained silent, the Blessed One said: 'It is afflicted, therefore…' etc.

Bhijjatīti sītādisannipāte visadisasantānuppattidassanato purimasantānassa bhedaṃ sandhāyāha. Bhedo ca visadisatāvikārāpattīti bhijjatīti vikāraṃ āpajjatīti attho. Vikārāpatti ca sītādisannipāte visadisarūpuppattiyeva. Arūpakkhandhānaṃ pana atilahuparivattito yathā rūpadhammānaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇe sītādīhi samāgamo hoti, yena tattha utuno ṭhitippattassa purimasadisasantānuppādanasamatthatā na hoti āhārādikassa vā, evaṃ aññehi samāgamo natthi. Saṅghaṭṭanena ca vikārāpattiyaṃ ruppana-saddo niruḷho, tasmā arūpadhammānaṃ saṅghaṭṭanavirahitattā rūpadhammānaṃ viya pākaṭassa vikārassa abhāvato ca “ruppantī”ti “ruppanalakkhaṇā”ti ca na vuccanti. Jighacchāpipāsāhi ruppanañca udaraggisannipātena hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca kuppatīti etena kattuatthe rūpapadasiddhiṃ dasseti, ghaṭṭīyati pīḷīyatīti etehi kammatthe. Kopādikiriyāyeva hi ruppanakiriyāti. So pana kattubhūto kammabhūto ca attho bhijjamāno hotīti imassatthassa dassanatthaṃ “bhijjatīti attho”ti vuttaṃ. Atha vā ruppatīti rūpanti kammakattutthe rūpapadasiddhi vuttā. Vikāro hi ruppananti. Teneva “bhijjatīti attho”ti kammakattutthena bhijjati-saddena atthaṃ dasseti. Yaṃ pana ruppati bhijjati, taṃ yasmā kuppati ghaṭṭīyati pīḷīyati, tasmā etehi ca padehi padattho pākaṭo katoti. “Kenaṭṭhenā”ti pucchāsabhāgavasena “ruppanaṭṭhenā”ti vuttaṃ. Na kevalaṃ saddatthoyeva ruppanaṃ, tassa panatthassa lakkhaṇañca hotīti atthalakkhaṇavasena “ruppanalakkhaṇena rūpantipi vattuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha.

'It is broken' (`bhijjati`) is said with reference to the breaking of the preceding continuum, since one sees the arising of a dissimilar continuum on account of an encounter with cold, etc. And breaking is the undergoing of alteration into dissimilarity; thus 'it is broken' means it undergoes alteration. And undergoing alteration is just the arising of dissimilar form on account of an encounter with cold, etc. But for the immaterial aggregates, because of their extremely rapid change, there is no encounter with other things as there is for material phenomena. For material phenomena, at their moment of presence, there is an encounter with cold, etc., whereby the temperature element that has reached its moment of presence, or nutriment, etc., lacks the capacity to produce a continuum similar to the preceding one. The word 'affliction' (`ruppana`) is established in usage for alteration by impact. Therefore, because immaterial phenomena are without impact and lack a manifest alteration like material phenomena, they are not called 'afflicted' or 'having the characteristic of affliction.' It should be understood that affliction by hunger and thirst occurs through an encounter with the internal fire. Here, by 'it is disturbed' (`kuppati`), he shows the derivation of the word 'form' (`rūpa`) in the agent sense; by 'it is struck' (`ghaṭṭīyati`) and 'it is oppressed' (`pīḷīyati`), in the patient sense. For the action of being disturbed, etc., is indeed the action of being afflicted. But to show this meaning—that the agentive and patient meaning is 'that which is being broken'—it is said, 'the meaning is, "it is broken."' Or, 'it is afflicted, therefore it is form' (`ruppatīti rūpaṃ`): the derivation of the word 'form' is stated in the medio-passive sense. For alteration is 'being afflicted.' For that reason, with the word 'it is broken' (`bhijjati`), which has a medio-passive sense, he shows the meaning. But since that which is afflicted and broken is also disturbed, struck, and oppressed, the meaning of the word is therefore made clear by these terms. In conformity with the question, 'By what meaning?', it is said, 'By the meaning of affliction.' Affliction is not merely the meaning of the word, but it is also the characteristic of its referent. Therefore, in terms of the meaning and the characteristic, he says: 'It is also proper to say: "Form has the characteristic of affliction."'

Chijjitvāti mucchāpattiyā muccitvā aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ chedanavasena vā chijjitvā. Accantakhārena sītodakenāti atisītabhāvameva sandhāya accantakhāratā vuttā siyā. Na hi taṃ [V 0.0006] kappasaṇṭhānaṃ udakaṃ sampattikaraṃ pathavīsandhārakaṃ kappavināsaudakaṃ viya khāraṃ bhavituṃ arahati. Tathā hi sati pathavī vilīyeyyāti. Avīcimahānirayeti saussadaṃ avīcinirayaṃ vuttaṃ. Teneva “tattha hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Petti…pe… na hontīti evaṃvidhāpi sattā atthīti adhippāyo evaṃvidhāyeva hontīti niyamābhāvato. Evaṃ kālakañjikādīsupīti. Sarantā gacchantīti sarīsapa-saddassa atthaṃ vadati.

'Having been severed' (`chijjitvā`): having been freed from a state of fainting, or having been severed in the sense of the cutting off of limbs and appendages. 'With extremely caustic cold water': the term 'extremely caustic' might be said with reference to its extreme coldness. For that water which sustains the aeon, which brings prosperity and supports the earth, cannot be caustic like the water at the dissolution of the aeon. For if it were so, the earth would dissolve. 'The great Avīci hell' means the Avīci hell with its surrounding minor hells. Therefore it is said, 'For there…' etc. 'Ghosts… are not': the intention is that beings of this kind also exist, since there is no rule that they must be only of this kind. Similarly in the case of the Kālakañjika asuras, etc. He states the meaning of the word 'reptile' (`sarīsapa`) as 'they go by sliding.'

Abhisaññūhitvāti [M 0.0006] ettha samūhaṃ katvātipi attho. Etena sabbaṃ rūpaṃ…pe… dassitaṃ hotīti etena rūpakkhandha-saddassa samānādhikaraṇasamāsabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tenevāha “na hi rūpato…pe… atthī”ti.

'Having heaped together' (`abhisaññūhitvā`): here the meaning is also 'having made a collection.' By this, 'all form…' is shown. By this he shows that the word 'form-aggregate' (`rūpakkhandha`) is a descriptive determinative compound. Therefore he said: 'For apart from form… there is not…'

3. Pakkhipitvāti ettha ekādasokāsesu rūpaṃ pakkhipitvāti attho. Na hi tattha mātikaṃyeva pakkhipitvā mātikā ṭhapitā, atha kho pakaraṇappattaṃ rūpanti.

3. 'Having included' (`pakkhipitvā`): here the meaning is 'having included form in the eleven instances.' For the matrix (`mātikā`) was not established by including just the matrix itself, but rather by including form, which is the subject of the treatise.

Aparo nayo…pe… ettheva gaṇanaṃ gatanti etena atītaṃsenāti bhummatthe karaṇavacananti dasseti. Yena pakārena gaṇanaṃ gataṃ, taṃ dassetuṃ “cattāro ca mahābhūtā”tiādi vuttanti imasmiṃ atthe sati mahābhūtupādāyarūpabhāvo atītakoṭṭhāse gaṇanassa kāraṇanti āpajjati. Na hi atītaṃsānaṃ vedanādīnaṃ nivattanatthaṃ idaṃ vacanaṃ “yaṃ rūpa”nti eteneva tesaṃ nivattitattā, nāpi rūpassa aññappakāranivattanatthaṃ sabbappakārassa tattha gaṇitattā, na ca anāgatapaccuppannākāranivattanatthaṃ atītaṃsavacanena taṃnivattanatoti. Atha pana yaṃ atītaṃsena gaṇitaṃ, taṃ cattāro ca…pe… rūpanti evaṃ gaṇitanti ayamattho adhippeto, evaṃ sati gaṇanantaradassanaṃ idaṃ siyā, na atītaṃsena gaṇitappakāradassanaṃ, taṃdassane pana sati bhūtupādāyarūpappakārena atītaṃse gaṇitaṃ taṃsabhāvattāti āpannameva hoti, na ca evaṃsabhāvatā atītaṃse gaṇitatāya kāraṇaṃ bhavituṃ arahati evaṃsabhāvasseva paccuppannānāgatesu gaṇitattā sukhādisabhāvassa ca atītaṃse gaṇitattā, tasmā purimanayo eva yutto. Ajjhattabahiddhāniddesesupi tādiso evattho labbhatīti.

'Another method… is included in the count here': by this he shows that 'by the past portion' (`atītaṃsena`) is an instrumental expression in the sense of the locative. To show the way in which it is included in the count, it is said, 'The four great elements…' etc. If this is the meaning, it would follow that the state of being form derived from the great elements is the reason for its inclusion in the count in the past portion. This statement is not for the purpose of excluding feelings, etc., from the past portion, because they are already excluded by the words 'whatever form.' Nor is it for excluding other kinds of form, since all kinds are counted therein. Nor is it for excluding the future and present kinds, since they are already excluded by the very mention of 'the past portion'. But if the intended meaning is that what is counted by 'the past portion' is counted thus: 'The four great elements… and form,' then this would be the showing of another count, not the showing of the way of counting by 'the past portion.' But if that way is shown, it would indeed follow that what is counted in the past portion is counted in the manner of form as elemental and derived because that is its nature. But such a nature cannot be the reason for its being counted in the past portion, since what has that very nature is also counted in the present and future, and since what has the nature of pleasure, etc., is also counted in the past portion. Therefore, the former method is correct. A similar meaning is obtained also in the expositions of the internal and external.

Suttantapariyāyatoti pariyāyadesanattā suttassa vuttaṃ. Abhidhammaniddesatoti nippariyāyadesanattā abhidhammassa nicchayena deso niddesoti katvā vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpītiādīsu ayamadhippāyo [V 0.0007] – suttantabhājanīyattā yathā “atītaṃ nanvāgameyyā”tiādīsu addhānavasena atītādibhāvova vutto, tathā idhāpi niddisitabbo (ma. ni. 3.272, 275; apa. thera 2.55.244) siyā. Evaṃ santepi suttantabhājanīyampi abhidhammadesanāyeva suttante vuttadhamme vicinitvā vibhajanavasena pavattāti abhidhammaniddeseneva atītādibhāvo niddiṭṭhoti.

'By the Suttanta method' (`suttantapariyāyato`): this is said because a sutta is a teaching with an indirect meaning. 'By the Abhidhamma exposition' (`abhidhammaniddesato`): this is said because the Abhidhamma is a teaching without an indirect meaning, and it is called an 'exposition' (`niddesa`) because it is a teaching (`deso`) with certainty (`nicchayena`). In 'Although…' (`kiñcāpi`), etc., this is the intention: because it is the Suttanta analysis, just as in such texts as 'One should not trace back the past,' the state of being past, etc., is spoken of in terms of time, so too it should be expounded here. Even so, although it is the Suttanta analysis, it is still an Abhidhamma teaching because it proceeds by way of investigating and classifying the phenomena taught in the Sutta; therefore the state of being past, etc., is expounded by means of the Abhidhamma exposition.

Addhāsantatisamayakhaṇavasenāti [M 0.0007] ettha cutipaṭisandhiparicchinne kāle addhā-saddo vattatīti “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhāna”ntiādisuttavasena (ma. ni. 1.18; saṃ. ni. 2.20) viññāyati. “Tayome, bhikkhave, addhā. Katame tayo? Atīto addhā, anāgato addhā, paccuppanno addhā”ti (itivu. 63; dī. ni. 3.305) ettha pana paramatthato paricchijjamāno addhā niruttipathasuttavasena (saṃ. ni. 3.62) khaṇaparicchinno yutto. Tattha hi “yaṃ, bhikkhave, rūpaṃ jātaṃ pātubhūtaṃ, ‘atthī’ti tassa saṅkhā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.62) vijjamānassa paccuppannatā tato pubbe pacchā ca atītānāgatatā vuttāti. Yebhuyyena pana cutipaṭisandhiparicchinno (dī. ni. 3.305; itivu. 63) suttesu atītādiko addhā vuttoti so eva idhāpi “addhāvasenā”ti vutto. Sītaṃ sītassa sabhāgo, tathā uṇhaṃ uṇhassa. Yaṃ pana sītaṃ uṇhaṃ vā sarīre sannipatitaṃ santānavasena pavattamānaṃ anūnaṃ anadhikaṃ ekākāraṃ, taṃ eko utūti vuccati. Sabhāgautuno anekantasabhāvato ekagahaṇaṃ kataṃ, evaṃ āhārepi. Ekavīthiekajavanasamuṭṭhānanti pañcachaṭṭhadvāravasena vuttaṃ. Santatisamayakathā vipassakānaṃ upakāratthāya aṭṭhakathāsu kathitā.

In the phrase 'by way of period, continuity, time, and moment,' the term 'period' (addhā) here refers to the time defined by death and rebirth-linking, as is understood from suttas such as 'Was I in the past period?' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.18; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.20). In the passage, 'Monks, there are these three periods. What three? The past period, the future period, and the present period' (Itivuttaka 63; Dīgha Nikāya 3.305), however, when the period is defined in an ultimate sense, it is more fitting for it to be defined by the moment, in accordance with the sutta on the path of language (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.62). For there it is said: 'Monks, whatever material form has been born, has manifested, its designation is "it exists"' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.62). The present is what exists; what precedes and follows it is said to be the past and the future. Generally, however, in the suttas (Dīgha Nikāya 3.305; Itivuttaka 63), the past period, etc., is spoken of as defined by death and rebirth-linking, and so it is this that is meant here by 'by way of period.' Cold is cognate with cold, and similarly heat with heat. But when cold or heat has accumulated in the body and proceeds by way of a continuum, being neither deficient nor excessive but uniform, that is called one season. Since a cognate season is not of a single nature, it is taken as one. The same applies to nutriment. 'Arising from a single cognitive process and a single impulsion' is stated by way of the five and the sixth doors. The discussion on continuity and time is given in the commentaries for the benefit of insight meditators.

Niṭṭhitahetupaccayakiccaṃ, niṭṭhitahetukiccamaniṭṭhitapaccayakiccaṃ, ubhayakiccamasampattaṃ, sakiccakkhaṇe paccuppannaṃ. Janako hetu, upatthambhako paccayo, tesaṃ uppādanaṃ upatthambhanañca kiccaṃ. Yathā bījassa aṅkuruppādanaṃ pathavīādīnañca tadupatthambhanaṃ kammassa kaṭattārūpavipākuppādanaṃ āhārādīnaṃ tadupatthambhanaṃ, evaṃ ekekassa kalāpassa cittuppādassa ca janakānaṃ kammānantarādipaccayabhūtānaṃ upatthambhakānañca sahajātapurejātapacchājātānaṃ kiccaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tattha uppādakkhaṇe hetukiccaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tīsupi khaṇesu paccayakiccaṃ. Pathavīādīnaṃ sandhāraṇādikaṃ phassādīnaṃ phusanādikañca attano attano kiccaṃ sakiccaṃ, tassa karaṇakkhaṇo sakiccakkhaṇo. Saha vā kiccena sakiccaṃ, yasmiṃ khaṇe sakiccaṃ rūpaṃ vā arūpaṃ vā hoti, so sakiccakkhaṇo, tasmiṃ khaṇe paccuppannaṃ.

(1) The function of the cause and condition is completed; (2) the function of the cause is completed but the function of the condition is not completed; (3) the function of both is unfulfilled; (4) present at the moment of its own function. The generator is the cause; the supporter is the condition. Their function is generating and supporting. Just as there is the seed's production of a sprout and the earth element's, etc., support of it, and kamma's production of resultant kamma-produced material form and nutriment's, etc., support of it, so too for each material group and each arising of consciousness, the function of the generating conditions—such as kamma, contiguity, etc.—and of the supporting conascence, prenascence, and postnascence conditions should be connected as is appropriate. Here, the function of the cause should be seen at the moment of arising; the function of the condition, in all three moments. The supporting, etc., of the earth element, etc., and the contacting, etc., of contact, etc., is each its own function. The moment of performing it is the moment of its own function. Or, `sakicca` means 'that which is with its function.' The moment in which a material or immaterial phenomenon has its own function, that is the moment of its own function; at that moment it is present.

6. Ettakamevāti [V 0.0008] “tesaṃ tesa”nti iminā āmeḍitavacanena abhibyāpanatthena vuttatthameva. “Aparassa aparassā”ti dīpanaṃ aparadīpanaṃ. Pariyesatūti [M 0.0008] etena pariyesanāya aniṭṭhanāmanivattanassa akāraṇabhāvaṃ dasseti. Kammadosena hi cittavipallāsadosena ca gūthabhakkhapāṇādayo ummattakādayo ca pariyeseyyuṃ diṭṭhivipallāsena ca yonakādayo na ārammaṇassa pariyesitabbasabhāvattā, apariyesitabbasabhāvattā pana etassa aniṭṭhamicceva nāmanti attho.

6. 'Just this much' means the very meaning stated with a sense of comprehensive inclusion by the repetitive expression 'of those, of those.' 'Of another and another' is an explanation, a further explanation. By 'let him seek,' it shows that seeking is not a reason for an undesirable name to be averted. For due to the fault of kamma and the fault of mental distortion, dung-eating creatures and the like, and the insane and the like would seek it; and due to distortion of view, the Yavanas and others would seek it. This is not because the object has a nature that ought to be sought; rather, because it has a nature that ought not to be sought, its name is simply 'undesirable'—this is the meaning.

Sampattivirahatoti rūpādīnaṃ devamanussasampattibhave kusalakammaphalatā samiddhasobhanatā ca sampatti, tabbirahatoti attho. Tato eva taṃ na pariyesitabbanti. Sobhanāni ca kānici hatthirūpādīni akusalakammanibbattāni na tesaṃyeva hatthiādīnaṃ sukhassa hetubhāvaṃ gacchantīti tesaṃ saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ “akanta”nti vuttaṃ. Tassa tasseva hi sattassa attanā katena kusalena nibbattaṃ sukhassa paccayo hoti, akusalena nibbattaṃ dukkhassa. Tasmā kammajānaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhatā kammakārakasattassa vasena yojanārahā siyā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “kusalakammajaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ nāma natthī”ti idameva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “akusalakammajaṃ iṭṭhaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Tena akusalakammajampi sobhanaṃ parasattānaṃ iṭṭhanti anuññātaṃ bhavissati. Kusalakammajaṃ pana sabbesaṃ iṭṭhamevāti vadanti. Tiracchānagatānaṃ pana kesañci manussarūpaṃ amanāpaṃ, yato te disvāva palāyanti. Manussā ca devatārūpaṃ disvā bhāyanti, tesampi vipākaviññāṇaṃ taṃ rūpaṃ ārabbha kusalavipākaṃ uppajjati, tādisassa pana puññassa abhāvā na tesaṃ tattha abhirati hotīti adhippāyo. Kusalakammajassa pana aniṭṭhassābhāvo viya akusalakammajassa sobhanassa iṭṭhassa abhāvo vattabbo. Hatthiādīnampi hi akusalakammajaṃ manussānaṃ akusalavipākasseva ārammaṇaṃ, kusalakammajaṃ pana pavatte samuṭṭhitaṃ kusalavipākassa. Iṭṭhārammaṇena pana vomissakattā appakaṃ akusalakammajaṃ bahulaṃ akusalavipākuppattiyā kāraṇaṃ na bhavissatīti sakkā vattunti. Vipākaṃ pana katthaci na sakkā vañcetunti vipākavasena iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇavavatthānaṃ suṭṭhu vuttaṃ. Tasmā taṃ anugantvā sabbattha iṭṭhāniṭṭhatā yojetabbā.

'Because of being devoid of attainment' means being devoid of the attainment of material forms, etc., in the existences of gods and humans; attainment is the state of being the fruit of wholesome kamma and the state of being successful and beautiful. 'Being devoid of that' is the meaning. Therefore it is said that one should not seek it. 'Undesirable' is said in order to include certain splendid material forms, such as those of elephants, which are produced by unwholesome kamma and do not become a cause of happiness for those very elephants, etc. For any given being, what is produced by the wholesome kamma done by oneself becomes a condition for happiness, while what is produced by unwholesome kamma becomes a condition for suffering. Therefore, the desirability and undesirability of things born of kamma should be applied according to the being who is the doer of the kamma. In the commentary, however, only this is stated: 'There is nothing called undesirable that is born of wholesome kamma'; it is not stated: 'There is nothing called desirable that is born of unwholesome kamma.' By this it will be conceded that even something splendid born of unwholesome kamma is desirable to other beings. But they say that what is born of wholesome kamma is desirable to all. For some animals, however, the human form is disagreeable, since on seeing it they flee. And humans are frightened on seeing the form of a deity, yet for them too, resultant consciousness arises taking that form as object as a wholesome result; but because they lack such merit, they have no delight in it—this is the intention. However, just as there is an absence of anything undesirable born of wholesome kamma, the statement that there is an absence of anything splendid and desirable born of unwholesome kamma should be refuted. For even elephants, etc., born of unwholesome kamma are an object only for the unwholesome result of humans, while what is born of wholesome kamma, having arisen in the course of existence, is an object for a wholesome result. But because of being mixed with a desirable object, it can be said that a small amount of what is born of unwholesome kamma will not be a cause for the arising of much unwholesome result. Since, however, result cannot be deceived anywhere, the determination of desirable and undesirable objects by way of result is well stated. Therefore, following this, desirability and undesirability should be applied everywhere.

Aniṭṭhā pañca kāmaguṇāti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu “cakkhuviññeyyāni rūpāni iṭṭhānī”ti (ma. ni. 1.166; 2.155; 3.190; saṃ. ni. 5.30) evamādinā iṭṭhāneva rūpādīni “kāmaguṇā”ti vuttānīti? Kāmaguṇasadisesu [M 0.0009] kāmaguṇavohārato, sadisatā ca rūpādibhāvoyeva[V 0.0009], na iṭṭhatā. “Aniṭṭhā”ti vā vacanena akāmaguṇatā dassitāti kāmaguṇavisabhāgā rūpādayo “kāmaguṇā”ti vuttā asive “sivā”ti vohāro viya. Sabbāni vā iṭṭhāniṭṭhāni rūpādīni taṇhāvatthubhāvato kāmaguṇāyeva. Vuttañhi “rūpā loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa”ntiādi (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.133; vibha. 203). Atisayena pana kāmanīyattā suttesu “kāmaguṇā”ti iṭṭhāni rūpādīni vuttānīti.

Why is it said, 'The five cords of sensual pleasure are undesirable'? Is it not the case that in such passages as 'Material forms cognizable by the eye are desirable…' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.166; 2.155; 3.190; Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.30), it is desirable material forms and so on that are called 'cords of sensual pleasure'? It is because of the conventional designation 'cords of sensual pleasure' for things similar to them; the similarity lies in their being material forms and so on, not in their being desirable. Or, by the word 'undesirable,' their nature of not being cords of sensual pleasure is shown. Thus material forms and so on that are dissimilar to cords of sensual pleasure are called 'cords of sensual pleasure,' like the conventional usage 'auspicious' for what is inauspicious. Or, all material forms and so on, whether desirable or undesirable, are cords of sensual pleasure because they are a basis for craving. For it is said: 'Material forms in the world are a pleasing form, an agreeable form…' (Dīgha Nikāya 2.400; Majjhima Nikāya 1.133; Vibhaṅga 203). However, in the suttas, it is desirable material forms and so on that are called 'cords of sensual pleasure' because they are extremely desirable.

Dvīsupi hīnapaṇītapadesu “akusalakammajavasena kusalakammajavasenā”ti vacanaṃ “tesaṃ tesaṃ sattāna”nti sattavasena niyametvā vibhajitattā, ayañcattho “tesaṃ tesa”nti avayavayoge sāmivacanaṃ katvā vuttoti veditabbo. Sattasantānapariyāpannesu kammajaṃ visiṭṭhanti “kammajavasenā”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi pana tehi tehīti etasmiṃ atthe tesaṃ tesanti sāmivacanaṃ, visayavisayīsambandhe vā, na kammajavaseneva rūpādīni vibhattāni, sabbesaṃ pana indriyabaddhānaṃ vasena vibhattānīti viññāyanti. Ettha ca pākaṭehi rūpādīhi nayo dassitoti cakkhādīsupi hīnapaṇītatā yojetabbā.

In both sections on the inferior and the sublime, the statement 'by way of what is born of unwholesome kamma and by way of what is born of wholesome kamma' is made because the analysis is restricted by way of beings, as 'of those particular beings.' And this meaning should be understood as stated by taking 'of those' as a genitive of relation to a part. 'By way of what is born of kamma' is said because what is born of kamma is distinguished among what is included in the continuity of a being. If, however, 'of those' is a genitive in the sense of 'by those,' or in the sense of the relation between object and subject, then it is to be understood that material forms, etc., are not distinguished only by way of what is born of kamma, but are distinguished by way of all that is bound up with the faculties. And here the method is shown by way of manifest material forms, etc., so inferiority and sublimity should be applied also to the eye faculty, etc.

Manāpapariyantanti manāpaṃ pariyantaṃ mariyādābhūtaṃ pañcasu kāmaguṇesu vadāmīti attho. Kiṃ kāraṇanti? Yasmā te ekaccassa manāpā honti, ekaccassa amanāpā, yassa yeva manāpā, tassa teva paramā, tasmā tassa tassa ajjhāsayavasena kāmaguṇānaṃ paramatā hoti, na tesaṃyeva sabhāvato.

'The agreeable has a limit' means: 'I say that the agreeable is the limit, the boundary, among the five cords of sensual pleasure.' What is the reason? Because for some they are agreeable, for others they are disagreeable. For whomever they are agreeable, for them they are supreme. Therefore the supremacy of the cords of sensual pleasure is due to the disposition of each individual, not to their own intrinsic nature.

Evanti imasmiṃ sutte vuttanayena. Ekasmiṃyeva assādanakujjhanato ārammaṇasabhāvasseva iṭṭhāniṭṭhābhāvato aniṭṭhaṃ “iṭṭha”nti gahaṇato ca, iṭṭhaṃ “aniṭṭha”nti gahaṇato ca iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ paṭivibhattaṃ natthīti attho. Saññāvipallāsena cātiādinā nibbāne viya aññesu ārammaṇesu saññāvipallāsena iṭṭhāniṭṭhaggahaṇaṃ hoti. Pittummattādīnaṃ khīrasakkarādīsu dosussadasamuṭṭhitasaññāvipallāsavasena tittaggahaṇaṃ viyāti imamatthaṃ sandhāya manāpapariyantatā vuttāti dasseti.

'Thus' means: in the way stated in this sutta. The meaning is that because one finds gratification and irritation in one and the same thing, because of the absence of desirability and undesirability in the intrinsic nature of the object itself, and because one grasps the undesirable as 'desirable' and the desirable as 'undesirable,' there is no such thing as desirable and undesirable that is individually distinct. By 'and through distortion of perception, etc.,' it is shown that the grasping of desirable and undesirable occurs in other objects through distortion of perception, just as in the case of Nibbāna. It shows that 'the agreeable has a limit' was stated with reference to this meaning: just as for those mad from bile, etc., there is a grasping of bitterness in milk, sugar, etc., by way of a distortion of perception that has arisen from an excess of a humor.

Vibhattaṃ [M 0.0010] atthīti ca vavatthitaṃ atthīti attho, aṭṭhakathācariyehi vibhattaṃ pakāsitanti vā. Tañca majjhimakasattassa vasena vavatthitaṃ pakāsitañca, aññesañca vipallāsavasena idaṃ iṭṭhaṃ [V 0.0010] aniṭṭhañca hotīti adhippāyo. Evaṃ vavatthitassa paniṭṭhāniṭṭhassa aniṭṭhaṃ iṭṭhanti ca gahaṇe na kevalaṃ saññāvipallāsova kāraṇaṃ, dhātukkhobhavasena indriyavikārāpattiādinā kusalākusalavipākuppattihetubhāvopīti sakkā vattuṃ. Tathā hi sītudakaṃ ghammābhitattānaṃ kusalavipākassa kāyaviññāṇassa hetu hoti, sītābhibhūtānaṃ akusalavipākassa. Tūlapicusamphasso vaṇe dukkho nivaṇe sukho, mudutaruṇahatthasambāhanañca sukhaṃ uppādeti, teneva hatthena paharaṇaṃ dukkhaṃ, tasmā vipākavasena ārammaṇavavatthānaṃ yuttaṃ.

And 'it exists as analyzed' means 'it exists as determined'; or, 'it was analyzed and revealed by the commentary masters.' And that is determined and revealed by way of a middling being, and for others, by way of distortion, this becomes desirable or undesirable—such is the intention. However, in grasping what is thus determined as undesirable to be desirable, and vice versa, the cause is not only perceptual distortion; it can also be said to be a condition for the arising of wholesome and unwholesome resultants by way of a disturbance of the elements, the occurrence of impairment of the faculties, and so on. For example, for those afflicted by heat, cold water is a cause for wholesome resultant body-consciousness; for those overcome by cold, it is a cause for an unwholesome resultant. The touch of a cotton swab is painful on a wound but pleasant on an unwounded spot. A massage with a soft, tender hand produces pleasure, but a blow with that same hand produces pain. Therefore, the determination of an object by way of its resultant is proper.

Kiñcāpītiādinā satipi saññāvipallāse buddharūpadassanādīsu kusalavipākasseva gūthadassanādīsu ca akusalavipākassa uppattiṃ dassento tena vipākena ārammaṇassa iṭṭhāniṭṭhataṃ dasseti. Vijjamānepi saññāvipallāse ārammaṇena vipākaniyamadassanaṃ ārammaṇaniyamadassanatthameva katanti.

With the phrase beginning 'Even though,' he shows that even when there is perceptual distortion, there is the arising of only a wholesome resultant in cases such as seeing the Buddha's form, and of an unwholesome resultant in cases such as seeing excrement, thereby showing the desirable or undesirable nature of the object through that resultant. Even when perceptual distortion exists, the demonstration of the determination of the resultant by the object is done solely for the purpose of showing the determination by the object.

Apica dvāravasenapītiādinā dvārantare dukkhassa sukhassa ca paccayabhūtassa dvārantare sukhadukkhavipākuppādanato vipākena ārammaṇaniyamadassanena ekasmiṃyeva ca dvāre samānasseva maṇiratanādiphoṭṭhabbassa saṇikaṃ phusane pothane ca sukhadukkhuppādanato vipākavasena iṭṭhāniṭṭhatā dassitāti viññāyati.

Furthermore, by the phrase beginning 'Also, by way of the doors,' it is understood that the desirable and undesirable nature is shown by way of the resultant. This is because of the production of pleasant and painful resultants at one door by what is a condition for pain and pleasure at another door, thereby demonstrating the determination of the object by the resultant; and because, at one and the same door, pleasure and pain are produced by the gentle touching and the striking of the very same tangible object, such as a gem.

Heṭṭhimanayoti majjhimakasattassa vipākassa ca vasena vavatthitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ gahetvā “tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ uññāta”nti (vibha. 6) ca ādinā vuttanayo. Sammutimanāpanti majjhimakasattassa vipākassa ca vasena sammataṃ vavatthitaṃ manāpaṃ, taṃ pana sabhāveneva vavatthitanti abhinditabbatova na bhindatīti adhippāyo. Saññāvipallāsena nerayikādīhipi puggalehi manāpanti gahitaṃ puggalamanāpaṃ “taṃ taṃ vā panā”tiādinā bhindati. Vemānikapetarūpampi akusalakammajattā kammakāraṇādidukkhavatthubhāvato ca “manussarūpato hīna”nti vuttaṃ.

'The lower method' is the method stated in the passage beginning 'known to those various beings' (Vibh 6), which takes the object as determined by way of a middling being and by way of the resultant. 'The conventionally agreeable' is what is agreed upon and determined as agreeable by way of a middling being and by way of the resultant. The intention is that since this is determined by its own nature, he does not deconstruct it because it is not to be deconstructed. He deconstructs 'the personally agreeable'—what is grasped as agreeable by individuals such as hell-beings due to perceptual distortion—with the phrase beginning 'or this or that.' The form of a vemānika-peta is also said to be 'inferior to a human form' because it is born of unwholesome kamma and because it is a basis for suffering due to kamma, its cause, and so on.

7. Oḷārikarūpānaṃ [M 0.0011] vatthārammaṇapaṭighātavasena supariggahitatā, sukhumānaṃ tathā abhāvato duppariggahitatā ca yojetabbā. Duppariggahaṭṭheneva lakkhaṇaduppaṭivijjhanatā daṭṭhabbā. Dasavidhanti “dūre”ti avuttassa dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Vuttampi pana okāsato dūre hotiyeva.

7. The easy graspability of gross material forms should be connected with their impinging by way of basis and object, and the difficult graspability of subtle forms with the absence of this. The difficulty of penetrating their characteristics should be seen as being for the very reason of their difficult graspability. 'Tenfold' is stated to show what was not stated under 'far.' However, what has been stated is indeed far in terms of location.

Heṭṭhimanayoti [V 0.0011] “itthindriyaṃ…pe… idaṃ vuccati rūpaṃ santike”ti (vibha. 7) evaṃ lakkhaṇato dvādasahatthavasena vavatthitaokāsato ca dassetvā niyyātitanayo. So lakkhaṇokāsavasena dūrasantikena saha gahetvā niyyātitattā bhindamāno missakaṃ karonto gato. Atha vā bhindamānoti sarūpadassanena lakkhaṇato yevāpanakena okāsatoti evaṃ lakkhaṇato okāsato ca visuṃ karonto gatoti attho. Atha vā lakkhaṇato santikadūrānaṃ okāsato dūrasantikabhāvakaraṇena santikabhāvaṃ bhinditvā dūrabhāvaṃ, dūrabhāvañca bhinditvā santikabhāvaṃ karonto pavattoti “bhindamāno gato”ti vuttaṃ. Idha panāti “taṃ taṃ vā pana rūpaṃ upādāya upādāyā”ti idha purimanayena lakkhaṇato dūraṃ okāsato santikabhāvakaraṇena na bhindati bhagavā, na ca okāsadūrato visuṃ karaṇena, nāpi okāsadūrena vomissakakaraṇenāti attho. Kiṃ pana karotīti? Okāsato dūrameva bhindati. Ettha pana na pubbe vuttanayena tidhā attho daṭṭhabbo. Na hi okāsato dūraṃ lakkhaṇato santikaṃ karoti, lakkhaṇato vā visuṃ tena vā vomissakanti. Okāsato dūrassa pana okāsatova santikabhāvakaraṇaṃ idha “bhedana”nti veditabbaṃ. Idha pana na lakkhaṇato dūraṃ bhindatīti etthāpi vā na pubbe vuttanayena tidhā bhedassa akaraṇaṃ vuttaṃ, lakkhaṇato santikadūrānaṃ pana lakkhaṇato upādāyupādāya dūrasantikabhāvo natthīti lakkhaṇato dūrassa lakkhaṇatova santikabhāvākaraṇaṃ lakkhaṇato dūrassa abhedananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Purimanayo viya ayaṃ nayo na hotīti ettakameva hi ettha dassetīti bhindamānoti ettha ca aññathā bhedanaṃ vuttaṃ, bhedanaṃ idha ca aññathā vuttanti.

'The lower method' is the method set forth by showing the distinction from the perspective of characteristic and from the perspective of location established as a twelve-cubit range, as in the passage: 'The female faculty... this is called form that is near' (Vibh 7). Since that method was set forth by taking what is far and near by way of characteristic and location together, it proceeds by deconstructing and mixing. Alternatively, 'deconstructing' means it proceeds by separating characteristic from location by showing its intrinsic nature. Or, by making what is near and far by characteristic into far and near by location, it proceeds by deconstructing the state of nearness into farness, and by deconstructing the state of farness into nearness; thus it is said, 'it proceeds by deconstructing.' Here, however, in the phrase 'depending on this or that form,' the Blessed One does not deconstruct what is far by characteristic by making it near by location, as in the previous method; nor by separating it from what is far by location, nor by mixing it with what is far by location. What then does he do? He deconstructs only what is far by location. Here, however, the meaning should not be seen in three ways as in the previously stated method. For he does not make what is far by location near by characteristic, nor does he separate it by characteristic, nor mix it with that. Rather, the making of what is far by location into a state of nearness by location itself should be understood here as 'deconstruction.' Furthermore, in the statement 'Here, however, he does not deconstruct what is far by characteristic,' the non-performance of deconstruction is not stated in the three ways of the previous method. Rather, since for what is near and far by characteristic there is no state of being far and near by repeatedly depending on characteristic, the non-making of what is far by characteristic into a state of nearness by characteristic itself should be seen as the non-deconstruction of what is far by characteristic. This method is not like the previous one; this much is shown here. Thus, 'deconstructing' is stated differently there, and 'deconstruction' is stated differently here.

Rūpakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the aggregate of form is completed.

2. Vedanākkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Exposition of the Feeling Aggregate

8. Cakkhādayo [M 0.0012] pasādā oḷārikamanomayattabhāvapariyāpannā kāyavohāraṃ arahantīti tabbatthukā adukkhamasukhā “kāyikā”ti pariyāyena vuttā, na kāyapasādavatthukattā. Na hi cakkhādayo kāyapasādā hontīti. Santativasena khaṇādivasena cāti ettha addhāsamayavasena atītādibhāvassa [V 0.0012] avacanaṃ sukhādivasena bhinnāya atītādibhāvavacanato. Na hi sukhāyeva addhāvasena samayavasena ca atītādikā hoti, tathā dukkhā adukkhamasukhā ca kāyikacetasikādibhāvena bhinnā. Tena vedanāsamudayo addhāsamayavasena atītādibhāvena vattabbataṃ arahati samudāyassa tehi paricchinditabbattā, vedanekadesā pana ettha gahitāti te santatikhaṇehi paricchedaṃ arahanti tattha tathāparicchinditabbānaṃ gahitattāti. Ekasantatiyaṃ pana sukhādianekabhedasabbhāvena tesu yo bhedo paricchinditabbabhāvena gahito, tassa ekappakārassa pākaṭassa paricchedikā taṃsahitadvārālambanappavattā, avicchedena taduppādakekavidhavisayasamāyogappavattā ca santati bhavituṃ arahatīti tassa bhedantaraṃ anāmasitvā paricchedakabhāvena gahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Lahuparivattino vā dhammā parivattaneneva paricchedaṃ arahantīti santatikhaṇavasena paricchedo vutto. Pubbantāparantamajjhagatāti etena hetupaccayakiccavasena vuttanayaṃ dasseti.

8. The eye and other sensitive faculties, being included in the gross mind-made existence, are fit for the designation 'body.' Therefore, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling based on them is figuratively called 'bodily,' not because it is based on the body faculty, for the eye and other faculties are not the body faculty. As for 'by way of continuity, by way of moment, etc.': here the state of being past, etc., is not mentioned in terms of duration and time because it is mentioned as distinguished by way of pleasure, etc. For it is not pleasure alone that becomes past, etc., by way of duration and time, but also pain and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, which are distinguished as bodily, mental, etc. Therefore, the origin of feeling deserves to be described as past, etc., in terms of duration and time, because the aggregate is to be defined by them. Here, however, only a part of feeling is taken, so these are fit for delimitation by continuity and moments, since what is to be so delimited there is taken in that way. Furthermore, in a single continuity, since there exist many distinctions such as pleasure, etc., when one distinction among them is taken as what is to be delimited, the continuity that delimits that one particular manifest kind is fit to be so. This continuity proceeds with its associated door and object and through uninterrupted conjunction with a single kind of object that produces it. Therefore, it is taken as the delimiter without referring to another distinction. Or, since phenomena that change quickly are fit for delimitation just by their changing, delimitation by way of continuity and moment is stated. By 'gone to the past, future, and present,' this indicates the method stated in terms of the function of cause and condition.

11. Kilesaggisampayogato sadarathā. Etena sabhāvato oḷārikataṃ dasseti, dukkhavipākaṭṭhenāti etena oḷārikavipākanipphādanena kiccato. Kammavegakkhittā kammapaṭibaddhabhūtā ca kāyakammādibyāpāravirahato nirussāhā vipākā, saussāhā ca kiriyā avipākā. Savipākā ca sagabbhā viya oḷārikāti tabbipakkhato avipākā sukhumāti vuttā.

11. They are accompanied by distress due to association with the fires of defilements. By this, it shows their coarseness by nature; and by 'being a painful result,' it shows their coarseness by function, through the production of a coarse result. Resultants are impelled by the force of kamma, bound to kamma, and without exertion due to the absence of the activity of bodily action, etc. Functional consciousness, however, is with exertion and is non-resultant. And those with resultants are coarse like one who is pregnant; in contrast to them, the non-resultants are said to be subtle.

Asātaṭṭhenāti amadhuraṭṭhena. Tena sātapaṭipakkhaṃ aniṭṭhasabhāvaṃ dasseti. Dukkhaṭṭhenāti dukkhamaṭṭhena. Tena dukkhānaṃ santāpanakiccaṃ dasseti. “Yāyaṃ, bhante, adukkhamasukhā vedanā, santasmiṃ esā paṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti (ma. ni. 2.88; saṃ. ni. 4.267) vacanato adukkhamasukhā pharaṇasabhāvavirahato asantānaṃ kāmarāgapaṭighānusayānaṃ [M 0.0013] anusayanassa aṭṭhānattā santā, sukhe nikantiṃ pariyādāya adhigantabbattā padhānabhāvaṃ nītāti paṇītāti. Tathā anadhigantabbā ca kāmāvacarajātiādisaṅkaraṃ akatvā samānajātiyaṃ ñāṇasampayuttavippayuttādike samānabhede sukhato paṇītāti yojetabbā. Upabrūhitānaṃ dhātūnaṃ paccayabhāvena sukhā khobheti vibādhitānaṃ paccayabhāvena dukkhā ca. Ubhayampi kāyaṃ byāpentaṃ viya uppajjatīti pharati. Madayamānanti madaṃ karontaṃ. Chādayamānanti icchaṃ uppādentaṃ, avattharamānaṃ vā. Ghammābhitattassa sītodakaghaṭena āsittassa yathā kāyo upabrūhito hoti, evaṃ sukhasamaṅginopīti katvā “āsiñcamānaṃ viyā”ti vuttaṃ. Ekattanimitteyevāti pathavīkasiṇādike [V 0.0013] ekasabhāve eva nimitte. Caratīti nānāvajjane javane vedanā viya vipphandanarahitattā sukhumā.

'By the meaning of unpleasurable' means by the meaning of not sweet. By this it shows the undesirable nature which is the opposite of the pleasurable. 'By the meaning of painful' means by the meaning of suffering. By this it shows the tormenting function of sufferings. As it is said: 'Venerable sir, this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is declared by the Blessed One to be peaceful and sublime.' The neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is peaceful because it lacks a pervasive nature and because it is not a basis for the underlying of the unpeaceful latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion; and because it is to be attained by completely mastering craving for pleasure, it is brought to a state of prominence and is thus sublime. Similarly, without confusing it with the sense-sphere class, etc., which are not to be attained, it should be understood as 'more sublime than pleasure' within the same class, which has similar distinctions such as being associated or dissociated with knowledge. Pleasure agitates by being a condition for nourished elements, and pain by being a condition for afflicted elements. Both arise as if pervading the body; thus 'it pervades.' 'Intoxicating' means causing intoxication. 'Covering' means producing desire, or overwhelming. Just as the body of one afflicted by heat is nourished when sprinkled with a pot of cool water, so too for one endowed with pleasure; thus it is said 'as if sprinkling.' 'In a single sign only' means in a sign of a single nature only, such as the earth kasiṇa. 'It moves': it is subtle because it is free from agitation, unlike the feeling in various advertings and impulsions.

Adhippāye akusalatāya akovido. Kusalattike…pe… āgatattāti “kusalākusalā vedanā oḷārikā, abyākatā vedanā sukhumā”ti evaṃ āgatattā. Bhūmantarabhede dassetuṃ “yampī”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Iminā nīhārenāti etena “kāmāvacarasukhato kāmāvacarupekkhā sukhumā”tiādinā sabhāvādibhedena ca oḷārikasukhumabhāvaṃ tatra tatreva kathento na bhindatīti nayaṃ dasseti.

Unskilled in the meaning of unwholesomeness. Because in the wholesome triad... and so on... it is stated thus: 'Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are gross, indeterminate feeling is subtle.' To show the distinction between other planes, 'And whatever...' and so on, is begun. By 'by this method': by this, he indicates the method of explaining the gross and subtle nature in each respective case—with distinctions of nature and so forth, such as 'sense-sphere equanimity is more subtle than sense-sphere pleasure'—without breaking the sequence.

Lokiyalokuttaramissakā kathitā, tasmā ekantapaṇīte hīnapaṇītānaṃ uddhaṭattā evameva ekantahīne ca yathāsambhavaṃ hīnapaṇītatā uddharitabbāti anuññātaṃ hotīti ubhayattha taduddharaṇe na kukkuccāyitabbanti attho.

They are said to be a mixture of worldly and supramundane. Therefore, since the inferior and the sublime have been extracted from the exclusively sublime, just so, from the exclusively inferior too, the state of being inferior and sublime should be extracted as may be the case; this is permitted. Thus, the meaning is that one should not have scruples about extracting them in both cases.

Akusalānaṃ kusalādīhi sukhumattābhāvato pāḷiyā āgatassa aparivattanīyabhāvena “heṭṭhimanayo na oloketabbo”ti vuttanti vadanti, taṃtaṃvāpanavasena kathanepi parivattanaṃ natthīti na parivattanaṃ sandhāya “heṭṭhimanayo na oloketabbo”ti vuttaṃ, heṭṭhimanayassa pana vuttattā avuttanayaṃ gahetvā “taṃ taṃ vā panā”ti vattuṃ yuttanti “heṭṭhimanayo na oloketabbo”ti vuttanti veditabbo. Bahuvipākā akusalā dosussannatāya oḷārikā, tathā appavipākā kusalā. Mandadosattā appavipākā akusalā sukhumā, tathā bahuvipākā kusalā ca. Oḷārikasukhumanikantivatthubhāvato kāmāvacarādīnaṃ oḷārikasukhumatā[M 0.0014]. Sāpīti bhāvanāmayāya bhedanena dānamayasīlamayānañca paccekaṃ bhedanaṃ nayato dassitanti veditabbaṃ. Sāpīti vā tividhāpīti yojetabbaṃ.

Some say that because unwholesome states lack subtlety compared to wholesome ones and so forth, what is stated in the Pāḷi is unalterable, hence the statement, 'The lower method should not be considered.' However, the statement 'The lower method should not be considered' was not made with reference to non-alteration, for even when speaking by way of 'sowing this or that,' there is no alteration. Rather, it should be understood that 'The lower method should not be considered' is said because, since the lower method has been stated, it is proper to say 'this or that, however' by taking up the unstated method. Unwholesome states that are rich in results are coarse due to the prevalence of hatred; likewise wholesome states that are poor in results. Unwholesome states that are poor in results are subtle due to weakness of hatred; likewise wholesome states that are rich in results. The coarseness and subtlety of the sense-sphere and so forth is due to their being objects of coarse and subtle craving. 'That too': it should be understood that by the division of what is based on development, the division of what is based on giving and on virtue is also shown individually, according to the method. Or 'that too' should be connected as 'all three also.'

13. Jātiādivasena asamānakoṭṭhāsatā visabhāgaṭṭho. Dukkhavipākatādivasena asadisakiccatā, asadisasabhāvatā vā visaṃsaṭṭho, na asampayogo. Yadi siyā, dūravipariyāyena santikaṃ hotīti saṃsaṭṭhaṭṭhena santikatā āpajjati, na ca vedanāya vedanāsampayogo atthi. Santikapadavaṇṇanāya ca “sabhāgaṭṭhena sarikkhaṭṭhena cā”ti vakkhatīti vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

13. Being in an unequal division by way of class and so forth is the meaning of 'dissimilar.' Dissimilarity of function or dissimilarity of nature, by way of resulting in suffering and so forth, is the meaning of 'unmixed,' not 'unassociated.' If it were the latter, then 'near' would be the opposite of 'far,' and nearness would follow from the meaning of 'mixed,' but there is no association of a feeling with a feeling. And in the commentary on the word 'near,' it will be said, 'by the meaning of being of the same kind and by the meaning of resemblance'; thus the meaning should be understood in the way already stated.

Na [V 0.0014] dūrato santikaṃ uddharitabbanti kasmā vuttaṃ, kiṃ yathā santikato akusalato akusalā dūreti uddharīyati, tathā tato dūrato kusalato kusalā santiketi uddharituṃ na sakkāti? Na sakkā. Tathā hi sati kusalā kusalāya santiketi katvā santikato santikatā eva uddharitā siyā, tathā ca sati santikasantikataratāvacanameva āpajjati, upādāyupādāya dūrasantikatāva idha vuccati, tasmā dūrato dūruddharaṇaṃ viya santikato santikuddharaṇañca na sakkā kātuṃ dūradūrataratāya viya santikasantikataratāya ca anadhippetattā. Atha pana vadeyya “na kusalā kusalāya eva santiketi uddharitabbā, atha kho yato sā dūre, tassā akusalāyā”ti, tañca natthi. Na hi akusalāya kusalā kadāci santike atthīti. Athāpi vadeyya “yā akusalā kusalāya santike, sā tato dūrato kusalato uddharitabbā”ti, tadapi natthi. Na hi kusale akusalā atthi, yā tato santiketi uddhariyeyya, tasmā idha vuttassa dūrassa dūrato accantavisabhāgattā dūre santikaṃ natthīti na sakkā dūrato santikaṃ uddharituṃ, santike panidha vutte bhinne tattheva dūraṃ labbhatīti āha “santikato pana dūraṃ uddharitabba”nti.

Why is it said, 'The near should not be extracted from the far'? Is it that just as from a near unwholesome state, another unwholesome state is extracted as 'far,' so too from a far wholesome state, another wholesome state cannot be extracted as 'near'? It is not possible. For if that were so, then by taking the wholesome as near to the wholesome, nearness would be extracted from nearness itself. In that case, it would just result in speaking of 'near' and 'nearer,' but here relative farness and nearness are spoken of. Therefore, just as it is not possible to extract 'far' from 'far,' so it is not possible to extract 'near' from 'near,' because a progression of 'far, farther' or 'near, nearer' is not intended. But if one were to say, 'The wholesome should not be extracted as near to the wholesome, but rather to the unwholesome from which it is far'—that too is not the case. For the wholesome is never near to the unwholesome. And if one were to say, 'The unwholesome that is near to the wholesome should be extracted from the wholesome that is far from it'—that too is not the case. For there is no unwholesome in the wholesome that could be extracted as near to it. Therefore, because the 'far' spoken of here is utterly dissimilar, there is no 'near' in the 'far,' so it is not possible to extract 'near' from 'far.' But when 'near' is spoken of here as distinct, 'far' can be found in that very context; therefore he said, 'But from the near, the far should be extracted.'

Upādāyupādāya dūrato ca santikaṃ na sakkā uddharituṃ. Lobhasahagatāya dosasahagatā dūre lobhasahagatā santiketi hi vuccamāne santikatova santikaṃ uddharitaṃ hoti. Tathā dosasahagatāya lobhasahagatā dūre dosasahagatā santiketi etthāpi [M 0.0015] sabhāgato sabhāgantarassa uddhaṭattā, na ca sakkā “lobhasahagatāya dosasahagatā dūre sā eva ca santike”ti vattuṃ dosasahagatāya santikabhāvassa akāraṇattā, tasmā visabhāgatā bhedaṃ aggahetvā na pavattatīti sabhāgābyāpakattā dūratāya dūrato santikuddharaṇaṃ na sakkā kātuṃ. Na hi dosasahagatā akusalasabhāgaṃ sabbaṃ byāpetvā pavattatīti. Sabhāgatā pana bhedaṃ antogadhaṃ katvā pavattatīti visabhāgabyāpakattā santikatāya santikato dūruddharaṇaṃ sakkā kātuṃ. Akusalatā hi lobhasahagatādisabbavisabhāgabyāpikāti. Tenāha “na dūrato santikaṃ uddharitabba”ntiādi.

Relatively, it is not possible to extract the near from the far. For when it is said, 'In relation to a state accompanied by greed, a state accompanied by hatred is far and a state accompanied by greed is near,' then the near is extracted from the near itself. Similarly, in relation to a state accompanied by hatred, a state accompanied by greed is far and a state accompanied by hatred is near; here too, since one extracts from a similar state to another similar state, it is not possible to say, 'In relation to a state accompanied by greed, a state accompanied by hatred is far, and that very same state is near,' because there is no reason for a state accompanied by hatred to be near. Therefore, since dissimilarity does not proceed without grasping a distinction, it is not possible to extract the near from the far, because farness does not pervade what is of a similar kind. For a state accompanied by hatred does not proceed by pervading the entire class of similar unwholesome states. But similarity proceeds having included the distinction; thus, because nearness pervades the dissimilar, it is possible to extract the far from the near. For unwholesomeness pervades all dissimilar states such as those accompanied by greed. Hence it is said, 'The near should not be extracted from the far,' and so on.

Vedanākkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the aggregate of feeling is finished.

3. Saññākkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Perception

17. Cakkhusamphassajā [V 0.0015] saññāti ettha yadipi vatthuto phassassa nāmaṃ phassato ca saññāya, vatthuvisiṭṭhaphassena pana visiṭṭhasaññā vatthunā ca visiṭṭhā hoti phassassa viya tassāpi tabbatthukattāti “vatthuto nāma”nti vuttaṃ. Paṭighasamphassajā saññāti etthāpi yathā phasso vatthārammaṇapaṭighaṭṭanena uppanno, tathā tato jātasaññāpīti “vatthārammaṇato nāma”nti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca paṭighajo samphasso, paṭighaviññeyyo vā samphasso paṭighasamphassoti uttarapadalopaṃ katvā vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

17. Regarding 'perception born of eye-contact': Here, although the name of contact is from the physical basis, and of perception from contact, yet a specific perception is specified by the specific contact on that physical basis, and is specified by the physical basis itself, because like contact, it too has that physical basis as its support. Thus it is said to be 'named from the physical basis.' Regarding 'perception born of impingement-contact': Here too, just as contact arises from the impingement of the physical basis and the object, so too does the perception born from it. Thus it is said to be 'named from the physical basis and the object.' And here it should be understood that 'impingement-contact' is stated with the elision of the latter part of the compound, meaning either 'contact born of impingement' or 'contact cognizable through impingement.'

Viññeyyabhāve vacanaṃ adhikicca pavattā, vacanādhīnā vā arūpakkhandhā, adhivacanaṃ vā etesaṃ pakāsanaṃ atthīti “adhivacanā”ti vuccanti, tatojo samphasso adhivacanasamphasso, samphassoyeva vā yathāvuttehi atthehi adhivacano ca samphasso cāti adhivacanasamphasso, adhivacanaviññeyyo vā samphasso adhivacanasamphasso, tato tasmiṃ vā jātā adhivacanasamphassajā. Pañcadvārikasamphassepi yathāvutto attho sambhavatīti tena pariyāyena tatojāpi saññā “adhivacanasamphassajā”ti vuttā. Yathā pana aññappakārāsambhavato manosamphassajā nippariyāyena “adhivacanasamphassajā”ti vuccati, na evaṃ ayaṃ paṭighasamphassajā āveṇikappakārantarasambhavatoti adhippāyo.

Because they proceed in dependence on speech with regard to what is cognizable, or because the formless aggregates are dependent on speech, or because there is designation as their clarification, they are called 'designations.' Contact born from that is 'designation-contact.' Or contact itself, in the senses already stated, is both designation and contact, thus 'designation-contact.' Or contact cognizable through designation is 'designation-contact'; what is born from that or therein is 'born of designation-contact.' Since the aforesaid meaning is also possible in the case of five-door contact, by that alternative method perception born from it is also called 'born of designation-contact.' But just as perception born of mind-contact is called 'born of designation-contact' unequivocally, as no other mode is possible, so this is not the case for perception born of impingement-contact, since another specific mode is possible. This is the intended meaning.

Yadi [M 0.0016] evaṃ cattāro khandhāpi yathāvuttasamphassato jātattā “adhivacanasamphassajā”ti vattuṃ yuttā, saññāva kasmā evaṃ vuttāti? Tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ atthavasena attano pattampi nāmaṃ yattha pavattamāno adhivacanasamphassaja-saddo niruḷhatāya dhammābhilāpo hoti, tassā saññāya eva āropetvā sayaṃ nivattanaṃ hoti. Tenāha “tayo hi arūpino khandhā”tiādi. Atha vā saññāya paṭighasamphassajāti aññampi visiṭṭhaṃ nāmaṃ atthīti adhivacanasamphassajānāmaṃ tiṇṇaṃyeva khandhānaṃ bhavituṃ arahati. Te pana attano nāmaṃ saññāya datvā nivattāti imamatthaṃ sandhāyāha “tayo hi arūpino khandhā”tiādi. Pañcadvārikasaññā oloketvāpi jānituṃ sakkāti idaṃ tena tenādhippāyena hatthavikārādikaraṇe tadadhippāyavijānananimittabhūtā viññatti viya rajjitvā olokanādīsu rattatādivijānananimittaṃ olokanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇavisayasamāgame pākaṭaṃ hotīti taṃsampayuttāya saññāyapi tathāpākaṭabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

If so, since the four aggregates are also born from the aforesaid contact, it would be proper to call them 'born of designation-contact.' Why is only perception so called? Because in the case of the three aggregates, the term 'born of designation-contact'—which by its established usage is a conventional expression—having also attained its own name in terms of meaning, is attributed to perception alone, and they themselves withdraw. Therefore it is said, 'the three formless aggregates,' etc. Alternatively, since perception has another specific name, 'born of impingement-contact,' the name 'born of designation-contact' should belong to the three aggregates alone. But they, having given their own name to perception, withdraw. With reference to this meaning it is said, 'the three formless aggregates,' etc. That five-door perception can be known even by observing: this is said with reference to the fact that just as intimation, which is the sign for knowing the intention behind making hand gestures and so on, becomes the sign for knowing such things as lust when looking with lust, etc., so observation becomes manifest at the conjunction of eye-consciousness and its object, and thus the associated perception is similarly manifest.

Rajjitvā [V 0.0016] olokanādivasena pākaṭā javanappavattā bhavituṃ arahatīti etissā āsaṅkāya nivattanatthaṃ “pasādavatthukā evā”ti āha. Aññaṃ cintentanti yaṃ pubbe tena cintitaṃ ñātaṃ, tato aññaṃ cintentanti attho.

To dispel the doubt that, being manifest by way of looking with lust, etc., it might be fit to occur as a process of impulsion, he said, 'they are based on the sensitive matter itself.' 'Thinking of something else' means thinking of something other than what was previously thought and known by him; that is the meaning.

Saññākkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the aggregate of perception is concluded.

4. Saṅkhārakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Formations

20. Heṭṭhimakoṭiyāti ettha bhummaniddesova. Tattha hi padhānaṃ dassitanti. Yadi evaṃ uparimakoṭiyā taṃ na dassitanti āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, uparimakoṭigatabhāvena vinā heṭṭhimakoṭigatabhāvābhāvato. Heṭṭhimakoṭi hi sabbabyāpikāti. Dutiye karaṇaniddeso, heṭṭhimakoṭiyā āgatāti sambandho. Purimepi vā “heṭṭhimakoṭiyā”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, tañca padhānasaṅkhāradassanavasenāti sambandhakaraṇena karaṇaniddesova. Taṃsampayuttā saṅkhārāti ekūnapaññāsappabhede saṅkhāre āha. Gahitāva honti tappaṭibaddhattā.

20. In the phrase 'at the lower limit,' this is an exposition in the locative case, for there the principal is shown. If so, does it follow that it is not shown for the upper limit? It does not follow, because without the state of having reached the upper limit, there is no state of having reached the lower limit. For the lower limit is all-pervasive. In the second instance, it is an exposition in the instrumental case; the connection is 'having come from the lower limit.' Or, what was said previously, 'by the lower limit,' is also an exposition in the instrumental case by way of connection, in the sense of showing the principal formations. 'Formations associated with that' refers to the forty-nine kinds of formations. They are included because they are connected with it.

Saṅkhārakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the aggregate of formations is concluded.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discourse

Samuggama-saddo [M 0.0017] sañjātiyaṃ ādiuppattiyaṃ niruḷho. Taṃtaṃpaccayasamāyoge hi purimabhavasaṅkhātā purimantato uddhaṅgamanaṃ samuggamo, sandhiyaṃ vā paṭisandhiyaṃ uggamo samuggamo. So pana yattha pañcakkhandhā paripuṇṇā samuggacchanti, tattheva dassito. Etena nayena aparipuṇṇakhandhasamuggamo ekavokāracatuvokāresu sakkā viññātunti. Atha vā yathādhigatānaṃ pañcannampi khandhānaṃ saha uggamo uppatti samuggamo. Etasmiṃ atthe vikaluppatti asaṅgahitā hoti. Himavantappadese jātimantaeḷakalomaṃ jātiuṇṇā. Sappimaṇḍabindūti evaṃ etthāpi bindu-saddo [V 0.0017] yojetabbo. Evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāganti evaṃvaṇṇaṃ evaṃsaṇṭhānañca. Paṭibhajanaṃ vā paṭibhāgo, sadisatābhajanaṃ sadisatāpattīti attho. Evaṃvidho vaṇṇappaṭibhāgo etassāti evaṃvaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ.

The word 'samuggama' is established in the sense of birth and initial arising. For when the respective conditions come together, the rising up from the prior end, known as the previous existence, is 'samuggama'; or the rising at the junction, at rebirth-linking, is 'samuggama.' But this is shown only where the five aggregates arise in full. By this method, the arising of incomplete aggregates in the one-constituent and four-constituent existences can be understood. Alternatively, 'samuggama' is the simultaneous arising, the origination, of all five aggregates as they have been acquired. In this sense, defective origination is not included. In the Himalayan region, the wool of a sheep of good breed is 'jātiuṇṇā.' As in 'a drop of the cream of ghee,' so here too the word 'drop' should be connected. 'Of such a counterpart-color' means of such a color and such a shape. Or 'paṭibhāga' is 'paṭibhajanaṃ' (resembling); the meaning is attaining similarity, reaching likeness. 'It has a counterpart of such a kind of color'; thus it is 'of such a counterpart-color.'

Santatisīsānīti santatimūlāni, santatikoṭṭhāsā vā. Anekindriyasamāhārabhāvato hi padhānaṅgaṃ “sīsa”nti vuccati, evaṃ vatthudasakādikoṭṭhāsā anekarūpasamudāyabhūtā “sīsānī”ti vuttānīti.

'Heads of continuity' means roots of continuity, or portions of continuity. For because it is a collection of many faculties, the principal part is called the 'head.' Similarly, the portions such as the base-decad, being a collection of many material phenomena, are called 'heads.'

Pañcakkhandhā paripuṇṇā hontīti gaṇanāpāripūriṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na tassa tassa khandhassa paripuṇṇataṃ. Kammasamuṭṭhānapaveṇiyā vuttattā “utucittāhārajapaveṇī ca ettakaṃ kālaṃ atikkamitvā hotī”tiādinā vattabbā siyā, taṃ pana “pubbāparato”ti ettha vakkhatīti akathetvā kammajapaveṇī ca na sabbā vuttāti avuttaṃ dassetuṃ opapātikasamuggamo nāma dassito. Evaṃ…pe… pañcakkhandhā paripuṇṇā hontīti paripuṇṇāyatanānaṃ vasena nayo dassito, aparipuṇṇāyatanānaṃ pana kāmāvacarānaṃ rūpāvacarānaṃ parihīnāyatanassa vasena santatisīsahāni veditabbā.

'The five aggregates are complete' is said with reference to completeness in number, not the completeness of each individual aggregate. Since the series originating from kamma has been mentioned, it might be said: 'The series originating from temperature, mind, and nutriment also occurs after such and such a time has passed.' But since this will be spoken of in the section on 'earlier and later,' it is not stated here. And to show what is unstated—that the kamma-born series is not fully described—the arising of spontaneous beings is shown. Thus... 'the five aggregates are complete': this method is shown by way of the complete sense bases.
