But for those with incomplete sense bases—those of the sense-sphere and the form-sphere—the loss of the heads of continuity should be understood by way of the deficient sense bases.

Pubbāparatoti ayaṃ vicāraṇā na pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ uppattiyaṃ, atha kho tesaṃ rūpasamuṭṭhāpaneti daṭṭhabbā. Taṃ dassento āha “evaṃ panā”tiādi. Apacchāapure uppannesūti etena saṃsayakāraṇaṃ dasseti. Sahuppannesu hi idameva paṭhamaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, idaṃ pacchāti adassitaṃ na sakkā viññātuṃ. Ettha ca “pubbāparato”ti etissā vicāraṇāya vatthubhāvena paṭisandhiyaṃ uppannā pavattā pañcakkhandhā gahitā. Tattha ca niddhāraṇe [M 0.0018] bhummaniddesoti “rūpaṃ paṭhamaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetī”ti āha. Aññathā bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇatthe bhummaniddese sati rūpassa rūpasamuṭṭhāpanakkhaṇe kammassapi rūpasamuṭṭhānaṃ vadantīti ubhayanti vattabbaṃ siyāti. Rūpārūpasantatiñca gahetvā ayaṃ vicāraṇā pavattāti “rūpaṃ paṭhamaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetī”ti vuttaṃ. Aññathā paṭisandhikkhaṇe eva vijjamāne gahetvā vicāraṇāya kariyamānāya arūpassa rūpasamuṭṭhāpanameva natthīti pubbāparasamuṭṭhāpanavicāraṇāva idha na upapajjatīti vattabbaṃ siyāti. Vatthu uppādakkhaṇe dubbalaṃ hotīti sabbarūpānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe dubbalataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tadā hi taṃ pacchājātapaccayarahitaṃ āhārādīhi ca anupatthaddhanti “dubbala”nti vuttaṃ. Kammavegakkhittattāti [V 0.0018] idaṃ satipi bhavaṅgassa kammajabhāve sāyaṃ vipākasantati paṭisandhikkhaṇe purimabhavaṅgasamuṭṭhāpakato aññena kammunā khittā viya appatiṭṭhitā, tato parañca samānasantatiyaṃ anantarapaccayaṃ purejātapaccayañca labhitvā patiṭṭhitāti imamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

This investigation concerning 'earlier and later' is not about the arising of the five aggregates, but should be understood as being about their origination of material form. To explain this, he says, 'Thus, moreover,' etc. By 'when arisen not later and not earlier,' he indicates the reason for doubt. For among things arisen simultaneously, it cannot be known without it being shown that 'this one originates material form first, this one later.' And here, for this investigation of 'earlier and later,' the five aggregates that have arisen at rebirth-linking and are proceeding are taken as the basis. And there, it is an exposition in the locative case of specification, thus he says: 'Material form first originates material form.' Otherwise, if there were an exposition in the locative case in the sense of the characteristic of one state being conditioned by another, it would have to be said 'both,' as they say that at the moment of the origination of material form by material form, there is also origination of material form by kamma. This investigation proceeds by taking the continuity of material and immaterial phenomena, hence it is said, 'Material form first originates material form.' Otherwise, if the investigation were conducted by taking only what exists at the moment of rebirth-linking, there would be no origination of material form by the immaterial, so it would have to be said that the investigation into earlier and later origination is not applicable here. 'The physical basis is weak at the moment of arising' is said with reference to the weakness of all material phenomena at the moment of arising. For then, being devoid of postnascence condition and unsupported by nutriment, etc., it is called 'weak.' 'Because of being cast by the force of kamma'—this is said with reference to this meaning: although the life-continuum is kamma-born, this resultant continuity, at the moment of rebirth-linking, is as if cast by a kamma different from that which originated the previous life-continuum, and is thus unestablished; but thereafter, in the same continuity, having obtained contiguity condition and prenascence condition, it becomes established.

Paveṇī ghaṭiyatīti cakkhādivatthusantati ekasmiṃ vijjamāne eva aññassa nirodhuppattivasena ghaṭiyati, na cutipaṭisandhinissayavatthūnaṃ viya vicchedappavattīti attho. Aṅgatoti jhānaṅgato. Jhānaṅgāni hi cittena saha rūpasamuṭṭhāpakāni, tesaṃ anubaladāyakāni maggaṅgādīni tesu vijjamānesu visesarūpappavattidassanato. Atha vā yāni cittaṅgāni cetanādīni cittassa rūpasamuṭṭhāpane aṅgabhāvaṃ sahāyabhāvaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ baladāyakehi jhānaṅgādīhi aparihīnanti attho. Tato parihīnattā hi cakkhuviññāṇādīni rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpentīti. Yo pana vadeyya “paṭisandhicittena sahajātavatthu tassa ṭhitikkhaṇe ca bhaṅgakkhaṇe ca purejātanti katvā paccayavekallābhāvato tasmiṃ khaṇadvaye rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpetū”ti, taṃ nivārento āha “yadi hi citta”ntiādi. Tattha ṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇesupi tesaṃ dhammānaṃ vatthu purejātaṃ na hotīti na vattabbamevetanti anujāni, tatthāpi dosaṃ dasseti. Yadi tadā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeyya, tava matena paṭisandhicittampi samuṭṭhāpeyya, tadā pana rūpuppādanameva natthi. Yadā ca rūpuppādanaṃ, tadā uppādakkhaṇe tava matenapi paccayavekallameva paṭisandhikkhaṇe purejātanissayābhāvato, tasmā paṭisandhicittaṃ rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpetīti ayamettha adhippāyo. Uppādakkhaṇe aṭṭha rūpāni gahetvā [M 0.0019] uṭṭhahati. Kasmā? Arūpadhammānaṃ anantarādipaccayavasena savegānaṃ paripuṇṇabalānameva uppattito.

'The series is connected' means that the continuity of the physical bases of the eye, etc., is connected by way of the cessation and arising of another while one still exists; the meaning is that its proceeding is not interrupted like that of the physical bases dependent on death and rebirth-linking. 'From the factor' means from the jhāna factor. For the jhāna factors, together with consciousness, are originators of material form, because when path factors and so on, which give them strength, are present, the proceeding of special material phenomena is seen. Alternatively, the meaning is that those mental factors such as volition, which become factors and helpers for consciousness in originating material form, are not deficient because of the strength given by the jhāna factors and so on. For because of being deficient in that, eye-consciousness and so on do not originate material form. But as to one who might say: 'Since the physical basis co-nascent with the rebirth-linking consciousness is pre-nascent at its moment of presence and moment of dissolution, let it originate material form in those two moments due to the absence of a deficiency of conditions'—refuting him, he says: 'If consciousness...' and so on. Therein he concedes: 'It should not be said that the physical basis of those states is not pre-nascent even at the moments of presence and dissolution,' but he also points out a fault therein. If it were to originate material form then, according to your view, the rebirth-linking consciousness too would originate it; but then there is no production of material form at all. And when there is production of material form, then at the moment of arising, even according to your view, there is a deficiency of conditions because at the moment of rebirth-linking there is an absence of a pre-nascent support. Therefore, the rebirth-linking consciousness does not originate material form—this is the intention here. At the moment of arising, it arises having grasped eight material phenomena. Why? Because immaterial states arise only with their full strength and impetus, by way of contiguity condition and so on.

Avisayatāyāti agatapubbassa gāmassa āgantukassa avisayabhāvato. Appahutatāyāti tattha tassa anissarabhāvato. Cittasamuṭṭhāna…pe… ṭhitānīti idaṃ yehākārehi cittasamuṭṭhānarūpānaṃ cittacetasikā paccayā honti, tehi sabbehi paṭisandhiyaṃ cittacetasikā samatiṃsakammajarūpānaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ paccayā hontīti katvā vuttaṃ.

'Because of not being its domain' means because of a village not previously gone to being outside the domain of a newcomer. 'Because of not having power' means because of his lack of mastery there. 'Mind-originated... established'—this is said because the mind and mental factors at rebirth-linking are conditions for the thirty kinds of kamma-originated material phenomena, as may be the case, in all the ways that mind and mental factors are conditions for mind-originated material phenomena.

Vaṭṭamūlanti taṇhā avijjā vuccati. Cuticittena uppajjamānaṃ rūpaṃ tato purimatarehi uppajjamānaṃ viya na bhavantare uppajjatīti vaṭṭamūlassa vūpasantattā anuppatti vicāretabbā.

'The root of the round'—craving and ignorance are so called. The material form arising with the death-consciousness does not arise in another existence like the material form arising with earlier moments; its non-arising should be considered as due to the pacification of the root of the round.

Rūpassa [V 0.0019] natthitāyāti rūpānaṃ nissaraṇattā arūpassa, virāgavasena pahīnattā uppādetabbassa abhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Rūpokāse vā rūpaṃ atthīti katvā rūpapaccayānaṃ rūpuppādanaṃ hoti, arūpaṃ pana rūpassa okāso na hotīti yasmiṃ rūpe sati cittaṃ aññaṃ rūpaṃ uppādeyya, tadeva tattha natthīti attho. Purimarūpassapi hi paccayabhāvo atthi puttassa pitisadisatādassanatoti.

'Because of the non-existence of material form' is said with reference to the absence of what is to be produced, because the formless realm is an escape from material phenomena and because of abandonment by way of dispassion. Or, since material form exists in the form-plane, there is production of material form by material-form conditions. But the formless realm is not a plane for material form, so the meaning is that that very material form, in the presence of which the mind could produce other material form, does not exist there. For even a preceding material form has the state of a condition, as seen from the resemblance of a son to his father.

Utu pana paṭhamaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe samuṭṭhāpanatoti adhippāyo. Utu nāma cesa dandhanirodhotiādi utussa ṭhānakkhaṇe uppādane kāraṇadassanatthaṃ arūpānaṃ uppādakāladassanatthañca vuttaṃ. Dandhanirodhattā hi so ṭhitikkhaṇe balavāti tadā rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, tasmiṃ dharante eva khippanirodhattā soḷasasu cittesu uppannesu paṭisandhianantaraṃ cittaṃ utunā samuṭṭhite rūpe puna samuṭṭhāpetīti adhippāyo. Tasmiṃ dharante eva soḷasa cittāni uppajjitvā nirujjhantīti etena pana vacanena yadi uppādanirodhakkhaṇā dharamānakkhaṇe eva gahitā, “soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukaṃ rūpa”nti vuttaṃ hoti, athuppādakkhaṇaṃ aggahetvā nirodhakkhaṇova gahito, “sattarasacittakkhaṇāyuka”nti, sace nirodhakkhaṇaṃ aggahetvā uppādakkhaṇo gahito, “adhikasoḷasacittakkhaṇāyuka”nti, yadi pana uppādanirodhakkhaṇā dharamānakkhaṇe na gahitā, “adhikasattarasacittakkhaṇāyuka”nti. Yasmā pana “tesu paṭisandhianantara”nti [M 0.0020] paṭisandhipi tassa dharamānakkhaṇe uppannesu gahitā, tasmā uppādakkhaṇo dharamānakkhaṇe gahitoti nirodhakkhaṇe aggahite adhikasoḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatā vakkhamānā, gahite vā soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatā adhippetāti veditabbā.

Temperature, however, first originates material form; the meaning is that it originates it at the moment of presence of the rebirth-linking consciousness. And this 'temperature' is said to be 'slow in ceasing, etc.' to show the cause for its origination at the moment of duration of temperature and also to show the time of arising of immaterial phenomena. For because it is slow in ceasing, it is strong at the moment of presence and thus originates material form. The meaning is that while that material form endures, because of the rapid cessation of consciousness, after sixteen consciousnesses have arisen, the consciousness subsequent to rebirth-linking again originates material form in the temperature-originated material form. But with this statement, 'while it endures, sixteen consciousnesses arise and cease,' if the moments of arising and cessation are included within the moment of duration itself, it is said, 'material form has a lifespan of sixteen thought-moments.' If, however, the arising-moment is not included and only the cessation-moment is included, it is said, 'it has a lifespan of seventeen thought-moments.' If the cessation-moment is not included and the arising-moment is included, it is said, 'it has a lifespan of more than sixteen thought-moments.' If, however, the moments of arising and cessation are not included in the moment of duration, it is said, 'it has a lifespan of more than seventeen thought-moments.' However, since in the phrase 'among them, after rebirth-linking,' the rebirth-linking itself is included among what has arisen during its duration, the arising-moment is thereby included in the moment of duration. Therefore, it should be understood that when the cessation-moment is not included, a lifespan of more than sixteen thought-moments is to be stated, or when it is included, a lifespan of sixteen thought-moments is intended.

Ojā kharāti savatthukaṃ ojaṃ sandhāyāha. Sabhāvato sukhumāya hi ojāya vatthuvasena atthi oḷārikasukhumatāti.

'Nutritive essence is coarse': this is said referring to nutritive essence that has a physical basis. For although nutritive essence is subtle by its intrinsic nature, by way of its physical basis there is coarseness and subtlety.

Cittañcevāti cittassa pubbaṅgamatāya vuttaṃ, taṃsampayuttakāpi pana rūpasamuṭṭhāpakā hontīti. Yathāha “hetū hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo”tiādi (paṭṭhā. 1.1.1). Cittanti vā cittuppādaṃ gaṇhāti, na kammacetanaṃ viya ekadhammameva avijjamānaṃ. Kammasamuṭṭhānañca taṃsampayuttehipi samuṭṭhitaṃ hotūti ce? Na, tehi samuṭṭhitabhāvassa avuttattā, avacanañca tesaṃ kenaci paccayena paccayabhāvābhāvato.

'And consciousness': this is said because of the primacy of consciousness. However, its associated factors also originate material form. As it is said: 'Root is a condition for root-associated states and for the material phenomena originated thereby by way of root condition,' etc. (Paṭṭh. 1.1.1). Or, by 'consciousness' is meant the conscious unit, not, like kamma-volition, a single phenomenon that is no longer present. If it is asked: 'Might kamma-originated form also be originated by its associated factors?' No, because its being originated by them has not been stated; and this is not stated because they are not a condition by way of any specific condition.

Addhānaparicchedatoti [V 0.0020] kālaparicchedato. Tattha “sattarasa cittakkhaṇā rūpassa addhā, rūpassa sattarasamo bhāgo arūpassā”ti eso addhānaparicchedo adhippeto. Paṭisandhikkhaṇeti idaṃ nayadassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ tato parampi rūpārūpānaṃ sahuppattisabbhāvato, na panetaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe asahuppattiabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇesupi rūpuppattiṃ sayameva vakkhatīti. Phalappattanidassanena ca rūpārūpānaṃ asamānakālataṃ nidasseti, na sahuppādaṃ tadatthaṃ anāraddhattā. Sahuppādena pana asamānakālatā sukhadīpanā hotīti taṃdīpanatthameva sahuppādaggahaṇaṃ.

'By the demarcation of the lifespan' means by the demarcation of time. Here, 'seventeen thought-moments are the lifespan of material form, and a seventeenth part of the lifespan of material form is the lifespan of immaterial form'—this is the intended demarcation of the lifespan. 'At the moment of rebirth-linking': this should be seen as a mere indication of the method, since even after that, the co-arising of material and immaterial phenomena exists. But it should be understood that this was not said with reference to the presence of co-nascence at the moment of rebirth-linking, for it will be stated that material form arises even at the moments of presence and dissolution of the rebirth-linking consciousness. And by showing the attainment of fruition, it indicates the non-synchronicity of the material and the immaterial, not their co-nascence, as that was not the purpose undertaken. However, their non-synchronicity is easily explained by way of co-nascence, so the mention of co-nascence is just for the purpose of that explanation.

Yadi evaṃ rūpārūpānaṃ asamānaddhattā arūpaṃ ohāya rūpassa pavatti āpajjatīti etassā nivāraṇatthamāha “tattha kiñcāpī”tiādi. Ekappamāṇāvāti nirantaraṃ pavattamānesu rūpārūpadhammesu nicchiddesu arūparahitaṃ rūpaṃ, rūparahitaṃ vā arūpaṃ natthīti katvā vuttaṃ. Ayañca kathā pañcavokāre kammajarūpappavattiṃ nibbānapaṭibhāganirodhasamāpattirahitaṃ sandhāya katāti daṭṭhabbā. Pade padanti attano pade eva padaṃ nikkhipanto viya lahuṃ lahuṃ akkamitvāti attho. Anohāyāti yāva cuti, tāva [M 0.0021] avijahitvā, cutikkhaṇe pana saheva nirujjhantīti. Yasmiñcaddhāne aññamaññaṃ anohāya pavatti, so ca paṭisandhicutiparicchinno ukkaṃsato etesaṃ addhāti. Evanti etena pubbe vuttaṃ avakaṃsato addhāpakāraṃ imañca saṅgaṇhātīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

To prevent the objection, 'If so, then because material and immaterial phenomena have unequal lifespans, it would follow that the occurrence of material form happens having left behind the immaterial,' he says, 'Therein, although...' etc. 'Of equal measure': this is said on the grounds that among material and immaterial phenomena that occur continuously without a gap, there is no material form devoid of the immaterial, or immaterial form devoid of the material. And this statement should be understood as made with reference to the occurrence of kamma-born material form in the five-constituent existence, excluding the attainment of cessation, which is the counterpart of Nibbāna. 'Step by step' means treading lightly, lightly, as if placing a foot right in one's own footstep. 'Without abandoning' means without leaving behind up to the moment of death; at the moment of death, however, they cease together. And the time-span in which they occur without abandoning one another, that, being demarcated by rebirth-linking and death, is their lifespan at its maximum. 'Thus': by this is included both the previously stated type of lifespan at its minimum and this one. It should be understood thus.

Ekuppādanānānirodhatoti etaṃ dvayamapi saha gahetvā rūpārūpānaṃ “ekuppādanānānirodhato”ti eko daṭṭhabbākāro vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ ito paresupi. Pacchimakammajaṃ ṭhapetvāti tassa cuticittena saha nirujjhanato nānānirodho natthīti katvā vuttanti vadanti. Tassa pana ekuppādopi natthi heṭṭhā soḷasake pacchimassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppattivacanato. Yadi pana yassa ekuppādanānānirodhā dvepi na santi, taṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sabbampi cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ siyā, pacchimakammajassa pana uppattito parato cittesu pavattamānesu kammajarūpassa anuppattito vajjetabbaṃ gahetabbañca tadā natthīti “pacchimakammajaṃ ṭhapetvā”ti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tato pubbe pana aṭṭhacattālīsakammajarūpapaveṇī atthīti tattha yaṃ cittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ, taṃ aññassa uppādakkhaṇe nirujjhatīti “ekuppādanānānirodha”nti gahetvā ṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇesu uppannarūpāni vajjetvā evaṃ ekuppādanānānirodhato veditabbāti yojanā [V 0.0021] katāti daṭṭhabbā. Tañhi rūpaṃ arūpena, arūpañca tena ekuppādanānānirodhanti. Tattha saṅkhalikassa viya sambandho paveṇīti katvā aṭṭhacattālīsakammajiyavacanaṃ kataṃ, aññathā ekūnapaññāsakammajiyavacanaṃ kattabbaṃ siyā.

'From single arising and diverse cessations': it should be understood that by taking this pair together for material and immaterial phenomena, one aspect to be seen is stated. So too in the subsequent cases. 'Excluding the last kamma-born material form': they say this is said on the grounds that since it ceases together with the death-consciousness, it does not have diverse cessations. But for that, there is not even a single arising, because below, in the section on the sixteen, its arising is spoken of at the dissolution moment of the last consciousness. However, if for something both single arising and diverse cessations do not exist, that should be excluded. All that arises at the dissolution moment of consciousness might have to be excluded. But it should be understood that 'excluding the last kamma-born' is said because for the last kamma-born, after its arising, while other consciousnesses are occurring, kamma-born material form does not arise, so there is nothing to be excluded and included then. Before that, however, there is a series of forty-eight kamma-born material forms. Therein, what arises at the arising-moment of one consciousness ceases at the arising-moment of another. Thus, taking it as 'single arising and diverse cessations,' and excluding the material forms that arise at the moments of presence and dissolution, it should be understood that the connection is made in this way: 'from single arising and diverse cessations.' For that material form with the immaterial, and the immaterial with it, have single arising and diverse cessations. Therein, because the connection, the series, is like a chain, the statement of 'forty-eight kamma-borns' is made; otherwise, the statement of 'forty-nine kamma-borns' would have to be made.

Nānuppāda…pe… pacchimakammajena dīpetabbāti tena sudīpanattā vuttaṃ. Etena hi nayena sakkā tato pubbepi ekassa cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannarūpaṃ aññassapi bhaṅgakkhaṇe eva nirujjhatīti taṃ arūpena, arūpañca tena nānuppādaṃ ekanirodhanti viññātunti. Ubhayatthāpi pana aññassa cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannaṃ rūpaṃ aññassa ṭhitikkhaṇe, tassa ṭhitikkhaṇe uppajjitvā ṭhitikkhaṇe eva nirujjhanakaṃ arūpañca na saṅgahitaṃ, taṃ “nānuppādato nānānirodhato”ti ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchatīti veditabbaṃ. Catusantatikarūpena hi nānuppādanānānirodhatādīpanā ettha ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannassa dassitattā adassitassa vasena nayadassanaṃ hotīti. Samatiṃsakammajarūpesu eva ṭhitassapi gabbhe gatassa maraṇaṃ atthīti tesaṃ eva vasena pacchimakampi yojitaṃ. Amarā nāma bhaveyyuṃ, kasmā? Yathā channaṃ vatthūnaṃ pavatti[M 0.0022], evaṃ taduppādakakammeneva bhavaṅgādīnañca tabbatthukānaṃ pavattiyā bhavitabbanti. Na hi taṃ kāraṇaṃ atthi, yena taṃ kammajesu ekaccaṃ pavatteyya, ekaccaṃ na pavatteyyāti. Tasmā āyuusmāviññāṇādīnaṃ jīvitasaṅkhārānaṃ anūnattā vuttaṃ “amarā nāma bhaveyyu”nti.

'Non-co-arising… etc. … should be explained by the last kamma-born material form': this is said because it is well explained by that. For by this method it can be known that even before that, material form arisen at the dissolution moment of one consciousness ceases at the dissolution moment of another; thus that material form with the immaterial, and the immaterial with it, are non-co-arising and have a single cessation. However, in both cases, neither material form arisen at the presence moment of one consciousness and ceasing at the presence moment of another, nor the immaterial which, having arisen at its presence moment, ceases at that very same presence moment, are included. It should be understood that this is included right here under 'from non-co-arising and diverse cessations.' For here the explanation of non-co-arising and diverse cessations by way of the four continuities of material form is shown for what arises at the presence moment; thus the method is shown by way of what is not shown. Since even for one who has gone to the womb and is established among the thirty kamma-born material forms, death exists, by way of these the last one is also connected. 'They would be immortal': why? Because just as there is the occurrence of the six bases, so too there must be the occurrence of the life-continuum, etc., and the things based on them, by that very kamma that produces them. For there is no reason why among the kamma-born, one part should occur and another part should not. Therefore, because the life-sustaining formations—life faculty, heat, consciousness, etc.—are not deficient, it is said, 'They would be immortal'.

“Uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ aññassa uppādakkhaṇe nirujjhati, ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannaṃ aññassa ṭhitikkhaṇe, bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannaṃ aññassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe nirujjhatī”ti idaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatattā vuttanti adhippāyo. Attano panādhippāyaṃ uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nirodhakkhaṇe, ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannañca uppādakkhaṇe, bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇe nirujjhatīti dīpetiyeva. Evañca katvā addhānaparicchede “taṃ pana sattarasamena cittena saddhiṃ nirujjhatī”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 26 pakiṇṇakakathā) vuttaṃ. Imāya pāḷiyā virujjhati, kasmā? Catusamuṭṭhānikarūpassapi samānāyukatāya bhavitabbattāti adhippāyo. Yathā pana etehi yojitaṃ, tathā rūpassa ekuppādanānānirodhatā nānuppādekanirodhatā ca natthiyeva.

'What has arisen at an arising-moment ceases at another's arising-moment; what has arisen at a presence-moment ceases at another's presence-moment; what has arisen at a dissolution-moment ceases at another's dissolution-moment.' The meaning is that this is said because it comes in the Commentary. But he indeed explains his own view that what has arisen at an arising-moment ceases at a dissolution-moment; what has arisen at a presence-moment ceases at an arising-moment; and what has arisen at a dissolution-moment ceases at a presence-moment. And having done so, in the demarcation of the lifespan it is said: 'But that ceases together with the seventeenth consciousness' (Vibh-a 26, Miscellaneous Discussion). This contradicts the Pāḷi. Why? The meaning is: because material form with four origins must also have an equal lifespan. However, as it has been construed by them, material form has neither single arising and diverse cessations, nor non-co-arising and single cessation.

Yā pana etehi rūpassa sattarasacittakkhaṇāyukatā vuttā, yā ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tatiyabhāgādhikasoḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatā, sā paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 227) atītārammaṇāya [V 0.0022] cutiyā anantarā paccuppannārammaṇaṃ paṭisandhiṃ dassetuṃ “ettāvatā ekādasa cittakkhaṇā atītā honti, tathā pañcadasa cittakkhaṇā atītā honti, athāvasesapañcacittaekacittakkhaṇāyuke tasmiṃ yevārammaṇe paṭisandhicittaṃ uppajjatī”ti dassitena soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukabhāvena virujjhati. Na hi sakkā “ṭhitikkhaṇe eva rūpaṃ āpāthamāgacchatī”ti vattuṃ. Tathā hi sati na rūpassa ekādasa vā pañcadaseva vā cittakkhaṇā atītā, atha kho atirekaekādasapañcadasacittakkhaṇā. Tasmā yadipi pañcadvāre ṭhitippattameva rūpaṃ pasādaṃ ghaṭṭetīti yujjeyya, manodvāre pana uppādakkhaṇepi āpāthamāgacchatīti icchitabbametaṃ. Na hi manodvāre atītādīsu kiñci āpāthaṃ nāgacchatīti. Manodvāre ca evaṃ vuttaṃ “ekādasa cittakkhaṇā atītā, athāvasesapañcacittakkhaṇāyuke”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 227).

But as to the statement about the seventeen-mind-moment lifespan of matter, and the statement in the commentary about a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments plus a third part, this is contradicted by the state of having a sixteen-mind-moment lifespan shown in the commentary on the Analysis of Dependent Origination. There, to illustrate how the rebirth-linking consciousness with a present object arises immediately after the death consciousness with a past object, it is shown thus: “By this point, eleven mind-moments have passed; similarly, fifteen mind-moments have passed; then, in that very same object which has a remaining lifespan of five mind-moments or one mind-moment, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises.” For it cannot be said that “matter comes into range only at its static moment.” If that were so, not just eleven or fifteen mind-moments of matter would have passed, but more than eleven or fifteen mind-moments. Therefore, although it might be plausible that in the five sense-doors matter impinges on the sense faculty only when it has reached its static moment, it must be accepted that in the mind-door it comes into range even at its arising moment. For in the mind-door, it is not the case that nothing among past objects, etc., comes into range. And in the mind-door, it is stated thus: “Eleven mind-moments have passed, and with a remaining lifespan of five mind-moments….”

Yo cettha cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇo vutto, so ca atthi natthīti vicāretabbo. Cittayamake (yama. 2.cittayamaka.102) hi “uppannaṃ uppajjamānanti? Bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannaṃ, no [M 0.0023] ca uppajjamāna”nti ettakameva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “ṭhitikkhaṇe bhaṅgakkhaṇe cā”ti. Tathā “nuppajjamānaṃ nuppannanti? Bhaṅgakkhaṇe nuppajjamānaṃ, no ca nuppanna”nti ettakameva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “ṭhitikkhaṇe bhaṅgakkhaṇe cā”ti. Evaṃ “na niruddhaṃ na nirujjhamānaṃ, na nirujjhamānaṃ na niruddha”nti etesaṃ paripuṇṇavissajjane “uppādakkhaṇe anāgatañcā”ti vatvā “ṭhitikkhaṇe”ti avacanaṃ, atikkantakālavāre ca “bhaṅgakkhaṇe cittaṃ uppādakkhaṇaṃ vītikkanta”nti vatvā “ṭhitikkhaṇe”ti avacanaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇābhāvaṃ cittassa dīpeti. Suttesupi hi “ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ paññāyatī”ti tasseva (saṃ. ni. 3.38; a. ni. 3.47) ekassa aññathattābhāvato “yassā aññathattaṃ paññāyati, sā santatiṭhitī”ti na na sakkā vattunti, vijjamānaṃ vā khaṇadvayasamaṅgiṃ ṭhitanti.

Here, what is called the static moment of the mind should be investigated as to whether it exists or not. For in the Cittayamaka it is said only this much: “Is what has arisen arising? At the moment of dissolution, it has arisen but is not arising”; it is not said: “at the static moment and at the moment of dissolution.” Similarly, it is said only this much: “Is what is not arising not arisen? At the moment of dissolution, it is not arising but is not unarisen”; it is not said: “at the static moment and at the moment of dissolution.” Thus, in the complete answer to the questions “not ceased and not ceasing, not ceasing and not ceased,” the non-mentioning of “at the static moment” after stating “at the moment of arising and in the future,” and in the section on past time, the non-mentioning of “at the static moment” after stating “the mind at the moment of dissolution has passed the moment of arising,” indicates the absence of a static moment for the mind. For even in the suttas it is said: “Alteration is discerned in what is static.” Since there is no alteration in that single moment, it is not impossible to say that “what is discerned as having alteration is the stability of the continuity,” or that stability is something existing endowed with two moments.

Yo cettha cittanirodhakkhaṇe rūpuppādo vutto, so ca vicāretabbo “yassa vā pana samudayasaccaṃ nirujjhati, tassa dukkhasaccaṃ uppajjatīti? Noti vutta”nti (yama. 1.saccayamaka.136). Yo ca cittassa uppādakkhaṇe rūpanirodho vutto, so ca vicāretabbo “yassa kusalā dhammā uppajjanti, tassa abyākatā dhammā nirujjhantīti? Notiādi (yama. 3.dhammayamaka.163) vutta”nti. Na ca cittasamuṭṭhānarūpameva sandhāya paṭikkhepo katoti sakkā vattuṃ [V 0.0023] cittasamuṭṭhānarūpādhikārassa abhāvā, abyākatasaddassa ca cittasamuṭṭhānarūpesveva appavattito. Yadi saṅkhārayamake kāyasaṅkhārassa cittasaṅkhārena sahuppādekanirodhavacanato abyākata-saddena cittasamuṭṭhānamevettha gahitanti kāraṇaṃ vadeyya, tampi akāraṇaṃ. Na hi tena vacanena aññarūpānaṃ cittena sahuppādasahanirodhapaṭikkhepo kato, nāpi nānuppādanānānirodhānujānanaṃ, neva cittasamuṭṭhānato aññassa abyākatabhāvanivāraṇañca kataṃ, tasmā tathā appaṭikkhittānānuññātānivāritābyākatabhāvānaṃ sahuppādasahanirodhādikānaṃ kammajādīnaṃ etena cittassa uppādakkhaṇe nirodho paṭikkhittoti na sakkā kammajādīnaṃ cittassa uppādakkhaṇe nirodhaṃ vattuṃ. Yamakapāḷianussaraṇe ca sati uppādānantaraṃ cittassa bhijjamānatāti tasmiṃ khaṇe cittaṃ na ca rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti vinassamānattā, nāpi ca aññassa rūpasamuṭṭhāpakassa sahāyabhāvaṃ gacchatīti paṭisandhicittena sahuppanno utu tadanantarassa cittassa uppādakkhaṇe rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeyya. Evañca sati rūpārūpānaṃ ādimhi saha rūpasamuṭṭhāpanato pubbāparatoti idampi natthi, atilahuparivattañca [M 0.0024] cittanti yena sahuppajjati, taṃ cittakkhaṇe rūpaṃ uppajjamānamevāti sakkā vattuṃ. Teneva hi taṃ paṭisandhito uddhaṃ acittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ attanā saha uppajjamānānaṃ na kenaci paccayena paccayo hoti, tadanantarañca taṃ ṭhitippattanti tadanantaraṃ cittaṃ tassa pacchājātapaccayo hoti, na sahajātapaccayoti. Yadi evaṃ “yassa kāyasaṅkhāro uppajjati, tassa vacīsaṅkhāro nirujjhatīti? No”ti (yama. 2.saṅkhārayamaka.128), vattabbanti ce? Na, cittanirodhakkhaṇe rūpuppādārambhābhāvatoti. Nippariyāyena hi cittassa uppādakkhaṇe eva rūpaṃ uppajjamānaṃ hoti, cittakkhaṇe pana avītivatte taṃ attano rūpasamuṭṭhāpanapurejātapaccayakiccaṃ na karoti, arūpañca tassa pacchājātapaccayo na hotīti ṭhitippattivisesālābhaṃ sandhāya pariyāyena idaṃ vuttanti.

And the statement made here about the arising of matter at the moment of the mind’s cessation should also be investigated, for it is said: “For one for whom the truth of the origin is ceasing, is the truth of suffering arising? No.” And the statement made about the cessation of matter at the moment of the mind’s arising should also be investigated, for it is said: “For one for whom wholesome states are arising, are indeterminate states ceasing? No,” etc. And it cannot be said that this rejection is made with reference only to mind-originated matter, because there is no section dealing with mind-originated matter, and because the term ‘indeterminate’ does not apply exclusively to mind-originated matter. If one were to give the reason that in the Saṅkhārayamaka, from the statement about the co-arising and co-cessation of bodily formation with mental formation, the term ‘indeterminate’ is here taken as only mind-originated, that too is not a reason. For that statement does not reject the co-arising and co-cessation of other kinds of matter with the mind, nor does it permit their non-arising and separate cessation, nor does it prevent what is other than mind-originated from being indeterminate. Therefore, since for kamma-originated matter, etc., their indeterminate nature and their co-arising, co-cessation, etc., are thus un-rejected, un-permitted, and un-prevented, their cessation at the arising moment of the mind is rejected by this Yamaka passage. Thus it is not possible to state that kamma-originated matter, etc., ceases at the arising moment of the mind. And, recalling the Yamaka Pāḷi, since the mind breaks up immediately after arising, at that moment the mind, being in the process of perishing, does not generate matter, nor does it act as a support for another generator of matter. Thus, the temperature that arose together with the rebirth-linking consciousness would generate matter at the arising moment of the subsequent consciousness. This being so, since matter is generated simultaneously at the beginning of the material and the immaterial, this distinction of prior and posterior does not exist. And because the mind is extremely quick to change, it can be said that matter arises at the very same mind-moment with which it co-arises. For that very reason, from rebirth-linking onwards, it is not a condition by any mode of conditionality for non-mind-originated things that are arising together with it. And subsequently, when that matter has reached its static moment, the subsequent mind is its postnascence condition, not its conascence condition. If so, should it be said: “For one for whom bodily formation is arising, is verbal formation ceasing? No”? No, because there is no beginning of the arising of matter at the moment of the mind’s cessation. For, in a non-figurative sense, matter arises at the very moment of the mind’s arising; but while that mind-moment has not yet passed, it does not perform its function as a prenascence condition for generating its own matter, and the immaterial is not its postnascence condition. Thus this is said figuratively, with reference to the non-attainment of a special static moment.

Tato paraṃ panāti etassa “ettha pana yadeta”ntiādikāyapi saṅgahakathāya niṭṭhitāya purimakathāya sanniṭṭhānato “tato paṭṭhāya kammajarūpapaveṇī na pavattatī”ti etena saha sambandhoti cutito paranti attho.

As to the phrase Tato paraṃ pana (“But after that”): since the previous discussion was concluded with the summary statement beginning ettha pana yadetaṃ, this phrase is connected with the statement tato paṭṭhāya kammajarūpapaveṇī na pavattatī (“from that point onwards the lineage of kamma-originated matter does not proceed”). The meaning is “after death.”

Rūpaṃ pana rūpena sahātiādinā yathā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, tathā ekuppādekanirodhatā rūpānaṃ arūpehi, arūpānaṃ rūpehi ca natthīti katvā rūpānaṃ rūpeheva, arūpānañca arūpehi yojitā.

By the phrase beginning Rūpaṃ pana rūpena saha (“But matter with matter…”), just as was stated in the commentary, on the grounds that a state of single arising and single cessation does not exist for material phenomena with immaterial phenomena, nor for immaterial phenomena with material phenomena, the connection is applied of material phenomena with material phenomena only, and of immaterial phenomena with immaterial phenomena only.

Sarīrassa [V 0.0024] rūpaṃ avayavabhūtanti attho, ghanabhūto puñjabhāvo ghanapuñjabhāvo, na tilamuggādipuñjā viya sithilasambandhanānaṃ puñjoti attho. Ekuppādāditāti yathāvutte tayo pakāre āha.

Sarīrassa rūpaṃ avayavabhūtanti means that the matter of the body is its constituent parts. Ghanabhūto puñjabhāvo is a solid mass; the meaning is that it is not a heap of loosely connected things like a pile of sesame seeds or mung beans. Ekuppādādīti refers to the three modes as stated above.

Heṭṭhāti rūpakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ. Parinipphannāva hontīti vikārarūpādīnañca rūpakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyaṃ parinipphannatāpariyāyo vuttoti katvā vuttaṃ. Parinipphannanipphannānaṃ ko visesoti? Pubbantāparantaparicchinno paccayehi nipphādito tilakkhaṇāhato sabhāvadhammo parinipphanno, nipphanno pana asabhāvadhammopi hoti nāmaggahaṇasamāpajjanādivasena nipphādiyamānoti. Nirodhasamāpatti panāti etena sabbampi upādāpaññattiṃ tadekadesena dassetīti veditabbaṃ.

Heṭṭhā means in the explanation of the section on matter. The statement Parinipphannāva honti (“They are indeed completely produced”) is made on the grounds that the section on the completely produced nature of material qualities of alteration, etc., is stated in the explanation of the section on matter. What is the difference between parinipphanna and nipphanna? Parinipphanna is an actual phenomenon, defined by a beginning and an end, produced by conditions, and stamped with the three characteristics. Nipphanna, however, can also be a non-actual phenomenon, being produced by way of naming, attainment, and so on. As for the phrase Nirodhasamāpatti pana, it should be understood that by this, all concepts derived from a basis are illustrated by means of a single part.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the miscellaneous section is concluded.

Kamādivinicchayakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Analysis of Kamma and so forth.

Dassanena [M 0.0025] pahātabbātiādinā paṭhamaṃ pahātabbā paṭhamaṃ vuttā, dutiyaṃ pahātabbā dutiyanti ayaṃ pahānakkamo. Anupubbapaṇītā bhūmiyo anupubbena vavatthitāti tāsaṃ vasena desanāya bhūmikkamo. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādiko (saṃ. ni. 5.372, 382, 383; vibha. 355) ekakkhaṇepi satipaṭṭhānādisambhavato desanākkamova. Dānakathādayo anupubbukkaṃsato kathitā, uppattiādivavatthānābhāvato pana dānādīnaṃ idha desanākkamavacanaṃ. Desanākkamoti ca yathāvuttavavatthānābhāvato anekesaṃ vacanānaṃ saha pavattiyā asambhavato yena kenaci pubbāpariyena desetabbattā tena tenādhippāyena desanāmattasseva kamo vuccati. Abhedena hīti rūpādīnaṃ bhedaṃ akatvā piṇḍaggahaṇenāti attho. Cakkhuādīnampi visayabhūtanti ekadesena rūpakkhandhaṃ samudāyabhūtaṃ vadati. Evanti ettha vuttanayenāti adhippāyo. “Chadvārādhipati rājā”ti (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.erakapattanāgarājavatthu) “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā”ti (dha. pa. 1-2) ca vacanato viññāṇaṃ adhipati.

"To be abandoned by seeing" and so on—first, what is to be abandoned first is stated first; second, what is to be abandoned second is stated second—this is the order of abandonment. The successively sublime stages are progressively established—thus, the sequence of stages in the teaching is based on them. "The four establishments of mindfulness" and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.372, 382, 383; Vibhaṅga 355)—since the establishments of mindfulness and the like can arise in a single moment, this is merely the order of teaching. Discourses on giving and so forth are taught in an ascending sequence of excellence, but since there is no fixed progression in their arising and so on, here the statement is about the order of teaching regarding giving and the like. The order of teaching—because there is no fixed arrangement as previously explained, and because many statements cannot occur simultaneously, they must be taught in some sequence, earlier or later. Thus the order is spoken of merely for the teaching itself, in accordance with this or that intention. Without distinction—meaning without making a distinction of form and the like, but taking them as a whole. Being the objective field of the eye and so on—this refers to the form aggregate, which is a totality, by way of one of its parts. Thus—here, the meaning is "in the manner explained." From the sayings, "The king, lord of the six sense-doors" (Dhammapada Aṭṭhakathā 2, Erakapattanāgarāja story) and "Mind is the forerunner of all things" (Dhammapada 1-2)—consciousness is the ruler.

Rūpakkhandhe [V 0.0025] “sāsavaṃ upādāniya”nti vacanaṃ anāsavānaṃ dhammānaṃ sabbhāvato rūpakkhandhassa taṃsabhāvatānivattanatthaṃ, na anāsavarūpanivattanatthanti. Anāsavāva khandhesu vuttāti ettha aṭṭhānappayutto eva-saddo daṭṭhabbo, anāsavā khandhesveva vuttāti attho.

In the form aggregate, the statement 'tainted and subject to clinging' is for the purpose of precluding that the form aggregate has the same nature as taintless phenomena—since such phenomena exist—not for the purpose of precluding taintless form. Regarding the statement 'The taintless are spoken of in the aggregates,' here the word 'eva' should be seen as misplaced; the meaning is, 'The taintless are spoken of only in the aggregates.'

Sabbasaṅkhatānaṃ sabhāgena ekajjhaṃ saṅgaho sabbasaṅkhatasabhāgekasaṅgaho. Sabhāgasabhāgena hi saṅgayhamānā sabbasaṅkhatā phassādayo pañcakkhandhā honti. Tattha ruppanādisāmaññena samānakoṭṭhāsā “sabhāgā”ti veditabbā. Tesu saṅkhatābhisaṅkharaṇakiccaṃ āyūhanarasāya cetanāya balavanti sā “saṅkhārakkhandho”ti vuttā, aññe ca ruppanādivisesalakkhaṇarahitā phassādayo saṅkhatābhisaṅkharaṇasāmaññenāti daṭṭhabbā. Phusanādayo pana sabhāvā visuṃ khandha-saddavacanīyā na hontīti dhammasabhāvaviññunā tathāgatena phassakhandhādayo na vuttāti daṭṭhabbāti. “Ye keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā sassatavādā sassataṃ lokañca paññapenti attānañca, sabbe te imeyeva pañcupādānakkhandhe nissāya paṭicca, etesaṃ vā aññatara”ntiādīnañca suttānaṃ vasena attattaniyagāhavatthussa etaparamatā daṭṭhabbā, etena ca vakkhamānasuttavasena ca khandhe eva nissāya [M 0.0026] parittārammaṇādivasena na vattabbā ca diṭṭhi uppajjati, khandhanibbānavajjassa sabhāvadhammassa abhāvatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Aññesañca khandha-saddavacanīyānaṃ sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ sabbhāvato na pañcevāti etaṃ codanaṃ nivattetumāha “aññesañca tadavarodhato”ti.

The inclusion of all conditioned phenomena together by way of a common part is the 'inclusion-as-one-by-a-common-part-of-all-conditioned-phenomena.' For when all conditioned phenomena, such as contact and so on, are included by way of a common part, they become the five aggregates. Herein, those that are of a similar division by the common characteristic of being afflicted, etc., should be known as 'common parts.' Among these, volition, which is powerful in the function of volitionally forming conditioned things, with its function of accumulation, is called the 'aggregate of formations.' The others, like contact and so on, which are devoid of specific characteristics such as being afflicted, should be seen as having the general characteristic of volitionally forming conditioned things. However, contact and the like, by their own natures, are not separately designated by the term 'aggregate'; thus it should be understood that the Tathāgata, who comprehends the true nature of phenomena, did not designate an 'aggregate of contact' and so on. Furthermore, based on suttas such as: 'Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins who are eternalists proclaim the world and the self as eternal—all of them do so dependent on these five aggregates subject to clinging, or on one of them,' and so on—it should be seen that this is the ultimate basis for grasping at self and what belongs to self. And by this and by the sutta about to be mentioned, it is said that views, which are not to be described in terms of limited objects and so on, arise dependent on the aggregates alone, because there is no phenomenon with an intrinsic nature apart from the aggregates and Nibbāna. And to refute the objection that 'they are not just five,' since there exist other things designated by the word 'aggregate,' such as the aggregate of virtue and so on, it is said: 'and because of their inclusion in that.'

Dukkhadukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhatāvasena vedanāya ābādhakattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Rāgādisampayuttassa vipariṇāmādidukkhassa itthipurisādiākāraggāhikā taṃtaṃsaṅkappamūlabhūtā saññā samuṭṭhānaṃ. Rogassa pittādīni viya āsannakāraṇaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ, utubhojanavesamādīni viya mūlakāraṇaṃ nidānaṃ. “Cittassaṅgabhūtā cetasikā”ti cittaṃ gilānūpamaṃ vuttaṃ, sukhasaññādivasena vedanākāraṇāya hetubhāvato vedanābhojanassa chādāpanato ca saññā aparādhūpamā byañjanūpamā ca, “pañca vadhakā paccatthikāti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ adhivacana”nti āsivisūpame (saṃ. ni. 4.238) vadhakāti vuttā, “bhāroti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ adhivacana”nti bhārasutte (saṃ. ni. 3.22) bhārāti, “atītaṃpāhaṃ addhānaṃ rūpena khajjiṃ, seyyathāpāhaṃ etarahi paccuppannena rūpena khajjāmi, ahañceva kho pana anāgataṃ rūpaṃ abhinandeyyaṃ, anāgatenapāhaṃ rūpena khajjeyyaṃ. Seyyathāpetarahi khajjāmī”tiādinā khajjanīyapariyāyena (saṃ. ni. 3.79) khādakāti[V 0.0026], “so aniccaṃ rūpaṃ ‘aniccaṃ rūpa’nti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātī”tiādinā yamakasutte (saṃ. ni. 3.85) aniccādikāti. Yadipi imasmiṃ vibhaṅge avisesena khandhā vuttā, bāhullena pana upādānakkhandhānaṃ tadantogadhānaṃ daṭṭhabbatā vuttāti veditabbāti.

The affliction of feeling should be seen by way of suffering as pain, suffering due to change, and the suffering of conditioned formations. Perception—which grasps features such as 'man' and 'woman' and is rooted in such and such conceptions—is the source of suffering due to change and so on when it is associated with lust and the like. The proximate cause (samuṭṭhāna) is like bile and so on for a disease; the root cause (nidāna) is like climate, food, attire, and so on. By the words 'mental factors are components of the mind,' the mind is said to be like a sick person. Because it is a cause for feeling by way of pleasant perception and so on, and because it covers the 'food' of feeling, perception is like a culprit and like a condiment. In the simile of the viper (SN 4.238), they are called 'murderers,' as in: 'Bhikkhus, “murderous enemies” is a designation for these five aggregates subject to clinging.' In the Bhāra Sutta (SN 3.22), they are called 'a burden,' as in: 'Bhikkhus, “a burden” is a designation for these five aggregates subject to clinging.' In the discourse on being devoured (SN 3.79), they are called 'devourers,' as in: 'In the past I was devoured by form, just as I am now devoured by present form. And if I were to delight in future form, I would be devoured by future form, just as I am now devoured.' In the Yamaka Sutta (SN 3.85), they are called 'impermanent, etc.,' as in: 'He does not understand impermanent form as “impermanent form” as it really is.' Although in this Vibhaṅga the aggregates are spoken of without distinction, it should be understood that what is stated should be seen predominantly as the aggregates subject to clinging, which are included therein.

Desitādiccabandhunāti desitaṃ ādiccabandhunā, desitāni vā. Gāthāsukhatthaṃ anunāsikalopo, nikāralopo vā kato.

Taught by the Kinsman of the Sun: this means 'taught (singular) by the Kinsman of the Sun,' or 'things taught (plural).' For the sake of metrical ease, the elision of a nasal or the elision of the syllable 'ni' is made.

Gahetuṃ na sakkāti niccādivasena gahetuṃ na yuttanti attho.

It cannot be grasped: the meaning is that it is not fitting to grasp it as permanent, etc.

Rūpena saṇṭhānena phalakasadiso dissamāno kharabhāvābhāvā phalakakiccaṃ na karotīti “na sakkā taṃ gahetvā phalakaṃ vā āsanaṃ vā kātu”nti āha. Na tathā tiṭṭhatīti niccādikā na hotīti attho, taṇhādiṭṭhīhi vā niccādiggahaṇavasena uppādādianantaraṃ bhijjanato gahitākārā hutvā na tiṭṭhatīti attho. Koṭisatasahassasaṅkhyāti idaṃ [M 0.0027] na gaṇanaparicchedadassanaṃ, bahubhāvadassanameva panetaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Udakajallakanti udakalasikaṃ. Yathā udakatale bindunipātajanito vāto udakajallakaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā puṭaṃ katvā pupphuḷaṃ nāma karoti, evaṃ vatthumhi ārammaṇāpāthagamanajanito phasso anupacchinnaṃ kilesajallaṃ sahakārīpaccayantarabhāvena saṅkaḍḍhitvā vedanaṃ nāma karoti. Idañca kilesehi mūlakāraṇabhūtehi ārammaṇassādanabhūtehi ca nibbattaṃ vaṭṭagatavedanaṃ sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena vā cattāro paccayā vuttā, ūnehipi pana uppajjateva.

Appearing similar to a plank in form and shape, it does not perform the function of a plank because of the absence of solidity; hence it is said, 'It is not possible to take that and make a plank or a seat.' 'It does not remain so' means it is not permanent, etc. Alternatively, the meaning is: because it is grasped as permanent, etc., by craving and views, it breaks up immediately after arising and does not remain having the form in which it was grasped. 'A hundred thousand koṭis': this is not to show a numerical limit, but it should be seen as showing abundance. 'Water film' means a water film. Just as wind, generated by a drop falling on the water's surface, draws together the water film, makes a pocket, and creates what is called a bubble, so too, contact—arising from an object coming into range of the sense base—draws together the unbroken film of defilements, acting as another cooperative condition, and produces what is called feeling. This should be understood as referring to feeling that has entered the round of existence, produced by defilements, which are the root cause and which savor the object. Alternatively, the four conditions are stated as the maximum limit, but it arises even with fewer.

Nānālakkhaṇoti vaṇṇagandharasaphassādīhi nānāsabhāvo. Māyāya dassitaṃ rūpaṃ “māyā”ti āha. Pañcapi upādānakkhandhā asubhādisabhāvā eva kilesāsucivatthubhāvāditoti asubhādito daṭṭhabbā eva. Tathāpi katthaci koci viseso sukhaggahaṇīyo hotīti āha “visesato cā”tiādi. Tattha cattāro satipaṭṭhānā catuvipallāsappahānakarāti tesaṃ gocarabhāvena rūpakkhandhādīsu asubhādivasena daṭṭhabbatā vuttā.

Of various characteristics: this means of various natures due to color, odor, taste, touch, etc. The form displayed by a magician is called 'magic.' The five aggregates subject to clinging are indeed of the nature of foulness, etc., because they are the ground for defilements, impurity, and so on; thus they are indeed to be seen as foul, etc. Nevertheless, because in some instances a particular distinction is easy to grasp as pleasant, it is said, 'and especially,' etc. Herein, since the four establishments of mindfulness bring about the abandoning of the four distortions, it is said that the aggregates of form, etc., are to be seen as foul, etc., by way of being their domain.

Khandhehi na vihaññati parividitasabhāvattā. Vipassakopi hi tesaṃ vipattiyaṃ na dukkhamāpajjati, khīṇāsavesu pana vattabbameva natthi. Te hi āyatimpi khandhehi na bādhīyantīti[V 0.0027]. Kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ parijānātīti “āhārasamudayā rūpasamudayo”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.56-57) vuttattā ajjhattikarūpe chandarāgaṃ pajahanto tassa samudayabhūte kabaḷīkārāhārepi chandarāgaṃ pajahatīti attho, ayaṃ pahānapariññā. Ajjhattikarūpaṃ pana pariggaṇhanto tassa paccayabhūtaṃ kabaḷīkārāhārampi pariggaṇhātīti ñātapariññā. Tassa ca udayavayānupassī hotīti tīraṇapariññā ca yojetabbā. Kāmarāgabhūtaṃ abhijjhaṃ sandhāya “abhijjhākāyagantha”nti āha. Asubhānupassanāya hi kāmarāgappahānaṃ hotīti. Kāmarāgamukhena vā sabbalobhappahānaṃ vadati. “Phassapaccayā vedanā”ti vuttattā āhāraparijānane vuttanayena phassaparijānanañca yojetabbaṃ.

One is not vexed by the aggregates because their nature has been fully comprehended. For even an insight meditator does not fall into suffering at their dissolution, so what need be said of those in whom the cankers are destroyed? For they will not be oppressed by the aggregates in the future either. 'He fully understands edible food': because it is said, 'With the arising of food, there is the arising of form' (SN 22.56), the meaning is that in abandoning desire and lust for internal form, one also abandons desire and lust for the edible food that is its origin. This is full understanding as abandoning. Further, in comprehending internal form, one also comprehends the edible food that is its condition; this is full understanding as knowing. And full understanding as scrutinizing should be connected with being one who contemplates its arising and passing away. With reference to covetousness, which is sensual lust, it is called 'the bodily knot of covetousness.' For the abandoning of sensual lust occurs through the contemplation of foulness. Or, by way of sensual lust, he speaks of the abandoning of all greed. Because it is said, 'With contact as condition, feeling arises,' the full understanding of contact should also be connected in the way explained for the full understanding of food.

Sukhatthameva bhavapatthanā hotīti vedanāya taṇhaṃ pajahanto bhavoghaṃ uttarati. Sabbaṃ vedanaṃ dukkhato passanto attano parena apubbaṃ dukkhaṃ uppāditaṃ, sukhaṃ [M 0.0028] vā vināsitaṃ na passati, tato “anatthaṃ me acarī”tiādiāghātavatthuppahānato byāpādakāyaganthaṃ bhindati. “Sukhabahule sugatibhave suddhī”ti gahetvā gosīlagovatādīhi suddhiṃ parāmasanto sukhapatthanāvaseneva parāmasatīti vedanāya taṇhaṃ pajahanto sīlabbatupādānaṃ na upādiyati. Manosañcetanā saṅkhārakkhandhova, saññā pana taṃsampayuttāti saññāsaṅkhāre anattato passanto manosañcetanāya chandarāgaṃ pajahati eva, tañca pariggaṇhāti tīreti cāti “saññaṃ saṅkhāre…pe… parijānātī”ti vuttaṃ.

The aspiration for existence is indeed for the sake of pleasure; by abandoning craving in regard to feeling, one crosses the flood of existence. Seeing all feeling as suffering, one does not see that suffering has been newly inflicted on oneself by another, or that one's pleasure has been destroyed. Then, by abandoning the grounds for resentment such as, 'He has done me harm,' one breaks the bodily knot of ill will. By grasping 'there is purity in a good destination abounding in pleasure,' and by misapprehending purity through such things as the cow-duty and the goat-duty, one misapprehends this simply because of the aspiration for pleasure. By abandoning craving in regard to feeling, one does not cling to the clinging to rules and observances. Mental volition is the aggregate of formations, but perception is associated with it. Seeing perception and formations as not-self, one abandons desire and lust for mental volition, and one also comprehends it and makes a determination about it; thus it is said: 'One fully understands perception and formations...'

Avijjāya viññāṇe ghanaggahaṇaṃ hotīti ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā taṃ aniccato passanto avijjoghaṃ uttarati. Mohabaleneva sīlabbataparāmāsaṃ hotīti taṃ pajahanto sīlabbataparāmāsakāyaganthaṃ bhindati.

Through ignorance there is a dense grasp on consciousness. Having made an analysis of the dense mass and seeing it as impermanent, one crosses the flood of ignorance. It is by the power of delusion that there is misapprehension of rules and observances. By abandoning that, one breaks the bodily knot of the misapprehension of rules and observances.

“Yañca kho etaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccati cittaṃ itipi mano itipi viññāṇaṃ itipi, tatrāssutavā puthujjano nālaṃ nibbindituṃ, nālaṃ virajjituṃ, nālaṃ vimuccituṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Dīgharattaṃhetaṃ, bhikkhave, assutavato puthujjanassa ajjhositaṃ mamāyitaṃ parāmaṭṭhaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.61) –

Bhikkhus, in regard to what is called mind and mind-organ and consciousness, the uninstructed worldling is incapable of becoming disenchanted with it, dispassionate toward it, and liberated from it. For what reason? For a long time, bhikkhus, this has been held fast to, held dear, and misapprehended by the uninstructed worldling thus: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.'

Vacanato [V 0.0028] viññāṇaṃ niccato passanto diṭṭhupādānaṃ upādiyatīti aniccato passanto taṃ na upādiyatīti.

According to this statement, by seeing consciousness as permanent one clings to the clinging to views, but by seeing it as impermanent one does not cling to it.

Kamādivinicchayakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the commentary on the discourse analyzing sensual pleasure and so on.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the Commentary on the Suttanta Exposition.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition

34. Evaṃ yā ekavidhādinā vuttavedanānaṃ bhūmivasena jānitabbatā, taṃ vatvā puna sampayuttato dassitatādijānitabbappakāraṃ vattumāha “apicā”tiādi. Aṭṭhavidhena tatthāti tattha-saddassa sattavidhabhedeneva yojanā chabbidhabhedena yojanāya sati aṭṭhavidhattābhāvato.

34. Thus, having stated how the feelings spoken of by way of the onefold method and so on are to be known according to their plane, he now says 'Moreover,' etc., in order to state the mode of knowing them as shown by way of association and so on. In the phrase 'there in eight ways,' the word 'there' is to be connected with the sevenfold division, for if it were connected with the sixfold division, there would be no eightfoldness.

Pūraṇatthameva vuttoti dasavidhatāpūraṇatthameva vutto, na navavidhabhede viya nayadānatthaṃ. Kasmā? Tattha nayassa dinnattā. Bhinditabbassa hi bhedanaṃ nayadānaṃ, tañca tattha katanti. Yathā ca kusalattiko, evaṃ “kāyasamphassajā [M 0.0029] vedanā atthi sukhā, atthi dukkhā”ti idampi pūraṇatthamevāti dīpitaṃ hoti aṭṭhavidhabhede nayassa dinnattā.

'It is stated only for the sake of completion' means it is stated only for the sake of completing the tenfoldness, not, as in the ninefold division, for the sake of giving a method. Why? Because the method has been given there. For the giving of a method is the dividing of what is to be divided, and that has been done there. And just as in the case of the wholesome triad, so this—'there is feeling born of body-contact that is pleasant, there is that which is painful'—is also shown to be merely for the sake of completion, because the method has been given in the eightfold division.

Pubbe gahitato aññassa gahaṇaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ gahaṇavaḍḍhanavasena, na purimagahite ṭhite aññupacayavasena. Vaḍḍhana-saddo vā chedanattho kesavaḍḍhanādīsu viyāti pubbe gahitassa aggahaṇaṃ chindanaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ, dukatikānaṃ ubhayesaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ ubhayavaḍḍhanaṃ, ubhayato vā pavattaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ ubhayavaḍḍhanaṃ, tadeva ubhatovaḍḍhanakaṃ, tena nayanīharaṇaṃ ubhatovaḍḍhanakanīhāro. Vaḍḍhanakanayo vā vaḍḍhanakanīhāro, ubhayato pavatto vaḍḍhanakanīhāro ubhatovaḍḍhanakanīhāro. Tattha dukamūlakatikamūlakaubhatovaḍḍhanakesu duvidhatividhabhedānaṃyeva hi viseso. Aññe bhedā avisiṭṭhā, tathāpi paññāppabhedajananatthaṃ dhammavitakkena ñātivitakkādiniratthakavitakkanivāraṇatthaṃ imañca pāḷiṃ vitakkentassa dhammupasaṃhitapāmojjajananatthaṃ ekekassa vārassa gahitassa niyyānamukhabhāvato ca duvidhatividhabhedanānattavasena itarepi bhedā vuttāti veditabbā aññamaññāpekkhesu [V 0.0029] ekassa visesena itaresampi visiṭṭhabhāvato. Na kevalaṃ ekavidhova, atha kho duvidho ca. Na ca ekaduvidhova, atha kho tividhopi. Nāpi eka…pe… navavidhova, atha kho dasavidhopīti hi evañca te bhedā aññamaññāpekkhā, tasmā eko bhedo visiṭṭho attanā apekkhiyamāne, attānañca apekkhamāne aññabhede visesetīti tassa vasena tepi vattabbataṃ arahantīti vuttāti daṭṭhabbā.

The taking of another after having taken a previous one is 'increase' (vaḍḍhana) in the sense of 'taking-increase' (gahaṇavaḍḍhana), not in the sense of an addition to what was previously taken. Or the word 'increase' (vaḍḍhana) has the meaning of 'cutting,' as in 'hair-cutting' (kesavaḍḍhana), etc.; thus the non-taking of what was previously taken is a cutting, an 'increase.' For the dyads and triads, the increase of both is 'both-increase' (ubhayavaḍḍhana); or an increase proceeding from both sides is 'both-increase.' That itself is 'from-both-increase' (ubhatovaḍḍhanaka), and the extraction of the method by means of it is 'from-both-increase-extraction' (ubhatovaḍḍhanakanīhāra). Or the method of increase is 'increase-extraction' (vaḍḍhanakanīhāra); an increase-extraction proceeding from both sides is 'from-both-increase-extraction.' Therein, in the cases of the dyad-based, triad-based, and from-both-increase, the distinction is only of twofold and threefold divisions. Other divisions are not specified. Nevertheless, for the sake of generating varieties of wisdom, for preventing useless thoughts such as those based on hearsay, for generating joy connected with the Dhamma in one who reflects on this Pāḷi text, and because each instance taken is a gateway to deliverance, it should be understood that the other divisions are also stated on account of the diversity of the twofold and threefold divisions. For in things that are mutually dependent, when one is distinguished, the others also become distinguished. Not only onefold, but also twofold. Not only onefold and twofold, but also threefold. Not only onefold... up to... ninefold, but also tenfold. Thus these divisions are mutually dependent. Therefore, it should be seen that since one division, being distinguished, distinguishes the other divisions that are dependent on it and that it is dependent on, they too deserve to be stated on that account and are so stated.

Sattavidhenātiādayo aññappabhedanirapekkhā kevalaṃ bahuppakāratādassanatthaṃ vuttāti sabbehi tehi pakārehi “bahuvidhena vedanākkhandhaṃ dassesī”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāvisayo rājā viya savisaye bhagavāpi mahāvisayatāya appaṭihato yathā yathā icchati, tathā tathā desetuṃ sakkoti sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇayogatoti attho. Duke vatvā tikā vuttāti tikā dukesu pakkhittāti yuttaṃ, dukā pana kathaṃ tikesu pakkhittāti? Parato vuttepi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ tike apekkhakāpekkhitabbavasena dukānaṃ yojitattā.

The phrases 'in seven ways,' etc., are stated without reference to other divisions, merely for the purpose of showing the manifoldness. It is by all these modes that it is said, 'He showed the aggregate of feeling in many ways.' The meaning is: just as a king with a great domain is unimpeded in his own domain, so the Blessed One, because of his great domain, is unimpeded and is able to teach in whatever way he wishes, because he is endowed with the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience. After the dyads are stated, the triads are stated; thus it is fitting that the triads are included in the dyads. But how are the dyads included in the triads? Because, although stated subsequently, in each respective triad the dyads are connected by way of mutual dependence.

Kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanavasena labbhatīti vuttaṃ, āvajjanā pana cakkhusamphassapaccayā na hoti. Na hi samānavīthiyaṃ pacchimo dhammo purimassa [M 0.0030] koci paccayo hoti. Ye ca vadanti “āvajjanavedanāva cakkhusaṅghaṭṭanāya uppannattā evaṃ vuttā”ti, tañca na yuttaṃ. Na hi “cakkhurūpapaṭighāto cakkhusamphasso”ti katthaci sutte vā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vā vuttaṃ. Yadi so ca cakkhusamphasso siyā, cakkhuviññāṇasahajātāpi vedanā cakkhusamphassapaccayāti sā idha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ na vajjetabbā siyā. Pāḷiyañca “cakkhusamphassapaccayā vedanā atthi abyākatā”ti ettha saṅgahitattā puna “cakkhusamphassajā vedanā”ti na vattabbaṃ siyāti. Ayaṃ panetthādhippāyo – āvajjanavedanaṃ vinā cakkhusamphassassa uppatti natthīti taduppādikā sā tappayojanattā pariyāyena cakkhusamphassapaccayāti vattuṃ yuttāti, nippariyāyena pana cakkhusamphassassa paratova vedanā labbhanti.

It is said that the functional mind-element is obtained by way of adverting. But adverting is not conditioned by eye-contact, for in the same cognitive process a later state is in no way a condition for an earlier one. And the view of those who say, 'The feeling of adverting is so described because it arises from the impact on the eye,' is not correct. For it is not stated anywhere in a sutta or a commentary that 'the impact of eye and form is eye-contact.' If that were eye-contact, then the feeling co-nascent with eye-consciousness, being conditioned by eye-contact, should not be excluded here in the commentary. And in the Pāḷi, since it is included in the statement 'There is indeterminate feeling conditioned by eye-contact,' it would not need to be said again, 'feeling born of eye-contact.' But this is the intention here: since the arising of eye-contact does not occur without the feeling of adverting, the latter, being its producer and its purpose, may figuratively be said to be conditioned by eye-contact. But strictly speaking, feelings are obtained only subsequent to eye-contact.

Catuttiṃsacittuppādavasenāti ettha rūpārūpāvacarānaṃ aggahaṇaṃ tesaṃ sayameva manodvārabhūtattā. Sabbabhavaṅgamano hi manodvāraṃ, cutipaṭisandhiyo ca tato anaññāti. Imasmiṃ pana catuvīsatividhabhede cakkhusamphassapaccayādikusalādīnaṃ samānavīthiyaṃ labbhamānatā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttā, pāḷiyaṃ pana ekūnavīsaticatuvīsatikā saṅkhipitvā āgatāti “cakkhusamphassapaccayā [V 0.0030] vedanākkhandho atthi anupādinnaanupādāniyo asaṃkiliṭṭhaasaṃkilesiko avitakkaavicāro”tiādinā nānāvīthigatānaṃ labbhamānatāya vuttattā kusalattikassapi nānāvīthiyaṃ labbhamānatā yojetabbā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana samānavīthiyaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayādikatā ekantikāti katvā ettha labbhamānatā dassitā, na pana asamānavīthiyaṃ labbhamānatā paṭikkhittā. Teneva “tāni sattavidhādīsu yattha katthaci ṭhatvā kathetuṃ vaṭṭantī”ti āha. Na hi samānavīthiyaṃyeva upanissayakoṭisamatikkamabhāvanāhi labbhamānatā hoti. Tidhāpi ca labbhamānataṃ sandhāya “yattha katthaci ṭhatvā kathetuṃ vaṭṭantī”ti vuccati.

In the phrase 'by way of the thirty-four consciousness-arisings,' the non-inclusion of the fine-material and immaterial sphere consciousnesses is because they themselves constitute the mind door. For all life-continuum mind is the mind door, and the death and rebirth-linking consciousnesses are not other than that. But in this twenty-fourfold division, the commentary states their availability in the same cognitive process for wholesome states, etc., conditioned by eye-contact, etc. But in the Pāḷi the nineteen and twenty-four are given in summary, as in the phrase: 'There is an aggregate of feeling conditioned by eye-contact that is not clung to and not a basis for clinging, that is undefiled and not a basis for defilement, that is without thought and examination,' etc. Because their availability in different cognitive processes is stated, the availability of the wholesome triad should also be connected with different cognitive processes. But in the commentary, their availability is shown here by taking the eye-contact-conditioned nature, etc., in the same cognitive process as certain, but their availability in different cognitive processes is not rejected. For that reason he said: 'These can be discussed by taking their stand anywhere in the sevenfold division, etc.' For their availability is not only in the same cognitive process, but also by way of dependence, culmination, surmounting, and development. And it is with reference to their threefold availability that it is said: 'They can be discussed by taking their stand anywhere.'

Etānīti yathādassitāni kusalādīni cittāni vadati, vedanāniddesepi ca etasmiṃ pubbaṅgamassa cittassa vasena kathetuṃ sukhanti cittasambandho kato. Teneva pana cittāni sattavidhabhede tikabhūmivasena, catuvīsatividhabhede dvāratikavasena, tiṃsavidhabhede dvārabhūmivasena, bahuvidhabhede dvāratikabhūmivasena dīpitānīti “tesu yattha [M 0.0031] katthaci ṭhatvā kathetuṃ vaṭṭantī”ti vuttaṃ. Kusalādīnaṃ dīpanā kāmāvacarādibhūmivasena kātabbā, tā ca bhūmiyo tiṃsavidhabhede sayamevāgatā, na ca sattavidhabhede viya dvāraṃ anāmaṭṭhaṃ, atibyattā ca ettha samānāsamānavīthīsu labbhamānatāti tiṃsavidhe…pe… sukhadīpanāni hontī”ti vuttaṃ. Kasmā pana tiṃsavidhasmiṃyeva ṭhatvā dīpayiṃsu, nanu dvāratikabhūmīnaṃ āmaṭṭhattā bahuvidhabhede ṭhatvā dīpetabbānīti? Na, dīpetabbaṭṭhānātikkamato. Sattavidhabhedo hi dvārassa anāmaṭṭhattā dīpanāya aṭṭhānaṃ, catuvīsatividhabhede āmaṭṭhadvāratikā na bhūmiyo apekkhitvā ṭhapitā, tiṃsavidhabhede āmaṭṭhadvārabhūmiyo vuttā. Ye ca ṭhapitā, te cettha tikā apekkhitabbarahitā kevalaṃ bhūmīhi saha dīpetabbāva. Tenedaṃ dīpanāya ṭhānaṃ, tadatikkame pana ṭhānātikkamo hotīti.

By 'these' is meant the wholesome and other types of minds as shown. In the exposition of feeling, the connection to the mind is made because it is easy to speak of it in relation to the preceding mind. Thus, the minds are explained in a sevenfold division by way of the triads and planes, in a twenty-fourfold division by way of the doors and triads, in a thirtyfold division by way of the doors and planes, and in a manifold division by way of the doors, triads, and planes. It is said, 'Among these, wherever one stands, they can be spoken of.' The exposition of the wholesome and other types should be done according to the planes such as the sense-sphere plane, etc. Those planes themselves appear in the thirtyfold division, and unlike the sevenfold division, the door is not untouched here. Moreover, in this case, their obtainment in similar and dissimilar cognitive processes is very clear. Thus, it is said that in the thirtyfold division... the expositions are easy. But why were they explained based only on the thirtyfold division? Shouldn’t they have been explained based on the manifold division, since the doors, triads, and planes are touched upon? No, because that would exceed the proper scope of exposition. The sevenfold division is unsuitable for exposition because the door is untouched. In the twenty-fourfold division, the touched-upon doors and triads are established without reference to the planes. In the thirtyfold division, the touched-upon doors and planes are mentioned. And those triads that are established here are to be explained only in conjunction with the planes, without requiring further consideration. Thus, this is the proper place for exposition. To go beyond it would be to exceed the proper scope.

Upanissayakoṭiyāti ettha “saddhaṃ upanissāya dānaṃ detī”tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.423) nānāvīthiyaṃ pakatūpanissayo vuttoti ekavīthiyaṃ kusalādīnaṃ cakkhusamphassādayo tadabhāve abhāvato jāti viya jarāmaraṇassa upanissayalesena paccayoti vattuṃ yujjeyya, idha pana “kasiṇarūpadassanahetuuppannā parikammādivedanā cakkhusamphassapaccayā”ti vakkhati, tasmā nānāvīthiyaṃ gatāni etāni cittāni cakkhusamphassapaccayā labbhamānānīti na upanissayaleso upanissayakoṭi, balavabalavānaṃ pana parikammādīnaṃ upanissayānaṃ sabbesaṃ ādibhūto [V 0.0031] upanissayo upanissayakoṭi. “Vālakoṭi na paññāyatī”tiādīsu viya hi ādi, avayavo vā koṭi. Kasiṇarūpadassanato pabhuti ca kāmāvacarakusalādīnaṃ vedanānaṃ upanissayo pavattoti taṃ dassanaṃ upanissayakoṭi. Parikammādīni viya vā na balavaupanissayo dassananti tassa upanissayantabhāvena upanissayakoṭitā vuttā. Ghānādidvāresu tīsu upanissayakoṭiyā labbhamānattābhāvaṃ vadanto idha samānavīthi na gahitāti dīpeti. Dassanasavanāni viya hi kasiṇaparikammādīnaṃ ghāyanādīni upanissayā na hontīti tadalābho dīpitoti. Yadipi vāyokasiṇaṃ phusitvāpi gahetabbaṃ, purimena pana savanena vinā taṃ phusanaṃ sayameva mūlupanissayo yebhuyyena na hotīti tassa upanissayakoṭitā na vuttā.

Here, regarding the category of decisive support, in the phrase 'relying on faith, one gives a gift,' etc. (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.423), natural decisive support condition is mentioned in relation to different cognitive processes. In a single cognitive process, it would be appropriate to say that eye-contact, etc., for wholesome states, etc., is a condition by way of a trace of decisive support—since in their absence these states are absent, just as aging-and-death is absent in the absence of birth. Here, however, it will be said: 'The feelings of preliminary work and access arising from seeing a kasiṇa-object are conditioned by eye-contact.' Therefore, since these consciousnesses occurring in different cognitive processes are obtainable as conditioned by eye-contact, this is not a mere trace of decisive support but the category of decisive support. For the strong and weak decisive supports of preliminary work, etc., the decisive support that is the beginning of them all is the category of decisive support. For just as in such phrases as 'the tip of a hair is not discerned,' the term 'tip' (koṭi) refers to the beginning or a part. From the seeing of a kasiṇa-object onwards, the decisive support for the feelings of sense-sphere wholesome states, etc., proceeds; thus that seeing is the category of decisive support. Alternatively, since seeing is not a strong decisive support like the preliminary work and access states, its status as the category of decisive support is stated because it serves as a decisive support. In speaking of the non-obtainment through the category of decisive support in the three doors of the nose, etc., he shows that here a similar cognitive process is not taken. For smelling, etc., are not decisive supports for the preliminary work on a kasiṇa, unlike seeing and hearing; thus their non-obtainment is shown. Although the air kasiṇa is to be grasped by touching it, without prior hearing that touching by itself would generally not be the root decisive support; hence its status as the category of decisive support is not stated.

Ajjhāsayena [M 0.0032] sampattigato ajjhāsayasampanno, sampannajjhāsayoti vuttaṃ hoti. Vattappaṭivattanti khuddakañceva mahantañca vattaṃ, pubbe vā kataṃ vattaṃ, pacchā kataṃ paṭivattaṃ. Evaṃ cakkhuviññāṇanti ādimhi uppannaṃ āha, tato paraṃ uppannānipi pana kasiṇarūpadassanakalyāṇamittadassanasaṃvegavatthudassanādīni upanissayapaccayā hontiyevāti. Tena tadupanissayaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassetīti veditabbaṃ.

One who has attained success through disposition is endowed with disposition; this is the meaning of the term. Duties and counter-duties refers to both minor and major duties; a 'duty' is one done before, and a 'counter-duty' is one done afterward. Thus, 'eye-consciousness' is spoken of as arising first, but even what arises subsequently—such as seeing kasiṇa-objects, seeing good friends, seeing objects that inspire a sense of spiritual urgency, and so on—occurs conditioned by decisive support. Therefore, it should be understood that he shows that eye-consciousness is a decisive support for those subsequent states.

Yathābhūtasabhāvādassanaṃ asamapekkhanā. “Asmī”ti rūpādīsu vinibandhassa. Sabhāvantarāmasanavasena parāmaṭṭhassa, parāmaṭṭhavatoti attho. Ārammaṇādhigahaṇavasena anu anu uppajjanadhammatāya thirabhāvakilesassa thāmagatassa, appahīnakāmarāgādikassa vā. Pariggahe ṭhitoti vīmaṃsāya ṭhito. Ettha ca asamapekkhanāyātiādinā mohādīnaṃ kiccena pākaṭena tesaṃ uppattivasena vicāraṇā daṭṭhabbā. Rūpadassanena uppannakilesasamatikkamavasena pavattā rūpadassanahetukā hotīti “cakkhusamphassapaccayā nāma jātā”ti āha. Ettha ca cakkhusamphassassa catubhūmikavedanāya upanissayabhāvo eva pakārantarena kathito, tathā “bhāvanāvasenā”ti ettha ca.

Non-consideration is the failure to see the true nature of things. Of the bondage to 'I am' in regard to form, etc. Of what is misapprehended by way of touching upon another nature; this is the meaning of 'of what is misapprehended.' Of the defilement that has become firm and gained strength, or of one for whom sensual lust, etc., has not been abandoned, because of the nature of arising again and again by way of grasping the object. Established in grasping means established in inquiry. And here, by 'non-consideration,' etc., since the function of delusion and other defilements is manifest, their investigation should be seen by way of their arising. Because it proceeds by way of overcoming the defilements that have arisen through seeing a form, it is caused by seeing a form. Hence he said, 'It is born conditioned by eye-contact.' And here the status of eye-contact as a decisive support for feeling in the four planes is stated in another way; and likewise in the passage 'by way of development.'

Kalāpasammasanena tīṇi lakkhaṇāni āropetvā udayabbayānupassanādikāya vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā ādimhi rūpārammaṇapariggahena rūpārammaṇaṃ sammasitvā, taṃmūlakaṃ vā sabbaṃ sammasanaṃ ādibhūte rūpārammaṇe pavattatīti katvā āha “rūpārammaṇaṃ sammasitvā”ti. Ettha ca [V 0.0032] nāmarūpapariggahādi sabbaṃ sammasanaṃ bhāvanāti veditabbā. Rūpārammaṇaṃ sammasitvāti ca yathāvuttacakkhuviññāṇassa ārammaṇabhūtaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ vuttaṃ, na yaṃ kiñci. Ārammaṇena hi cakkhusamphassaṃ dassetīti. Evaṃ “rūpārammaṇe uppannaṃ kilesa”nti etthāpi veditabbaṃ.

Having ascribed the three characteristics by way of comprehension by groups, and having comprehended the form-object at the beginning of the sequence of insight practice—which starts with the contemplation of rise and fall, etc.—by discerning the form-object; or because all comprehension rooted in that proceeds with the initial form-object as its basis, he said, 'having comprehended the form-object.' And here, all comprehension, beginning with the discernment of name-and-form, should be understood as development. And by 'having comprehended the form-object' is meant the form-object that is the object of the aforesaid eye-consciousness, not just any form-object. For he shows eye-contact by way of the object. Similarly, it should be understood also in the phrase 'the defilement that has arisen in regard to the form-object.'

Idaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ kiṃnissitanti cakkhudvāre viya yojanāya yathāsambhavaṃ āpodhātuyā aññamaññassa ca vasena mahābhūtanissitatā yojetabbā.

On what does this tangible object depend? Just as in the case of the eye-door, its dependence on the great elements should be connected up, as is possible, by way of the water element and of each other.

Jāti…pe… balavapaccayo hotīti yathāvuttānaṃ bhayato dissamānānaṃ jātiādīnaṃ balavapaccayabhāvena tesaṃ bhayato dassanena sahajātassa manosamphassassa, tassa vā dassanassa dvārabhūtassa bhavaṅgamanosamphassassa balavapaccayabhāvaṃ dasseti.

By 'Birth... is a strong condition,' he shows the status of birth, etc.—which are seen as fearful as was stated—as a strong condition for the mental contact that is co-nascent with the seeing of them as fearful, or for the life-continuum mental contact that has become the door for that seeing.

Dhammārammaṇeti [M 0.0033] na pubbe vutte jātiādiārammaṇeva, atha kho sabbasmiṃ rāgādivatthubhūte dhammārammaṇe. Vatthunissitanti ettha vedanādisaṅkhātassa dhammārammaṇekadesassa pariggahamukhena dhammārammaṇapariggahaṃ dasseti.

By mind-object is meant not only the objects such as birth, etc., mentioned before, but any mind-object that has become the basis for lust and so on. Here, by 'dependent on the basis,' he shows the discernment of the mind-object by way of discerning a portion of the mind-object, designated as feeling, etc.

Manosamphassoti viññāṇaṃ samphassassa kāraṇabhāvena gahitaṃ, tadeva attano phalasseva phalabhāvena vattuṃ na yuttaṃ kāraṇaphalasaṅkarabhāvena sotūnaṃ sammohajanakattāti āha “na hi sakkā viññāṇaṃ manosamphassajanti niddisitu”nti, na pana viññāṇassa manosamphassena sahajātabhāvassa abhāvā. Yasmā vā yathā “tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”ti (ma. ni. 1.204; 3.420, 425-426; saṃ. ni. 4.60) vacanato indriyavisayā viya viññāṇampi phassassa visesapaccayo, na tathā phasso viññāṇassa, tasmā indriyavisayā viya viññāṇampi cakkhusamphassajādivacanaṃ na arahatīti cakkhusamphassajādibhāvo na katoti veditabbo.

By mind-contact, consciousness is taken as the cause of contact. It is not proper to speak of that same thing as the effect of its own effect, as this would cause confusion for the hearers by confounding cause and effect. Thus he said: 'For it is not possible to point out consciousness as born from mind-contact.' This is not, however, because of the absence of a state of co-nascence for consciousness with mind-contact. Or, since, according to the saying, 'The meeting of the three is contact,' consciousness, like the faculty and the object, is a specific condition for contact, but contact is not so for consciousness, therefore consciousness, like the faculty and the object, does not merit the expression 'born from eye-contact,' etc. Thus it should be understood that the state of being 'born from eye-contact,' etc., is not stated for it.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
