The commentary on the Abhidhamma Analysis is concluded.

3. Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Questioner

150. Cittuppādarūpavasena [V 0.0033] taṃ taṃ samudāyaṃ ekekaṃ dhammaṃ katvā “pañcapaṇṇāsa kāmāvacaradhamme”ti āha. Rajjantassātiādīsu rāgādayo chasu dvāresu sīlādayo ca pañca saṃvarā yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbā, sammasanaṃ pana manodvāre eva. Rūpārūpāvacaradhammesu abhijjhādomanassādiuppatti atthīti tato satisaṃvaro ñāṇavīriyasaṃvarā ca yathāyogaṃ yojetabbā. Pariggahavacanena sammasanapaccavekkhaṇāni saṅgaṇhāti. Teyevāti cattāro khandhā vuttā.

150. By way of the arising of mind and form, having treated each and every aggregate as a single phenomenon, he said: 'fifty-five sense-sphere phenomena.' In such phrases as 'for one who is lustful,' lust and so on at the six doors, and the five restraints beginning with virtue, should be connected as is possible. But comprehension occurs only at the mind door. Since the arising of covetousness, discontent, and so on exists in the form-sphere and formless-sphere phenomena, restraint by mindfulness and the restraints by knowledge and energy should be connected there as is appropriate. By the word 'inclusion,' he includes comprehension and reviewing. 'Just those' refers to the four aggregates that were mentioned.

Samāne desitabbe desanāmattassa parivaṭṭanaṃ parivaṭṭo. Tīsupi parivaṭṭesu katthaci kiñci ūnaṃ adhikaṃ vā natthīti katvā āha “ekova paricchedo”ti.

When the same thing is to be taught, a 'turning' is merely a turning of the teaching. Having considered that in all three turnings there is nowhere anything deficient or excessive, he said: 'There is only one section.'

Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Questioner is finished.

Khandhavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Aggregates is finished.

2. Āyatanavibhaṅgo

2. The Analysis of the Bases

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Exposition in the Sutta Manner

152. Visesatoti [M 0.0034][V 0.0034] āyatana-saddattho viya asādhāraṇato cakkhādisaddatthatoti attho. Assādetīti cakkhati-saddo “madhuṃ cakkhati byañjanaṃ cakkhatī”ti rasasāyanattho atthīti tassa vasena atthaṃ vadati. “Cakkhuṃ kho, māgaṇḍiya, rūpārāmaṃ rūparataṃ rūpasammudita”nti (ma. ni. 2.209) vacanato cakkhu rūpaṃ assādeti. Satipi sotādīnaṃ saddārammaṇādiratibhāve niruḷhattā cakkhumhiyeva cakkhu-saddo pavattati padumādīsu paṅkajādisaddā viyāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vibhāveti cāti saddalakkhaṇasiddhassa cakkhati-saddassa vasena atthaṃ vadati. Cakkhatīti hi ācikkhati, abhibyattaṃ vadatīti attho. Nayanassa ca vadantassa viya samavisamavibhāvanameva ācikkhananti katvā āha “vibhāveti cāti attho”ti. Anekatthattā vā dhātūnaṃ vibhāvanatthatā cakkhu-saddassa daṭṭhabbā. Rattaduṭṭhādikālesu kakaṇṭakarūpaṃ viya uddarūpaṃ viya ca vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ rūpaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ rūpayati rūpamiva pakāsaṃ karoti, saviggahamiva katvā dassetīti attho. Vitthāraṇaṃ vā rūpa-saddassa attho, vitthāraṇañca pakāsanamevāti āha “pakāsetī”ti. Anekatthattā vā dhātūnaṃ pakāsanatthoyeva rūpa-saddo daṭṭhabbo, vaṇṇavācakassa rūpa-saddassa rūpayatīti nibbacanaṃ, rūpavācakassa ruppatīti ayaṃ viseso.

152. 'Especially' (visesato) means: because of being uncommon, just as the meaning of the word 'base' (āyatana), so is the meaning of the words 'eye,' etc. The word 'cakkhati' has the meaning of savoring a taste, as in 'he tastes honey,' 'he tastes a curry,' and on that basis he states the meaning. In accordance with the text, 'The eye, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in forms, is fond of forms, rejoices in forms,' the eye savors form. It should be seen that although the ear, etc., also take delight in objects such as sounds, because it is so established, the word 'eye' is used only for the eye, just like words such as 'mud-born' are used for lotuses, etc. And 'it clarifies' (vibhāveti ca): he states the meaning on the basis of the word 'cakkhati' as established by its linguistic characteristic. For 'cakkhati' means 'it points out, it speaks distinctly.' And since the pointing out of the eye is just the clarifying of the even and uneven, like someone speaking, he said: 'and it clarifies' is the meaning. Or, because roots have many meanings, the meaning 'clarification' for the word 'eye' should be seen. At times of lust, hatred, etc., form, undergoing a change of color like the form of a chameleon and like that of an otter, impresses its state upon the heart, makes it manifest as if it were a form; the meaning is that it shows it as if it had a body. Or the meaning of the word 'rūpa' is 'spreading out,' and since spreading out is just manifestation, he says 'it manifests.' Or, because roots have many meanings, the word 'rūpa' should be seen as having just the meaning 'manifestation.' The derivation of the word 'rūpa' that denotes color is 'rūpayati' (it impresses); for the one that denotes material form, it is 'ruppati' (it is afflicted). This is the distinction.

Udāharīyatīti vuccatīti-atthe vacanameva gahitaṃ siyā, na ca vacana-saddoyeva ettha saddo, atha kho sabbopi sotaviññeyyoti sappatīti sakehi paccayehi sappīyati sotaviññeyyabhāvaṃ gamīyatīti attho. Sūcayatīti attano vatthuṃ gandhavasena apākaṭaṃ “idaṃ sugandhaṃ [V 0.0035] duggandha”nti pakāseti, paṭicchannaṃ vā pupphādivatthuṃ “ettha pupphaṃ atthi campakādi, phalamatthi ambādī”ti pesuññaṃ karontaṃ viya hotīti attho. Rasaggahaṇamūlakattā āhārajjhoharaṇassa jīvitahetumhi āhārarase ninnatāya jīvitaṃ avhāyatīti jivhā vuttā niruttilakkhaṇena. Kucchitānaṃ sāsavadhammānaṃ āyoti visesena kāyo vutto anuttariyahetubhāvaṃ anāgacchantesu kāmarāganidānakammajanitesu kāmarāgassa ca visesapaccayesu [M 0.0035] ghānajivhākāyesu kāyassa visesatarasāsavapaccayattā. Tena hi phoṭṭhabbaṃ assādentā sattā methunampi sevanti. Uppattidesoti uppattikāraṇanti attho. Kāyindriyavatthukā vā cattāro khandhā balavakāmāsavādihetubhāvato visesena “sāsavā”ti vuttā, tesaṃ uppajjanaṭṭhānanti attho. Attano lakkhaṇaṃ dhārayantīti ye visesalakkhaṇena āyatanasaddaparā vattabbā, te cakkhādayo tathā vuttāti aññe manogocarabhūtā dhammā sāmaññalakkhaṇeneva ekāyatanattaṃ upanetvā vuttā. Oḷārikavatthārammaṇamananasaṅkhātehi visayavisayibhāvehi purimāni pākaṭānīti tathā apākaṭā ca aññe manogocarā na attano sabhāvaṃ na dhārentīti imassatthassa dīpanattho dhamma-saddoti.

'It is uttered' (udāharīyati): in the sense of 'it is said,' the mere utterance might be taken. But here 'sound' (sadda) is not just the word 'utterance'; rather, it is everything cognizable by the ear. 'It goes' (sappati): the meaning is that by its own conditions it is made to go, it reaches the state of being cognizable by the ear. 'It indicates' (sūcayati): by means of smell it reveals its own unmanifest basis, saying, 'This is fragrant, this is foul-smelling.' Or it is as if it were slandering a hidden object like a flower, etc., saying, 'Here there is a flower, a campaka, etc.; here there is a fruit, a mango, etc.' That is the meaning. Because the swallowing of food is rooted in the grasping of taste, and because it is inclined towards the taste of food which is the cause of life, it 'calls to' (avhāyati) life; thus it is called 'tongue' (jivhā) according to the characteristic of etymology. The body (kāyo) is especially so called because it is an 'abode' (āya) for 'despicable' (kucchita) tainted states. For among the sense faculties of nose, tongue, and body, which do not become a cause for the supreme, which are generated by kamma born of sensual craving, and which are specific conditions for sensual craving, the body is a still more specific condition for the taints. For by savoring the tangible, beings also engage in sexual intercourse. 'A place of origin' (uppattideso) means a cause of origin. Or, the four aggregates that have the body faculty as their physical basis are especially called 'tainted' because they are a cause for strong taints such as the taint of sensual pleasure; the meaning is that it is their place of arising. Those that 'uphold' their own characteristic are to be spoken of by the word 'base' through their specific characteristic; thus the eye, etc., are so called. Other phenomena, which are the domain of the mind, are brought under the heading of a single base only by way of a general characteristic. Because the former are manifest through the subject-object relationships designated as gross physical basis, object, and mind, and thus the other mental objects are unmanifest and do not uphold their own nature—the word 'dhamma' is for the purpose of clarifying this meaning.

Vāyamantīti attano kiccaṃ karonticceva attho. Imasmiñca atthe āyatanti etthāti āyatananti adhikaraṇattho āyatana-saddo, dutiyatatiyesu kattuattho. Te cāti cittacetasikadhamme. Te hi taṃtaṃdvārārammaṇesu āyanti āgacchanti pavattantīti āyāti. Vitthārentīti pubbe anuppannattā līnāni apākaṭāni pubbantato uddhaṃ pasārenti pākaṭāni karonti uppādentīti attho.

'They exert' (vāyamanti) just means 'they perform their own function.' And in this sense, the word 'base' (āyatana) has the meaning of a location: 'that in which they exert.' In the second and third etymologies, it has the meaning of an agent. 'And those' refers to the phenomena of consciousness and mental factors. For they 'come' (āyanti), arrive, and proceed at their respective doors and objects; thus they are 'comings' (āyā). 'They stretch out' (vitthārenti) means: they extend upwards from a previous state those things that were formerly unarisen, hence dormant and unmanifest; they make them manifest, they produce them. That is the meaning.

Ruḷhīvasena āyatana-saddassatthaṃ vattuṃ “apicā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Taṃ nissitattāti ettha mano manoviññāṇādīnaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ nissayapaccayo na hotīti tassa nesaṃ dvārabhāvo nissayabhāvoti daṭṭhabbo. Atthatoti vacanatthato, na vacanīyatthato. Vacanattho hettha vutto “cakkhatī”tiādinā, na vacanīyattho “yaṃ cakkhu catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya pasādo”tiādinā (dha. sa. 597) viyāti.

To state the meaning of the word 'base' by way of its established usage, the passage beginning 'Moreover...' was started. Herein, regarding 'because it is depended on': since the mind-organ is not a support condition for consciousness and mental factors such as mind-consciousness, it should be seen that its being a door for them constitutes its state of being a support. 'From the meaning' means from the verbal meaning, not from the meaning of what is to be expressed. For here the verbal meaning is stated by 'cakkhati,' etc., not the meaning of what is to be expressed, as in 'that eye which is the sensitivity derived from the four great elements,' etc.

Tāvatvatoti anūnādhikabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tattha dvādasāyatanavinimuttassa kassaci dhammassa abhāvā adhikabhāvato codanā natthi, salakkhaṇadhāraṇaṃ pana sabbesaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇanti ūnacodanā [V 0.0036] sambhavatīti dassento āha “cakkhādayopi hī”tiādi. Asādhāraṇanti cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ. Satipi asādhāraṇārammaṇabhāve cakkhādīnaṃ dvārabhāvena gahitattā dhammāyatane aggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dvārārammaṇabhāvehi vā asādhāraṇataṃ sandhāya “asādhāraṇa”nti vuttaṃ.

'Just so much' shows the state of being neither deficient nor excessive. Therein, since there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is separate from the twelve bases, there is no charge of excessiveness. But since the upholding of a specific characteristic is a general characteristic of all, a charge of deficiency is possible. Showing this, he says: 'For the eye, etc., too...' 'Uncommon' means uncommon to eye-consciousness, etc. Although they have the state of being an uncommon object, it should be seen that the eye, etc., are not included in the dhamma-base because they are taken as doors. Or 'uncommon' is said with reference to their being uncommon by way of being doors and objects.

Yebhuyyasahuppattiādīhi [M 0.0036] uppattikkamādiayutti yojetabbā. Ajjhattikesu hīti etena ajjhattikabhāvena visayibhāvena ca ajjhattikānaṃ paṭhamaṃ desetabbataṃ dasseti. Tesu hi paṭhamaṃ desetabbesu pākaṭattā paṭhamataraṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ desitanti. Tato ghānāyatanādīnīti ettha bahūpakārattābhāvena cakkhusotehi purimataraṃ adesetabbāni saha vattuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā ekena kamena desetabbānīti ghānādikkamena desitānīti adhippāyo. Aññathāpi hi desitesu na na sakkā codetuṃ, na ca sakkā sodhetabbāni na desetunti. Gocaro visayo etassāti gocaravisayo, mano. Kassa pana gocaro etassa visayoti? Cakkhādīnaṃ pañcannampi. Viññāṇuppattikāraṇavavatthānatoti etena ca cakkhādianantaraṃ rūpādivacanassa kāraṇamāha.

The rationale for the order of arising, etc., should be connected with factors such as arising together for the most part. By 'For among the internal,' he shows that the internal bases should be taught first because of their internality and their being the subject. For among those that should be taught first, the eye-base is taught first of all because it is the most manifest. Then 'the nose-base, etc.': here the intention is that because they are not as helpful as the eye and ear, they should not be taught before them; and because they cannot be spoken of together, they must be taught in a certain order, and so they are taught in the order beginning with the nose. For if they were taught otherwise, one could indeed raise an objection, but it is not that what is to be purified could not be taught. 'The domain is its object,' hence 'domain-object': this is the mind. But whose domain is its object? Of all five, beginning with the eye. And by 'because of the determination of the cause for the arising of consciousness,' he states the reason for mentioning form, etc., immediately after the eye, etc.

Paccayabhedo kammādibhedo. Nirayādiko apadādigatinānākaraṇañca gatibhedo. Hatthiassādiko khattiyādiko ca nikāyabhedo. Taṃtaṃsattasantānabhedo puggalabhedo. Yā ca cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ anantabhedatā vuttā, soyeva hadayavatthussa ca bhedo hoti. Tato manāyatanassa anantappabhedatā yojetabbā dukkhāpaṭipadādito ārammaṇādhipatiādibhedato ca. Imasmiṃ suttantabhājanīye vipassanā vuttāti vipassanupagamanañca viññāṇaṃ gahetvā ekāsītibhedatā manāyatanassa vuttā niddesavasena. Nīlaṃ nīlasseva sabhāgaṃ, aññaṃ visabhāgaṃ, evaṃ kusalasamuṭṭhānādibhedesu yojetabbaṃ. Tebhūmakadhammārammaṇavasenāti pubbe vuttaṃ cakkhādivajjaṃ dhammārammaṇaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

'Distinction of conditions' is the distinction of kamma, etc. 'Distinction of destination' is the distinction of hell, etc., and the variety of destinations such as the footless, etc. 'Distinction of group' is the distinction of elephants, horses, etc., and of warriors, etc. 'Distinction of individual' is the distinction of the continuities of this or that being. And the infinite variety of the physical bases of the eye, etc., that was mentioned, that same variety is also the variety of the heart-basis. From that, the infinite variety of the mind-base should be connected, from the distinctions of painful practice, etc., and from the distinctions of object-predominance, etc. Since insight is spoken of in this Sutta-style Exposition, taking consciousness that pertains to insight, the eighty-onefold variety of the mind-base is stated by way of the Exposition. Blue is similar to blue itself; another is dissimilar. This should be applied in the case of the distinctions of wholesome-rooted, etc. 'By way of phenomena of the three planes as object' is said with reference to the previously mentioned dhamma-object, exclusive of the eye, etc.

Saparipphandakiriyāvasena īhanaṃ īhā. Cintanavasena byāpārakaraṇaṃ byāpāro. Tattha byāpāraṃ dassento āha “na hi cakkhu rūpādīnaṃ evaṃ hotī”ti. Īhaṃ dassento āha “na ca tānī”tiādi. Ubhayampi pana īhā ca hoti byāpāro cāti uppaṭipāṭivacanaṃ. Dhammatāvāti sabhāvova, kāraṇasamatthatā vā. Īhābyāpārarahitānaṃ dvārādibhāvo dhammatā. Imasmiñca atthe yanti etassa yasmāti attho. Purimasmiṃ sambhavanavisesanaṃ yaṃ-saddo. “Suñño [V 0.0037] gāmoti kho, bhikkhave, channetaṃ ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacana”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.238) vacanato suññagāmo viya daṭṭhabbāni. Annapānasamohitanti [M 0.0037] gahite suññagāme yaññadeva bhājanaṃ parāmasīyati, taṃ taṃ rittakaṃyeva parāmasīyati, evaṃ dhuvādibhāvena gahitāni upaparikkhiyamānāni rittakāneva etāni dissantīti. Cakkhādidvāresu abhijjhādomanassuppādakabhāvena rūpādīni cakkhādīnaṃ abhighātakānīti vuttāni. Ahisusumārapakkhikukkurasiṅgālamakkaṭā cha pāṇakā. Visamabilākāsagāmasusānavanāni tesaṃ gocarā. Tattha visamādiajjhāsayehi cakkhādīhi visamabhāvabilākāsagāmasusānasannissitasadisupādinnadhammavanabhāvehi abhiramitattā rūpādīnampi visamādisadisatā yojetabbā.

Striving (īhā) is exertion by way of agitated action. Activity (byāpāra) is engagement by way of thinking. In this context, to illustrate activity, it is said: ‘For the eye does not have this [thought] towards forms, etc.’ To illustrate striving, it is said: ‘Nor do they,’ etc. But this statement of striving and activity is in reverse order. ‘Natural principle’ (dhammatā) means intrinsic nature, or the capacity to be a cause. It is the natural principle for the doors, etc., to be devoid of striving and activity. In this context, ‘yanti’ means ‘because of which’ (yasmā). In the former, ‘yaṃ’ is a qualifier of possibility. As stated in the phrase, ‘Bhikkhus, “an empty village” is a designation for these six internal sense bases’ (SN 35.241), they should be regarded like an empty village. ‘Engrossed in food and drink’: just as in an empty village that has been entered, whatever vessel one touches, one touches only an empty one, so too, when these [sense bases], grasped as permanent, etc., are examined, they are seen to be just empty. Forms, etc., are said to be assailants of the eye, etc., because they produce covetousness and displeasure at the eye-door, etc. The six creatures—a snake, a crocodile, a bird, a dog, a jackal, and a monkey—have as their pasture uneven ground, a hole, the open sky, a village, a charnel ground, and a forest. There, because the eye, etc., have dispositions for the uneven, etc., and delight in states similar to uneven ground, a hole, the open sky, a village, a charnel ground, and a forest—which are similar to their supports and to clung-to phenomena—the similarity of forms, etc., to the uneven, etc., should be connected.

Hutvā abhāvaṭṭhenāti idaṃ itaresaṃ catunnaṃ ākārānaṃ saṅgahakattā visuṃ vuttaṃ. Hutvā abhāvākāro eva hi uppādavayattākārādayoti. Tattha hutvāti etena purimantavivittatāpubbakaṃ majjhe vijjamānataṃ dasseti, taṃ vatvā abhāvavacanena majjhe vijjamānatāpubbakaṃ, aparante avijjamānataṃ, ubhayenapi sadā abhāvo aniccalakkhaṇanti dasseti. Sabhāvavijahanaṃ vipariṇāmo, jarābhaṅgehi vā parivattanaṃ, santānavikārāpatti vā. Sadā abhāvepi ciraṭṭhānaṃ siyāti taṃnivāraṇatthaṃ “tāvakālikato”ti āha. Uppādavayaññathattarahitaṃ niccaṃ, na itarathāti niccapaṭikkhepato aniccaṃ, niccapaṭipakkhatoti adhippāyo.

‘In the sense of having become non-existent after having been’: this is stated separately because it includes the other four aspects. For the aspect of having become non-existent after having been is indeed the aspects of arising, passing away, alteration, and so on. Therein, by ‘having been,’ he shows its presence in the middle, which is preceded by its separation from the prior end. Having said that, by the word ‘non-existence,’ he shows its non-existence at the subsequent end, which is preceded by its presence in the middle. By both, he shows that its constant non-existence is the characteristic of impermanence. Change (vipariṇāma) is the abandoning of its intrinsic nature, or transformation through decay and breakup, or the undergoing of alteration in the continuum. Since even with constant non-existence there might be long duration, to prevent that he says ‘because it is temporary.’ What is devoid of arising, passing away, and alteration is permanent, not otherwise; thus, by the rejection of the permanent, it is impermanent. The intention is that it is the opposite of the permanent.

Jātidhammatādīhi aniṭṭhatā paṭipīḷanaṃ. Paṭipīḷanaṭṭhenāti ca yassa taṃ pavattati, taṃ puggalaṃ paṭipīḷanato, sayaṃ vā jarādīhi paṭipīḷanattāti attho. Parittaṭṭhitikassapi attano vijjamānakkhaṇe uppādādīhi abhiṇhaṃ sampaṭipīḷanattā “abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanato”ti purimaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ visesetvā vadati, puggalassa pīḷanato dukkhamaṃ. Sukhapaṭipakkhabhāvato dukkhaṃ sukhaṃ paṭikkhipati nivāreti, dukkhavacanaṃ vā atthato sukhaṃ paṭikkhipatīti āha “sukhapaṭikkhepato”ti.

Oppression is undesirability due to being subject to birth, etc. And ‘in the sense of oppression’ means because it oppresses the person in whom it occurs, or because it is itself oppressed by aging, etc. Because even what has a brief duration is constantly oppressed by arising, etc., at the moment of its existence, he specifies the former general characteristic by saying ‘because of constant oppression.’ It is suffering because of the oppression of the person. Because it is the opposite of pleasure, suffering rejects and wards off pleasure; or the word ‘suffering’ by its meaning rejects pleasure. Thus he says ‘because of the rejection of pleasure.’

Natthi etassa vasavattanako, nāpi idaṃ vasavattanakanti avasavattanakaṃ, attano parasmiṃ parassa ca attani vasavattanabhāvo vā vasavattanakaṃ, taṃ etassa natthīti avasavattanakaṃ, avasavattanakassa avasavattanako vā attho sabhāvo avasavattanakaṭṭho, idañca sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ. Tenāti parassa attani vasavattanākārena suññaṃ. Imasmiñca atthe suññatoti etasseva [V 0.0038] visesanaṃ “assāmikato”ti. Atha vā “yasmā [M 0.0038] vā etaṃ…pe… mā pāpuṇātū”ti evaṃ cintayamānassa kassaci tīsu ṭhānesu vasavattanabhāvo natthi, suññaṃ taṃ tena attanoyeva vasavattanākārenāti attho. Na idaṃ kassaci kāmakāriyaṃ, nāpi etassa kiñci kāmakāriyaṃ atthīti akāmakāriyaṃ. Etena avasavattanatthaṃ visesetvā dasseti.

‘There is no one who exercises control over it, nor does it exercise control’: thus it is uncontrollable (avasavattanakaṃ). The state of exercising control over another, or of another exercising control over oneself, is ‘controllable’ (vasavattanakaṃ). That does not exist for this, thus it is uncontrollable. The meaning or intrinsic nature of ‘uncontrollable’ is the sense of being uncontrollable; and this is a general characteristic. Therefore, it is empty of the mode of another exercising control over oneself. And in this sense, ‘because it is ownerless’ is a qualifier of this very ‘emptiness.’ Alternatively, for someone who thinks, ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus,’ there is no state of exercising control in the three instances. The meaning is that it is empty of that very mode of exercising control over oneself. It does not do anyone’s will, nor is there anything that does its will; thus it is ‘not subject to will’ (akāmakāriyaṃ). By this he shows, specifying it, the meaning of being uncontrollable.

Vibhavagati vināsagamanaṃ. Santatiyaṃ bhavantaruppattiyeva bhavasaṅkantigamanaṃ. Santatiyā yathāpavattākāravijahanaṃ pakatibhāvavijahanaṃ. “Cakkhu anicca”nti vutte cakkhuanicca-saddānaṃ ekatthattā aniccānaṃ sesadhammānampi cakkhubhāvo āpajjatīti etissā codanāya nivāraṇatthaṃ visesasāmaññalakkhaṇavācakānañca saddānaṃ ekadesasamudāyabodhanavisesaṃ dīpetuṃ “apicā”tiādimāha.

The course to non-existence is the going to destruction. In the continuum, the arising of another existence is the transition of existence. The abandoning of the mode in which the continuum proceeds is the abandoning of its natural state. To prevent the objection that, when it is said ‘The eye is impermanent,’ because the words ‘eye’ and ‘impermanent’ have a single meaning, the state of being an eye would also apply to the other impermanent phenomena, and to illuminate the specific way of understanding a part and the whole of words that express specific and general characteristics, he said ‘Moreover,’ etc.

Kiṃ dassitanti vipassanācāraṃ kathentena kiṃ lakkhaṇaṃ dassitanti adhippāyo. “Katamā cānanda, anattasaññā? Idhānanda, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā iti paṭisañcikkhati ‘cakkhu anattā’ti…pe… ‘dhammā anattā’ti. Iti imesu chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu anattānupassī viharatī”ti (a. ni. 10.60) avisesesu āyatanesu anattānupassanā vuttāti kāraṇabhūtānaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ, phalabhūtānañca cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ kāraṇaphalamattatāya anattatāya anattalakkhaṇavibhāvanatthāya āyatanadesanāti āha “dvādasannaṃ…pe… anattalakkhaṇa”nti. Yadipi aniccadukkhalakkhaṇāni ettha dassitāni, tehi ca anattalakkhaṇameva visesena dassitanti adhippāyo. Veti cāti ettha iti-saddo samāpanattho. Iccassāti ettha iti-saddo yathāsamāpitassa āropetabbadosassa nidassanattho. Evanti “cakkhu attā”ti evaṃ vāde satīti attho. Iccassāti vā iti-saddo “iti vadantassā”ti paravādissa dosalakkhaṇākāranidassanattho. Evanti dosagamanappakāranidassanattho. Rūpe attani “evaṃ me rūpaṃ hotū”ti attaniye viya sāminiddesāpattīti ce? Na, “mama attā”ti gahitattā. “Mama attā”ti hi gahitaṃ rūpaṃ vasavattitāya “evaṃ me hotū”ti icchiyamānañca tatheva bhaveyya, icchatopi hi tassa rūpasaṅkhāto attā avasavatti cāti. Ābādhāyāti evaṃ dukkhena. Paññāpananti [M 0.0039] paresaṃ ñāpanaṃ. Anattalakkhaṇapaññāpanassa aññesaṃ avisayattā anattalakkhaṇadīpakānaṃ aniccadukkhalakkhaṇānañca paññāpanassa avisayatā dassitā hoti.

‘What is shown?’: the intention is, when explaining the practice of insight, what characteristic is shown? ‘And what, Ānanda, is the perception of not-self? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu—gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling—reflects thus: “The eye is not-self”… up to … “mental phenomena are not-self.” Thus he dwells contemplating not-self in these six internal and external sense bases’ (AN 10.60). Since the contemplation of not-self is taught in regard to the sense bases in general, the teaching on the sense bases is for the purpose of analyzing the characteristic of not-self by way of the mere cause-and-effect nature of the causal factors, the eye, etc., and the resultant factors, eye-consciousness, etc. Thus he says: ‘of the twelve… the characteristic of not-self.’ Although the characteristics of impermanence and suffering are shown here, the intention is that the characteristic of not-self is shown specifically by means of them. In ‘veti cāti,’ the word ‘iti’ has the sense of conclusion. In ‘iccassāti,’ the word ‘iti’ serves to indicate the fault to be imputed to what has been concluded. ‘Evanti’ means: when there is the view, ‘The eye is self.’ Alternatively, in ‘iccassāti,’ the word ‘iti’ serves to indicate the reason for the faulty characteristic in the opponent who speaks thus. ‘Evanti’ serves to indicate the way the fault proceeds. (Objection:) If, with regard to form as self, one thinks, ‘Let my form be thus,’ does this not amount to a declaration of ownership, like a master over his property? (Reply:) No, because it is grasped as ‘my self.’ For form grasped as ‘my self,’ if it were subject to control, would be just as one wishes it to be: ‘Let it be thus for me.’ But even though one wishes this, the self designated as form is not subject to control. ‘For affliction’ (ābādhāya): thus, with suffering. ‘Making known’ (paññāpanaṃ) is making it known to others. Since the making known of the characteristic of not-self is not the domain of others, it is shown that the making known of the characteristics of impermanence and suffering, which illuminate the characteristic of not-self, is also not their domain.

Evaṃ [V 0.0039] pana duppaññāpanatā etesaṃ durūpaṭṭhānatāya hotīti tesaṃ anupaṭṭhahanakāraṇaṃ pucchanto āha “imāni panā”tiādi. Ṭhānādīsu nirantaraṃ pavattamānassa heṭṭhā vuttassa abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanassa. Dhātumattatāya cakkhādīnaṃ samūhato vinibbhujjanaṃ nānādhātuvinibbhogo. Ghanenāti cattāripi ghanāni ghanabhāvena ekattaṃ upanetvā vadati. Paññāyeva santativikopanāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yāthāvasarasatoti aviparītasabhāvato. Sabhāvo hi rasiyamāno aviraddhapaṭivedhena assādiyamāno “raso”ti vuccati. Aniccādīhi aniccalakkhaṇādīnaṃ aññattha vacanaṃ ruppanādivasena pavattarūpādiggahaṇato visiṭṭhassa aniccādiggahaṇassa sabbhāvā. Na hi nāmarūpaparicchedamattena kiccasiddhi hoti, aniccādayo ca rūpādīnaṃ ākārā daṭṭhabbā. Te panākārā paramatthato avijjamānā rūpādīnaṃ ākāramattāyevāti katvā aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 350) lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāya khandhārammaṇatā vuttāti adhippāyamatte ṭhātuṃ yuttaṃ, nātidhāvituṃ. “Anicca”nti ca gaṇhanto “dukkhaṃ anattā”ti na gaṇhāti, tathā dukkhādiggahaṇe itarassāgahaṇaṃ. Aniccādiggahaṇāni ca niccasaññādinivattanakāni saddhāsamādhipaññindriyādhikāni tividhavimokkhamukhabhūtāni. Tasmā etesaṃ ākārānaṃ pariggayhamānānaṃ aññamaññaṃ viseso ca atthīti tīṇi lakkhaṇāni vuttāni.

However, since their difficulty of being made known is due to their being difficult to attend to, questioning the reason for their non-appearance, he says: ‘But these…,’ etc. [The question concerns] the non-appearance of the constant oppression mentioned above, which occurs continuously in states, etc. The discrimination of the various elements is the dissecting of the eye, etc., from the mass by way of their being mere elements. By ‘solid,’ he speaks bringing the four solids to oneness by way of their solid nature. It should be seen that it is wisdom itself that shatters the continuity. ‘According to its real essence’ (yāthāvasarasato): because of its unperverted intrinsic nature. For intrinsic nature, when savored, when enjoyed with unerring penetration, is called ‘essence’ (raso). The statement elsewhere of the characteristics of impermanence, etc., by means of impermanence, etc., is because there exists a grasping of impermanence, etc., that is distinct from the grasping of form, etc., which proceeds by way of being afflicted, etc. For the task is not accomplished by the mere defining of name-and-form; impermanence, etc., must be seen as modes of form, etc. But since those modes are ultimately non-existent and are mere modes of form, etc., it is said in the Aṭṭhasālinī (DhsA 350) that insight meditation that takes the characteristics as its object has the aggregates as its object. It is proper to stand on the mere intention and not to run on too far. One who grasps ‘impermanent’ does not grasp ‘suffering’ or ‘not-self’; similarly, when grasping suffering, etc., the other is not grasped. The graspings of impermanence, etc., are what dispel the perceptions of permanence, etc.; they are predominated by the faculties of faith, concentration, and wisdom, and are the three gateways to liberation. Therefore, since there is a distinction among these modes when they are comprehended, the three characteristics are spoken of.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Suttanta Exposition is concluded.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Abhidhamma Division

167. Nāmarūpaparicchedakathā abhidhammakathāti suttante viya paccayayugaḷavasena akathetvā ajjhattikabāhiravasena abhiññeyyāni āyatanāni abbokārato abhidhammabhājanīye kathitāni. Āgammāti sabbasaṅkhārehi nibbindassa visaṅkhāraninnassa gotrabhunā vivaṭṭitamānasassa maggena sacchikaraṇenāti attho. Sacchikiriyamānañhi taṃ adhigantvā ārammaṇapaccayabhūtañca [M 0.0040] paṭicca adhipatipaccayabhūte ca tamhi paramassāsabhāvena vinimuttasaṅkhārassa ca gatibhāvena patiṭṭhānabhūte patiṭṭhāya khayasaṅkhāto maggo rāgādayo khepetīti taṃsacchikaraṇābhāve rāgādīnaṃ anuppattinirodhagamanābhāvā “taṃ āgamma rāgādayo khīyantī”ti [V 0.0040] vuttaṃ. Suttato muñcitvāti suttapadāni muñcitvā. Añño suttassa attho “mātaraṃ pitaraṃ hantvā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 294-295) viya āharitabbo, natthi suttapadeheva nīto atthoti attho.

167. The discourse on the delimitation of name-and-form is called the Abhidhamma discourse. Unlike in the Suttas, this is not explained in terms of pairs of conditions; rather, in the Abhidhamma Division, the sense bases to be directly known are explained in terms of internal and external, without omission. 'Relying on it' means: by its realization through the path for one whose mind is turned away by the change-of-lineage consciousness, who is disenchanted with all formations and inclined toward the unformed. For when that is being realized, having attained it and being established in it—which is relied upon as both an object-condition and a dominance-condition, as a state of supreme relief, and as a resort and foundation for one liberated from formations—the path, known as 'destruction,' eradicates lust and so on. Since in the absence of its realization, lust and so on do not arrive at non-arising and cessation, it is said: 'Relying on that, lust and so on are destroyed.' 'Having been released from the Sutta' means having released the words of the Sutta. Another meaning of the Sutta should be adduced, as in the case of 'Having slain mother and father,' etc. (Dhp 294–295); the meaning is that the meaning is not conveyed by the words of the Sutta alone.

Ekaṃ nānanti cuṇṇitaṃ khuddakaṃ vā karaṇaṃ, cuṇṇīkaraṇanti abahumānena vadati. Na tvaṃ ekaṃ nānaṃ jānāsīti kiṃ ettakaṃ tvameva na jānāsīti attho. Nanu ñāteti “yadipi pubbe na ñātaṃ, adhunāpi ñāte nanu sādhu hotī”ti attano jānanaṃ paṭicchādetvā vikkhepaṃ karontaṃ nibandhati. Vibhajitvāti akkharatthamatte aṭṭhatvā līnaṃ atthaṃ vibhajitvā uddharitvā nīharitvā kathitanti attho. Rāgādīnaṃ khayo nāma abhāvamatto, na ca abhāvassa bahubhāvo atthi attano abhāvattāti vadantassa vacanapacchindanatthaṃ pucchati “rāgakkhayo nāma rāgasseva khayo”tiādi. Yadi hi rāgakkhayo dosādīnaṃ khayo na hoti, dosakkhayādayo ca rāgādīnaṃ khayā, aññamaññavisiṭṭhā bhinnā āpannā hontīti bahunibbānatā āpannā eva hoti, aññamaññaviseso ca nāma nissabhāvassa natthīti sasabhāvatā ca nibbānassa. Nava taṇhāmūlakā “taṇhaṃ paṭicca pariyesanā”ti (dī. ni. 2.103; 3.359; a. ni. 9.23; vibha. 963) ādayo, tesu pariyesanādayo ca pariyesanādikarakilesā daṭṭhabbā. Diyaḍḍhakilesasahassaṃ nidānakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

'One thing and various things' means making something pulverized or small; 'pulverization' is said with disrespect. 'You do not know one thing and various things' means: 'Do you not know even this much?' 'But surely it is known': with this, he presses the one who, concealing his own knowledge, creates a distraction by saying, 'Even if it was not known before, now that it is known, is it not good?' 'Having analyzed' means: not being satisfied with the mere literal meaning, but having analyzed, uplifted, and extracted the concealed meaning, it is explained. To cut off the speech of one who says: 'The destruction of lust and so on is mere absence, and absence, being absence, has no multiplicity,' he asks: 'Is the destruction of lust the destruction of lust only?' and so on. For if the destruction of lust is not the destruction of hatred and so on, and the destructions of hatred and so on are not the destructions of lust and so on, they would become distinct from one another and separate, and a multiplicity of Nibbānas would result. And since there is no particularity for what is without an intrinsic nature, Nibbāna would have to have an intrinsic nature. The nine states rooted in craving are those beginning with 'Dependent on craving, there is seeking' (DN 15, etc.). Among them, seeking and so on should be understood as the defilements that perform the acts of seeking and so on. The one and a half thousand defilements are mentioned in the Nidānakathā.

Oḷārikatāya kāretabboti atisukhumassa nibbānassa oḷārikabhāvadosāpattiyā bodhetabbo, niggahetabbo vā. Vatthunti upādinnakaphoṭṭhabbaṃ methunaṃ. Acchādīnampi nibbānappatti kasmā vuttā, nanu “kilesānaṃ accantaṃ anuppattinirodho nibbāna”nti icchantassa kilesānaṃ vināso kañci kālaṃ appavatti nibbānaṃ na hotīti? Na, abhāvasāmaññato. Accantāpavatti hi kañci kālañca appavatti abhāvoyevāti natthi viseso. Savisesaṃ vā vadantassa abhāvatā āpajjatīti. Tiracchānagatehipi pāpuṇitabbattā tesampi pākaṭaṃ piḷandhanaṃ viya oḷārikaṃ thūlaṃ. Kevalaṃ pana kaṇṇe piḷandhituṃ na sakkoti, piḷandhanatopi vā thūlattā na sakkāti uppaṇḍento viya niggaṇhāti.

He should be made to understand, or be rebuked, for the fault of attributing coarseness to the extremely subtle Nibbāna. 'Object' means sexual intercourse, which is clung-to tangible matter. Why is the attainment of Nibbāna mentioned even for coverings and so on? Is it not that for one who holds that 'Nibbāna is the utter non-arising and cessation of the defilements,' the destruction of the defilements and their non-occurrence for some time is not Nibbāna? No, because of the commonality of absence. For utter non-occurrence and non-occurrence for some time are both just absence, so there is no difference. Or, for one who speaks of it with distinctions, it results in mere absence-ness. Because it can be attained even by those in the animal realm, for them too it is coarse and gross like a conspicuous ornament. But one cannot simply wear it on the ear; or because it is even grosser than an ornament, one cannot. Thus he rebukes him as if in jest.

Nibbānārammaṇakaraṇena [M 0.0041] gotrabhukkhaṇe kilesakkhayappatti panassa āpannāti maññamāno āha “tvaṃ akhīṇesuyevā”tiādi. Nanu ārammaṇakaraṇamattena kilesakkhayo anuppattoti na sakkā [V 0.0041] vattuṃ. Cittañhi atītānāgatādisabbaṃ ālambeti, na nipphannamevāti gotrabhupi maggena kilesānaṃ yā anuppattidhammatā kātabbā, taṃ ārabbha pavattissatīti? Na, appattanibbānassa nibbānārammaṇañāṇābhāvato. Na hi aññadhammā viya nibbānaṃ, taṃ pana atigambhīrattā appattena ālambituṃ na sakkā. Tasmā tena gotrabhunā pattabbena tikālikasabhāvātikkantagambhīrabhāvena bhavitabbaṃ, kilesakkhayamattataṃ vā icchato gotrabhuto puretaraṃ nipphannena kilesakkhayena. Tenāha “tvaṃ akhīṇesuyeva kilesesu kilesakkhayaṃ nibbānaṃ paññapesī”ti. Appattakilesakkhayārammaṇakaraṇe hi sati gotrabhuto puretaracittānipi ālambeyyunti.

Thinking that one attains the destruction of the defilements at the moment of change-of-lineage by making Nibbāna its object, the protagonist says: 'You, with defilements still undestroyed…' and so on. Surely, it cannot be said that the destruction of defilements is attained merely by making it an object. For the mind takes as object everything—past, future, etc.—not only what has been produced. Therefore, will the change-of-lineage consciousness also proceed by taking as its object that state of non-arising of the defilements that is to be effected by the path? No, because one who has not attained Nibbāna does not have the knowledge that takes Nibbāna as its object. For Nibbāna is not like other dhammas; because it is extremely profound, it cannot be taken as an object by one who has not attained it. Therefore, that which is to be attained by the change-of-lineage consciousness must have a profound nature that transcends the nature of the three time periods. Or, for one who desires the mere destruction of the defilements, that destruction of the defilements must have been produced before the change-of-lineage. Therefore he said: 'You, with the defilements still undestroyed, designate the destruction of defilements as Nibbāna.' For if it were possible to make the unattained destruction of defilements an object, then even minds prior to the change-of-lineage consciousness could take it as an object.

Maggassa kilesakkhayaṃ nibbānanti maggassa ārammaṇabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ katamanti attho. Maggotiādinā purimapucchādvayameva vivarati.

'Nibbāna, the destruction of defilements, for the path' means that Nibbāna has been made the object of the path. By the words 'of the path,' and so on, he explains the previous two questions.

Na ca kiñcīti rūpādīsu nibbānaṃ kiñci na hoti, na ca kadāci hoti, atītādibhāvena na vattabbanti vadanti, taṃ āgamma avijjātaṇhānaṃ kiñci ekadesamattampi na hoti, tadeva taṃ āgamma kadāci na ca hotīti attho yutto.

As to 'and not anything': some say that Nibbāna is not anything among form and so on, that it never exists, and that it cannot be spoken of in terms of past, etc. But the proper meaning is this: relying on that Nibbāna, not even the slightest portion of ignorance and craving exists; and relying on it, that very ignorance and craving never exists at any time.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Division is finished.

3. Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Questioner

168. Na…pe… navattabbadhammārammaṇattāti yathā sārammaṇā parittādibhāvena navattabbaṃ kiñci ārammaṇaṃ karonti, evaṃ kiñci ālambanato na navattabbakoṭṭhāsaṃ bhajatīti attho.

168. Not... because its object is a phenomenon that is unspecifiable. The meaning is that just as states that have an object, by way of being limited and so on, take as their object something unspecifiable, so too, by taking something as a support, it does not fall into the category of 'unspecifiable'.

Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Questioner is finished.

Āyatanavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Bases is finished.

3. Dhātuvibhaṅgo

3. The Analysis of Elements

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta Exposition

172. Yadipi [M 0.0042][V 0.0042] dhātusaṃyuttādīsu “dhātunānattaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi, katamañca, bhikkhave, dhātunānattaṃ? Cakkhudhātu…pe… manoviññāṇadhātū”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.85) aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo āgatā, tā pana abhidhamme ca āgatāti sādhāraṇattā aggahetvā suttantesveva āgate tayo dhātuchakke gahetvā suttantabhājanīyaṃ vibhattanti veditabbaṃ. Sabbā dhātuyoti aṭṭhārasapi. Suññe sabhāvamatte niruḷho dhātu-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Asamphuṭṭhadhātūti catūhi mahābhūtehi abyāpitabhāvoti attho.

172. Although in the Connected Discourses on the Elements and other texts the eighteen elements are presented, as in the passage beginning: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the diversity of elements. And what, bhikkhus, is the diversity of elements? The eye element … the mind-consciousness element” (SN 14.1), since these are also presented in the Abhidhamma and are thus common to both, they are not taken up here. It should be understood that the Sutta Exposition is set forth by taking the three six-fold groups of elements that are found only in the suttas. “All the elements” means all eighteen. The term “element” should be understood as established in the sense of mere intrinsic nature, which is empty. “Uncontacted element” means the state of not being pervaded by the four great elements; this is the meaning.

173. Pathavīdhātudvayanti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ paduddhāro kato, pāḷiyaṃ pana “dveya”nti āgacchati, attho pana yathāvuttova. Dvayanti pana pāṭhe sati ayampi attho sambhavati. Dve avayavā etassāti dvayaṃ, pathavīdhātūnaṃ dvayaṃ pathavīdhātudvayaṃ, dvinnaṃ pathavīdhātūnaṃ samudāyoti attho. Dve eva vā avayavā samuditā dvayaṃ, pathavīdhātudvayanti. “Tattha katamā pathavīdhātu? Pathavīdhātudvayaṃ, esā pathavīdhātū”ti saṅkhepena vissajjeti. Atthi ajjhattikā atthi bāhirāti ettha ajjhattikabāhira-saddā na ajjhattikaduke viya ajjhattikabāhirāyatanavācakā, nāpi ajjhattattike vuttehi ajjhattabahiddhā-saddehi samānatthā, indriyabaddhānindriyabaddhavācakā pana ete. Tena “sattasantānapariyāpannā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Niyakajjhattāti ca na paccattaṃ attani jātataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, atha kho sabbasattasantānesu jātatanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ajjhattaṃ paccattanti vacanena hi sattasantānapariyāpannatāya ajjhattikabhāvaṃ dasseti, na pāṭipuggalikatāya. Sabhāvākāratoti āpādīhi visiṭṭhena attano eva sabhāvabhūtena gahetabbākārena.

173. In the commentary, the phrase `pathavīdhātudvayaṃ` is analyzed, but in the Pāli text it appears as `dveyaṃ`; the meaning, however, is as stated. When the reading is `dvayaṃ`, this meaning is also possible: `dvayaṃ` means 'it has two parts,' so `pathavīdhātudvayaṃ` is a pair of earth elements, meaning the aggregate of the two earth elements. Or `dvayaṃ` is simply the two parts combined, hence `pathavīdhātudvayaṃ`. It answers concisely: “Therein, what is the earth element? The pair of earth elements. This is the earth element.” Here, in the phrase “there is the internal and there is the external,” the terms “internal” and “external” do not denote the internal and external sense bases as in the Duka on the internal, nor do they have the same meaning as the terms “internal” and “external” used in the Tika on the internal. Rather, these terms denote what is bound to the faculties and what is not bound to the faculties. Therefore it is said, “included in a being’s continuity,” etc. And “one’s own internal” is not said with reference to what has arisen in oneself personally, but it should be understood as what has arisen in the continuities of all beings. For the expression “internal, personal” indicates its internal nature by way of its inclusion in a being’s continuity, not by way of individual particularity. “By its own characteristic mark” means by the mode of apprehension that is its own intrinsic nature, distinguished by such qualities as solidity.

Kesā [V 0.0043] kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇāti kakkhaḷatādhikatāya vuttā. Pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāsoti pathavīkoṭṭhāsamatto suññoti attho. Matthaluṅgaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaggahaṇena gahitanti idha visuṃ na vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

“Hair has the characteristic of hardness”: this is said because of its predominance of hardness. “A separate portion”: this means it is empty, merely a portion of the earth element. It should be understood that the brain is included under the heading of bone marrow, and thus it is not mentioned separately here.

Imināti [M 0.0043] “seyyathidaṃ kesā”tiādinā. Kammaṃ katvāti payogaṃ vīriyaṃ āyūhanaṃ vā katvāti attho. Bhogakāmena kasiyādīsu viya arahattakāmena ca imasmiṃ manasikāre kammaṃ kattabbanti. Pubbapalibodhāti āvāsādayo dīghakesādike khuddakapalibodhe aparapalibodhāti apekkhitvā vuttā.

“By this” means by the passage beginning “that is, hair of the head….” “Having done the work” means having made an effort, exertion, or application; this is the meaning. Just as one desiring wealth should work at farming and the like, so one desiring arahantship should do the work on this meditation subject. “Earlier impediments” refers to residence and so on; this is said in contrast to the minor impediments such as long hair, which are the “later impediments.”

Vaṇṇādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ vasena manasikāro dhātupaṭikūlavaṇṇamanasikārānaṃ sādhāraṇo pubbabhāgoti nibbattitadhātumanasikāraṃ dassetuṃ “avasāne evaṃ manasikāro pavattetabbo”ti āha. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitāti kāraṇassa ca phalassa ca abyāpāratāya dhātumattataṃ dasseti. Ābhogapaccavekkhaṇādīnampi evameva abyāpāratā daṭṭhabbā. Na hi tāni, tesañca kāraṇāni ābhujitvā paccavekkhitvā ca uppajjanti karonti cāti. Lakkhaṇavasenāti “kakkhaḷaṃ kharigata”ntiādivacanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

The contemplation by way of the five aspects beginning with color is a preliminary part common to the contemplation of the elements and the contemplation of the sign of repulsiveness. To show the developed contemplation of the elements, it is said: “At the end, contemplation should be conducted in this way.” “Devoid of mutual application and review” shows the state of being a mere element because of the non-activity of cause and effect. The non-activity of application, review, and so on should be understood in the same way. For they do not arise and act after applying and reviewing their causes. “By way of characteristic” is said with reference to such statements as “hard, hardness.”

Vekantakaṃ ekā lohajāti. Nāganāsikalohaṃ lohasadisaṃ lohavijāti haliddivijāti viya. Tiputambādīhi missetvā kataṃ karaṇena nibbattattā kittimalohaṃ. Morakkhādīni evaṃnāmānevetāni. Sāmuddikamuttāti nidassanamattametaṃ, sabbāpi pana muttā muttā eva.

`Vekantaka` is a type of metal. `Nāganāsika` metal is a variety of metal similar to iron, like the `halidda` variety. `Kittima` metal is so called because it is produced by manufacture, made by mixing with tin, copper, and so on. `Morakkha` and so on are just their names. “Ocean pearl” is merely a designation, for any pearl is just a pearl.

174. Appetīti āpo, ābandhanavasena sesabhūtattayaṃ pāpuṇāti silesatīti attho. Yūsabhūtoti rasabhūto. Vakkahadayayakanapapphāsāni tementanti ettha yakanaṃ heṭṭhābhāgapūraṇena, itarāni tesaṃ upari thokaṃ thokaṃ paggharaṇena temeti. Heṭṭhā leḍḍukhaṇḍāni temayamāneti temakatemitabbānaṃ abyāpārasāmaññanidassanatthāyeva upamā daṭṭhabbā, na ṭhānasāmaññanidassanatthāya. Sannicitalohitena temetabbānaṃ kesañci heṭṭhā, kassaci upari ṭhitatañhi satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅge vakkhatīti, yakanassa heṭṭhābhāgo “ṭhitaṃ mayi lohita”nti na jānāti, vakkādīni “amhe temayamānaṃ lohitaṃ ṭhita”nti na jānantīti evaṃ yojanā kātabbā. Yathā [V 0.0044] pana bhesajjasikkhāpade niyamo atthi “yesaṃ maṃsaṃ kappati, tesaṃ khīra”nti, evamidha natthi.

174. “It pervades” (`appeti`), thus it is water (`āpo`); the meaning is that it reaches and binds the other three great elements. “Become like juice” means become fluid. “The kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs are moistened”: here, it moistens the liver by filling its lower part, and the others by trickling a little over them. The simile “as it moistens the clods of earth below” should be seen as illustrating only the general non-volitional nature of the moistener and the moistened, not for illustrating a similarity of place. For it will be said in the Analysis of the Establishment of Mindfulness that of the things to be moistened by the accumulated blood, some are situated below and some above. The connection should be made thus: the lower part of the liver does not know, “Blood is situated in me,” and the kidneys and so on do not know, “The blood that moistens us is situated here.” Just as in the training rule on medicines there is a rule, “For those whose flesh is allowable, their milk is also allowable,” there is no such rule here.

175. Tejanavasenāti nisitabhāvena tikkhabhāvena. Sarīrassa pakatiṃ atikkamitvā uṇhabhāvo santāpo, sarīradahanavasena pavatto [M 0.0044] mahādāho paridāho. Ayametesaṃ viseso. Yena jīrīyatīti ekāhikādijararogena jīrīyatītipi attho yujjati. Satavāraṃ tāpetvā udake pakkhipitvā uddhaṭasappi satadhotasappīti vadanti. Rasasoṇitamedamaṃsanhāruaṭṭhiaṭṭhimiñjā rasādayo. Keci nhāruṃ apanetvā sukkaṃ sattamadhātuṃ avocunti. Pākatikoti khobhaṃ appatto sadā vijjamāno. Petaggi mukhato bahi niggatova idha gahito.

175. “By way of heating” means by its sharp and keen nature. Heat that surpasses the body’s normal state is “burning” (`santāpa`); a great burning that proceeds by way of consuming the body is “scorching” (`paridāha`). This is the difference between them. “By which one is consumed”: the meaning “is consumed by a feverish illness such as a one-day fever” is also fitting. They call ghee that has been heated a hundred times, placed in water, and then removed, “hundred-times-washed ghee.” Nutritional essence, blood, fat, flesh, sinews, bones, and bone marrow are the nutritional essences and so on. Some, omitting sinews, have said that semen is the seventh primary element. “Natural” means not having reached a state of disturbance, always present. The fire of hungry ghosts is here taken as that which has come out of the mouth.

176. Vāyanavasenāti savegagamanavasena, samudīraṇavasena vā.

176. “By way of blowing” means by way of forceful movement or by way of impelling.

177. Iminā yasmiṃ ākāse…pe… taṃ kathitanti idaṃ kasiṇugghāṭimākāsassa akathitataṃ, ajaṭākāsassa ca kathitataṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ.

177. This is said in order to show that by the words “in whatever space … that is described,” the space of the removed kasiṇa is not described, while the unentangled space is described.

179. Sukhadukkhānaṃ pharaṇabhāvo sarīraṭṭhakautussa sukhadukkhaphoṭṭhabbasamuṭṭhānapaccayabhāvena yathābalaṃ sarīrekadesasakalasarīrapharaṇasamatthatāya vutto, somanassadomanassānaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhacittajasamuṭṭhāpanena tatheva pharaṇasamatthatāya. Evaṃ etesaṃ sarīrapharaṇatāya ekassa ṭhānaṃ itaraṃ paharati, itarassa ca aññanti aññamaññena sappaṭipakkhataṃ dasseti, aññamaññapaṭipakkhaoḷārikappavatti eva vā etesaṃ pharaṇaṃ. Vatthārammaṇāni ca pabandhena pavattihetubhūtāni pharaṇaṭṭhānaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, ubhayavato ca puggalassa vasena ayaṃ sappaṭipakkhatā dassitā sukhadassanīyattā.

179. The pervasion by pleasure and pain is spoken of because it is a condition for the arising of bodily pleasure and pain from tangible objects, and because of its ability to pervade a part of the body or the entire body according to its strength. Similarly, the pervasion by joy and sorrow is spoken of because of their ability to pervade in the same way by producing desirable and undesirable mind-born states. Thus, because they pervade the body, one strikes the place of the other, and the other strikes the place of the one; this shows their mutual opposition. Or their pervasion is simply their gross occurrence in mutual opposition. The bases and objects, which are the cause for their continuous occurrence, should be seen as the place of pervasion. This mutual opposition is shown with respect to a person who possesses both, for the sake of easy comprehension.

181. Kilesakāmaṃ sandhāyāti “saṅkappo kāmo rāgo kāmo”ti (mahāni. 1; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 8) ettha vuttaṃ saṅkappaṃ sandhāyāti adhippāyo. Sopi hi vibādhati upatāpeti cāti kilesasanthavasambhavato kilesakāmo vibhatto kilesavatthusambhavato vā. Kāmapaṭisaṃyuttāti kāmarāgasaṅkhātena kāmena sampayuttā, kāmapaṭibaddhā vā. Aññesu ca kāmapaṭisaṃyuttadhammesu vijjamānesu vitakkeyeva kāmopapado dhātusaddo niruḷho veditabbo vitakkassa [V 0.0045] kāmappasaṅgappavattiyā sātisayattā. Esa nayo byāpādadhātuādīsu. Parassa attano ca dukkhāyanaṃ vihiṃsā. Vihiṃsantīti hantuṃ icchanti.

181. “With reference to sensual desire as a defilement”: the intention is that this refers to the thought mentioned in the passage: “Thought is sensual desire, lust is sensual desire” (Mahanid. 1; Culanid. Ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 8). For that too obstructs and torments. Thus “sensual desire as a defilement” is distinguished because it arises from the constitution of defilements, or because it arises from the object of defilements. “Connected with sensual desire” means associated with the desire called sensual lust, or bound to sensual desire. Although there are other phenomena connected with sensual desire, the term “element” qualified by “sensual desire” should be understood as established only in relation to thought, because thought’s tendency to be inclined towards sensual desire is excessive. This same method applies to the element of ill will and so on. Cruelty is the causing of suffering to others and to oneself. “They are cruel” means they wish to harm.

182. Ubhayattha uppannopi abhijjhāsaṃyogena kammapathajananato anabhijjhākammapathabhindanato ca kāmavitakko “kammapathabhedo”ti vutto[M 0.0045]. Byāpādo panāti byāpādavacanena byāpādavitakkaṃ dasseti. So hi byāpādadhātūti. Tathā vihiṃsāya vihiṃsādhātuyā ca byāpādavasena yathāsambhavaṃ pāṇātipātādivasena ca kammapathabhedo yojetabbo. Etthāti dvīsu tikesu. Sabbakāmāvacarasabbakusalasaṅgāhakehi itare dve dve saṅgahetvā kathanaṃ sabbasaṅgāhikakathā. Etthāti pana etasmiṃ chakketi vuccamāne kāmadhātuvacanena kāmāvacarānaṃ nekkhammadhātuādīnañca gahaṇaṃ āpajjati.

182. Even when arising in both ways, a thought of sensual desire is called 'a breach in the path of action' because it generates a path of action through its connection with covetousness and because it breaches the path of non-covetousness. As to 'ill will,' this indicates a thought of ill will by the term 'ill will.' For that is the element of ill will. Similarly, a breach in the path of action should be connected with cruelty and the element of cruelty by way of ill will and, as may be the case, by way of killing living beings and so on. Here, in the two triads, the statement is an all-inclusive one, made by including the other two members of each triad under the all-inclusive terms for all that pertains to the sensual sphere and all that is wholesome. But here, when this sixfold set is spoken of, the term 'element of sensuality' would entail the inclusion of things belonging to the sensual sphere and also of the element of renunciation and so on.

Labhāpetabbāti cakkhudhātādibhāvaṃ labhamānā dhammā nīharitvā dassanena labhāpetabbā. Carati etthāti cāro, kiṃ carati? Sammasanaṃ, sammasanassa cāro sammasanacāro, tebhūmakadhammānaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

'To be made available': phenomena that are attaining the state of the eye-element and so on are to be made available by drawing them out and showing them. 'One ranges here' (carati ettha), thus it is a 'range' (cāro). What ranges? Comprehension. The range of comprehension is the 'comprehension-range' (sammasanacāro), a designation for the phenomena of the three planes.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Suttanta Analysis is finished.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Analysis

183. Cakkhussāti visesakāraṇaṃ asādhāraṇasāmibhāvena niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tañhi puggalantarāsādhāraṇaṃ nīlādisabbarūpasādhāraṇañca. Vidahatīti evaṃ evañca tayā pavattitabbanti viniyujjamānaṃ viya uppādetīti attho. Vidahatīti ca dhātuattho eva visiṭṭho upasaggena dīpitoti vināpi upasaggena dhātūti eso saddo tamatthaṃ vadatīti daṭṭhabbo. Kattukammabhāvakaraṇaadhikaraṇesu dhātupadasiddhi hotīti pañcapi ete atthā vuttā. Suvaṇṇarajatādidhātuyo suvaṇṇādīnaṃ bījabhūtā selādayo.

183. 'Of the eye': this indicates a specific cause by way of unique ownership. For it is not shared with another person, but it is common to all forms such as blue, etc. 'It arranges' (vidahati): this means it generates, as if enjoining, 'Thus and thus should you proceed.' And as to 'it arranges,' the meaning of the root (dhā) is here illuminated as a specific one by the prefix (vi-), but it should be seen that even without the prefix, this word 'dhātu' conveys that meaning. The formation of the word from the root occurs in the senses of agent, object, state, instrument, and location; thus these five meanings are stated. The primary elements (dhātuyo) such as gold and silver are rocks and so on, which are the seeds of gold and so on.

Attano sabhāvaṃ dhārentīti dhātuyoti etthāpi dhātīti dhātūti padasiddhi veditabbā. Dhātu-saddo [V 0.0046] eva hi dhāraṇatthopi hotīti. Kattuatthopi cāyaṃ purimena asadisoti nissattasabhāvamattadhāraṇañca dhātu-saddassa padhāno atthoti visuṃ vutto. Dhātuyo viya dhātuyoti ettha sīha-saddo viya kesarimhi niruḷho purisesu, selāvayavesu niruḷho dhātu-saddo ca cakkhādīsu upacarito daṭṭhabbo. Ñāṇañca ñeyyañca ñāṇañeyyāni, tesaṃ avayavā tappabhedabhūtā dhātuyo ñāṇañeyyāvayavā. Tattha ñāṇappabhedā dhammadhātuekadeso, ñeyyappabhedā aṭṭhārasāpīti ñāṇañeyyāvayavamattā dhātuyo [M 0.0046] honti. Atha vā ñāṇena ñātabbo sabhāvo dhātusaddena vuccamāno aviparītato ñāṇañeyyo, na diṭṭhiādīhi viparītaggāhakehi ñeyyoti attho. Tassa ñāṇañeyyassa avayavā cakkhādayo. Visabhāgalakkhaṇāvayavesu rasādīsu niruḷho dhātu-saddo tādisesu aññāvayavesu cakkhādīsu upacarito daṭṭhabbo, rasādīsu viya vā cakkhādīsu niruḷhova. Nijjīvamattassetaṃ adhivacananti etena nijjīvamattapadatthe dhātu-saddassa niruḷhataṃ dasseti. Cha dhātuyo etassāti chadhātuyo, yo loke “puriso”ti dhammasamudāyo vuccati, so chadhāturo channaṃ pathavīādīnaṃ nijjīvamattasabhāvānaṃ samudāyamatto, na ettha jīvo puriso vā atthīti attho.

'They bear their own intrinsic nature,' thus they are 'elements' (dhātuyo). Here too, the formation of the word `dhātu` from `dhāti` (it bears) should be understood. For the word `dhātu` also has the meaning of bearing. And since this agent-meaning is dissimilar to the previous one, it is stated separately that the primary meaning of the word `dhātu` is the bearing of a mere non-sentient nature. In the phrase 'elements like the primary elements,' just as the word 'lion' (sīha), established in the sense of a maned beast, is used figuratively for men, so the word 'element' (dhātu), established in the sense of components of rock, should be seen as used figuratively for the eye and so on. Knowledge and the knowable are 'knowledge-and-knowable'; their parts, which are their divisions, are the elements, the 'parts of knowledge-and-knowable.' Therein, the divisions of knowledge are a portion of the element of phenomena, and the divisions of the knowable are all eighteen elements. Thus the elements are merely parts of knowledge and the knowable. Alternatively, an intrinsic nature to be known by knowledge, when designated by the word 'element,' is what is knowable without distortion, meaning it is not what is knowable by those who grasp in a distorted way, such as by views and so on. The parts of that which is knowable by knowledge are the eye and so on. The word 'element,' established in the sense of components with dissimilar characteristics such as tastes, should be seen as used figuratively for other such components like the eye, or it is established in the eye and so on just as in tastes and so on. 'This is a designation for what is merely lifeless': by this he shows that the word 'element' is established in the meaning of the term 'merely lifeless.' 'He has six elements,' thus he is 'one of six elements' (chadhātuyo). That collection of phenomena which in the world is called a 'person' is one of six elements, a mere collection of the six things that are merely lifeless intrinsic natures, beginning with earth. The meaning is that there is no soul or person here.

Cakkhādīnaṃ kamo pubbe vuttoti idha ekekasmiṃ tike tiṇṇaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhātūnaṃ kamaṃ dassento āha “hetuphalānupubbavavatthānavasenā”ti. Hetuphalānaṃ anupubbavavatthānaṃ hetuphalabhāvova. Tattha hetūti paccayo adhippeto. Phalanti paccayuppannanti āha “cakkhudhātū”tiādi. Manodhātudhammadhātūnañca manoviññāṇassa hetubhāvo yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbo, dvārabhūtamanovasena vā tassā manodhātuyā.

Since the sequence of the eye and so on was stated previously, here, showing the sequence of the three elements in each triad, he says: 'by way of the sequential arrangement of cause and effect.' The sequential arrangement of cause and effect is simply the state of being cause and effect. Therein, by 'cause,' 'condition' is intended. By 'effect' is meant 'what has arisen from a condition,' as when he says, 'the eye-element,' and so on. The status of the mind-element and the element of phenomena as a cause for mind-consciousness should be connected as is appropriate, either by way of the mind that has become the door or in respect of that mind-element.

Sabbāsaṃ vasenāti yathāvuttānaṃ ābhādhātuādīnaṃ pañcatiṃsāya dhātūnaṃ vasena. Aparamatthasabhāvassa paramatthasabhāvesu na kadāci antogadhatā atthīti āha “sabhāvato vijjamānāna”nti. Candābhāsūriyābhādikā vaṇṇanibhā evāti āha “rūpadhātuyeva hi ābhādhātū”ti. Rūpādipaṭibaddhāti rāgavatthubhāvena gahetabbākāro subhanimittanti sandhāya “rūpādayovā”ti avatvā paṭibaddhavacanaṃ āha. Asatipi rāgavatthubhāve “kusalavipākārammaṇā subhā dhātū”ti dutiyo vikappo vutto. Vihiṃsādhātu cetanā, paraviheṭhanachando vā. Avihiṃsā karuṇā.

'By way of all': this means by way of the thirty-five elements as mentioned, beginning with the element of radiance. Because what does not have an ultimate nature is never included among things that have an ultimate nature, he says, 'of those existing by their own nature.' Because the radiance of the moon, sun, and so on is merely the appearance of color, he says, 'for the element of radiance is just the element of form.' 'Bound to form, etc.': with reference to the beautiful sign—the aspect to be grasped as a basis for lust—he did not say 'forms, etc.' but used the word 'bound.' Even when there is no basis for lust, a second alternative is stated: 'the beautiful element as an object for wholesome resultant consciousness.' The element of cruelty is volition, or the desire to harass others. The element of non-cruelty is compassion.

Ubhopīti [V 0.0047] dhammadhātumanoviññāṇadhātuyo. Hīnādīsu purimanayena hīḷitā cakkhādayo hīnā, sambhāvitā paṇītā, nātihīḷitā nātisambhāvitā majjhimāti khandhavibhaṅge āgatahīnadukatoyeva nīharitvā majjhimā dhātu vuttāti veditabbā. Viññāṇadhātu yadipi chaviññāṇadhātuvasena vibhattā, tathāpi “viññāṇadhātuggahaṇena tassā purecārikapacchācārikattā manodhātu gahitāva hotī”ti vuttattā āha [M 0.0047] “viññāṇadhātu…pe… sattaviññāṇasaṅkhepoyevā”ti. Anekesaṃ cakkhudhātuādīnaṃ, tāsu ca ekekissā nānappakāratāya nānādhātūnaṃ vasena anekadhātunānādhātuloko vuttoti āha “aṭṭhārasadhātuppabhedamattamevā”ti.

'Both': the element of phenomena and the element of mind-consciousness. In 'inferior, etc.,' in accordance with the previous method, the eye and so on, being despised, are inferior; being esteemed, they are superior; being neither too despised nor too esteemed, they are middling. Thus it should be understood that the middling element is spoken of by extracting it from the dyad of the inferior that comes in the Analysis of the Aggregates. Although the consciousness-element is divided by way of the six consciousness-elements, still, because it has been said, 'by the grasping of the consciousness-element, the mind-element is also grasped, on account of its being its forerunner and follower,' he says: 'the consciousness-element... is just a summary of the seven consciousnesses.' Because there are many elements such as the eye-element, and because of the diversity of each one of them, the world is said to be of 'many elements' and 'diverse elements.' Therefore he says: 'it is merely the division into eighteen elements.'

“Cakkhusotaghānajivhākāyamanomanoviññāṇadhātubhedenā”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ likhitaṃ. Tattha na cakkhādīnaṃ kevalena dhātu-saddena sambandho adhippeto vijānanasabhāvassa pabhedavacanato. Viññāṇadhātu-saddena sambandhe kariyamāne dve manogahaṇāni na kattabbāni. Na hi dve manoviññāṇadhātuyo atthīti. “Cakkhu…pe… kāyamanoviññāṇamanodhātū”ti vā vattabbaṃ atulyayoge dvandasamāsābhāvato. Ayaṃ panettha pāṭho siyā “cakkhu…pe… kāyaviññāṇamanomanoviññāṇadhātubhedenā”ti.

In the commentary it is written: 'by the division into the eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, mind-, and mind-consciousness-elements.' Therein, a connection of 'eye,' etc., with the mere word 'element' is not intended, because this is a statement about the divisions of the nature of cognition. When the connection is made with the word 'consciousness-element,' two graspings of 'mind' should not be made, for there are not two mind-consciousness-elements. Or it should be stated as 'the eye... up to body, mind-consciousness, and mind-element,' because there is no dvandva compound in an unequal combination. The reading here might be: 'by the division into the eye... up to body-consciousness, mind-, and mind-consciousness-elements.'

Khandhāyatanadesanā saṅkhepadesanā, indriyadesanā vitthāradesanāti tadubhayaṃ apekkhitvā nātisaṅkhepavitthārā dhātudesanā. Atha vā suttantabhājanīye vuttadhātudesanā atisaṅkhepadesanā, ābhādhātuādīnaṃ anekadhātunānādhātuantānaṃ vasena desetabbā ativitthāradesanāti tadubhayaṃ apekkhitvā ayaṃ “nātisaṅkhepavitthārā”ti.

The teaching on the aggregates and bases is a teaching in brief, while the teaching on the faculties is a teaching in detail. In consideration of both, the teaching on the elements is neither too brief nor too detailed. Alternatively, the teaching on the elements spoken of in the Suttanta Analysis is an extremely brief teaching, whereas the teaching that is to be delivered by way of the many elements and diverse elements ending with the element of radiance and so on is an extremely detailed teaching. In consideration of both, this is said to be 'neither too brief nor too detailed.'

Bherītalaṃ viya cakkhudhātu saddassa viya viññāṇassa nissayabhāvato. Etāhi ca upamāhi nijjīvānaṃ bherītaladaṇḍādīnaṃ samāyoge nijjīvānaṃ saddādīnaṃ viya nijjīvānaṃ cakkhurūpādīnaṃ samāyoge nijjīvānaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ pavattīti kāraṇaphalānaṃ dhātumattattā kārakavedakabhāvavirahaṃ dasseti.

The eye-element is like the surface of a drum in that it is a support for consciousness, just as the drum surface is for sound. And by these similes—just as lifeless sounds and so on arise from the conjunction of lifeless things such as a drum surface and a drumstick, so lifeless eye-consciousness and so on arise from the conjunction of the lifeless eye and forms—he shows the absence of a doer and an experiencer, since cause and effect are merely elements.

Purecarānucarā viyāti nijjīvassa kassaci keci nijjīvā purecarānucarā viyāti attho. Manodhātuyeva vā attano khaṇaṃ anativattantī attano khaṇaṃ anativattantānaṃyeva cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ avijjamānepi purecarānucarabhāve pubbakālāparakālatāya purecarānucarā viya daṭṭhabbāti [V 0.0048] attho. Sallamiva sūlamiva tividhadukkhatāsamāyogato daṭṭhabbo. Āsāyeva dukkhaṃ āsādukkhaṃ, āsāvighātaṃ dukkhaṃ vā. Saññā hi abhūtaṃ dukkhadukkhampi subhādito sañjānantī taṃ āsaṃ tassā ca vighātaṃ [M 0.0048] āsīsitasubhādiasiddhiyā janetīti. Kammappadhānā saṅkhārāti “paṭisandhiyaṃ pakkhipanato”tiādimāha. Jātidukkhānubandhanatoti attanā nibbattiyamānena jātidukkhena anubandhattā. Bhavapaccayā jāti hi jātidukkhanti. Padumaṃ viya dissamānaṃ khuracakkaṃ viya rūpampi itthiyādibhāvena dissamānaṃ nānāvidhupaddavaṃ janeti. Sabbe anatthā rāgādayo jātiādayo ca visabhūtā asantā sappaṭibhayā cāti tappaṭipakkhabhūtattā amatādito daṭṭhabbā.

'Like forerunners and followers': the meaning is that for some lifeless thing, certain other lifeless things are like forerunners and followers. Or, the meaning is that the mind-element itself, not overstepping its own moment, should be seen as being like a forerunner and follower to eye-consciousness and so on—which also do not overstep their own moments—in terms of earlier and later time, even though a real state of being forerunner and follower does not exist. 'Like a dart, like a stake': this should be seen as due to its connection with the threefold suffering. 'Longing is suffering' (āsādukkhaṃ) means either that longing itself is suffering, or that the frustration of longing is suffering. For perception, by falsely perceiving what is actually suffering upon suffering as pleasant and so on, generates that longing and its frustration through the non-attainment of the desired pleasantness and so on. 'Formations are kamma-prominent': he says, 'because of depositing into rebirth-linking,' and so on. 'Because it is bound up with the suffering of birth': because it is followed by the suffering of birth that is produced by it. For birth conditioned by becoming is the suffering of birth. Form, appearing like a lotus but being like a razor-wheel, also generates various calamities by appearing in the guise of a woman and so on. All baneful things—lust and so on, and birth and so on—are like poison, unreal, and perilous; therefore, being their opposites, Nibbāna and so on should be seen as the deathless and so on.

Muñcitvāpi aññaṃ gahetvāvāti etena makkaṭassa gahitaṃ sākhaṃ muñcitvāpi ākāse ṭhātuṃ asamatthatā viya gahitārammaṇaṃ muñcitvāpi aññaṃ aggahetvā pavattituṃ asamatthatāya makkaṭasamānataṃ dasseti. Aṭṭhivedhaviddhopi damathaṃ anupagacchanto duṭṭhasso assakhaḷuṅko. Raṅgagato naṭo raṅganaṭo.

“Having let go, it grasps another”—by this, it shows the similarity to a monkey, in that just as a monkey is unable to remain in the air after letting go of a grasped branch, so too is there an inability to continue without grasping another object after letting go of the grasped object. Even though pierced by eight arrows, a vicious, untamed horse does not undergo taming. An actor who has gone onto the stage is a stage actor.

184. Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe cātiādinā dvārārammaṇesu ekavacanabahuvacananiddesā ekanānāsantānagatānaṃ ekasantānagataviññāṇapaccayabhāvato ekanānājātikattā ca.

184. The indication of singular and plural regarding the doors and objects in phrases like “dependent on the eye and forms,” etc., is because they, existing in single or multiple continua, are a condition for consciousness, which exists in a single continuum, and also because they are of single and multiple kinds.

Sabbadhammesūti ettha sabba-saddo adhikāravasena yathāvuttaviññāṇasaṅkhāte ārammaṇasaṅkhāte vā padesasabbasmiṃ tiṭṭhatīti daṭṭhabbo. Manoviññāṇadhātuniddese “cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā uppajjitvā niruddhasamanantarā uppajjati manodhātu, manodhātuyāpi uppajjitvā niruddhasamanantarā uppajjati citta”nti cakkhuviññāṇadhātānantaraṃ manodhātu viya manodhātānantarampi uppajjati cittanti yāva aññā manodhātu uppajjissati, tāva pavattaṃ sabbaṃ cittaṃ ekattena gahetvā vuttanti evampi attho labbhati. Evañhi sati manoviññāṇadhātānantaraṃ uppannāya manodhātuyā manoviññāṇadhātubhāvappasaṅgo na hotiyeva. Pañcaviññāṇadhātumanodhātukkamanidassanañhi tabbidhurasabhāvena uppattiṭṭhānena ca paricchinnassa cittassa manoviññāṇadhātubhāvadassanatthaṃ, na anantaruppattimattenāti tabbidhurasabhāve ekattaṃ upanetvā dassanaṃ yujjati. Anupanītepi ekatte tabbidhurasabhāve ekasmiṃ dassite sāmaññavasena aññampi sabbaṃ taṃ sabhāvaṃ dassitaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pi-saddena manoviññāṇadhātusampiṇḍane [V 0.0049] ca sati “manoviññāṇadhātuyāpi samanantarā uppajjati cittaṃ…pe… tajjā manoviññāṇadhātū”ti [M 0.0049] manoviññāṇadhātuggahaṇena bhavaṅgānantaraṃ uppannaṃ manodhātucittaṃ nivattitaṃ hotīti ce? Na, tassā manoviññāṇadhātubhāvāsiddhito. Na hi yaṃ codīyati, tadeva parihārāya hotīti.

In the phrase 'sabbadhammesu' (in all phenomena), the word 'sabba' (all) should be understood as standing, by way of the topic, for the entire scope, whether in terms of consciousness (viññāṇa) or object (ārammaṇa) as previously mentioned. In the exposition of the mind-consciousness element, it is said: 'After the eye-consciousness element has arisen and ceased, the mind-element arises immediately; and after the mind-element has arisen and ceased, consciousness (citta) arises immediately.' Thus, just as the mind-element arises immediately after the eye-consciousness element, so too does consciousness arise immediately after the mind-element; all consciousness that occurs until another mind-element arises is spoken of as a unity. This meaning is also obtained. If this were the case, there would be no occasion for the mind-element arising immediately after the mind-consciousness element to become the mind-consciousness element. For the showing of the sequence of the five sense-consciousness elements and the mind-element is for the purpose of showing that consciousness (citta), delimited by its distinct nature and its basis of arising, is the mind-consciousness element, not merely by its immediate arising. Thus, it is appropriate to show the unity by bringing it to its distinct nature. Even without explicitly unifying them, when one instance of their distinct nature is shown, all others of the same nature are implicitly indicated. If, by the particle 'pi' (also), the mind-consciousness element were also included, so that it is said: 'Immediately after the mind-consciousness element also, consciousness arises... and the corresponding mind-consciousness elements,' would this inclusion of the mind-consciousness element imply that the mind-element consciousness arising after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is excluded? No, because its nature as mind-consciousness is not established. For what is questioned is not itself the answer.

Manodhātuyāpi manoviññāṇadhātuyāpīti manadvayavacanena dvinnaṃ aññamaññavidhurasabhāvatā dassitāti teneva manodhātāvajjanassa manoviññāṇadhātubhāvo nivattitoti daṭṭhabbo. Vutto hi tassa manoviññāṇadhātuvidhuro manodhātusabhāvo “sabbadhammesu vā pana paṭhamasamannāhāro uppajjatī”tiādinā. Sā sabbāpīti etaṃ mukhamattanidassanaṃ. Na hi javanapariyosānā eva manoviññāṇadhātu, tadārammaṇādīnipi pana hontiyevāti. Evaṃ pañcaviññāṇadhātumanodhātuvisiṭṭhasabhāvavasena sabbaṃ manoviññāṇadhātuṃ dassetvā puna manodvāravasena sātisayaṃ javanamanoviññāṇadhātuṃ dassento “manañca paṭiccā”tiādimāha. Yadi pana channaṃ dvārānaṃ vasena javanāvasānāneva cittāni idha “manoviññāṇadhātū”ti dassitānīti ayamattho gayheyya, cutipaṭisandhibhavaṅgānaṃ aggahitattā sāvasesā desanā āpajjati, tasmā yathāvuttena nayena attho veditabbo. Chadvārikacittehi vā samānalakkhaṇāni aññānipi “manoviññāṇadhātū”ti dassitānīti veditabbāni.

The phrase 'manodhātuyāpi manoviññāṇadhātuyāpi' (also the mind-element, also the mind-consciousness element) indicates the mutual distinctness of the two by mentioning the two minds; thus, it should be understood that, by that very fact, the mind-element of adverting is excluded from being the mind-consciousness element. For its nature as the mind-element, distinct from the mind-consciousness element, is stated in phrases like 'or when the first mental engagement arises regarding all phenomena,' etc. The phrase 'sā sabbāpi' (all of it) here merely serves as an introductory illustration. For the mind-consciousness element is not limited to just the conclusion of the impulsion phase, but it also includes the registration phase and others. Having thus explained the entire mind-consciousness element by distinguishing its specific nature from the five sense-consciousness elements and the mind-element, he now emphasizes the impulsion mind-consciousness element in particular, associated with the mind-door, by stating, 'dependent on the mind,' etc. However, if one were to interpret that only the consciousnesses at the end of impulsion arising through the six doors are here referred to as the 'mind-consciousness element,' the teaching would be incomplete, as it would exclude death, rebirth-linking, and life-continuum states. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as explained above. Alternatively, it should be understood that other states sharing the same characteristics as the six-door consciousnesses are also referred to as the 'mind-consciousness element.'

Paṭiccāti āgataṭṭhāneti ettha “mano ca nesaṃ gocaravisayaṃ paccanubhotī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.455) visuṃ kātuṃ yuttaṃ, idha pana “cakkhuñca paṭiccā”tiādīsu ca-saddena sampiṇḍetvā āvajjanassapi cakkhādisannissitatākaraṇaṃ viya manañca paṭiccāti āgataṭṭhāne manodvārasaṅkhātabhavaṅgasannissitameva āvajjanaṃ kātabbanti adhippāyo.

In passages where 'paṭicca' (dependent on) occurs, such as 'the mind also experiences their object-field' (MN 1.455), it is appropriate to distinguish separately. But here, in passages like 'dependent on the eye and,' etc., by combining with the particle 'ca' (and), just as adverting is made dependent on the eye and other bases, so too, in passages where 'dependent on the mind' occurs, the adverting should be made dependent solely on the life-continuum, which is designated as the mind-door—this is the intention.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Abhidhamma Analysis is concluded.

3. Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā

3. Exposition on the Question Section

Pañhapucchakaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānamevāti.

The Question Section is self-explanatory, as the method has been stated above.

Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the Question Section is concluded.

Dhātuvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Analysis of Elements is concluded.

4. Saccavibhaṅgo

4. The Analysis of the Truths

1. Suttantabhājanīyaṃ

1. The Sutta-based Analysis

Uddesavaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Outline

189. Sāsanakkamoti [M 0.0050][V 0.0050] ariyasaccāni vuccanti ariyasaccadesanā vā. Sakalañhi sāsanaṃ bhagavato vacanaṃ saccavinimuttaṃ natthīti saccesu kamati, sīlasamādhipaññāsaṅkhātaṃ vā sāsanaṃ etesu kamati, tasmā kamati etthāti kamo, kiṃ kamati? Sāsanaṃ, sāsanassa kamo sāsanakkamoti saccāni sāsanapavattiṭṭhānāni vuccanti, taṃdesanā ca tabbohārenāti.

189. The 'course of the Dispensation' refers to the Noble Truths, or the exposition of the Noble Truths. For the Blessed One's entire Dispensation, his word, is not devoid of truth; thus, it proceeds in the truths. Or, the Dispensation, consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, proceeds in these. Therefore, 'course' (kamo) is so called because one proceeds (kamati) in it. What proceeds? The Dispensation. The course of the Dispensation is 'sāsanakkamo.' Thus, the truths are called the grounds for the proceeding of the Dispensation, and the exposition of them is so called by that designation.

Tathāti taṃsabhāvāva. Avitathāti amusāsabhāvā. Anaññathāti aññākārarahitā. Dukkhadukkhatātaṃnimittatāhi aniṭṭhatā pīḷanaṭṭho, dvidhāpi paridahanaṃ, kilesadāhasamāyogo vā santāpaṭṭhoti ayametesaṃ viseso. Puggalahiṃsanaṃ vā pīḷanaṃ, attano eva tikhiṇabhāvo santāpanaṃ santāpoti.
