Ettha ca pīḷanaṭṭho dukkhassa saraseneva āvibhavanākāro, itare yathākkamaṃ samudayamagganirodhadassanehi āvibhavanākārāti ayaṃ catunnampi viseso. Tatratatrābhinandanavasena byāpetvā ūhanaṃ rāsikaraṇaṃ dukkhanibbattanaṃ āyūhanaṃ, samudayato āgacchatīti vā āyaṃ, dukkhaṃ. Tassa ūhanaṃ pavattanaṃ āyūhanaṃ, sarasāvibhāvanākāro eso. Nidadāti dukkhanti nidānaṃ, “idaṃ taṃ dukkha”nti sampaṭicchāpentaṃ viya samuṭṭhāpetīti attho. Dukkhadassanena cāyaṃ nidānaṭṭho āvi bhavati. Saṃyogapalibodhaṭṭhā nirodhamaggadassanehi, te ca saṃsārasaṃyojanamagganivāraṇākārā daṭṭhabbā.

'True' means it is of that very nature. 'Not false' means it is of a non-deceptive nature. 'Not otherwise' means it is devoid of another mode. The meaning of oppression is undesirability, on account of suffering as suffering and its being a sign; in both ways it is a burning. Or, the meaning of torment is the association with the burning of defilements—this is the distinction among these. Or, oppression is the harming of beings; its own acute nature is tormenting, is torment. And here, the meaning of oppression is the mode of manifestation of suffering by its own essence, while the others are modes of manifestation in due order through the seeing of origination, path, and cessation—this is the distinction among all four. Impulsion (āyūhana) is piling up, making a heap, and producing suffering by pervading through delight in this and that. Or, because it comes from origination, it is 'income' (āyaṃ), which is suffering. Its piling up and continuation is 'impulsion' (āyūhana)—this is its mode of manifestation by its own essence. Because 'it lays down suffering' (nidadāti dukkhaṃ), it is the source (nidāna); the meaning is that it causes suffering to arise as if presenting it for acceptance, saying, 'This is that suffering.' And this meaning of source becomes manifest through the seeing of suffering. The meanings of connection and obstruction become manifest through the seeing of cessation and the path, and these should be seen as the modes of being the fetter of saṃsāra and the prevention of the path, respectively.

Nissaranti [V 0.0051] ettha sattā, sayameva vā nissaṭaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ sabbasaṅkhatehi sabbupadhipaṭinissaggabhāvatoti nissaraṇaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāvena āvibhavanākāro. Vivekāsaṅkhatāmataṭṭhā samudayamaggadukkhadassanāvibhavanākārā, samudayakkhayaappaccayaavināsitā vā. Saṃsārato niggamanaṃ niyyānaṃ. Ayamassa sarasena pakāsanākāro, itare samudayanirodhadukkhadassanehi. Tattha palibodhupacchedavasena nibbānādhigamova nibbānanimittatā [M 0.0051] hetvaṭṭho. Paññāpadhānattā maggassa nibbānadassanaṃ, catusaccadassanaṃ vā dassanaṭṭho. Catusaccadassane kilesadukkhasantāpavūpasamane ca ādhipaccaṃ karonti maggaṅgadhammā sampayuttadhammesūti so maggassa adhipateyyaṭṭhoti. Visesato vā ārammaṇādhipatibhūtā maggaṅgadhammā honti “maggādhipatino dhammā”ti vacanatoti so tesaṃ ākāro adhipateyyaṭṭho. Evamādi āhāti sambandho. Tattha abhisamayaṭṭhoti abhisametabbaṭṭho, abhisamayassa vā visayabhūto attho abhisamayaṭṭho, abhisamayasseva vā pavattiākāro abhisamayaṭṭho, so cettha abhisametabbena pīḷanādinā dassitoti daṭṭhabbo.

Beings escape from this, or it is itself released, disconnected from all conditioned things, because it is the state of relinquishing all acquisitions—this is 'escape' (nissaraṇa). This is its mode of manifestation by its intrinsic nature. The meanings of seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless are modes of manifestation through the seeing of origination, path, and suffering; or through the destruction of origination, being without condition, and indestructibility. Departure from saṃsāra is 'the way out' (niyyāna). This is its mode of elucidation by its essence, while the others are through the seeing of origination, cessation, and suffering. Therein, the attainment of Nibbāna itself, by way of cutting off obstructions, is its being a sign of Nibbāna, which is the meaning of 'cause'. Because wisdom is predominant in the path, the seeing of Nibbāna, or the seeing of the four truths, is the meaning of 'seeing'. In the seeing of the four truths and in the pacification of the torment of defilements and suffering, the path factors exercise dominance over their associated states—thus, this is the meaning of 'dominance' for the path. Or, specifically, because the path factors have become the dominant object, as stated in the phrase 'states for which the path is dominant'—this mode of theirs is the meaning of 'dominance'. Thus he said 'and so on'; this is the connection. Therein, 'the meaning of breakthrough' is the meaning of what is to be broken through; or 'the meaning of breakthrough' is the meaning that is the object of breakthrough; or 'the meaning of breakthrough' is the very mode of occurrence of breakthrough. And here it should be understood as being shown by means of what is to be broken through, such as oppression and so on.

Kucchitaṃ khaṃ dukkhaṃ. “Samāgamo sameta”ntiādīsu kevalassa āgama-saddassa eta-saddassa ca payoge saṃyogatthassa anupalabbhanato saṃ-saddassa ca payoge upalabbhanato “saṃyogaṃ dīpetī”ti āha, evaṃ “uppannaṃ udita”nti etthāpi. Aya-saddo gatiatthasiddho hetu-saddo viya kāraṇaṃ dīpeti attano phalanipphādanena ayati pavattati, eti vā etasmā phalanti ayoti, saṃyoge uppattikāraṇaṃ samudayoti ettha visuṃ payujjamānāpi upasagga-saddā sadhātukaṃ saṃyogatthaṃ uppādatthañca dīpenti kiriyāvisesakattāti veditabbā.

Because it is contemptible and a void, it is suffering. In phrases such as 'samāgamo sameta' (coming together, met), because the meaning of connection is not found when only the word 'āgama' or 'eta' is used, but is found when the word 'saṃ' is used, he said, 'it indicates connection.' Similarly, also in the case of 'uppannaṃ udita' (arisen, appeared). The word 'aya', established in the meaning of motion, indicates a cause, like the word 'hetu', because it goes towards or proceeds to the production of its own result; or because results come from it, it is 'aya'. Thus, 'samudaya' is the cause of arising in connection. Here, it should be understood that even when used separately, these prefix-words, along with the root, indicate the meaning of connection and the meaning of arising, because they are qualifiers of the action.

Abhāvo ettha rodhassāti nirodhoti etena nibbānassa dukkhavivekabhāvaṃ dasseti. Samadhigate tasmiṃ tadadhigamavato puggalassa rodhābhāvo pavattisaṅkhātassa rodhassa paṭipakkhabhūtāya nivattiyā adhigatattāti etasmiñcatthe abhāvo etasmiṃ rodhassāti nirodhoicceva padasamāso. Dukkhābhāvo panettha puggalassa, na nibbānasseva. Anuppādo eva nirodho anuppādanirodho. Āyatibhavādīsu appavatti, na pana bhaṅgoti bhaṅgavācakaṃ nirodha-saddaṃ nivattetvā anuppādavācakaṃ gaṇhāti. Etasmiṃ atthe kāraṇe phalopacāraṃ katvā nirodhapaccayo nirodhoti vutto. Paṭipadā ca hoti puggalassa dukkhanirodhappattiyā. Nanu sā eva dukkhanirodhappattīti tassā eva sā paṭipadāti na yujjatīti? Na, puggalādhigamassa yehi so adhigacchati, tesaṃ [V 0.0052] kāraṇabhūtadhammānañca pattibhāvena paṭipadābhāvena ca vuttattā. Sacchikiriyāsacchikaraṇadhammānaṃ aññattābhāvepi hi puggalasacchikiriyadhammabhāvehi nānattaṃ katvā niddeso [M 0.0052] kato. Atha vā dukkhanirodhappattiyā niṭṭhānaṃ phalanti tassā dukkhanirodhappattiyā paṭipadatā daṭṭhabbā.

'The absence of imprisonment herein is cessation' (ni-rodha); by this he shows Nibbāna's state of being secluded from suffering. When that has been attained, for the person who has attained it, the absence of imprisonment is due to the attainment of cessation, which is the opposite of the imprisonment known as ongoing occurrence. In this sense, the compound word 'nirodha' is 'the absence of imprisonment in this.' The absence of suffering here, however, pertains to the person, not to Nibbāna itself. Non-arising itself is cessation—cessation as non-arising. In future existences and so on, there is non-occurrence, not destruction; thus, rejecting the word 'nirodha' which signifies destruction, he adopts the one signifying non-arising. In this sense, by applying the metaphor of the result to the cause, the condition for cessation is called 'cessation.' And there is the path for a person's attainment of the cessation of suffering. Is it not so that that very attainment of the cessation of suffering is the path for that same attainment? That is not logical. No, because it is spoken of as the path for the person's attainment and as the attainment of those causal phenomena by which one attains. For even though there is no otherness between the act of realizing and the phenomena that are the means of realizing, the explanation is given by making a distinction between the person's act of realizing and the nature of the phenomena. Or else, since the culmination in the attainment of the cessation of suffering is the fruit, the path-nature of that attainment of the cessation of suffering should be understood.

Buddhādayo ariyā paṭivijjhantīti ettha paṭividdhakāle pavattaṃ buddhādivohāraṃ “agamā rājagahaṃ buddho”tiādīsu (su. ni. 410) viya purimakālepi āropetvā “buddhādayo”ti vuttaṃ. Te hi buddhādayo catūhi maggehi paṭivijjhantīti. Ariyapaṭivijjhitabbāni saccāni ariyasaccānīti cettha purimapade uttarapadalopo daṭṭhabbo. Ariyā imanti paṭivijjhitabbaṭṭhena ekattaṃ upanetvā “ima”nti vuttaṃ. Tasmāti tathāgatassa ariyattā tassa saccānīti ariyasaccānīti vuccantīti attho. Tathāgatena hi sayaṃ adhigatattā, teneva pakāsitattā, tato eva ca aññehi adhigamanīyattā tāni tassa hontīti. Ariyabhāvasiddhitopīti ettha ariyasādhakāni saccāni ariyasaccānīti pubbe viya uttarapadalopo daṭṭhabbo. Ariyāni saccānītipīti ettha avitathabhāvena araṇīyattā adhigantabbattā ariyāni, ariyavohāro vā ayaṃ avisaṃvādako avitatharūpo daṭṭhabbo.

Regarding the phrase 'Noble ones, such as Buddhas, penetrate': here the designation 'Buddhas and others', which applies at the time of penetration, is retrospectively applied to an earlier time, as in phrases like 'The Buddha went to Rājagaha.' For those noble ones, such as Buddhas, penetrate by means of the four paths. Because they are truths to be penetrated by noble ones, they are 'noble truths'; here the elision of the latter part of the first word in the compound should be understood. Therefore, because the Tathāgata is noble, his truths are called 'noble truths'—this is the meaning. For they are his because they were realized by himself, revealed by him, and are to be realized by others through him. Also, because they accomplish the noble state, they are 'noble truths'; here, as before, the elision of the latter part of the word in the compound should be understood. Or again, they are 'noble truths' because they are noble, being unerring, to be resorted to, and to be attained. Alternatively, this designation 'noble' should be understood as non-deceptive and true in nature.

Bādhanalakkhaṇanti ettha dukkhadukkhatannimittabhāvo bādhanā, udayabbayapīḷitatā vā. Bhavādīsu jātiādivasena cakkhurogādivasena ca anekadhā dukkhassa pavattanameva puggalassa santāpanaṃ, tadassa kiccaṃ raso. Pavattinivattīsu saṃsāramokkhesu pavatti hutvā gayhatīti pavattipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Pabhavati etasmā dukkhaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ nibbattati purimabhavena pacchimabhavo ghaṭito saṃyutto hutvā pavattatīti pabhavo. “Evampi taṇhānusaye anūhate nibbattatī dukkhamidaṃ punappuna”nti (dha. pa. 338) evaṃ punappunaṃ uppādanaṃ anupacchedakaraṇaṃ. Bhavanissaraṇanivāraṇaṃ palibodho. Rāgakkhayādibhāvena sabbadukkhasantatā santi. Accutirasanti accutisampattikaṃ. Cavanaṃ vā kiccanti tadabhāvaṃ kiccamiva voharitvā accutikiccanti attho. Acavanañca sabhāvassāpariccajanaṃ avikāratā daṭṭhabbā. Pañcakkhandhanimittasuññatāya aviggahaṃ hutvā gayhatīti animittapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Anusayupacchedanavasena saṃsāracārakato niggamanūpāyabhāvo niyyānaṃ. Nimittato pavattato ca cittassa vuṭṭhānaṃ hutvā gayhatīti vuṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

The characteristic of affliction: here, the state of being a sign of suffering as suffering is affliction, or being oppressed by arising and passing away. In states of existence and so on, by way of birth and so forth, and by way of eye-diseases and the like, the very occurrence of suffering in many ways is the tormenting of the individual—that is its function, its essence. In continuation and cessation, in saṃsāra and liberation, it is grasped as continuation; thus, its manifestation is continuation. It is the source (pabhava): from this, suffering arises; in rebirth-linking, the subsequent existence is produced, connected and joined to the previous existence, and thus continues. 'As long as the latent tendency of craving is not eradicated, this suffering arises again and again' (Dhp. 338)—thus, its repeated production is the causing of non-cessation. Obstruction (palibodha) is the prevention of escape from existence. Through the destruction of lust and so on, the entire continuity of suffering is stilled. The deathless (accuti) is the attainment of non-passing away. Or, passing away is its function—by treating its absence as if it were a function, the meaning is the function of non-passing away. And non-passing away should be understood as the non-abandonment of its intrinsic nature, its unalterable state. Because it is empty of the sign of the five aggregates, it is grasped as ungraspable; thus, its manifestation is the signless. By way of cutting off the latent tendencies, it is the state of being the means of exit from the wandering in saṃsāra—this is the escape. The mind's emergence from the sign and from continuation is grasped; thus, its manifestation is emergence.

Asuvaṇṇādi [M 0.0053][V 0.0053] suvaṇṇādi viya dissamānaṃ māyāti vatthusabbhāvā tassā viparītatā vuttā. Udakaṃ viya dissamānā pana marīci upagatānaṃ tucchā hoti, vatthumattampi tassā na dissatīti visaṃvādikā vuttā. Marīcimāyāattānaṃ vipakkho bhāvo tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvo. Ariyañāṇassāti avitathagāhakassa ñāṇassa, tena paṭivedhapaccavekkhaṇāni gayhanti, tesañca gocarabhāvo paṭivijjhitabbatāārammaṇabhāvo ca daṭṭhabbo. Aggilakkhaṇaṃ uṇhattaṃ. Tañhi katthaci kaṭṭhādiupādānabhedepi visaṃvādakaṃ viparītaṃ abhūtaṃ vā kadāci na hoti. “Byādhidhammā jarādhammā, atho maraṇadhammino”ti (a. ni. 3.39; 5.57) ettha vuttā jātiādikā lokapakati. Manussānaṃ uddhaṃ dīghatā, ekaccānaṃ tiracchānānaṃ tiriyaṃ dīghatā, vuddhiniṭṭhaṃ pattānaṃ puna avaḍḍhanaṃ evamādikā cāti vadanti. Tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvesu pacchimo tathatā, paṭhamo avitathatā, majjhimo anaññathatāti ayametesaṃ viseso.

What is not gold, etc., appearing as if it were gold, etc., is illusion (māyā); because its substance is unreal, its contrariness is stated. But a mirage, appearing like water, is empty for those who approach it; not even a mere substance is seen in it, thus it is called deceptive. The state opposite to that of mirages and illusions is the state of being true, not contrary, and real. 'Of the noble knowledge' means of the knowledge that grasps what is not unreal. By that, penetration and reflection are grasped; and their sphere should be seen as the state of being what is to be penetrated and the state of being an object. The characteristic of fire is heat. For that is never deceptive, contrary, or unreal, even when there is a difference in its fuel, such as wood. 'Subject to sickness, subject to aging, and also subject to death' (AN 3.39; 5.57)—here, birth and so forth are spoken of as the natural condition of the world. They say that for humans, length is upwards; for some animals, length is horizontal; and for those who have reached the limit of growth, there is no further increase, and so on. Among the states of being true, not contrary, and real, the last is suchness (tathatā), the first is non-unreality (avitathatā), and the middle is non-otherness (anaññathatā)—this is the distinction among them.

Dukkhā aññaṃ na bādhakanti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu taṇhāpi jāti viya dukkhanimittatāya bādhikāti? Na, bādhakapabhavabhāvena visuṃ gahitattā. Jātiādīnaṃ viya vā dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvo dukkhadukkhatā ca bādhakatā, na dukkhassa pabhavakatāti natthi taṇhāya pabhavakabhāvena gahitāya bādhakattappasaṅgo. Tenāha “dukkhā aññaṃ na bādhaka”nti. Bādhakattaniyāmenāti dukkhaṃ bādhakameva, dukkhameva bādhakanti evaṃ dvidhāpi bādhakattāvadhāraṇenāti attho. Taṃ vinā nāññatoti satipi avasesakilesaavasesākusalasāsavakusalamūlāvasesasāsavakusaladhammānaṃ dukkhahetubhāve na taṇhāya vinā tesaṃ dukkhahetubhāvo atthi, tehi pana vināpi taṇhāya dukkhahetubhāvo atthi kusalehi vinā akusalehi, rūpāvacarādīhi vinā kāmāvacarādīhi ca taṇhāya dukkhanibbattakattā. Tacchaniyyānabhāvattāti dvidhāpi niyamena taccho niyyānabhāvo etassa, na micchāmaggassa viya viparītatāya, lokiyamaggassa viya vā anekantikatāya atacchoti tacchaniyyānabhāvo, maggo. Tassa bhāvo tacchaniyyānabhāvattaṃ, tasmā tacchaniyyānabhāvattā. Sabbattha dvidhāpi niyamena tacchāviparītabhūtabhāvo vuttoti āha “iti tacchāvipallāsā”tiādi.

Why is it said, 'Nothing other than suffering is an afflicter'? Is it not that craving also, like birth, is an afflicter because it is a cause of suffering? No, because it is taken separately as the origin of what afflicts. Or, like birth and so on, the state of being the basis of suffering and suffering-as-suffering is what constitutes being an afflicter, not the state of being the origin of suffering. Therefore, there is no occasion for craving, taken as the origin, to be an afflicter. Hence, it is said, 'Nothing other than suffering is an afflicter.' 'By the rule of being an afflicter' means: suffering is indeed the afflicter, and only suffering is the afflicter; thus, the meaning is by the twofold determination of what it is to be an afflicter. 'Without that, there is no other': Even though the remaining defilements, remaining unwholesome states, wholesome roots with taints, and remaining wholesome states with taints are causes of suffering, without craving, they do not have the nature of being a cause of suffering. Yet, even without them, craving has the nature of being a cause of suffering, because craving produces suffering without wholesome states by means of unwholesome states, and without form-sphere states by means of sense-sphere states. 'Because of its nature as the true escape': its nature is definitively the true escape in two ways; it is not untrue like the wrong path, due to perversion, nor like the worldly path, due to being inconclusive. Thus, it is the true escape, the path. Its state is the nature of being the true escape; therefore, because of its nature as the true escape. Everywhere, the state of being true and unperverted is stated with a twofold determination. Hence, it is stated, 'Thus, the true non-perversion,' and so on.

Sacca-saddassa [M 0.0054] sambhavantānaṃ atthānaṃ uddharaṇaṃ, sambhavante vā atthe vatvā adhippetatthassa uddharaṇaṃ atthuddhāro. Viratisacceti musāvādaviratiyaṃ. Na hi aññaviratīsu sacca-saddo niruḷhoti. “Idameva saccaṃ, moghamañña”nti gahitā diṭṭhi diṭṭhisaccaṃ. “Amosadhammaṃ nibbānaṃ[V 0.0054], tadariyā saccato vidū”ti (su. ni. 763) amosadhammattā nibbānaṃ paramatthasaccaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa pana taṃsampāpakassa ca maggassa pajānanā paṭivedho avivādakāraṇanti dvayampi “ekañhi saccaṃ na dutiyamatthi, yasmiṃ pajā no vivade pajāna”nti (su. ni. 890; mahāni. 119) missā gāthāya saccanti vuttaṃ.

The extraction of the possible meanings of the word 'truth' (sacca), or, having stated the possible meanings, the extraction of the intended meaning, is the 'extraction of meaning' (atthuddhāro). 'Truth of abstinence' (viratisacca) refers to abstinence from false speech, for the word 'truth' is not established in other abstinences. The view grasped as 'This alone is true, all else is futile' is 'truth of view' (diṭṭhisacca). Nibbāna is called the ultimate truth because of its non-deceptive nature, as in, 'Nibbāna is the non-deceptive Dhamma, which the noble ones know as truth' (su. ni. 763). However, both the penetration of it and the path that leads to its attainment, being a cause of non-dispute, are also called 'truth,' as stated in the composite verse: 'For truth is one, there is no second, about which one who knows might dispute with others who know' (su. ni. 890; mahāni. 119).

Netaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti āgaccheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti etena jātiādīnaṃ dukkhaariyasaccabhāve aviparītataṃ dasseti, aññaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti āgaccheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatīti iminā dukkhaariyasaccabhāvassa jātiādīsu niyatataṃ. Sacepi kathañci koci evaṃcitto āgaccheyya, paññāpane pana sahadhammena paññāpane attano vādassa ca paññāpane samattho natthīti dassetuṃ “ahametaṃ…pe… paññāpessāmīti āgaccheyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Jātiādīnaṃ anaññathatā aññassa ca tathābhūtassa abhāvoyevettha ṭhānābhāvo. Sacepi koci āgaccheyya, āgacchatu, ṭhānaṃ pana natthīti ayamettha suttattho. Esa nayo dutiyasuttepi. Tattha pana sampattatā paccakkhatā ca paṭhamatā, taṃnimittatā dutiyatā, tadupasamatā tatiyatā, taṃsampāpakatā catutthatāti daṭṭhabbā.

By the phrase, 'One might come [and say], 'This is not the noble truth of suffering,'—this is not possible,' he shows the unperverted nature of birth and so on as the noble truth of suffering. By the phrase, 'One might come [and say], 'Another is the noble truth of suffering,'—this is not possible,' he demonstrates the fixed nature of the noble truth of suffering in birth and so on. To show that even if someone were somehow to come with such a thought, they would not be capable of establishing it with a valid argument, nor of establishing their own thesis, it is said: 'One might come [thinking], 'I will establish this...'; this is not possible.' The impossibility here is precisely the unalterable nature of birth and so on, and the absence of any other such thing. Even if someone were to come [with such a claim], let them come, but there is no basis for it—this is the meaning of the sutta here. This same method applies to the second sutta as well. There, however, it should be understood that attainment and direct experience are the first, its cause is the second, its pacification is the third, and that which leads to its attainment is the fourth.

Nibbutikāmena parijānanādīhi aññaṃ kiñci kiccaṃ kātabbaṃ natthi, dhammañāṇakiccaṃ vā ito aññaṃ natthi, pariññeyyādīni ca etapparamānevāti cattāreva vuttāni. Taṇhāya ādīnavadassāvīnaṃ vasena “taṇhāvatthuādīnaṃ etaṃparamatāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā ālaye pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhāte, sakalavatthukāmasaṅkhāte, bhavattayasaṅkhāte vā dukkhe dosadassāvīnaṃ vasena “ālayādīnaṃ etaṃparamatāyā”ti vuttaṃ.

For one desiring quenching, there is no other task to be done apart from full understanding and so on; or, there is no other task for the knowledge of the Dhamma than this. And since the things to be fully understood and so on have this as their highest limit, only the four have been stated. For those who see the danger in craving, it is said, 'because this is the highest limit for the objects of craving and so on.' Similarly, for those who see the fault in suffering—designated as attachment (ālaya), which is the five strands of sensual pleasure; or as all objects of sensual pleasure; or as the three realms of existence—it is said, 'because this is the highest limit for attachment and so on.'

Sahetukena dukkhenāti etena dukkhassa abbocchinnatādassanena atisaṃvegavatthutaṃ dasseti.

By the phrase 'with suffering that has a cause,' he shows that it is a basis for extreme spiritual urgency by revealing the uninterrupted nature of suffering.

Na [M 0.0055] paṭivedhañāṇaṃ viya sakideva bujjhati, atha kho anu anu bujjhanato anubodho, anussavākāraparivitakkadiṭṭhinijjhānakkhantianugato vā bodho anubodho. Na hi so paccakkhato bujjhati, anussavādivasena pana kappetvā gaṇhātīti. Kiccatoti parijānanādito. Taṃkiccakaraṇeneva hi tāni tassa pākaṭāni. Vivaṭṭānupassanāya hi saṅkhārehi patilīyamānamānasassa uppajjamānaṃ maggañāṇaṃ visaṅkhāraṃ dukkhanissaraṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā [V 0.0055] dukkhaṃ paricchindati, dukkhagatañca taṇhaṃ pajahati, nirodhañca phusati ādicco viya pabhāya, sammāsaṅkappādīhi saha uppannaṃ taṃ maggaṃ bhāveti, na ca saṅkhāre amuñcitvā pavattamānena ñāṇena etaṃ sabbaṃ sakkā kātuṃ nimittapavattehi avuṭṭhitattā, tasmā etāni kiccāni karontaṃ taṃ ñāṇaṃ dukkhādīni vibhāveti tattha sammohanivattanenāti “cattāripi saccāni passatī”ti vuttaṃ.

It does not awaken all at once like the knowledge of penetration; rather, there is gradual awakening (`anubodha`) from awakening little by little. Or, awakening (`bodha`) accompanied by tradition, reasoning, reflection, and contemplative acceptance of a view is gradual awakening. For it does not awaken directly, but grasps by inferring through tradition and so on. By 'function' (`kicca`) is meant from full understanding onwards. For by performing its tasks, these truths become clear to it. Through the contemplation of turning away, when the mind is withdrawing from formations, the arising path-knowledge, having taken the unformed—the escape from suffering—as its object, fully understands suffering, abandons craving related to suffering, and realizes cessation like the sun with its light. This path, arisen together with right thought and other factors, is developed. But it is not possible to accomplish all this with knowledge operating without releasing the formations, because it has not emerged from the occurrence of their sign. Therefore, while performing these tasks, that knowledge clarifies suffering and so forth by dispelling delusion about them. Hence, it is said, 'one sees all four truths.'

Dukkhasamudayampi so passatīti kālantaradassanaṃ sandhāya vuttanti ce? Na, “yo nu kho, āvuso, dukkhaṃ passati, dukkhasamudayampi so passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.1100) ekadassino aññattayadassitāvicāraṇāya tassā sādhanatthaṃ gavaṃpatittherena imassa suttassa āharitattā paccekañca saccesu dissamānesu aññattayadassanassa yojitattā. Aññathā anupubbābhisamaye purimadiṭṭhassa pacchā adassanato samudayādidassino dukkhādidassanatā na yojetabbā siyāti. Suddhasaṅkhārapuñjamattadassanato sakkāyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhānaṃ nivāreti. “Lokasamudayaṃ kho, kaccāna, yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya passato yā loke natthitā, sā na hotī”ti vacanato samudayadassanaṃ hetuphalappabandhāvicchedadassanavasena ucchedadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhānaṃ nivatteti. “Lokanirodhaṃ kho…pe… passato yā loke atthitā, sā na hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.15) vacanato nirodhadassanaṃ hetunirodhā phalanirodhadassanavasena sassatadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhānaṃ nivāreti. Attakārassa paccakkhadassanato maggadassanena “natthi attakāre, natthi parakāre, natthi purisakāre”tiādikaṃ (dī. ni. 1.168) akiriyadiṭṭhipariyuṭṭhānaṃ pajahati. “Natthi hetu, natthi paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya, ahetū appaccayā sattā saṃkilissanti. Natthi hetu…pe… visuddhiyā, ahetū appaccayā sattā visujjhantī”tiādikā ahetukadiṭṭhi ca idha akiriyadiṭṭhiggahaṇena gahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Sāpi hi visuddhimaggadassanena pahīyatīti.

If it is asked, 'Does one also see the origin of suffering? Is this said with reference to seeing at a later time?' No, because the Elder Gavampati cited this discourse to establish, by examining the showing of the threefold difference for one who sees a single thing, that 'one who sees suffering, friend, also sees the origin of suffering,' and so on (SN 5.1100); and because the seeing of the threefold difference was applied to each of the truths as they are seen. Otherwise, in a gradual realization, if what was seen first is not seen later, the seeing of the origin and so on could not be connected with the seeing of suffering and so on. By seeing a mere mass of pure formations, one prevents the obsession of the identity view. From the statement, 'When, Kaccāna, one sees with right wisdom the arising of the world as it really is, the notion of non-existence in the world does not arise,' the seeing of the origin, by way of seeing the unbroken continuity of cause and effect, prevents the obsession of the annihilation view. From the statement, 'When one sees the cessation of the world… as it really is, the notion of existence in the world does not arise,' the seeing of cessation, by way of seeing the cessation of the cause bringing about the cessation of the effect, prevents the obsession of the eternalist view. By directly seeing the agent, the seeing of the path abandons the obsession of the inaction view, such as 'There is no agent, no other-agent, no personal action' (DN 1.168). The view of non-causality, such as 'There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause or condition. There is no cause… for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause or condition,' should be understood as included here under the inaction view. For that too is abandoned by seeing the path to purification.

Dukkhañāṇaṃ [M 0.0056] samudayaphalassa dukkhassa adhuvādibhāvaṃ passatīti phale vippaṭipattiṃ nivatteti. “Issaro lokaṃ pavatteti nivatteti cā”ti issarakāraṇino vadanti, padhānato āvi bhavati, tattheva ca patilīyatīti padhānakāraṇino. “Kālavaseneva pavattati nivattati cā”ti kālavādino. “Sabhāveneva sambhoti vibhoti cā”ti sabhāvavādino. Ādi-saddena aṇūhi loko pavattati, sabbaṃ pubbekatahetūti evamādi akāraṇapariggaho daṭṭhabbo. Rāmudakāḷārādīnaṃ viya arūpaloke, nigaṇṭhādīnaṃ viya lokathupikāya apavaggo mokkhoti gahaṇaṃ[V 0.0056]. Ādi-saddena padhānassa appavatti, guṇaviyuttassa attano sakattani avaṭṭhānaṃ, brahmunā salokatā, diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādāti evamādiggahaṇañca daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha guṇaviyuttassāti buddhisukhadukkhaicchādosapayattadhammādhammasaṅkhārehi navahi attaguṇehi vippayuttassāti kaṇādabhakkhavādo. Indriyatappanaputtamukhadassanādīhi vinā apavaggo natthīti gahetvā tathāpavattanaṃ kāmasukhallikānuyogo.

The knowledge of suffering, by seeing the impermanent nature and so on of suffering which is the fruit of the origin, dispels the wrong view about the fruit. "A Lord creates and dissolves the world," so say those who hold a Lord to be the cause. "From primal matter it becomes manifest, and right there it is reabsorbed," so say those who hold primal matter to be the cause. "By the force of time alone it arises and ceases," so say the proponents of time. "By its own nature alone it comes to be and perishes," so say the proponents of its own nature. By the word "etc.," the grasping of a non-cause should be understood, such as the views that the world proceeds from atoms, or that everything is due to past deeds. Also to be understood is the grasping of liberation as an escape in the formless world, like that of Udaka Rāmaputta and Āḷāra Kālāma, or at the summit of the world, like that of the Nigaṇṭhas. By the word "etc.," should also be understood the grasping of such views as: the non-activity of primal matter; the subsistence of the self in its own selfhood, devoid of qualities; co-existence with Brahmā; and the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life. Here, "devoid of qualities" refers to being dissociated from the nine qualities of the self—intelligence, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, virtue, vice, and dispositions—which is the doctrine of Kaṇāda. Grasping that "without the gratification of the senses, seeing the faces of one's children, etc., there is no liberation," and acting accordingly, is the indulgence in sensual pleasures.

Ajjhattikabāhiresu dvādasasu āyatanesu kāmabhavavibhavataṇhāvasena dvādasa tikā chattiṃsa taṇhāvicaritāni. Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅge vā āgatanayena kālavibhāgaṃ anāmasitvā vuttāni. Vīmaṃsiddhipādādayo bodhipakkhiyā kiccanānattena vuttā, atthato ekattā sammādiṭṭhimukhena tattha antogadhā. Tayo nekkhammavitakkādayoti lokiyakkhaṇe alobhamettākaruṇāsampayogavasena bhinnā maggakkhaṇe lobhabyāpādavihiṃsāsamucchedavasena tayoti ekopi vutto. Esa nayo sammāvācādīsu. Appicchatāsantuṭṭhitānaṃ pana bhāve sammāājīvasambhavato tena tesaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Bhavantarepi jīvitahetupi ariyehi avītikkamanīyattā ariyakantānaṃ sammāvācādisīlānaṃ gahaṇena yena saddhāhatthena tāni pariggahetabbāni, so saddhāhattho gahitoyeva hotīti tato anaññāni saddhindriyasaddhābalāni tattha antogadhāni honti. Tesaṃ atthitāyāti saddhindriyasaddhābalachandiddhipādānaṃ atthitāya sīlassa atthibhāvato tividhenapi sīlena te tayopi gahitāti tattha antogadhā. Cittasamādhīti cittiddhipādaṃ vadati. “Cittaṃ paññañca bhāvaya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.23, 192) hi cittamukhena samādhi [M 0.0057] vuttoti samādhimukhena cittampi vattabbataṃ arahati. Cittiddhipādabhāvanāya pana samādhipi adhimatto hotīti vīmaṃsiddhipādādivacanaṃ viya cittiddhipādavacanaṃ avatvā idha “cittasamādhī”ti vuttaṃ. “Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.359; saṃ. ni. 5.376; a. ni. 3.96; 11.12) vacanato samādhiupakārā pītipassaddhiyo, tasmā samādhiggahaṇena gahitā, upekkhā pana samādhiupakārakato taṃsadisakiccato ca, tasmā sammāsamādhivasena etesaṃ antogadhatā daṭṭhabbā.

In the twelve internal and external sense bases, there are thirty-six courses of craving, as twelve triads based on craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. Or, they are stated without touching upon the division by time, in accordance with the method that comes in the Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga. The wings to awakening, such as the bases for spiritual power beginning with discrimination, are spoken of with a diversity of function, but in meaning they are one, included therein by way of right view. The three thoughts of renunciation, etc., are distinct at the mundane moment through their association with non-greed, loving-kindness, and compassion, but at the path moment, through the eradication of greed, ill will, and cruelty, they are also spoken of as one. The same principle applies to right speech, etc. But since right livelihood arises in one who has few wishes and is content, their inclusion should be understood through that. Because right speech and the other virtues, which are dear to the noble ones, are not to be transgressed by them even in another existence or for the sake of life, by grasping them with the hand of faith, that hand of faith is itself grasped; thus the faith faculty and the faith power, not being other than that, are included therein. Because of their existence—that is, because of the existence of the faith faculty, the faith power, and the basis for spiritual power consisting of zeal—virtue exists; thus, by the threefold virtue, those three are grasped and are included therein. "Concentration of mind" refers to the basis for spiritual power consisting of mind. For it is said, "Develop mind and wisdom," where concentration is spoken of by way of the mind; thus, the mind also deserves to be spoken of by way of concentration. But since concentration becomes pre-eminent in the development of the basis for spiritual power consisting of mind, instead of saying "the basis for spiritual power consisting of mind," as one might say "the basis for spiritual power consisting of discrimination," here it is called "concentration of mind." Based on the statement, "For one with a joyful mind, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, one feels pleasure; for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated," joy and tranquility are assistants to concentration; therefore, they are included by the term concentration. Equanimity, however, is included because it assists concentration and because its function is similar. Therefore, their inclusion by way of right concentration should be understood.

Bhāro viya vighātakattā. Dubbhikkhamiva bādhakattā. “Nibbānaparamaṃ sukha”nti (ma. ni. 2.215, 217; dha. pa. 203, 204) sukhabhāvato [V 0.0057] subhikkhamiva. Aniṭṭhabhāvato sāsaṅkasappaṭibhayato ca dukkhaṃ verīvisarukkhabhayaorimatīrūpamaṃ.

Like a burden, because it is crushing. Like a famine, because it is afflicting. "Nibbāna is the supreme happiness" (MN 75; Dhp 203–204); because of its nature as happiness, it is like a time of abundance. Because it is undesirable and because it is perilous and fearful, suffering is comparable to an enemy, a poisonous tree, and the fearful near bank.

Tathatthenāti tathasabhāvena, pariññeyyabhāvenāti attho. Etena ariyasaccadvayaṃ siyā dukkhaṃ, na ariyasaccaṃ, siyā ariyasaccaṃ, na dukkhanti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Ariyasacca-saddaparā hi dukkhādisaddā pariññeyyādibhāvaṃ vadanti. Teneva ariyasacca-saddānapekkhaṃ dukkha-saddaṃ sandhāya maggasampayuttasāmaññaphaladhammānaṃ ādipadasaṅgaho vutto, tadapekkhaṃ sandhāya catutthapadasaṅgaho. Samudayādīsu avasesakilesādayo samudayo, na ariyasaccaṃ, saṅkhāranirodho nirodhasamāpatti ca nirodho, na ariyasaccaṃ, ariyamaggato aññāni maggaṅgāni maggo, na ariyasaccanti iminā nayena yojanā kātabbā. Dukkhaṃ vedanīyampi santaṃ vedakarahitaṃ, kevalaṃ pana tasmiṃ attano paccayehi pavattamāne dukkhaṃ vedetīti vohāramattaṃ hoti. Evaṃ itaresupi.

"In its suchness" means in its real nature; the meaning is, in its being something to be fully understood. By this he shows the following meaning regarding the pair of terms, noble truth and suffering: something may be suffering but not a noble truth, and something may be a noble truth but not suffering. For the words "suffering," etc., when qualified by the word "noble truth," speak of the state of being something to be fully understood, and so on. For that reason, with reference to the word "suffering" irrespective of the word "noble truth," the inclusion by the initial term is stated for states associated with the path and for the general fruits; with reference to it as a noble truth, the inclusion by the fourth term is stated. Regarding the origin, etc.: the remaining defilements and so on are an origin but not a noble truth; the cessation of formations and the attainment of cessation are cessation but not a noble truth; path factors other than the noble path are the path but not a noble truth. The application should be made in this way. Although suffering is felt, it is devoid of a feeler; it is merely a conventional expression that "one feels suffering" when it is occurring due to its own conditions. So too with the others.

Kiriyāva vijjatīti samudayameva vadati, tassa vā dukkhapaccayabhāvaṃ. Maggo atthīti vattabbe “maggamatthī”ti okārassa abhāvo katoti daṭṭhabbo. Gamakoti gantā. Sāsavatā asubhatāti katvā nirodhamaggā subhā eva. Dukkhādīnaṃ pariyāyena samudayādibhāvo ca atthi, na pana nirodhabhāvo, nirodhassa vā dukkhādibhāvoti na aññamaññasamaṅgitāti āha “nirodhasuññāni vā”tiādi. Samudaye dukkhassābhāvatoti ponobbhavikāya taṇhāya punabbhavassa abhāvato. Yathā vā pakativādīnaṃ vikārāvibhāvato pubbe paṭippalīnā ca pakatibhāveneva tiṭṭhanti, na evaṃ [M 0.0058] samudayasampayuttampi dukkhaṃ samudayabhāvena tiṭṭhatīti āha “samudaye dukkhassābhāvato”ti. Yathā avibhattehi vikārehi mahantā visesindriyabhūtavisesehi pakatibhāveneva ṭhitehi pakati sagabbhā pakativādīnaṃ, evaṃ na phalena sagabbho hetūti attho. Dukkhasamudayānaṃ nirodhamaggānañca asamavāyāti etaṃ vivaranto āha “na hetusamavetaṃ hetuphala”ntiādi. Tattha idha tantūsu paṭo, kapālesu ghaṭo, biraṇesu kaṭo, dvīsu aṇūsu dviaṇukantiādinā idha buddhivohārajanako avisuṃ siddhānaṃ sambandho samavāyo, tena samavāyena kāraṇesu dvīsu aṇūsu dviaṇukaṃ phalaṃ samavetaṃ ekībhūtamiva sambandhaṃ, tīsu aṇūsu tiaṇukanti evaṃ mahāpathavimahāudakamahāaggimahāvātakkhandhapariyantaṃ phalaṃ attano kāraṇesu samavetanti samavāyavādino vadanti. Evaṃ pana vadantehi aparimāṇesu kāraṇesu mahāparimāṇaṃ [V 0.0058] ekaṃ phalaṃ samavetaṃ attano antogadhehi kāraṇehi sagabbhaṃ asuññanti vuttaṃ hoti, evamidha samavāyābhāvā phale hetu natthīti hetusuññaṃ phalanti attho.

"There is only action"—thus he speaks of the origin itself, or of its being a condition for suffering. When it should be said maggo atthi ("the path exists"), it should be understood that the vowel 'o' has been elided to make maggamatthi. A gamaka is a goer. Because of being with cankers and being foul, cessation and the path are indeed beautiful. Suffering, etc., can be synonymous with the origin, etc., but not with cessation, nor can cessation be synonymous with suffering, etc. Because they are not mutually connected, he says, "or they are void of cessation," etc. "Because of the absence of suffering in the origin" means that in the craving that leads to renewed existence, there is an absence of that renewed existence. Or, just as for the proponents of primal nature, transformations, having been reabsorbed before their manifestation, subsist in the state of primal nature, it is not the case that suffering associated with the origin subsists in the state of the origin. Thus he says, "because of the absence of suffering in the origin." Just as for the proponents of primal nature, primal nature is "pregnant" with unmanifested transformations, so too the cause is not "pregnant" with the effect; this is the meaning. Explaining that suffering and the origin, and cessation and the path, are not in a relationship of inherence, he says, "the effect does not inhere in the cause," etc. Here, in the Vaiśeṣika system, inherence is the relation of things established as inseparable—such as cloth in threads, a pot in potsherds, a mat in rushes, a dyad in two atoms—which generates the intellectual convention of unity. By that relation of inherence, the effect, such as a dyad, inheres in its causes, the two atoms, connected as if unified. Similarly, a triad in three atoms, and so on up to the great earth, great water, great fire, and great wind, the effect inheres in its causes—so say the proponents of inherence. But when they speak thus, it is said that a single effect of great magnitude inheres in innumerable causes, and being "pregnant" with its inherent causes, it is not void. Thus here, in Buddhism, because of the absence of inherence, the cause is not in the effect; the meaning is that the effect is void of the cause.

Pavattibhāvatoti saṃsārassa pavattibhāvato. Catuāhārabhedatoti iminā cattāro āhārabhede tehi bhinne tappaccayadhammabhede ca saṅgaṇhāti. Rūpābhinandanādibhedo rūpādikhandhavasena, ārammaṇavasena vā. Upādānehi upādīyatīti upādi, upādānakkhandhapañcakaṃ. Nibbānañca taṃnissaraṇabhūtaṃ tassa vūpasamo taṃsantīti katvā tassa yāva pacchimaṃ cittaṃ, tāva sesataṃ, tato parañca anavasesataṃ upādāya “saupādisesanibbānadhātu anupādisesanibbānadhātū”ti dvidhā voharīyatīti. “Sammādiṭṭhi sammāsaṅkappo vipassanā, itare samatho”ti vadanti. Sīlampi hi samathassa upakārakattā samathaggahaṇena gayhatīti tesaṃ adhippāyo. Atha vā yānadvayavasena laddho maggo samatho vipassanāti āgamanavasena vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Sappadesattāti sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ ekadesattāti attho. Sīlakkhandhādayo hi sabbalokiyalokuttarasīlādisaṅgāhakā, ariyamaggo lokuttaroyevāti tadekadeso hoti.

"Because of its nature as occurrence" means because of the occurrence of saṃsāra. "By the division of the four nutriments": by this he includes the divisions of the four nutriments, the things divided by them, and the divisions of the phenomena conditioned by them. The division by delight in form, etc., is by way of the aggregates of form, etc., or by way of the object. That which is clung to by the clingings is the "basis of clinging," that is, the five aggregates subject to clinging. And Nibbāna is the escape from that, its appeasement, its peace. Because of this, with respect to its having a remainder as long as the last consciousness exists, and its being without remainder after that, it is designated in two ways as "the Nibbāna element with residue remaining" and "the Nibbāna element without residue remaining." Some say: "Right view and right thought are insight; the others are serenity." Their intention is that since virtue is an assistant to serenity, it is included by the term serenity. Or, it should be understood that "the path attained by way of the two vehicles is serenity and insight" is said according to the textual tradition. "Because it is partial" means because it is a part of the aggregates of virtue, etc. For the aggregates of virtue, etc., are inclusive of all mundane and supramundane virtue, etc., whereas the noble path is only supramundane; thus it is a part of them.

Onatasahāyo viya vāyāmo paggahakiccasāmaññato. Aṃsakūṭaṃ datvā ṭhitasahāyo viya sati apilāpanavasena niccalabhāvakaraṇasāmaññato. Sajātitoti savitakkasavicārādibhedesu samānāya samādhijātiyāti [M 0.0059] attho. Kiriyatoti samādhianurūpakiriyato. Tato eva hi “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā samādhinimittā, cattāro sammappadhānā samādhiparikkhārā”ti (ma. ni. 1.462) sativāyāmānaṃ samādhissa nimittaparikkhārabhāvo vuttoti.

Like a friend who helps carry the burden, effort is similar in its function of upholding. Like a steadfast friend giving support by the shoulder, mindfulness, by preventing distraction, is similar in its function of making it steady. "Of the same kind" means of the same kind of concentration, in divisions such as with initial and sustained thought, and so forth. "In action" means acting in accordance with concentration. For it is said: 'The four foundations of mindfulness are the signs for concentration, the four right efforts are the requisites for concentration' (MN 1.462). Thus, the role of mindfulness and effort as signs and requisites for concentration is stated.

Ākoṭentena viyāti “aniccaṃ anicca”ntiādinā paññāsadisena kiccena samantato ākoṭentena viya “aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena, dukkhaṃ bhayaṭṭhenā”tiādinā parivattantena viya ca ādāya ūhitvā dinnameva paññā paṭivijjhati. Dvinnaṃ samānakālattepi paccayabhāvena saṅkappassa purimakālassa viya niddeso kato. Sajātitoti “dukkhe ñāṇa”ntiādīsu samānāya paññājātiyā. Kiriyatoti ettha paññāsadisakiccaṃ kiriyāti vuttaṃ, pubbe pana samādhiupakārakaṃ tadanurūpaṃ kiccanti ayamettha viseso. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññeyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.46) vacanato [V 0.0059] cattāripi abhimukhaṃ paccakkhato ñātabbāni, abhivisiṭṭhena vā ñāṇena ñātabbānīti abhiññeyyāni.

As if striking all around with a function similar to wisdom, such as 'impermanent, impermanent,' and as if turning it over with phrases like 'impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of fear,' and so forth, wisdom penetrates what is given, having taken it up and considered it. Though the two occur simultaneously, the indication is made as if thought (saṅkappa) comes first, due to its being a condition. 'Of the same kind' means of the same kind of wisdom as in phrases like 'knowledge of suffering,' and so forth. As for 'in action,' here a function similar to wisdom is called 'action,' but previously it was said to be a function in accordance with and helpful to concentration—this is the distinction here. From the statement, 'Monks, all is to be fully known' (SN 4.46), the four are to be known directly, face to face, or known by a more distinguished knowledge—thus, they are to be fully known.

Durabhisambhavataranti abhisambhavituṃ sādhetuṃ asakkuṇeyyataraṃ, sattivighātena duradhigamanti attho. Bādhakapabhavasantiniyyānalakkhaṇehi vavatthānaṃ salakkhaṇavavatthānaṃ. Duravagāhatthena gambhīrattāti oḷārikā dukkhasamudayā. Tiracchānagatānampi hi dukkhaṃ āhārādīsu ca abhilāso pākaṭo, pīḷanādiāyūhanādivasena pana “idaṃ dukkhaṃ, idamassa kāraṇa”nti yāthāvato ogāhituṃ asakkuṇeyyattā gambhīrā, saṇhasukhumadhammattā nirodhamaggā sabhāvato eva gambhīrattā duravagāhā, teneva uppanne magge natthi nirodhamaggānaṃ yāthāvato anavagāhoti. Nibbānampi maggena adhigantabbattā tassa phalanti apadissatīti āha “phalāpadesato”ti. Vuttañhi “dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 719). Maggopi nirodhassa sampāpakabhāvato hetūti apadissatīti āha “hetuapadesato”ti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 719). Iti vijaññāti iti-saddena vijānanakkamaṃ dasseti. Evaṃ pakārehīti evaṃ-saddena vijānanakāraṇabhūte naye.

Harder to fully comprehend means harder to achieve or accomplish; that is, hard to penetrate due to the obstruction of faculties. The distinguishing of intrinsic characteristics is by means of the characteristics of oppression, origination, tranquility, and exit. Because of their depth, they are hard to delve into—suffering and its origin are coarse. For even in the case of animals, suffering and desire for food and so forth are evident, but because of their inability to fully grasp 'this is suffering, this is its cause' by way of affliction, accumulation, and so on, these truths are profound. Cessation and the path, due to their nature as subtle and refined phenomena, are hard to penetrate because they are profound by their very nature. For that very reason, when the path has arisen, there is no non-penetration of cessation and the path as they truly are. Nibbāna, being attainable by the path, is designated as its fruit; hence, it is said, 'by designation as fruit.' For it is said: 'Knowledge of the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning' (Vibh. 719). The path, too, being the cause for accomplishing cessation, is designated as the cause; hence, it is said, 'by designation as cause.' And this is also stated: 'Knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of phenomena' (Vibh. 719). 'Thus one should understand'—with the word 'thus,' it shows the manner of understanding. 'By such means'—with the word 'such,' it refers to the methods that are the reasons for understanding.

Uddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the outline is concluded.

1. Dukkhasaccaniddeso

1. The Exposition of the Truth of Suffering

Jātiniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of Birth

190. Tattha [M 0.0060] …pe… ayaṃ mātikāti niddesavāraādimhi vutte jātiādiniddese tesaṃ jātiādīnaṃ niddesavasena dukkhassa ariyasaccassa kathanatthāya, tesu vā jātiādīsu tesañca dukkhaṭṭhe veditabbe jātiādīnaṃ niddesavasena dukkhassa ariyasaccassa kathanatthāya dukkhadukkhantiādikā dukkhamātikā veditabbāti attho. Atha vā tatthāti tasmiṃ niddesavāre. “Jātipi dukkhā…pe… saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti ayaṃ dukkhassa ariyasaccassa kathanatthāya mātikāti yathādassitassa jātiādiniddesassa mātikābhāvaṃ [V 0.0060] dīpeti. Taṃ dīpetvā puna yasmiṃ padadvaye ṭhatvā dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ kathetabbaṃ, tassa niddhāraṇatthaṃ sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ saṅkaḍḍhento āha “idañhi dukkhaṃ nāmā”tiādi.

190. Herein... this is the matrix. In the section on exposition, at the beginning of the recitation, in the exposition of birth and so on, for the purpose of explaining the Noble Truth of Suffering by way of the exposition of birth and so on; or, with regard to birth and so on, when their nature as suffering is to be understood, for the purpose of explaining the Noble Truth of Suffering by way of the exposition of birth and so on, the matrix of suffering, beginning with 'suffering as suffering,' is to be understood. This is the meaning. Alternatively, 'herein' means in that section on exposition. 'Birth is suffering... in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering'—this is the matrix for the purpose of explaining the Noble Truth of Suffering; thus it clarifies the nature as a matrix of the exposition of birth and so on, as has been shown. Having clarified that, then, in order to determine the two terms upon which the Noble Truth of Suffering is to be explained, drawing together all suffering, he says, 'This, indeed, is called suffering,' and so on.

Sabhāvatoti dukkhavedayitasabhāvato. Nāmatoti teneva sabhāvena laddhanāmato. Tena na aññena pariyāyena idaṃ dukkhaṃ nāma, atha kho dukkhattāyevāti sabhāvena nāmaṃ viseseti. Atha vā nāmatoti udayabbayavantatāya laddhanāmato. Yathā aññe udayabbayavanto dhammā na sabhāvato dukkhā, na evaṃ idaṃ, atha kho sabhāvato dukkhā, bhūtamevedaṃ dukkhanti purimena dukkha-saddena pacchimaṃ viseseti. Vipariṇāmavantatāya sukhaṃ aniṭṭhameva hotīti dukkhaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Tenevāha “dukkhuppattihetuto”ti. Kaṇṇasūlādīhi abhibhūtassa nitthunanādīhi dukkhābhibhūtatāya viññāyamānāyapi kiṃ tava rujjatīti pucchitvāva kaṇṇasūlādidukkhaṃ jānitabbaṃ hotīti paṭicchannadukkhatā tassa vuttā. Upakkamassa ca pākaṭabhāvatoti kāraṇāvasena dukkhavisesassa pākaṭabhāvaṃ dasseti.

'By its intrinsic nature' means by its intrinsic nature as painful feeling. 'By name' means by the name acquired through that very intrinsic nature. Thus, this is not called suffering by any other mode, but rather precisely because of its nature as suffering; in this way, it qualifies the name by the intrinsic nature. Alternatively, 'by name' means by the name acquired on account of possessing arising and passing away. Just as other phenomena that possess arising and passing away are not suffering by their intrinsic nature, this is not so; rather, it is suffering by its intrinsic nature. 'This is truly suffering'—with the first word 'suffering,' it qualifies the second. Because it possesses the nature of change, pleasure becomes indeed undesirable; thus, the name 'suffering' has arisen. For that reason, it is said, 'due to being the cause for the arising of suffering.' Although for one afflicted by an earache and so on, the affliction by suffering is discerned through groaning and the like, the suffering of the earache and so on must be known only after asking, 'What pains you?'; thus, its concealed nature as suffering is stated. 'And because its cause is manifest' shows the manifest nature of a specific suffering by way of its cause.

Sabhāvaṃ muñcitvā pakārantarena dukkhanti vuccamānaṃ pariyāyadukkhaṃ. Kathetabbattā paṭiññātaṃ yathā kathetabbaṃ, taṃpakāradassanatthaṃ “ariyasaccañca nāmeta”ntiādimāha. Saṅkhepo sāmaññaṃ, sāmaññañca visese antokaritvā pavattatīti tattha ubhayathāpi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Vitthāro pana viseso jātiādiko, viseso ca visesantaranivattakoti jātiādīsu jarādīnaṃ saṅkhipanaṃ na sakkā kātunti tattha vitthāreneva kathetabbaṃ.

That which is called suffering in a different mode, having set aside its intrinsic nature, is figurative suffering. In order to show the manner in which what was undertaken to be explained should be explained, he says, 'And it is named the Noble Truth,' and so on. The summary is the general, and the general proceeds by including the specific; therefore, it is fitting to explain it in both ways. The detailed explanation, however, is the specific, such as birth and so on. And the specific is that which excludes other specifics; thus, with regard to birth and so on, it is not possible to summarize aging and so on. Therefore, it must be explained in detail.

191. “Aparassa [M 0.0061] aparassā”ti dīpanaṃ aparatthadīpanaṃ. Sāmiatthepi hi aparattha-saddo sijjhatīti. Tesaṃ tesanti vā sāmivasena vuttaṃ atthaṃ bhummavasena vattukāmatāya āha “aparatthadīpana”nti, aparasmiṃ aparasmiṃ dīpananti attho. Aparassa aparassa vā jātisaṅkhātassa atthassa dīpanaṃ aparatthadīpanaṃ. Pañcagativasena ekekāyapi gatiyā khattiyādibhummadevādihatthiādijātivasena cāti gatijātivasena.

191. The elucidation 'of each particular one' is aparatthadīpanaṃ. For the word aparattha is also formed in the sense of the genitive. Or, the meaning expressed in the genitive as 'of those respective beings' is stated as aparatthadīpanaṃ due to the desire to express it in the locative; the meaning is 'elucidation in each particular case.' Or, aparatthadīpanaṃ is the elucidation of the thing designated as birth for each particular being. This is by way of destiny and birth: in terms of the five destinies, and within each single destiny, by way of births such as Khattiyas, earth-deities, elephants, and so on.

Tiṇākāro tiṇajāti, so ca upādāpaññattīti “paññattiya”nti āha. Tadupādāyāti taṃ paṭhamaṃ viññāṇaṃ upādāya ayaṃ jāti, nāssa kutoci niggamanaṃ upādāya. Yasmā ca evaṃ, tasmā sāvassa jāti paṭhamaviññāṇasaṅkhātāti attho. Atha vā tadupādāya sajātoti vuccatīti [V 0.0061] sāvassa jāti paṭhamaviññāṇasaṅkhātāti attho. Viññāṇamukhena ca pañcapi khandhā vuttā hontīti “paṭisandhiya”nti āha. Ariyabhāvakaraṇattā ariyasīlanti pātimokkhasaṃvaro vuccati. Jātiādīnipi lakkhaṇāni dhammānaṃ ākāravikārāti katvā sahuppādakā sahavikārakāti vuttā. Jāyanaṭṭhenātiādi āyatanavasena yonivasena ca dvīhi dvīhi padehi sabbasatte pariyādiyitvā jātiṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Purimanaye pana ekekeneva padena sabbasatte pariyādiyitvā jāti dassitāti ayaṃ viseso. Keci pana “purimanaye kattuniddeso, pacchimanaye bhāvaniddeso kato”ti vadanti, “tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ jātī”ti pana kattari sāminiddesassa katattā ubhayatthāpi bhāvaniddesova yutto. Sampuṇṇā jāti sañjāti. Pākaṭā nibbatti abhinibbatti. “Tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ…pe… abhinibbattī”ti sattavasena pavattattā sammutikathā.

'A kind of grass' means a species of grass, and since that is a derived concept, it is said 'by concept.' 'Dependent on that' means this birth is dependent on that first consciousness; it is not dependent on an emergence from anywhere. Since this is so, the meaning is that its birth is designated as the first consciousness. Alternatively, because it is said to be 'born together with' by depending on that, the meaning is that its birth is designated as the first consciousness. And because by way of consciousness the five aggregates are also stated, it is said 'by relinking.' Because it brings about the noble state, the Pātimokkha restraint is called 'noble virtue.' Birth and other characteristics, being modes and alterations of phenomena, are said to be co-arising and co-altering. 'By the meaning of being born,' and so on, is said to show birth by encompassing all beings with each of the two terms, by way of sense-bases and by way of wombs. In the former method, however, birth was shown by encompassing all beings with each single term; this is the difference. Some say, 'In the former method, the agent is indicated; in the latter, the state is indicated.' But since the phrase 'the birth of those respective beings' is an indication of the owner in the agentive sense, an indication of the state is appropriate in both cases. Complete birth is sañjāti. Manifest production is nibbatti. Full production is abhinibbatti. The phrase 'of those respective beings... full production' is conventional speech because it proceeds by way of beings.

Tatra tatrāti ekacatuvokārabhavesu dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ, sese rūpadhātuyaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe uppajjamānānaṃ pañcannaṃ, kāmadhātuyaṃ vikalāvikalindriyānaṃ vasena sattannaṃ navannaṃ dasannaṃ puna dasannaṃ ekādasannañca āyatanānaṃ vasena saṅgaho veditabbo. Ekabhavapariyāpannassa khandhasantānassa paṭhamābhinibbattibhūtā paṭisandhikkhandhāti āha “paṭhamābhinibbattilakkhaṇā”ti. Tameva santānaṃ niyyātentaṃ viya “handa gaṇhathā”ti paṭicchāpentaṃ viya pavattatīti niyyātanarasā. Santatiyā eva ummujjanaṃ hutvā gayhatīti ummujjanapaccupaṭṭhānā. Dukkharāsissa vicittatā dukkhavicittatā, dukkhavisesā vā tadavayavā, taṃ paccupaṭṭhāpeti phalatīti dukkhavicittatāpaccupaṭṭhānā.

'In each case' means that the inclusion of sense-bases should be understood as two each in the one-constituent and four-constituent existences; as five for those arising at the moment of relinking in the remaining form realm; and in the desire realm, according to the deficiency or completeness of faculties, as seven, nine, ten, again ten, and eleven. Because the relinking-aggregates are the first production of the aggregate-continuum comprised in a single existence, it is said they have 'the characteristic of first production.' It proceeds as if entrusting that very continuum, as if making it be accepted with the words, 'Here, take this!'; thus, its function is entrusting. It is grasped after having emerged from the continuity itself; thus, its manifestation is emergence. The variegation of the mass of suffering is dukkhavicittatā; or, the specific sufferings are its components. It presents this, it brings it to fruition; thus, its manifestation is the presentation of the variegation of suffering.

Pariyāyanippariyāyadukkhesu [M 0.0062] yaṃ dukkhaṃ jāti hoti, taṃ dukkhabhāvoyeva tassā dukkhaṭṭho. Yadi akkhānena pāpuṇitabbaṃ siyā, bhagavā ācikkheyya. Bhagavatāpi –

Among the various kinds of suffering, the suffering that is birth is indeed the very state of suffering; that is its meaning as suffering. If it could be conveyed through explanation, the Blessed One would explain it. Even by the Blessed One—

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamo nu kho mahantataro? Yo cāyaṃ mayā paritto pāṇimatto pāsāṇo gahito, yo ca himavā pabbatarājāti. Appama…pe… gahito, himavantaṃ pabbatarājānaṃ upanidhāya saṅkhampi na upeti, kalabhāgampi na upeti, upanidhampi na upeti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yaṃ so puriso tīhi sattisatehi haññamāno [V 0.0062] tatonidānaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti, taṃ nerayikassa dukkhassa upanidhāya saṅkhampi…pe… upanidhampi na upetī”ti (ma. ni. 3.250) –

"What do you think, monks, which is greater? This small, hand-sized pebble I have taken, or Himavā, the king of mountains?" "Venerable sir, this small pebble you have taken is insignificant; compared to Himavā, the king of mountains, it does not amount to a calculation, it does not amount to a fraction, it does not amount to a comparison." "In the same way, monks, the suffering and displeasure that a person experiences on that account, being struck with three hundred spears, compared to the suffering of hell, does not amount to a calculation... it does not amount to a comparison."

Upamāvasena pakāsitaṃ āpāyikadukkhaṃ. Sukhuppattikāraṇāni sucīni uppalādīnīti katvā tattha nibbattinivāraṇena jātiyā dukkhavatthubhāvaṃ dasseti “atha kho”tiādinā. Dukkhuppattikāraṇe nibbattanena gabbhapariharaṇūpakkamena vinā mātukucchisambhavameva dukkhaṃ gabbhokkantimūlakaṃ aññānapekkhattā, upakkamanibbattaṃ pana pariharaṇamūlakaṃ okkantimattānapekkhattā. Ayametesaṃ viseso.

The suffering of the woeful states has been explained by way of simile. Having considered that the causes for the arising of happiness are pure, like lotuses and so on, he shows, by preventing rebirth there, that birth is the basis for suffering, with the words beginning 'atha kho'. The suffering of arising in a mother's womb itself—which occurs in a cause for the arising of suffering, without the effort of avoiding the womb—is rooted in the descent into the womb, as it is not dependent on anything else. That which is produced by effort, however, is rooted in avoidance, as it is not dependent merely on the descent. This is the distinction between them.

Attano abhimukhaṃ kaḍḍhanaṃ ākaḍḍhanaṃ, parito sabbatobhāgena kaḍḍhanaṃ parikaḍḍhanaṃ. Adho dhunanaṃ odhunanaṃ, tiriyaṃ, sabbato vā dhunanaṃ nidhunanaṃ. Tacchetvā khārapakkhipanaṃ khārāpaṭicchakaṃ.

Drawing towards oneself is pulling (ākaḍḍhana). Drawing from all around, in every direction, is drawing all around (parikaḍḍhana). Shaking downwards is shaking off (odhunana). Shaking sideways or in all directions is shaking completely (nidhunana). Slicing and applying lye is the lye application (khārāpaṭicchaka).

Sakalasarīranhāpanaṃ nhāpanaṃ, ekadesadhovanaṃ dhovanaṃ, sūriyābhimukhapavattanena ātāpanaṃ, pañcaggitāpena paritāpanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabboyeva vā tāpo dvidhāpi vutto.

Bathing the entire body is bathing; washing one part is washing. Heating by turning towards the sun is sunning; scorching by the five fires should be understood as intense heating. Or, all heating is spoken of in both these ways.

Kuhiṃ nu patiṭṭhaṃ labhetha, jātiyā vinā na tassa dukkhassa patiṭṭhānaṃ atthīti attho, jātiyā vā vinā so satto kuhiṃ nu patiṭṭhaṃ, kattha nu patiṭṭhanto taṃ dukkhaṃ labhethāti attho. Tattha tiracchānesu kathaṃ dukkhaṃ bhaveyya tahiṃ tiracchānesu jātiṃ vinā. Na cassāti na ce assa. Nanu nevatthīti sambandho kātabbo, nanu āhāti vā. Yadatoti yasmā nevatthi, tasmā āhāti attho.

Where indeed could one find a footing? The meaning is: without birth, there is no basis for that suffering. Or, the meaning is: without birth, where indeed could that being find a footing? Standing where, indeed, could one experience that suffering? In that regard, how could there be suffering among animals without birth among those animals? 'Na cassā' means 'na ce assa' (and if it were not). The connection should be made as, 'Is it not so that it does not exist?' or, 'Did he not say?'. 'Yadato' means: because it does not exist, therefore he said.

Jarāniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Analysis of Aging

192. Jīraṇameva [M 0.0063] jīraṇatā, jīraṇassa vā ākāro tā-saddena vutto.

192. The state of aging is simply the process of aging; or, the mode of aging is expressed by the word 'tā'.

Yathāpure asallakkhenteti gāravakaraṇaupaṭṭhānādīni asallakkhente taṃnimittaṃ domanassaṃ uppajjatīti attho.

The phrase 'as they do not regard as before' means: when others do not show them respect, service, and so on, displeasure arises on that account.

Satādīnanti [V 0.0063] satisutavīriyapaññādīnaṃ vippavāsanimittaṃ attanā apasādetabbehipi attano puttadārehi apasādanīyato. Avasavattaṅgapaccaṅgatāya suciasuciādivicāraṇavirahena ca bālakumārakakālo viya jiṇṇakālo hotīti āha “bhiyyo bālattappattiyā”ti.

'Of mindfulness and so on' refers to the cause for the departure of mindfulness, learning, energy, wisdom, and other such qualities, and to being dismissed by one's own children and wife, who ought to be dismissed by oneself. Due to the state of having uncontrolled limbs and faculties, and the absence of discrimination between pure and impure and so on, the time of old age becomes like the time of a young boy; thus he says, 'through the attainment of further childishness'.

Maraṇaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Analysis of Death

193. “Kālassa antakassa kiriyā”ti yā loke vuccati, sā cuti, maraṇanti attho. Cavanakāloyeva vā anatikkamanīyattā visesena kāloti vutto, tassa kiriyā cutikkhandhānaṃ bhedappattiyeva. Maccu maraṇanti etthāpi samāsaṃ akatvā yo maccu vuccati bhedo, yañca maraṇaṃ pāṇacāgo, idaṃ vuccati maraṇanti visuṃ sambandho na na yujjati.

193. That which is called in the world 'the act of Time, the end-maker,' means passing away, death. Or, the time of passing away itself, because it cannot be transgressed, is specifically called 'Time'; its act is precisely the attainment of the breakup of the aggregates at death. Here too, regarding 'death' (maccu) and 'dying' (maraṇaṃ), without forming a compound, it is not unsuitable to connect them separately thus: that which is called 'death' (maccu) is the breakup, and that which is 'dying' (maraṇaṃ) is the abandoning of life-breath; this is called death.

Yassa khandhabhedassa pavattattā “tisso mato, phusso mato”ti vohāro hoti, so khandhappabandhassa anupacchinnatāya “sammutimaraṇa”nti vutto, pabandhasamucchedo ca “samucchedamaraṇa”nti. Maraṇampi dukkhanti imasmiṃ panatthe dukkhasaccakathā vaṭṭakathāti katvā “sammutimaraṇaṃ adhippeta”nti āha. Tasseva nāmanti tabbhāvato tadekadesabhāvato ca maraṇa-saddabahutte asammohatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Cutilakkhaṇanti “cavanatā”ti nidassitacavanalakkhaṇameva vadati. Sampattibhavakhandhehi viyojetīti viyogarasaṃ, viyogakiriyābhūtatāya vā “viyogarasa”nti vuttaṃ. Sattassa purimabhavato vippavāso hutvā upaṭṭhātīti vippavāsapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

That breakup of the aggregates on account of which the convention, 'Tissa is dead, Phussa is dead,' arises, is called 'conventional death' due to the non-interruption of the series of aggregates; and the cutting off of the series is called 'death by cutting off.' But in this context, 'death is suffering,' having considered that the talk on the truth of suffering is a talk on the round of existence, he said, 'conventional death is intended.' 'Its name' is said to avoid confusion amidst the many uses of the word 'death,' with respect to its essential nature and its partial aspects. 'The characteristic of passing away' refers only to the characteristic of passing away indicated as 'the state of passing away.' Its function is separation, as it separates one from the aggregates of the attained existence; or it is called 'the function of separation' because it is the action of separation. Its manifestation is separation, as it appears as the separation of a being from the previous existence.

Maraṇantikāti maraṇassa āsannā. Yadi maraṇaṃ na bhavissati, yathāvuttaṃ kāyikaṃ cetasikañca dukkhaṃ na bhavissatīti āha “dvinnampi dukkhānaṃ vatthubhāvenā”ti.

`Maraṇantikā` means near death. If there were no death, the aforesaid physical and mental suffering would not exist; hence it is said, 'because it is the basis for both kinds of suffering.'

Pāpakammādinimittanti [M 0.0064] pāpakammanimittaṃ pāpagatinimittañcāti attho, kammampi vā ettha “nimitta”nti vuttaṃ upapattinimittabhāvena upaṭṭhānato. Tadupaṭṭhānepi hi “akataṃ vata me kalyāṇa”ntiādinā anappakaṃ domanassaṃ uppajjatīti. Bhaddassāti kalyāṇakammassāti attho. Avisesatoti “sabbesa”nti etena yojetabbaṃ. Sabbesanti ca yesaṃ kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, teyeva sabbe gahitā “vitujjamānamammāna”nti visesitattā. Sandhīnaṃ bandhanāni sandhibandhanāni[V 0.0064], tesaṃ chedanena nibbattaṃ dukkhaṃ “sandhibandhanacchedana”nti vuttaṃ. Ādi-saddo vā kāraṇattho, sandhibandhanacchedanamūlakanti attho.

'The sign of evil deeds and so on' means the sign of evil action and the sign of an evil destination. Or here, action itself is called 'sign' because it appears as a sign of rebirth. For when that appears, considerable displeasure arises, with such thoughts as, 'Alas, I have not done good.' 'Of the good' means of good action. 'Without distinction' should be connected with 'of all.' And by 'of all,' all those are taken for whom bodily suffering arises, because they are specified as 'of those whose vital spots are being pierced.' 'Bonds of the joints' are the connections of the joints; the suffering produced by the cutting of them is called 'the cutting of the bonds of the joints.' Or the word 'ādi' has the meaning of cause; the meaning is 'rooted in the cutting of the bonds of the joints.'

Anayabyasanāpādanaṃ viyāti anayabyasanāpatti viyāti attho. Vāḷādīhi kate hi anayabyasanāpādane antogadhā anayabyasanāpatti ettha nidassananti.

'Like causing misfortune and disaster' means 'like the occurrence of misfortune and disaster.' For the occurrence of misfortune and disaster is included within the causing of misfortune and disaster done by beasts of prey and so on; this is the example here.

Sokaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Analysis of Sorrow

194. Sukhakāraṇaṃ hitaṃ, tassa phalaṃ sukhaṃ. Ñātikkhayoti bhogādīhi ñātīnaṃ parihāni maraṇañca. Ayaṃ pana visesoti bhogabyasanādipadatthavisesaṃ rogabyasanādīsu samāsavisesañca sandhāyāha. Ñātibhogā paññattimattā tabbināsāvāti iminā adhippāyena aparinipphannataṃ sandhāya “anipphannānī”ti āha. Aparinipphannataṃyeva hi sandhāya visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 2.447 ādayo) ca “dasa rūpāni anipphannānī”ti vuttaṃ. Rūpakaṇḍavaṇṇanāyañhi (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 975 pakiṇṇakakathā) ni “aparinipphannānī”ti vuttāni. Khandhavibhaṅge ca nipphādetabbassa nirodhasamāpattiādikassa nipphannatā vuttāti asabhāvadhammassa ca nipphannatā, nibbānasseva anipphannatāti.

194. Welfare is the cause of happiness; happiness is its fruit. 'Destruction of relatives' means the decline of relatives with regard to possessions and so on, and their death. 'This, however, is a distinction'—he says this referring to the specific meaning of terms like 'disaster of possessions' and the specific compound in 'disaster of disease' and so on. With the intention that 'relatives and possessions are mere concepts, as is their destruction,' and referring to their unproduced nature, he said 'unproduced.' Indeed, it is with reference to their unproduced nature that in the Visuddhimagga it is said, 'Ten forms are unproduced.' In the commentary on the Section on Form, they are also said to be 'unproduced.' And in the Analysis of the Aggregates, the produced nature of that which is to be produced—such as the attainment of cessation—is stated, as is the produced nature of a phenomenon without intrinsic nature, whereas only Nibbāna is unproduced.

Dhamma-saddo hetuatthoti āha “dukkhassa uppattihetunā”ti. Jhāmanti daḍḍhaṃ. Pubbe vuttalakkhaṇādikā domanassavedanā sokoti tassa puna lakkhaṇādayo na vattabbā siyuṃ, tathāpi domanassavisesattā sokassa ca visiṭṭhā lakkhaṇādayo vattabbāti “kiñcāpī”tiādimāha. Visārarahitaṃ anto eva saṅkucitaṃ cintanaṃ, sukkhanaṃ vā antonijjhānaṃ. Parinijjhāyanaṃ dahanaṃ. Ñātibyasanādianurūpaṃ socanaṃ anusocanaṃ, taṃ taṃ vā guṇaṃ dosañca anugantvā socanaṃ tappanaṃ anusocanaṃ.

The term 'dhamma' means cause; hence it is said, 'as the cause for the arising of suffering.' 'Jhāma' means burnt. Although the characteristics, etc., of the mental pain (domanassavedanā) that is sorrow were stated previously, and thus its characteristics, etc., should not be stated again, nevertheless, because sorrow is a specific kind of mental pain, its distinct characteristics, etc., should be stated—hence it is said, 'although,' etc. Thought that is devoid of expansion, contracted inwardly; or inward brooding that is drying up. Burning thoroughly. Grieving in accordance with the loss of relatives, etc., is lamentation; or it is grieving and tormenting, following after this or that virtue and fault.

Javanakkhaṇeti [M 0.0065] manodvārajavanakkhaṇe. Tathā hi taṃ dassento “ettakā me”tiādimāha. Kāyaviññāṇādivīthiyampi pana javanakkhaṇe domanassassa paccayo hoti eva. Teneva “javanakkhaṇe cā”ti āha. Aññathā kāyikacetasikadukkhānaṃ kāyavatthukamanodvārappavattānameva paccayoti gaṇheyya tattha visesena kāyikacetasikasaddappavattito.

"At the moment of impulsion" means at the moment of impulsion in the mind-door process. To show this, it is said, "so much for me," etc. However, in body-consciousness processes, etc., mental pain also has a condition at the moment of impulsion. Therefore, it is said, "and at the moment of impulsion." Otherwise, it would be understood that only bodily and mental sufferings arising through the body-base and mind-door have this as their condition, specifically from the occurrence of the terms 'bodily' and 'mental' there.

Tujjatīti [V 0.0065] “tudatī”ti vattabbe byattayavasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

'Tujjati'—it should be understood that this is said by way of transposition, when 'tudati' could have been said.

Paridevaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Lamentation

195. Ādevanti etenāti ādevoti ādevana-saddaṃ katvā assuvimocanādivikāraṃ āpajjantānaṃ tabbikārāpattiyā so saddo karaṇabhāvena vuttoti. Vīhipalāpādayo viya tucchaṃ vacanaṃ palāpo. Guṇadose kitteti bodhetīti guṇadosakittanaraso lālappa-saddo. Atthānatthe hiriyitabbajane ca avicāretvā puggalassa sambhamabhāvo hutvā paridevana-saddo upaṭṭhātīti “sambhamapaccupaṭṭhāno”ti vutto, sokavatthuavighātena vā sambhamo, na uttāsasambhamo, so ca paridevana-saddena pākaṭo hotīti paridevo “sambhamapaccupaṭṭhāno”ti vutto.

195. They cry out with this, hence it is called 'ādeva.' For those who, making the sound of lamentation, undergo changes such as shedding tears, that sound is described in the instrumental sense because of their undergoing that change. Like rice chaff, empty speech is prattle. The sound of 'lālappa' has the characteristic of proclaiming virtues and faults, for it proclaims and makes them known. Because a state of agitation arises in a person who does not consider what is beneficial and unbeneficial or those who should be respected, and the sound of lamentation appears, it is said to 'manifest as agitation.' Or, agitation arises due to the destruction of the basis for sorrow; it is not the agitation of terror. And since that agitation becomes evident through the sound of lamentation, lamentation is said to 'manifest as agitation.'

Sokābhibhūto paridevananimittaṃ muṭṭhipothanādīni karoti, paridevananimittameva ca ñātiabbhatthaṅgamanādīni cintetīti paridevassa dukkhadomanassānaṃ vatthubhāvo vutto.

Overcome by sorrow, one performs signs of lamentation such as beating one's breast, and one thinks of things like the death of relatives precisely as a cause for lamentation—thus, lamentation is said to be the basis of suffering and mental pain.

Bhiyyoti yena vinā na hoti, tato paridevasamuṭṭhāpakadomanassato, pubbe vuttadukkhato vā bhiyyo, kaṇṭhoṭṭhatāluādisosajatopi vā bhiyyoti aññañca kāyikaṃ cetasikaṃ taṃnidānadukkhaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

By 'more' is meant that which is more than the mental pain that gives rise to lamentation—without which it does not occur—or more than the suffering previously mentioned, or more than that arising from dryness of throat, lips, palate, etc. It also encompasses other physical and mental suffering originating from that.

Dukkhadomanassaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Suffering and Mental Pain

196-7. Kāyikaṃ dukkhaṃ kāyikassa dukkhassa upanissayapaccayoti “dukkhitassa dukkhaṃ uppajjatī”ti vuttaṃ. Etena dukkhena abhibhūtattā nakkhattaṃ kīḷituṃ [M 0.0066] na labhāmīti balavadomanassaṃ uppajjatīti dukkhassa domanassavatthutā hoti.

196-7. Bodily suffering is the decisive support condition for bodily suffering—thus it is said, "suffering arises for one who is suffering." Because one is overwhelmed by this suffering, one thinks, "I cannot enjoy the festival," and thus strong mental pain arises. In this way, suffering is the basis for mental pain.

Attano pavattikkhaṇaṃ sandhāya “pīḷetī”ti vuttaṃ kāyikadukkhaṃ, tadupanissayato vā.

Bodily suffering is said to 'oppress' with reference to its own moment of occurrence, or by way of its decisive support.

Āvaṭṭantīti parivaṭṭanti. Vivaṭṭantīti pabbhāre khittatthambho viya ludhanti. Mūlacchinnarukkho viya chinnapapātaṃ papatanti, paridayhamānacittā purimadomanassupanissayavasena cintenti, vigate domanasse tathācintanaṃ natthīti.

"Whirling" means turning around. "Rolling away" means tumbling down like a pillar thrown down a slope. Like a tree with severed roots, they fall as if from a precipice. With minds burning, they think by way of previous mental pain as a decisive support. When that mental pain is gone, such thinking does not occur.

Upāyāsaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Despair

198. Sabbavisayappaṭipattinivāraṇavasena [V 0.0066] samantato sīdanaṃ saṃsīdanaṃ, uṭṭhetumpi asakkuṇeyyatākaraṇavasena atibalavaṃ, virūpaṃ vā sīdanaṃ visīdanaṃ. Aññaṃ visayaṃ agantvā ñātibyasanādīsu virūpo āsaṅgo tattheva avabandhatā byāsatti. Nitthunanakaraṇato nitthunanaraso. Visīdanaṃ visādo.

198. Sinking down completely, by way of obstructing engagement with all objects, is 'saṃsīdana.' It is extremely powerful, as it makes one unable even to rise. Or, distorted sinking is 'visīdana.' Distorted attachment to misfortunes such as the loss of relatives, without going to another object, being bound right there, is 'byāsatti.' Its characteristic is groaning, as it causes groaning. Sinking down is dejection.

Sayaṃ na dukkho dosattā saṅkhārakkhandhapariyāpannadhammantarattā vā. Ye pana domanassameva upāyāsoti vadeyyuṃ, te “upāyāso tīhi khandhehi ekenāyatanena ekāya dhātuyā sampayutto, ekena khandhena ekenāyatanena ekāya dhātuyā kehici sampayutto”ti (dhātu. 249) imāya pāḷiyā paṭikkhipitabbā. Visādappattiyā sukhadukkhakāraṇaṃ agaṇayitvā dukkhaṭṭhānādīni karontānaṃ upāyāso kāyikadukkhassa vatthu hoti, visādanavaseneva ñātivināsādīni cintentānaṃ domanassassa. Attano pavattikkhaṇeyeva upāyāso domanassasampayogato cittaṃ paridahati, avipphārikatākaraṇavasena kāyaṃ visādeti, tadubhayakaraṇeneva tato paraṃ taṃnimittaṃ kāyikaṃ cetasikañca adhimattaṃ dukkhaṃ janayatīti dukkho vutto.

In itself it is not suffering, because it is aversion, or because it is another phenomenon included in the aggregate of formations. But those who would say that despair is merely mental pain should be refuted by this passage: 'Despair is associated with three aggregates, one sense-sphere, and one element; in some cases, it is associated with one aggregate, one sense-sphere, and one element' (Dhātukathā 249). For those who, having fallen into dejection, do such things as make places of suffering without considering the causes of pleasure and pain, despair becomes the basis of bodily suffering; and for those who, merely through the force of dejection, contemplate the loss of relatives and so on, it becomes the basis of mental pain. At the very moment of its arising, despair, through its association with mental pain, burns the mind, and by causing a lack of expansiveness, it makes the body sink; by doing both of these, it later generates intense bodily and mental suffering having that as its cause—therefore it is called suffering.

Appiyasampayoganiddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Association with the Disagreeable

199. Na appiyantīti na gamiyanti, na pavesīyantīti attho. Anatthanti byasanaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā. Ahitanti tassa hetuṃ.
