Seeing a form with the eye, he becomes attached to agreeable forms and is repelled by disagreeable forms. And he dwells with mindfulness of the body unestablished and with a limited mind. He does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen in him cease without remainder. He, having thus fallen into conformity and opposition, whatever feeling he feels—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains attached to it."

Evaṃ vuttassa. Evaṃ sotadvārādīsupi. Abhivadatoti “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti vacībhedakarappattāya balavataṇhāya “ahaṃ mamā”ti abhivadato. Tato balavatiyā mocetuṃ asakkuṇeyyabhāvena ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato. Tatopi balavatī upādānabhūtā taṇhā nandī. Ettha ca abhinandanādinā taṇhā vuttā, nandīvacanena tappaccayaṃ upādānaṃ catubbidhampi nanditātadavippayogatāhi taṇhādiṭṭhābhinandanabhāvehi cāti veditabbaṃ. “Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”ntiādikañca tattheva mahātaṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttisutte (ma. ni. 1.402-403) vuttaṃ.

Of what was thus said. Similarly, also in the case of the ear-door and so on. 'Welcomes' (abhivadati) means welcoming with 'I' and 'mine' due to strong craving that has reached the point of breaking into speech, such as, 'Oh, happiness! Oh, happiness!' Then, because of being unable to be freed from that stronger craving, one remains attached. Even stronger than that is delight (nandī), which is craving that has become clinging. And here, craving is expressed by 'delighting' (abhinandanā) and so on; by the word 'delight' (nandī), it should be understood that the fourfold clinging conditioned by it arises from delighting, from not being separated from that, and from the states of delighting in craving and views. And 'With birth as condition, aging and death,' etc., is stated in that very Great Discourse on the Destruction of Craving (Majjhima Nikāya 1.402–403).

Vipākavaṭṭabhūte paṭisandhipavattiphassādayo kammasamuṭṭhānañca ojaṃ sandhāya “cattāro āhārā taṇhānidānā”tiādi vuttaṃ, vaṭṭūpatthambhakā pana itarepi āhārā taṇhāpabhave tasmiṃ avijjamāne na vijjantīti “taṇhānidānā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭanti.

With reference to rebirth-linking, contact in the course of existence, and so on, which constitute the cycle of results, and also to the nutritive essence arisen from kamma, it is said, 'The four nutriments have craving as their source,' and so on. However, the other nutriments, which support the cycle, are also born of craving; when that is not present, they do not exist. Thus, it is fitting to say they 'have craving as their source.'

Tato tatoti catubbidhāsu desanāsu tato tato desanāto. Ñāyappaṭivedhāya saṃvattatīti ñāyoti [V 0.0086] maggo, soyeva vā paṭiccasamuppādo “ariyo cassa ñāyo paññāya sudiṭṭho hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.41) vacanato. Sayameva hi samantabhadrakattā tathā tathā paṭivijjhitabbattā tāya tāya desanāya attano paṭivedhāya saṃvattatīti. Samantabhadrakattaṃ desanāvilāsappatti ca catunnampi desanānaṃ samānaṃ kāraṇanti visesakāraṇaṃ [M 0.0086] vattukāmo āha “visesato”ti. Assa bhagavato desanā, assa vā paṭiccasamuppādassa desanāti yojetabbaṃ. Pavattikāraṇavibhāgo avijjādikova, kāraṇanti vā gahitānaṃ pakatiādīnaṃ avijjādīnañca akāraṇatā kāraṇatā ca. Tattha sammūḷhā keci akāraṇaṃ “kāraṇa”nti gaṇhanti, keci na kiñci kāraṇaṃ bujjhantīti tesaṃ yathāsakehi anurūpehi kāraṇehi saṅkhārādipavattisandassanatthaṃ anulomadesanā pavattā, itarāsaṃ tadatthatāsambhavepi na tāsaṃ tadatthameva pavatti atthantarasabbhāvato. Ayaṃ pana tadatthā evāti etissā tadatthatā vuttā. Pavattiādīnavapaṭicchādikā avijjā ādi, tato saṅkhārā uppajjanti tato viññāṇanti evaṃ pavattiyā uppattikkamasandassanatthañca.

'From this and that' means from each of the fourfold teachings. 'It leads to the penetration of the method': 'method' (ñāya) is the path, or it is dependent origination itself, as stated: 'And for him the noble method is well seen with wisdom' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.41). Indeed, because it is itself universally good and must be penetrated in various ways, it leads to one's own penetration through each of those teachings. The universally good nature and the attainment of grace in the teaching are a common reason for all four teachings. Wishing to state a special reason, he says 'especially.' This should be construed as 'the teaching of this Blessed One' or 'the teaching of this dependent origination.' The analysis of the cause of the process of existence concerns ignorance and so on, or it concerns the non-causality and causality of things—such as nature, etc., and ignorance, etc.—that are taken as 'cause.' In this regard, some deluded people take a non-cause as 'cause'; some do not understand any cause at all. For them, the forward teaching was set forth to show the occurrence of formations, etc., through causes appropriate to their respective views. Although this purpose is possible for the other teachings, they are not set forth for this purpose alone, since another meaning exists. But this teaching is indeed for that purpose; thus its being for that purpose is stated. It is also for showing the order of arising of the process of existence in this way: ignorance, which conceals the danger of the process of existence, is the beginning; from that, formations arise; from that, consciousness.

Anuvilokayato yo sambodhito pubbabhāge taṃtaṃphalapaṭivedho pavatto, tadanusārena tadanugamena jarāmaraṇādikassa jātiādikāraṇaṃ yaṃ adhigataṃ, tassa sandassanatthaṃ assa paṭilomadesanā pavattā, anuvilokayato paṭilomadesanā pavattāti vā sambandho. Desentopi hi bhagavā kicchāpannaṃ lokaṃ anuviloketvā pubbabhāga…pe… sandassanatthaṃ desetīti. Āhārataṇhādayo paccuppannaddhā, saṅkhārāvijjā atītaddhāti iminā adhippāyenāha “yāva atītaṃ addhānaṃ atiharitvā”ti, āhārā vā taṇhāya pabhāvetabbā anāgato addhā, taṇhādayo paccuppanno, saṅkhārāvijjā atītoti. Paccakkhaṃ pana phalaṃ dassetvā taṃnidānadassanavasena phalakāraṇaparamparāya dassanaṃ yujjatīti āhārā purimataṇhāya uppāditā paccuppanno addhā, taṇhādayo atīto, saṅkhārāvijjā tatopi atītataro saṃsārassa anādibhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttoti yāva atītaṃ addhānanti yāva atītataraṃ addhānanti attho yutto.

For him who was reviewing, the penetration of the respective fruits occurred in the preliminary stage of enlightenment. In accordance with that, following that, this reverse teaching was set forth to show that cause of aging-and-death, etc.—namely birth, etc.—which was understood. Or, the connection is that the reverse teaching was set forth for one who was reviewing. For even when teaching, the Blessed One, having reviewed the world that has fallen into suffering, teaches... to show it. 'Nutriment, craving, etc., are the present time; formations and ignorance are the past time'—with this intention it is said, 'having carried it back as far as the past time.' Or: nutriments, which are to be generated by craving, are the future time; craving, etc., is the present; formations and ignorance are the past. However, it is appropriate to show the succession of cause and fruit by way of showing its source after having shown the directly visible fruit. Thus: nutriments produced by previous craving are the present time; craving, etc., is the past; formations and ignorance are a still more remote past—this is said to show the beginninglessness of saṃsāra. Therefore, 'as far as the past time' has the fitting meaning 'as far as the more remote past time.'

Āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattiāhārakā vā cattāro āhārā –

Or, the four nutriments are nutriment for the production of renewed existence in the future—

“Āhāretīti ahaṃ na vadāmi, āhāretīti cāhaṃ vadeyyuṃ, tatrassa kallo pañho [V 0.0087] ‘ko nu kho, bhante, āhāretī’ti. Evaṃ cāhaṃ na vadāmi, evaṃ pana avadantaṃ maṃ yo evaṃ puccheyya ‘kissa nu kho, bhante, viññāṇāhāro’ti. Esa kallo [M 0.0087] pañho, tatra kallaṃ veyyākaraṇaṃ, viññāṇāhāro āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbattiyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.12) –

"I do not say, 'One takes nutriment.' If I were to say, 'One takes nutriment,' then this would be a proper question: 'Venerable sir, who takes nutriment?' But I do not speak thus. However, as I do not speak thus, if someone were to ask me, 'Venerable sir, for what is consciousness-nutriment a condition?'—this is a proper question. To that, the proper answer is: 'Consciousness-nutriment is a condition for the production of renewed existence in the future.'" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.12)

Vacanato taṃsampayuttattā phassacetanānaṃ tappavattihetuttā ca kabaḷīkārāhārassa. Tena hi upatthambhitarūpakāyassa, tañca icchantassa kammaviññāṇāyūhanaṃ hoti. Bhojanañhi saddhādīnaṃ rāgādīnañca upanissayoti vuttanti. Tasmā “te kammavaṭṭasaṅgahitā āhārā paccuppanno addhā”ti imasmiṃ pariyāye purimoyevattho yutto. Atītaddhuto pabhuti “iti kho, bhikkhave, avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.3) atīte tato parañca hetuphalapaṭipāṭiṃ paccakkhānaṃ āhārānaṃ nidānadassanavasena ārohitvā nivattanena vinā abujjhantānaṃ taṃsandassanatthaṃ sā ayaṃ desanā pavattāti attho. Anāgataddhuno sandassanatthanti anāgataddhuno duppaṭivijjhantānaṃ apassantānaṃ paccakkhaṃ paccuppannaṃ hetuṃ dassetvā hetuphalaparamparāya tassa sandassanatthanti attho.

[The inclusion of] physical food is because of the statement, because contact and volition are associated with it, and because it is a cause for their occurrence. For by that, for one whose physical body is sustained and who desires that, there is an accumulation of kamma and consciousness. For food is said to be a decisive support condition for faith, etc., and for lust, etc. Therefore, in this exposition, 'those nutriments included in the kamma-cycle are the present time,' the former meaning is fitting. The meaning is that this teaching is set forth to show this to those who do not understand without ascending and then turning back, by showing the source of the directly visible nutriments, thereby showing the sequence of cause and effect from the past time onward and beyond, beginning with 'Thus, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, formations...' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.3). 'For the purpose of showing the future time' means: for those who find the future time difficult to penetrate, who do not see it, it is for the purpose of showing it through the succession of cause and effect, by showing the directly visible present cause.

Mūlakāraṇasaddaṃ apekkhitvā “na akāraṇa”nti napuṃsakaniddeso kato. Akāraṇaṃ yadi siyā, suttaṃ paṭibāhitaṃ siyāti dassento suttaṃ āharati. Vaṭṭakathāya sīsabhāvo vaṭṭahetuno kammassapi hetubhāvo. Tattha bhavataṇhāyapi hetubhūtā avijjā, tāya paṭicchāditādīnave bhave taṇhuppattitoti avijjā visesena sīsabhūtāti “mūlakāraṇa”nti vuttā. Purimāya koṭiyā apaññāyamānāya uppādavirahato niccataṃ gaṇheyyāti āha “evañcetaṃ, bhikkhave, vuccatī”tiādi. Tena ito pubbe uppannapubbatā natthīti apaññāyanato purimakoṭiapaññāyanaṃ vuttanti imamatthaṃ dasseti.

Having considered the word 'root cause,' the neuter designation 'not without a cause' is made. To show that if it were without a cause, the sutta would be refuted, he cites the sutta. The state of being the head in the discourse on the round is the state of being a cause even for kamma, which is the cause of the round. Therein, ignorance is a cause for craving for existence, and because craving arises in an existence where the dangers are concealed by it, ignorance is thus called the 'root cause,' being pre-eminent in a special sense. Lest one might assume permanence due to the absence of origination if the prior limit were not discernible, he said, 'And so, bhikkhus, it is said,' etc. By this, he shows the meaning that the non-discernment of a prior limit is stated because it is not discerned that there was any prior arising before this.

Avijjātaṇhāhetukkamena phalesu vattabbesu “sugatiduggatigāmino”ti vacanaṃ saddalakkhaṇāvirodhanatthaṃ. Dvande hi pūjitassa pubbanipātoti. Savarā kira maṃsassa aṭṭhinā alagganatthaṃ punappunaṃ tāpetvā koṭṭetvā uṇhodakaṃ pāyetvā virittaṃ sūnaṃ aṭṭhito muttamaṃsaṃ gāviṃ mārenti. Tenāha “aggisantāpi”ccādi. Tattha yathā vajjhā gāvī ca avijjābhibhūtatāya yathāvuttaṃ uṇhodakapānaṃ ārabhati, evaṃ puthujjano yathāvuttaṃ duggatigāmikammaṃ. Yathā pana sā uṇhodakapāne [V 0.0088] ādīnavaṃ disvā [M 0.0088] taṇhāvasena sītudakapānaṃ ārabhati, evamayaṃ avijjāya mandattā duggatigāmikamme ādīnavaṃ disvā taṇhāvasena sugatigāmikammaṃ ārabhati. Dukkhe hi avijjaṃ taṇhā anuvattati, sukhe taṇhaṃ avijjāti.

When the results are to be stated according to the causal sequence of ignorance and craving, the expression 'going to good and bad destinations' is used in order not to contradict grammatical convention. For in a dvandva compound, the honored term is placed first. It is said that butchers, in order to prevent the meat from sticking to the bone, repeatedly heat and pound the cow, make it drink hot water, and then kill it, its meat having been released from the bone. Therefore, he said, 'tormented by fire,' etc. Therein, just as the cow to be slaughtered, being overcome by ignorance, starts to drink the hot water as described, so too the ordinary person undertakes action leading to a bad destination. And just as that cow, seeing the danger in drinking hot water, starts to drink cold water because of craving, so too this person, due to the weakness of ignorance, seeing the danger in action leading to a bad destination, undertakes action leading to a good destination because of craving. For in suffering, craving follows ignorance; in happiness, ignorance follows craving.

Evanti avijjāya nivutattā taṇhāya saṃyuttattā ca. Ayaṃ kāyoti saviññāṇakakāyo khandhapañcakaṃ, “saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso”ti vacanato phassakāraṇañcetaṃ vuccatīti āyatanachakkaṃ vā. Samudāgatoti uppanno. Bahiddhā ca nāmarūpanti bahiddhā saviññāṇakakāyo khandhapañcakaṃ, saḷāyatanāni vā. Itthetanti itthaṃ etaṃ. Attano ca paresañca pañcakkhandhā dvādasāyatanāni ca dvārārammaṇabhāvena vavatthitāni dvayanāmānīti attho. “Dvayaṃ paṭicca phassoti aññattha cakkhurūpādīni dvayāni paṭicca cakkhusamphassādayo vuttā, idha pana ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni. Mahādvayaṃ nāma kireta”nti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.19) vuttaṃ. Ayamettha adhippāyo – aññattha “cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.43) “cakkhu ceva rūpā ca…pe… mano ceva dhammā cā”ti vuttāni dvayāni paṭicca cakkhusamphassādayo vuttā, idha pana “ayañceva kāyo”ti cakkhādinissaye sesadhamme cakkhādinissite eva katvā vuttaṃ, cakkhādikāyaṃ ekattena “ajjhattikāyatana”nti gahetvā “bahiddhā nāmarūpa”nti vuttaṃ, rūpādiārammaṇaṃ ekatteneva bāhirāyatananti tāni ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni paṭicca phasso vutto, tasmā mahādvayaṃ nāmetanti. Evañca katvā “attano ca parassa ca pañcahi khandhehi chahāyatanehi cāpi ayamattho dīpetabbovā”ti (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.2.19) vuttaṃ. “Ayaṃ kāyo”ti hi vuttāni sanissayāni cakkhādīni attano pañcakkhandhā, “bahiddhā nāmarūpa”nti vuttāni rūpādīni paresaṃ. Tathā ayaṃ kāyo attanova ajjhattikāni āyatanāni, bahiddhā nāmarūpaṃ paresaṃ bāhirānīti. Aññathā ajjhattikāyatanamatte eva “ayaṃ kāyo”ti vutte na ajjhattikāyatanāneva attano pañcakkhandhā hontīti attano ca paresañca pañcakkhandhehi dīpanā na sambhaveyyāti. Saḷevāyatanānīti saḷeva samphassakāraṇāni, yehi kāraṇabhūtehi āyatanehi uppannena phassena phuṭṭho bālo sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti.

Thus: because of being shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving. 'This body' means the conscious body, the five aggregates, or the six sense bases, because it is also called the cause of contact by the statement 'Contact arises dependent on the six sense bases.' 'Samudāgato' means 'uppanno' (arisen). 'And externally, name-and-form' means externally the conscious body, the five aggregates, or the six sense bases. 'Itthetaṃ' means 'itthaṃ etaṃ' (thus this). The five aggregates of oneself and others, and the twelve sense bases, are distinguished by their roles as doors and objects; this is the meaning of 'the twofold.' 'Contact arises dependent on the twofold': elsewhere, the twofold, such as the eye and forms, etc., are said to be the cause of eye-contact, etc. Here, however, it refers to the internal and external sense bases. It is called the 'great twofold,' as stated (in the commentary, Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 2.2.19). The meaning here is this: elsewhere, it is said, 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact,' etc. (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.43), where the twofold (eye and forms... mind and mental phenomena) gives rise to eye-contact, etc. Here, however, 'this very body' is stated, treating the remaining phenomena dependent on the eye, etc., as dependent on the eye, etc. The eye, etc., as a group, are taken as the 'internal sense base,' while 'external name-and-form' is stated, treating the objects like forms, etc., as a single 'external sense base.' Thus, contact is said to arise dependent on these internal and external sense bases; hence it is called the 'great twofold.' And having done so, it is said (in the commentary, Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā 2.2.19), 'This meaning should be explained through the five aggregates of oneself and others, as well as the six sense bases.' For 'this body' refers to the eye, etc., with their supports, which are one's own five aggregates, while 'external name-and-form' refers to forms, etc., of others. Similarly, 'this body' refers to one's own internal sense bases, and 'external name-and-form' refers to the external sense bases of others. Otherwise, if 'this body' were stated to mean only the internal sense bases, then the internal sense bases alone would not be one's own five aggregates, and thus the explanation through the five aggregates of oneself and others would not be possible. 'Only the six sense bases' means only these six are the causes of contact, and being struck by the contact that arises from these causal sense bases, the fool experiences pleasure and pain.

Ādi-saddena [M 0.0089] “etesaṃ vā aññatarena avijjānīvaraṇassa, bhikkhave, paṇḍitassa taṇhāya [V 0.0089] saṃyuttassā”tiādi yojetabbaṃ. Tasmiñhi sutte saṅkhāre avijjātaṇhānissite eva katvā kāyaggahaṇena viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanāni gahetvā etasmiñca kāye saḷāyatanānaṃ phassaṃ taṃnissitameva katvā vedanāya visesapaccayabhāvaṃ dassentena bhagavatā bālapaṇḍitānaṃ atītaddhāvijjātaṇhāmūlako vedanānto paṭiccasamuppādo dassito. Puna ca bālapaṇḍitānaṃ visesaṃ dassentena –

By the word 'etcetera,' it should be connected thus: '...of the wise person, bhikkhus, hindered by ignorance and bound by craving,' etc. In that sutta, having treated formations as based on ignorance and craving, and having taken consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases by the term 'body,' and having treated the contact of the six sense bases in this body as dependent on that, the Blessed One, showing the specific condition for feeling, has thus explained dependent origination as rooted in past ignorance and craving, ending in feeling, for both the fool and the wise. Again, showing the distinction between the fool and the wise—

“Yāya ca, bhikkhave, avijjāya nivutassa bālassa yāya ca taṇhāya saṃyuttassa ayaṃ kāyo samudāgato, sā ceva avijjā bālassa appahīnā, sā ca taṇhā aparikkhīṇā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na, bhikkhave, bālo acari brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhakkhayāya, tasmā bālo kāyassa bhedā kāyūpago hoti, so kāyūpago samāno na parimuccati jātiyā…pe… dukkhasmāti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.19) –

"Bhikkhus, this body has arisen for the fool who is shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving. That very ignorance of the fool is not abandoned, and that craving is not exhausted. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, the fool has not lived the holy life rightly for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, when the fool’s body breaks up, he is reborn in a body. Being reborn in a body, he is not freed from birth... I say he is not freed from suffering." (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.19)

Vedanāpabhavaṃ sāvijjaṃ taṇhaṃ dassetvā upādānabhave ca taṃnissite katvā “kāyūpago hotī”tiādinā jātiādike dassentena paccuppannahetusamuṭṭhānato pabhuti ubhayamūlova paṭiccasamuppādo vutto, tabbipariyāyena ca paṇḍitassa paccuppannahetuparikkhayato pabhuti ubhayamūlako paṭilomapaṭiccasamuppādoti.

Having shown craving—which originates from feeling and is accompanied by ignorance—and having treated clinging and becoming as dependent on it, and by showing birth and so on with 'he goes to a body,' etc., dependent origination with both roots is stated as proceeding from the arising of the present cause. And conversely, for the wise, dependent origination in reverse with both roots is stated as proceeding from the exhaustion of the present cause.

Duggatigāmikammassa visesapaccayattā avijjā “avindiyaṃ vindatī”ti vuttā, tathā visesapaccayo vindiyassa na hotīti “vindiyaṃ na vindatī’ti ca. Attani nissitānaṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ pavattanaṃ uppādanaṃ āyatanaṃ. Sammohabhāveneva anabhisamayabhūtattā aviditaṃ aññātaṃ karoti. Antavirahite javāpetīti ca vaṇṇāgamavipariyāyavikāravināsadhātuatthavisesayogehi pañcavidhassa niruttilakkhaṇassa vasena tīsupi padesu a-kāra vi-kāra ja-kāre gahetvā aññesaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ lopaṃ katvā ja-kārassa ca dutiyassa āgamaṃ katvā “avijjā”ti vuttā. Byañjanatthaṃ dassetvā sabhāvatthaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādimāha. Cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ vatthārammaṇāni “idaṃ vatthu, idamārammaṇa”nti avijjāya ñātuṃ [M 0.0090] na sakkāti avijjā tappaṭicchādikā vuttā. Vatthārammaṇasabhāvacchādanato eva avijjādīnaṃ paṭiccasamuppādabhāvassa, jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ paṭiccasamuppannabhāvassa ca chādanato paṭiccasamuppādapaṭiccasamuppannachādanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Due to its being a special condition for kamma leading to a bad destination, ignorance is called 'avindiyaṃ vindatī' (it finds what is not to be found). Likewise, because it is not a special condition for what is to be found, it is also said 'vindiyaṃ na vindatī' (it does not find what is to be found). The proceeding and arising of eye-consciousness and so forth, which are dependent on oneself, is their sphere. Because of its nature as delusion, being uncomprehended, it makes the unknown known. And it is described as 'antavirahite javāpeti' (it propels in the endless). Through the fivefold characteristics of etymology—based on letter-addition, letter-inversion, letter-alteration, letter-destruction, and the application of a special meaning to the root—by taking the syllables 'a,' 'vi,' and 'ja' in the three places, eliding the other letters, and adding a second 'ja,' the term 'avijjā' is said to be formed. Having shown the etymological meaning, to show the meaning of its intrinsic nature, the text begins with 'Furthermore' (apicā). Because the bases and objects of eye-consciousness and the like—'this is the base, this is the object'—cannot be known through ignorance, ignorance is said to be that which conceals them. Precisely from its concealment of the intrinsic nature of bases and objects, and from its concealment of the state of dependent origination for ignorance and so forth, and the state of being dependently arisen for aging and death and so forth, its concealment of the dependently originating and the dependently arisen should be understood.

Saṅkhāra-saddaggahaṇena [V 0.0090] āgatā saṅkhārā saṅkhāra-saddena āgatasaṅkhārā. Yadipi avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāpi saṅkhāra-saddena āgatā, te pana imissā desanāya padhānāti visuṃ vuttā. Tasmā “duvidhā”ti ettha abhisaṅkharaṇakasaṅkhāraṃ saṅkhāra-saddenāgataṃ sandhāya tattha vuttampi vajjetvā saṅkhārasaddena āgatasaṅkhārā yojetabbā. “Saṅkhāra-saddenāgatasaṅkhārā”ti vā samudāyo vutto, tadekadeso ca idha vaṇṇitabbabhāvena “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti, tasmā vaṇṇitabbasabbasaṅgahaṇavasena duvidhatā vuttāti veditabbā. Paṭhamaṃ nirujjhati vacīsaṅkhārotiādinā vitakkavicāraassāsapassāsasaññāvedanāvacīsaṅkhārādayo vuttā, na avijjāsaṅkhāresu vuttā kāyasañcetanādayo.

The formations that come by the term 'formations' are the formations designated by the word 'formations'. Although the formations conditioned by ignorance also come by the term 'formations', they are mentioned separately as they are primary in this discourse. Therefore, here, regarding the statement 'twofold', one should exclude what was said there with reference to the formative formations that come by the word 'formations', and instead apply the formations that come by the word 'formations'. Or, the phrase 'formations that come by the term "formations"' is stated as a collection, and a part of that, namely 'formations conditioned by ignorance', is to be described here; therefore, it should be understood that the twofold nature is stated by way of including all that is to be described. In the passage beginning 'the verbal formation ceases first,' thinking, pondering, in-breathing, out-breathing, perception, feeling, and verbal formations are mentioned, but not bodily volition and so forth, which are mentioned among the formations conditioned by ignorance.

Paritassatīti pipāsati. Bhavatīti upapattibhavaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, bhāvayatīti kammabhavaṃ. Cuti khandhānaṃ maraṇanti “maranti etenā”ti vuttaṃ. “Dukkhā vedanā uppādadukkhā ṭhitidukkhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.465) vacanato dvedhā khaṇati. Āyāsoti parissamo visādo. Kevala-saddo asammissavācako hoti “kevalā sālayo”ti, niravasesavācako ca “kevalā aṅgamagadhā”ti, tasmā dvedhāpi atthaṃ vadati. Tattha asammissassāti sukharahitassa. Na hi ettha kiñci uppādavayarahitaṃ atthīti.

'He is agitated' means he thirsts. 'It becomes' is said with reference to rebirth-becoming, while 'it causes to become' refers to kamma-becoming. Death is the passing away of the aggregates; it is said, 'they die by this.' From the statement, 'Painful feeling is painful in arising and painful in persisting' (MN 1.465), it torments in two ways. 'Distress' means exhaustion and despair. The word 'kevala' (entire) is used to denote unmixed, as in 'unmixed sal trees,' and to denote complete, as in 'the whole of Aṅga and Magadha.' Thus, it conveys both meanings. Here, 'unmixed' means devoid of happiness. Indeed, nothing here is without arising and passing away.

Taṃsampayutte, puggalaṃ vā sammohayatīti sammohanarasā. Ārammaṇasabhāvassa chādanaṃ hutvā gayhatīti chādanapaccupaṭṭhānā. “Āsavasamudayā avijjāsamudayo”ti (ma. ni. 1.103) vacanato āsavapadaṭṭhānā. Paṭisandhijananatthaṃ āyūhanti byāpāraṃ karontīti āyūhanarasā, rāsikaraṇaṃ vā āyūhanaṃ. Nāmarūpassa purecārikabhāvena pavattatīti pubbaṅgamarasaṃ. Purimabhavena saddhiṃ ghaṭanaṃ hutvā gayhatīti paṭisandhipaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Viññāṇena saha sampayujjatīti sampayogarasaṃ. Aññamaññaṃ sampayogābhāvato rūpaṃ vikiratīti vikiraṇarasaṃ. Evañca katvā pisiyamānā taṇḍulādayo vikiranti cuṇṇī bhavantīti. Nāmassa kadāci kusalādibhāvo ca atthīti tato [M 0.0091] visesanatthaṃ “abyākatapaccupaṭṭhāna”nti āha. “Acetanā abyākatā”ti ettha viya anārammaṇatā vā abyākatatā daṭṭhabbā. Āyatanalakkhaṇanti ghaṭanalakkhaṇaṃ, āyānaṃ tananalakkhaṇaṃ vā. Dassanādīnaṃ kāraṇabhāvo dassanādirasatā. Akusalavipākupekkhāya aniṭṭhabhāvato dukkhena itarāya ca iṭṭhabhāvato sukhena saṅgahitattā “sukhadukkhapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti āha. Dukkhasamudayattā hetulakkhaṇā taṇhā. “Tatratatrābhinandinī”ti (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.133, 460; vibha. 203) vacanato [V 0.0091] abhinandanarasā. Cittassa, puggalassa vā rūpādīsu atittabhāvo hutvā gayhatīti atittabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Taṇhādaḷhattaṃ hutvā kāmupādānaṃ, sesāni diṭṭhi hutvā upaṭṭhahantīti taṇhādaḷhattadiṭṭhipaccupaṭṭhānā. Kammupapattibhavavasena bhavassa lakkhaṇādayo yojetabbā.

Associated with that, it deludes a person—thus its essence is delusion. Concealing the inherent nature of the object, it is grasped—thus its manifestation is concealment. From the statement, 'With the arising of the taints, ignorance arises' (MN 1.103), its proximate cause is the taints. They exert effort for the purpose of generating rebirth—thus their essence is exertion, or accumulation is exertion. It occurs as the forerunner of name-and-form—thus its essence is being the precursor. Connecting with the previous existence, it is grasped—thus its manifestation is rebirth-linking. It is associated with consciousness—thus its essence is association. Because there is no mutual association, form scatters—thus its essence is scattering. And in this way, when being pounded, rice and the like scatter and become powder. Since name sometimes has the nature of wholesome qualities and so forth, to distinguish it from that, it is said to manifest as indeterminate. Here, as in 'unconscious and indeterminate,' non-objectiveness or indeterminacy should be regarded. The characteristic of the sense-base is the characteristic of connection, or the characteristic of extension or proliferation. Its essence is being the cause of seeing and so forth. Because unwholesome-resultant equanimity, due to its undesirable nature, is included under suffering, and the other kind, due to its desirable nature, is included under pleasure, its manifestation is said to be pleasure and pain. Because it is the origin of suffering, craving has the characteristic of a root cause. From the statement, 'Delighting in this and that' (DN 2.400; MN 1.133, 460; Vibh 203), its essence is delight. For the mind or the person, being insatiable in forms and so forth, it is grasped—thus its manifestation is insatiability. Being the firmness of craving, it manifests as clinging to sensual pleasures; the others, being views, manifest—thus its manifestation is the firmness of craving and views. The characteristics and so forth of existence should be connected in terms of kamma-existence and rebirth-existence.

Ādi-saddena anubodhādibhāvaggahaṇaṃ. Dukkhādīsu aññāṇaṃ appaṭipatti, asubhādīsu subhādivipallāsā micchāpaṭipatti. Diṭṭhivippayuttā vā appaṭipatti, diṭṭhisampayuttā micchāpaṭipatti. Na avijjāya eva chadvārikatā chaḷārammaṇatā ca, atha kho aññesupi paṭiccasamuppādaṅgesu arūpadhammānanti āha “sabbesupī”ti. Nobhayagocaranti manāyatanamāha. Na hi arūpadhammānaṃ desavasena āsannatā dūratā ca atthi asaṇṭhānattā, tasmā manāyatanassa gocaro na manāyatanaṃ sampatto asampatto vāti vuccatīti.

By the word 'ādi' (and so forth), the inclusion of states such as comprehension is indicated. Regarding suffering and so forth, ignorance is non-practice; regarding the unattractive and so forth, the perversions of perceiving them as attractive and so forth are wrong practice. Alternatively, non-practice is dissociated from views, while wrong practice is associated with views. It is not only ignorance that has six doors and six objects, but also the other immaterial factors of dependent origination—thus it is said, 'in all cases.' It is said that the mind-base is 'not a domain of both,' that is, of near and far. For immaterial phenomena, there is no nearness or distance by way of location, because they are without physical shape. Therefore, it is not said of the domain of the mind-base that it is reached or not reached.

Sokādīnaṃ sabbhāvā aṅgabahuttappasaṅge “dvādasevā”ti aṅgānaṃ vavatthānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Na hi sokādayo aṅgabhāvena vuttā, phalena pana kāraṇaṃ avijjaṃ mūlaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ te vuttāti. Jarāmaraṇabbhāhatassa hi bālassa te sambhavantīti sokādīnaṃ jarāmaraṇakāraṇatā vuttā. “Sārīrikāya dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.252) ca sutte jarāmaraṇanimittañca dukkhaṃ saṅgahitanti taṃtaṃnimittānaṃ sādhakabhāvena vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana jarāmaraṇeneva sokādīnaṃ ekasaṅkhepo kato, tasmā tesaṃ jātipaccayatā yujjati. Jarāmaraṇapaccayabhāve hi avijjāya ekasaṅkhepo kātabbo siyā, jātipaccayā pana jarāmaraṇaṃ sokādayo ca sambhavantīti. Tattha jarāmaraṇaṃ ekantikaṃ aṅgabhāveneva gahitaṃ, sokādayo [M 0.0092] pana rūpabhavādīsu abhāvato anekantikā kevalaṃ pākaṭena phalena avijjānidassanatthaṃ gahitā. Tena anāgate jātiyā sati tato parāya paṭisandhiyā hetuhetubhūtā avijjā dassitāti bhavacakkassa avicchedo dassito hotīti. Suttañca sokādīnaṃ avijjā kāraṇanti etassevatthassa sādhakaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na sokādīnaṃ bālassa jarāmaraṇanimittatāmattassa. “Assutavā puthujjano”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.252) hi vacanena avijjā sokādīnaṃ kāraṇanti dassitā, na ca jarāmaraṇanimittameva dukkhaṃ dukkhanti.

Due to the existence of sorrow and so forth, and the possibility of a multiplicity of factors, the determination of the factors as 'only twelve' should be understood. For sorrow and the like are not mentioned as factors themselves, but they are stated to show ignorance, the root factor, through their effects. Indeed, sorrow and the like arise in a fool afflicted by aging and death—thus, sorrow and the like are said to be caused by aging and death. Moreover, in the sutta, 'afflicted by bodily painful feeling' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.252), suffering is included as a sign of aging and death, and thus it is said to be instrumental as a proof of their respective signs. However, since sorrow and the like are collectively summarized with aging and death alone, their conditionality by birth is justified. For if they were conditioned by aging and death, a single summary would have to be made with respect to ignorance; but when birth is the condition, aging and death as well as sorrow and the like arise. Here, aging and death are invariably included as factors, whereas sorrow and the like, being absent in the form realm and other existences, are not invariably included and are only included to demonstrate ignorance through their evident effects. Thus, in the future, when birth exists, ignorance is shown as the root cause for the subsequent rebirth-linking, thereby demonstrating the unbroken continuity of the wheel of existence. Furthermore, the sutta should be seen as supporting the idea that ignorance is the cause of sorrow and the like, not merely that sorrow and the like are a sign of aging and death for a fool. For the statement, 'the uninstructed ordinary person' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.252), shows that ignorance is the cause of sorrow and the like, and not that suffering is merely the sign of aging and death.

Uddesavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the chapter on the outline is completed.

Avijjāpadaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Ignorance'

226. “Avijjāpaccayā 92 saṅkhārā”ti hi vuttanti etena avijjāya visesanabhāvena saṅkhārānañca padhānabhāvena vuttattā saṅkhārānaṃ niddisitabbabhāvassa kāraṇaṃ dasseti. Pitā kathīyati “dīgho sāmo, mitto rasso, odāto datto”ti.

226. Indeed, it is said: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations.' By this, because it is stated that ignorance is a specifying factor and volitional formations are primary, the reason for the need to expound on volitional formations is shown. A father is spoken of thus: 'Dīgha, the dark one; Mitta, the short one; Datta, the fair one.'

Rasitabbo paṭivijjhitabbo sabhāvo raso, attano raso saraso, yāthāvo saraso yāthāvasaraso, so eva lakkhitabbattā lakkhaṇanti yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ. “Katamā ca, bhikkhave, avijjā? Dukkhe aññāṇa”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.2; ma. ni. 1.103) sutte cattāreva vuttānīti “suttantikapariyāyenā”ti āha. Nikkhepakaṇḍe panātiādinā idha catūsu ṭhānesu kathitāya eva avijjāya nikkhepakaṇḍe aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu kiccajātito pañcavīsatiyā padehi lakkhaṇato ca kathitattā tadatthasaṃvaṇṇanāvasena vibhāvanaṃ karoti. Ahāpetvā vibhajitabbavibhajanañhi abhidhammapariyāyo.

Essence (rasa) is a nature that should be tasted and penetrated; its own essence is 'sarasa'; the true 'sarasa' is 'yāthāvasarasa.' Since it is to be characterized as such, the characteristic is the 'characteristic of true essence' (yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇa). 'And what, bhikkhus, is ignorance? Ignorance of suffering,' and so forth—in the Sutta (Saṃ. Ni. 2.2; Ma. Ni. 1.103) only four are mentioned; thus he says, 'according to the Suttanta method.' In the Nikkhepakaṇḍa, however, and so on—here, although ignorance is spoken of in four places, in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa it is spoken of in eight places in terms of function-type, and in twenty-five terms in terms of characteristic; thus, for the purpose of elucidating its meaning, an explanation is made. For the Abhidhamma method is analysis, dividing what should be divided, without omitting anything.

Jāyati etthāti jāti, uppattiṭṭhānaṃ. Yadipi nirodhamagge avijjā ārammaṇaṃ na karoti, te pana jānitukāmassa tappaṭicchādanavasena anirodhamaggesu nirodhamaggaggahaṇakaāraṇavasena ca pavattamānā tattha uppajjatīti vuccatīti tesampi avijjāya uppattiṭṭhānatā hoti, itaresaṃ ārammaṇabhāvena [M 0.0093] cāti. Saṅghikabaladevagoṇādīnaṃ saṅghāṭinaṅgalādīni viya aññasetādīnaṃ avijjāya dukkhādivisayānaṃ andhattakarānaṃ lobhādīnaṃ nivattako aññāṇādisabhāvo lakkhaṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

It arises therein, thus 'birth' (jāti), the place of arising. Although ignorance does not make the path of cessation its object, yet for one who desires to know, because it operates by concealing that state and, in the non-cessation paths, by causing the path of cessation to be apprehended as a non-cessation path, it is said to arise there. Thus, even for these, there is a place of arising for ignorance; and for others, it is by way of being an object. Just as robes and plows belong to the Sangha, oxen to Baladeva, and so on, so too, the characteristic of ignorance is to be understood as the nature of not-knowing and so forth, which causes blindness regarding the objects of suffering and so on, and which prevents the turning away from greed and other defilements.

Atthatthanti phalaphalaṃ. Āmeḍitavacanañhi sabbesaṃ atthānaṃ visuṃ visuṃ pākaṭakaraṇabhāvappakāsanatthaṃ. Attho eva vā attho atthatthoti atthassa aviparītatādassanatthaṃ atthenevatthaṃ visesayati. Na hi ñāṇaṃ anatthaṃ atthoti gaṇhātīti. Evaṃ kāraṇakāraṇanti etthāpi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃ ākāranti atthatthādiākāraṃ. Gahetvāti citte pavesetvā, cittena puggalena vā gahitaṃ katvā. Paṭividdhassa puna avekkhaṇā paccavekkhaṇā. Duccintitacintitādilakkhaṇassa bālassa bhāvo bālyaṃ. Pajānātīti pakārehi jānāti. Balavamohanaṃ pamoho. Samantato mohanaṃ sammoho.

The meaning of 'atthattha' is the fruit of the fruit. The reduplicated word is indeed for the purpose of revealing the distinct manifestation of each and every meaning. Or, 'atthattha' means 'meaning is indeed meaning,' to show the non-perversion of the meaning. It specifies the meaning by the meaning itself. For knowledge does not grasp what is not the meaning as the meaning. Similarly, 'cause of cause' (kāraṇakāraṇa) should be seen here as well. That mode (ākāra) means the mode of 'atthattha' and so on. 'Having grasped' (gahetvā) means having entered it into the mind, or having made it grasped by the mind or the individual. For one who has penetrated, the repeated reviewing is re-examination (paccavekkhaṇā). The state of a fool, characterized by ill-conceived thinking and the like, is foolishness (bālya). 'Pajānāti' means one knows in various ways. Strong delusion is 'pamoho.' Utter delusion is 'sammoho.'

Dukkhārammaṇatāti [V 0.0093] dukkhārammaṇatāya, yāya vā avijjāya chādentiyā dukkhārammaṇā taṃsampayuttadhammā, sā tesaṃ bhāvoti dukkhārammaṇatā, ārammaṇameva vā ārammaṇatā, dukkhaṃ ārammaṇatā etissāti dukkhārammaṇatā.

'Dukkhārammaṇatā' means by way of having suffering as an object. Or, by which obscuring ignorance the associated states come to have suffering as their object, that state of theirs is `dukkhārammaṇatā`. Or, object-ness is simply the object; for this, suffering is its object-ness, thus `dukkhārammaṇatā`.

Duddasattā gambhīrā na sabhāvato, tasmā tadārammaṇatā avijjā uppajjati, itaresaṃ sabhāvato gambhīrattā tadārammaṇatā nuppajjatīti adhippāyo. Apica kho panāti maggassa saṅkhatasabhāvattā tatopi nirodhassa gambhīratarataṃ dasseti.

They are profound due to being hard to see, not by their intrinsic nature; therefore, ignorance with them as its object arises. But for others, because they are profound by their intrinsic nature, ignorance with them as its object does not arise—this is the meaning. Moreover, it shows the even greater profundity of cessation than that of the path, because the path has a conditioned nature.

Avijjāpadaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Ignorance' is concluded.

Saṅkhārapadaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Volitional Formations'

Punātīti sodheti apuññaphalato dukkhasaṃkilesato ca, hitasukhajjhāsayena puññaṃ karotīti taṃnipphādanena kārakassajjhāsayaṃ pūretīti puñño, pūrako pujjanibbattako ca niruttilakkhaṇena “puñño”ti veditabbo. Samādhipaccanīkānaṃ atidūratāya na iñjati na calatīti attho. Kāyassāti dvārassa sāmibhāvena niddeso kato.

'Punāti' means it purifies, it cleanses from the fruit of demerit and from suffering and defilement. By the intention for welfare and happiness, one performs merit (puñña); by accomplishing that, it fulfills (pūreti) the doer's intention—thus, it is called 'puñña.' It is to be understood by the characteristic of etymology as 'that which fills' (pūraka) and 'that which produces honor' (pujjanibbattaka). Due to being very far from the opponents of concentration, it does not waver or move—this is the meaning. 'Of the body' (kāyassa) is a designation made by way of it being the master of the door.

Puññupaganti [M 0.0094] bhavasampattupagaṃ. Tatthāti vibhaṅgasutte (saṃ. ni. 2.2). Tañhi padhānabhāvena gahitanti. Sammādiṭṭhisutte (ma. ni. 1.102) pana “tayome, āvuso, saṅkhārā”ti āgatanti. Sabbaññujinabhāsito pana ayaṃ, na paccekajinabhāsito, imassatthassa dīpanatthaṃ etesaṃ suttānaṃ vasena te gahitā. Kathaṃ panetena gahaṇenāyamattho dīpito hotīti taṃdassanatthamāha “abhidhammepi hi suttepi ekasadisāva tanti niddiṭṭhā”ti. Sabbaññubhāsitoti pākaṭena suttantena sadisattā ayampi sabbaññubhāsitoti ñāyatīti vuttaṃ hotīti.

'Puññupaga' (merit-bound) means bound for the attainment of existence. 'Therein' refers to the Vibhaṅga Sutta (Saṃ. Ni. 2.2), for it is taken as primary. In the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta (Ma. Ni. 1.102), however, it appears thus: 'These, friends, are the three kinds of volitional formations.' But this is spoken by the All-knowing Conqueror, not by a Paccekajina; to clarify this meaning, they are taken by way of these suttas. How, then, is this meaning clarified by this citation? To show this, it is said: 'For in both the Abhidhamma and the Suttas, the very same doctrine is indicated.' Because this is similar to a manifest Suttanta, it is understood that this too is spoken by the All-knowing One—so it is said.

“Terasāpī”ti vuttaṃ, tattha ñāṇavippayuttānaṃ na bhāvanāmayatā pākaṭāti “yathā hī”tiādimāha[V 0.0094]. Pathavī pathavītiādibhāvanā ca kasiṇaparikammakaraṇaṃ maṇḍalakaraṇañca bhāvanaṃ bhajāpenti.

'All thirteen' is said. Herein, for those dissociated from knowledge, their nature as mental cultivation is not manifest. Thus, he says, 'as indeed,' and so forth. And the cultivation of 'earth, earth,' and so forth, the preliminary work for the kasinas, and the making of the circle, lead to participation in cultivation.

Dānavasena pavattā cittacetasikā dhammā dānaṃ. Tattha byāpārabhūtā āyūhanacetanā dānaṃ ārabbha dānaṃ adhikicca uppajjatīti vuccati, evaṃ itaresu. Somanassacittenāti anumodanāpavattinidassanamattametaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Upekkhāsahagatenapi hi anussarati evāti.

The mental and mental factors that arise by way of giving are 'giving' (dāna). Herein, the accumulating volition, which is the active function, is said to arise concerning giving, with reference to giving; similarly in the other cases. 'With a joyful mind' (somanassacittena) should be regarded merely as an instance showing the occurrence of appreciation. For one does indeed recollect even with a mind accompanied by equanimity.

Asarikkhakampi sarikkhakena catutthajjhānavipākena vehapphalādīsu vināpi asaññesu kaṭattārūpaṃ. Rūpameva saphandanattā “saiñjana”nti vuttaṃ iñjanakaranīvaraṇādīnaṃ avikkhambhanato, rūpataṇhāsaṅkhātassa iñjanakassa kāraṇattā vā. Teneva rūpārammaṇaṃ nimittārammaṇañca sabbampi catutthajjhānaṃ nippariyāyena “aniñjana”nti na vuccatīti. Mahātulāya dhārayamāno nāḷiyā minamāno ca samudāyameva dhāreti minati ca, na ekekaṃ guñjaṃ, ekekaṃ taṇḍulaṃ vā, evaṃ bhagavāpi aparimāṇā paṭhamakusalacetanāyo samudāyavaseneva gahetvā ekajātikattā ekameva katvā dasseti. Evaṃ dutiyādayopīti.

Even the dissimilar is similar to the fourth-jhāna-resultant in the Vehapphala realm and so on—even apart from the non-percipient beings—in having karmically produced form. Because form itself has vibration, it is called 'with vibration' (saiñjana), due to the non-suppression of the causes of vibration, such as the hindrances, or because it is a cause of that which vibrates, which is craving for form. For that reason, not every fourth jhāna with a form-object or a sign-object is called 'non-vibrating' (aniñjana) without qualification. Just as one weighing with a large scale or measuring with a nāḷi measure weighs or measures the whole collection, not each single guñja seed or each single grain of rice, so too the Blessed One, taking the immeasurable first wholesome volitions by way of a collection, shows them as one because they are of a single genesis. So too for the second and the others.

“Kāyadvāre pavattā”ti avatvā “ādānaggahaṇacopanaṃ pāpayamānā uppannā”tipi vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti vacanavisesamattameva dasseti. Kāyadvāre pavatti eva hi ādānādipāpanāti. Purimena vā dvārassa upalakkhaṇabhāvo vutto, pacchimena cetanāya saviññattirūpasamuṭṭhāpanaṃ. Tattha ākaḍḍhitvā gahaṇaṃ ādānaṃ, sampayuttassa gahaṇaṃ gahaṇaṃ, phandanaṃ copanaṃ.

Instead of saying 'it occurs at the body-door' (kāyadvāre pavattā), it can also be said 'arisen while causing seizing, grasping, and agitation' (ādānaggahaṇacopanaṃ pāpayamānā uppannā); this only shows a difference in expression. For occurrence at the body-door is indeed the causing of seizing and so on. Alternatively, by the former, the characteristic of the door is stated; by the latter, volition's origination of form-with-intimation. Therein, 'ādāna' is grasping after drawing near; 'gahaṇa' is grasping what is associated; 'copana' is trembling.

Etthāti [M 0.0095] kāyavacīsaṅkhāraggahaṇe, kāyavacīsañcetanāgahaṇe vā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ abhiññācetanā na gahitā viññāṇassa paccayo na hotīti. Kasmā pana na hoti, nanu sāpi kusalā vipākadhammā cāti? Saccaṃ, anupacchinnataṇhāvijjāmāne pana santāne sabyāpārappavattiyā tassā kusalatā vipākadhammatā ca vuttā, na vipākuppādanena, sā pana vipākaṃ uppādayantī rūpāvacarameva uppādeyya. Na hi aññabhūmikaṃ kammaṃ aññabhūmikaṃ vipākaṃ uppādetīti. Attanā sadisārammaṇañca tiṭṭhānikaṃ taṃ uppādeyya cittuppādakaṇḍe rūpāvacaravipākassa kammasadisārammaṇasseva vuttattā, na ca rūpāvacaravipāko parittādiārammaṇo atthi, abhiññācetanā ca parittādiārammaṇāva hoti, tasmā vipākaṃ na uppādetīti [V 0.0095] viññāyati. Kasiṇesu ca uppāditassa catutthajjhānasamādhissa ānisaṃsabhūtā abhiññā. Yathāha “so evaṃ samāhite citte”tiādi (dī. ni. 1.244-245; ma. ni. 1.384-386). Tasmā samādhiphalasadisā sā, na ca phalaṃ detīti dānasīlānisaṃso tasmiṃ bhave paccayalābho viya sāpi vipākaṃ na uppādeti. Yathā ca abhiññācetanā, evaṃ uddhaccacetanāpi na hotīti idaṃ uddhaccasahagate dhamme visuṃ uddharitvā “tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti (vibha. 725) vuttattā vicāretabbaṃ.

'Here' (ettha) refers to the grasping of bodily and verbal formations, or the grasping of bodily and verbal volitions. In the Commentary, the volition of direct knowledge (abhiññācetanā) is not included, as it is not a condition for consciousness. But why not? Is it not also wholesome and a state that produces a result? True, but in a continuity where craving and ignorance remain unbroken, its wholesomeness and its nature of producing a result are spoken of in terms of its active operation, not in terms of producing a result. Moreover, if it were to produce a result, it would produce only a form-sphere result. For kamma of one sphere does not produce a result in another sphere. It would produce a result that is of the same plane and has an object similar to its own, because in the section on the arising of consciousness it is said that form-sphere results have objects similar to the kamma. But there is no form-sphere result that has a limited object, etc., whereas the volition of direct knowledge has only a limited object, etc. Therefore, it is understood that it does not produce a result. And direct knowledge is a benefit of the fourth-jhāna concentration produced in relation to the kasiṇas, as it is said: 'With his mind thus concentrated...' (Dī. Ni. 1.244–245; Ma. Ni. 1.384–386). Therefore, it is similar to the fruit of concentration, but it does not give a fruit. Just like the benefit of giving and virtue, which is the obtaining of requisites in that very life, it too does not produce a result. The proposition that 'just as the volition of direct knowledge does not, so too the volition accompanied by restlessness does not' should be investigated, since, having separately extracted the states associated with restlessness, it is said: 'In their result there is knowledge, the analytical knowledge of meaning' (Vibh. 725).

Ayaṃ panettha amataggapathānugato vinicchayo – dassanabhāvanānaṃ abhāvepi yesaṃ puthujjanānaṃ sekkhānañca dassanabhāvanāhi bhavitabbaṃ, tesaṃ taduppattikāle tehi pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā akusalā “dassanena pahātabbā bhāvanāya pahātabbā”ti ca vuccanti, puthujjanānaṃ pana bhāvanāya abhāvā bhāvanāya pahātabbacintā natthi. Tena tesaṃ pavattamānā te dassanena pahātuṃ asakkuṇeyyāpi “bhāvanāya pahātabbā”ti na vuccanti. Yadi vucceyyuṃ, dassanena pahātabbā bhāvanāya pahātabbānaṃ kesañci keci kadāci ārammaṇārammaṇādhipatiupanissayapaccayehi paccayo bhaveyyuṃ, na ca paṭṭhāne “dassanena pahātabbā bhāvanāya pahātabbānaṃ kesañci kenaci paccayena paccayo”ti vuttā. Sekkhānaṃ pana vijjamānā bhāvanāya pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā bhāvanāya pahātabbā. Teneva sekkhānaṃ dassanena pahātabbā cattattā vantattā muttattā pahīnattā paṭinissaṭṭhattā ukkheṭitattā samukkheṭitattā assāditabbā abhinanditabbā [M 0.0096] ca na honti, pahīnatāya eva somanassahetubhūtā avikkhepahetubhūtā ca na domanassaṃ uddhaccañca uppādentīti na te tesaṃ ārammaṇārammaṇādhipatibhāvaṃ pakatūpanissayabhāvañca gacchanti. Na hi pahīne upanissāya ariyo rāgādikilese uppādeti.

Herein, this is the determination that follows the path to the Deathless: For those ordinary people and trainees by whom seeing and development are to be cultivated, even in the absence of actualized seeing and development, the unwholesome states that could be abandoned by them at the time of the arising of those paths are called 'to be abandoned by seeing' and 'to be abandoned by development.' But for ordinary people, since they lack development, there is no consideration of what is to be abandoned by development. Therefore, the unwholesome states occurring in them, even those that cannot be abandoned by seeing, are not called 'to be abandoned by development.' If they were so called, then some states to be abandoned by seeing would, for some, at some time, be a condition for some states to be abandoned by development by way of object, object-predominance, or decisive support condition. Yet in the Paṭṭhāna it is not said: 'States to be abandoned by seeing are a condition for some states to be abandoned by development by any condition.' For trainees, however, the states that can be abandoned by development, which is present for them, are 'to be abandoned by development.' For that very reason, for trainees, the states to be abandoned by seeing are given up, disgorged, released, abandoned, relinquished, uprooted, and thoroughly uprooted; they are not to be savored or delighted in. Precisely because they are abandoned, they are not a cause for mental joy or for non-distraction, and they do not produce mental pain or restlessness. Therefore, they do not attain for them the state of object, object-predominance, or natural decisive support. For a noble one does not generate defilements such as greed by depending on what has been abandoned.

Vuttañca “sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchati…pe… arahattamaggena…pe… na paccāgacchatī”ti (mahāni. 80; cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 27), na ca puthujjanānaṃ dassanena pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā itaresaṃ na kenaci paccayena paccayo hontīti sakkā vattuṃ “diṭṭhiṃ assādeti abhinandati, taṃ ārabbha rāgo uppajjati, diṭṭhi vicikicchā uddhaccaṃ uppajjati. Vicikicchaṃ ārabbha vicikicchā diṭṭhi uddhaccaṃ uppajjatī”ti diṭṭhivicikicchānaṃ uddhaccārammaṇapaccayabhāvassa vuttattā. Ettha hi uddhaccanti uddhaccasahagataṃ cittuppādaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evañca katvā adhipatipaccayaniddese “diṭṭhiṃ garuṃ [V 0.0096] katvā assādeti abhinandati, taṃ garuṃ katvā rāgo uppajjati, diṭṭhi uppajjatī”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.409) ettakameva vuttaṃ, na vuttaṃ “uddhaccaṃ uppajjatī”ti. Tasmā dassanabhāvanāhi pahātabbānaṃ atītādibhāvena navattabbattepi yādisānaṃ tāhi anuppattidhammatā āpādetabbā, tesu puthujjanesu vattamānā dassanaṃ apekkhitvā tena pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā dassanena pahātabbā, sekkhesu vattamānā bhāvanaṃ apekkhitvā tāya pahātuṃ sakkuṇeyyā bhāvanāya pahātabbā. Tesu bhāvanāya pahātabbā sahāyavirahā vipākaṃ na janayantīti bhāvanāya pahātabbacetanāya nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayabhāvo na vutto, apekkhitabbadassanabhāvanārahitānaṃ pana puthujjanesu uppajjamānānaṃ sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgādīnaṃ uddhaccasahagatacittuppādassa ca saṃyojanattayatadekaṭṭhakilesānaṃ anupacchinnatāya aparikkhīṇasahāyānaṃ vipākuppādanaṃ na sakkā paṭikkhipitunti uddhaccasahagatadhammānaṃ vipāko vibhaṅge vuttoti.

And it is said: 'The defilements abandoned by the path of stream-entry—those defilements he does not return to, does not revert to, does not come back to… and so on… by the path of arahantship… he does not come back to' (Mahāni. 80; Cūḷani. Mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa 27). And it cannot be said that the defilements that can be abandoned by seeing in ordinary people are not a condition in any way for the other defilements, because it has been stated that views and doubt are an object-condition for restlessness, as in: 'One savors and delights in a view; with that as basis, greed arises; view, doubt, and restlessness arise. With doubt as basis, doubt, view, and restlessness arise.' Here, 'restlessness' is said with reference to a consciousness-moment accompanied by restlessness. And so, in the exposition of the predominance condition, only this much is said: 'Having made a view important, one savors and delights in it; having made that important, greed arises, a view arises' (Paṭṭhā. 1.1.409); it is not said 'restlessness arises.' Therefore, although the defilements to be abandoned by seeing and development cannot be spoken of as past, etc., the quality of non-arising must be brought about for them by means of those paths. Among these, those present in ordinary people that can be abandoned by relying on seeing are 'to be abandoned by seeing'; those present in trainees that can be abandoned by relying on development are 'to be abandoned by development.' Among these, for a trainee, those to be abandoned by development, being deprived of their allies, do not generate a result; therefore, for the volition associated with what is to be abandoned by development, the state of being a different-moment kamma-condition is not mentioned. However, for ordinary people who are devoid of the seeing and development that should be relied upon, when desire and greed for their own belongings and consciousness-moments accompanied by restlessness arise, since the three fetters and the defilements of a single substance with them are not cut off and their allies are not exhausted, the production of a result cannot be denied. Thus, the result of states accompanied by restlessness is mentioned in the Vibhaṅga.

Yadi evaṃ, apekkhitabbadassanabhāvanārahitānaṃ akusalānaṃ nevadassanenanabhāvanāyapahātabbatā āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati, appahātabbānaṃ “neva dassanena na bhāvanāya pahātabbā”ti (dha. sa. tikamātikā 8) vuttattā, appahātabbaviruddhasabhāvattā ca akusalānaṃ. Evampi tesaṃ imasmiṃ tike navattabbatā āpajjatīti? Nāpajjati cittuppādakaṇḍe dassitānaṃ dvādasaakusalacittuppādānaṃ dvīhi padehi saṅgahitattā. Yathā hi dhammavasena saṅkhatadhammā [M 0.0097] sabbe saṅgahitāti uppannattike kālavasena asaṅgahitāpi atītā navattabbāti na vuttā cittuppādarūpabhāvena gahitesu navattabbassa abhāvā, evamidhāpi cittuppādabhāvena gahitesu navattabbassa abhāvā navattabbatā na vuttāti veditabbā. Yattha hi cittuppādo koci niyogato navattabbo atthi, tattha tesaṃ catuttho koṭṭhāso atthīti yathāvuttapadesu viya tatthāpi bhinditvā bhajāpetabbe cittuppāde bhinditvā bhajāpeti “siyā navattabbā parittārammaṇā”tiādinā. Tadabhāvā uppannattike idha ca tathā na vuttā.

If so, does it follow that unwholesome states, which are devoid of the required seeing and development, are not to be abandoned either by seeing or by development? It does not follow, because for the unabandonable states it is said, 'not to be abandoned either by seeing or by development' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Tika Mātikā 8), and because unwholesome states are of a nature contrary to what is unabandonable. Even so, does it follow that they are 'not to be stated' in this triad? It does not follow, because the twelve unwholesome consciousness-arisings, shown in the chapter on the arising of consciousness, are included by two terms. For just as in the triad of the arisen, all conditioned phenomena are included by way of phenomena, so even the past, though not included by way of time, is not said to be 'not to be stated,' because among those grasped as the arising of consciousness and form, there is nothing 'not to be stated.' Similarly here, it should be understood that since among those grasped as the arising of consciousness there is nothing 'not to be stated,' 'not to be stated' is not mentioned. For wherever a consciousness-arising is necessarily 'not to be stated,' there is a fourth category for them, just as in the aforementioned sections, where a consciousness-arising that is to be divided and classified is divided and classified, as in: 'They may be not to be stated, with limited objects,' and so on. Due to the absence of that, it is not stated thus, either in the triad of the arisen or here.

Atha vā yathā sappaṭighehi samānasabhāvattā rūpadhātuyaṃ tayo mahābhūtā “sappaṭighā”ti vuttā. Yathāha “asaññasattānaṃ anidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ ekaṃ mahābhūtaṃ paṭicca dve mahābhūtā, dve mahābhūte paṭicca ekaṃ mahābhūta”nti (paṭṭhā. 2.22.9). Evaṃ puthujjanānaṃ pavattamānā bhāvanāya pahātabbasamānasabhāvā “bhāvanāya pahātabbā”ti vucceyyunti natthi navattabbatāpasaṅgo. Evañca sati puthujjanānaṃ pavattamānāpi bhāvanāya pahātabbā sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgādayo [V 0.0097] parabhaṇḍe chandarāgādīnaṃ upanissayapaccayo, rāgo ca rāgadiṭṭhīnaṃ adhipatipaccayoti ayamattho laddho hoti. Yathā pana aphoṭṭhabbattā rūpadhātuyaṃ tayo mahābhūtā na paramatthato sappaṭighā, evaṃ apekkhitabbabhāvanārahitā puthujjanesu pavattamānā sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgādayo na paramatthato bhāvanāya pahātabbāti bhāvanāya pahātabbānaṃ nānākkhaṇikakammapaccayatā na vuttā, na ca “dassanena pahātabbā bhāvanāya pahātabbānaṃ kenaci paccayena paccayo”ti vuttā. Ye hi dassanena pahātabbapaccayā kilesā, na te dassanato uddhaṃ pavattanti, dassanena pahātabbapaccayassapi pana uddhaccasahagatassa sahāyavekallamattameva dassanena kataṃ, na tassa koci bhāvo dassanena anuppattidhammataṃ āpāditoti tassa ekantabhāvanāya pahātabbatā vuttā. Tasmā tassa tādisasseva sati sahāye vipākuppādanavacanaṃ, asati ca vipākānuppādanavacanaṃ na virujjhatīti.

Alternatively, just as the three great elements in the form realm are called 'with resistance' because they share the same nature as things with resistance, as it is said: 'For non-percipient beings, the invisible with resistance is one great element dependent on two great elements, and two great elements dependent on one great element' (Paṭṭhā. 2.22.9). In the same way, that which occurs in ordinary people and shares the same nature as what is to be abandoned by development may be called 'to be abandoned by development,' and thus there is no occasion for it to be 'not to be stated.' This being the case, the meaning is obtained that even what occurs in ordinary people is to be abandoned by development; desire and lust, etc., regarding one's own possessions are a decisive support condition for desire and lust, etc., regarding others' possessions, and lust is a predominance condition for lust and views. However, just as the three great elements in the form realm are not ultimately 'with resistance' because they are intangible, similarly, the desire and lust, etc., occurring in ordinary people regarding their own possessions—being devoid of the required development—are not ultimately 'to be abandoned by development.' Thus, the conditionality of karma of different moments for what is to be abandoned by development is not stated, nor is it said, 'What is to be abandoned by seeing is a condition in any way for what is to be abandoned by development.' For those defilements which are conditions to be abandoned by seeing do not persist after the seeing. Yet, even for that which is a condition to be abandoned by seeing and is accompanied by restlessness, only the mere lack of a companion is effected by the seeing—no aspect of it is brought by the seeing to a state of non-arising. Thus, its being exclusively 'to be abandoned by development' is stated. Therefore, when a companion of such a kind exists, the statement of the arising of a result, and when it does not exist, the statement of the non-arising of a result, is not contradictory.

Sāpi viññāṇapaccayabhāve yadi apanetabbā, kasmā “samavīsati cetanā”ti vuttanti tassa kāraṇaṃ dassento āha “avijjāpaccayā pana [M 0.0098] sabbāpetā hontī”ti. Yadi evaṃ, abhiññācetanāya saha “ekavīsatī”ti vattabbanti? Na, avacanassa vuttakāraṇattā, taṃ pana itarāvacanassapi kāraṇanti samānacetanāvacanakāraṇavacanena yaṃ kāraṇaṃ apekkhitvā ekā vuttā, tena kāraṇena itarāyapi vattabbataṃ, yañca kāraṇaṃ apekkhitvā itarā na vuttā, tena kāraṇena vuttāyapi avattabbataṃ dasseti. Āneñjābhisaṅkhāro cittasaṅkhāro evāti bhedābhāvā pākaṭoti na tassa saṃyogo dassito.

If even that volition should be excluded on the basis of being conditioned by consciousness, why then is it said, 'There are twenty volitions'? Showing the reason for that, he says, 'But all these are conditioned by ignorance.' If so, should it not be said, 'There are twenty-one,' including the volition of direct knowledge? No, because the reason for not stating it has been given. And that is also the reason for the non-statement of the other. By stating the reason for stating similar volitions, it shows that by the reason for which one was stated, by that same reason the other also should have been stated; and by the reason for which the other was not stated, by that same reason even the one that was stated should not have been stated. The imperturbable formation is simply the mental formation—thus, due to the absence of difference, it is clear, so its conjunction is not shown.

Sukhasaññāya gahetvāti etena taṇhāpavattiṃ dasseti. Taṇhāparikkhāreti taṇhāya parivāre, taṇhāya “sukhaṃ subha”ntiādinā saṅkhate vā alaṅkateti attho. Taṇhā hi dukkhassa samudayoti ajānanto “aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ vā sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya”nti saṅkhāre parikkharotīti. Amaraṇatthāti gahitā dukkarakiriyā amaratapo, devabhāvatthaṃ tapo vā, dukkhattā vā maro mārako tapo amaratapo. Diṭṭhe adiṭṭha-saddo viya maresu amara-saddo daṭṭhabbo.

With 'by having grasped the perception of pleasure,' it shows the occurrence of craving. 'Craving furnishes' (`Taṇhāparikkhāreti`) means it is in the retinue of craving, or the meaning is that it is prepared or adorned by craving with notions such as 'pleasant, beautiful.' For, not knowing that craving is the origin of suffering, one furnishes formations, thinking, 'Oh, that after the breakup of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of wealthy nobles!' 'For the sake of deathlessness' (`Amaraṇatthāti`) means the difficult practice undertaken, the 'deathless austerity'; or it is austerity for the sake of becoming a deva; or, because suffering is death, the austerity that is the killer of death is 'deathless austerity.' Just as the word 'unseen' (`adiṭṭha`) is used for the seen (`diṭṭha`), so the word 'deathless' (`amara`) should be understood in the case of mortals.

Jātiādipapātadukkhajananato marupapātasadisatā puññābhisaṅkhārassa vuttā. Ramaṇīyabhāvena [V 0.0098] ca assādabhāvena ca gayhamānaṃ puññaphalaṃ dīpasikhāmadhulittasatthadhārāsadisaṃ, tadattho ca puññābhisaṅkhāro taṃnipātalehanasadiso.

Because it generates the suffering of the fall into birth and so forth, the meritorious formation is said to be similar to a fall from a desert precipice. And the fruit of merit, being grasped through its delightful nature and its sweetness, is like a lamp flame or a honey-smeared sword blade; and the meritorious formation for the sake of that is like licking a drop of it.

“Sukho imissā paribbājikāya taruṇāya mudukāya lomasāya bāhāya samphasso”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.469) sukhasaññāya bālo viya gūthakīḷanaṃ kilesābhibhūtatāya kodhāratiabhibhūto asavaso maritukāmo viya visakhādanaṃ karaṇaphalakkhaṇesu jigucchanīyaṃ dukkhañca apuññābhisaṅkhāraṃ ārabhati. Lobhasahagatassa vā gūthakīḷanasadisatā, dosasahagatassa visakhādanasadisatā yojetabbā. Kāmaguṇasamiddhiyā sabhayassapi pisācanagarassa sukhavipallāsahetubhāvo viya arūpavipākānaṃ nirantaratāya anupalakkhiyamānauppādavayānaṃ, dīghasantānatāya agayhamānavipariṇāmānaṃ, saṅkhāravipariṇāmadukkhabhūtānampi niccādivipallāsahetubhāvoti tesaṃ pisācanagarasadisatā, tadabhimukhagamanasadisatā ca āneñjābhisaṅkhārassa yojetabbā.

Through the perception of pleasure, as in 'Pleasant is the touch of this young, tender, soft-haired female wanderer's arm,' and so on (M.N. 1.469), one undertakes demeritorious formations, which are repulsive in their performance, result, and characteristics, and are suffering. This is like a fool playing with excrement, or, being overwhelmed by defilements, overcome by anger and discontent, and helpless, it is like one who wishes to die eating poison. The similarity to playing with excrement should be applied to that which is accompanied by greed; the similarity to eating poison should be applied to that which is accompanied by hatred. Just as the abundance of sensual pleasures, even in a frightful city of goblins, is a cause for the perversion of perception regarding pleasure, so too for the formless results—which, due to their uninterruptedness, have an unperceivable arising and passing away; due to their long continuity, have an ungraspable transformation; and although they are suffering due to the transformation of formations—there is a cause for the perversion of perception regarding permanence, etc. Thus, their similarity to a city of goblins, and the similarity of heading towards it, should be applied to the imperturbable formation.

Tāvāti [M 0.0099] vattabbantarāpekkho nipāto, tasmā avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayoti idaṃ tāva siddhaṃ, idaṃ pana aparaṃ vattabbanti attho. Avijjāpaccayā pana sabbāpetā hontīti vuttanti abhiññācetanānaṃ paccayabhāvaṃ dasseti. Cetopariyapubbenivāsaanāgataṃsañāṇehi paresaṃ attano ca samohacittajānanakāleti yojetabbā.

The particle `tāva` is one that anticipates something further to be said. Therefore, the meaning is: 'Ignorance is a condition for formations'—this much is established; 'this, however, is something further to be stated.' By the statement, 'But all these are conditioned by ignorance,' it shows that ignorance is a condition for the volitions of direct knowledge. This should be connected with the time of knowing the deluded minds of others and of oneself through the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the future.

Avijjāsammūḷhattāti bhavādīnavapaṭicchādikāya avijjāya sammūḷhattā. Rāgādīnanti rāgadiṭṭhivicikicchuddhaccadomanassānaṃ avijjāsampayuttarāgādiassādanakālesu avijjaṃ ārabbha uppatti veditabbā. Garuṃ katvā assādanaṃ rāgadiṭṭhisampayuttāya eva avijjāya yojetabbaṃ, assādanañca rāgo, tadavippayuttā ca diṭṭhīti assādanavacaneneva yathāvuttaṃ avijjaṃ garuṃ karontī diṭṭhi ca vuttāti veditabbā. Rāgādīhi ca pāḷiyaṃ sarūpena vuttehi taṃsampayuttasaṅkhārassa avijjārammaṇāditaṃ dasseti. Anavijjārammaṇassa paṭhamajavanassa ārammaṇādhipatianantarādipaccayavacanesu avuttassa vuttassa ca sabbassa saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ “yaṃ kiñcī”ti āha. Vuttanayenāti samatikkamabhavapatthanāvasena vuttanayena.

“Blinded by ignorance” means being blinded by ignorance, which conceals the dangers of existence. “By lust and so on”—meaning the arising of lust, views, doubt, restlessness, and displeasure—should be understood as occurring in relation to ignorance when experiencing gratification associated with lust and the like, conjoined with ignorance. Taking gratification seriously should be connected to ignorance associated with lust and views, for gratification is lust, and views are inseparable from it. Thus, by the term “gratification,” it should be understood that both views and ignorance, which takes gratification seriously, are mentioned. And when lust and the like are mentioned in the Pāli text by their own nature, this indicates that the volitional formations associated with them have ignorance as their object, etc. To encompass all that is unstated and stated regarding the object condition, dominance condition, proximity condition, etc., of the first impulsion whose object is not ignorance, the phrase “whatever” is used. “In the way stated” means in the way stated by means of the desire for a surpassing existence.

Ekakāraṇavādo āpajjatīti dosappasaṅgo vutto. Aniṭṭho hi ekakāraṇavādo sabbassa sabbakāle [V 0.0099] sambhavāpattito ekasadisasabhāvāpattito ca. Yasmā tīsu pakāresu avijjamānesu pārisesena catutthe eva ca vijjamāne ekahetuphaladīpane attho atthi, tasmā na nupapajjati.

“The doctrine of a single cause is incurred” means that the implication of a fault is stated. For the doctrine of a single cause is undesirable because it implies the arising of everything at all times and the arising of a uniform nature for everything. Since in the three modes it is non-existent, but exists only in the fourth by elimination, and since there is indeed a purpose in pointing out a single cause and effect, therefore it is not unreasonable.

Yathāphassaṃ vedanāvavatthānatoti “sukhavedanīyaṃ, bhikkhave, phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhā vedanā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.62), “cakkhuñca paṭicca…pe… tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.43) ca sukhavedanīyādicakkhusamphassādianurūpena sukhavedanādicakkhusamphassajāvedanādīnaṃ vavatthānato, samānesu cakkhurūpādīsu phassavasena sukhādivipariyāyābhāvato, samānesu ca rūpamanasikārādīsu cakkhādisaṅghaṭṭanavasena cakkhusamphassajādivipariyāyābhāvato, aññapaccayasāmaññepi phassavasena sukhādicakkhusamphassajādīnaṃ oḷārikasukhumādisaṅkarābhāvato cāti attho. Sukhādīnaṃ yathāvuttasamphassassa aviparīto paccayabhāvo [M 0.0100] eva yathāvedanaṃ phassavavatthānaṃ, kāraṇaphalavisesena vā phalakāraṇavisesanicchayo hotīti ubhayatthāpi nicchayo vavatthānanti vutto. Kammādayoti kammāhārautuādayo apākaṭā semhapaṭikārena rogavūpasamato.

“The distinguishing of feeling according to contact” means that, as it is said: “Bhikkhus, dependent on a contact to be felt as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises,” and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.62), and “Dependent on the eye… the coming together of the three is contact; from contact as a condition, feeling arises,” and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.43). This means that pleasant feelings, etc., arising from eye-contact, etc., are distinguished according to their corresponding pleasant-to-be-felt eye-contacts, etc. Even when the eye, forms, etc., are the same, there is no variation of pleasant feelings, etc., due to contact; and similarly, there is no variation of feelings born of eye-contact, etc., due to the collision of the eye, etc., even when forms and mental attention, etc., are the same; and also, even when other conditions are generally the same, there is no mixing of gross and subtle qualities in pleasant feelings born of eye-contact, etc., due to contact. The non-reversed conditionality of the aforementioned contact in relation to pleasant feelings, etc., is precisely the distinguishing of contact according to feeling. Alternatively, the determination of the distinction between cause and effect, or effect and cause, is what is meant; in both cases, this determination is called distinguishing. “Kamma, etc.” refers to kamma, nutriment, temperature, and so on, which are not obvious, as is seen from the pacification of a disease by a remedy for phlegm.

“Assādānupassino taṇhā pavaḍḍhatī”ti vacanatoti “saṃyojanīyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati, taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ, upādānapaccayā bhavo”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.53-54) iminā suttena taṇhāya saṅkhārakāraṇabhāvassa vuttattāti attho. Puna tassāpi avijjā kāraṇanti dassanatthaṃ “avijjāsamudayā āsavasamudayoti vacanato”ti āha. Taṇhā vā caturupādānabhūtā kāmabhavadiṭṭhāsavā ca saṅkhārassa kāraṇanti pākaṭāti suttadvayenapi avijjāya saṅkhārakāraṇabhāvameva dasseti. Assādānupassinoti hi vacanena ādīnavapaṭicchādanakiccā avijjā taṇhāya kāraṇanti dassitā hotīti. Yasmā avidvā, tasmā puññābhisaṅkhārādike abhisaṅkharotīti avijjāya saṅkhārakāraṇabhāvassa pākaṭattā aviddasubhāvo saṅkhārakāraṇabhāvena vutto khīṇāsavassa saṅkhārābhāvato asādhāraṇattā ca. Puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ sādhāraṇāni vatthārammaṇādīnīti puññabhavādiādīnavapaṭicchādikā avijjā puññābhisaṅkhārādīnaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇanti vā attho daṭṭhabbo. Ṭhānaviruddhoti atthitāviruddho. Keci pana “paṭisandhiādīni ṭhānānī”ti vadanti, evaṃ sati purimacittaṃ pacchimacittassa ṭhānaviruddho paccayoti na idaṃ ekantikaṃ siyā. Bhavaṅgampi [V 0.0100] hi bhavaṅgassa anantarapaccayo, javanaṃ javanassāti, na ca sippādīnaṃ paṭisandhiādiṭhānaṃ atthīti na taṃ idha adhippetaṃ. Kammaṃ rūpassa namanaruppanavirodhā sārammaṇānārammaṇavirodhā ca sabhāvaviruddho paccayo, khīrādīni dadhiādīnaṃ madhurambilarasādisabhāvavirodhā. Avijānanakicco āloko vijānanakiccassa viññāṇassa, amadanakiccā ca guḷādayo madanakiccassa āsavassa.

“By contemplating gratification, craving increases.” This statement means that by this sutta—“Bhikkhus, when one dwells contemplating gratification in things that are conducive to bondage, craving increases; from craving as a condition, clinging arises; from clinging as a condition, existence arises” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.53-54)—the causal nature of craving for volitional formations is stated. Furthermore, to indicate that ignorance is also the cause of that craving, it is said: “With the arising of ignorance, the arising of taints occurs.” It is clear that craving, which becomes the four kinds of clinging, and the taints of sensuality, existence, and views are a cause of volitional formations, as shown by these two suttas, which thereby demonstrate the causal nature of ignorance for volitional formations. For by the phrase “contemplating gratification,” it is shown that ignorance, whose function is to cover over danger, is the cause of craving. Because one is ignorant, one forms meritorious volitional formations and the like—thus, the causal nature of ignorance for volitional formations is clear. The nature of the ignorant person is stated as the cause of volitional formations because formations cease in one whose taints are destroyed, making it a unique cause. Common causes for meritorious volitional formations and the like include base, object, etc., but ignorance—which conceals the dangers of merit, existence, and so on—is the unique cause of meritorious volitional formations and the like. This meaning should be understood. “Opposed in position” means opposed to existence. Some say, “Rebirth-linking and such are positions.” If so, a preceding mind being a condition for a subsequent mind would not be an invariable rule, as it would be opposed in position. For life-continuum is an immediate condition for life-continuum, and impulsion for impulsion. But skills and the like have no position such as rebirth-linking, so that is not what is intended here. Kamma is a condition by nature opposed to form, due to the opposition of bending and being afflicted, and due to the opposition of having an object and not having an object. Milk and the like are opposed by nature to curd and other products due to the opposition of sweet, sour, and other tastes. Light, whose function is not to cognize, is opposed to consciousness, whose function is to cognize. Sugarcane products and the like, whose function is non-intoxication, are opposed to the taints, whose function is intoxication.

Golomāvilomāni dabbāya paccayo, dadhiādīni bhūtiṇakassa. Ettha ca avīti rattā eḷakā vuccanti. Vipākāyeva te ca na, tasmā dukkhavipākāyapi [M 0.0101] avijjāya tadavipākānaṃ puññāneñjābhisaṅkhārānaṃ paccayattaṃ na na yujjatīti attho. Tadavipākattepi sāvajjatāya tadaviruddhānaṃ taṃsadisānañca apuññābhisaṅkhārānameva paccayo, na itaresanti etassa pasaṅgassa nivāraṇatthaṃ “viruddho cāviruddho ca, sadisāsadiso tathā. Dhammānaṃ paccayo siddho”ti vuttaṃ, tasmā tamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto “iti ayaṃ avijjā”tiādimāha.

The twisting of cow hair clockwise and counter-clockwise is a condition for the churning stick, and curds and such are conditions for bhūtiṇaka grass. Here, red sheep are called “avī.” And they are not merely results. Therefore, it is not unreasonable that ignorance, which has a painful result, is a condition for those meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations that are not its results. This is the meaning. To prevent the objection that, even though they are not its results, ignorance is still a condition only for unwholesome volitional formations, which are blameworthy and not opposed to it, as well as for those similar to them, but not for others, it is said: “Opposed and unopposed, similar and dissimilar—thus the condition for phenomena is established.” Therefore, to clarify that meaning, he states: “Thus, this ignorance…” and so on.

Acchejjasuttāvutābhejjamaṇīnaṃ viya pubbāpariyavavatthānaṃ niyati, niyatiyā, niyati eva vā saṅgati samāgamo niyatisaṅgati, tāya bhāvesu pariṇatā manussadevavihaṅgādibhāvaṃ pattā niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā. Niyatiyā saṅgatiyā bhāvena ca pariṇatā nānappakārataṃ pattā niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatāti ca atthaṃ vadanti. Etehi ca vikappanehi avijjā akusalaṃ cittaṃ katvā puññādīsu yattha katthaci pavattatīti imamatthaṃ dassento āha “so evaṃ avijjāyā”tiādi.

Just as the sequential arrangement of gems on an unbreakable string is fixed, so too is connection and meeting determined by necessity; the association, the coming together, is a determined association. Through that, beings are transformed, having attained states such as human, divine, or avian existence—transformed by the condition of determined association. Or they say the meaning is that beings, transformed by necessity, association, and state, attain various conditions and are molded by the transformation of the condition of determined association. Showing this meaning—that through these alternatives, ignorance, having made the mind unwholesome, operates wherever in regard to merit or other qualities—he says: “Thus, through ignorance…” and so on.

Apariṇāyako bāloti arahattamaggasampaṭipādakakalyāṇamittarahitoti attho. Arahattamaggāvasānaṃ vā ñāṇaṃ samavisamaṃ dassetvā nibbānaṃ nayatīti pariṇāyakanti vuttaṃ, tena rahito apariṇāyako. Dhammaṃ ñatvāti sappurisūpanissayena catusaccappakāsakasuttādidhammaṃ ñatvā, maggañāṇeneva vā sabbadhammapavaraṃ nibbānaṃ ñatvā, taṃjānanāyattattā pana sesasaccābhisamayassa samānakālampi taṃ purimakālaṃ viya katvā vuttaṃ.

“Without a guide, the fool” means lacking a noble friend who leads to the path to arahantship. Or, a guide is so called because, by showing the even and the uneven, it leads to Nibbāna, the knowledge that concludes the path to arahantship. Being devoid of that, one is without a guide. “Having known the Dhamma” means knowing the Dhamma, such as the discourses that reveal the four truths, through reliance on a good person. Alternatively, it means knowing Nibbāna, the foremost of all dhammas, through the knowledge of the path. Yet, because the comprehension of the remaining truths depends on that knowledge, it is spoken of as if it were prior, even though the comprehension occurs simultaneously.

Saṅkhārapadaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
