Alternatively, having made a single-residue formation of 'the sixth sense base and the mind-base are the sixth sense base,' or 'the mind-base,' or 'the sixth sense base and the sixth sense base are the sixth sense base,' or 'the mind-base and the mind-base are the mind-base,' it is called 'the six sense bases' together with the eye-base, etc. And showing in terms of meaning that this very single-residue formation is made by way of the mind-base, which is a condition for name alone and for name-and-form, he says: 'of the single-residue formation made thus: "the sixth sense base and the six sense bases are the six sense bases."' For indeed, the single-residue formation as stated is, in terms of meaning, made thus: 'the sixth sense base and the six sense bases,' and is so named. And it should be seen that everywhere, when a single-residue formation is made, the designation in the singular is made because of the commonality of being expressible by terms such as 'six sense bases' for those things formed into a single residue. Regarding the statement, 'He will explain it in the indeterminate section': although in the unwholesome and wholesome sections it is said, 'The sixth sense base is conditioned by name,' it should be understood that they cite only the indeterminate section as proof with the intention that in the Suttanta classification, only the resultant sixth sense base is taken. However, in the Conditional Method, a condition even for a non-resultant is extracted with the words, 'The sixth arises from that, partially,' etc. It should be understood that this is extracted out of a desire to speak without omission. 'Included here' means included here by the method of single-residue formation. 'There, in the indeterminate section, it is analyzed in the classification of mundane resultants'—this should be known to be the intended meaning.

Neyyanti ñeyyaṃ. Ukkaṃsāvakaṃsoti ettha sattadhā paccayabhāvato ukkaṃso aṭṭhadhā paccayabhāvo, tato pana navadhā tato vā dasadhāti ayaṃ ukkaṃso, avakaṃso pana dasadhā paccayabhāvato navadhā paccayabhāvo, tato aṭṭhadhā, tato sattadhāti evaṃ veditabbo, na pana sattadhā paccayabhāvato eva dvepi ukkaṃsāvakaṃsā yojetabbā tato avakaṃsābhāvatoti.

`Neyyaṃ` means `ñeyyaṃ` (to be known). Regarding 'maximization and diminution': here, maximization is the eightfold conditionality from the sevenfold conditionality, and from that, the ninefold, or from that, the tenfold—this is maximization. Diminution, however, is the ninefold conditionality from the tenfold conditionality, and from that, the eightfold, and from that, the sevenfold—thus it should be understood. But both maximization and diminution should not be connected only from the sevenfold conditionality, for from that point there would be no diminution.

Hadayavatthuno sahāyaṃ hutvāti etena arūpe viya asahāyaṃ nāmaṃ na hoti, hadayavatthu ca [V 0.0117] nāmena saha chaṭṭhāyatanassa paccayo hotīti ettakameva dasseti, na pana yathā hadayavatthu paccayo hoti, tathā nāmampīti ayamattho adhippeto. Vatthu hi vippayuttapaccayo hoti, na nāmaṃ, nāmañca vipākahetādipaccayo hoti, na vatthūti. Pavatte arūpadhammā kammajarūpassa ṭhitippattasseva paccayā honti, na uppajjamānassāti vippayuttaatthiavigatā ca pacchājātavippayuttādayo eva cakkhādīnaṃ yojetabbā.

By the phrase 'having become a companion to the heart-basis,' it is shown only that, unlike in the formless realm, name is not without a companion, and that the heart-basis together with name is a condition for the sixth sense base. The intended meaning is not that name is a condition in the same way that the heart-basis is. For the physical basis is a dissociation-condition, not name; and name is a resultant-cause-condition, etc., not the physical basis. In the course of existence, formless phenomena are conditions only for kamma-born form that has reached the stage of presence, not for that which is arising. Thus, dissociation, presence, non-disappearance, post-nascence-dissociation, and other such conditions should be applied to the eye-base, etc.

Avasesamanāyatanassāti ettha “pañcakkhandhabhave panā”ti etassa anuvattamānattā pañcavokārabhave eva pavattamānaṃ pañcaviññāṇehi avasesamanāyatanaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nāmarūpassa sahajātādisādhāraṇapaccayabhāvo sampayuttādiasādhāraṇapaccayabhāvo ca yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbo.

Regarding 'of the remaining mind-base': here, since the phrase 'but in the five-aggregate existence' is carried forward, it should be understood that what is spoken of is the remaining mind-base—occurring only in the five-constituent existence—apart from the five consciousnesses. The common conditionality of name-and-form, such as co-nascence, and the uncommon conditionality, such as association, should be applied as is appropriate.

Saḷāyatanapadaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Section on the Six Sense Bases is concluded.

Phassapadaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Section on Contact

230. “Chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā [M 0.0119] phasso”ti abhidhammabhājanīyapāḷi āruppaṃ sandhāya vuttāti “chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā phassoti pāḷianusārato”ti āha. Ajjhattanti sasantatipariyāpannameva gaṇhāti. Tañhi sasantatipariyāpannakammanibbattaṃ tādisassa phassassa paccayo hoti, rūpādīni pana bahiddhā anupādinnāni ca phassassa ārammaṇaṃ honti, na tāni cakkhādīni viya sasantatipariyāpannakammakilesanimittapavattibhāvena phassassa paccayoti paṭhamācariyavāde na gahitāni, dutiyācariyavāde pana yathā tathā vā paccayabhāve sati na sakkā vajjetunti gahitānīti.

230. The Pāḷi text from the Abhidhamma Classification, 'Contact is conditioned by the sixth sense base,' was stated with reference to the formless realm; therefore, he says, 'The phrase "Contact is conditioned by the sixth sense base" is according to the Pāḷi.' By 'internal,' he takes only what is included in one's own continuity. For that which is included in one's own continuity and produced by kamma is a condition for such contact. But external forms, etc., which are ungrasped, are objects for contact; they are not conditions for contact in the way the eye, etc., are—by way of occurring as signs of kamma and defilements included in one's own continuity. Thus, they were not included in the doctrine of the first teachers. However, in the doctrine of the second teachers, they are included because, since they are conditions in one way or another, they cannot be excluded.

Yadi sabbāyatanehi eko phasso sambhaveyya, “saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso”ti ekassa vacanaṃ yujjeyya. Athāpi ekamhā āyatanā sabbe phassā sambhaveyyuṃ, tathāpi sabbāyatanehi sabbaphassasambhavato āyatanabhedena phassabhedo natthīti tadabhedavasena ekassa vacanaṃ yujjeyya, tathā pana asambhavato na yuttanti codeti “na sabbāyatanehī”tiādinā. Aññassapi vā asambhavantassa [V 0.0118] vidhānassa bodhanatthameva “nāpi ekamhā āyatanā sabbe phassā”ti vuttaṃ, “na sabbāyatanehi eko phasso sambhotī”ti idameva pana ekaphassavacanassa ayuttadīpakaṃ kāraṇanti veditabbaṃ. Nidassanavasena vā etaṃ vuttaṃ, nāpi ekamhā āyatanā sabbe phassā sambhonti, evaṃ na sabbāyatanehi eko phasso sambhoti, tasmā ekassa vacanaṃ ayuttanti. Parihāraṃ pana anekāyatanehi ekaphassassa sambhavatoti dassento “tatridaṃ vissajjana”ntiādimāha. Ekopi anekāyatanappabhavo ekopanekāyatanappabhavo. Chadhāpaccayatte pañcavibhāvayeti evaṃ sesesupi yojanā. Tathā cāti paccuppannāni rūpādīni paccuppannañca dhammāyatanapariyāpannaṃ rūparūpaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ārammaṇapaccayamattenāti taṃ sabbaṃ apaccuppannaṃ aññañca dhammāyatanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

If a single contact were to arise from all the sense bases, the statement, 'dependent on the six sense bases is contact,' would be appropriate for a single one. And even if all contacts were to arise from a single sense base, then, because all contacts would arise from all the sense bases, there would be no distinction of contact based on the distinction of the sense bases; therefore, due to that lack of distinction, the statement of a single one would be appropriate. But since that is not possible, it is not appropriate—thus he objects with 'not from all the sense bases,' and so on. Alternatively, it is said, 'nor do all contacts arise from a single sense base,' merely for the purpose of clarifying another impossible arrangement. This alone, however, should be understood as the reason indicating the inappropriateness of speaking of a single contact. Or this is said by way of illustration: 'nor do all contacts arise from a single sense base,' thus a single contact does not arise from all the sense bases; therefore, the statement of a single one is inappropriate. However, showing the solution—that a single contact arises from multiple bases—he says, 'Here is the explanation,' and so on. A single one has multiple sense bases as its source; a single one has multiple sense bases as its source. In the state of being a sixfold condition, he analyzes it as fivefold—thus the application should be made in the remaining cases as well. And so, it is said with reference to present forms, etc., and present materiality and immateriality included in the mind-base. 'Merely by way of object condition'—this is said with reference to all that is non-present and other phenomena included in the mind-base.

Phassapadaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Contact' is concluded.

Vedanāpadaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Feeling'

231. “Sesāna”nti [M 0.0120] ettha sampaṭicchanassa cakkhusamphassādayo pañca yadipi anantarādīhipi paccayā honti, anantarādīnaṃ pana upanissaye antogadhattā santīraṇatadārammaṇānañca sādhāraṇassa tassa vasena “ekadhā”ti vuttaṃ.

231. Herein, regarding 'of the remaining,' this refers to the five, beginning with eye-contact, of the receiving consciousness. Although these are conditions by way of immediacy, etc., it is said 'in one way' because immediacy, etc., are included within decisive support, and by way of that which is common to the investigating and registering consciousnesses.

Tebhūmakavipākavedanānampi sahajātamanosamphassasaṅkhāto so phasso aṭṭhadhā paccayo hotīti yojetabbaṃ. Paccayaṃ anupādinnampi keci icchantīti “yā panā”tiādinā manodvārāvajjanaphassassa paccayabhāvo vutto, tañca mukhamattadassanatthaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etena nayena sabbassa anantarassa anānantarassa ca phassassa tassā tassā vipākavedanāya upanissayatā yojetabbāti.

It should be understood that that contact, designated as mental contact co-arisen with resultant feelings of the three planes, is a condition in eight ways. Because some desire even the unappropriated to be a condition, with 'But which...' and so on, the conditionality of the mind-door-adverting contact is stated; and that should be seen merely for the purpose of showing the introduction. By this method, the nature as decisive support of every immediate and non-immediate contact for those respective resultant feelings should be understood.

Vedanāpadaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Feeling' is concluded.

Taṇhāpadaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Craving'

232. Mamattenāti [V 0.0119] sampiyāyamānena, assādanataṇhāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha putto viya vedanā daṭṭhabbā, khīrādayo viya vedanāya paccayabhūtā rūpādayo, khīrādidāyikā dhāti viya rūpādichaḷārammaṇadāyakā cittakārādayo cha. Tattha vejjo rasāyanojāvasena tadupatthambhitajīvitavasena ca dhammārammaṇassa dāyakoti daṭṭhabbo. Ārammaṇapaccayo uppajjamānassa ārammaṇamattameva hoti, na upanissayo viya uppādakoti uppādakassa upanissayasseva vasena “ekadhāvā”ti vuttaṃ. Upanissayena vā ārammaṇūpanissayo saṅgahito, tena ca ārammaṇabhāvena taṃsabhāvo aññopi ārammaṇabhāvo dīpito hotīti upanissayavaseneva paccayabhāvo vuttoti veditabbo.

232. 'By my-ness' means by being cherished; this is said to be craving for enjoyment. Herein, feeling should be seen as the child; forms and so on, which are conditions for feeling, as milk and so on; the six, such as the painter, who are providers of the six sense-objects beginning with form, as the wet-nurse who provides milk and so on. Herein, the physician should be seen as the provider of the mind-object by way of the power of elixirs and by way of life being supported by that. The object condition is merely the object for that which is arising; it is not a producer like the decisive support. Therefore, it is said 'in one way' by way of the decisive support alone, which is the producer. Or, the object-decisive support is included by decisive support, and by that state of being an object, its own nature, another state of being an object, is also revealed; thus it should be understood that the state of being a condition is stated only in terms of the decisive support.

Yasmā vātiādinā na kevalaṃ vipākasukhavedanā eva, tissopi pana vedanā vipākā visesena taṇhāya upanissayapaccayo, avisesena itarā cāti dasseti. Upekkhā pana santattā, sukhamicceva bhāsitāti tasmā sāpi bhiyyo icchanavasena taṇhāya upanissayoti adhippāyo[M 0.0121]. Upekkhā pana akusalavipākabhūtā aniṭṭhattā dukkhe avarodhetabbā, itarā iṭṭhattā sukheti sā dukkhaṃ viya sukhaṃ viya ca upanissayo hotīti sakkā vattunti. “Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā”ti vacanena sabbassa vedanāvato paccayassa atthitāya taṇhuppattippasaṅge taṃnivāraṇatthamāha “vedanāpaccayā cāpī”tiādi.

By 'Because...' and so on, he shows that not only pleasant resultant feeling, but also all three resultant feelings are a decisive support condition for craving—the former specifically, and the others non-specifically. Neutral feeling, however, being peaceful, is spoken of as 'pleasant'; therefore, the intention is that it too is a decisive support for craving by way of being more desirable. However, neutral feeling that is the result of the unwholesome, being undesirable, should be included in suffering; the other, being desirable, is included in pleasure. Thus it can be said that it is a decisive support like suffering and like pleasure. Due to the statement, 'Dependent on feeling, craving arises,' there is the unwanted consequence of craving arising for every being that has feeling, since the condition exists. To prevent that, he says, 'And also dependent on feeling...' and so on.

Nanu “anusayasahāyā vedanā taṇhāya paccayo hotī”ti vacanassa abhāvā atippasaṅganivattanaṃ na sakkā kātunti? Na, vaṭṭakathāya pavattattā. Vaṭṭassa hi anusayavirahe abhāvato anusayasahitāyeva paccayoti atthato vuttametaṃ hotīti. Atha vā “avijjāpaccayā”ti anuvattamānattā anusayasahitāva paccayoti viññāyati. “Vedanāpaccayā taṇhā”ti ca ettha vedanāpaccayā eva taṇhā, na vedanāya vināti ayaṃ niyamo viññāyati, na vedanāpaccayā taṇhā hoti evāti, tasmā atippasaṅgo natthi evāti.

Is it not so that, due to the absence of the statement, 'feeling accompanied by latent tendencies is a condition for craving,' it is not possible to prevent the excessive implication? No, because this proceeds as a discourse on the round of existence. For since the round does not exist in the absence of latent tendencies, it is thereby said in meaning that the condition is only that which is accompanied by latent tendencies. Or, because 'dependent on ignorance' is carried forward, it is understood that the condition is only that which is accompanied by latent tendencies. And here, in 'dependent on feeling, craving,' this rule is understood: craving is dependent on feeling only, not without feeling; it is not that craving necessarily arises when there is feeling. Therefore, there is no excessive implication at all.

Vusīmatoti vusitavato, vusitabrahmacariyavāsassāti attho. Vussatīti vā “vusī”ti maggo [V 0.0120] vuccati, so etassa vuttho atthīti vusīmā. Aggaphalaṃ vā pariniṭṭhitavāsattā “vusī”ti vuccati, taṃ etassa atthīti vusīmā.

'Vusīmā' means one who has lived; the meaning is one who has lived the holy life to completion. Or, because one dwells (vussati), the path is called 'vusī'; he has dwelt it (vuttho), thus he is 'vusīmā'. Or, the highest fruit is called 'vusī' because the dwelling is perfected; he possesses this, thus he is 'vusīmā'.

Taṇhāpadaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Craving' is concluded.

Upādānapadaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Clinging'

233. Sassato attāti idaṃ purimadiṭṭhiṃ upādiyamānaṃ uttaradiṭṭhiṃ nidassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā hi esā diṭṭhi daḷhīkaraṇavasena purimaṃ uttarā upādiyati, evaṃ “natthi dinna”ntiādikāpīti. Attaggahaṇaṃ pana attavādupādānanti na idaṃ diṭṭhupādānadassananti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Loko cāti vā attaggahaṇavinimuttaṃ gahaṇaṃ diṭṭhupādānabhūtaṃ idha purimadiṭṭhiuttaradiṭṭhivacanehi vuttanti veditabbaṃ. “Dhammasaṅkhepavitthāre pana saṅkhepato taṇhādaḷhattaṃ, saṅkhepato diṭṭhimattameva, vitthārato panā”ti evaṃ dhammasaṅkhepavitthārato saṅkhepaṃ vitthārañca niddhāretīti. Dhammasaṅkhepavitthāreti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

233. 'The self is eternal'—this is stated to indicate the subsequent view, which takes up the former view. For just as this subsequent view takes up the former by way of strengthening it, so too do views like 'There is nothing given,' and so on. However, the grasping of a self is clinging to a doctrine of self; this should be understood as not a demonstration of clinging to views. Or, it should be understood that here, in the statements about the former and subsequent views, the grasping that is free from the grasping of a self—such as 'the world'—which constitutes clinging to views, is stated. In the 'Summary and Detailed Exposition of the Dhamma,' however, it determines both the concise and the elaborate thus: 'Briefly, it is the firmness of craving; briefly, it is merely the view; but in detail…' In 'Dhammasaṅkhepavitthāre,' the locative case should be understood as indicating determination.

Pakatiaṇuādīnaṃ [M 0.0122] sassatagāhapubbaṅgamo, sarīrassa ucchedaggāhapubbaṅgamo ca tesaṃ sāmibhūto koci sassato ucchijjamāno vā attā atthīti attaggāho kadāci hotīti “yebhuyyenā”ti vuttaṃ. Yebhuyyena paṭhamaṃ attavādupādānantiādinā vā sambandho.

Because the grasping of a self—the view that there is some self which is their master, either eternal or being annihilated, which is preceded by the grasping of eternalism concerning primordial atoms, etc., and preceded by the grasping of annihilationism concerning the body—sometimes arises, it is said 'for the most part'. Or, the connection is with 'for the most part, firstly clinging to a doctrine of self,' and so on.

Yadipi bhavarāgajavanavīthi sabbapaṭhamaṃ pavattati gahitappaṭisandhikassa bhavanikantiyā pavattitabbattā, so pana bhavarāgo taṇhādaḷhattaṃ na hotīti maññamāno na kāmupādānassa paṭhamuppattimāha. Taṇhā kāmupādānanti pana vibhāgassa akaraṇe sabbāpi taṇhā kāmupādānanti, karaṇepi kāmarāgato aññāpi taṇhā daḷhabhāvaṃ pattā kāmupādānanti tassa arahattamaggavajjhatā vuttā.

Although the impulse-process of lust for existence occurs first of all for one who has taken rebirth, because it must proceed due to delight in existence, yet he, thinking that this lust for existence is not a firm state of craving, does not state the first arising of clinging to sensual pleasures. However, when no distinction is made, then all craving is clinging to sensual pleasures, in the sense that 'craving is clinging to sensual pleasures.' And even when a distinction is made, it is said that craving other than lust for sensual pleasures, having reached a state of firmness, is clinging to sensual pleasures, and that its abandonment by the path of arahantship is stated.

Uppattiṭṭhānabhūtā cittuppādā visayo. Pañcupādānakkhandhā ālayo, tattha ramatīti ālayarāmā[V 0.0121], pajā. Teneva sā ālayarāmatā ca sakasantāne parasantāne ca pākaṭā hotīti. Upanissayavacanena ārammaṇānantarapakatūpanissayā vuttāti anantarapaccayādīnampi saṅgaho kato hoti.

The arising of consciousness, which is the place of origin, is the sphere. The five aggregates subject to clinging are the abode; beings delight therein, hence they are called ‘delighting in the abode.’ For this reason, that delight in the abode becomes evident in one’s own continuum and in others’ continuum. By the term ‘powerful support condition,’ the object-condition, the immediately contiguous condition, and the natural powerful support condition are stated; thus, the immediately contiguous condition and so on are included.

Upādānapadaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Clinging' is concluded.

Bhavapadaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Becoming'

234. Phalavohārena kammabhavo bhavoti vuttoti upapattibhavanibbacanameva dvayassapi sādhāraṇaṃ katvā vadanto āha “bhavatīti bhavo”ti. Bhavaṃ gacchatīti nipphādanaphalavasena attano pavattikāle bhavābhimukhaṃ hutvā pavattatīti attho, nibbattanameva vā ettha gamanaṃ adhippetaṃ.

234. It is said that kamma-becoming is called becoming by way of its result. Thus, speaking by making the definition of rebirth-becoming common to both, he says: ‘It becomes, therefore it is becoming.’ ‘It goes to becoming’ means that, at the time of its occurrence, it proceeds facing becoming by way of the result of production. Or, here, ‘going’ is intended to mean simply ‘production’.

Saññāvataṃ bhavo saññābhavoti ettha vantu-saddassa lopo daṭṭhabbo, tassa vā atthe akāraṃ katvā “saññabhavo”tipi pāṭho. Vokirīyati pasārīyati vitthārīyatīti vokāro, vokiraṇaṃ vā vokāro, so ekasmiṃ pavattattā eko vokāroti vutto, padesapasaṭuppattīti attho.

Here, in ‘the becoming of those possessing perception is perception-becoming,’ the elision of the suffix ‘-vantu’ should be understood. Or, by making ‘a’ in its place, the reading ‘saññābhava’ is also found. That which is scattered, spread out, or expanded is ‘vokāra’; or, scattering itself is ‘vokāra’. Because it occurs in one, it is called ‘a single constituent,’ meaning its arising is spread out in a region.

Cetanāsampayuttā [M 0.0123] vā…pe… saṅgahitāti ācayagāmitāya kammasaṅkhātataṃ dassetvā kammabhave saṅgahitabhāvaṃ pariyāyena vadati, nippariyāyena pana cetanāva kammabhavo. Vuttañhi “kammabhavo tīhi khandhehi ekenāyatanena ekāya dhātuyā sampayutto, ekena khandhena ekenāyatanena ekāya dhātuyā kehici sampayutto”ti (dhātu. 244). Upapattibhavo tīhipi tikehi vuttā upapattikkhandhāva. Yathāha “upapattibhavo kāmabhavo saññābhavo pañcavokārabhavo pañcahi khandhehi ekādasahāyatanehi sattarasahi dhātūhi saṅgahito”tiādi (dhātu. 67). Yadi hi anupādinnakānampi gahaṇaṃ siyā, “dvādasahāyatanehi aṭṭhārasahi dhātūhī”ti vattabbaṃ siyāti.

‘Associated with volition,’ etc., ‘included’—thus, by showing that it is designated as kamma by way of its tendency to accumulate, it speaks figuratively of its inclusion in kamma-becoming. But literally, volition itself is kamma-becoming. For it is said: ‘Kamma-becoming is associated with three aggregates, one sense-base, and one element; with one aggregate, one sense-base, and one element, it is associated in some cases’ (Dhatukathā 244). Rebirth-becoming is just the rebirth-aggregates stated by all three triads. As it is said: ‘Rebirth-becoming, sensual-realm becoming, perception-becoming, five-constituent becoming—is included by five aggregates, eleven sense-bases, and seventeen elements,’ etc. (Dhatukathā 67). For if what is not clung to were also included, it would have to be said: ‘with twelve sense-bases and eighteen elements.’

Saṅkhārabhavānaṃ dhammabhedato na saṅkhārā eva puna vuttāti “sātthakamevidaṃ punavacana”nti etaṃ na [V 0.0122] yuttanti ce? Na, bhavekadesabhāvena saṅkhārānaṃ bhavoti puna vuttattā. Parena vā dhammavisesaṃ agaṇetvā punavacanaṃ coditanti codakābhilāsavasena “sātthakamevidaṃ punavacana”nti vuttaṃ.

If it is said: 'It is not appropriate to say, “This repetition is meaningful,” because in the case of formations-becoming, due to the distinction of phenomena, it is not that formations are simply stated again,' [we reply]: No, because formations are called ‘becoming’ again due to their being a part of becoming. Or, the repetition is questioned by another without considering the distinction of phenomena, and thus, in accordance with the questioner’s intention, it is said, ‘This repetition is indeed meaningful.’

Kāmabhavādinibbattanakassa kammassa kāmabhavādibhāvo phalavohārena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto. Antogadhe visuṃ agaṇetvā abbhantaragate eva katvā kāmabhavādike kammupapattibhavavasena duguṇe katvā āha “cha bhavā”ti.

In the commentary, the nature of kamma that produces sensual-realm becoming, etc., as sensual-realm becoming, etc., is stated by way of its result. Not counting those included separately, but considering only those internal, and doubling the sensual-realm becoming, etc., by way of kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming, it is said: ‘There are six becomings.’

Avisesenāti upādānabhedaṃ akatvāti attho. Upādānabhedākaraṇeneva ca dvādasappabhedassa saṅgahavasena saṅgahato “cha bhavā”ti vuttaṃ.

‘Without distinction’ means: without making a division of clinging—this is the meaning. And precisely by not making a division of clinging, the twelvefold classification is included by way of a comprehensive enumeration; hence it is said: ‘six becomings.’

Gosīlena kukkurasīlena ca samattena samādinnena gunnaṃ kukkurānañca sahabyatā vuttāti sīlabbatupādānavato jhānabhāvanā na ijjhatīti maññamānā tena rūpārūpabhavā na hontīti keci vadanti, vakkhamānena pana pakārena paccayabhāvato “taṃ na gahetabba”nti āha. Asuddhimagge ca suddhimaggaparāmasanaṃ sīlabbatupādānanti suddhimaggaparāmasanena rūpārūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ nibbattanaṃ na yujjatīti. Purāṇabhāratasītāharaṇapasubandhavidhiādisavanaṃ asaddhammasavanaṃ. Ādi-saddena asappurisūpanissayaṃ pubbe [M 0.0124] ca akatapuññataṃ attamicchāpaṇidhitañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tadantogadhā evāti tasmiṃ duccaritanibbatte sucaritanibbatte ca kāmabhave antogadhā evāti attho.

Some say that because the companionship of cows and dogs is stated as resulting from the complete undertaking of cow-duty and dog-duty, those who possess clinging to rules and observances do not succeed in developing jhānas, and therefore for them there are no form and formless becomings. However, he says that ‘that should not be accepted’ because of its conditionality in the manner to be explained. And on the impure path, the misapprehension of the pure path is clinging to rules and observances, meaning that by misapprehending the pure path, the arising of form and formless sphere jhānas is not possible. Listening to ancient Bhārata tales, the abduction of Sītā, animal sacrifice rituals, etc., is listening to false Dhamma. By the word ‘etc.,’ association with ignoble persons, lack of merit previously done, and wrong aspiration for oneself are included. ‘They are included within that’ means they are indeed included within that sensual-realm becoming, whether produced by misconduct or by good conduct.

Antogadhāti ca saññābhavapañcavokārabhavānaṃ ekadesena antogadhattā vuttaṃ. Na hi te niravasesā kāmabhave antogadhāti. Sappabhedassāti sugatiduggatimanussādippabhedavato. Kamena ca avatvā sīlabbatupādānassa ante bhavapaccayabhāvavacanaṃ attavādupādānaṃ viya abhiṇhaṃ asamudācaraṇato attavādupādānanimittattā ca.

And ‘included’ is stated because it is included in part in perception-becoming and five-constituent becoming. For they are not entirely included in sensual-realm becoming. ‘Of various kinds’ refers to having distinctions such as happy and unhappy destinies, human existence, etc. And without stating it in sequence, the statement of clinging to rules and observances as a condition for becoming at the end is like clinging to a doctrine of self—because of its infrequent occurrence and because it is a cause for clinging to a doctrine of self.

Hetupaccayappabhedehīti ettha maggapaccayo ca vattabbo. Diṭṭhupādānādīni hi maggapaccayā hontīti.

Here, in ‘by way of the classifications of cause-condition,’ etc., the path-condition should also be stated. For clinging to views, etc., are path-conditions.

Bhavapadaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Term 'Becoming' is concluded.

Jātijarāmaraṇādipadaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Terms Beginning with Birth, Ageing, and Death

235. Upapattibhavuppattiyeva [V 0.0123] jātīti āha “na upapattibhavo”ti. Jāyamānassa pana jāti jātīti upapattibhavopi asati abhāvā jātiyā paccayoti sakkā vattuṃ. Jāyamānarūpapadaṭṭhānatāpi hi rūpajātiyā vuttā “upacitarūpapadaṭṭhāno (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 641) upacayo, anuppabandharūpapadaṭṭhānā santatī”ti.

235. He says that birth is precisely the arising of rebirth-becoming, not rebirth-becoming itself. However, for one who is being born, birth is called ‘birth,’ and even rebirth-becoming, in the absence of which birth is absent, can be said to be a condition for birth. For the state of being a basis for arising form is also described as the birth of form: ‘The state of being a basis for accumulated form is accumulation; continuity is the state of being a basis for uninterrupted form.’

Khandhānaṃ jātānaṃ uññātatānuññātatāca hīnapaṇītatā. Ādi-saddena suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇādivisesaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ajjhattasantānagatato aññassa visesakārakassa kāraṇassa abhāvā “ajjhattasantāne”ti āha.

Of the born aggregates, there is being known and unknown, and inferiority and superiority. By the word ‘etc.’ are included distinctions such as good and bad complexion. Because there is no other distinguishing cause apart from what is internal to one's own continuum, he says ‘within one's own continuum.’

Tena tenāti ñātibyasanādinā jarāmaraṇato aññena dukkhadhammena. Upanissayakoṭiyāti upanissayaṃsena, upanissayalesenāti attho. Yo hi paṭṭhāne anāgato sati bhāvā asati ca abhāvā suttantikapariyāyena upanissayo, so “upanissayakoṭī”ti vuccati.

‘By that, by that’ means: by other phenomena of suffering apart from ageing and death, such as the calamity of relatives and so on. ‘By way of the category of decisive support’ means by way of a part of decisive support, or by way of a trace of decisive support. For that which, though not explicitly mentioned in the Paṭṭhāna, is decisive support according to the Suttanta method—namely, when it exists, a state arises, and when it does not exist, it does not arise—that is called 'the category of decisive support.'

Jātijarāmaraṇādipadaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Terms Beginning with Birth, Ageing, and Death is concluded.

Bhavacakkakathāvaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Discourse on the Wheel of Becoming

242. Samitanti [M 0.0125] saṅgataṃ, abbocchinnanti attho. Kāmayānassāti kāmayamānassa, kāmo yānaṃ etassāti vā kāmayāno, tassa kāmayānassa. Ruppatīti sokena ruppati.

242. ‘Samitaṃ’ means assembled, uninterrupted—this is the meaning. ‘Kāmayānassa’ means for one who is desiring; or, ‘kāmayāna’ means ‘one for whom desire is the vehicle’; for that one who is desiring. ‘It is afflicted’ means it is afflicted by sorrow.

Pariyuṭṭhānatāya tiṭṭhanasīlo pariyuṭṭhānaṭṭhāyī. “Pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino”ti vā pāṭho, tattha pariyuṭṭhātīti pariyuṭṭhaṃ, diṭṭhipariyuṭṭhaṃ, tena tiṭṭhatīti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyīti attho daṭṭhabbo. Pañca pubbanimittānīti “mālā milāyanti, vatthāni kilissanti, kacchehi sedā muccanti, kāye vevaṇṇiyaṃ okkamati, devo devāsane nābhiramatī”ti (itivu. 83) vuttāni pañca maraṇapubbanimittānīti attho. Tāni hi disvā kammanibbattakkhandhasaṅkhāte upapattibhave bhavachandabalena [V 0.0124] devānaṃ balavasoko uppajjatīti. Bāloti avidvā. Tena avijjāya kāraṇabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tividhanti tassāruppakathāsavanakammakāraṇādassanamaraṇakālakammopaṭṭhānanidānaṃ sokādidukkhaṃ. Āsave sādhentīti āsave gamenti bodhentīti attho.

One whose nature is to persist through obsession is a 'persister in obsession.' Alternatively, the reading is 'pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino.' There, 'pariyuṭṭha' means 'that which obsesses,' as in 'obsessed by views.' One who persists by that is called a 'persister in obsession'—this meaning should be understood. The five premonitory signs: this means the five premonitory signs of death mentioned as 'the garlands wither, the clothes become soiled, sweat flows from the armpits, a discoloration appears on the body, and the god no longer delights in his divine seat' (Itivuttaka 83). For upon seeing these, intense sorrow arises in the gods due to the power of craving for existence in rebirth-becoming, which consists of the aggregates produced by kamma. 'Fool' means the ignorant one. This shows the causal nature of ignorance. 'Threefold' refers to the suffering of sorrow, etc., which is caused by not seeing the cause of his improper talk, hearing, and deeds, and which is rooted in the presentation of kamma at the time of death. 'They cultivate the taints' means they lead to or make known the taints—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ satīti aviditāditāya anādibhāve sati. Ādimattakathanantiādi etassa atthīti ādimaṃ, bhavacakkaṃ. Tassa bhāvo ādimattaṃ, tassa kathanaṃ ādimattakathanaṃ. Visesanivattiattho vā matta-saddo, sati anādibhāve avijjā ādimhi majjhe pariyosāne ca sabbattha siyāti ādimattāya avijjāya kathanaṃ virujjhatīti attho. Avijjāggahaṇenāti avijjāya uppādanena kathanena, appahānena vā, attano santāne sannihitabhāvakaraṇenāti attho. Kammādīnīti kammavipākavaṭṭāni. Vaṭṭakāraṇabhāvena padhānattā “padhānadhammo”ti avijjā kathitā. Vadatīti vado. Vedeti, vediyatīti vā vedeyyo, sukhādiṃ anubhavati, sabbavisaye vā jānāti, “sukhito”tiādinā attanā parehi ca jānāti ñāyati cāti attho. Brahmādinā vā attanā vāti vā-saddo ca-saddattho. Tenāha “kārakavedakarahita”nti ca-saddatthasamāsaṃ.

Thus, when it is so: this means when there is a beginningless state due to its beginning not being known. Speaking of the mere beginning: that which has a beginning (ādi) is 'ādimaṃ', the cycle of existence. Its state is 'ādimattaṃ' (mere beginning); speaking of that is 'ādimattakathanaṃ' (speaking of the mere beginning). Alternatively, the word 'matta' has the meaning of excluding a specific quality. Since ignorance exists everywhere—at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end—even when there is a beginningless state, speaking of ignorance as merely having a beginning is contradicted—this is the meaning. By the grasping of ignorance: this means by speaking of the arising of ignorance, or by not abandoning it, or by causing its presence in one's own continuum—this is the meaning. Kamma, etc.: this means the cycles of kamma and result. Because it is primary as the cause of the cycle, ignorance is called 'the primary phenomenon.' He speaks (vadati), thus he is a speaker (vado). He feels (vedeti), or he is felt (vediyati), thus he is one who experiences (vedeyyo); he experiences pleasure, etc., or he knows all objects; or he is known and is recognized by himself and by others as 'happy,' etc.—this is the meaning. Or by Brahmā, or by oneself: the word 'vā' (or) here has the meaning of 'ca' (and). Therefore, he said 'devoid of agent and experiencer'—a compound with the meaning of the word 'and'.

Dvādasavidhasuññatāsuññanti avijjādīnaṃ dvādasavidhānaṃ suññatāya suññaṃ, catubbidhampi vā suññataṃ ekaṃ katvā dvādasaṅgatāya dvādasavidhāti tāya dvādasavidhāya suññatāya suññanti attho.

Empty by the twelvefold emptiness: this means empty by the emptiness of the twelvefold things, beginning with ignorance; or, by combining the fourfold emptiness into one, it is twelvefold due to its twelve factors; thus, empty by that twelvefold emptiness—this is the meaning.

Pubbantāharaṇatoti [M 0.0126] pubbantato paccuppannavipākassa āharaṇato paricchinnavedanāvasānaṃ etaṃ bhavacakkanti attho. Bhavacakkekadesopi hi bhavacakkanti vuccati. Vedanā vā taṇhāsahāyāya avijjāya paccayo hotīti vedanāto avijjā, tato saṅkhārāti sambajjhanato vedanāvasānaṃ bhavacakkanti yuttametaṃ, evaṃ taṇhāmūlake ca yojetabbaṃ. Dvinnampi hi aññamaññaṃ anuppaveso hotīti. Avijjā dhammasabhāvaṃ paṭicchādetvā viparītābhinivesaṃ karontī diṭṭhicarite saṃsāre nayati, tesaṃ vā saṃsāraṃ saṅkhārādipavattiṃ nayati pavattetīti “saṃsāranāyikā”ti vuttā. Phaluppattiyāti kattuniddeso. Viññāṇādipaccuppannaphaluppatti hi idha diṭṭhā, adiṭṭhānañca purimabhave attano hetūnaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārānaṃ phalaṃ ajanetvā anupacchijjanaṃ pakāseti. Atha vā purimabhavacakkaṃ dutiyena sambandhaṃ vuttanti vedanāsaṅkhātassa phalassa uppattiyā taṇhādīnaṃ hetūnaṃ anupacchedaṃ pakāseti, tasmā phaluppattiyā kāraṇabhūtāya paṭhamassa bhavacakkassa hetūnaṃ anupacchedappakāsanatoti attho. Saṅkhārādīnameva vā phalānaṃ uppattiyā [V 0.0125] avijjādīnaṃ hetūnaṃ phalaṃ ajanetvā anupacchedameva, viññāṇādihetūnaṃ vā saṅkhārādīnaṃ anubandhanameva pakāseti paṭhamaṃ bhavacakkaṃ, na dutiyaṃ viya pariyosānampīti “phaluppattiyā hetūnaṃ anupacchedappakāsanato”ti vuttaṃ. “Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti ettha aparipuṇṇāyatanakalalarūpaṃ vatvā tato uddhaṃ “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti saḷāyatanappavatti vuttāti āha “anupubbapavattidīpanato”ti. “Bhavapaccayā jātī”ti ettha na āyatanānaṃ kamena uppatti vuttāti āha “sahuppattidīpanato”ti.

By 'bringing from the past end': this means that by bringing the present result from the past end, this cycle of existence is defined as ending with feeling—this is the meaning. For even a part of the cycle of existence is called the cycle of existence. Or, since feeling, with craving as its companion, is a condition for ignorance, and from feeling comes ignorance, and from that, formations—due to this connection, it is fitting that the cycle of existence ends with feeling. Similarly, it should be connected to craving as its root, for there is mutual entry between the two. Ignorance, by concealing the true nature of phenomena and causing wrong adherence, leads one in saṃsāra characterized by wrong views, or it leads their saṃsāra, that is, it causes the process of formations, etc., to proceed—thus it is called 'the guide of saṃsāra.' By 'the arising of the result': this is a designation in the agentive sense. Here, the arising of present results such as consciousness is seen, and it reveals the non-cessation of one's own unseen causes from a previous existence—ignorance and formations—which are not cut off, though not yet generating their result. Alternatively, since the previous cycle of existence is said to be connected with the second, by the arising of the result designated as feeling, it reveals the non-cessation of the causes, craving and so on. Therefore, the meaning is: by the arising of the result, which is the cause, the non-cessation of the causes of the first cycle of existence is revealed. Or, by the arising of the results, namely formations and so on, the first cycle of existence reveals only the non-cessation of the causes, ignorance and so on, which do not yet generate their full result; or it reveals only the continuation of formations and so on as causes for consciousness and so on. It does not, like the second cycle, also reveal an end; thus, it is said, 'by the arising of the result, the non-cessation of the causes is revealed.' In the phrase 'dependent on consciousness, name-and-form,' after mentioning the embryonic form with its incomplete sense bases, and from there onward, in 'dependent on name-and-form, the six sense bases,' the process of the six sense bases is explained—hence it is said, 'by showing the successive process.' In the phrase 'dependent on existence, birth,' the arising of the sense bases is not explained in sequence—hence it is said, 'by showing simultaneous arising.'

Hetuādipubbakā tayo sandhī etassāti hetuphalahetupubbakatisandhi, bhavacakkaṃ. Hetuphalahetuphalavasena catuppabhedo aṅgānaṃ saṅgaho etassāti catubhedasaṅgahaṃ. Sarūpato avuttāpi tasmiṃ tasmiṃ saṅgahe ākirīyanti avijjāsaṅkhārādiggahaṇehi pakāsīyantīti ākārā, atītahetuādīnaṃ vā pakārā ākārā. Kilesakammavipākā vipākakilesakammehi sambandhā hutvā punappunaṃ parivattantīti tesu vaṭṭanāmaṃ āropetvā “tivaṭṭa”nti vuttaṃ, vaṭṭekadesattā vā “vaṭṭānī”ti vuttāni.

That which has three links preceded by cause, etc., is 'hetuphalahetupubbakatisandhi' (having three links preceded by cause-result-cause), i.e., the cycle of existence. That which has a grouping of factors into four divisions by way of cause-result-cause-result is 'catubhedasaṅgahaṃ' (the fourfold grouping). Though not stated in their own nature, they are scattered within each grouping and are revealed by the inclusion of ignorance, formations, etc.—these are the 'ākārā' (modes). Or, the 'ākārā' are the aspects of past causes, etc. Defilements, kamma, and results, being connected with results, defilements, and kamma, revolve again and again; thus, by applying the name 'cycle' to them, they are called the 'three cycles.' Or, because they are parts of the cycle, they are called 'cycles.'

Sandhīnaṃ ādipariyosānavavatthitāti sandhīnaṃ pubbāparavavatthitāti attho.

The links are established as having a beginning and an end: this means the links are established in their prior and subsequent sequence.

“Yā [M 0.0127] kāci vā pana cetanā bhavo, cetanāsampayuttā āyūhanasaṅkhārā”ti idaṃ imissā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇabhājanīye vuttāya paṭisambhidāpāḷiyā (paṭi. ma. 1.47) vasena vuttaṃ. Ettha hi “cetanā bhavo”ti āgatāti. Bhavaniddese pana “sātthato”ti ettha “cetanāva saṅkhārā, bhavo pana cetanāsampayuttāpī”ti vibhaṅgapāḷiyā vasena dassitaṃ. “Tattha katamo puññābhisaṅkhāro? Kusalā cetanā kāmāvacarā”tiādinā hi saṅkhārānaṃ cetanābhāvo vibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ (vibha. 226) vuttoti. Tattha paṭisambhidāpāḷiyaṃ “cetanāsampayuttā vipākadhammattā savipākena āyūhanasaṅkhātena saṅkhatābhisaṅkharaṇakiccena saṅkhārā”ti vuttā. Vibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ (vibha. 234) “sabbampi bhavagāmikammaṃ kammabhavo”ti bhavassa paccayabhāvena bhavagāmibhāvato kammasaṃsaṭṭhasahāyatāya kammabhāvato ca upapattibhavaṃ bhāventīti bhavoti vuttā, upapattibhavabhāvanakiccaṃ pana cetanāya sātisayanti paṭisambhidāpāḷiyaṃ cetanā “bhavo”ti vuttā, bhavābhisaṅkharaṇakiccaṃ cetanāya sātisayanti vibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ “kusalā cetanā”tiādinā cetanā “saṅkhārā”ti vuttā, tasmā tena tena pariyāyena ubhayaṃ ubhayattha vattuṃ yuttanti natthettha virodho[V 0.0126]. Gahaṇanti kāmupādānaṃ kiccenāha. Parāmasananti itarāni. Āyūhanāvasāneti tīsupi atthavikappesu vuttassa āyūhanassa avasāne.

'Whatever volition there is, that is becoming; the volition-associated formations of striving'—this is stated according to the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.47), in the exposition on the knowledge of the stability of phenomena. For here, 'volition is becoming' is stated. However, in the explanation of becoming, in the section 'with meaning,' it is shown according to the Vibhaṅga that 'volition itself is formations, but becoming can also be associated with volition.' For in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 226), it is stated: 'Here, what is the meritorious formation? It is wholesome volition pertaining to the sense-sphere,' and so on, showing that formations are volition. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it is said: 'Associated with volition, having the nature of result, conditioned by that which has a result, namely the striving formation, they are formations because of the function of forming the conditioned.' In the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 234), it is said: 'All kamma leading to becoming is kamma-becoming.' It is called 'becoming' because it brings about rebirth-becoming, due to being a condition for becoming, leading to becoming, being associated with and a companion to kamma, and having the nature of kamma. However, since the function of bringing about rebirth-becoming is exceedingly performed by volition, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga volition is called 'becoming.' Since the function of forming for becoming is exceedingly performed by volition, in the Vibhaṅga, in the passage beginning 'Wholesome volition,' volition is called 'formations.' Therefore, according to the respective contexts, it is fitting to say both in both places, and there is no contradiction here. 'Grasping': he says this with reference to the function of sensual clinging. 'Adhering': this refers to the others. 'At the end of striving': this means at the end of the striving mentioned in all three alternative meanings.

Dvīsu atthavikappesu vutte āyūhanasaṅkhāre “tassa pubbabhāgā”ti āha, tatiye vutte “taṃsampayuttā”ti. Daharassa cittappavatti bhavaṅgabahulā yebhuyyena bhavantarajanakakammāyūhanasamatthā na hotīti “idha paripakkattā āyatanāna”nti vuttaṃ. Kammakaraṇakāle sammohoti etena kammassa paccayabhūtaṃ sammohaṃ dasseti, na kammasampayuttameva.

Regarding the striving formation mentioned in the two alternative meanings, he said 'its preliminary part'; regarding the third, he said 'associated with it.' The mental process of a young person is mostly composed of the life-continuum and is generally not capable of the kamma-striving that generates another existence; hence, it is said, 'here, due to the maturity of the sense bases.' 'At the time of performing kamma, there is delusion'—by this he shows the delusion that is a condition for kamma, not merely that which is associated with kamma.

Kammāneva vipākaṃ sambharanti vaḍḍhentīti kammasambhārā, kammaṃ vā saṅkhārabhavā, tadupakārakāni avijjātaṇhupādānāni kammasambhārā, paṭisandhidāyako vā bhavo kammaṃ, tadupakārakā yathāvuttaāyūhanasaṅkhārā avijjādayo ca kammasambhārāti kammañca kammasambhārā ca kammasambhārāti ekasesaṃ katvā “kammasambhārā”ti āha. Dasa dhammā kammanti avijjādayopi kammasahāyatāya kammasarikkhakā tadupakārakā cāti “kamma”nti vuttā.

They are 'kammasambhārā' (kamma-requisites) because they gather and increase the result of kamma itself. Or, kamma is the formations-existence, and ignorance, craving, and clinging, which are helpful to it, are the kamma-requisites. Alternatively, the existence that gives rebirth is kamma, and the aforementioned striving formations, ignorance, etc., which are helpful to it, are the kamma-requisites. Thus, having made 'kamma and kamma-requisites' into a single-remainder compound, he said 'kammasambhārā.' The ten things are kamma: ignorance and the rest are also called 'kamma' because they are companions to kamma, resemble kamma, and are helpful to it.

Saṅkhippanti [M 0.0128] ettha avijjādayo viññāṇādayo cāti saṅkhepo, kammaṃ vipāko ca. Kammaṃ vipākoti evaṃ saṅkhipīyatīti vā saṅkhepo, avijjādayo viññāṇādayo ca. Saṅkhepabhāvasāmaññena pana ekavacanaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saṅkhepasaddo vā bhāgādhivacananti kammabhāgo kammasaṅkhepo.

Herein, ignorance and so on, and consciousness and so on, are summarized—this is 'saṅkhepo' (summary), meaning kamma and its result. Or, because kamma and its result are thus summarized, it is 'saṅkhepo,' meaning ignorance and so on, and consciousness and so on. However, the singular number should be understood as used because of the generality of the state of being a summary. Or, the word 'saṅkhepa' signifies a part; therefore, the part of kamma is the summary of kamma.

Evaṃ samuppannanti kammato vipāko. Tatthāpi avijjāto saṅkhārāti evaṃ samuppannaṃ, tisandhiādivasena vā samuppannaṃ idaṃ bhavacakkanti attho. Ittaranti gamanadhammaṃ, vinassadhammanti attho. Tena uppādavayavantatādīpakena anicca-saddena vikārāpattidīpakena cala-saddena ca adīpitaṃ kālantaraṭṭhāyitāpaṭikkhepaṃ dīpeti, adhuvanti etena thirabhāvapaṭikkhepaṃ nissārataṃ. Hetū eva sambhārā hetusambhārā. “Ṭhānaso hetuso”ti ettha evaṃ vuttaṃ vā ṭhānaṃ, aññampi tassa tassa sādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇaṃ sambhāro, asādhāraṇaṃ hetu. Evanti evaṃ hetuto dhammamattasambhave hetunirodhā ca vaṭṭupacchede dhamme ca taṃnirodhāya desite satīti attho. Brahmacariyaṃ idha brahmacariyidha. Satte cāti ettha ca-saddo evaṃ brahmacariyañca vijjati, sassatucchedā ca na hontīti samuccayattho. Evañhi [V 0.0127] hetuāyatte dhammamattasambhave satto nupalabbhati, tasmiñca upalabbhante sassato ucchedo vā siyā, nupalabbhante tasmiṃ nevucchedo na sassatanti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Thus arisen' means the result from kamma. In that context, 'from ignorance, formations arise'—thus arisen, or this wheel of existence has arisen by way of the threefold connection, etc.—this is the meaning. 'Transient' means having the nature of going, meaning having the nature of perishing. By this, it reveals the rejection of lastingness over time, which is not indicated by the word 'impermanent,' which indicates possessing arising and ceasing, nor by the word 'unstable,' which indicates undergoing change. By 'non-enduring,' it indicates the rejection of a stable nature and insubstantiality. Causes themselves are the conditions; hence, 'causal conditions.' In the phrase 'by way of basis, by way of cause,' the basis is what is thus stated; any other common cause for this or that is a condition, while the specific cause is the cause. 'Thus' means: when there is the arising of mere phenomena from causes, and the cutting off of the round of existence through the cessation of causes, and when the Dhamma is taught for that cessation—this is the meaning. 'The holy life here' is a contraction for 'the holy life is here.' In 'and beings,' the word 'and' has a conjunctive sense, meaning: thus the holy life exists, and eternalism and annihilationism do not occur. For thus, when there is the arising of mere phenomena dependent on causes, a being is not found. And if a being were found, there would be either eternalism or annihilationism. But since no being is found, there is neither annihilationism nor eternalism—this is what is said.

Saccappabhavatoti saccato, saccānaṃ vā pabhavato. Kusalākusalaṃ kammanti vaṭṭakathāya vattamānattā sāsavanti viññāyati. Avisesenāti cetanā cetanāsampayuttakāti visesaṃ akatvā sabbampi taṃ kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ “samudayasacca”nti vuttanti attho. “Taṇhā ca…pe… avasesā ca sāsavā kusalā dhammā”ti hi cetanācetanāsampayuttavisesaṃ akatvā vuttanti, ariyasaccavisesaṃ vā akatvā samudayasaccanti vuttanti attho.

'Because it is the origin of truth' means because it arises from truth, or because it is the origin of truths. 'Wholesome and unwholesome kamma' is understood as being with taints because it occurs in the discourse on the round of existence. 'Without distinction' means that without making a distinction between volition and what is associated with volition, all that wholesome and unwholesome kamma is called 'the truth of the origin'—this is the meaning. For it is said, 'Craving and... the remaining wholesome states with taints,' without making a distinction between volition and what is associated with volition, or without making a distinction among the noble truths; it is called 'the truth of the origin.' This is the meaning.

Vatthūsūti ārammaṇesu, cakkhādīsu vā paṭicchādetabbesu vatthūsu. Sokādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānattāti tesaṃ kāraṇattā, tehi siddhāya avijjāya sahitehi saṅkhārehi paccayo ca hoti bhavantarapātubhāvāyāti adhippāyo. Cuticittaṃ vā paṭisandhiviññāṇassa anantarapaccayo hotīti “paccayo ca hoti bhavantarapātubhāvāyā”ti vuttaṃ[M 0.0129]. Taṃ pana cuticittaṃ avijjāsaṅkhārarahitaṃ bhavantarassa paccayo na hotīti tassa sahāyadassanatthamāha “sokādīnaṃ adhiṭṭhānattā”ti. Dvidhāti attanoyeva sarasena dhammantarapaccayabhāvena cāti dvidhā.

'In bases' means in objects, or in the bases to be covered over, such as the eye, etc. 'Because they are the foundation of sorrow, etc.' means because they are the cause of these; the intention is that they are also a condition for the appearance of another existence, by means of formations accompanied by the ignorance that is established through them. Or, the death-consciousness is the immediate condition for the rebirth-linking consciousness—thus it is said, 'it is also a condition for the appearance of another existence.' However, that death-consciousness, if devoid of ignorance and formations, is not a condition for another existence. To show its assisting factor, it says, 'because they are the foundation of sorrow, etc.' 'Twofold' means in two ways: by its own intrinsic nature and by being a condition for another phenomenon.

Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti etena saṅkhārānaṃ paccayuppannatādassanena “ko nu kho abhisaṅkharotīti esa no kallo pañho”ti dasseti. Tenetaṃ kārakadassananivāraṇanti. Evamādidassananivāraṇanti etena “socati paridevati dukkhito”tiādidassananivāraṇamāha. Sokādayopi hi paccayāyattā avasavattinoti “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ soka…pe… sambhavantī”ti etena vuttanti.

'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise'—by showing the conditionally arisen nature of volitional formations, this indicates, 'Who, indeed, forms these formations? This is not a valid question.' Thus, it is a prevention of the view of a doer. By this, it states the prevention of such views as 'one grieves, laments, suffers,' etc. For sorrow and the like are also dependent on conditions and not under one's control, as is said by this: 'With birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow... arise.'

Gaṇḍabhedapīḷakā viyāti gaṇḍabhedanatthaṃ paccamāne gaṇḍe tassapi upari jāyamānakhuddakapīḷakā viya, gaṇḍassa vā anekadhābhede pīḷakā viya. Gaṇḍavikārā sūnatāsarāgapubbagahaṇādayo.

'Like small pustules on a bursting boil' means like small pustules appearing on top of a ripening boil for the purpose of bursting it, or like pustules when a boil breaks into many parts. The disorders of a boil are swelling, redness, accumulation of pus, and so on.

Paṭalābhibhūtacakkhuko rūpāni na passati, kiñcipi passanto ca viparītaṃ passati, evaṃ avijjābhibhūto dukkhādīni na paṭipajjati na passati, micchā vā paṭipajjatīti paṭalaṃ viya avijjā[V 0.0128], kiminā viya attanā katattā vaṭṭassa attanoyeva paribbhamanakāraṇattā ca kosappadesā viya saṅkhārā, saṅkhārapariggahaṃ vinā patiṭṭhaṃ alabhamānaṃ viññāṇaṃ pariṇāyakapariggahaṃ vinā patiṭṭhaṃ alabhamāno rājakumāro viyāti pariggahena vinā patiṭṭhālābho ettha sāmaññaṃ. Upapattinimittanti kammādiārammaṇamāha. Parikappanatoti ārammaṇakaraṇato, sampayuttena vā vitakkena vitakkanato. Devamanussamigavihaṅgādivividhappakāratāya māyā viya nāmarūpaṃ, patiṭṭhāvisesena vuḍḍhivisesāpattito vanappagumbo viya saḷāyatanaṃ. Āyatanānaṃ visayivisayabhūtānaṃ aññamaññābhimukhabhāvato āyatanaghaṭṭanato. Ettha ca saṅkhārādīnaṃ kosappadesapariṇāyakādīhi dvīhi dvīhi sadisatāya dve dve upamā vuttāti daṭṭhabbā.

One whose eyes are covered by a cataract does not see forms, or if seeing anything, sees it distorted. Similarly, one overcome by ignorance does not understand or see suffering, etc., or understands wrongly. Thus, ignorance is like a cataract. Formations are like a worm, because they are made by oneself and are the cause of one's own whirling in the round; and they are also like the husk of a grain. Consciousness, not obtaining a footing without the support of formations, is like a prince not obtaining a footing without the support of a retinue. Here, the commonality is the non-attainment of a footing without support. 'The sign of rebirth' refers to the object of kamma, etc. 'From conceiving' means from making it an object, or from thinking with associated thought. Name-and-form is like an illusion due to its various kinds, such as gods, humans, beasts, and birds. The six sense bases are like a forest thicket because of attaining particular growth from a particular establishment. The striking of the sense bases occurs from the mutual confrontation of the sense-faculties and their sense-fields. Here, it should be understood that for formations and so on, two similes each are given, due to their similarity to two things each, such as the husk of a grain, the retinue, and so on.

Gambhīro eva hutvā obhāsati pakāsati dissatīti gambhīrāvabhāso. Jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭhoti jātipaccayā sambhūtaṃ hutvā sahitassa attano paccayānurūpassa uddhaṃ uddhaṃ āgatabhāvo, anuppabandhoti attho. Atha vā sambhūtaṭṭho ca samudāgataṭṭho ca sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho. “Na jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na hoti, na ca jātiṃ vinā [M 0.0130] aññato hotī”ti hi jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭho vutto. Itthañca jātito samudāgacchatīti paccayasamudāgataṭṭho, yā yā jāti yathā yathā paccayo hoti, tadanurūpapātubhāvoti attho.

Being deep, it thus shines, illuminates, and appears; hence it is called 'of deep appearance.' The meaning of 'arisen and come forth from birth as condition' is this: having arisen from birth as condition, it is the state of having come forth continuously, in conformity with its own cause with which it is conjoined; the meaning is 'unbroken continuity.' Or alternatively, the meaning of 'arisen' and the meaning of 'come forth' together form 'the meaning of arisen and come forth.' For it is said, 'Aging and death do not exist apart from birth, nor do they arise from anything other than birth'—thus, the meaning of 'arisen from the condition of birth' is stated. And so, 'it comes forth from birth' is the meaning of 'come forth from a condition'; that is, whatever birth occurs, in whatever way it is a condition, its manifestation is in accordance with that.

Anulomapaṭilomatoti idha pana paccayuppādā paccayuppannuppādasaṅkhātaṃ anulomaṃ, nirodhā nirodhasaṅkhātaṃ paṭilomañcāha. Ādito pana antagamanaṃ anulomaṃ, antato ca ādigamanaṃ paṭilomamāhāti. “Ime cattāro āhārā kiṃnidānā”tiādikāya (saṃ. ni. 2.11) vemajjhato paṭṭhāya paṭilomadesanāya, “cakkhuṃ paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso, phassapaccayā vedanā”tiādikāya (saṃ. ni. 2.43-44; 2.4.60) anulomadesanāya ca dvisandhitisaṅkhepaṃ, “saṃyojanīyesu, bhikkhave, dhammesu assādānupassino viharato taṇhā pavaḍḍhati, taṇhāpaccayā upādāna”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.53-54) ekasandhidvisaṅkhepaṃ.

'Forward and backward order': Here, however, the arising of the conditioned from the arising of its cause is called the forward order, and cessation from cessation is called the backward order. From the beginning to the end is called the forward order, and from the end back to the beginning is called the backward order. In teachings like, 'These four nutriments—what is their source?' (SN 2.11), beginning from the middle, the explanation proceeds in reverse order. In teachings like, 'Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is a condition for feeling' (SN 2.43-44; 2.4.60), the explanation follows the forward order, summarizing two links. In passages like, 'Monks, when one dwells contemplating gratification in things that tend to fetter, craving increases. Craving is a condition for clinging' (SN 2.53-54), there is a summary of one link.

Avijjādīnaṃ sabhāvo paṭivijjhīyatīti paṭivedho. Vuttañhi “tesaṃ tesaṃ vā tattha tattha vuttadhammānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo salakkhaṇasaṅkhāto aviparītasabhāvo paṭivedho”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. nidānakathā). Apuññābhisaṅkhārekadeso sarāgo, añño virāgo, rāgassa vā apaṭipakkhabhāvato [V 0.0129] rāgappavaḍḍhako sabbopi apuññābhisaṅkhāro sarāgo, itaro paṭipakkhabhāvato virāgo. “Dīgharattañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, assutavato puthujjanassa ajjhositaṃ mamāyitaṃ parāmaṭṭhaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.62) attaparāmāsassa viññāṇaṃ visiṭṭhaṃ vatthu vuttanti viññāṇassa suññataṭṭho gambhīro, attā vijānāti saṃsaratīti sabyāpāratāsaṅkantiabhinivesabalavatāya abyāpāraṭṭhaasaṅkantipaṭisandhipātubhāvaṭṭhā ca gambhīrā, nāmassa rūpena, rūpassa ca nāmena asampayogato vinibbhogo, nāmassa nāmena avinibbhogo yojetabbo. Ekuppādekanirodhehi avinibbhoge adhippete rūpassa ca rūpena labbhati. Atha vā ekacatuvokārabhavesu nāmarūpānaṃ asahavattanato aññamaññavinibbhogo, pañcavokārabhave sahavattanato avinibbhogo ca veditabbo.

Penetration is so called because the intrinsic nature of ignorance and so forth is penetrated. For it is said: 'Penetration is the undistorted intrinsic nature, designated as the individual characteristic, of those various phenomena taught in each case, which is to be penetrated' (Dhs.A. Nidānakathā). A portion of demeritorious formations is accompanied by lust; another is free from lust. Or, because it is not the counterpart to lust, all demeritorious formation that increases lust is accompanied by lust; the other, because it is the counterpart, is free from lust. 'For a long time, monks, this has been clung to, appropriated, and misapprehended by the uninstructed worldling thus: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self"' (SN 22.62). Because consciousness is said to be the special basis for the misapprehension of self, the meaning of emptiness in regard to consciousness is profound. Due to the strength of the adherence that 'a self cognizes and transmigrates'—which involves activity and transition—the meaning of being without activity, without transition, and the state of the manifestation of relinking are also profound. The disassociation of mentality from materiality, and of materiality from mentality, is due to non-conjunction; the non-disassociation of mentality from mentality should be connected. When non-disassociation is intended due to simultaneous arising and ceasing, this also applies to materiality with materiality. Alternatively, in the one- and four-constituent existences, the mutual disassociation of mentality and materiality is to be understood as due to their non-coexistence, whereas in the five-constituent existence, their non-disassociation is to be understood as due to their coexistence.

Adhipatiyaṭṭho [M 0.0131] nāma indriyapaccayabhāvo. “Lokopeso dvārāpesā khettampeta”nti (dha. sa. 598-599) vuttā lokādiatthā cakkhādīsu pañcasu yojetabbā. Manāyatanassapi lujjanato manosamphassādīnaṃ dvārakhettabhāvato ca ete atthā sambhavanteva. Āpāthagatānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ pakāsanayogyatālakkhaṇaṃ obhāsanaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ visayibhāvo, manāyatanassa vijānanaṃ. Saṅghaṭṭanaṭṭho visesena cakkhusamphassādīnaṃ pañcannaṃ, itare channampi yojetabbā. Phusanañca phassassa sabhāvo, saṅghaṭṭanaṃ raso, itare upaṭṭhānākārā. Ārammaṇarasānubhavanaṭṭho rasavasena vutto, vedayitaṭṭho lakkhaṇavasena. Attā vedayatīti abhinivesassa balavatāya nijjīvaṭṭho vedanāya gambhīro. Nijjīvāya vedanāya vedayitaṃ nijjīvavedayitaṃ, nijjīvavedayitameva attho nijjīvavedayitaṭṭho.

The meaning of dominance is the state of being a faculty condition. The meanings of 'world,' etc., stated in the passage, 'This is the world, this is the door, this is the field' (Dhs. §§598-599), should be applied to the five faculties beginning with the eye. Since the mind-base also perishes, and since it is the door and field for mental contact and so forth, these meanings are indeed possible for it as well. The illumination of forms, etc., that have come into range—which is characterized by the suitability for being revealed—is the function of the eye, etc., as subject; for the mind-base, it is cognizing. The meaning of impact applies especially to the five types of contact beginning with eye-contact; the other meanings should be applied to all six. Touching is the intrinsic nature of contact, impact is its function, and the others are modes of manifestation. The meaning of experiencing the flavor of the object is stated by way of its function, while the meaning of feeling is stated by way of its characteristic. Due to the strength of the adherence that 'a self feels,' the meaning of lifelessness in regard to feeling is profound. What is felt by a lifeless feeling is a lifeless feeling; the meaning is simply lifeless feeling—this is the meaning of 'lifeless feeling'.

Ādānaṭṭho catunnampi upādānānaṃ samāno, gahaṇaṭṭho kāmupādānassa, itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ abhinivesādiattho. “Diṭṭhikantāro”ti hi vacanato diṭṭhīnaṃ duratikkamanaṭṭhopīti. Daḷhagahaṇattā vā catunnampi duratikkamanaṭṭho yojetabbo. Yonigatiṭhitinivāsesukhipananti samāse bhummavacanassa alopo daṭṭhabbo, tasmā tena āyūhanābhisaṅkharaṇapadānaṃ samāso hoti. Jarāmaraṇaṅgaṃ maraṇappadhānanti maraṇaṭṭhā eva khayādayo gambhīrā dassitā. Navanavānañhi parikkhayena khaṇḍiccādiparipakkappavatti jarāti, khayaṭṭho vā jarāya vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Navabhāvāpagamo hi khayoti vattuṃ yuttoti. Vipariṇāmaṭṭho dvinnampi. Santativasena vā jarāya khayavayabhāvo, sammutikhaṇikavasena maraṇassa bhedavipariṇāmatā yojetabbā.

The meaning of 'taking up' is common to all four kinds of clinging; the meaning of 'grasping' applies to clinging to sensual pleasures, while for the other three the meaning is adherence, and so on. For, from the statement, 'the wilderness of views,' it is also meant that views are difficult to traverse. Alternatively, due to their firm grasping, the meaning of being difficult to traverse should be connected with all four. In the compound `yonigatiṭhitinivāsesukhipana`, the non-elision of the locative case ending should be noted; therefore, with that, there is a compound of the words `āyūhana` and `abhisaṅkharaṇa`. The factor of aging-and-death is 'death-prominent,' meaning that profound aspects such as destruction, which pertain to death, are shown. For aging is the process of maturing into brokenness of teeth, etc., through the wearing away of what is new; or, it should be understood that the meaning of destruction is stated for aging. For it is fitting to say that destruction is the departure of newness. The meaning of alteration applies to both. Alternatively, for aging, there is decay and passing away by way of continuity; for death, breaking up and alteration should be connected by way of the conventional and the momentary.

Atthanayāti [V 0.0130] atthānaṃ nayā. Avijjādiatthehi ekattādī sena bhāvena nīyanti gammentīti ekattādayo tesaṃ nayāti vuttā. Nīyantīti hi nayāti. Atthā eva vā ekattādibhāvena nīyamānā ñāyamānā “atthanayā”ti vuttā. Nīyanti etehīti vā nayā, ekattādīhi ca atthā “eka”ntiādinā nīyanti, tasmā ekattādayo atthānaṃ nayāti atthanayā. Santānānupacchedena bījaṃ rukkhabhāvaṃ pattaṃ rukkhabhāvena pavattanti ekattena vuccatīti santānānupacchedo ekattaṃ, evamidhāpi avijjādīnaṃ santānānupacchedo ekattanti dasseti.

`Atthanayā` means 'methods of meaning.' Unity and so on are called their methods because by them the meanings of ignorance and so forth are led, that is, understood, in their respective ways. For 'methods' (`nayā`) are so called because meanings are led (`nīyanti`) by them. Or, the meanings themselves, being led and known through the state of unity and so on, are called 'methods of meaning.' Or, 'methods' are that by which meanings are led; and by unity and so on, the meanings are led as 'one,' etc. Therefore, unity and so on are the methods of the meanings, hence `atthanayā`. Just as a seed, having reached the state of a tree, proceeds as a tree without interruption of its continuity—this is called unity. So too here, the uninterrupted continuity of ignorance and so on is shown to be unity.

Bhinnasantānassevāti [M 0.0132] sambandharahitassa nānattassa gahaṇato sattantaro ucchinno sattantaro uppannoti gaṇhanto ucchedadiṭṭhimupādiyati.

Of a broken continuity itself: due to grasping at a diversity that is devoid of connection, one who holds that 'one being is annihilated, another being has arisen' adopts the annihilationist view.

Yato kutocīti yadi aññasmā aññassuppatti siyā, vālikato telassa, ucchuto khīrassa kasmā uppatti na siyā, tasmā na koci kassaci hetu atthīti ahetukadiṭṭhiṃ, avijjamānepi hetumhi niyatatāya tilagāvīsukkasoṇitādīhi telakhīrasarīrādīni pavattantīti niyativādañca upādiyatīti viññātabbaṃ yathārahaṃ.

From whatever source: if one thing could arise from another, why would oil not arise from sand, or milk from sugarcane? Therefore, holding that 'nothing is a cause for anything,' one adopts the view of causelessness. And holding that 'even without an existing cause, due to fixed nature, oil, milk, bodies, etc., proceed from sesame seeds, cows, semen and blood, etc.,' one adopts the doctrine of fatalism. This should be understood as appropriate.

Kasmā? Yasmā idañhi bhavacakkaṃ apadāletvā saṃsārabhayamatīto na koci supinantarepi atthīti sambandho. Durabhiyānanti duratikkamaṃ. Asanivicakkamivāti asanimaṇḍalamiva. Tañhi nimmathanameva, nānimmathanaṃ pavattamānaṃ atthi, evaṃ bhavacakkampi ekantaṃ dukkhuppādanato “niccanimmathana”nti vuttaṃ.

Why? The connection is: because without shattering this wheel of existence, there is no one who has transcended the fear of saṃsāra, not even in a dream. `Durabhiyāna` means difficult to overcome. `Asanivicakkamiva` means like a thunderbolt's sphere. For that is sheer destruction; it does not proceed without destroying. Similarly, the wheel of existence, because it exclusively produces suffering, is called 'constantly destructive.'

Ñāṇāsinā apadāletvā saṃsārabhayaṃ atīto natthīti etassa sādhakaṃ dassento āha “vuttampi ceta”ntiādi. Tantūnaṃ ākulakaṃ tantākulakaṃ, tantākulakamiva jātā tantākulakajātā, kilesakammavipākehi atīva jaṭitāti attho. Guṇāya sakuṇiyā nīḍaṃ guṇāguṇḍikaṃ. Vaḍḍhiabhāvato apāyaṃ dukkhagatibhāvato duggatiṃ sukhasamussayato vinipātattā vinipātañca catubbidhaṃ apāyaṃ, “khandhānañca paṭipāṭī”tiādinā vuttaṃ saṃsārañca nātivattati. Saṃsāro eva vā sabbo idha vaḍḍhiapagamādīhi atthehi apāyādināmako vutto kevalaṃ dukkhakkhandhabhāvato.

To show the proof for the statement, 'There is no one who has transcended the fear of saṃsāra without shattering it with the sword of wisdom,' the author says, 'And this has been stated,' etc. A tangle of threads is a `tantākulaka`; 'become like a tangled skein' (`tantākulakajātā`) means being exceedingly entangled by defilements, kamma, and its results. 'Become like a ball of string' (`guṇāguṇṭhikajātā`). One does not transcend the fourfold plane of misery (`apāya`)—so called because of the absence of progress (`vaḍḍhi`), the bad destination (`duggati`) because it is a course of suffering, and ruin (`vinipāta`) because it is a falling away from the accumulation of happiness—nor saṃsāra, described as 'the sequence of the aggregates,' etc. Or indeed, all of saṃsāra here is called by names such as 'plane of misery,' with meanings such as 'absence of progress,' simply because it is a mass of suffering.

Bhavacakkakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the discourse on the Wheel of Existence.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the explanation of the Suttanta Analysis.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Abhidhamma Analysis

243. Pathavīākāsā [V 0.0131] viya paṭiccasamuppādo mahāpatthaṭavitthāritānaṃ atthānaṃ parikappavasena kathito. Tañhi apatthaṭaṃ avitthatañca pathaviṃ ākāsañca pattharanto vitthārayanto viya ca ekekacittāvaruddhaṃ akatvā [M 0.0133] sabbasattasabbacittasādhāraṇavasena patthaṭavitthataṃ katvā suttantabhājanīyena bhagavā dasseti. Tattha nānācittavasenāti asahajātānaṃ sahajātānañca paccayapaccayuppannānaṃ nānācittagatānaṃ dassitabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Nava mūlapadāni etesanti navamūlapadā, nayā. “Ekekena nayena catunnaṃ catunnaṃ vārānaṃ saṅgahitattā”ti vuttaṃ, ettha “ekekena catukkenā”ti vattabbaṃ. Nayacatukkavārā hi ettha vavatthitā dassitānaṃ catukkānaṃ nayabhāvāti.

243. Like the earth and space, dependent origination is taught by way of delimitation with regard to vast and extensive meanings. For just as one might spread out and extend the unspread and unextended earth and space, so too the Blessed One teaches it in the Suttanta Analysis, not by confining it to a single mind-moment, but by making it spread out and extensive, as common to all beings and all minds. Therein, the phrase 'by way of various minds' is said with reference to the fact that conditions and conditioned phenomena, whether non-co-arisen or co-arisen, are shown as pertaining to various minds. The methods have nine root terms, thus they are 'the nine-root-termed.' It is said, 'because by each method four turns each are included'; here, it should be said, 'by each tetrad.' For here the turns of the tetrads of methods are established as being the methods for the tetrads that have been shown.

1. Paccayacatukkavaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Tetrad of Conditions

Avijjaṃ aṅgaṃ aggahetvā tato paraṃ “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro”tiādīni paccayasahitāni paccayuppannāni aṅgabhāvena vuttānīti āha “na, tassa anaṅgattā”ti. Evañca katvā niddese (vibha. 226) “tattha katamā avijjā”ti avijjaṃ visuṃ vissajjetvā “tattha katamo avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro”tiādinā taṃtaṃpaccayavanto saṅkhārādayo vissajjitāti. Tīsu pakāresu paṭhamapaṭhamavāro dutiyavārādīsu pavisanto paccayavisesādisabbanānattasādhāraṇattā te vāravisese gaṇhātīti “sabbasaṅgāhako”ti vutto. Paṭhamavāro eva hi na kevalaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanameva, atha kho nāmañca phassassa paccayo, nāmaṃ vā na kevalaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanasseva, atha kho phassassāpīti paccayavisesadassanatthaṃ, yena atthavisesena mahānidānasuttadesanā pavattā, taṃdassanatthañca chaṭṭhāyatanaṅgaṃ parihāpetvā vuttoti tassa dutiyavāre ca paveso vutto, na sabbaṅgasamorodhato.

Not taking ignorance as a factor, thereafter, 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations,' etc.—conditioned phenomena together with their conditions—are spoken of as factors. Thus it is said, 'No, because it is not a factor.' And having done so, in the Exposition (Vibhaṅga 226), after explaining ignorance separately with 'Therein, what is ignorance?', volitional formations and so on, each with their respective conditions, are explained with 'Therein, what are volitional formations conditioned by ignorance?' and so on. Among the three kinds, the very first turn, entering into the second turn and so on, takes up those specific turns due to being common to all diversity, such as distinctions of conditions; thus, it is called 'all-inclusive.' For the first turn does not merely deal with the sixth sense-base, but also that name is a condition for contact, and name is not limited to just the sixth sense-base but also pertains to contact. This is to show the distinctions among conditions, and to show that specific meaning by which the teaching of the Great Discourse on Origination proceeds. For this purpose, the sixth sense-base as a factor is omitted and spoken of, and thus its entry into the second turn is stated, not from the inclusion of all factors.

Yatthāti vāracatukke ekekavāre ca. Aññathāti suttantabhājanīyato aññathā saṅkhāroti vuttaṃ. Avuttanti “rūpaṃ saḷāyatana”nti, tesupi ca vāresu catūsupi sokādayo avuttā suttantabhājanīyesu vuttā. Tattha ca vuttameva idha “chaṭṭhāyatana”nti aññathā vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Where' (yatthā) refers to the fourfold division of turns and to each single turn. 'Otherwise' (aññathā) means that 'volitional formations' is stated differently from in the Suttanta Analysis. 'Not stated' (avuttaṃ) refers to 'form, the six sense-bases'; and in those four turns as well, sorrow and the like are not stated, though they are stated in the Suttanta Analysis. And it should be understood that what is stated there is stated differently here as 'the sixth sense-base'.

Sabbaṭṭhānasādhāraṇatoti [V 0.0132] vuttanayena sabbavārasādhāraṇato, sabbaviññāṇapavattiṭṭhānabhavasādhāraṇato vā. Vinā abhāvena viññāṇassa khandhattayampi samānaṃ phalaṃ paccayo cāti āha “avisesenā”ti. “Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso”ti (ma. ni. 1.204; saṃ. ni. 2.43) vacanato pana viññāṇaṃ phassassa visesapaccayoti tassa phasso visiṭṭhaṃ phalaṃ, satipi paccayasampayuttānaṃ āhārapaccayabhāve manosañcetanāya viññāṇāharaṇaṃ visiṭṭhaṃ kiccanti saṅkhāro cassa visiṭṭho paccayo. Acittakkhaṇamattānīti [M 0.0134] cittakkhaṇappamāṇarahitāni. Tassatthoti tassa vuttassa avijjādikassa attho suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

'Common to all bases' (sabbaṭṭhānasādhāraṇato) means it is common to all turns in the manner stated, or common to all states of existence which are the place for the arising of consciousness. With the presence of consciousness, the three aggregates are also a common result and condition—hence it is said 'without distinction.' However, according to the statement, 'Contact is the meeting of the three' (Majjhima Nikāya 1.204; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.43), consciousness is a specific condition for contact; therefore, contact is its distinctive result. Even with the presence of nutriment as a condition for associated states, the bringing forth of consciousness by mental volition is a distinctive function, and thus formations are its distinctive condition. 'Devoid of even a moment of mind' (acittakkhaṇamattāni) means lacking the measure of a mind-moment. 'The meaning of that' (tassattho) refers to the meaning of what was stated—ignorance, etc.—and should be understood in the same way as explained in the commentary on the Suttanta Analysis.

Hetukādīnīti ettha yasmiṃ catukke hetuka-saddo vutto, taṃ hetuka-saddasahacaritattā “hetuka”nti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Hetu-saddo gatisūcako avigatatā ca vigatatānivāraṇavasena gati eva hotīti hetukacatukkaṃ avigatapaccayavasena vuttanti vuttaṃ.

'Beginning with hetuka' (hetukādīni) means that here, the tetrad in which the word 'hetuka' is stated should be understood as being called 'hetuka' because it is associated with the word 'hetuka.' The word 'hetu' indicates a going, and since non-disappearance prevents disappearance, it is indeed a going. Therefore, it is said that the 'hetuka' tetrad is stated by way of the non-disappearance condition.

Tidhā catudhā pañcadhā vāti vā-saddo “chadhā vā”tipi vikappetīti daṭṭhabbo. Samādhi hi sādhāraṇehi tīhi jhānindriyamaggapaccayehi ca paccayoti. Upādānaṃ bhavassa maggapaccayena cāti sattadhāti kāmupādānavajjānaṃ vasena vadati. Kāmupādānaṃ pana yathā bhavassa paccayo hoti, so pakāro taṇhāyaṃ vutto evāti na vutto.

The word 'vā' (or), in 'threefold, fourfold, or fivefold,' should be understood as also allowing for the alternative 'or sixfold.' For concentration is a condition by way of the three common conditions: jhāna, faculty, and path. That clinging is a condition for becoming also by way of the path condition, thus making it sevenfold, is said with respect to the kinds of clinging excluding sensual clinging. However, the way in which sensual clinging is a condition for becoming is not stated here, as that manner has already been explained in relation to craving.

Imasmiṃ catukke sahajātapaccayena paccayā hontīti vacanavasenāti adhippāyo. Attho hi na katthaci attano paccayuppannassa yathāsakehi paccayo na hoti, sahajātapaccayavaseneva pana imassa catukkassa vuttattā soyevettha hotīti vadanti. Paṭhamavāroti paṭhamacatukkoti evaṃ vattabbaṃ. Bhavādīnaṃ tathā abhāvanti yadi sahajātapaccayavaseneva paṭhamacatukko vutto, bhavo jātiyā, jāti ca maraṇassa sahajātapaccayo na hotīti yathā avigatacatukkādīsu “bhavapaccayā jāti bhavahetukā”tiādi na vuttaṃ bhavādīnaṃ avigatādipaccayatāya abhāvato, evamidhāpi “bhavapaccayā jātī”tiādi na vattabbaṃ siyā. Paccayavacanameva hi tesaṃ sahajātasūcakaṃ āpannaṃ avigatacatukkādīsu viya idha paccayavisesasūcakassa vacanantarassa abhāvā, na ca taṃ na vuttaṃ, na ca bhavādayo sahajātapaccayā honti, tasmā na sahajātapaccayavasenevāyaṃ catukko vutto. Sesapaccayānañca sambhavanti idaṃ “bhavādīna”nti etena [V 0.0133] saha ayojetvā sāmaññena avijjādīnaṃ sahajātena saha sesapaccayabhāvānañca sambhavaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha attho – paccayavisesasūcakassa vacanantarassa abhāvā sahajātato aññe paccayabhāvā avijjādīnaṃ na sambhavantīti sahajātapaccayavasenevāyaṃ catukko [M 0.0135] āraddhoti vucceyya, na ca te na sambhavanti, tasmā nāyaṃ tathā āraddhoti.

The intention is that in this tetrad, it is by way of the statement that things are conditions through the co-arisen condition. For a thing is always a condition for its own conditioned phenomenon in its own ways; however, since this tetrad is stated by way of the co-arisen condition, they say that this alone is the case here. It is said 'the first turn,' but it should be called 'the first tetrad.' For if the first tetrad were stated solely by way of the co-arisen condition, then since becoming is a condition for birth, but birth is not a co-arisen condition for death, it would follow that 'becoming is a condition for birth,' etc., should not be stated here. This is just as in the tetrads beginning with non-disappearance, where 'becoming is a condition for birth, birth is caused by becoming,' etc., is not stated, because becoming and so on are not conditions by way of non-disappearance. For here, the mere statement of 'condition' would imply co-arising, due to the absence of another word indicating a specific condition, as in the tetrads beginning with non-disappearance. And it is not that this is unstated, nor that becoming and so on are co-arisen conditions. Therefore, this tetrad is not stated solely by way of the co-arisen condition. And the statement that other conditions are possible is said with reference to the general possibility of ignorance and so on having other conditions besides the co-arisen one, not by connecting it with 'for becoming and so on.'
