The meaning here is this: if it were said that this tetrad is established solely by way of the co-arisen condition because, in the absence of another word indicating a specific condition, other types of conditionality besides co-arising are not possible for ignorance and so on, this would be incorrect, for they are indeed possible. Therefore, this tetrad is not established in that way.

“Mahānidānasuttante ekādasaṅgiko paṭiccasamuppādo vutto”ti vuttaṃ, tattha pana “nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, nāmapaccayā phasso”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.97) dvikkhattuṃ āgate nāmarūpe ekadhā gahite navaṅgiko, dvidhā gahite dasaṅgiko vutto, aññattha pana vuttesu avijjāsaṅkhāresu addhattayadassanatthaṃ yojiyamānesu ekādasaṅgiko hotīti katvā evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Mahānidānasuttantadesanāya pariggahatthanti tattha hi cakkhāyatanādīni viya rūpe chaṭṭhāyatanañca nāme antogadhaṃ katvā phassassa niravasesarūpapaccayaṃ viya niravasesanāmapaccayañca dassetuṃ “nāmarūpapaccayā phasso”ti vuttaṃ, evamidhāpi tattha dassitavisesadassanena taṃdesanāpariggahatthaṃ ekacittakkhaṇike paṭiccasamuppāde chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ nāmantogadhaṃ katvā “nāmapaccayā phasso”ti vuttanti attho.

It is said, 'In the Mahānidānasutta, dependent origination is taught as having eleven factors.' It should be understood that it is said thus because, although in that Sutta—where name-and-form appears twice in the reciprocal conditioning of consciousness—it is spoken of as having nine factors if name-and-form is taken as one, and ten factors if taken as two, it becomes eleven-factored when ignorance and formations, stated elsewhere, are applied to show the three periods of time. The exposition in the Mahānidānasutta is for the purpose of comprehensive inclusion. For there, just as the eye-base and so on are included in form, the sixth sense-base is also included in name, and in order to show that contact has form as its complete condition and name as its complete condition, it is said, 'with name-and-form as condition, contact.' Similarly here, for the purpose of including that teaching by showing the distinctions demonstrated there, in the single-moment dependent origination, the sixth sense-base is included in name, and thus it is said, 'with name as condition, contact'—this is the meaning.

Rūpappavattidesaṃ sandhāya desitattā “imassā”ti vacanaseso, na purimānanti, teneva “ayañhī”tiādimāha.

Because it was taught with reference to the teaching on the arising of form, the remainder of the phrase is 'of this' (imassā), not 'of the former' (purimānaṃ). For that very reason, it says, 'for this indeed' (ayañhi), and so on.

Yonivasena opapātikānanti cettha saṃsedajayonikāpi paripuṇṇāyatanabhāvena opapātikasaṅgahaṃ katvā vuttāti daṭṭhabbā. Padhānāya vā yoniyā sabbaparipuṇṇāyatanayoniṃ dassetuṃ “opapātikāna”nti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ saṅgahanidassanavaseneva hi dhammahadayavibhaṅgepi (vibha. 1009) “opapātikānaṃ petāna”ntiādinā opapātikaggahaṇameva kataṃ, na saṃsedajaggahaṇanti. Ekacittakkhaṇe chahāyatanehi phassassa pavatti natthi, na cekassa akusalaphassassa chaṭṭhāyatanavajjaṃ āyatanaṃ samānakkhaṇe pavattamānaṃ paccayabhūtaṃ atthi, ārammaṇapaccayo cettha pavattako na hotīti na gayhati, tasmā “saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso”ti na sakkā vattunti dassanatthaṃ “yasmā paneso”tiādimāha.

Regarding 'by way of birth, for the spontaneously born': here it should be understood that even those born from moisture are spoken of by including them in the category of the spontaneously born, due to their having fully developed sense bases. Alternatively, to indicate the birth-mode with all sense bases fully developed as the principal birth-mode, the term 'for the spontaneously born' is used. For in the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga, by way of showing inclusion in this way, only the spontaneously born are taken, not the moisture-born, as in such phrases as 'for the spontaneously born spirits.' In a single mind-moment, contact does not arise through all six sense bases. Nor, for a single instance of unwholesome contact, is there any sense base, apart from the sixth, that occurs simultaneously as its condition. Here, the object condition is not the instigator, so it is not taken. Therefore, to show that it cannot be said 'contact is conditioned by the six sense bases,' the passage beginning 'but because this...' is stated.

Purimayonidvaye sambhavantampi kesañci saḷāyatanaṃ kalalādikāle na sambhavatīti “sadā asambhavato”ti [V 0.0134] āha. Pacchimayonidvaye pana yesaṃ [M 0.0136] sambhavati, tesaṃ sadā sambhavatīti. Itoti imasmā catukkato, nayato vā, yo viseso.

Even for some beings arising in the first two modes of birth, the six sense bases do not arise at the kalala stage and so on; hence it is said, 'because of the constant non-arising.' However, for those for whom they arise in the last two modes of birth, for them they always arise. 'From this' (ito) means the distinction from this tetrad, or from this method.

Paccayacatukkavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Tetrad of Conditions is concluded.

2. Hetucatukkavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Tetrad of Causes

244. Jātikkhaṇamatte eva abhāvatoti tato uddhaṃ bhāvatoti attho. Avigatapaccayaniyamābhāvato bhave upādānahetukaggahaṇaṃ na kataṃ, abhāvato avigatapaccayassa jātiādīsu bhavahetukādiggahaṇaṃ na katanti yojetabbaṃ. Yathā pana yāva vatthu, tāva anupalabbhamānassa viññāṇassa vatthu avigatapaccayo hoti viññāṇato uddhaṃ pavattanakampi, evaṃ upādānaṃ bhavasaṅgahitānaṃ jātiādīnaṃ, bhavo ca jātiyā avigatapaccayo siyā. Atha na siyā, saṅkhārakkhandhe jātiādīnaṃ saṅgahitattā viññāṇaṃ nāmassa, nāmañca atakkhaṇikasambhavā chaṭṭhāyatanassa avigatapaccayo na siyāti idha viya tatthāpi hetukaggahaṇaṃ na kattabbaṃ siyā, tasmā yāva upādānaṃ, tāva jātiādīnaṃ anupalabbho, jātikkhaṇamatte eva bhavassa abhāvo ca kāraṇanti na sakkā kātuṃ. Saṅkhatalakkhaṇānaṃ pana jātiādīnaṃ asabhāvadhammānaṃ bhavena saṅgahitattā asabhāvadhammassa ca paramatthato bhavantarassa abhāvato hetuādipaccayā na santīti bhavassa upādānaṃ na niyamena avigatapaccayo, bhavo pana jātiyā, jāti jarāmaraṇassa neva avigatapaccayoti avigatapaccayaniyamābhāvato abhāvato ca avigatapaccayassa bhavādīsu hetukaggahaṇaṃ na katanti yuttaṃ.

244. The meaning is: because of non-existence at the mere moment of birth, and because of existence thereafter. Because there is no fixed rule for the non-disappearance condition, the taking of clinging as a cause is not done in the case of existence. And because of the absence of the non-disappearance condition, the taking of existence as a cause for birth, etc., is not done in the case of birth, etc.—this should be connected. Just as, as long as the base exists, the base is a non-disappearance condition for consciousness which is not yet apprehended, and also for its continuation after consciousness; so too clinging might be a non-disappearance condition for birth, etc., which are included in existence, and existence might be a non-disappearance condition for birth. But if it were not so, then because birth, etc., are included in the aggregate of formations, consciousness would not be a non-disappearance condition for name, and name, because its arising is not momentary, would not be a non-disappearance condition for the sixth sense-base; thus, here as there, the taking of a cause should not be done. Therefore, it cannot be made a reason that as long as there is clinging, birth, etc., are not apprehended, and that at the mere moment of birth there is the absence of existence. However, since conditioned characteristics like birth, etc., are phenomena without intrinsic nature and are included in existence, and since for a phenomenon without intrinsic nature there is ultimately no other existence, the conditions of cause, etc., do not exist. Thus, clinging is not invariably a non-disappearance condition for existence; but existence is for birth, while birth is certainly not a non-disappearance condition for aging-and-death. Therefore, it is correct that due to the absence of a fixed rule for the non-disappearance condition, and due to the absence of the non-disappearance condition, the taking of a cause in the case of existence, etc., is not done.

Nanu evaṃ “nāmaṃ viññāṇahetukaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ nāmahetuka”nti vacanaṃ na vattabbaṃ. Na hi nāmasaṅgahitānaṃ jātiādīnaṃ avigatapaccayo aññassa avigatapaccayabhāvo ca atthi asabhāvadhammattāti? Na, tesaṃ nāmena asaṅgahitattā. Namanakiccaparicchinnañhi nāmaṃ, tañca kiccaṃ sabhāvadhammānameva hotīti sabhāvadhammabhūtā eva tayo khandhā “nāma”nti vuttā, tasmā tattha hetukaggahaṇaṃ yuttaṃ, idha pana bhavatīti bhavo, na ca jātiādīni na bhavanti “bhavapaccayā [V 0.0135] jāti sambhavati, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sambhavatī”ti yojanato[M 0.0137], tasmā saṅkharaṇato saṅkhāre viya bhavanato bhave jātiādīni saṅgahitānīti niyamābhāvābhāvehi yathāvuttehi hetukaggahaṇaṃ na katanti.

Surely, in that case, the statement 'name is caused by consciousness, the sixth sense-base is caused by name' should not be made. For there is no non-disappearance condition for birth, etc., included in name, nor a state of being a non-disappearance condition for another, due to their being phenomena without intrinsic nature. No, because they are not included in name. For name is defined by its function of bending towards an object, and that function pertains only to phenomena with intrinsic nature. Therefore, only the three aggregates that are phenomena with intrinsic nature are called 'name.' Hence, the taking of a cause there is appropriate. But here, 'it becomes' (bhavati), therefore it is 'becoming' (bhavo); and it is not that birth and the like do not become, since the connection is made: 'conditioned by becoming, birth arises; conditioned by birth, aging and death arise.' Therefore, just as formations are included in 'formations' due to their forming, so too are birth and the like included in 'becoming' due to their becoming. Thus, because of the aforementioned absence of a fixed rule and absence, the taking of a cause is not done here.

Keci panātiādinā revatattheramataṃ vadati. Arūpakkhandhā hi idha bhavoti āgatā. Vuttañhi “tattha katamo upādānapaccayā bhavo, ṭhapetvā upādānaṃ vedanākkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho”ti (vibha. 249).

With 'Some, however,' etc., he states the opinion of the Elder Revata. For here, the formless aggregates are what is meant by 'existence.' For it was said: 'Herein, what is existence conditioned by clinging? Excluding clinging, it is the feeling aggregate... the consciousness aggregate' (Vibh. 249).

“Vattabbapadesābhāvato”ti vuttaṃ, satipi pana padese upādānaṃ viya sabhāvāni jātiādīni na hontīti ṭhapetabbassa bhāvantarassa abhāvato eva ṭhapanaṃ na kātabbanti yuttaṃ. Jāyamānānaṃ pana jāti, jātānañca jarāmaraṇanti “bhavapaccayā jāti, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”nti (vibha. 225) vuttaṃ. Yathā pana “nāmapaccayā phassoti tattha katamaṃ nāmaṃ? Ṭhapetvā phassaṃ vedanākkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho. Idaṃ vuccati nāma”nti (vibha. 259), “nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatananti atthi nāmaṃ atthi rūpaṃ. Tattha katamaṃ nāmaṃ? Vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho. Idaṃ vuccati nāmaṃ. Tattha katamaṃ rūpaṃ? Cattāro mahābhūtā yañca rūpaṃ nissāya manodhātu manoviññāṇadhātu vattati, idaṃ vuccati rūpa”nti (vibha. 261) ca yaṃ nāmarūpañca phassassa saḷāyatanassa paccayo, tassa vattabbapadeso niddiṭṭho, evaṃ yo bhavo jātiyā paccayo, tassapi ṭhapetabbagahetabbavisese sati na sakkā vattabbapadeso natthīti vattunti.

It is said, 'because there is no basis for designation'; but even if there were a basis, birth and so on are not phenomena with intrinsic nature like clinging is. Therefore, it is appropriate that no exclusion be made, precisely because there is no other state of being to be excluded. However, for those being born, there is birth, and for those who have been born, there is aging and death—as stated: 'Conditioned by becoming, there is birth; conditioned by birth, there is aging and death' (Vibh. 225). Just as it is said: 'Conditioned by name, there is contact. Herein, what is name? Excluding contact, it is the feeling aggregate… the consciousness aggregate. This is called name' (Vibh. 259). And: 'Conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases. There is name, there is form. Herein, what is name? The feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate. This is called name. Herein, what is form? The four great elements and that form depending on which the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element operate. This is called form' (Vibh. 261). Thus, the basis for designation of that name-and-form which is the condition for contact and the six sense bases has been specified. Similarly, regarding that becoming which is the condition for birth, since there are specific distinctions between what is to be excluded and what is to be taken, it cannot be said that there is no basis for designation.

Hetucatukkavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Tetrad of Causes is concluded.

4. Aññamaññacatukkavaṇṇanā

4. The Explanation of the Tetrad of Reciprocity

246. Nippadesattā bhavena upādānaṃ saṅgahitanti paccayuppannassa upādānassa visuṃ ṭhitassa abhāvā “bhavapaccayāpi upādāna”nti na sakkā vattunti dassetuṃ “yasmā pana bhavo [V 0.0136] nippadeso”tiādimāha. Evaṃ sati “nāmapaccayāpi viññāṇa”nti na vattabbaṃ siyā, nāmaṃ pana paccayuppannabhūtaṃ paccayabhūtañca sappadesameva gahitanti adhippāyo. Yathā pana “nāmapaccayā chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ, nāmapaccayā phasso”tiādīsu (vibha. 150-154) paccayuppannaṃ ṭhapetvā nāmaṃ [M 0.0138] gahitaṃ, evaṃ “bhavapaccayāpi upādāna”nti idhāpi paccayuppannaṃ ṭhapetvā bhavassa gahaṇaṃ na na sakkā kātuṃ, tasmā upādānassa avigatapaccayaniyamābhāvo viya aññamaññapaccayaniyamābhāvo bhave pubbe vuttanayena atthīti “bhavapaccayāpi upādāna”nti na vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

246. To show that it cannot be said 'clinging is also conditioned by existence'—because existence is without specific designation, clinging is included in existence, and thus there is no conditioned clinging standing separately—he says, beginning with 'because existence is without specific designation,' etc. If this were so, it should not be said that 'consciousness is also conditioned by name,' but the intention is that name, being both conditioned and a condition, is taken as having specific designation. Just as in the statements 'the sixth sense-base is conditioned by name,' 'contact is conditioned by name,' etc., name is taken excluding what is conditioned, so too here, in the case of 'clinging is also conditioned by existence,' the taking of existence excluding what is conditioned is not impossible. Therefore, it should be understood that just as there is an absence of a fixed rule for the non-disappearance condition for clinging, so too there is an absence of a fixed rule for the reciprocity condition in the case of existence, in the manner previously explained; thus, 'clinging is also conditioned by existence' was not stated.

Aññamaññapaccayoti cettha sampayuttavippayuttaatthipaccayo adhippeto siyā. “Nāmarūpapaccayāpi viññāṇa”nti hi vuttaṃ, na ca vatthu akusalaviññāṇassa aññamaññapaccayo hoti, purejātavippayutto pana hotīti. Tathā “chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayāpi nāmarūpa”nti vuttaṃ, na ca chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ cakkhāyatanupacayādīnaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānarūpassa ca aññamaññapaccayo hoti, pacchājātavippayutto pana hotīti.

Here, by 'reciprocity condition,' the association, dissociation, and presence conditions may be intended. For it is said, 'Consciousness is also conditioned by name-and-form,' yet the physical base is not a reciprocity condition for unwholesome consciousness, but rather a pre-nascence dissociation condition. Similarly, it is said, 'Name-and-form is also conditioned by the sixfold base,' yet the sixfold base is not a reciprocity condition for the accumulation of the eye-base and so on, and for mind-originated matter, but rather a post-nascence dissociation condition.

Aññamaññacatukkavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Tetrad of Reciprocity is concluded.

Saṅkhārādimūlakanayamātikāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Matrix of Methods Rooted in Formations and so on

247. “Apubbassa aññassa avijjāpaccayassa vattabbassa abhāvato bhavamūlakanayo na vutto”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati “chaṭṭhāyatanapaccayā avijjā”tiādikā chaṭṭhāyatanādimūlakā ca na vattabbā siyuṃ. “Nāmapaccayā avijjā”ti ettha hi avijjāpaccayā sabbe cattāro khandhā nāmanti vuttāti. Tatthāyaṃ adhippāyo siyā – nāmavisesānaṃ chaṭṭhāyatanādīnaṃ avijjāya paccayabhāvo vattabboti chaṭṭhāyatanādimūlakā vuttā. Yadeva pana nāmaṃ avijjāya paccayo, tadeva bhavapaccayā avijjāti etthāpi vucceyya, na vattabbaviseso koci, tasmā apubbābhāvato na vuttoti. Bhavaggahaṇena ca idha avijjāya paccayabhūtā sabhāvadhammā gaṇheyyaṃu, na jātiādīnīti apubbābhāvato na vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. “Avijjāpaccayā avijjātipi [V 0.0137] vuttaṃ siyā”ti vuttaṃ, yathā pana “nāmapaccayā phasso”ti vutte “phassapaccayā phasso”ti vuttaṃ na hoti paccayuppannaṃ ṭhapetvā paccayassa gahaṇato, evamidhāpi na siyā, tasmā bhavanavasena sabhāvadhammāsabhāvadhammesu sāmaññena pavatto bhava-saddoti na so avijjāya paccayoti sakkā vattuṃ. Tena bhavamūlakanayo na vuttoti veditabbo.

247. It was said: 'Because another condition for ignorance, not previously mentioned, which should be stated, is absent, the method rooted in existence was not stated.' This being so, methods such as 'the sixth sense-base is a condition for ignorance' and others rooted in the sixth sense-base and so on should not be stated. For here, in the phrase 'name is a condition for ignorance,' it is said that all four aggregates, which are a condition for ignorance, are 'name'. The intention here might be that the conditionality of specific aspects of name, such as the six sense-bases and so on, for ignorance, is to be stated—thus, those rooted in the six sense-bases and so on are mentioned. However, the very 'name' that is a condition for ignorance could also be stated here as 'existence is a condition for ignorance,' and there is no special distinction to be stated. Therefore, because of the absence of a new condition, it was not stated. And by the term 'existence' here, the intrinsic phenomena that are conditions for ignorance should be understood, not birth and so on—thus, it should be understood that it was not stated due to the absence of a new condition. It was said: 'It might also be said, “Ignorance is a condition for ignorance.”' But just as when 'name is a condition for contact' is said, 'contact is a condition for contact' is not said, because the condition is taken excluding the conditioned phenomenon, so too here it should not be. Therefore, since the word 'existence' occurs generally in intrinsic and non-intrinsic phenomena in the sense of becoming, it cannot be said that it is a condition for ignorance. Hence, it should be understood that the method rooted in existence was not stated.

“Upādānapaccayā [M 0.0139] bhavo”ti ettha viya bhavekadese visuṃ pubbe aggahite bhava-saddo paccayasodhanatthaṃ ādito vuccamāno niravasesabodhako hoti, na nāma-saddo. Evaṃsabhāvā hi etā niruttiyoti imināvā adhippāyena “avijjāpaccayā avijjātipi vuttaṃ siyā”ti āhāti daṭṭhabbaṃ, imināva adhippāyena “bhavassa nippadesattā bhavapaccayāpi upādānanti na vutta”nti ayamattho aññamaññapaccayavāre vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Tattha pacchinnattāti etena jātijarāmaraṇānaṃ avijjāya paccayabhāvo anuññāto viya hoti. Jāyamānānaṃ pana jāti, na jātiyā jāyamānā, jīyamānamīyamānañca jarāmaraṇaṃ, na jarāmaraṇassa jīyamānamīyamānāti jātiādīni ekacittakkhaṇe na avijjāya paccayo honti, tasmā asambhavato eva tammūlakā nayā na gahitā, pacchedopi pana atthīti “tattha pacchinnattā”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Teneva “apicā”tiādimāha.

'With clinging as condition, existence'—here, just as when a part of existence has not been previously grasped separately, the word 'existence', when stated from the beginning for the purpose of clarifying the condition, conveys the meaning completely, unlike the word 'name.' For this is the very nature of these expressions. It should be understood that it was with this intention that he said, 'It might also be said, “Ignorance is a condition for ignorance.”' It should be seen that it was with this same intention that this meaning was stated in the section on reciprocal conditionality: 'Because existence is without parts, it is not said that clinging is also conditioned by existence.' There, by the phrase 'because of being cut off,' the fact that ignorance is a condition for birth, aging, and death is seemingly acknowledged. But birth is of those being born, not those being born of birth; and aging and death are of those aging and dying, not those aging and dying of aging and death. Thus, birth and the like are not conditions for ignorance in a single mind-moment; therefore, methods rooted in them are not accepted due to their very impossibility. However, since there is also a cutting off, it is said, 'because of being cut off'—this should be understood. For that very reason, he said, 'furthermore' and so on.

Mātikāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Matrix is completed.

Akusalaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Unwholesome

248-249. Upādānassa upādānapaccayattaṃ āpajjeyyāti nanu nāyaṃ doso. Kāmupādānañhi diṭṭhupādānassa, tañca itarassa paccayo hotīti? Saccaṃ, kāmupādānassa pana taṇhāgahaṇena gahitattā nāme viya visesapaccayattābhāvā ca upādānaggahaṇena taṇhāpaccayā bhavassa ca paccayabhūtā diṭṭhi eva gahitāti ayaṃ doso vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā ca upādānaṭṭhāne paccayuppannaṃ paccayo ca ekameva, tasmā “nāmapaccayā phasso, nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatana”nti etesaṃ niddesesu viya “upādānapaccayā bhavo”ti etassa niddese paccayo visuṃ [V 0.0138] na vibhatto. Satipi vā bhavassa paccayabhāvena kāmupādānassapi gahaṇe “ṭhapetvā upādāna”nti avuccamāne kāmupādānaṃ kāmupādānassa, diṭṭhi ca diṭṭhiyā paccayoti āpajjeyyāti paccayapaccayuppannatānivāraṇatthaṃ “ṭhapetvā upādāna”nti vuttanti dasseti.

248-249. 'Would it not lead to the fault of clinging becoming a condition for clinging?' Surely this is not a fault. For sensual clinging is a condition for view-clinging, and that in turn is a condition for the other, is it not? True. However, it should be understood that this fault is mentioned because sensual clinging is included by the grasping of craving, and because there is an absence of specific conditionality as in the case of name, and because by the grasping of 'clinging', only view-clinging—which is conditioned by craving and is a condition for becoming—is taken. And because at the stage of clinging the condition and the conditioned phenomenon are one and the same, therefore, just as in the expositions 'name is a condition for contact' and 'name-and-form is a condition for the six sense-bases,' so too in the exposition 'clinging is a condition for becoming,' the condition is not separately distinguished. Or, even if sensual clinging is included as a condition for becoming, if the phrase 'excluding clinging' were not stated, it would follow that sensual clinging is a condition for sensual clinging, and view-clinging for view-clinging. He shows that the phrase 'excluding clinging' is stated to prevent the condition from being the conditioned phenomenon.

252. Cakkhāyatanādiupatthambhakassa [M 0.0140] cittasamuṭṭhānarūpassa janakaṃ viññāṇaṃ cakkhāyatanupacayādīnaṃ paccayoti vuttaṃ tadajanakampīti adhippāyena “yassa cittasamuṭṭhānarūpassā”tiādimāha. Tāsampi hīti utuāhārajasantatīnampi hi upatthambhakasamuṭṭhāpanapacchājātapaccayavasena viññāṇaṃ paccayo hoti evāti attho.

252. It is said that consciousness, which generates the mind-originated matter that supports the eye-base and so on, is a condition for the growth of the eye-base and the other bases. The phrase 'of whatever mind-originated matter' is stated with the intention of including even that which it does not generate. The meaning is that consciousness is indeed also a condition for those—namely, the continuities originating from temperature and nutriment—by way of support condition, origination condition, and post-nascence condition.

254. Yathānurūpanti mahābhūtasaṅkhātaṃ pañcannaṃ sahajātādipaccayo, vatthusaṅkhātaṃ chaṭṭhassa purejātādipaccayo, nāmaṃ pañcannaṃ pacchājātādipaccayo, chaṭṭhassa sahajātādipaccayoti esā yathānurūpatā.

254. 'As is suitable' means: that which is designated as the great elements is the conascence condition, etc., for the five; that which is designated as the base is the prenascence condition, etc., for the sixth; name is the postnascence condition, etc., for the five; and for the sixth, it is the conascence condition, etc. This is what is meant by 'suitability'.

264. Yassāti yassa paccayuppannassa nāmassa viññāṇassa sampayuttapaccayabhāvo hotīti yojetabbaṃ.

264. The phrase 'for which' should be construed as: for which conditioned name and consciousness it is an association condition.

272. “Phassapaccayāpi nāma”nti phassapaccayabhāvena vattabbasseva nāmassa attano paccayuppannena pavatti dassitāti “ṭhapetvā phassa”nti puna vacane koci attho atthīti na vuttanti dassento “tathāpī”tiādimāha.

272. He said 'nevertheless,' and so on, showing that the phrase 'excluding contact' is not repeated because there is no meaning in it, since the statement 'name is also conditioned by contact' shows the occurrence of that very name—which is to be stated as conditioned by contact—through its own conditioned phenomenon.

280. Yasmā adhimokkhopi natthi, tasmā upādānaṭṭhānaṃ parihīnamevāti sambandho. Balavakilesena pana padapūraṇassa kāraṇaṃ taṇhāya abhāvo domanassasahagatesu vutto evāti tassa tena sambandho yojetabbo. Sabbatthāti tatiyacittādīsu “taṇhāpaccayā adhimokkho”tiādimhi vissajjanameva visesaṃ dassetvā pāḷi saṃkhittā. Heṭṭhāti cittuppādakaṇḍādīsu.

280. The connection is: because there is no conviction, the ground for clinging is entirely diminished. But the reason for the word-filler is the strong defilement; its connection should be construed with that which has already been stated, namely, the absence of craving in states accompanied by displeasure. 'In all cases' means in the third consciousness, and so on; in the passage beginning 'conviction is conditioned by craving,' the Pāli is concise, showing the distinction only in the explanation. 'Below' means in the chapter on the arising of consciousness, and so on.

Akusalaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Unwholesome is completed.

Kusalābyākataniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Wholesome and the Indeterminate

292. Pasādoti [V 0.0139] saddhā.

292. Serenity means faith.

306. “Alobho nidānaṃ kammānaṃ samudayāyā”tiādivacanato (a. ni. 3.34) sabyāpārāni kusalamūlāni saṅkhārānaṃ nidānāni honti, na kammavegakkhittesu [M 0.0141] vipākesu alobhādisahagatakammapaṭibimbabhūtā viya pavattamānā alobhādayoti pañcaviññāṇesu viya nidānarahitatā sotapatitatāti daṭṭhabbā. Kiriyadhammā kiriyamattattā kammanidānarahitāicceva parihīnāvijjāṭṭhānā veditabbā.

306. From the statement, 'Non-greed is the source for the arising of actions,' etc. (AN 3.34), the active wholesome roots are the sources for volitional formations, not the non-greed and so on that occur in resultants propelled by karmic force, which are like mere reflections of actions accompanied by non-greed, etc. It should be seen that their state of being without a source is like the fivefold consciousness and like having fallen into a stream. Functional phenomena, being merely functional, are devoid of karmic sources and should thus be understood as states where the ground of ignorance has been abandoned.

Tatiyacatutthavārā asambhavato evāti kasmā vuttaṃ, kiṃ cakkhuviññāṇādīni cakkhāyatanupacayādīnaṃ pacchājātapaccayā na hontīti? Honti, tadupatthambhakassa pana cittasamuṭṭhānassa asamuṭṭhāpanaṃ sandhāya “asambhavato”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sahajātapacchājātaviññāṇassa pana vasena tadāpi viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, pacchājātasahajātanāmassa sahajātapurejātabhūtacakkhādirūpassa ca vasena nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanañca labbhatīti tatiyacatutthavārā na na sambhavantīti.

Why is it said that the third and fourth sections are impossible? Is it that eye-consciousness, etc., are not post-nascence conditions for the accumulation of the eye-base, etc.? They are; but it should be understood that the statement 'impossible' is made with reference to the non-origination of mind-originated matter that would support them. However, by way of co-nascent and post-nascent consciousness, 'name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness' is obtained; and by way of post-nascent and co-nascent name, and of co-nascent and pre-nascent matter such as the eye, 'the six sense-bases are conditioned by name-and-form' is also obtained. Thus, the third and fourth sections are not impossible.

Kusalābyākataniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Wholesome and the Indeterminate is completed.

Avijjāmūlakakusalaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the Wholesome Rooted in Ignorance

334. Sammohavasenāti kusalaphale aniccāditāya sabhaye sādurasavisarukkhabījasadise taṃnibbattakakusale ca anādīnavadassitāvasena. Samatikkamatthaṃ bhāvanā samatikkamabhāvanā, tadaṅgavikkhambhanavasena samatikkamabhūtā vā bhāvanā samatikkamabhāvanā.

334. 'By the power of delusion' means: through not seeing the danger in wholesome results—which are fearsome due to impermanence and so on, and are like the seed of a delicious-tasting poisonous tree—and in the wholesome states that produce them. 'Overcoming-development' is development for the purpose of overcoming; or it is the development that has become overcoming by means of the suppression of its factors.

Tathā idha na labbhantīti avijjāya eva saṅkhārānaṃ avigatādipaccayattābhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, viññāṇādīnaṃ pana saṅkhārādayo avigatādipaccayā hontīti avijjāpaccayā saṅkhāro, saṅkhārapaccayā [V 0.0140] viññāṇaṃ saṅkhārahetukantiādinā yojanā na na sakkā kātunti avigatacatukkādīnipi na idha labbhanti. Viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ viññāṇasampayuttaṃ nāmantiādinā hi yathālābhayojanāya nayo dassitoti.

Therefore, the statement 'it is not obtained here' is made with reference to the absence of the state of being a condition of non-disappearance, etc., for volitional formations on account of ignorance. However, for consciousness and so on, volitional formations and the like are conditions of non-disappearance, etc. Thus, while a connection such as 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness' and 'volitional formations being the cause' can be made, the tetrad of non-disappearance, etc., is also not obtained here. For, by such statements as 'with consciousness as condition, name-and-form' and 'name is that which is associated with consciousness,' the method of connection according to what is available is shown.

Avijjāmūlakakusalaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Wholesome Rooted in Ignorance is concluded.

Kusalamūlakavipākaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of Results Rooted in the Wholesome

343. “Nānākkhaṇikakammapaccaye [M 0.0142] pana vattabbameva natthī”ti vuttaṃ, kiṃ kusalamūlaṃ akusalamūlañca kammapaccayo hotīti? Na hoti, kammapaccayabhūtāya pana cetanāya saṃsaṭṭhaṃ kammaṃ viya paccayo hoti. Tena ekībhāvamiva gatattāti evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā kusalākusalamūlehi vinā kammaṃ vipākaṃ na janetīti tāni vipākassa pariyāyena upanissayoti vuttāni, evaṃ kammena ekībhūtāni saṃsaṭṭhāni hutvā kammajānaṃ paccayā hontīti pariyāyena tesaṃ kammapaccayatā vuttā. Esāti esa kusalamūlapaccayo akusalamūlapaccayo cāti yojetabbaṃ.

343. But regarding the different-moment kamma condition, it is said, 'there is absolutely nothing to be said.' Is it that the wholesome root and the unwholesome root are a kamma condition? No, they are not. However, associated with the volition that is the kamma condition, they act as a condition, as if they were kamma itself. It should be understood that it is stated thus because they have, as it were, attained a state of oneness. Just as, without wholesome and unwholesome roots, kamma does not generate a result, thus those roots are said to be a decisive support for the result indirectly; so too, having become one with kamma and associated with it, they serve as conditions for kamma-born phenomena; thus, their conditionality as a kamma condition is stated indirectly. 'This' means this wholesome-root condition and unwholesome-root condition; thus it should be connected.

Kusalākusalavipākānaṃ viya kiriyānaṃ uppādakāni avijjākusalākusalamūlāni ca na hontīti āha “upanissayataṃ na labhantī”ti. Manasikāropi javanavīthipaṭipādakamattattā kusalākusalāni viya avijjaṃ upanissayaṃ na karoti, avijjūpanissayānaṃ pana pavattiatthaṃ bhavaṅgāvaṭṭanamattaṃ hoti, pahīnāvijjānañca kiriyānaṃ avijjā nevuppādikā, ārammaṇamattameva pana hoti. Evañca katvā “kusalo dhammo abyākatassa dhammassa upanissayapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.423), “vipākadhammadhammo nevavipākanavipākadhammadhammassa upanissayapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.3.103) ca evamādīsu kiriyānaṃ akusalā upanissayapaccayabhāvena na uddhaṭāti. Apica “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”ti etassa vasena avijjāmūlako kusalanayo vutto, “saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇa”nti etassa vasena kusalākusalamūlako [V 0.0141] vipākanayo, kiriyānaṃ pana neva saṅkhāraggahaṇena, na ca viññāṇaggahaṇena gahaṇaṃ gacchatīti taṃmūlako kiriyānayo na labbhatīti na vuttoti daṭṭhabbo.

Ignorance and wholesome and unwholesome roots are not the producers of functional actions, just as they are not for wholesome and unwholesome results; therefore, it is said, 'They do not obtain the state of being a decisive support.' Attention also, being merely that which establishes the cognitive process, does not make ignorance a decisive support in the way that wholesome and unwholesome states do. For the occurrence of states that have ignorance as a decisive support, there is merely the adverting of the life-continuum. And for the functional actions of those who have abandoned ignorance, ignorance is not a producer; it is, however, merely an object. And so, in such passages as 'A wholesome state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of decisive support condition' (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.423), and 'A resultant-state-and-state is a condition for a neither-resultant-nor-resultant-state-and-state by way of decisive support condition' (Paṭṭhāna 1.3.103), unwholesome states are not cited as being a decisive support condition for functional actions. Furthermore, it should be understood that by way of 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations,' the wholesome method rooted in ignorance is stated; by way of 'with volitional formations as condition, consciousness,' the resultant method rooted in the wholesome and unwholesome is stated. However, functional actions are not included either by the term 'volitional formations' or by the term 'consciousness.' Therefore, a method rooted in them is not found and so is not stated.

Anekabhedatoti avijjādīnaṃ mūlapadānaṃ ekacittakkhaṇikānaṃ kiriyante paṭhamanaye sahajātādianekapaccayabhāvena gahitattā tesaṃ paccayānaṃ vasena navādimūlapadānaṃ nayānaṃ vasena, anekappakārato catunnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasenāti vā adhippāyo. Kusalākusalānaṃ pana vipāke cāti ettha kusalākusalesu kusalākusalānaṃ vipāke cāti vattabbaṃ. Purimapacchimesu hi nayesu yathā paccayākāro vutto, taṃdassanatthaṃ [M 0.0143] “anekabhedato ekadhāvā”ti vuttaṃ, na ca pacchimanaye kusale anekabhedato paccayākāro vutto, atha kho “ekadhāvā”ti. Ekadhāvāti ca mūlapadekapaccayatāvasena, ekasseva vā nayassa vasena ekappakārenāti attho, paṭhamacatukkasseva vasenāti vā adhippāyo. Dhammapaccayabhedeti avijjādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ paccayabhāvabhede jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ jātiādipaccayabhede, taṃtaṃcittuppādasamayaparicchinnānaṃ vā phassādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ ekakkhaṇikāvijjādipaccayabhede. Pariyattiādīnaṃ kamo pariyatti…pe… paṭipattikkamo. Paccayākāre hi pāḷipariyāpuṇanatadatthasavanapāḷiatthacintanāni “jarāmaraṇaṃ aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ…pe… nirodhadhamma”ntiādinā bhāvanāpaṭipatti ca kamena kātabbāti kama-ggahaṇaṃ karoti. Tatoti ñāṇappabhedajanakato kamato. Aññaṃ karaṇīyataraṃ natthi. Tadāyattā hi dukkhantakiriyāti.

'Of manifold divisions' means that because the root-terms, ignorance and so on, which are of a single mind-moment, are taken in the first method at the end of the functional section as having manifold conditions such as co-nascence, etc., the meaning is 'by way of these conditions,' or 'by way of the methods of the nine and other root-terms,' or 'in manifold ways by way of the four tetrads.' Regarding 'and in the result of wholesome and unwholesome,' it should be stated as 'in wholesome and unwholesome states, and in the result of wholesome and unwholesome states.' For in the earlier and later methods, the mode of conditionality is explained accordingly. To illustrate this, it is said, 'of manifold divisions or in one way.' However, in the later method, the mode of conditionality for the wholesome is not described as 'of manifold divisions,' but rather as 'in one way.' 'In one way' means by way of the conditionality of a single root-term, or by way of a single method in a uniform manner; or the intention is by way of the first tetrad alone. 'In the division of the conditionality of phenomena' refers to the division in the state of being a condition for phenomena such as ignorance, etc.; the division of the conditions such as birth, etc., for phenomena such as aging-and-death, etc.; or the division of the single-moment conditions, such as ignorance, etc., for phenomena such as contact, etc., which are delimited by the time of the arising of this or that consciousness. The sequence of learning, etc., is: learning… the sequence of practice. For in the mode of conditions, the mastering of the Pāli text, listening to its meaning, reflecting on the Pāli and its meaning, and the practice of development by way of 'aging-and-death is impermanent, conditioned… subject to cessation,' etc., should be done in sequence; thus the text includes the word 'sequence' (kama). 'From that' (tato) means from that sequence which generates distinctions of knowledge. There is nothing more important to be done, for the making of an end to suffering depends on it.

Kusalamūlakavipākaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Results Rooted in the Wholesome is concluded.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Division is concluded.

Paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of Dependent Origination is concluded.

7. Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgo

7. The Analysis of the Foundations of Mindfulness

1. Suttantabhājanīyaṃ

1. The Sutta Division

Uddesavāravaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Summary Section

355. Tayo [M 0.0144][V 0.0142] satipaṭṭhānāti satipaṭṭhāna-saddassa atthuddhāraṃ karoti, na idha pāḷiyaṃ vuttassa satipaṭṭhāna-saddassa atthadassanaṃ. Ādīsu hi satigocaroti ādi-saddena “phassasamudayā vedanānaṃ samudayo, nāmarūpasamudayā cittassa samudayo, manasikārasamudayā dhammānaṃ samudayo”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.408) satipaṭṭhānanti vuttānaṃ satigocarānaṃ dīpake suttappadese saṅgaṇhāti. Evaṃ paṭisambhidāpāḷiyampi avasesapāḷippadesadassanattho ādi-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Dānādīnipi karontassa rūpādīni kasiṇādīni ca satiyā ṭhānaṃ hotīti taṃnivāraṇatthamāha “padhānaṃ ṭhāna”nti. Pa-saddo hi padhānatthadīpakoti adhippāyo.

355. 'Three foundations of mindfulness': here, an extraction of the meaning of the word 'satipaṭṭhāna' is being done, not an explanation of the meaning of the word 'satipaṭṭhāna' as stated here in the Pāli text. For in 'in the beginning, the object of mindfulness,' the word 'ādi' (beginning, etc.) includes the sutta passages that illuminate the objects of mindfulness which are called 'foundations of mindfulness', such as: "With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling; with the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of consciousness; with the arising of attention, there is the arising of phenomena" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.408). In the same way, in the Pāli of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the word 'ādi' should be seen as indicating the remaining Pāli passages. To prevent the notion that for one performing giving and other such actions, material forms and kasiṇas are also a station for mindfulness, it is said, 'the principal station.' The prefix 'pa-' indeed signifies the meaning of 'principal'; this is the intention.

Ariyoti ariyaṃ seṭṭhaṃ sammāsambuddhamāha. Etthāti etasmiṃ saḷāyatanavibhaṅgasutteti attho. Suttekadesena hi suttaṃ dasseti. Tattha hi –

'The noble one' means the noble, supreme, Perfectly Enlightened Buddha. 'Here' means in this Salāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta. For a portion of the sutta indicates the whole sutta. Therein—

“Tayo satipaṭṭhānā yadariyo…pe… arahatīti iti kho panetaṃ vuttaṃ, kiñcetaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, satthā sāvakānaṃ dhammaṃ deseti anukampako hitesī anukampaṃ upādāya ‘idaṃ vo hitāya idaṃ vo sukhāyā’ti. Tassa sāvakā na sussūsanti, na sotaṃ odahanti, na aññā cittaṃ upaṭṭhāpenti, vokkamma ca satthusāsanā vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato na ceva anattamano hoti, na ca anattamanataṃ [V 0.0143] paṭisaṃvedeti, anavassuto ca viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Yadariyo…pe… arahati.

“Three foundations of mindfulness, which the noble one… is worthy of. Now, this was said, but with reference to what was it said? Here, monks, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to his disciples, compassionate and seeking their welfare, out of compassion, thinking, ‘This is for your welfare, this is for your happiness.’ But his disciples do not want to listen, do not lend an ear, do not apply their minds to final knowledge, and they turn away from the Teacher’s instruction. In this case, monks, the Tathāgata is neither displeased nor does he experience displeasure. He dwells untainted, mindful and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is the first foundation of mindfulness, which the noble one… is worthy of.

“Puna caparaṃ bhikkhave satthā…pe… idaṃ vo sukhāyāti. Tassa ekacce sāvakā na sussūsanti…pe… vattanti. Ekacce sāvakā sussūsanti [M 0.0145]…pe… na ca vokkamma satthusāsanā vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato na ceva attamano hoti, na ca attamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Na ceva anattamano hoti, na ca anattamanataṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Attamanatañca anattamanatañca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhako ca viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, dutiyaṃ…pe….

“Furthermore, monks, the Teacher… ‘This is for your happiness.’ Some of his disciples do not want to listen… and turn away. Some disciples want to listen… and do not turn away from the Teacher’s instruction. In this case, monks, the Tathāgata is neither gratified, nor does he experience gratification. He is neither displeased, nor does he experience displeasure. Having avoided both gratification and displeasure, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. This, monks, is the second…

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… sukhāyāti. Tassa sāvakā sussūsanti…pe… vattanti. Tatra, bhikkhave, tathāgato attamano ceva hoti, attamanatañca paṭisaṃvedeti, anavassuto ca viharati sato sampajāno. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, tatiya”nti (ma. ni. 3.311) –

“Again, monks… ‘This is for your happiness.’ His disciples listen… they act accordingly. In this case, monks, the Tathāgata is pleased and feels pleasure, yet he dwells unattached, mindful and fully aware. This, monks, is the third.”

Evaṃ paṭighānunayehi anavassutatā, niccaṃ upaṭṭhitasatitā, tadubhayavītivattatā satipaṭṭhānanti vuttā. Buddhānameva kira niccaṃ upaṭṭhitasatitā hoti, na paccekabuddhādīnanti.

Thus, untaintedness by aversion and inclination, constant mindfulness, and transcendence of both are spoken of as the foundations of mindfulness. Indeed, it is said that only the Buddhas possess constant mindfulness, not Paccekabuddhas and others.

Pa-saddo ārambhaṃ joteti, ārambho ca pavattīti katvā āha “pavattayitabbatoti attho”ti. Satiyā karaṇabhūtāya paṭṭhānaṃ paṭṭhāpetabbaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Ana-saddañhi bahulaṃ-vacanena kammatthaṃ icchanti saddavidū, tatheva kattuatthampi icchantīti puna tatiyanaye “patiṭṭhātīti paṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha pa-saddo bhusatthaṃ pakkhandanaṃ dīpetīti “okkantitvā pakkhanditvā vattatīti attho”ti āha. Puna bhāvatthe sati-saddaṃ paṭṭhāna-saddañca vaṇṇento “atha vā”tiādimāha. Tena purimatthe sati-saddo paṭṭhāna-saddo ca kattuatthoti viññāyati.

The prefix "pa-" signifies commencement, and considering commencement as continuity, it is said, "The meaning is 'should be set in motion'." The foundation (paṭṭhāna) should be established with mindfulness (sati) as the instrumental cause—hence, satipaṭṭhāna. Indeed, grammarians often desire the passive sense by the frequent use of the suffix '-ana', and similarly, they also desire the active sense. Therefore, in the third method, it is said, "Because it stands firm, it is a 'foundation' (paṭṭhāna)." Here, the prefix "pa-" conveys the meaning of intensity and propulsion—thus, it is said, "The meaning is 'having advanced, it rushes forward and proceeds.'" Again, explaining the words "sati" and "paṭṭhāna" in the sense of abstract quality, it is said, "Or alternatively," etc. By this, in the previous sense, the word "sati" and the word "paṭṭhāna" are understood to convey the active sense.

Visesena kāyo ca vedanā ca assādassa kāraṇanti tappahānatthaṃ tesaṃ taṇhāvatthūnaṃ oḷārikasukhumānaṃ asubhadukkhatādassanāni mandatikkhapaññehi taṇhācaritehi sukarānīti tāni tesaṃ visuddhimaggoti vuttāni, evaṃ diṭṭhiyā visesakāraṇesu cittadhammesu aniccānattatādassanāni nātipabhedātipabhedagatesu tesu tappahānatthaṃ mandatikkhānaṃ diṭṭhicaritānaṃ sukarānīti [V 0.0144] tesaṃ tāni visuddhimaggoti. Tikkho samathayāniko oḷārikārammaṇaṃ pariggaṇhanto tattha aṭṭhatvā jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya vedanaṃ pariggaṇhātīti āha “oḷārikārammaṇe asaṇṭhahanato”ti. Vipassanāyānikassa [M 0.0146] sukhume citte dhammesu ca cittaṃ pakkhandatīti tadanupassanānaṃ taṃvisuddhimaggatā vuttā.

The body and feelings are especially the causes of gratification, and to abandon them, contemplation of the foulness and suffering of those craving-objects, whether gross or subtle, is easy for those whose wisdom is dull or keen who are inclined to craving. These are called their path of purification. Similarly, regarding mental phenomena as special causes of views, contemplation of impermanence and non-self in those phenomena—whether not too diverse or extremely diverse—is easy for those whose wisdom is dull or keen who are inclined to views, for the purpose of abandoning those phenomena. These are called their path of purification. One who is keen and whose vehicle is serenity meditation, taking a gross object, not being established there, attains jhāna, arises, and then contemplates feeling. Hence, it is said, "from not being established on a gross object." For one whose vehicle is insight meditation, the mind inclines towards subtle mental phenomena, and it is said that those contemplations are their path to purification.

Tesaṃ tatthāti ettha tattha-saddassa pahānatthanti etena yojanā. Pañca kāmaguṇā savisesā kāye labbhantīti visesena kāyo kāmoghassa vatthu, bhave sukhaggahaṇavasena bhavassādo hotīti bhavoghassa vedanā, santatighanaggahaṇavasena citte attābhiniveso hotīti diṭṭhoghassa cittaṃ, dhammavinibbhogassa dhammānaṃ dhammamattatāya ca duppaṭivijjhattā sammoho hotīti avijjoghassa dhammā, tasmā tesu tesaṃ pahānatthaṃ cattārova vuttā, dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo anusetīti dukkhadukkhavipariṇāmadukkhasaṅkhāradukkhabhūtā vedanā visesena byāpādakāyaganthassa vatthu, citte niccaggahaṇavasena sassatassa attano sīlena suddhītiādiparāmasanaṃ hotīti sīlabbataparāmāsassa cittaṃ, nāmarūpaparicchedena bhūtaṃ bhūtato apassantassa bhavavibhavadiṭṭhisaṅkhāto idaṃsaccābhiniveso hotīti tassa dhammā…pe… sukhavedanāssādavasena paralokanirapekkho “natthi dinna”ntiādiparāmāsaṃ uppādetīti diṭṭhupādānassa vedanā. Santatighanaggahaṇavasena sarāgādicitte sammoho hotīti mohāgatiyā cittaṃ, dhammasabhāvānavabodhena bhayaṃ hotīti bhayāgatiyā dhammā…pe… avuttānaṃ vuttanayena vatthubhāvo yojetabbo.

In the phrase `tesaṃ tattha`, the word 'therein' is to be connected with the meaning 'for the purpose of their abandonment'. The five strands of sensual pleasure are obtained distinctly in the body; thus, the body is especially the basis for the flood of sensuality. By grasping pleasure in existence, there arises delight in existence; thus, feeling is the basis for the flood of existence. By grasping continuity and solidity in the mind, there arises adherence to self; thus, the mind is the basis for the flood of views. Due to the analysis of phenomena and the difficulty of penetrating the mere phenomenal nature of phenomena, delusion arises; thus, phenomena are the basis for the flood of ignorance. Therefore, for the purpose of abandoning these, all four are mentioned. The underlying tendency of aversion lies latent in painful feeling; thus, this feeling—which is the pain of pain, the pain of change, and the pain of conditioned formations—is especially the basis of the bodily knot of ill-will. By grasping permanence in the mind, there arises the misapprehension that an eternal self attains purity through virtue and asceticism, and so on; thus, the mind is the basis for adherence to rites and rituals. For one who, in the determination of name-and-form, does not see what has come to be as it has come to be, there arises adherence to 'this is the truth,' which is characterized as views of existence and non-existence; the basis for this is phenomena… Through relishing pleasant feeling, being indifferent to the next world, one gives rise to the misapprehension 'there is no giving,' and so on; thus, feeling is the basis for clinging to views. By grasping continuity and solidity in a mind affected by lust and so on, delusion arises; thus, the mind is the basis for the wrong course of delusion. Through non-comprehension of the true nature of phenomena, fear arises; thus, phenomena are the basis for the wrong course of fear… The unstated items should be connected as a basis in the manner explained.

“Āhārasamudayā kāyasamudayo, phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo (saṃ. ni. 5.408), saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti (ma. ni. 3.126; saṃ. ni. 2.1; udā. 1) vacanato kāyādīnaṃ samudayabhūtā kabaḷīkārāhāraphassamanosañcetanāviññāṇāhārā kāyādiparijānanena pariññātā hontīti āha “catubbidhāhārapariññattha”nti. Pakaraṇanayoti tambapaṇṇibhāsāya vaṇṇanānayo. Nettipeṭakappakaraṇe dhammakathikānaṃ yojanānayotipi vadanti.

“With the arising of nutriment, the body arises; with the arising of contact, feeling arises (Saṃ. Ni. 5.408). With formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises” (Ma. Ni. 3.126; Saṃ. Ni. 2.1; Udā. 1). Thus, the nutriments—physical food, contact, mental volition, and consciousness—which are the cause of the arising of the body and so on, are fully understood by thoroughly knowing the body and so on. This is what is meant by “the purpose of fully understanding the four kinds of nutriment.” The method of the treatise is the style of commentary in the Tambapaṇṇi language. Some also say it is the method of exposition for Dhamma speakers found in the Nettipakaraṇa.

Saraṇavasenāti kāyādīnaṃ kusalādidhammānañca dhāraṇatāvasena. Saranti gacchanti etāyāti satīti imasmiṃ atthe ekatte nibbāne samāgamo ekattasamosaraṇaṃ. Etadeva hi dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādimāha. Ekanibbānappavesahetubhūto vā samānatāya eko satipaṭṭhānasabhāvo [M 0.0147][V 0.0145] ekattaṃ, tattha samosaraṇaṃ taṃsabhāgatā ekattasamosaraṇaṃ. Ekanibbānappavesahetubhāvaṃ pana dassetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādimāha. Etasmiṃ atthe saraṇekattasamosaraṇāni saha satipaṭṭhānekabhāvassa kāraṇattena vuttānīti daṭṭhabbāni, purimasmiṃ visuṃ. Saraṇavasenāti vā gamanavasenāti atthe sati tadeva gamanaṃ samosaraṇanti samosaraṇe vā sati-saddatthavasena avuccamāne dhāraṇatāva satīti sati-saddatthantarābhāvā purimaṃ satibhāvassa kāraṇaṃ, pacchimaṃ ekabhāvassāti nibbānasamosaraṇepi sahitāneva tāni satipaṭṭhānekabhāvassa kāraṇāni.

By means of recollection (saraṇa), it is in the sense of sustaining (dhāraṇa) wholesome qualities and so on in the body and so forth. "They go, they proceed by this"—thus sati (mindfulness). In this sense, convergence into the oneness that is Nibbāna is ekattasamosaraṇa (convergence into unity). Indeed, to show this, he said, "Just as..." etc. Or, the state of having one satipaṭṭhāna nature due to the cause of entering the single Nibbāna, is ekatta (oneness); convergence into that, being of the same nature as that, is ekattasamosaraṇa (convergence into unity). To show the state of being the cause for entering the single Nibbāna, he said, "Just as..." etc. In this sense, recollection, oneness, and convergence are to be understood as stated as the cause for the unity of the foundations of mindfulness. In the previous explanation, they were treated separately. Alternatively, "by means of recollection" or "by means of going"—when there is the sense of going, that very going is samosaraṇa (convergence). Or, if the meaning of the word 'sati' is not stated in terms of 'samosaraṇa', then 'sati' means 'sustaining'. Because there is no other meaning of the word sati, the former explanation is the cause for the state of mindfulness, and the latter is the cause for unity. Even in the convergence into Nibbāna, those causes for the unity of satipaṭṭhāna are included together.

Cuddasavidhenāti idaṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutte (dī. ni. 2.372 ādayo; ma. ni. 1.105 ādayo) vuttānaṃ ānāpānapabbādīnaṃ vasena. Tathā pañcavidhena dhammānupassananti etthāpi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ettha ca uṭṭhānakabhaṇḍasadisatā taṃtaṃsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanānubhāvassa daṭṭhabbā. Bhikkhugocarā hi ete. Vuttañhi “gocare, bhikkhave, caratha sake pettike visaye”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.372; dī. ni. 3.80).

By 'in fourteen ways' (cuddasavidhena), this refers to what is stated in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta (Dī. Ni. 2.372 ff.; Ma. Ni. 1.105 ff.) in terms of the section on mindfulness of breathing, etc. Similarly, 'the fivefold contemplation of phenomena' should also be understood in this context. Here, the nature of being like a merchant's stock-in-trade should be understood as the influence of the development of each respective foundation of mindfulness. For these are the bhikkhus' domain. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, wander in your own ancestral domain,' etc. (Saṃ. Ni. 5.372; Dī. Ni. 3.80).

Kāyānupassanādipaṭipattiyā bhikkhu hotīti bhikkhuṃ “kāyānupassī viharatī”tiādinā dasseti bhikkhumhi taṃniyamato. Tenāha “paṭipattiyā vā bhikkhubhāvadassanato”ti.

One becomes a bhikkhu by the practice of contemplation of the body and so on. Thus, with the words 'dwells contemplating the body,' etc., he indicates a bhikkhu, as this is prescribed for a bhikkhu. Therefore, it is said: 'or by showing the state of being a bhikkhu through practice.'

Samaṃ careyyāti kāyādivisamacariyaṃ pahāya kāyādīhi samaṃ careyya. Rāgādivūpasamena santo, indriyadamanena danto, catumagganiyamena niyato, seṭṭhacāritāya brahmacārī. Kāyadaṇḍādioropanena nidhāya daṇḍaṃ. So evarūpo bāhitapāpasamitapāpabhinnakilesatāhi brāhmaṇādisamañño veditabbo.

By 'should walk evenly' (samaṃ careyya), it means having abandoned uneven conduct of body and so on, one should conduct oneself evenly with body and so on. Peaceful through the calming of lust and so on, tamed through the restraint of the senses, controlled through the discipline of the four paths, a holy one through supreme conduct. Having laid down the rod by refraining from bodily punishment and so on. Such a one, with evil expelled, evil calmed, and defilements shattered, should be known by designations such as 'brahmin' and the like.

Kāyānupassanāuddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition on Contemplation of the Body

Asammissatoti vedanādayopi ettha sitā, ettha paṭibaddhāti kāye vedanādianupassanāpasaṅgepi āpanne tadamissatoti attho. Avayavīgāhasamaññātidhāvanasārādānābhinivesanisedhanatthaṃ kāyaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgehi, tāni ca kesādīhi, kesādike ca bhūtupādāyarūpehi [V 0.0146] vinibbhujjanto [M 0.0148] “tathā na kāye”tiādimāha. Pāsādādinagarāvayavasamūhe avayavīvādinopi avayavīgāhaṃ na karonti. Nagaraṃ nāma koci attho atthīti pana kesañci samaññātidhāvanaṃ siyāti itthipurisādisamaññātidhāvane nagaranidassanaṃ vuttaṃ.

By 'not mixed' (asammissato), it means that feelings and other things are also situated here, bound here—thus, even if the contemplation of feelings and so on is included in the body, the meaning is that they are not mixed with it. To negate the grasping of a whole, the running after designations, the taking of essence, and the clinging to them, he analyzes the body into major and minor parts, and those into hair and so on, and hair and so on into the derived materiality of the elements. By dissecting in this way, he says, 'Thus, not in the body,' and so on. Even those who assert a whole in relation to a collection of parts like a palace or a city do not engage in the grasping of a whole. However, because for some the running after designations might occur, thinking, 'There is some entity called a city,' the example of a city is given to illustrate the running after designations like 'man' or 'woman.'

Yaṃ passati itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā, nanu cakkhunā itthipurisadassanaṃ natthīti? Saccaṃ natthi, “itthiṃ passāmi, purisaṃ passāmī”ti pana pavattasaññāya vasena “yaṃ passatī”ti vuttaṃ. Micchādassane vā diṭṭhiyā yaṃ passati, na taṃ diṭṭhaṃ, taṃ rūpāyatanaṃ na hoti, rūpāyatanaṃ vā taṃ na hotīti attho. Atha vā taṃ kesādibhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhātaṃ diṭṭhaṃ na hoti, diṭṭhaṃ vā yathāvuttaṃ na hotīti attho. Yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṃ na passatīti yaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ, kesādibhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhātaṃ vā diṭṭhaṃ, taṃ paññācakkhunā bhūtato na passatīti attho.

When one sees a woman or a man, is there not the seeing of a woman or a man by the eye? Truly, there is not. Yet, it is said, 'one sees,' based on the current perception that 'I see a woman, I see a man.' Or, in wrong seeing, with wrong view, what one sees is not truly seen—that is, it is not the form-base, or the form-base is not that—this is the meaning. Alternatively, that which is seen, reckoned as the aggregate of derived materiality beginning with hair, is not truly seen, or what is seen is not as described—this is the meaning. By 'what is seen, one does not see,' it means that the form-base, or what is seen reckoned as the aggregate of derived materiality beginning with hair, one does not see truly with the eye of wisdom—this is the meaning.

Na aññadhammānupassīti na aññasabhāvānupassī, asubhādito aññākārānupassī na hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Pathavīkāyanti kesādipathaviṃ dhammasamūhattā kāyoti vadati, lakkhaṇapathavimeva vā anekappabhedasakalasarīragataṃ pubbāpariyabhāvena pavattamānaṃ samūhavasena gahetvā kāyoti vadati, evaṃ aññatthāpi.

By 'not contemplating other dhammas' (na aññadhammānupassī), it means not contemplating other natures; it is said that one does not contemplate aspects other than foulness and so on. By 'earth-element body' (pathavīkāyaṃ), it refers to the earth element in the body, such as hair, etc.; because it is a collection of dhammas, it is called a body. Alternatively, it refers to the earth element as its characteristic, present throughout the entire body in its various divisions, and occurring continuously from beginning to end; taking it as a collection, it is called a body. The same applies elsewhere.

Ajjhattabahiddhāti ajjhattabahiddhādhammānaṃ ghaṭitārammaṇaṃ ekato ārammaṇabhāvo natthīti attho, ajjhattabahiddhā dhammā vā ghaṭitārammaṇaṃ idaṃ natthīti attho. Tīsu bhavesu kilesānanti bhavattayavisayānaṃ kilesānanti attho.

By 'internal and external' (ajjhattabahiddhā), it means that for internal and external phenomena there is no single combined object; or it means that internal and external phenomena are not this combined object. By 'defilements in the three existences' (tīsu bhavesu kilesānaṃ), it means defilements pertaining to the three realms of existence.

Sabbatthikanti sabbattha bhavaṃ. Sabbasmiṃ līne uddhaṭe ca citte icchitabbattā, sabbe vā līne uddhaṭe ca bhāvetabbā bojjhaṅgā atthikā etāyāti sabbatthikā. Antosaṅkhepoti antoolīyanā kosajjanti attho.

By 'universal' (sabbatthika), it means existing everywhere. Because in every situation, when the mind is sluggish or agitated, it is desirable; or because all the factors of enlightenment are to be cultivated when the mind is sluggish or agitated, they are present in it—hence, it is universal. By 'inward shrinking' (antosaṅkhepo), it means inward sluggishness, which is laziness.

Avisesena dvīhipi nīvaraṇappahānaṃ vuttanti katvā puna ekekena vuttappahānavisesaṃ dassetuṃ “visesenā”ti āha, “vineyya nīvaraṇānī”ti avatvā abhijjhādomanassavinayassa vā payojanaṃ dassento “visesenā”tiādimāha. Kāyānupassanābhāvanāya ujuvipaccanīkānaṃ anurodhavirodhādīnaṃ [V 0.0147] pahānadassanañhi etassa payojananti. Kāyabhāvanāyāti [M 0.0149] kāyānupassanābhāvanā adhippetā. Tenāti anurodhādippahānavacanena.

Having stated that the abandonment of the hindrances was spoken of without distinction, to then show the distinctive abandonment of each individually, he says 'distinctively' (visesena). Without saying 'having removed the hindrances' (vineyya nīvaraṇāni), but instead showing the purpose of removing covetousness and displeasure, he says 'distinctively' and so on. For the development of contemplation of the body, indeed, the purpose is to show the abandoning of conformity, opposition, and the like, which are directly opposed. By 'development of the body' (kāyabhāvanāya), the development of contemplation of the body is intended. By 'by that' (tena), it means by the statement of the abandoning of conformity and so on.

Sabbatthikakammaṭṭhānaṃ buddhānussati mettā maraṇassati asubhabhāvanā ca. Satisampajaññena etena yoginā parihariyamānaṃ taṃ sabbatthikakammaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ satisampajaññabalena avicchinnassa tassa pariharitabbattā, satiyā vā samatho vutto samādhikkhandhasaṅgahitattā.

The universal meditation subjects are: recollection of the Buddha, loving-kindness, mindfulness of death, and contemplation of unattractiveness. This is called a universal meditation subject when practiced by a yogi with mindfulness and clear comprehension, because it must be maintained continuously by the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension. Or, by mindfulness, tranquility is meant, because it is included in the aggregate of concentration.

Kāyānupassanāuddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Summary on the Contemplation of the Body is concluded.

Vedanānupassanādiuddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Summary on the Contemplation of Feelings and so on

Kevalaṃ panidhātiādinā idha ettakaṃ veditabbanti veditabbaṃ paricchedaṃ dasseti. Addamadakkhīti dvepi ekatthā. Sammaddasoti sammā passako.

Here, by the phrase 'but only here' and so on, he shows the limit of what should be understood, namely, 'this much should be understood.' 'He saw' (addam) and 'he saw' (adakkhī) both have the same meaning. 'One who saw rightly' (sammaddaso) means one who sees correctly.

Sukhadukkhatopi cāti sukhādīnaṃ ṭhitivipariṇāmañāṇasukhatāya, vipariṇāmaṭṭhitiaññāṇadukkhatāya ca vuttattā tissopi ca sukhato tissopi ca dukkhato anupassitabbāti attho.

'And also from pleasure and pain' means that, because it is said that the knowledge of the stability and change of pleasure and so on is happiness, and the ignorance of change and stability is suffering, therefore, all three feelings should be contemplated as happiness, and all three as suffering. This is the meaning.

Rūpādiārammaṇachandādiadhipatiñāṇādisahajātakāmāvacarādibhūminānattabhedānaṃ kusalākusalatabbipākakiriyānānattabhedassa ca ādi-saddena sasaṅkhārikāsaṅkhārikasavatthukāvatthukādinānattabhedānañca vasenāti yojetabbaṃ. Suññatādhammassāti “dhammā honti, khandhā hontī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 121) suññatāvāre āgatasuññatāsabhāvassa vasena. Kāmañcetthātiādinā pubbe pahīnattā puna pahānaṃ na vattabbanti codanaṃ dasseti, maggacittakkhaṇe vā ekattha pahīnaṃ sabbattha pahīnaṃ hotīti visuṃ visuṃ na vattabbanti. Tattha purimacodanāya nānāpuggalaparihāro, pacchimāya nānācittakkhaṇikaparihāro. Lokiyabhāvanāya hi kāye pahīnaṃ na vedanādīsu vikkhambhitaṃ hoti. Yadipi na pavatteyya, na paṭipakkhabhāvanāya [V 0.0148] tattha sā abhijjhādomanassassa appavatti hotīti puna tappahānaṃ vattabbamevāti. Ubhayattha vā ubhayaṃ sambhavato yojetabbaṃ. Ekattha pahīnaṃ [M 0.0150] sesesupi pahīnaṃ hotīti maggasatipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ, lokiyabhāvanāya vā sabbattha appavattimattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. “Pañcapi khandhā loko”ti hi catūsupi vuttanti.

It should be construed that by the word 'ādi' (and so on), the diversity of objects such as form, the diversity of dominant conditions like desire, the diversity of co-nascent factors like knowledge, the diversity of planes such as the sense sphere, and the diversity of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional states, as well as the diversity of prompted, unprompted, with a basis, without a basis, and so on, are included. The phrase 'of the phenomenon of emptiness' refers to the nature of emptiness as it appears in the chapter on emptiness, beginning with 'there are phenomena, there are aggregates' (Dhs 121). By 'And if here' (Kāmañcettha) and so on, he shows the objection that since something has already been abandoned before, its abandonment should not be stated again. Alternatively, at the moment of path-consciousness, what is abandoned in one place is abandoned in all places—it should not be stated separately. There, the resolution for the first objection pertains to different individuals, while for the latter, it pertains to different moments of consciousness. For in mundane development, what is abandoned in regard to the body is not suppressed in feelings and so on. Even if it does not arise, that non-arising of covetousness and displeasure there is not due to the counteractive development; thus, its abandonment must still be stated. Alternatively, both should be construed where both are possible. The statement 'what is abandoned in one place is abandoned in the rest' refers either to the development of the foundations of mindfulness on the path or to the mere non-arising in all places in mundane development. For it is said that 'the five aggregates are the world' applies to all four.

Vedanānupassanādiuddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Summary on the Contemplation of Feelings and so on is concluded.

Uddesavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chapter on the Summary is concluded.

Kāyānupassanāniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Detailed Exposition of the Contemplation of the Body

356. Sabbappakāravacanena uddese dassitā ajjhattādianupassanā pakārā ca gahitā. Tattha antogadhā cuddasa pakārā, kāyagatāsatisutte vuttā kesādivaṇṇakasiṇārammaṇacatukkajjhānappakārā, lokiyādippakārā cāti tepi gahitā eva. Niddese hi ekappakāraniddesena nidassanamattaṃ katanti, sabbappakāraggahaṇañca bāhiresupi ekadesasambhavato katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

356. By the comprehensive statement, the various modes of contemplation, such as internal contemplation, shown in the summary, have been included. Among these, fourteen modes are included within, and also those modes mentioned in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta—the modes of the four jhānas with colored kasiṇas of hair and so on as their object, and worldly modes, and so on—are also included. For in the detailed exposition, presenting only a single mode of detailed exposition serves as a mere illustration, and the inclusion of all modes should be understood as being made because of the possibility of some aspects also occurring in external objects.

Tiriyaṃ tacaparicchinnanti ettha nanu kesalomanakhānaṃ atacaparicchinnatā tacassa ca atthīti? Yadipi atthi, tacaparicchinnabahulatāya pana tacaparicchinnatā na na hoti kāyassāti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Taco pariyanto assāti tacapariyantoti vuttoti etena pana vacanena kāyekadesabhūto taco gahito eva. Tappaṭibaddhā ca kesādayo tadanupaviṭṭhamūlā tacapariyantāva hontīti dvattiṃsākārasamūho sabbopi kāyo tacapariyantoti vuttoti veditabbo.

Regarding the phrase 'enclosed by skin all around' (tiriyaṃ tacaparicchinnaṃ): is it not the case that hair, body hair, and nails are not enclosed by skin, and that the skin itself is also not? Even if that is so, because the greater part is enclosed by skin, the body is indeed enclosed by skin—thus it is said. Furthermore, by the statement 'bounded by skin' (tacapariyanta), which means 'skin is its boundary,' the skin, being a part of the body, is indeed included. And since the hair and so on are attached to it, with their roots penetrating it, they too are bounded by skin. Thus, it should be understood that the entire body, the collection of thirty-two parts, is said to be 'bounded by skin'.

“Pūraṃ nānappakārassā”ti vuttaṃ, ke pana te pakārā? Yehi nānappakāraṃ asuci vuttanti kesā lomātiādi vuttanti imamatthaṃ dīpento āha “ete kesādayo ākārā”ti. Ākārā pakārāti hi eko attho.

It is said, 'Full of various kinds.' But what are those kinds? Explaining this meaning, namely, 'by which it is said to be impure in various ways, such as hair, body hair, and so on,' he says, 'These aspects, beginning with hair, and so on.' For 'ākārā' (aspects) and 'pakārā' (kinds) have the same meaning.

Nisinnassa [V 0.0149] yāva aparipphandanisajjāmūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajjati, yāvatā uṭṭhāti vā, tāva eko nisajjavāro. Yena vidhinā uggahe kusalo hoti, so sattavidho vidhi “uggahakosalla”nti vuccati, taṃnibbattaṃ vā ñāṇaṃ.

For one who is seated, for as long as suffering rooted in unmoving sitting arises, or until one stands up, that constitutes one session of sitting. The method by which one becomes skilled in grasping is called 'skill in grasping,' which is sevenfold, or the knowledge born from that.

Pathavīdhātubahulabhāvato matthaluṅgassa karīsāvasāne tantiāropanamāha. Ettha pana maṃsaṃ…pe… vakkaṃ…pe… kesāti evaṃ vakkapañcakādīsu [M 0.0151] anulomasajjhāyaṃ vatvā paṭilomasajjhāyo purimehi sambandho vutto. Svāyaṃ ye parato visuṃ tipañcāhaṃ, purimehi ekato tipañcāhanti chapañcāhaṃ sajjhāyā vakkhamānā, tesu ādiantadassanavasena vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Anulomapaṭilomasajjhāyepi hi paṭilomasajjhāyo antimoti. Sajjhāyappakārantaraṃ vā etampīti veditabbaṃ. Hatthasaṅkhalikā aṅgulipanti. Lakkhaṇapaṭivedhassāti asubhalakkhaṇapaṭivedhassa, dhātulakkhaṇapaṭivedhassa vā.

Due to the predominance of the earth element, he speaks of placing the thread on the brain, ending with excrement. Here, regarding flesh… and so on… kidneys… and so on… hair—thus, having stated the forward recitation in the fivefold group beginning with kidneys and so on, the reverse recitation is stated in connection with the former. This recitation, which will be spoken of—reciting separately for three or five days, and together with the former for three or five days, or for six or five days—should be understood as stated with regard to seeing the beginning and the end in them. For even in forward and reverse recitation, the reverse recitation is the last. Alternatively, this should also be understood as another mode of recitation. 'Hatthasaṅkhalikā' means the row of fingers. 'For the penetration of characteristics' means for the penetration of the characteristic of repulsiveness or the penetration of the characteristic of the elements.

Attano bhāgo sabhāgo, sabhāgena paricchedo sabhāgaparicchedo, heṭṭhuparitiriyantehi sakakoṭṭhāsikakesantarādīhi ca paricchedoti attho.

One's own part is 'sabhāga'; delimitation by one's own part is 'sabhāgaparicchedo'. The meaning is delimitation below, above, and sideways by one's own parts, such as the hairs within one's own sections.

Dhātuvibhaṅgo (ma. ni. 3.342 ādayo) pukkusātisuttaṃ. Sādhāraṇavasenāti ettakeneva siddhe sabba-ggahaṇaṃ vaṇṇakasiṇavasena catukkajjhānikasamathasādhāraṇattassa ca dassanatthaṃ.

The Dhātuvibhaṅga (Analysis of the Elements) (Majjhima Nikāya 3.342, etc.) is the Pukkusāti Sutta. Although 'in a general sense' suffices, the inclusion of 'all' is to show the commonality with regard to the color kasiṇas and the four jhānas in serenity meditation.

Okkamanavissajjananti paṭipajjitabbavajjetabbe maggeti attho. Bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇeti ettha kāyānupassanaṃ hitvā subhādivasena gayhamānā kesādayopi bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇānevāti veditabbā. Ukkuṭṭhukkaṭṭhiṭṭhāneyeva uṭṭhahitvāti pubbe viya ekattha katāya ukkuṭṭhiyā kamena sabbatālesu patitvā uṭṭhahitvā pariyantatālaṃ āditālañca agantvā tato tato tattha tattheva katāya ukkuṭṭhiyā uṭṭhahitvāti attho.

'Entering and emerging' means the path that should be practiced and avoided. Here, regarding 'external, diverse objects,' it should be understood that even the hair and so on, when grasped as beautiful, etc., abandoning the contemplation of the body, are also external, diverse objects. 'Having stood up right there in the squatting posture' means that, as before, having stood up from the squatting posture done in one place, gradually stepping on all the squares, and without going to the outermost and the initial square, but standing up right there from the squatting posture done again and again at each square—this is the meaning.

Adhicittanti samathavipassanācittaṃ. Anuyuttenāti yuttapayuttena, bhāventenāti attho. Samādhinimittaṃ upalakkhaṇākāro samādhiyeva. Manasi kātabbanti citte kātabbaṃ, uppādetabbanti attho. Samādhikāraṇaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ samādhinimittaṃ āvajjitabbanti attho. Ṭhānaṃ atthīti vacanaseso, taṃ cittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyya, etassa saṃvattanassa kāraṇaṃ atthīti [V 0.0150] attho. Taṃ vā manasikaraṇaṃ cittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyyāti etassa ṭhānaṃ kāraṇanti attho. Na ca pabhaṅgūti kammaniyabhāvūpagamanena ca pabhijjanasabhāvanti attho.

'Adhicitta' (higher mind) means the mind associated with serenity and insight. 'Anuyuttena' (engaged) means properly engaged, developing it—this is the meaning. The sign of concentration is the characteristic of observation, which is concentration itself. 'It should be kept in mind' means it should be done in the mind, it should be produced—this is the meaning. Alternatively, the object that causes concentration is the sign of concentration that should be attended to—this is the meaning. 'There is a possibility' is the remainder of the statement, that the mind might tend toward laziness, meaning there is a cause for this tendency. Or, that very directing of the mind might cause the mind to tend toward laziness—this is the meaning: there is a cause for this. 'And it is not fragile' means it approaches workability and does not have a nature of being easily broken.

Ālimpetīti ādīpeti jāleti. Tañcāti taṃ piḷandhanavikatisaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ payojanaṃ. Assāti suvaṇṇakārassa anubhoti sambhoti sādheti[M 0.0152]. Assa vā suvaṇṇassa taṃ atthaṃ suvaṇṇakāro anubhoti pāpuṇāti.

'Ālimpeti' (he kindles) means he ignites and inflames. 'And that' refers to that purpose, known as the flaw of ornaments. 'Assa' (he experiences) means the goldsmith undergoes, obtains, or accomplishes it. Or, the goldsmith obtains that purpose from the gold.

Abhiññāya iddhividhādiñāṇena sacchikaraṇīyassa iddhividhapaccanubhavanādikassa abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyassa. Paccakkhaṃ yassa atthi, so sakkhi, sakkhino bhabbatā sakkhibhabbatā, sakkhibhavanatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sakkhi ca so bhabbo cāti vā sakkhibhabbo. Ayañhi iddhividhādīnaṃ bhabbo, tattha ca sakkhīti sakkhibhabbo, tassa bhāvo sakkhibhabbatā, taṃ pāpuṇāti. Āyataneti pubbahetādike kāraṇe sati.

'Of what is to be realized by direct knowledge' refers to that which is to be realized, such as the experience of psychic powers and so on, by means of the knowledge of psychic powers and the like. One who has direct perception is a witness; the state of being a witness is 'sakkhibhabbatā', meaning the state of being a witness. Or, he is both a witness and capable, thus 'sakkhibhabbo'. For he is capable of psychic powers and the like, and a witness to them, thus he is a 'capable witness'; his state is 'sakkhibhabbatā', which he attains. 'Āyatane' refers to when there is a cause, such as a prior cause.

Sītibhāvanti nibbānaṃ, kilesadarathavūpasamaṃ vā. Sampahaṃsetīti samapavattaṃ cittaṃ tathāpavattiyā paññāya toseti uttejeti. Yadā vā nirassādaṃ cittaṃ bhāvanāya na pakkhandati, tadā jātiādīni saṃvegavatthūni paccavekkhitvā sampahaṃseti samuttejeti.

'Sītibhāva' (cooling) means Nibbāna, or the subsiding of the fever of the defilements. 'Sampahaṃseti' (he gladdens) means he gladdens and uplifts the mind that proceeds evenly, delighting it with wisdom that proceeds in that way. Or, when the mind, finding no relish, does not incline towards development, then he reflects on things that cause spiritual urgency, such as birth, etc., and gladdens and uplifts it.

Tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā, kathaṃ? Dve kesā ekato natthīti. Āsayoti nissayo, paccayoti attho.

Sideways, they are distinct from each other. How so? Because two hairs are not together.

Nakhā tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnāti visuṃ vavatthitataṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tameva hi atthaṃ dassetuṃ “dve nakhā ekato natthī”ti āhāti.

'Nails are distinct from each other sideways'—this is said with reference to their being separately established. To illustrate this very meaning, it is said, 'Two nails are not together.'

Sukhumampīti yathāvuttaoḷārikacammato sukhumaṃ antomukhacammādi. Koṭṭhāsesu vā tacena paricchinnattā yaṃ durupalakkhaṇīyaṃ, taṃ “sukhuma”nti vuttaṃ. Tañhi vuttanayena tacaṃ vivaritvā passantassa pākaṭaṃ hotīti.

'Even the subtle' means what is subtle compared to the coarse skin previously described, such as the skin inside the mouth, etc. Or, because it is confined by skin in the sections, what is difficult to perceive is called 'subtle.' For when one opens the skin and looks in the manner described, it becomes evident.

Tālaguḷapaṭalaṃ [V 0.0151] nāma pakkatālaphalalasikaṃ tālapaṭṭikāya limpitvā sukkhāpetvā uddharitvā gahitapaṭalaṃ.

The 'tālaguḷapaṭala' is a layer of ripe palm fruit juice smeared on a palm strip, dried, and then lifted off as a sheet.

Evaṃ timattānīti evaṃ-matta-saddehi gopphakaṭṭhikādīni avuttānipi dassetīti veditabbaṃ. Kīḷāgoḷakāni suttena bandhitvā aññamaññaṃ ghaṭṭetvā kīḷanagoḷakāni.

'Thus, only these three' means that even unmentioned things like ankle bones etc. are indicated by the words 'evaṃ' and 'matta'—this should be understood. Play balls are balls for playing that are tied with thread and struck against each other.

Tattha jaṅghaṭṭhikassa patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānanti jaṇṇukaṭṭhimhi pavisitvā ṭhitaṭṭhānanti adhippāyo. Tena aṭṭhinā patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ yaṃ kaṭiṭṭhino, taṃ aggachinnamahāpunnāgaphalasadisaṃ. Sīsakapaṭṭaveṭhakaṃ veṭhetvā ṭhapitasīsamayaṃ paṭṭakaṃ. Suttakantanasalākāviddhā [M 0.0153] goḷakā vaṭṭanāti vuccanti, vaṭṭanānaṃ āvali vaṭṭanāvali. Avalekhanasatthakaṃ ucchutacāvalekhanasatthakaṃ.

Here, 'the standing place of the shin bone' means the place where it enters and stands in the knee bone; this is the intention. The standing place of the hip bone, supported by that bone, resembles a great punnāga fruit severed at the top. `Sīsakapaṭṭaveṭhakaṃ` is a leaden plate placed by wrapping it around. Balls pierced with thread-spinning spindles are called `vaṭṭanā`, and a row of `vaṭṭanā` is called a `vaṭṭanāvali`. `Avalekhanasatthakaṃ` is a small knife for scraping sugarcane bark.

Vakkabhāgena paricchinnanti vakkapariyantabhāgena paricchinnaṃ.

'Bounded by the kidney portion' means bounded by the perimeter portion of the kidney.

Sakkharasudhāvaṇṇanti marumpehi katasudhāvaṇṇaṃ. “Setasakkharasudhāvaṇṇa”nti ca pāṭhaṃ vadanti, setasakkharāvaṇṇaṃ sudhāvaṇṇañcāti attho.

'Having the color of sugar and plaster' means having the color of plaster made with gravel. Some state the reading as 'having the color of white sugar and plaster,' meaning the color of white sugar and the color of plaster.

Yattha annapānaṃ nipatitvā tiṭṭhatīti sambandho.

The connection is: where food and drink fall and remain.

Visamacchinnakalāpo visamaṃ udakaṃ paggharati, evameva sarīraṃ kesakūpādivivarehi upari heṭṭhā tiriyañca visamaṃ paggharatīti dassetuṃ visamacchinna-ggahaṇaṃ karoti.
