Now, to show that learning and so on are not strong conditions for attainment, but that prior practice is a strong condition, he said, 'Learning, hearing, and questioning indeed...' Here, 'there is no analytical knowledge' is intended to mean that there is no attainment of analytical knowledge. Now, to show what has been said, he stated, 'But these...' For prior practice and attainment are both causes of clarity, so it was said, 'Prior practice is a strong condition for differentiation.'

Saṅgahavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Section on Inclusion is concluded.

2. Saccavārādivaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Section on Truths and so on.

719. Hetuvāre [M 0.0194] kālattayepi hetuphaladhammā “atthā”ti vuttā, tesañca hetudhammā “dhammā”ti, dhammavāre veneyyavasena atītānañca saṅgahitattā “uppannā samuppannā”tiādi na vuttanti atītapaccuppannā “atthā”ti vuttā, taṃnibbattakā ca “dhammā”ti idametesaṃ dvinnampi vārānaṃ nānattaṃ.

719. In the Section on Conditions, phenomena that are causes and results in the three times are called 'things' (attha), and the phenomena that are their causes are called 'dhammas.' In the Section on Phenomena, because past phenomena are also included for the sake of those to be trained, terms like 'arisen, produced,' and so on are not used; past and present phenomena are called 'things' (attha), and those that produce them are called 'dhammas.' This is the difference between these two sections.

Saccavārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Section on Truths and so on is concluded.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Suttanta Division is concluded.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Division

725. Avuttattāti “tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇa”nti sāmaññena vatvā visesena avuttattāti adhippāyo. Ettha ca kiriyānaṃ avipākattā dhammabhāvo na vuttoti. Yadi evaṃ vipākā na hontīti atthabhāvo ca na vattabboti? Na, paccayuppannattā. Evañce kusalākusalānampi atthabhāvo āpajjatīti. Nappaṭisiddho, vipākassa pana padhānahetutāya pākaṭattā dhammabhāvova tesaṃ vutto. Kiriyānaṃ paccayattā dhammabhāvo āpajjatīti ce? Nāyaṃ doso appaṭisiddhattā, kammaphalasambandhassa pana ahetuttā dhammabhāvo na vutto. Apica “ayaṃ imassa paccayo, idaṃ paccayuppanna”nti evaṃ bhedaṃ akatvā kevalaṃ kusalākusale vipākakiriyadhamme ca sabhāvato paccavekkhantassa dhammapaṭisambhidā atthapaṭisambhidā ca hotītipi tesaṃ atthadhammatā na vuttāti veditabbā[V 0.0196]. Kusalākusalavāresu ca dhammapaṭisambhidā kusalākusalānaṃ paccayabhāvaṃ sattivisesaṃ sanipphādetabbataṃ passantī nipphādetabbāpekkhā hotīti taṃsambandheneva “tesaṃ vipāke ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabhāvadassanamattameva pana atthapaṭisambhidāya kiccaṃ nipphannaphalamattadassanatoti tassā nipphādakānapekkhattā vipākavāre “tesaṃ vipaccanake ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā”ti na vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

725. 'Because it was not stated' is intended to mean: because after stating generally, 'knowledge of their results,' it was not stated in detail. And here, the nature of phenomena is not stated for functional consciousness, because it is not a result. If so, since they are not results, should their nature as meaning also not be stated? No, because they are conditionally arisen. If this were so, the nature as meaning would also apply to wholesome and unwholesome states. That is not denied; however, because of the prominence of the result as the principal cause, only their nature as phenomena is stated. If it is said that the nature of phenomena applies to functional consciousness because it is a condition, this is not a fault, as it is not denied; but because there is no cause in the connection between kamma and its fruit, its nature as phenomena is not stated. Moreover, it should be understood that their nature as meaning and phenomena is not stated because for one who, without making a distinction such as 'this is a condition, this is conditionally arisen,' merely reviews wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional phenomena according to their intrinsic nature, there arise both the analytical knowledge of phenomena and the analytical knowledge of meaning. And in the sections on wholesome and unwholesome states, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, seeing the state of being a condition, the specific potential, and the producibility of wholesome and unwholesome states, is dependent on what is to be produced. It is in relation to that, that it is said, 'knowledge of their results is the analytical knowledge of meaning.' However, since the function of the analytical knowledge of meaning is merely the seeing of intrinsic nature, which is the seeing of merely the produced fruit, it is not dependent on a producer. Therefore, it should be understood that in the section on results it is not said, 'knowledge of their ripening is the analytical knowledge of phenomena.'

Sabhāvapaññattiyāti na sattādipaññattiyā, aviparītapaññattiyā vā. Khobhetvāti lomahaṃsajananasādhukāradānādīhi khobhetvā. Puna dhammassavane [M 0.0195] jānissathāti appassutattā dutiyavāraṃ kathento tadeva kathessatīti adhippāyo.

'By designation of intrinsic nature' means not by designation of a being and so on, or by a non-perverted designation. 'Having stirred' means having stirred by causing the hair to stand on end, giving cries of approval, giving gifts, and so on. 'You will know upon hearing the Dhamma again' is intended to mean that because one has heard little, when the speaker speaks for a second time, he will say the very same thing.

746. Bhūmidassanatthanti ettha kāmāvacarā lokuttarā ca bhūmi “bhūmī”ti veditabbā, cittuppādā vāti.

746. 'For the purpose of seeing the planes' means that here, the sense-sphere and supramundane planes are to be understood as 'planes,' or alternatively, as arisings of consciousness.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Abhidhamma Division is concluded.

3. Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Section of Questions

747. Paccayasamuppannañca atthaṃ paccayadhammañcāti vacanehi hetādipaccayasamuppannānaṃ kusalākusalarūpānampi atthapariyāyaṃ, hetādipaccayabhūtānaṃ vipākakiriyarūpānampi dhammapariyāyañca dasseti. Paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāya kāmāvacaravipākārammaṇatā mahaggatārammaṇatā ca paṭisambhidāñāṇārammaṇatte na yujjati paṭisambhidāñāṇānaṃ kāmāvacaralokuttarakusalesu kāmāvacarakiriyālokuttaravipākesu ca uppattito. Sabbañāṇārammaṇatāya sati yujjeyya, “yena ñāṇena tāni ñāṇāni jānātī”ti (vibha. 726) vacanato pana na sabbañāṇārammaṇatāti kathayanti. Suttantabhājanīye pana “ñāṇesu ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā”ti avisesena vuttattā sabbañāṇārammaṇatā siyā. Abhidhammabhājanīyepi cittuppādavasena kathanaṃ niravasesakathananti yathādassitavisayavacanavasena “yena ñāṇena tāni ñāṇāni [V 0.0197] jānātī”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ aññārammaṇataṃ na paṭisedhetīti. Yathā ca atthapaṭisambhidāvisayānaṃ na niravasesena kathanaṃ abhidhammabhājanīye, evaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāvisayassapīti. Evaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidāya sabbañāṇavisayattā “tisso paṭisambhidā siyā parittārammaṇā siyā mahaggatārammaṇā siyā appamāṇārammaṇā”ti (vibha. 749) vuttā.

747. The terms 'meaning arisen from conditions' (paccayasamuppannaṃ atthaṃ) and 'condition-phenomena' (paccayadhammaṃ) show the meaning-aspect (atthapariyāyaṃ) of wholesome, unwholesome, and material phenomena produced by conditions such as roots, and the phenomena-aspect (dhammapariyāyaṃ) of resultant, functional, and material phenomena that are conditions such as roots. Regarding the analytical knowledge of ready wit (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā), its object cannot be sensual-sphere resultant states, sublime objects, or analytical knowledge as object, because the analytical knowledges arise in relation to sensual-sphere wholesome states, supramundane wholesome states, sensual-sphere functional states, and supramundane resultant states. If it were to take all knowledges as its object, it would be admissible; but according to the statement, 'By which knowledge one knows those knowledges' (Vibh. 726), they say it does not take all knowledges as its object. However, in the Suttanta division (suttantabhājanīye), since it is stated without distinction, 'Knowledge among knowledges is the analytical knowledge of ready wit,' it might take all knowledges as its object. Even in the Abhidhamma division (abhidhammabhājanīyepi), the explanation given in terms of the arising of consciousness is an exhaustive explanation; however, what was said as 'By which knowledge one knows those knowledges,' spoken in terms of the subject as shown, does not deny that it takes other objects. And just as the objects of the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) are not exhaustively explained in the Abhidhamma division, so too for the objects of the analytical knowledge of ready wit. Thus, since the analytical knowledge of ready wit has all knowledges as its object, it is said: 'The three analytical knowledges may have limited objects, or sublime objects, or measureless objects' (Vibh. 749).

Yadipi “siyā atthapaṭisambhidā na maggārammaṇā”ti (vibha. 749) vacanato abhidhammabhājanīye vuttapaṭisambhidāsveva pañhapucchakanayo pavatto. Na hi maggo paccayuppanno na hoti, abhidhammabhājanīye ca paṭisambhidāñāṇavisayā eva paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā vuttāti na tassā mahaggatārammaṇatāti. Evamapi dvepi etā pāḷiyo virujjhanti, tāsu balavatarāya ṭhatvā [M 0.0196] itarāya adhippāyo maggitabbo. Kusalākusalānaṃ pana paccayuppannattapaṭivedhopi kusalākusalabhāvapaṭivedhavinimutto natthīti nippariyāyā tattha dhammapaṭisambhidā ekantadhammavisayattā, tathā vipākakiriyānaṃ paccayabhāvapaṭivedhopi vipākakiriyabhāvapaṭivedhavinimutto natthīti nippariyāyā tattha atthapaṭisambhidā ekantikaatthavisayattā. Kiñci pana ñāṇaṃ appaṭibhānabhūtaṃ natthi ñeyyappakāsanatoti sabbasmimpi ñāṇe nippariyāyā paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā bhavituṃ arahati. Nippariyāyapaṭisambhidāsu pañhapucchakassa pavattiyaṃ dvepi pāḷiyo na virujjhanti.

Although it is said, 'There might be the analytical knowledge of meaning without the path as object' (Vibh. 749), in the Abhidhamma division, the method of questioning proceeds only with regard to the analytical knowledges mentioned. For the path is indeed arisen from conditions, and in the Abhidhamma division, the analytical knowledge of ready wit is stated as having only the analytical knowledges as its object; therefore, it does not have a sublime object. Even so, these two Pāli passages contradict each other. Standing by the stronger of them, the meaning of the other should be sought. As for wholesome and unwholesome states, the penetration of their nature as arisen from conditions is not separate from the penetration of their nature as wholesome or unwholesome. Thus, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā) there is without qualification, since its object is exclusively phenomena. Similarly, as for resultant and functional states, the penetration of their nature as conditions is not separate from the penetration of their nature as resultant or functional. Thus, the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) there is without qualification, since its object is exclusively meaning. Moreover, there is no knowledge that is devoid of ready wit, because it illuminates what is to be known. Therefore, the analytical knowledge of ready wit can exist without qualification in all knowledge. When the method of questioning proceeds with regard to the analytical knowledges without qualification, the two Pāli passages do not contradict.

Saddārammaṇattā bahiddhārammaṇāti ettha parassa abhilāpasaddārammaṇattāti bhavitabbaṃ. Na hi saddārammaṇatā bahiddhārammaṇatāya kāraṇaṃ saddassa ajjhattassa ca sabbhāvāti. Anuvattamāno ca so eva saddoti visesanaṃ na katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Regarding the statement, 'Because it has sound as its object, it is an external object,' here it should be understood as 'because its object is the sound of another's speech.' For the fact that it has sound as its object is not the reason for its being an external object, since sound that is internal also exists. And it should be understood that because that same sound is being carried forward, a specific qualifier was not made.

Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Questioner is concluded.

Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Discriminations is concluded.

16. Ñāṇavibhaṅgo

16. The Analysis of Knowledge

1. Ekakamātikādivaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Mātikās of Ones, etc.

751. Okāsaṭṭhena [M 0.0197][V 0.0198] sampayuttā dhammā ārammaṇañcāpi ñāṇassa vatthu. Yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanāti nahetādiavitathekappakāravatthuvibhāvanā. Yathā ekaṃ nahetu, tathā ekaṃ aññampīti hi gahetabbaṃ avitathasāmaññayuttaṃ ñāṇārammaṇaṃ yāthāvakavatthu. Yāthāvakena vā avitathasāmaññena vatthuvibhāvanā yāthāvakavatthuvibhāvanā.

751. Phenomena associated by way of opportunity are also the object and basis of knowledge. 'The discrimination of the object as it really is' means the discrimination of the object in the one true manner of non-roots, etc. For just as one is a non-root, so too is another; thus, an object of knowledge connected with true generality should be taken as the object as it really is. Or, the discrimination of an object by means of what is real or by true generality is the discrimination of the object as it really is.

Dukānurūpehīti dukamātikānurūpehīti vadanti. Osānadukassa pana dukamātikaṃ anissāya vuttattā dukabhāvānurūpehīti vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ tikānurūpehīti etthāpi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Osānaduke pana atthoti phalaṃ, anekatthattā dhātusaddānaṃ taṃ janetīti atthajāpikā, kāraṇagatā paññā. Jāpito janito attho etissāti jāpitatthā, kāraṇapaññāsadisī phalappakāsanabhūtā phalasampayuttā paññā.

They say 'in accordance with the dyads' (dukānurūpehīti) means 'in accordance with the dyad mātikās' (dukamātikānurūpehīti). However, since the final dyad is stated without relying on a dyad mātikā, it should be said to be 'in accordance with the nature of a dyad' (dukabhāvānurūpehīti). The same should be understood here too regarding 'in accordance with the triads' (tikānurūpehīti). In the final dyad, 'attha' means result. Because root-words have manifold meanings, 'it generates that' (taṃ janeti), thus it is called 'meaning-generating' (atthajāpikā), which is wisdom pertaining to the cause. 'The meaning is generated by it' (jāpito attho etissā), thus it is 'jāpitatthā'; this is wisdom similar to the wisdom of the cause, which has the nature of revealing the result and is associated with the result.

10. Dasakamātikāvaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Decad Matrix

760. “Catasso kho imā, sāriputta, yoniyo. Katamā…pe… yo kho maṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ jāna”nti (ma. ni. 1.152) vacanena catuyoniparicchedakañāṇaṃ vuttaṃ, “nirayañcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.153) pañcagatiparicchedakaṃ. “Saṃyuttake āgatāni tesattati ñāṇāni, sattasattati ñāṇānī”ti vuttaṃ, tattha pana nidānavagge sattasattati āgatāni catucattārīsañca, tesattati pana paṭisambhidāmagge sutamayādīni āgatāni [V 0.0199] dissanti, na saṃyuttaketi. Aññānipīti etena idha ekakādivasena vuttaṃ, aññattha ca “pubbante ñāṇa”ntiādinā, brahmajālādīsu ca “tayidaṃ tathāgato pajānāti ‘imāni diṭṭhiṭṭhānāni evaṃ gahitānī’ti”ādinā vuttaṃ anekañāṇappabhedaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Yāthāvapaṭivedhato sayañca akampiyaṃ puggalañca taṃsamaṅgiṃ ñeyyesu adhibalaṃ karotīti āha “akampiyaṭṭhena upatthambhakaṭṭhena cā”ti.

10. By the statement, "There are, Sāriputta, these four kinds of birth. Which four? ... He who knows me thus, Sāriputta" (MN 12), the knowledge that defines the four kinds of birth is stated. By the passage beginning, "I, Sāriputta, understand hell..." (MN 12), the knowledge that defines the five destinations is stated. It is said, "In the Saṃyutta Nikāya, seventy-three knowledges are found, and seventy-seven knowledges." However, in the Nidānavagga, seventy-seven and forty-four are found; whereas seventy-three, such as those arising from learning, are seen in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, not in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. By 'and others,' this includes what is stated here by way of the numerical lists starting with one, and elsewhere by such as 'knowledge of the past,' and in the Brahmajāla Sutta and others by such as 'This the Tathāgata understands: "These bases of views are thus held..."'—thus many kinds of knowledge are included. Because of penetrating things as they really are, it makes oneself unshakable and makes a person endowed with it powerful regarding what is to be known. Therefore, it is said, 'by the meaning of being unshakable and by the meaning of being a support.'

Seṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ [M 0.0198] sabbaññutaṃ. Paṭijānanavasena sabbaññutaṃ abhimukhaṃ gacchanti, aṭṭha vā parisā upasaṅkamantīti āsabhā, buddhā. Idaṃ panāti buddhānaṃ ṭhānaṃ sabbaññutameva vadati. Tiṭṭhamānovāti avadantopi tiṭṭhamānova paṭijānāti nāmāti attho. Aṭṭhasu parisāsu “abhijānāmahaṃ, sāriputta, anekasataṃ khattiyaparisaṃ…pe… tatra vata maṃ bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā okkamissatīti nimittametaṃ, sāriputta, na samanupassāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.151) vacanena dassitaakampiyañāṇayutto dasabalohanti abhītanādaṃ nadati. Sīhanādasuttena khandhakavagge āgatena.

760. The foremost state is omniscience. The Buddhas are called 'bulls' (āsabhā) because they go towards (abhimukhaṃ gacchanti) omniscience by way of declaration, or because the eight assemblies approach (upasaṅkamanti) them. But this speaks only of the Buddhas' state, which is omniscience. 'Standing firm' means that even without speaking, by merely standing firm one indeed makes a declaration. Endowed with the unshakable knowledge shown in the statement regarding the eight assemblies, "I recall, Sāriputta, having approached an assembly of many hundred nobles... That fear or timidity might overcome me there—I do not see that possibility" (MN 12), he, the one with ten powers, roars the fearless roar. This is from the Sīhanāda Sutta in the Khandhakavagga.

“Devamanussānaṃ catucakkaṃ vattatī”ti (a. ni. 4.31) suttasesena sappurisūpassayādīnaṃ phalasampatti pavatti, purimasappurisūpassayādiṃ upanissāya pacchimasappurisūpassayādīnaṃ sampatti pavatti vā vuttāti ādi-saddena tattha ca cakka-saddassa gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Paṭivedhaniṭṭhattā arahattamaggañāṇaṃ paṭivedhoti “phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Tena paṭiladdhassapi desanāñāṇassa kiccanipphattiparassa bujjhanamattena hotīti “aññāsikoṇḍaññassa sotāpattiphalakkhaṇe pavattaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Tato paraṃ pana yāva parinibbānā desanāñāṇappavatti tasseva pavattitassa dhammacakkassa ṭhānanti veditabbaṃ, pavattitacakkassa cakkavattino cakkaratanaṭṭhānaṃ viya.

"Among gods and humans, the four wheels turn" (AN 4.31). By the remainder of the sutta is meant the occurrence of the accomplishment of the fruit of such things as relying on a good person; or, it is said that the accomplishment and occurrence of later reliance on a good person and so on is dependent on the earlier reliance on a good person and so on. By the word 'ādi' (and so on) there, the inclusion of the word 'wheel' should be understood. Because it has penetration as its consummation, the knowledge of the path of arahantship is 'penetration'; as it is said, "it is what arises at the moment of fruition." Therefore, even for the knowledge of teaching thus attained, which is concerned with the accomplishment of its task, its function is fulfilled merely by awakening; hence it is said, "it occurred for Aññāsikoṇḍañña at the moment of stream-entry fruition." But thereafter, up to final Nibbāna, the continuation of the knowledge of teaching should be understood as the station of that very Dhamma-wheel that has been set in motion, like the station of the wheel-jewel for a wheel-turning monarch whose wheel has been set in motion.

Samādīyantīti samādānāni, tāni pana samādiyitvā katāni hontīti āha “samādiyitvā katāna”nti. Kammameva vā kammasamādānanti etena samādāna-saddassa apubbatthābhāvaṃ dasseti muttagata-sadde gata-saddassa viya.

They are undertaken, thus they are undertakings; but, having been undertaken, they are done, hence it is said, 'of those undertaken and done.' Or, action itself is the undertaking of action; by this, he shows the absence of a distinct meaning for the word 'undertaking,' just as with the word 'gone' in 'liberated-gone'.

Agatigāmininti [V 0.0200] nibbānagāminiṃ. Vuttañhi “nibbānañcāhaṃ, sāriputta, pajānāmi nibbānagāminiñca paṭipada”nti (ma. ni. 1.153).

"Leading to the Un-gone" means leading to Nibbāna. For it has been said: "Sāriputta, I understand Nibbāna and the path leading to Nibbāna" (MN 1.153).

Hānabhāgiyadhammanti hānabhāgiyasabhāvaṃ, kāmasahagatasaññādidhammaṃ vā. Taṃ kāraṇanti pubbeva katābhisaṅkhārādiṃ.

"A state conducive to decline" means the nature conducive to decline, or phenomena such as perceptions associated with sensual pleasures. "That cause" means previously performed volitional formations and the like.

“Idānī”ti etassa “iminā anukkamena vuttānīti veditabbānī”ti iminā saha yojanā kātabbā. Kilesāvaraṇaṃ tadabhāvañcāti kilesāvaraṇābhāvaṃ. Kilesakkhayādhigamassa hi kilesāvaraṇaṃ aṭṭhānaṃ, tadabhāvo ṭhānaṃ. Anadhigamassa kilesāvaraṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ, tadabhāvo [M 0.0199] aṭṭhānanti. Tattha tadabhāvaggahaṇena gahitaṃ “atthi dinna”ntiādikāya sammādiṭṭhiyā ṭhitiṃ tabbiparītāya ṭhānābhāvañca adhigamassa ṭhānaṃ passantena iminā ñāṇena adhigamānadhigamānaṃ ṭhānāṭṭhānabhūte kilesāvaraṇatadabhāve passati bhagavāti imamatthaṃ sādhento āha “lokiyasammādiṭṭhiṭhitidassanato niyatamicchādiṭṭhiṭhānābhāvadassanato cā”ti. Ettha ca adhigamaṭṭhānadassanameva adhippetaṃ upari bhabbapuggalavaseneva vipākāvaraṇābhāvadassanādikassa vakkhamānattā. Iminā pana ñāṇena sijjhanato pasaṅgena itarampi vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Dhātuvemattadassanatoti rāgādīnaṃ adhimattatādivasena taṃsahitānaṃ dhātūnaṃ vemattatādassanato, “ayaṃ imissā dhātuyā adhimattattā rāgacarito”tiādinā cariyāhetūnaṃ vā, rāgādayo eva vā pakatibhāvato dhātūti rāgādivemattadassanatoti attho. Payogaṃ anādiyitvāti santatimahāmattaaṅgulimālādīnaṃ viya kāmarāgabyāpādādivasena payogaṃ anādiyitvā.

The word 'idāni' should be connected with the phrase 'it should be understood that they are stated in this sequence'. 'The obstacle of defilements and its absence' means the absence of the obstacle of defilements. For the attainment of the destruction of defilements, the obstacle of defilements is an impossibility; its absence is a possibility. For non-attainment, the obstacle of defilements is a possibility; its absence is an impossibility. Here, by grasping its absence, the Blessed One, by this knowledge, sees the obstacle of defilements and its absence as the basis of possibility and impossibility for attainment and non-attainment, as one who sees that the stability of right view (such as, 'there is what is given') and the impossibility of the stability of its contrary is a possibility for attainment. To clarify this meaning, it is said: 'from seeing the stability of mundane right view and from seeing the impossibility of a basis for fixed wrong view.' And here, only the seeing of the possibility of attainment is intended, because the seeing of the absence of the obstacle of kamma-result and so on will be spoken of later with reference to capable individuals. It should be understood, however, that since this is accomplished by this knowledge, the other is also stated by implication. 'From seeing the diversity of elements' means from seeing the diversity of elements associated with them according to the degree of lust, etc., or of the causes of conduct, as in 'this person is of lustful conduct due to the high degree of this element,' etc.; or, that lust and so on are themselves elements due to their intrinsic nature—this is the meaning of 'from seeing the diversity of lust, etc.' 'Without taking up an effort' means without taking up an effort by way of sensual desire, ill will, etc., as in the case of Santati the great minister and Aṅgulimāla.

(1.) Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā

(1.) Commentary on the Exposition of Single Items

761. Na hetumevāti ettha ca na hetū evāti attho, byañjanasiliṭṭhatāvasena pana rassattaṃ ma-kāro ca kato “adukkhamasukhā”ti ettha viya. Imināpi nayenāti ettha purimanayena hetubhāvādipaṭikkhepo, pacchimanayena nahetudhammādikoṭṭhāsasaṅgahoti ayaṃ viseso veditabbo. Cutiggahaṇena cutiparicchinnāya ekāya jātiyā gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, bhavaggahaṇena navadhā vuttabhavassa. Tadantogadhatāya tattha tattha pariyāpannatā vuttā. Uppannaṃ manoviññāṇaviññeyyamevāti [V 0.0201] “na rūpaṃ viya uppannā chaviññāṇaviññeyyā”ti rūpato etesaṃ visesanaṃ karoti.

761. Here, 'na hetumeva' means 'not indeed causes,' but due to the compactness of the consonants, the shortening of the vowel and the letter 'm' are made, as in 'adukkhamasukhā.' In 'by this method as well,' it should be understood that this is the distinction: by the former method, there is the rejection of being a cause, etc.; by the latter method, there is the inclusion of the category of non-causal phenomena, etc. By the term 'cuti' (passing away), the taking of one birth delimited by passing away should be understood; by the term 'bhava' (existence), the ninefold existence as previously stated is understood. Because of being included within that, their inclusion here and there is stated. By 'arisen, knowable only by mind-consciousness,' he specifies their distinction from material form, stating that 'they are not knowable by the six consciousnesses when arisen, like material form'.

762. Kappato kappaṃ gantvāpi na uppajjatīti na kadāci tathā uppajjati. Na hi khīrādīnaṃ viya etesaṃ yathāvuttalakkhaṇavilakkhaṇatā atthīti dasseti.

762. "Even after going from aeon to aeon, it does not arise" means it never arises in that way. He shows that these things do not possess characteristics different from those described, unlike milk and so forth.

763. Samodhānetvāti loke vijjamānaṃ sabbaṃ rūpaṃ samodhānetvā. Etena mahattepi avibhāvakattaṃ dassento sukhumattā na vibhāvessatīti [M 0.0200] vādapathaṃ chindati. Cakkhupasāde mama vatthumhīti attho. Visayoti issariyaṭṭhānanti adhippāyo.

763. "Having combined" means having combined all form existing in the world. By this, showing that it cannot be discerned even when great, he cuts off the line of argument that it will not be discerned due to its subtlety. The meaning is: 'in my eye-sensitivity as the base.' The intention of 'visaya' (domain) is the place of mastery.

764. Abbokiṇṇāti abyavahitā, anantaritāti attho. Vavatthitānampi paṭipāṭiniyamo tena paṭikkhittoti attho. Anantaratāti anantarapaccayatā etena paṭikkhittāti attho.

764. "Uninterrupted" means without separation; the meaning is continuous. By that, the fixed sequence, even of established things, is rejected—this is the meaning. "Immediacy" means the condition of immediacy; by this, it is rejected—this is the meaning.

765. Samanantaratāti ca samanantarapaccayatā.

765. And "immediate contiguity" means the condition of immediate contiguity.

766. Ābhujanatoti ābhuggakaraṇato, nivattanato icceva attho. Ettha ca “pañca viññāṇā anābhogā”ti ābhogasabhāvā na hontīti attho, “pañcannaṃ viññāṇānaṃ natthi āvaṭṭanā vā”tiādīsupi āvaṭṭanabhāvo vātiādinā attho daṭṭhabbo.

766. "From bending" means from causing to bend, from turning back; this is indeed the meaning. Here, the phrase 'the five consciousnesses are without directing' means they do not have the nature of directing. And in statements like 'the five consciousnesses have no turning,' the meaning should be understood as the absence of the state of turning, and so on.

Na kañci dhammaṃ paṭivijānātīti ettha na sabbe rūpādidhammā dhammaggahaṇena gahitāti yathādhippetadhammadassanatthaṃ “manopubbaṅgamā dhammāti evaṃ vutta”nti āha.

Here, regarding 'does not recognize any phenomenon,' to show the intended phenomenon, he says that not all phenomena, such as form and so on, are included by the term 'phenomenon,' citing 'thus it was said, "phenomena are preceded by mind."

Rūpādīsu abhinipatanaṃ tehi samāgamo tesantipi vattuṃ yujjatīti āha “rūpādīnaṃ abhinipātamatta”nti. Kammatthe vā sāmivacanaṃ. Viññāṇehi abhinipatitabbāni hi rūpādīnīti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hotītiādīsu hi ayaṃ adhippāyo – ārammaṇakaraṇena paṭivijānitabbāni rūpādīni ṭhapetvā kusalākusalacetanāya taṃsampayuttānañca yathāvuttānaṃ sahajapubbaṅgamadhammena paṭivijānitabbānaṃ paṭivijānanaṃ etesaṃ natthīti. Evañca katvā “dassanādimattato [V 0.0202] pana muttā aññā etesaṃ kusalādipaṭiviññatti nāma natthī”ti kiccantaraṃ paṭisedheti.

He says 'merely the falling upon of forms, etc.' because it is appropriate to say that falling upon forms, etc., is an association with them. Or, the genitive is in the sense of the object, for forms, etc., are indeed to be fallen upon by consciousnesses. Indeed, in statements like 'this is what is meant,' this is the intention: setting aside forms, etc., which are to be recognized by being made an object, for these five consciousnesses there is no recognition of wholesome and unwholesome volitions and their associated states, which, as stated, are to be recognized by means of co-arisen and preceding phenomena. Having established this, he denies another function by stating: 'But apart from mere seeing, etc., there is no other designation of these as wholesome, etc.'

Avipākabhāvena aññaṃ abyākatasāmaññaṃ anivārento kusalākusalaggahaṇañca karotīti cavanapariyosānañca kiccaṃ. Pi-saddena sahajavanakāni vīthicittāni sampiṇḍetvā pañcadvāre paṭisedhane ayaṃ adhippāyo siyā – “manasā ce paduṭṭhena…pe… pasannena bhāsati vā karoti vā”ti (dha. pa. 1-2) evaṃ vuttā bhāsanakaraṇakarā, taṃsadisā ca sukhadukkhuppādakā balavanto chaṭṭhadvārikā eva dhammaggahaṇena gahitāti na tesaṃ pañcadvārikajavanena paṭivijānanaṃ atthi, dubbalānaṃ pana pubbaṅgamapaṭivijānanaṃ tattha na paṭisiddhaṃ “na [M 0.0201] kāyakammaṃ na vacīkammaṃ paṭṭhapetī”ti viññattidvayajanakasseva paṭṭhapanapaṭikkhepena dubbalassa manokammassa anuññātattā. Tathā kāyasucaritādikusalakammaṃ karomīti, tabbiparītaṃ akusalaṃ kammaṃ karomīti ca kusalākusalasamādānaṃ pañcadvārikajavanena na hoti. Tathā paṭiccasamuppādavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttā “pañcadvārikacuti ca na pañcadvārikacittehi hoti cuticittassa ataṃdvārikattā”ti. Yā panāyaṃ pāḷi “pañcahi viññāṇehi na kañci dhammaṃ paṭivijānāti aññatra abhinipātamattā”ti, tassā rūpādīnaṃ āpāthamattaṃ muñcitvā aññaṃ kañci dhammasabhāvaṃ na paṭivijānātīti ayamattho dissati. Na hi rūpaṃ paṭiggaṇhantampi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ rūpanti ca gaṇhātīti. Sampaṭicchanassapi rūpanīlādiākārapaṭivijānanaṃ natthīti kiñci dhammassa paṭivijānanaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ, pañcahi pana viññāṇehi sātisayaṃ tassa vijānananti “aññatra abhinipātamattā”ti na vuttaṃ. Yassa pāḷiyaṃ bahiddhāpaccuppannārammaṇatā vuttā, tato aññaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidaṃ icchantehi pañcadvārajavanena paṭisambhidāñāṇassa sahuppatti paṭisiddhā. Rūpārūpadhammeti rūpārūpāvacaradhammeti attho.

By not preventing another generally indeterminate state due to its non-resultant nature, it also performs the grasping of wholesome and unwholesome, and its function concludes with passing away. When the impulsion process consciousnesses are included by the particle 'pi', in the rejection at the five doors this might be the intention: those who perform speech and action as stated in 'manasā ce paduṭṭhena…pe… pasannena bhāsati vā karoti vā' (Dhp 1–2), and similarly those powerful sixth-door phenomena that produce pleasure and pain, are indeed grasped by the apprehension of dhammas; therefore, for them there is no recognition through a five-door impulsion. However, for the weak ones, a preliminary recognition is not denied there, since 'it does not establish bodily action nor verbal action' rejects the establishment only of that which generates the two kinds of intimation, thereby permitting weak mental action. Similarly, the undertaking of wholesome and unwholesome actions—such as 'I perform wholesome bodily conduct,' or its opposite, 'I perform unwholesome action'—does not occur through a five-door impulsion. Moreover, as stated in the explanation of dependent origination: 'Death at a five-door process does not occur with five-door consciousnesses, because the death consciousness is without that door.' As for the Pāḷi passage: 'With the five consciousnesses one does not recognize any phenomenon except for mere impact,' its meaning is seen as this: apart from merely the coming into range of forms and so forth, they do not recognize any other intrinsic nature of a phenomenon. For even when the eye-consciousness receives a form, it does not apprehend it as 'form.' For the receiving consciousness also, there is no recognition of the appearance of form, blue, etc.; thus, any recognition of a phenomenon is denied. However, the phrase 'except for mere impact' was not stated to mean that the five consciousnesses have a superior knowing of it. For those by whom an external present object is stated in the Pāḷi, and who desire another analytical knowledge of language, the co-arising of the knowledge of analytical insight with a five-door impulsion is denied. 'Phenomena of form and formlessness' means phenomena pertaining to the form and formless spheres.

Pañcadvārikacittena na paṭibujjhatīti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu rūpādīnaṃ āpāthagamane niddāpaṭibodho hotīti? Na, paṭhamaṃ manodvārikajavanassa uppattitoti dassento āha “niddāyantassa hī”tiādi. Palobhetvā saccasupinena.

Why is it said that one does not awaken by way of five-door consciousness? Is it not that when forms and so forth come into range, awakening from sleep occurs? No. Showing that the mind-door impulsion arises first, he says, 'For one who is sleeping,' and so on. Having enticed with a true dream.

Abyākatoyeva āvajjanamattasseva uppajjanatoti vadanti. Evaṃ vadantehi manodvārepi āvajjanaṃ dvattikkhattuṃ uppajjitvā javanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā bhavaṅgaṃ otaratīti adhippetanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

They say that it is merely indeterminate, arising only as an instance of advertence. When they speak thus, it should be understood that what is intended is that even at the mind-door, advertence arises two or three times, then stands at the impulsion phase, and finally sinks back into the life-continuum.

Tassā [V 0.0203] eva vasenāti tassā vasena ekavidhena ñāṇavatthu hotīti ca, veditabbanti ca yojanā kātabbā.

'Tassā eva vasena' means that by that very means it becomes a single kind of object for knowledge, and the construction with 'it is to be understood' should be made.

Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of Single Items is concluded.

(2.) Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Exposition of Pairs

767. Attha-saddo aññatra sabhāvaṃ gahetvā adhikaraṇesu pavattamāno adhikaraṇavasena liṅgaparivattiṃ gacchatīti adhippāyena jāpitā [M 0.0202] ca sā atthā cāti jāpitatthāti ayamattho vibhāvitoti daṭṭhabbo.

767. The word 'attha', apart from its inherent nature, when occurring in various contexts, undergoes a change of gender according to the context. With the intention that what is made known (jāpitā) and that which is its meaning (atthā) are both called 'jāpitattha', this meaning is to be understood as having been clearly explained.

Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Pairs is concluded.

(3.) Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Exposition of Triads

768. Paññāpariṇāmitesūti paññāya paripācitesu. “Yogavihitesūti idañca visayavisesanamattameva, tasmā yāni paññāya vihitāni ahesuṃ honti bhavissanti ca, sabbāni tāni yogavihitānīti daṭṭhabbāni. Sikkhitvā kātabbaṃ sippaṃ, itaraṃ kammaṃ. Ayametesaṃ viseso. Vaḍḍhakīkammanti ca asikkhitvāpi kātabbaṃ thūlakammaṃ “kamma”nti daṭṭhabbaṃ, paññā eva vā tattha tattha “kammaṃ sippa”nti ca veditabbā. Nāgamaṇḍalaṃ nāma maṇḍalaṃ katvā sappe vijjāya pakkositvā baliṃ datvā visāpanayanaṃ. Parittaṃ rakkhā, yena “phū”ti mukhavātaṃ datvā visaṃ apanayanti, so uṇṇanābhiādimanto phudhamanakamanto. “A ā”tiādikā mātikā “ka kā”tiādiko tappabhedo ca lekhā.

768. 'Paññāpariṇāmitesu' means matured by wisdom. 'Yogavihitesu' is merely a qualification of the object's sphere; therefore, whatever has been, is, or will be directed by wisdom should all be understood as 'yogavihita'. A craft (sippa) is work that is to be done after training; other work is 'kamma'. This is the distinction between them. Carpentry (vaḍḍhakīkamma) should be understood as coarse work done even without training, simply as 'kamma'. Or, wisdom itself in each particular instance should be understood as both 'kamma' and 'sippa'. The 'nāga-maṇḍala' refers to making a circle, summoning snakes through magical knowledge, offering oblations, and removing poison. 'Paritta' is a protection, by which they expel poison by blowing breath from the mouth, such as the spider-mantra and others, which is a blowing-mantra. The matrix letters like 'a, ā,' etc., and their variations like 'ka, kā,' etc., are writing (lekhā).

Kusalaṃ dhammaṃ sakaṃ, itaraṃ nosakaṃ. Catunnaṃ saccānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbānaṃ tappaṭivedhapaccayabhāvena anulomanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Pubbe “yogavihitesu vā kammāyatanesū”tiādinā paññā [V 0.0204] vuttā, puna tassā vevacanavasena “anulomikaṃ khanti”ntiādi vuttanti adhippāyena “anu…pe… paññāvevacanānī”ti āha. Ettha ca evarūpinti yathāvuttakammāyatanādivisayaṃ kammassakatasaccānulomikasabhāvaṃ aniccādipavattiākārañcāti attho. Yathāvuttā ca bhūmisabhāvapavattiākāraniddesā khantiādīhi yojetabbā. Yassā paññāya dhammā nijjhānapajānanakiccasaṅkhātaṃ olokanaṃ khamanti aviparītasabhāvattā, sā paññā dhammānaṃ nijjhānakkhamanaṃ etissā atthīti dhammanijjhānakkhantīti attho.

A wholesome quality is one's own; the other is not one's own. Conformity (anulomana) should be seen as the condition for the penetration of the four truths, which are to be penetrated. Previously, wisdom was spoken of with 'in the bases of action where effort is applied,' etc., and again, as a synonym for that, 'conformity, patience,' etc., were mentioned. With the intention that these are synonyms of wisdom, it says 'conformity… etc.… are synonyms of wisdom.' Herein, 'of such a kind' means the nature of conformity to the truth of ownership of action, which has as its sphere the aforesaid bases of action, etc., and the mode of occurrence as impermanent, etc. And the descriptions of the nature and mode of occurrence of the stages, as stated, should be connected with patience, etc. That wisdom by which phenomena endure examination—the function designated as 'scrutinizing and understanding'—because of their undistorted nature; that wisdom possesses the endurance for scrutinizing phenomena, hence it is called 'the patience for scrutinizing phenomena' (dhammanijjhānakkhanti). This is the meaning.

769. Asaṃvaraṃ muñcatīti samādānasampattaviratisampayuttacetanā “sīlaṃ pūrentassa muñcacetanā”ti vuttā. Pubbāparapaññāya ca dānasīlamayatāvacanato muñcaaparacetanāvasena “ārabbhā”ti, pubbacetanāvasena “adhikiccā”ti ca vattuṃ yuttanti “adhikiccā”tipi pāṭho yujjati.

769. 'Abandoning non-restraint' (Asaṃvaraṃ muñcati) refers to the volition associated with the attainment of undertaking and abstinence, which is called 'the abandoning volition of one fulfilling virtue.' And by means of prior and subsequent wisdom, and because of the statement about the nature of generosity and virtue, it is appropriate to say 'having begun' (ārabbhā) with reference to the subsequent abandoning volition, and 'having undertaken' (adhikiccā) with reference to the prior volition. Thus, the reading 'adhikiccā' is also justified.

770. Pañcasīladasasīlāni [M 0.0203] viññāṇassa jātiyā ca paccayabhūtesu saṅkhārabhavesu antogadhānīti “uppādā vā”tiādikāya dhammaṭṭhitipāḷiyā saṅgahitāni. Bhavanibbattakasīlassa paññāpanaṃ satipi savane na tathāgatadesanāyattanti bhikkhuādīnampi taṃ vuttaṃ.

770. The five precepts and the ten precepts are included within the formations-becoming, which are conditions for the birth of consciousness, and are thus included in the Pāḷi text on the stability of the Dhamma beginning 'uppādā vā'. The establishing of virtue that produces becoming, even when there is hearing, is not dependent on the Tathāgata's teaching; this has been stated even by monks and others.

Adhipaññāya paññāti adhipaññāya antogadhā paññā. Atha vā adhipaññānibbattesu, tadadhiṭṭhānesu vā dhammesu adhipaññā-saddo daṭṭhabbo, tattha paññā adhipaññāya paññā.

'Adhipaññāya paññā' means wisdom included in higher wisdom. Alternatively, the term 'adhipaññā' should be understood as referring to states generated by higher wisdom, or to things determined by it; in that context, wisdom is 'wisdom concerning higher wisdom'.

771. Apāyuppādanakusalatā apāyakosallaṃ siyāti maññamāno pucchati “apāyakosallaṃ kathaṃ paññā nāma jātā”ti. Taṃ pana parassa adhippāyaṃ nivattento “paññavāyeva hī”tiādimāha. Tatrupāyāti tatra tatra upāyabhūtā. Ṭhāne uppatti etassāti ṭhānuppattiyaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Kāraṇajānanaṃ, bhayādīnaṃ uppattikkhaṇe tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne lahuuppajjanakanti vuttaṃ hoti.

771. Thinking that proficiency in producing states of woe might be 'proficiency in states of woe' (apāyakosalla), one asks, "How has 'proficiency in states of woe' come to be called wisdom?" Refuting that person's intention, he said, 'Indeed, it is one with wisdom.' 'Tatrupāya' means being a means in each particular instance. 'Ṭhānuppatti' is 'its arising in a place'. What is that? Knowledge of the cause. This means it is said to be that which arises quickly in that very place at the moment of the arising of fear and so forth.

Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of Triads is concluded.

(4.) Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Exposition of Fours

793. Na [V 0.0205] paritassatīti “api nāma me taṇḍulādīni siyu”nti na pattheti, tadabhāvena vā na uttasati.

793. 'Na paritassati' (he is not anxious) means he does not yearn, thinking, "May I have rice, etc.," nor is he agitated by their absence.

796. Aparappaccayeti parena napattiyāyitabbe. Dhamme ñāṇanti saccavisayaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Ariyasaccesu hi dhamma-saddo tesaṃ aviparītasabhāvattāti. Saṅkhatapavaro vā ariyamaggo tassa ca phalaṃ dhammo, tattha paññā taṃsahagatā dhamme ñāṇaṃ. Na aññañāṇuppādanaṃ nayanayanaṃ, ñāṇasseva pana pavattivisesoti adhippāyenāha “paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa kicca”nti. Ettha ca iminā dhammenāti maggañāṇenāti vuttaṃ, duvidhampi pana maggaphalañāṇaṃ paccavekkhaṇāya ca mūlaṃ, kāraṇañca nayanayanassāti duvidhenapi tena dhammenāti na na yujjati, tathā catusaccadhammassa ñātattā, maggaphalasaṅkhātassa ca dhammassa saccapaṭivedhasampayogaṃ gatattā nayanaṃ hotīti tena iminā dhammena [M 0.0204] ñāṇavisayabhāvena, ñāṇasampayogena vā ñātenāti ca attho na na yujjati.

796. `Aparappaccaya` means not to be relied upon another. `Dhamme ñāṇa` means knowledge whose object is the truths. For in the Noble Truths, the word 'dhamma' is used because of their unperverted nature. Or, the Noble Path is the best of conditioned things, and its fruit is a dhamma; therein, the wisdom associated with it is `dhamme ñāṇa`. It is not the production of another knowledge, this leading (`nayana`); rather, it is a particular mode of functioning of knowledge itself. With this intention, it is said, 'the function of reviewing knowledge.' Here, 'by this dhamma' means 'by path-knowledge,' it is said. Indeed, both path- and fruition-knowledge are the root for reviewing and the cause for leading. Thus, it is not inappropriate to say 'by this dhamma' in both ways. Likewise, because the dhamma of the four truths is known, and because the dhamma designated as path and fruit has gone into association with the penetration of the truths, leading occurs. Therefore, the meaning 'known by this dhamma, through its being an object of knowledge or through its association with knowledge' is not inappropriate.

Yadipi sabbena sabbaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ dukkhaṃ abhijānanti, tathāpi paccuppanne sasantatipariyāpanne savisese abhiniveso hotīti āha “na taññeva ima”nti. Diṭṭhena adiṭṭhena nayato nayanañāṇaṃ, adiṭṭhassa diṭṭhatāya kāraṇabhūtattā kāraṇañāṇaṃ, anurūpatthavācako vā kāraṇa-saddoti dhamme ñāṇassa anurūpañāṇanti attho.

Although they fully know all suffering—past, future, and present—nevertheless, there is an adherence to the present, which is included in one's own continuity and is particular. Hence, it is said, 'not just this.' Knowledge that leads from the seen to the unseen is leading-knowledge. Because it is the cause for the unseen becoming seen, it is causal-knowledge. Or, the word `kāraṇa` is expressive of the meaning 'suitable'; thus, the meaning is that it is knowledge suitable for knowledge in the Dhamma.

Sammutimhi ñāṇanti dhamme ñāṇādīnaṃ viya sātisayassa paṭivedhakiccassa abhāvā visayobhāsanamattajānanasāmaññena ñāṇanti sammatesu antogadhanti attho. Sammutivasena vā pavattaṃ sammutimhi ñāṇaṃ, avasesaṃ pana itarañāṇattayavisabhāgaṃ ñāṇaṃ tabbisabhāgasāmaññena sammutiñāṇamhi paviṭṭhattā sammutiñāṇaṃ nāma hotīti.

`Sammutimhi ñāṇa` means that, unlike knowledge in the Dhamma and so forth, it lacks the function of penetrating the superior, and by the commonality of being a mere knowing that illuminates its object, it is included among what is conventionally known as 'knowledge.' This is the meaning. Alternatively, knowledge that operates by way of convention is `sammutimhi ñāṇa`. The remaining knowledge, however, being dissimilar to the other three types of knowledge, is called conventional knowledge because it is included under conventional knowledge by the commonality of being dissimilar to them.

797. Kilesamūlake cāti nīvaraṇamūlake ca kāmabhavadhamme.

797. `Kilesamūlake ca` means rooted in the hindrances and in the phenomena of sensual existence.

798. Sā hissāti ettha assāti yo “kāmesu vītarāgo hotī”ti evaṃ vutto, assa [V 0.0206] paṭhamajjhānasamaṅgissāti attho. Svevāti etena kāmesu vītarāgabhāvanāvatthasseva paṭhamajjhānasamaṅgissa gahaṇe pavatte tassa tato paraṃ avatthaṃ dassetuṃ “kāmesu vītarāgo samāno”ti vuttaṃ. Catutthamaggapaññā chaṭṭhābhiññābhāvappattiyā taṃ paṭivijjhati nāma, itarā tadupanissayattā. Yathānurūpaṃ vā āsavakkhayabhāvato, phale vā āsavakkhaye sati yathānurūpaṃ taṃnibbattanato catūsupi maggesu paññā chaṭṭhaṃ abhiññaṃ paṭivijjhatīti daṭṭhabbā.

798. In `Sā hi assā`, `assa` refers to the one who is said to be 'free from lust for sensual pleasures'; the meaning is, of one who possesses the first jhāna. By `Sveva`, it is indicated that when one who possesses the first jhāna is taken as being in the state of freedom from lust for sensual pleasures, to show the state subsequent to that, it is said 'being free from lust for sensual pleasures.' The wisdom of the fourth path penetrates the sixth higher knowledge by attaining that state, while the others serve as its supporting condition. Or, it should be seen that in all four paths, wisdom penetrates the sixth higher knowledge according to what is suitable: because of the state of the destruction of taints, or, when there is the destruction of taints in the fruition, because of its suitable production.

799. Kāmasahagatāti vatthukāmārammaṇā. Codentīti kāmābhimukhaṃ tanninnaṃ karontīti attho. Tadanudhammatāti tadanudhammā icceva vuttaṃ hoti. Tā-saddassa apubbatthābhāvatoti adhippāyenāha “tadanurūpasabhāvā”ti. Nikantiṃ, nikantisahagatacittuppādaṃ vā “micchāsatī”ti vadati. “Aho vata me avitakkaṃ uppajjeyyā”ti avitakkārammaṇā avitakkasahagatā.

799. `Kāmasahagatā` means having sensual objects as its object. `Codentī` means directing towards sensual pleasures, making one inclined to that; this is the meaning. `Tadanudhammatā` is simply said to mean 'in accordance with that.' Because the word `tā` has no meaning not previously stated, it is explained by intention as 'having a nature in accordance with that.' `Nikantiṃ`, or the arising of a mind associated with craving, is called `micchāsatī` (wrong mindfulness). 'Oh, that a thought-free state might arise for me!' means having a thought-free object, associated with being without thought.

801. Adhigamabhāvena [M 0.0205] abhimukhaṃ jānantassa abhijānantassa, abhivisiṭṭhena vā ñāṇena jānantassa, anārammaṇabhūtañca taṃ ṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ karontassāti attho.

801. The meaning is: of one who knows directly by way of attainment, who comprehends thoroughly, or who knows with superior knowledge, and who makes that objectless state apparent.

802. Vasitāpañcakarahitaṃ jhānaṃ appaguṇaṃ. Ettha catasso paṭipadā cattāri ārammaṇānīti paññāya paṭipadārammaṇuddesena paññā eva uddiṭṭhāti sā eva vibhattāti.

802. The jhāna lacking the five masteries is of little benefit. Here, with regard to the designation 'four paths and four objects,' by this designation of the path and object of wisdom, wisdom alone is designated, and it is precisely this that is analyzed.

Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Catukkaniddesa is concluded.

(5.) Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Exposition of the Fivefold

804. Pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhīti samādhiaṅgabhāvena paññā uddiṭṭhāti. Pītipharaṇatādivacanena hi tameva vibhajati, “so imameva kāyaṃ vivekajena pītisukhena abhisandetī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.226; ma. ni. 1.427) nayena pītiyā sukhassa ca pharaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pītipharaṇatāsukhapharaṇatāhi ārammaṇe ṭhatvā catutthajjhānassa uppādanato “pādā viyā”ti tā vuttā.

804. By 'right concentration with five factors,' wisdom is designated as a factor of concentration. For by such expressions as 'pervasion by rapture,' he analyzes that very thing. In the manner of 'he drenches, saturates, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion,' the pervading by rapture and pleasure should be understood. Because the pervasion by rapture and the pervasion by pleasure, having been established in the object, produce the fourth jhāna, they are called 'like feet'.

Dutiyapañcake [V 0.0207] ca “pañcañāṇiko”ti samādhimukhena pañcañāṇāneva uddiṭṭhāni niddiṭṭhāni cāti daṭṭhabbāni. Lokiyasamādhissa paccanīkāni nīvaraṇapaṭhamajjhānanikantiādīni niggahetabbāni. Aññe kilesā vāretabbā, imassa pana arahattasamādhissa paṭippassaddhasabbakilesattā na niggahetabbaṃ vāretabbañca atthīti maggānantaraṃ samāpattikkhaṇe ca appayogeneva adhigatattā ca ṭhapitattā ca, aparihānivasena ṭhapitattā vā na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato. Sativepullappattattāti etena appavattamānāyapi satiyā satibahulatāya sato eva nāmāti dasseti. Yathāparicchinnakālavasenāti etena paricchindanasatiyā satoti.

And in the second pentad, it should be understood that by 'endowed with five knowledges,' the five knowledges themselves are designated and explained by way of concentration. Obstacles to mundane concentration, such as the hindrances and craving for the first jhāna, etc., should be suppressed. Other defilements should be warded off. But for this concentration of an Arahant, since all defilements have been utterly allayed, there is nothing to suppress or ward off. Because it is attained without effort and established at the moment of fruition-attainment immediately following the path, or because it is established without decline, it is not subject to suppression or restraint through exertion. 'Due to mindfulness having reached fullness'—by this, he shows that even when mindfulness is not actively operating, one is still called 'mindful' because of the abundance of mindfulness. 'According to the limited time'—by this, he shows that one is mindful due to the mindfulness that delimits.

Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Fivefold is concluded.

(6.) Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixfold

805. Visuddhibhāvaṃ [M 0.0206] dassento “dūra…pe… rammaṇāyā”ti āha. Sotadhātuvisuddhīti ca cittacetasikā dhammā vuttāti tattha ñāṇaṃ sotadhātuvisuddhiyā ñāṇaṃ. “Cetopariyañāṇa”nti idameva atthavasena “paracitte ñāṇa”nti uddhaṭanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Cutūpapātañāṇassa dibbacakkhuñāṇekadesattā “vaṇṇadhātuārammaṇā”ti vuttaṃ. Muddhappattena cutūpapātañāṇasaṅkhātena dibbacakkhuñāṇena sabbaṃ dibbacakkhuñāṇanti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

805. Showing the state of purity, he says, 'distant... etc. ...delightful.' And by 'purity of the ear-element,' mind and mental factors are meant; the knowledge therein is 'knowledge of the purity of the ear-element.' It should be understood that 'knowledge of encompassing others’ minds' itself is cited by way of meaning as 'knowledge of another’s mind.' Because the knowledge of passing away and reappearance is a part of the divine eye knowledge, it is said to have 'the color element as object.' It should be understood that by the divine eye knowledge which is designated as the knowledge of passing away and reappearance and which has reached its culmination, all divine eye knowledge is spoken of.

Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Sixfold is concluded.

(7.) Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevenfold

806. Tadeva ñāṇanti chabbidhampi paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ vipassanārammaṇabhāvena saha gahetvā vuttanti adhippāyo. Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇenāti chapi ñāṇāni saṅkhipitvā vuttena ñāṇena. Khayadhammantiādinā [V 0.0208] hi pakārena pavattañāṇassa dassanaṃ, ñāṇavipassanādassanato vipassanāpaṭivipassanādassanamattamevāti na taṃ aṅganti adhippāyo. Pāḷiyaṃ pana sabbattha ñāṇavacanena aṅgānaṃ vuttattā nirodhadhammanti ñāṇanti iti-saddena pakāsetvā vuttaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ sattamaṃ ñāṇanti ayamattho dissati. Na hi yampi taṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ, tampi ñāṇanti sambandho hoti taṃñāṇaggahaṇe etasmiṃ ñāṇabhāvadassanassa anadhippetattā, “khayadhammaṃ…pe… nirodhadhamma”nti etesaṃ sambandhābhāvappasaṅgato cāti.

806. The intention is that 'that very knowledge' refers to the sixfold reviewing knowledge, spoken of as having been taken together with insight as its object. 'By knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma' means by the knowledge spoken of concisely, encompassing the six knowledges. For the showing of the knowledge that has occurred in the manner of 'subject to destruction,' etc., is, from the perspective of knowledge and insight, merely the seeing of insight and counter-insight; thus, the intention is that it is not a factor. However, in the Pāḷi, since the factors are spoken of everywhere by the word 'knowledge', this meaning is seen: that the insight knowledge, spoken of as 'knowledge that it is subject to cessation' and illuminated by the word `iti`, is the seventh knowledge. For there is no connection such that 'even that which is knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma, that too is knowledge,' because in the taking of that knowledge, the showing of its nature as knowledge is not intended here, and because it would lead to a lack of connection for the phrases 'subject to destruction... subject to cessation'.

Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Sevenfold is concluded.

(8.) Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Eightfold

808. Vihāritabbaṭṭhenāti paccanīkadhamme, dukkhaṃ vā vicchinditvā pavattetabbaṭṭhena.

808. 'By the meaning of 'to be dwelt in'': in regard to opposing qualities, or by the meaning of 'to be made to proceed after having cut off suffering'.

Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Eightfold is concluded.

(10.) Dasakaniddeso

10. The Exposition of the Tenfold

Paṭhamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Exposition of the First Power

809. Avijjamānaṃ [M 0.0207] ṭhānaṃ aṭṭhānaṃ, natthi ṭhānanti vā aṭṭhānaṃ. Esa “anavakāso”ti etthāpi nayo. Tadatthanigamanamattameva hi “netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti vacananti. Asukhe sukhanti diṭṭhivipallāsova idha sukhato upagamanassa ṭhānanti adhippetanti dassento “ekanta…pe… attadiṭṭhivasenā”ti padhānadiṭṭhimāha. Bhedānurūpassa sāvanaṃ anussāvanaṃ, bhedānurūpena vā vacanena viññāpanaṃ.

809. A non-existent possibility is an impossibility (aṭṭhānaṃ); or, 'there is no possibility' is an impossibility. This same principle applies to 'no opportunity' (anavakāso). For the statement, 'this possibility does not exist,' is merely a conclusion of that meaning. Showing that it is intended here that the basis for approaching what is suffering as happiness is a distortion of view, he states the primary wrong view by saying, 'entirely... by means of the view of self.' Making it heard in accordance with the division is 'proclamation' (anussāvanaṃ); or, making it understood through speech suitable to the division.

Liṅge [V 0.0209] parivatte ca so eva ekakammanibbattito bhavaṅgappabandho jīvitindriyappabandho ca, nāññoti āha “api parivattaliṅga”nti. Ayaṃ pañhoti ñāpanicchānibbattā kathā.

And in the case of a change of sex, it is that very same continuum of bhavaṅga and continuum of the life faculty, produced by a single kamma, and not another, that he speaks of, saying: 'even with a changed sex.' This is a question, a discussion born from the desire to make known.

Saṅgāmacatukkaṃ sapattavasena yojetabbaṃ. Sabbattha ca purimaṃ abhisandhicittaṃ appamāṇaṃ, vadhakacittaṃ pana tadārammaṇañca jīvitindriyaṃ ānantariyānānantariyabhāve pamāṇanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Puthujjanasseva taṃ dinnaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Yathā vadhakacittaṃ paccuppannārammaṇampi jīvitindriyappabandhavicchedanavasena ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattati, na evaṃ cāgacetanā. Sā hi cajitabbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā cajanamattameva hoti, aññasakakaraṇañca tassa cajanaṃ, tasmā yassa taṃ sakaṃ kataṃ, tasseva dinnaṃ hotīti.

The quartet on battle should be connected by way of the enemy. And in all cases, the prior mind of intention is immeasurable; but the killer's mind and its object, the life faculty, should be understood as the standard for the state of being an immediately resultant kamma or not. That gift is given only in the case of an ordinary person. Why? Because, just as the killer's mind, although its object is present, proceeds by making the severing of the continuum of the life faculty its object, the volition of giving is not so. For that volition, having made the object-to-be-relinquished its object, is merely an act of relinquishing; and that relinquishing is the making of it another's property. Therefore, it is given to that very one for whom it is made his own.

Saṇṭha…pe… kappavināseyeva muccatīti idaṃ kappaṭṭhakathāya na sameti. Tattha hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (kathā. aṭṭha. 654-657) vuttaṃ “āpāyikoti idaṃ suttaṃ yaṃ so ekaṃ kappaṃ asītibhāge katvā tato ekabhāgamattaṃ kālaṃ tiṭṭheyya, taṃ āyukappaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti. Kappavināseyevāti pana āyukappavināseyevāti atthe sati natthi virodho. Ettha ca saṇṭhahanteti idaṃ sve vinassissatīti viya abhūtaparikappavasena vuttaṃ. Ekadivasameva paccati tato paraṃ kappābhāvena āyukappassapi abhāvatoti avirodhato atthayojanā daṭṭhabbā.

'It persists... is freed only at the destruction of the aeon'—this does not agree with the commentary on the Kathāvatthu. For there, in the commentary (Kathā-aṭṭha. 654-657), it is said: 'This discourse on one "destined for the plane of misery" is spoken with reference to the lifespan-aeon, in a case where one, having divided one aeon into eighty parts, would remain for a period of just one part.' However, if the meaning of 'only at the destruction of the aeon' is 'only at the destruction of the lifespan-aeon,' there is no contradiction. And here, this phrase 'it persists' is spoken by way of a hypothetical assumption, like 'it will be destroyed tomorrow.' It ripens for only one day; thereafter, due to the absence of the aeon, there is also an absence of the lifespan-aeon. Thus, the application of the meaning should be seen as non-contradictory.

Pakatattoti anukkhitto. Samānasaṃvāsakoti apārājiko.

'One in a natural state' means one who is not suspended. 'One in communion' means one who has not committed a pārājika offense.

Kiṃ [M 0.0208] pana tanti yo so “niyato”ti vutto, taṃ kiṃ niyametīti attho. Tasseva pana yathāpucchitassa niyatassa micchattasammattaniyatadhammānaṃ viya sabhāvato vijjamānataṃ yathāpucchitañca niyāmakahetuṃ paṭisedhetvā yena “niyato”ti “sattakkhattuparamādiko”ti ca vuccati, taṃ yathādhippetakāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “sammāsambuddhena hī”tiādimāha. Jātassa kumārassa viya ariyāya jātiyā jātassa nāmamattametaṃ niyatasattakkhattuparamādikaṃ, niyatāniyatabhedaṃ nāmanti attho. Yadi pubbahetu niyāmako, sotāpanno ca niyatoti sotāpattimaggato uddhaṃ tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ upanissayabhāvato pubbahetukiccaṃ, tato pubbe pana pubbahetukiccaṃ natthīti sotāpattimaggassa upanissayābhāvo āpajjati. Yadi hi tassapi pubbahetu upanissayo siyā, so ca niyāmakoti sotāpattimagguppattito pubbe eva niyato siyā, tañca aniṭṭhaṃ, tasmāssa [V 0.0210] pubbahetunā ahetukatā āpannāti imamatthaṃ sandhāyāha “iccassa ahetu appaccayā nibbattiṃ pāpuṇātī”ti.

But what is that which is called 'determined'? The meaning is, 'What determines it?' However, having refuted both the existence by its own nature of that which was asked about—the determined one—like the states determined for wrongness and rightness, and the determining cause which was asked about, in order to show the intended reason why one is called 'determined' and 'at most seven times more,' he says, 'For by the Perfectly Enlightened One...' and so on. Just as for a newborn child, so for one born with the noble birth, this 'determined, at most seven times more' is merely a name; the meaning is, it is a name for the distinction between the determined and the undetermined. If a prior cause were the determiner, and a stream-enterer is determined, then because the three paths above the stream-entry path have it as a support condition, the prior cause has its function. But before that, the prior cause has no function, so it would follow that the stream-entry path lacks a support condition. For if that stream-entry path also had a prior cause as a support condition, and that were the determiner, then one would be determined even before the arising of the stream-entry path, and that is undesirable. Therefore, it would follow that it is without a cause from a prior cause. Intending this meaning, he says: 'Thus, its arising comes to be without cause, without condition.'

Paṭiladdhamaggo sotāpattimaggo, teneva sattakkhattuparamādiniyame sati sattamabhavādito uddhaṃ pavattanakassa dukkhassa mūlabhūtā kilesā teneva khīṇāti upari tayo maggā akiccakā hontīti attho. Yadi upari tayo maggā sattakkhattuparamādikaṃ niyamenti, tato ca añño sotāpanno natthīti sotāpattimaggassa akiccakatā nippayojanatā āpajjatīti attho. Atha sakkāyadiṭṭhādippahānaṃ dassanakiccaṃ, tesaṃ pahānena sattakkhattuparamāditāya bhavitabbaṃ. Sā cuparimaggehi eva hotīti sattamabhavādito uddhaṃ pavattito tena vinā vuṭṭhāne sakkāyadiṭṭhādippahānena ca tena vinā bhavitabbanti āha “paṭhamamaggena ca anuppajjitvāva kilesā khepetabbā hontī”ti. Na añño koci niyametīti nāmakaraṇanimittato vipassanāto añño koci niyāmako nāma natthīti attho. Vipassanāva niyametīti ca nāmakaraṇanimittataṃyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tenevāha “iti sammāsambuddhena gahitanāmamattameva ta”nti.

The path attained is the stream-entry path. The meaning is: since by that very path there is the determination of 'at most seven times more,' the defilements that are the root of the suffering that would occur from the seventh existence onwards are destroyed by that very path; thus the three higher paths become functionless. The meaning is: if the three higher paths determined the 'at most seven times more,' then there would be no other stream-enterer than that, so it would follow that the stream-entry path is functionless and useless. Furthermore, the abandoning of identity-view and so forth is the function of vision; by their abandonment, the state of 'at most seven times more' must come to be. And since that state comes about only through the higher paths, he says, 'and by the first path, the defilements must be destroyed without arising again,' meaning that without it, the first path, there would have to be an emerging from what occurs from the seventh existence onwards, and without it, an abandoning of identity-view and so forth. 'No other determines' means that there is no determiner other than insight, which is the reason for the naming. And 'insight alone determines' is said with reference to its being the reason for the naming. Therefore he says, 'Thus, it is merely a name adopted by the Perfectly Enlightened One.'

Na uppajjantīti pana atthīti “na me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjatī”tiādiṃ (ma. ni. 1.285; 2.341; mahāva. 11; kathā. 405) imissā lokadhātuyā ṭhatvā vadantena bhagavatā “kiṃ panāvuso [M 0.0209] sāriputta, atthetarahi aññe samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā bhagavatā samasamā sambodhiyanti evaṃ puṭṭhāhaṃ, bhante, noti vadeyya”nti (dī. ni. 3.161) vatvā tassa kāraṇaṃ dassetuṃ “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddhā”ti (ma. ni. 3.129) imaṃ suttaṃ dassentena dhammasenāpatinā ca buddhakkhettabhūtaṃ imaṃ lokadhātuṃ ṭhapetvā aññattha anuppatti vuttā hotīti adhippāyo.

However, that 'they do not arise' is supported by what was said by the Blessed One, standing in this world-system: 'I have no teacher; none equal to me exists,' and so on (MN 1.285; etc.); and by what was said by the General of the Dhamma, who, when asked, 'But, friend Sāriputta, are there now any other ascetics or brahmins equal to the Blessed One in supreme enlightenment?', replied, 'No, venerable sir' (DN 3.161), and to show the reason for that, presented this sutta: 'It is impossible, there is no opportunity, for two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, to arise in one world-system' (MN 3.129). The intention is that, this world-system being established as a Buddha-field, the non-arising of a second Buddha is spoken of with regard to any other place within it.

“Yo pana bhikkhū”tiādinā vuttāni sikkhāpadāni mātikā, tāya antarahitāya nidānuddesasaṅkhāte pātimokkhe pabbajjūpasampadākammesu ca sāsanaṃ tiṭṭhatīti attho. Pātimokkhe vā antogadhā pabbajjā upasampadā ca tadubhayābhāve pātimokkhābhāvato, tasmā pātimokkhe, tāsu ca sāsanaṃ tiṭṭhatīti vuttaṃ. Osakkitaṃ nāmāti pacchimapaṭivedhasīlabhedadvayaṃ ekato katvā tato paraṃ vinaṭṭhaṃ nāma hotīti attho.

The training rules stated beginning with 'Whatever monk...' are the mātikā. The meaning is that when that has disappeared, the teaching remains in the Pātimokkha—designated as the introduction and recitation—and in the formal acts of going forth and higher ordination. Or, the going forth and higher ordination are included in the Pātimokkha, because in the absence of those two, there is no Pātimokkha. Therefore, it is said that the teaching remains in the Pātimokkha and in those acts. The meaning of 'declined' is that, having taken together the pair—the final penetration and the breach of virtue—what is beyond that is called 'destroyed'.

Tāti rasmiyo. Kāruññanti paridevanakāruññaṃ.

'Those' (tā) means the rays. 'Compassion' (kāruññaṃ) means the compassion of lamentation.

Anacchariyattāti [V 0.0211] dvīsu uppajjamānesu acchariyattābhāvadosatoti attho. Vivādabhāvatoti vivādābhāvatthaṃ dve na uppajjantīti attho.

'Because of its not being marvelous' means: because of the fault of the absence of marvelousness when two arise. 'Because of the absence of dispute' means: two do not arise for the sake of the absence of dispute.

Ekaṃ buddhaṃ dhāretīti ekabuddhadhāraṇī. Etena evaṃsabhāvā ete buddhaguṇā, yena dutiyabuddhaguṇe dhāretuṃ asamatthā ayaṃ lokadhātūti dasseti. Paccayavisesanipphannānañhi dhammānaṃ sabhāvaviseso na sakkā dhāretunti. Samaṃ uddhaṃ pajjatīti samupādikā, udakassopari samaṃ gāminīti attho. Dvinnampīti dvepi, dvinnampi vā sarīrabhāraṃ. Chādentanti rocayamānaṃ. Sakiṃ bhuttovāti ekampi ālopaṃ ajjhoharitvāva mareyyāti attho.

Because it bears one Buddha, it is a 'bearer of one Buddha' (ekabuddhadhāraṇī). By this, he shows that these qualities of a Buddha are of such a nature that this world-system is incapable of bearing the qualities of a second Buddha. For the specific nature of phenomena produced from specific conditions cannot be borne. Because it goes evenly upwards, it is a samupādikā; the meaning is, 'going evenly over the water.' 'Of both' (dvinnampi) means 'both,' or 'the bodily burden of both.' 'Covering' (chādentaṃ) means 'pleasing.' 'Having eaten once' (sakiṃ bhutto vā) means: one would die even after swallowing a single morsel.

Atidhammabhārenāti dhammena nāma pathavī tiṭṭheyya, sā kiṃ teneva calatīti adhippāyo. Puna thero “ratanaṃ nāma loke kuṭumbaṃ sandhārentaṃ abhimatañca lokena attano garusabhāvatāya sakaṭabhaṅgassa kāraṇaṃ atibhārabhūtaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. Evaṃ dhammo ca hitasukhavisesehi taṃsamaṅginaṃ dhārento abhimato ca viññūhi gambhīrāppameyyabhāvena garusabhāvattā atibhārabhūto pathavīcalanassa kāraṇaṃ hotī”ti dassento [M 0.0210] “idha, mahārāja, dve sakaṭā”tiādimāha. Ekassāti ekasmā, ekassa vā sakaṭassa ratanaṃ, tasmā sakaṭato gahetvāti attho. Osāritanti pavesitaṃ āhaṭaṃ vuttanti attho.

`Atidhammabhārena` means: the earth, which by its nature should stand firm, why does it shake because of that very thing? This is the intended meaning. Again, the elder, to illustrate this, said: 'In the world, a jewel, while sustaining a household and being esteemed by the world, is seen as an excessive burden, being the cause of the cart's breaking due to its own heavy nature. Similarly, the Dhamma, while sustaining one endowed with special welfare and happiness, and being esteemed by the wise for its profound and immeasurable nature, becomes an excessive burden, causing the earth to shake, due to its heavy nature.' To illustrate this, he said, 'Here, great king, are two carts,' and so on. `Ekassā` means 'from one,' or 'of one cart's jewel'; therefore, the meaning is 'having taken it from that cart.' `Osāritaṃ` means entered, brought, or said—this is the meaning.

Sabhāvapakatikāti akittimapakatikāti attho. Kāraṇamahantattāti mahantehi pāramitākāraṇehi buddhaguṇānaṃ nibbattitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Pathavīādayo mahantā attano attano visaye ekekāva, evaṃ sammāsambuddhopi mahanto attano visaye eko eva. Ko ca tassa visayo? Yāvatakaṃ ñeyyaṃ, evaṃ ākāso viya anantavisayo bhagavā eko eva hotīti vadanto lokadhātvantaresupi dutiyassa abhāvaṃ dasseti.

`Sabhāvapakatikā` means having a non-artificial nature. `Kāraṇamahantattā` means that it is said that the Buddha's qualities arise from great causes, the perfections. Just as the earth and so on are great, each one being single in its own sphere, so too the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is great, being single in His sphere. And what is His sphere? As far as there is the knowable. Thus, like space, the Blessed One has an infinite sphere and is single. By stating this, he shows the absence of a second one even in other world-systems.

Pubbabhāge āyūhanavasena āyūhanasamaṅgitā sanniṭṭhānacetanāvasena cetanāsamaṅgitā ca veditabbā, santatikhaṇavasena vā. Vipākārahanti dutiyabhavādīsu vipaccanapakatitaṃ sandhāya vadati. Calatīti parivattati. Sunakhehi vajanasīlo sunakhavājiko.

In the initial stage, it should be understood as being endowed with accumulation in the sense of exertion, and endowed with volition in the sense of resolute volition, or in the sense of the moment of continuity. `Vipākārahaṃ` is said with reference to its nature of ripening in a second existence and so on. `Calati` means it revolves. One whose habit is to speak like dogs is a `sunakhavājiko`.

Paṭhamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition of the first power is completed.

Dutiyabalaniddesavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Exposition of the Second Power

810. Gatito [V 0.0212] aññā gatisampatti nāma natthīti dassento “sampannā gatī”ti āha. Mahāsudassanādisurājakālo paṭhamakappikādisumanussakālo ca kālasampatti.

810. To show that there is no such thing as an 'accomplishment of a destination' apart from the destination itself, he says, 'an accomplished destination.' The time of great kings such as Mahāsudassana and the time of good humans such as those of the first eon is an accomplishment of time.

Ekantaṃ kusalasseva okāsoti idaṃ yadipi koci kāyasucaritādipayogasampattiyaṃ ṭhitaṃ bādheyya, taṃ pana bādhanaṃ bādhakasseva issādinimittena viparītaggāhena jātaṃ. Sā payogasampatti sabhāvato sukhavipākasseva paccayo, na dukkhavipākassāti imamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Makkaṭo bhattapuṭaṃ bandhaṭṭhāne muñcitvā bhuñjituṃ na jānāti, yattha vā tattha vā bhinditvā vināseti, evaṃ anupāyaññūpi bhoge. Susāne chaḍḍetvātiādinā ghātetvā chaḍḍitassa vuṭṭhānābhāvo viya apāyato vuṭṭhānābhāvoti dasseti.

'There is exclusively an opportunity for the wholesome'—this is said with reference to the following meaning: even if someone were to obstruct one established in the accomplishment of application, such as bodily good conduct, that obstruction arises from the obstructor's own wrong grasp due to signs such as envy. That accomplishment of application is by its nature a condition only for a pleasant result, not for a painful result. Just as a monkey, having untied a food bundle at the place it was tied, does not know how to eat it but breaks it open here or there and destroys it, so too does one who does not know the proper means with regard to wealth. By the phrase 'having discarded in the charnel ground' and so on, it is shown that just as there is no rising again for one who has been killed and discarded there, so too there is no rising again from the plane of misery.

“Paccarī”tipi [M 0.0211] uḷumpassa nāmaṃ, tena ettha katā “mahāpaccarī”ti vuccati. Udake maraṇaṃ thale maraṇañca ekamevāti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu sakkena “samuddārakkhaṃ karissāmī”ti vuttanti? Saccaṃ vuttaṃ, jīvitassa lahuparivattitaṃ pakāsentehi therehi evaṃ vuttaṃ, lahuparivattitāya jīvitahetu na gamissāmāti adhippāyo. Atha vā udaketi nāgadīpaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, thaleti jambudīpaṃ.

`Paccarī` is also a name for a raft; therefore, the one made here is called `mahāpaccarī`. Why is it said that death in water and death on land are one and the same? Was it not said by Sakka, 'I will provide protection from the sea'? It is true that this was said, but the elders spoke thus to show the swift changing nature of life; the intention is, 'We will not go because of the swift changing nature of life.' Alternatively, 'in water' was said with reference to Nāgadīpa, and 'on land' with reference to Jambudīpa.

Thero na detīti kathamahaṃ etena ñāto, kenaci kiñci ācikkhitaṃ siyāti saññāya na adāsi. Teneva “mayampi na jānāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Aparassāti aparassa bhikkhuno pattaṃ ādāya…pe… therassa hatthe ṭhapesīti yojanā. Anāyataneti nikkāraṇe, ayutte vā nassanaṭṭhāne. Tuvaṃ attānaṃ rakkheyyāsi, mayaṃ pana mahallakattā kiṃ rakkhitvā karissāma, mahallakattā eva ca rakkhituṃ na sakkhissāmāti adhippāyo. Anāgāmittā vā thero attanā vattabbaṃ jānitvā ovadati.

The elder did not give, with the perception, 'How am I known by him? Someone must have told him something.' Because of this perception, he did not give. For that reason, it was said, 'We too do not know.' `Aparassa` means: taking the bowl of another monk... he placed it in the elder's hand—this is the connection. `Anāyatane` means without cause, or in an unsuitable place of destruction. The intention is: 'You should protect yourself. But we, being old, what shall we do by protecting ourselves? And just because we are old, we will not be able to protect ourselves.' Or, the elder, due to being a non-returner, advises, knowing what should be said by him.

Sammāpayogassa gatamaggoti sammāpayogena nipphāditattā tassa sañjānanakāraṇanti attho.

`Sammāpayogassa gatamaggo` means that because it is accomplished through right application, this is the reason for its being known. This is the meaning.

Bhūtamatthaṃ [V 0.0213] katvā abhūtopamaṃ kathayissatīti adhippāyo. Manussāti bhaṇḍāgārikādiniyuttā manussā mahantattā sampaṭicchituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu.

The intention is: having established the true meaning, he will state an unreal simile. `Manussā` means: the people appointed as treasurers and so on were unable to accept it due to their importance.

Dutiyabalaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition of the second power is completed.

Tatiyabalaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Third Power.

811. Añcitāti gatā. Peccāti puna, maritvāti vā attho. Ussannattāti vitakkabahulatāya ussannattāti vadanti, sūratādīhi vā ussannattā. Dibbantīti kīḷanti.

811. `Añcitā` means gone. `Pecca` means again, or the meaning is 'having died.' `Ussannattā` means due to abundance; they say it is due to abundance because of the multiplicity of thoughts, or due to abundance because of courage and so on. `Dibbanti` means they play.

Sañjīvakāḷasuttasaṅghātaroruvamahāroruvatāpanamahātāpanaavīciyo aṭṭha mahānirayā. Ekekassa cattāri dvārāni, ekekasmiṃ dvāre cattāro cattāro gūthanirayādayoti evaṃ soḷasa ussadaniraye vaṇṇayanti.

The eight great hells are: Sañjīva, Kāḷasutta, Saṅghāta, Roruva, Mahāroruva, Tāpana, Mahātāpana, and Avīci. Each of these has four gates, and at each gate there are four minor hells such as the dung-hell. Thus they describe sixteen Ussada hells.

Sakkasuyāmādayo [M 0.0212] viya jeṭṭhakadevarājā. Pajāpativaruṇaīsānādayo viya dutiyādiṭṭhānantarakārako paricārako hutvā.

Like Sakka, Suyāma, and so on, the chief deva kings. And like Pajāpati, Varuṇa, Īsāna, and so on, being an attendant who occupies the second rank and so forth.

Tatiyabalaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition of the third power is completed.

Catutthabalaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Fourth Power.

812. Kappoti dvedhābhūtaggo. Ettha ca bījādidhātunānattavasena khandhādidhātunānattaṃ veditabbaṃ.

812. `Kappo` means an aggregate of that which has become twofold. And here, the diversity of elements such as the aggregates should be understood by way of the diversity of elements such as seeds.

Catutthabalaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition of the fourth power is completed.

Pañcamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Fifth Power.

813. Ajjhāsayadhātūti [V 0.0214] ajjhāsayasabhāvo. Yathā gūthādīnaṃ dhātusabhāvo eso, yaṃ gūthādīheva saṃsandati, evaṃ puggalānaṃ ajjhāsayassevesa sabhāvo, yaṃ dussīlādayo dussīlādikeheva saṃsandantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhikkhūpi āhaṃsūti aññamaññaṃ āhaṃsu. Āvuso ime manussā “yathāsabhāgena paribhuñjathā”ti vadantā amhe sabhāgāsabhāge viditvā hīnajjhāsayapaṇītajjhāsayataṃ paricchinditvā dhātusaṃyuttakamme upanenti tassa payogaṃ daṭṭhukāmāti attho, evaṃ sabhāgavaseneva ajjhāsayadhātuparicchindanato ajjhāsayadhātusabhāgavasena niyametīti adhippāyo.

813. `Ajjhāsayadhātu` means the nature of disposition. Just as this is the elemental nature of excrement and so on, that it corresponds only with excrement and the like, so too this is the nature of persons' dispositions, that the immoral and so on correspond only with the immoral and the like—this is what is said. `Bhikkhūpi āhaṃsu` means they said to one another. The meaning is: 'Friends, these people, saying, "Partake according to your similar nature," having known what is similar and dissimilar in us, having distinguished the inferiority and superiority of our dispositions, lead us to work connected with our elemental nature, wishing to see its application.' The intention is: thus, because of discerning the disposition-element solely by way of its similar nature, they assign us according to the similarity of the disposition-element.

Pañcamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the exposition of the fifth power is completed.

Chaṭṭhabalaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Sixth Power.

Caritanti idha duccaritaṃ sucaritanti vuttaṃ. Apparajaṃ akkhaṃ etesanti apparajakkhāti attho vibhāvito, apparajaṃ akkhimhi etesanti apparajakkhātipi saddattho sambhavati. Ettha ca āsayajānanādinā yehi [M 0.0213] indriyehi paroparehi sattā kalyāṇapāpāsayādikā honti, tesaṃ jānanaṃ vibhāvetīti veditabbaṃ. Evañca katvā indriyaparopariyattaāsayānusayañāṇānaṃ visuṃ asādhāraṇatā, indriyaparopariyattanānādhimuttikatāñāṇānaṃ visuṃ balatā ca siddhā hoti.

`Caritaṃ` here is said to be misconduct and good conduct. The meaning of `apparajakkhā` is explained as 'those who have little dust in the eye.' Alternatively, the literal meaning `apparajakkhā` as 'those in whose eye there is little dust' is also possible. And here, it should be understood that it clarifies the knowledge of those superior and inferior faculties of others by which beings have good or bad dispositions, etc., through knowing their dispositions and so on.
