And by this, the distinct, uncommon nature of the knowledge of the faculties, dispositions, and latent tendencies of others is established, and the distinct power of the knowledge of the faculties and diverse inclinations of others is also established.

815. Yadariyāti ye ariyā. Āvasiṃsūti nissāya vasiṃsu. Ke pana te? “Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti chaḷaṅgasamannāgato ekārakkho caturāpasseno panuṇṇapaccekasacco samavayasaṭṭhesano anāvilasaṅkappo passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro suvimuttacitto suvimuttapañño”ti (dī. ni. 3.348; a. ni. 10.19) evaṃ vuttā. Etesu pañcaṅgavippahīnapaccekasaccapanodanaesanāsamavayasajjanāni “saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati adhivāseti parivajjeti vinodetī”ti (ma. ni. 2.168) vuttesu apassenesu vinodanañca maggakiccāneva, itare ca maggeneva samijjhanti. Tenāha “etañhi suttaṃ…pe… dīpetī”ti.

815. 'Yadariyā' means 'those who are noble.' 'Āvasiṃsu' means 'they dwelt relying on it.' And who are they? They are those described thus: 'Here, monks, a monk has abandoned five factors, possesses six factors, is guarded in one way, supported in four ways, has dispelled individual truths, is united in striving, free from troubled thoughts, with bodily formations calmed, with a mind and wisdom fully liberated' (DN 3.348; AN 10.19). Among these, the abandonment of five factors, the dispelling of individual truths, and the unification of striving are functions of the path, as is the removal among the supports mentioned as 'one resorts to, endures, avoids, removes by reflection' (MN 2.168). And the others are perfected by the path itself. Therefore, it is said, 'This sutta... illuminates.'

816. Ārammaṇasantānānusayanesu [V 0.0215] iṭṭhārammaṇe ārammaṇānusayanena anuseti. Āciṇṇasamāciṇṇāti etena samantato veṭhetvā viya ṭhitabhāvena anusayitataṃ dasseti. Bhavassapi vatthukāmattā, rāgavasena vā samānattā “bhavarāgānusayo…pe… saṅgahito”ti āha.

816. In the context of objects, continuity, and latent tendencies, one latently inclines towards a desirable object by means of the latent tendency regarding the object. 'Āciṇṇasamāciṇṇa' indicates the state of latent inclination as if encompassing it entirely. Because existence has the nature of a basis for sensual pleasure, or because of its similarity in the manner of lust, it is said, 'The latent tendency of lust for existence... is included.'

818. “Paṇītādhimuttikā tikkhindriyā, itare mudindriyā”ti evaṃ indriyavisesadassanatthameva adhimuttiggahaṇanti āha “tikkhindriyamudindriyabhāvadassanattha”nti.

818. 'Those inclined to the superior have keen faculties, others have dull faculties.' Thus, the term 'inclination' is used precisely to show the distinction in faculties, as stated: 'to show the state of keen and dull faculties.'

819. Pahānakkamavasenāti ettha pahātabbapajahanakkamo pahānakkamoti daṭṭhabbo, yassa pahānena bhavitabbaṃ, taṃ teneva pahānena paṭhamaṃ vuccati, tato appahātabbanti ayaṃ vā pahānakkamo.

819. 'In terms of the order of abandoning': Here, the order of abandoning should be understood as the sequence of abandoning what is to be abandoned. That which is to be abandoned is mentioned first by that very abandoning, and then what is not to be abandoned; this is the order of abandoning.

820. Maggassa upanissayabhūtāni indriyāni upanissayaindriyāni.

820. The faculties that are a strong support for the path are faculties of strong support.

826. Nibbutichandarahitattā acchandikaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhā. Yasmiṃ bhavaṅge pavattamāne taṃsantatiyaṃ lokuttaraṃ nibbattati, taṃ tassa pādakaṃ.

826. Because they lack desire for quenching, they have entered a state of desirelessness. That life-continuum, while it is occurring, in which continuity the supramundane arises, is its basis.

Chaṭṭhabalaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Sixth Power is concluded.

Sattamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Seventh Power

828. Niddāyitvāti [M 0.0214] kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karonto niddaṃ okkamitvā paṭibuddho samāpattiṃ samāpannomhīti attho. Nīvaraṇādīhi visuddhacittasantati eva cittamañjūsā, samādhi vā, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā. Cittaṃ ṭhapetunti samāpatticittaṃ ṭhapetuṃ. Saññāvedayitānaṃ apagamo eva apagamavimokkho.

828. “Having dozed off”: The meaning is that having fallen asleep while attending to the meditation subject, upon waking up, one mistakenly thinks, “I have attained absorption.” The stream of consciousness purified from hindrances and so forth is the mind-casket, or concentration, or the meditation subject. “To set the mind” means to set the mind of meditative attainment. The cessation of perception and feeling is itself the liberation through cessation.

Saññāmanasikārānaṃ kāmādidutiyajjhānādipakkhandanāni “hānabhāgiyavisesabhāgiyadhammā”ti [V 0.0216] dassitāni, tehi pana jhānānaṃ taṃsabhāvatā dhamma-saddena vuttā. Paguṇabhāvavodānaṃ paguṇavodānaṃ. Tadeva paṭhamajjhānādīhi vuṭṭhahitvā dutiyajjhānādiadhigamassa paccayattā “vuṭṭhānaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. “Vodānampi vuṭṭhānaṃ, tamhā tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhānampi vuṭṭhāna”nti imāya vuṭṭhānapāḷiyā asaṅgahitattā nirodhasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhānaṃ “pāḷimuttakavuṭṭhānaṃ nāmā”ti vuttaṃ. Ye pana “nirodhato phalasamāpattiyā vuṭṭhāna”nti pāḷi natthīti vadeyyuṃ, te “nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ phalasamāpattiyā anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.417) imāya pāḷiyā paṭisedhetabbā.

The plungings of perceptions and attentions into sensuality, etc., and into the second jhāna, etc., are shown as 'states pertaining to decline and distinction.' By these, the inherent nature of those jhānas is expressed by the word 'dhamma.' The purification of proficiency is called practiced purification. That very thing, being the condition for attaining the second jhāna and so forth after emerging from the first jhāna and so forth, is called 'emergence.' Because the statement, 'Purification is also emergence, and emergence from any given concentration is also emergence,' is not included in this scriptural passage on emergence, the emergence from the attainment of cessation is called 'emergence not included in the scriptures.' Those who would say, 'There is no scriptural passage on emergence from cessation into the attainment of fruition,' should be refuted by this passage: 'For one emerging from cessation, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of immediate condition' (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.417).

Sattamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Seventh Power is concluded.

Dasamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Tenth Power

831. Rāgādīhi cetaso vimuttibhūto samādhi cetovimutti. Paññāva vimutti paññāvimutti. Kammantaravipākantaramevāti kammantarassa vipākantaramevāti attho. Cetanācetanāsampayuttakadhamme nirayādinibbānagāminipaṭipadābhūte kammanti gahetvā āha “kammaparicchedamevā”ti. Appetuṃ na sakkoti aṭṭhamanavamabalāni viya, taṃsadisaṃ iddhividhañāṇaṃ viya vikubbituṃ. Etena dasabalasadisatañca vāreti, jhānādiñāṇaṃ viya vā appetuṃ vikubbituñca. Yadipi hi jhānādipaccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ sattamabalanti tassa savitakkasavicāratā vuttā, tathāpi jhānādīhi [M 0.0215] vinā paccavekkhaṇā natthīti jhānādisahagataṃ ñāṇaṃ tadantogadhaṃ katvā evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ jhānādikiccaṃ viya na sabbaṃ balakiccaṃ kātuṃ sakkotīti dassetuṃ “tañhi jhānaṃ hutvā appetuṃ iddhi hutvā vikubbituñca na sakkotī”ti vuttaṃ, na pana kassaci balassa jhānaiddhibhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

831. The concentration that is the mind’s liberation from lust and so forth is liberation of mind. Wisdom itself is liberation by wisdom. 'Merely the result of an interval of kamma' means merely the result of an interval of kamma. Taking volition and the states associated with volition—which constitute the path leading to hell, etc., and to Nibbāna—as kamma, it is said, 'It is merely the delimitation of kamma.' It cannot apply itself like the eighth and ninth powers, nor can it transform itself like the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power. By this, similarity to the ten powers is also precluded, and like the knowledge of jhāna, etc., it cannot apply or transform. For although the knowledge of reflecting on jhāna, etc., is called the seventh power, and its nature as being accompanied by initial and sustained thought is stated, still, since there is no reflection without jhāna, etc., it should be understood that the knowledge associated with jhāna, etc., is included therein, and thus it is stated. Alternatively, to show that the knowledge of omniscience cannot perform all the functions of the powers, as is the function of jhāna, etc., it is said, 'For it cannot apply itself by becoming a jhāna, nor transform itself by becoming a psychic power.' However, it should be understood that no power has the nature of jhāna or psychic power.

Dasamabalaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Exposition of the Tenth Power is concluded.

Ñāṇavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Analysis of Knowledge is concluded.

17. Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgo

17. The Analysis of Minor Matters

1. Ekakamātikādivaṇṇanā

1. The Explanation of the Numerical Lists and so forth

832. “Tettiṃsati [M 0.0216][V 0.0217] tikā”ti vuttaṃ, te pana pañcatiṃsa. Tathā “purisamalādayo aṭṭha navakā”ti vuttaṃ, te pana āghātavatthuādayo nava. Ye “dve aṭṭhārasakā”tiādimhi vuttā, te eva “iti atītāni chattiṃsā”tiādinā tayo chattiṃsakā katāti āha “cha aṭṭhārasakā”ti, dvāsaṭṭhi pana diṭṭhigatāni aññattha vuttabhāveneva idha nikkhittānīti na gahitānīti daṭṭhabbāni.

832. It is said, 'Thirty-three triads,' but they are actually thirty-five. Similarly, it is said, 'the eight nonads beginning with the defilements of a man,' but they are actually the nine beginning with the grounds for resentment. Those which are mentioned as 'two sets of eighteen,' etc., are made into three sets of thirty-six by the phrase 'thus, the past thirty-six,' etc., and so it is said, 'six sets of eighteen.' It should be understood that the sixty-two views, however, are not taken up here, being omitted because they are spoken of elsewhere.

Ekakamātikādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Numerical Lists and so forth is concluded.

(1.) Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā

(1.) The Explanation of the Exposition of Single Items

843-844. Atthi paṭiccaṃ nāmāti yathā “cakkhuñca paṭiccā”tiādīsu nissayādipaccayabhāvena paṭiccāti vuttaṃ, na tathā idha khattiyādijātīnaṃ paramatthato avijjamānānaṃ nissayādipaccayattassa abhāvā. Yesu pana khandhesu santesu khattiyādisammuti hoti, tesaṃ abbocchinnatāva khattiyādijātiyā atthitā, sā idha paṭicca-saddena vibhāvitāti attho. Ekissā seṇiyāti asambhinnāyāti attho.

843-844. “There is dependence, so-called”—as in “dependent on the eye” and so forth, where ‘dependent’ is stated in the sense of a support condition, etc., but not so here, because for castes like the Khattiya, which do not exist in an ultimate sense, there is an absence of being a support condition, etc. However, the unbroken continuity of those aggregates, in the presence of which the convention “Khattiya,” etc., occurs, is the existence of the Khattiya caste, etc. This is clarified here by the term “dependent.” “Of a single lineage” means unmixed.

Pañhavissajjanādikiriyāsu [V 0.0218] purato karaṇaṃ purekkhāro. Nikkheparāsīti nidhānarāsi. Patthaṭākittinoti vitthiṇṇākittino. Rattaññumadoti purāṇaññutāmadoti vadanti. Cirarattijātena, cirarattipabbajitena vā jānitabbassa, rattīnameva vā jānanamado. Upaṭṭhāpakamānoti āṇākaraṇamāno. Āṇākaraṇañhi vicāraṇaṃ idha “yaso”ti vuttanti. Parimaṇḍalattabhāvanissito māno pariṇāhamado. Sarīrasampattipāripūriyā mado pāripūrimado.

In actions such as answering questions, placing in front is 'purekkhāra.' 'Nikkheparāsi' means a heap of treasure. 'Patthaṭākittino' refers to those whose fame is widespread. 'Rattaññumado' is said to mean pride in ancient knowledge—that is, pride in what is to be known by one born long ago or ordained long ago, or pride in knowing the nights themselves. 'Upaṭṭhāpakamāno' means pride in giving orders, for here, deliberation in giving orders is called 'yaso' (fame). Pride based on a well-proportioned body is 'pariṇāhamado.' Pride in the perfection of bodily accomplishment is 'pāripūrimado.'

845. Vatthunā vināpi vattabbatāya avatthukaṃ, na vatthuno abhāvā.

845. It is 'avatthukaṃ' (without basis) because it can be spoken of even without a basis, not because of the absence of a basis.

846. Cittassa vossajjananti cittassa satito muccanaṃ, kāyaduccaritādīsu pakkhandanaṃ vā vossaggo. Patiṭṭhābhāvoti kusalakaraṇe aṭṭhānaṃ, anuṭṭhānanti [M 0.0217] attho. Pamādasaṅkhātassa atthassa kāyaduccarite cittassa vossaggo pāṇātipāte micchādiṭṭhiyaṃ kodhe upanāheti evamādiko pariyāyo apariyanto, tadatthatappariyāyappakāsako vossagganissaggādiko byañjanapariyāyo cāti sabbaṃ taṃ saṅkhipitvā evarūpoti idaṃ ākāranidassanaṃ sabbapariyāyassa vattuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā katanti dassento āha “pariyantābhāvato”ti. Vissaṭṭhākāroti satiyā paccanīkabhūte cattāro khandhe dasseti.

846. ‘Cittassa vossajjana’ means the mind’s release, that is, being freed from mindfulness, or its plunging into bodily misconduct and so forth. ‘Patiṭṭhābhāvo’ means the absence of a foundation for doing what is wholesome, that is, non-establishment. The release of the mind into bodily misconduct, characterized as negligence, leading to killing, wrong view, anger, grudge, and so on, is an endless process. The verbal expression beginning with ‘release’ and ‘relinquishment’ reveals that meaning and its method. Summarizing all that, this ‘such-like’ is an indication of the manner, made because it is impossible to state all the methods; showing this, he said, ‘due to the absence of limits.’ ‘Vissaṭṭhākāro’ shows the four aggregates that are opposed to mindfulness.

847. Cittassa thaddhatā tathāpavattacittamevāti vadanti, mānaviseso vā daṭṭhabbo. Upasaṅkamane vanditabbaṃ hotīti pariyanteneva carati.

847. ‘Cittassa thaddhatā’ is said to refer to rigidity of mind, or it should be regarded as a kind of conceit. ‘Upasaṅkamane vanditabbaṃ hoti’ means one behaves with restraint.

848. “Āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti vutte “āvuso, tvaṃ āpannosī”tiādinā tena vuttaṃ tasseva upari khipanavasena “paṭippharitvā”ti vadanti. “Tasmiṃ nāma dalidde, akusale vā idaṃ karonte ahaṃ kasmā na karomī”ti evaṃ idha paṭippharaṇaṃ yuttaṃ. Karaṇassa uttarakiriyā karaṇuttariyaṃ. Akusalapakkho esāti sārambhoti adhippāyo.

848. When told, “You have committed an offense,” replying, “Friend, you have committed an offense,” and so forth, by way of throwing it back upon the speaker, is called ‘paṭippharitvā.’ Here, such retaliation is fitting, as in thinking, “Why should I not do this when that wretched or unwholesome person does it?” ‘Karaṇuttariyaṃ’ means the subsequent action of doing. This is the unwholesome side—the meaning is contentiousness.

849. Aticca icchatīti aticciccho, tassa bhāvo aticcicchatāti vattabbe cci-kāralopaṃ katvā “aticchatā”ti vuttaṃ. Atricchatāti ca sā eva vuccatīti. Tatrāpi neruttikavidhānena padasiddhi veditabbā. Yathāladdhaṃ vā atikkamitvā atra atra icchanaṃ atricchatā, sā eva ra-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā “aticchatā”ti vuttā.

849. ‘He desires excessively’ (aticca icchati), thus he is one with excessive desire (aticciccho). When its state should be stated as ‘aticcicchatā,’ the syllable ‘cci’ is elided, and so it is called ‘aticchatā.’ That same state is also called ‘atricchatā.’ Here also, the formation of the word should be understood according to the etymological method. Or alternatively, ‘atricchatā’ is desiring here and there, having exceeded what has been obtained. That very word, with the letter ‘r’ changed to ‘t,’ is called ‘aticchatā.’

Atricchanti [V 0.0219] aticchaṃ, atra vā icchanto. Kena? Atilobhena atilobhamicchāsaṅkhātena atilobhamadena ca. Attano hitaṃ attāti vuttaṃ. Hāyati jīrati, ādiṇṇo vā attā, patto vā attā, naṃ jīrati candakinnariṃ patthayitvā asitābhūdeviyā vihīno viya.

Desiring excessively, or desiring here. By what? By excessive greed, characterized as excessive greed and wrong desire, and by the intoxication of excessive greed. One’s own welfare is called the self. It diminishes, it decays; or the self, being seized or attained, decays him, like one who is deprived of Asitābhūdevī after having longed for Candakinnarī.

Icchāhatassāti icchāya upaddutassa, mudditassa vā.

‘Of one struck by craving’ means of one oppressed by craving, or infatuated by it.

Atihīḷayānoti avamaññamāno. Malakanti evaṃnāmakaṃ janapadaṃ, abbhokāsaṃ vā. Kodaṇḍakenāti kudaṇḍakena rassadaṇḍakena. Gaddulenāti ca vadanti. Ruhiramakkhitaṅgoti ruhirasinnagatto.

‘Atihīḷayāno’ means disdaining excessively. ‘Malakaṃ’ means a country of that name, or an open space. ‘Kodaṇḍakena’ means with a bad stick, a short stick. They also call it a `gaddula`. ‘Ruhiramakkhitaṅgo’ means one whose body is wet with blood.

850. Jānantasseva [M 0.0218] bhiyyo bhiyyo codento viya sambhāvetukāmo hoti. Paccayeti upādānādipaccaye.

850. Even though he knows, as if admonishing him again and again, he wishes to esteem him. ‘In the conditions’ means in the conditions beginning with clinging.

851. Ye patirūpena vañcenti, te gaṇṭhikā, durācārena vā gaṇṭhibhūtā. Gaṇṭhikaputtā nāma gaṇṭhikā eva honti, tena saddhivihārikā gaṇṭhikabhāvena “thero…pe… dīghacaṅkame viharatī”ti vadanti.

851. Those who deceive with what is suitable are called tricksters, or those who, through misconduct, become like knots. The sons of tricksters are indeed tricksters; therefore their co-residents, due to his knotted nature, say, “The elder... dwells on a long walking path.”

Vaṭṭati bhanteti ayampi eko pakāro, lābhinā eva pana sakkā ñātunti attano samāpattilābhitaṃ sūcetīti attho. Pañcattayaṃ nāma uparipaṇṇāsake dutiyasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 3.21 ādayo). Tassa gambhīrattā vadati “pañcattayaṃ olokentassā”ti.

‘It is fitting, venerable sir’—this too is one way; but ‘only one who has gained it can know’—thus the meaning is that he indicates his own attainment of meditative absorption. ‘The Fivefold Three’ refers to the second discourse in the Upper Fifty (Majjhima Nikāya 3.21 ff.). Because of its profundity, he says, ‘for one examining the Fivefold Three.’

852. Siṅganti siṅgāraṃ. Tañhi kusalassa vijjhanato samāsevitatāya sīse parikkhataṃ sunikhataṃ visāṇaṃ viya, thirattā ca siṅgaṃ viyāti siṅgaṃ, taṃ panatthato rāgo.

852. ‘Siṅgaṃ’ means adornment or passion (siṅgāraṃ). For, because it pierces what is wholesome and is constantly practiced, it is like a well-fashioned, well-fixed horn on the head. And because of its firmness, it is like a horn (siṅgaṃ), thus it is called ‘siṅgaṃ.’ In meaning, however, it is lust.

853. Temanakaraṇatthe tintiṇa-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Khīyananti ca yena lobhena paraṃ mamanti vadantaṃ khīyati, so vutto. Khīyanaṃ bhaṇḍananti ca vadanti. Tintiṇanti vā loluppamicceva vuttaṃ hoti. Saññā-saddo hi eso loluppavācakoti.

853. The word ‘tintiṇa’ should be understood in the sense of ‘causing moistening.’ And ‘khīyana’ is said of that greed by which one disparages another who says ‘mine.’ They also say ‘khīyanaṃ’ means scolding. Or ‘tintiṇa’ is simply stated as intense greed. For this is indeed a term denoting intense greed.

854. Ūruppamāṇāpīti [V 0.0220] etena mahantaghanabhāvena apūtitaṃ dasseti. Athavātiādinā cīvaramaṇḍanādīnaṃ visesanāni “imassa vā pūtikāyassa bāhirānaṃ vā parikkhārānaṃ maṇḍanā”tiādīnīti dasseti. Cīvarena hi maṇḍanā cīvaramaṇḍanā, cīvarassa vā maṇḍanā cīvaramaṇḍanā, evaṃ pattamaṇḍanā senāsanamaṇḍanā cāti adhippāyo. Ūnaṭṭhānapūraṇaṃ chavirāgasusaṇṭhānādikaraṇañca cīvarādīsu kāye ca yathāyogaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Tadahujātadārako viya hotīti dārakacāpalyaṃ na muñcatīti attho.

854. ‘Even the size of a thigh’—by this, he shows that it is not putrid due to its great solidity. By ‘Or,’ etc., he indicates that the qualifiers of ‘robe-adornment,’ etc., are ‘adornments of this putrid body or of external requisites,’ and so forth. For, adornment by means of a robe is ‘robe-adornment,’ or adornment of a robe is ‘robe-adornment’; similarly, ‘bowl-adornment’ and ‘dwelling-adornment’—this is the meaning. Filling what is lacking, making the skin color good, and shaping it well, etc., should be applied appropriately to robes and to the body. ‘He is like a child born that very day’—the meaning is that he does not abandon childish restlessness.

855. Sadisā anurūpā bhatti sabhāgo, na sabhāgo asabhāgo, mānathaddhatā, virodho vā. Tenassa mātādīsu vattanaṃ asabhāgavuttitā. Evaṃvidhānaṃ mānādhikānaṃ akusalānamidaṃ nāmaṃ.

855. Similar, appropriate devotion is ‘shared’ (sabhāgo); what is not shared is ‘unshared’ (asabhāgo), or conceit and rigidity, or opposition. Therefore, his conduct toward his mother and others is ‘unshared conduct’ (asabhāgavuttitā). This is the name for such unwholesome states of those who are full of conceit.

856. Paritassitāti [M 0.0219] saṅkampanā, ukkaṇṭhitassa vā tassa tassa taṇhāyanā.

856. ‘Paritassitā’ means trembling, or the craving for this and that in one who is discontented.

857. Kusalakaraṇe kāyassa avipphārikatā līnatā jātiālasyaṃ, na rogautubhojanādīhi kāyagelaññaṃ tandī nāma, atha kho pakatiālasyanti attho. Kāyālasiyanti nāmakāyassa ālasiyaṃ, tadeva rūpakāyassāpīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

857. In performing wholesome deeds, the body's lack of vigor, its sluggishness, an innate laziness—not bodily sickness due to illness, climate, food, and so on—is called sloth (tandī); rather, the meaning is natural laziness. ‘Kāyālasiyaṃ’ is the laziness of the mental body; it should be understood that this also applies to the physical body.

858. Accasanādīhi uppannadhātukkhobhanimittaṃ ālasiyaṃ vijambhitā.

858. ‘Vijambhitā’ is laziness arising from the disturbance of the elements caused by overeating and so on.

859. Bhattanimittena uppannaṃ ālasyaṃ bhattasammado.

859. ‘Bhattasammado’ is the laziness that arises due to the sign of food.

860. Imehi panāti cittassa akalyatādīhi. Sabbattha kilesavasenāti thinamiddhakāraṇānaṃ rāgādīnaṃ vasenāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

860. ‘But by these’—that is, by the mind's unfitness, etc. ‘Everywhere by the power of defilements’ should be understood as by the power of lust, etc., which are the causes of sloth and torpor.

861. Sammāājīvato apeto katoti apakato. So ājīvupaddavena upaddutoti katvā āha “upaddutassāti attho”ti.

861. ‘Departed from right livelihood’ (sammāājīvato apeto) means ‘removed’ (apakato). Because he is afflicted by the distress of livelihood, he said the meaning is ‘of one afflicted’ (upaddutassa).

Tividhampi taṃ tattha āgataṃ tassa nissayabhūtāya imāya pāḷiyā dassetunti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

The meaning should be understood thus: that threefold aspect, having occurred there, is shown by this Pāli text, which serves as its basis.

Pāpaṇikānīti [V 0.0221] āpaṇato chaḍḍitāni. Nantakānīti antarahitāni, cīrāni vā. Gilānassa paccayabhūtā bhesajjasaṅkhātā jīvitaparikkhārā gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārā. Pūtimuttanti purāṇassa apurāṇassa ca sabbassa gomuttassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Pūtibhāvena chaḍḍitosadhantipi keci.

‘Pāpaṇikāni’ means things discarded from a shop. ‘Nantakāni’ means disappeared, or tattered garments. The life-requisites that are requisites for the sick and are counted as medicine are ‘gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārā.’ ‘Pūtimuttaṃ’ is the name for all cow urine, whether old or new. Some say it is medicine discarded due to its putrid state.

Agabbhikā ekadvārā dīghasālā kira uddaṇḍo. Kucchitarajabhūtāya pāpicchatāya niratthakakāyavacīvipphandaniggahaṇaṃ korajaṃ, taṃ etassa atthīti korajiko, ativiya korajiko korajikakorajiko. Atiparisaṅkitoti keci. Mukhasambhāvitoti korajikakorajikādibhāvena pavattavacanehi attano mukhamattena aññehi sambhāvito. So evarūpo evarūpatāya eva attānaṃ paraṃ viya katvā “ayaṃ samaṇo”tiādiṃ katheti.

A long hall without an inner chamber, with one door, is apparently a guardhouse (uddaṇḍo). ‘Korajaṃ’ is the restraint of useless bodily and verbal agitation due to vile desire that has become like dust. One who has this is ‘korajiko’; one who is extremely so is ‘korajikakorajiko.’ Some say ‘excessively apprehensive.’ ‘Mukhasambhāvito’ means esteemed by others merely through his own words, by speaking in the manner of a ‘korajikakorajiko,’ etc. Such a one, by his very nature, makes himself out to be like another and speaks, saying, “This ascetic,” etc.

Paṇidhāyāti “arahāti maṃ jānantū”ti cittaṃ ṭhapetvā, patthetvā vā. Āpāthakajjhāyīti manussānaṃ āpāthaṭṭhāne samādhiṃ samāpanno viya nisīdanto āpāthake janassa pākaṭaṭṭhāne jhāyī.

‘Paṇidhāya’ means having established the mind, “Let them know me as an arahant,” or having aspired. ‘Āpāthakajjhāyī’ means one who sits as if absorbed in concentration in a place within sight of people, meditating in a place visible to the public.

Aññaṃ [M 0.0220] viya katvā attano samīpe bhaṇanaṃ sāmantajappitaṃ. Ākārassa rassattaṃ katvā “aṭhapanā”ti vuttaṃ. Kuhanaṃ kuho, tassa ayanā pavatti kuhāyanā, kuhassa vā puggalassa ayanā gatikiriyā kuhāyanā.

Speaking near oneself as if to another is called ‘sāmantajappitaṃ.’ Having shortened the expression, it is called ‘aṭhapanā.’ ‘Kuhanaṃ’ is a deceitful person (kuho); its progression is ‘kuhāyanā,’ or the action of a deceitful person is ‘kuhāyanā.’

862. Puṭṭhassāti “ko tisso, ko rājapūjito”ti puṭṭhassa. Nahanāti bandhanā pariveṭhanā.

862. "When asked" (puṭṭhassa)—that is, when asked, "Who is Tissa, who is revered by the king?" "Nahanā" means bondage or surrounding.

863. Nimittena caranto jīvanto nimittakārako nemittiko, tassa bhāvo nemittikatā. Attano icchāya pakāsanaṃ obhāso. Ko pana soti? “Ajja bhikkhūnaṃ paccayā dullabhā jātā”tiādikā paccayapaṭisaṃyuttakathā. Icchitavatthussa samīpe kathanaṃ sāmantajappā.

863. One who lives by making signs is a sign-maker, a diviner; his state is divination. The manifestation of one's own desire is "radiance" (obhāso). "But what is that?"—it is talk connected to requisites, such as "Today, the requisites for the monks have become hard to obtain." Speaking near what one desires is "muttering nearby" (sāmantajappā).

864. Bahi chaḍḍanaṃ ukkhepanā. Parapiṭṭhimaṃsakhādanasīlo parapiṭṭhimaṃsiko, tassa bhāvo parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā.

864. Casting out (bahi chaḍḍanaṃ) is "rejection" (ukkhepanā). One who habitually eats the flesh from another's back (parapiṭṭhimaṃsakhādanasīlo) is a "back-flesh eater" (parapiṭṭhimaṃsiko); the state of being such is "back-flesh eating" (parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā).

865. Nikattuṃ [V 0.0222] appena lābhena bahukaṃ vañcetvā gahetuṃ icchanaṃ nijigīsanaṃ, tassa bhāvo nijigīsanatā. Tasseva icchanassa pavattiākāro, taṃsahajātaṃ vā gavesanakammaṃ.

865. The desire to cheat and to seize much by deceiving with a little gain is "acquisitiveness" (nijigīsanaṃ); its state is "acquisitiveness" (nijigīsanatā). It is the manner of that very desire's occurrence, or the accompanying act of searching.

866. Vaṇṇasampannaṃ pokkharaṃ vaṇṇapokkharanti uttarapadalopo pubbapadassa daṭṭhabbo, vaṇṇapāripūrī vā vaṇṇapokkharatā. “Atthajāpikā”ti ettha viya japa-saddo uppattivācakoti āha “pavattetī”ti.

866. A lotus endowed with beauty (vaṇṇasampannaṃ pokkharaṃ) is a 'beautiful lotus' (vaṇṇapokkharaṃ)—here, the elision of the latter part of the first word should be understood; or, the fullness of beauty is 'beautiful-lotus-ness' (vaṇṇapokkharatā). As in 'atthajāpikā,' here the word 'japa' indicates origin, so it is said 'it causes to proceed.'

867. Seyyasadisamānā unnativasena pavattāti ubhayatthāpi “mānaṃ jappetī”ti vuttaṃ.

867. Conceit regarding a superior and an equal operates by way of elevation—therefore, in both cases, it is said, "he mutters conceit" (mānaṃ jappeti).

868. Hīnamāno pana onativasena pavattito kevalena mānasaddena niddesaṃ nārahatīti taṃniddese “omānaṃ jappetī”ti (vibha. 874) vuttaṃ.

868. But inferior conceit, operating by way of lowliness, does not deserve description by the mere word "conceit." Therefore, in describing it, it is said, "he mutters lowly conceit" (omānaṃ jappeti) (Vibh. 874).

872. Rājabhogena raṭṭhabhuñjanako rājanissito raṭṭhiyo.

872. One who enjoys the kingdom with the king's revenue, dependent on the king, is a "state official" (raṭṭhiyo).

879. Puggalaṃ anāmasitvāti yathā seyyassa seyyamānādiniddesesu “parehi seyyaṃ attānaṃ dahatī”ti seyyādipuggalo mānuppādako [M 0.0221] āmaṭṭho, evametassa seyyamānabhāvepi mānuppādakapuggalavisesaṃ anāmasitvā “pare atimaññati”cceva vuttanti attho. Pare atikkamitvā maññanañhi yassa kassaci atimānoti.

879. "Without touching upon a person" (puggalaṃ anāmasitvā)—just as in the descriptions of conceit regarding a superior, etc., in phrases like "he considers himself superior to others," the superior person, etc., who gives rise to conceit is touched upon; similarly, even in the case of this conceit regarding a superior, without touching upon any specific person who might give rise to conceit, it is simply said, "he despises others"—this is the meaning. For thinking of oneself as having surpassed others is indeed anyone's excessive conceit (atimāno).

880. Purimamānassa uparimāno mānātimāno, ati-saddo upari-saddassa atthaṃ vadatīti daṭṭhabbo. Purimamānaṃ vā atikkanto māno mānātimāno.

880. Conceit above a previous conceit is "conceit-surpassing-conceit" (mānātimāno); the word "ati-" should be understood as conveying the meaning of the word "upari" (above). Or, conceit that surpasses a previous conceit is "conceit-surpassing-conceit."

881. Pakkhijātīsu vāyaso anto lāmakoti katvā “kākajāti viyā”ti vuttaṃ.

881. Among bird species, the crow is considered inwardly mean; thus, it is said, "like the crow species" (kākajāti viya).

882. Thero kira dosacarito ahosi, tasmā āditova “tumhe akhīṇāsavā”ti avatvā upāyena kathesīti vadanti, dosacaritattā vā khippaṃ tatiyapadavāre virāgaṃ uppādesīti adhippāyo.

882. The elder, it seems, was of a hateful disposition. Therefore, from the start, instead of saying, "You are not free from taints," he spoke skillfully—so they say. Or, due to his hateful disposition, he quickly aroused dispassion at the third repetition of the phrase—this is the meaning.

883. Mānaṃ [V 0.0223] anugatacchandoti mānasampayuttachando, mānasabhāvaṃ anugato mānacchando vā.

883. "Desire accompanied by conceit" (mānaṃ anugatacchando) means desire associated with conceit, or desire that follows the nature of conceit, which is "conceit-desire" (mānacchando).

884. “Vilambana”nti ca itthipurisasammānanādikiriyādivilambanapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kattabbaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha yuttamuttasiliṭṭhaṃ paṭibhānaṃ vilambanapaṭibhānaṃ.

884. "Delaying" (vilambana) should be understood as a task connected with delaying, such as the act of honoring women and men. Therein, apt, fluent, and smooth ready wit is "delaying ready wit" (vilambanapaṭibhānaṃ).

887. Amaravādapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko, attano amaraṇatthāya devabhāvatthāya vā vitakko amaravitakko.

887. A thought connected with the doctrine of immortality, or a thought for one's own deathlessness or for divine existence, is "the thought of immortality" (amaravitakko).

888. Paresu anuddayā rāgavasena anuddayakaraṇaṃ etassāti parānuddayo, tassa bhāvo parānuddayatā, paresu vā anuddayasseva sahananditādikassa bhāvo parānuddayatā, tādiso rāgo. Tatthāti parānuddayatāya saṃsaṭṭhavihārena dassitāyāti attho yujjati.

888. One who has compassion for others (parānuddayo) is one for whom there is acting with compassion due to the power of lust. The state of that is 'compassion for others' (parānuddayatā). Or, the state of delighting, rejoicing, etc., together with that very compassion for others is 'compassion for others'; such is this lust. There, the meaning is fittingly shown through a lifestyle connected with what is shown as 'compassion for others.'

890. Anavaññattiṃ patthento anavaññattatthameva kāmaguṇe ca patthetīti āha “pañcakāma…pe… nissito hutvā”ti.

890. One who, desiring non-disparagement, also desires sensual pleasures for the very sake of non-disparagement. Thus, it is said: "dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure..." (pañcakāma...pe... nissito hutvā).

Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of singles is concluded.

(2.) Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Exposition of Pairs

891. Upanayhatīti [M 0.0222] bandhati. A-kāro anantaratthavācako, mariyādavācakassa vā ākārassa rassattaṃ katvā “aṭṭhapanā”ti vuttanti “anantaraṭṭhapanā”tiādimāha. Tattha paṭhamuppannassa pavattākāro mariyādā, taṃ anatikkamitvā tasseva daḷhīkaraṇavasena ṭhapanā mariyādaṭṭhapanā. Pakatiṭṭhapanāmattameva, visesanarahitāti attho.

891. "Upanayhati" means to bind. The letter 'a' (in aṭṭhapanā) denotes the meaning of 'immediate', or 'aṭṭhapanā' is said to be stated by shortening the 'ā' of 'mariyādavācaka' (indicating a limit), as in 'anantaraṭṭhapanā' (immediate establishing) and so forth. There, the mode of occurrence of what first arises is the limit; establishing that does not transgress it, by way of strengthening that very thing, is limit-establishing. It is merely a natural establishing, devoid of specification—this is the meaning.

892. Niṭṭhuriyaṃ kheḷapātanaṃ, niṭṭhuriyaṃ viya niṭṭhuriyaṃ. Dassetvāti dantehi chinditvā. Tena [V 0.0224] pana dassanaṃ paḷāsoti dasseti. Paḷāsassa āyanāti yugaggāhappavatti. Samabhāvadahanaṃ jayo, tassa āharaṇato āhāro. Dhuraṃ na detīti pāmokkhaṃ na deti.

892. Harshness (niṭṭhuriyaṃ) is spitting saliva; it is like harshness, so it is called harshness. "Having shown" (dassetvā) means having cut with the teeth. By that showing, it shows malice (paḷāsa). The 'going' of malice is the progression of grasping the end of the yoke. Victory (jayo) is the burning of an even state; its acquisition (āharaṇa) is nutriment (āhāra). "Does not give the yoke" (dhuraṃ na deti) means "does not give prominence."

894. Kāyena cetiyaṅgaṇādivattaṃ karoti “evaṃ vattasampanno saddho kathaṃ kāyaduccaritādīni karissatī”ti paresaṃ ñāpanatthaṃ. Aticcāti accayaṃ katvā. Āsarantīti āgacchanti, puna paṭicchādane pavattantīti attho. Konāmevaṃ karotīti vocchindanacchādanā vā vocchādanā.

894. One performs bodily observances, such as duties at shrine courtyards, to make others know: "How could a faithful person, endowed with such conduct, commit bodily misconduct and so forth?" "Aticca" means having committed a transgression. "Āsaranti" means they come, that is, they proceed to conceal again. "Who indeed would do thus?" (konāmevaṃ karoti) is an explanation of "vocchādanā" as cutting off and concealing.

Na sammā bhāsitāti yo na sammā bhāsati, so saṭhoti dasseti. Kucchi vā piṭṭhi vā jānituṃ na sakkāti asantaguṇasambhāvaneneva cittānurūpakiriyāvirahato “evaṃcitto evaṃkiriyo”ti jānituṃ na sakkāti attho.

"Not rightly spoken" indicates that one who does not speak rightly is deceitful. "It is impossible to know the belly or the back" means that because of the absence of actions conforming to one's thoughts, due to the mere assumption of non-existent qualities, it is impossible to know "such is their mind, such are their actions"—this is the meaning.

Ajo eva ajāmigo. Nelakoti taruṇavaccho. Yathā so yakkho tādisaṃ rūpaṃ dassetvā “ajā”ti saññāya āgatāgate khādati, evamayampi taṃtaṃsadisaguṇasambhāvanena te te vañceti. Tenetaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ māyāto balavatarā vañcanāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Teneva “parikkhattatā”ti vuttaṃ.

A goat (ajo) is a goat-beast (ajāmigo). A 'nelaka' is a young calf. Just as that ogre, having shown such a form, devours those who come near under the perception 'it is a goat,' so too does this one deceive those people by feigning qualities similar to theirs. Therefore, this deceit (sāṭheyyaṃ) should be regarded as a deception more powerful than trickery (māyā). Hence, it is called 'encircling' (parikkhattatā).

908. Sakkāyadiṭṭhādīnaṃ abhāvepi yaṃ saṃyojanaṃ hoti, taṃ bahiddhā saṃyojanato bahiddhāsaṃyojanassa puggalassa visesanabhūtaṃ bahiddhāsaṃyojanaṃ nāma.

908. Even in the absence of identity view and the like, whatever fetter exists is called an external fetter because it fetters externally, being a distinguishing characteristic of a person with external fetters.

Dukaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Dukaniddesa is concluded.

(3.) Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Tikaniddesa

909. Akusalamūlāneva [M 0.0223] vaṭṭamūlānīti tehi kathitehi vaṭṭamūlasamudācāro kathito hotīti āha “tīhi…pe… kathito”ti.

909. The unwholesome roots are indeed the roots of the cycle of rebirth; thus, by stating them, the practice based on the roots of the cycle is stated. Therefore, it is said: "by these three... it is stated."

919. Sassato [V 0.0225] lokotiādidassanameva brahmacariyaṃ mokkhasampāpakaṃ uttamacariyanti diṭṭhigatikehi sammatanti āha “diṭṭhigatikasammatassā”ti. Rūpārūpāvacaravipākesu sātisayo bhavarāgoti adhippāyena vuttaṃ “mahābrahmāna”nti.

919. The view that the world is eternal and so forth is itself considered by those attached to views as the holy life, the supreme practice leading to liberation; hence it is said: "of that which is considered by those attached to views." The phrase "great Brahmā" is used with the intention that craving for existence is excessive in relation to the results in the form and formless realms.

920. Kathaṃvidhanti kenākārena saṇṭhitanti atthoti katvā āha “ākārasaṇṭhāna”nti. Mānaṭhapanāti seyyādivasena mānena ṭhapanā, mānasaṅkhātā vā ṭhapanā.

920. "How constituted" (kathaṃvidha) means "in what manner it is constituted"; having taken this as the meaning, it is said: "by mode of constitution." "Establishing of conceit" (mānaṭṭhapanā) means establishing by conceit in terms of being superior and so forth, or establishing that is designated as conceit.

921. Cetaso utrāso domanassaṃ, doso vā, taṃsampayuttā vā cetanādayo.

921. The trembling of the mind is mental pain, or aversion, or volitions and so forth associated therewith.

922. Desanāsukhatāyāti tiṇṇaṃ addhānaṃ vasena vicikicchāya desanā sukhā “kaṅkhati vicikicchatī”ti, na pana tathā mohenāti adhippāyo. Vaṇṇādibhedaṃ sutvāti keci kira vadanti “khattiyajīvo paṇḍuvaṇṇo. Kasmā? So hi pubbaṇhe ramati, pubbaṇhe ca chāyā paṇḍuvaṇṇā. Brāhmaṇavessasuddajīvā odātapītakāḷavaṇṇā. Te hi majjhanhasāyanharattīsu odātapītakāḷachāyā kāḷatamakālesu ramantī”ti tesaṃ vaṇṇabhedaṃ, “byāpī parimaṇḍalo”tiādinā kathentānaṃ saṇṭhānabhedañca sutvā.

922. 'The ease of teaching' means that teaching concerning doubt is easy with respect to the three periods of time, as in 'he doubts, he is uncertain,' but it is not so with delusion—this is the intended meaning. 'Having heard the distinctions of color and so forth'—some indeed say: 'The life-principle of a khattiya is pale in color. Why? Because he delights in the forenoon, and the shade in the forenoon is pale. The life-principles of brahmins, vessas, and suddas are white, yellow, and black in color. For they delight in the white, yellow, and black shades at midday, evening, and night, and in the dark and darkest times.' Having heard their distinctions of color, and the distinctions of form from those who speak of such things as 'pervasive, round,' and so forth.

923. Purisapuggaloti padadvayaṃ ekapadaṃ katvā jānantānaṃ vasenāyaṃ sammutikathā pavattā, padantarameva vā idaṃ puggalavācakanti dassento “ayaṃ panā”tiādimāha. Atha vā purisoti vutto ca puggalo eva, na purisindriyayuttovāti dassanatthampi “purisapuggalo”ti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Aṭṭhasu ābādhesūti pittasemhavātasamuṭṭhānautuvipariṇāmajaopakkamikavisamaparihārajasannipātajakammasamuṭṭhānesu. Pubbe katanti purāṇatarakammaṃ icchantīti upapajjavedanīyañca kira paṭikkhipanti. Āṇattimūlakena vāti yopi āṇāpetvā vadhabandhādidukkhaṃ uppādeti, tampi taṃmūlakaṃ na hoti, issaranimmānamūlamevāti adhippāyo.

923. 'Purisapuggala'—this conventional expression is used by those who understand these two words as a single term. Or, to show that this is another word denoting a person, he said 'ayaṃ panā' and so forth. Alternatively, it should be understood that 'purisapuggala' is stated to show that when 'purisa' is said, it refers to a person, not merely one possessing the male faculty. 'In the eight afflictions' means in those arising from bile, phlegm, and wind; those born of seasonal change; those born of improper care; those caused by external agency; those born of a combination of humors; and those arising from kamma. 'Previously done' means they desire only very old kamma, and indeed they reject kamma that is to be experienced in the next life. 'Or rooted in command' means that even if one, having given a command, causes suffering such as killing or imprisonment, this is not rooted in that command; it is rooted solely in the creation of a Lord—this is the intended meaning.

924. Mohassa [M 0.0224] anudahanaṃ dāhakāraṇatāya vuttaṃ, sabhāvatopi pana asampaṭivedho sampaṭivedhasukhassa paccanīkabhūto dukkho evāti anudahanatā veditabbā. Evañca katvā “upekkhā vedanā ñāṇasukhā aññāṇadukkhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.465) vuttā.

924. The burning of delusion is spoken of because it is a cause of torment; but by its very nature, non-penetration, being opposed to the happiness of penetration, is itself suffering. Thus, its nature as burning should be understood. And for this reason, it is said: 'Equanimous feeling is happiness when conjoined with knowledge, suffering when conjoined with ignorance' (MN 59).

926. Puthunimittārammaṇesūti [V 0.0226] subhanimittādivasena puthunimittasabhāvesu ārammaṇesu, puthusabhāvesu vā subhanimittādiārammaṇesu. Kosajjapamādaniddesānaṃ samānattepi avipphārikatāsaṅkhātā līnavuttitā kosajjaṃ, sativossaggasaṅkhātaṃ pamajjanaṃ pamādoti ayaṃ visesoti.

926. 'In objects that are diverse signs' means in objects that have the nature of diverse signs, such as the sign of the beautiful, or in objects of diverse natures, such as the sign of the beautiful. Although the descriptions of laziness and heedlessness are similar, laziness is a sluggish state, characterized as a lack of exertion, while heedlessness is negligence, characterized as the abandonment of mindfulness—this is the distinction.

931. Sagaruvāsanti saottappavāsamāha, sajeṭṭhakavāsanti sahirivāsaṃ. Anādiyanā anaddā ovādaaggahaṇaṃ, acittīkāroti attho. Sukkhakaṭṭhassa viya anallatā, amudutā vā anaddā. Asīlyanti asukhasīlatā amudutā eva.

931. 'Living with reverence' refers to living with moral dread; 'living with respect for elders' refers to living with moral shame. 'Disrespect' means not accepting advice, not taking it to heart. 'Anaddā' is non-pliancy or hardness, like that of dry wood. 'Intractability' is being of a difficult nature, which is just hardness.

934. Upārambho dosasampayuttacittuppādo siyā.

934. Reproach might be the arising of a mind associated with aversion.

936. “Idha pāsāṇaṃ karotī”tiādinā ṭhapanatthepi karoti-saddo yujjatīti āha “karotīti ṭhapetī”ti. Ettha cāyaṃ āvajjanā akusalānaṃ āsannakāraṇattā khuddakavatthūsu vuttāti veditabbā, tadanukūlakiccattā vā.

936. By the phrase 'Here, he makes a stone,' and so forth, the word 'karoti' (makes) is applicable even in the sense of placing; hence it is said: ''Karoti' means 'places'.' Here, this advertence should be understood as being mentioned in connection with minor matters because it is a proximate cause of unwholesome states, or because its function is conducive to them.

Tikaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Exposition of the Triads is concluded.

(4.) Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā

(4.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Fours

939. Itīti nidassane nipātoti evaṃ-saddena samānatthoti dasseti. Bhavābhavahetūtipīti ettha bhavanti jāyanti etenāti bhavo, sappiādibhesajjaṃ. Bhavo eva paṇītataro abhivuddho abhavo. Bhāvanārāmatāariyavaṃsappaheyyattā vā purimataṇhāttayavajjā sabbā taṇhā “bhavābhavahetu uppajjatī”ti vuttāti veditabbā.

939. The particle 'iti' is for illustration; this shows it is synonymous with the word 'evaṃ'. As to 'the cause of existence and non-existence': here, 'bhava' is that by which beings come to be, are born, such as medicinal ghee. A more refined and developed existence itself is 'abhava'. Alternatively, it should be understood that because of delighting in cultivation and because they are to be abandoned by the noble lineage, all craving, except for the three former types of craving, is said to arise as 'the cause of existence and non-existence'.

Etāyāti [M 0.0225] chandādiagatiyā. Na gacchantīti na pavattanti, taṃ taṃ kiriyaṃ na karontīti [V 0.0227] attho. Imināti chandādinā agatigamanena. Chandādīsu yena ninno, tena gamanaṃ yathāninnagamanaṃ.

'By this' means by the wrong course of desire and so forth. 'They do not go' means they do not proceed, they do not perform that particular action; this is the meaning. 'By this' means by going the wrong course due to desire and so forth. Among desire and so forth, going in whichever way one is inclined is like going down an incline.

“Rājā”tiādinā rājādinimitto viya ūmiādinimitto cittutrāso ūmiādibhayaṃ, “ūmibhayanti kho, bhikkhave, kodhupāyāsassetaṃ adhivacana”ntiādivacanato (ma. ni. 2.162; a. ni. 4.122; itivu. 109) kodhupāyāsaodarikattapañcakāmaguṇamātugāmā vā. Tattha pañcakāmaguṇamātugāmaggahaṇena tannissitachandarāgaggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, odarikattañca lobhova. Ukkhepanīyādikammaṃ vinayadaṇḍaṃ.

By 'king,' and so forth: just as there is mental agitation caused by a king and so forth, so the fear of waves and so forth is a mental agitation caused by waves and so forth. From statements such as, 'Monks, "fear of waves" is a designation for anger and despair' (M II 103; A II 124; It 114), it refers to anger, despair, gluttony, the five strands of sensual pleasure, or women. Here, by the mention of the five strands of sensual pleasure and women, the desire and lust dependent on them should be understood to be included; and gluttony is just greed.

“Atha kho timbaruko paribbājako yena bhagavā…pe… etadavoca ‘kiṃ nu kho, bho gotama, sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkha’nti? Mā hevaṃ timbarukāti bhagavā avocā”tiādinā nidānavagge (saṃ. ni. 2.18) āgatattā “timbarukadiṭṭhī”ti vuttā.

Because it appears in the Nidānavagga (SN 12.19) in the passage beginning, 'Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One... and said: "Master Gotama, is pleasure and pain self-made?" "Not so, Timbaruka," the Blessed One replied,' it is called 'Timbaruka's View.'

Catukkaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Fours is concluded.

(5.) Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā

(5.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Fives

940. Āgantuṃ pana na dentīti āgamanassa paccayā na hontīti attho daṭṭhabbo.

940. 'They do not give to one who comes' means that they do not become a condition for coming; this meaning should be understood.

941. Avadehanatoti pūraṇena maṃsūpacayahetutāya ca upacayanato. Gimhakāle bhuñjitvā sayantassa sukhaṃ hotīti taṃ utusukhaṃ “seyyasukha”nti vuttaṃ, sayaniriyāpathasukhanti attho. Vatanti dhutaṅgāni. Tapoti khandhakavattāni, vīriyaṃ vā. Sīlaggahaṇena khandhakavattamethunaviratīnaṃ gahitattā tapabrahmacariyaggahaṇaṃ na kattabbanti ce? Na, aññasīlato visesetvā tapabrahmacariyānaṃ devattakāraṇattaggahaṇassa dassanato, bāhirānañcassa vinibandhassa pavattidassanato vā. Tesañhi avihiṃsādigovatādidukkarakārikāmethunaviratiyo yathākkamaṃ sīlādīni, tāni ca te devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya carantīti. Aññathā ca saddhāruciādīhi “yato [V 0.0228] kho bho ayaṃ attā rūpī cātumahābhūtiko mātāpettikasambhavo kāyassa bhedā ucchijjatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.85) vikappetvā.

941. 'Due to filling up' means due to filling and, because it is a cause for the accumulation of flesh, due to increasing. In the hot season, the comfort one experiences after eating and lying down—that seasonal comfort is called 'sleeping comfort', meaning the happiness of the lying-down posture. 'Vows' refers to the ascetic practices. 'Austerity' refers to the monastic rules, or it is effort. If it is asked whether the inclusion of 'austerity' and 'celibacy' is unnecessary because the precepts already include monastic rules and abstaining from sexual misconduct, the answer is no. This is because 'austerity' and 'celibacy' are distinguished from other moral conduct due to their role as causes for attaining divine states, or because their observance leads to the breaking of external bonds. For them, non-violence and so forth, vow-based austerities and so forth, difficult practices, and abstaining from sexual misconduct are, in sequence, moral conduct and so forth. And they practice these, intending rebirth in divine realms. Otherwise, through faith, preference, and so forth, they speculate, saying, 'Since this self is material, composed of the four great elements, born from mother and father, it is annihilated upon the breakup of the body,' and so forth (DN 1).

942. Byasanesu [M 0.0226] ñātibhogarogabyasanaggahaṇena taṃnimittā sokādayo gahitāti daṭṭhabbā. Dassanasavanesu paṭikūlatā dassanasavanapaṭikūlatā. Ettha ca ādīnavehi pañcahi tesaṃ kāraṇabhūtā akkhantiyeva bhinditvā kathitāti veditabbā, akkhantimūlakā vā appiyatādihetubhūtā dukkaṭadubbhāsitatādidosā.

942. It should be understood that in the case of misfortunes, by the inclusion of misfortunes related to relatives, wealth, and illness, the sorrows and so forth caused by them are included. In the case of sights and sounds, 'repulsiveness' means repulsiveness to sights and sounds. Here, with the five drawbacks, it should be understood that intolerance itself, being their root cause, is spoken of by analyzing it; or that the faults of misconduct and wrong speech, which are rooted in intolerance, are the cause of dislike and other factors.

Micchājīvanimittaṃ maraṇakāle uppannabhayaṃ “ājīvakabhaya”nti vuttaṃ. “Ājīvikābhaya”nti pana pāṭhe paccayānuppattiṃ passato ājīvikanimitto cittutrāsoti attho daṭṭhabbo. Kittisaddo silokanti tappaṭipakkhā asilokaṃ akitti. Tenāha “garahabhaya”nti.

The fear arising at the time of death on account of wrong livelihood is called 'fear concerning livelihood' (ājīvakabhaya). However, with the reading 'fear of livelihood' (ājīvikābhaya), the meaning should be understood as mental terror on account of livelihood for one who sees the non-arising of requisites. The word 'kitti' (fame) means renown; its opposite, 'asiloka' (infamy), is 'akitti' (disrepute). Therefore, it is called 'fear of blame'.

943. Uppilāvitanti udaggatāsaṅkhāto avūpasamabhāvo, avūpasamahetubhūto vā pītiyā ākāro.

943. 'Elation' is a state of non-tranquility, characterized as excitement; or it is an aspect of joy that is the cause of non-tranquility.

Pañcakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Fives is completed.

(6.) Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā

(6.) Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixes

944. “Kodhano hoti upanāhī”tiādinā kodhādihetukā upanāhādayo kodhādīnaṃ sahāyakāraṇabhāvena suttante vuttāti kodhādayo eva vivādamūlāni, tenettha te eva vuttā. Sandiṭṭhiparāmasitā attano diṭṭhiyaṃ abhiniviṭṭhatā.

944. Because states such as bearing grudges, which are caused by anger and so forth, are mentioned in the suttas as auxiliary causes for anger and so forth, anger and so forth are themselves the roots of dispute; therefore, these very states are mentioned here. 'Clinging to one's own views' means being firmly attached to one's own opinions.

945. Appatissayoti patissayabhūtehi garūhi virahito. Appamādalakkhaṇanti satiavippavāsaṃ kusalānuyogasātaccaṃ vā.

945. 'Lacking in deference' (appatissaya) means being devoid of those worthy of reverence who are a support. 'The characteristic of heedfulness' (appamādalakkhaṇa) is either the non-deviation of mindfulness or persistent engagement in wholesome practices.

Yuttapayuttatāti [V 0.0229] tanninnatāvasena suṭṭhu yuttatā. Gaṇasaṅgaṇikā kilesavasena pavattā saṅgaṇikā. Itthipaṭisaṃyuttakathāsavane itthisaddasavane ca assādo savanasaṃsaggo. Itthiyā kassaci dānaggahaṇassādo paribhogasaṃsaggo.

'Being well-suited' (yuttapayuttatā) means being very well-suited due to that tendency. 'Association with groups' (gaṇasaṅgaṇikā) refers to association that occurs due to defilements. The pleasure in listening to talk connected with women or the sound of women's voices is the enjoyment of auditory association (savana-saṃsagga). The pleasure in a woman's giving or one's receiving of gifts is the enjoyment of association through use (paribhoga-saṃsagga).

946. Somanassena saddhiṃ upavicarantīti somanassupavicārāti akusalasomanassasahagatā rūpavicārādayo idhādhippetāti veditabbā, tathā upekkhupavicārā ca. Taṃsampayutto vāti etena vicāraggahaṇena vitakkopi [M 0.0227] gahitoti vitakkappavattanena “upavitakketī”ti idampi vuttaṃ hotīti dasseti.

946. 'Examining with joy' (somanassupavicārā) refers to investigations of forms and so forth accompanied by unwholesome joy, and should be understood as intended here. Similarly, 'examining with equanimity' (upekkhupavicārā) is also intended. 'Associated with that' (taṃsampayutto vā) shows that by the inclusion of investigation (vicāra), initial application (vitakka) is also included, and that through the activity of initial application, the expression 'he applies thought' (upavitakketi) is also stated.

947. Aññāṇasampayuttāti vicikicchuddhaccasahagatacittesu upekkhā mohoti vadanti, lobhasampayuttupekkhāpi pana gehassitā na na hoti.

947. 'Associated with ignorance' (aññāṇasampayuttā) refers to the equanimity in cittas accompanied by doubt and restlessness, which they call delusion (moha). However, equanimity associated with greed, being rooted in household life, is not absent.

948. Adhiccasamuppanniko “adhicca samuppanno attā uppanno bhavissatī”ti gaṇhanto sassatadiṭṭhiko hotīti evarūpassa diṭṭhi viyāti dassento “adhiccasamuppannikassevā”ti āha. Na so jātoti ettha “jātū”ti ayaṃ nipāto u-kārassa o-kāraṃ katvā jātoti vutto, tena vā samānatthaṃ nipātantaraṃ etaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sabbāsavadiṭṭhīti sabbāsavapariyāyena āgatā diṭṭhi.

948. The one who holds the view of 'arising by chance' (adhiccasamuppannika) becomes an eternalist by thinking, 'The self arises by chance and the self will come to be.' Thus, showing that the view of such a one passes away, he says 'of the one who holds the view of arising by chance' (adhiccasamuppannikasseva). As to 'he is not born' (na so jāto): here, the particle 'jātū' is stated as 'jāto' by changing the 'u' to 'o,' or another particle with the same meaning should be understood here. 'All-āsava view' (sabbāsavadiṭṭhi) means the view that comes by way of the category of all āsavas.

Chakkaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Sixes is completed.

(7.) Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevens

951. Dvāsaṭṭhiyā diṭṭhīsu sattakassa aññassa abhāvā satta ucchedavādā eva idha tathā avatvā “satta diṭṭhī”ti vuttā.

951. Among the sixty-two views, since there is no other group of seven, the seven annihilationist views alone are here called 'the seven views' without being specified as such.

Sattakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Sevens is finished.

(8.) Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Exposition of the Eights

952. “Kammaṃ [V 0.0230] kho me kattabbaṃ bhavissatī”tiādinā osīdanākārena pavattacittuppādā kosajjakāraṇāni, kosajjameva vā kosajjantarakāraṇatāya kosajjakāraṇānīti daṭṭhabbāni. Māsācitaṃ maññeti ettha ācita-saddo tinta-saddassa, maññe-saddo ca viya-saddassa atthaṃ vadatīti adhippāyena “tintamāso viyā”ti ayamattho vibhāvito, māsacayo viyāti vā attho.

952. The arisings of thought occurring in a sluggish manner, such as 'I will have work to do,' are causes of laziness. Or, laziness itself should be seen as the causes of laziness because it is a cause for further laziness. In the phrase 'he thinks it is māsācita,' the word ācita has the meaning of 'soaked,' and the word maññe has the meaning of 'like.' With this intention, the meaning is explained as 'like a soaked bean'; or the meaning is 'like a heap of beans.'

957. Pharatīti phusati, ghaṭṭetīti attho. Aññena kāraṇenāti “ajja tayā vikāle bhuttaṃ, tena tvaṃ āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti vutto “hiyyo [M 0.0228] mayā kāle bhuttaṃ, tenāhaṃ anāpanno”tiādinā aññena ayuttena kāraṇena aññaṃ yuttaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicchādetīti attho. Pucchitatthato bahiddhā yathā taṃ na allīyati, tathā kathāya apanayanaṃ vikkhipanaṃ bahiddhā apanāmanā.

957. 'It pervades' (pharati) means it touches (phusati); the meaning is it strikes (ghaṭṭeti). 'By another reason' means this: when told, 'Today you ate at the wrong time, and for that reason you have incurred an offense,' one conceals the correct reason with another, unsuitable reason, saying, 'Yesterday I ate at the proper time, and for that reason I am not at fault,' and so on. This is the meaning. To lead the conversation away, to scatter it, to turn it aside externally, so that it does not adhere to the matter being asked about.

958. Asaññīvādāti puggalehi diṭṭhiyo dasseti. Yehi vā abhinivesehi asaññī attānaṃ vadanti, te asaññīvādā. Arūpasamāpattinimittanti ākāsādiṃ.

958. 'Doctrine of the non-percipient' (asaññīvāda): this indicates the views by way of the persons holding them. Or, the adherences by which they declare the self to be non-percipient are the 'doctrines of the non-percipient.' 'The sign of the formless attainments' means space and so on.

Aṭṭhakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Eights is finished.

(9.) Navakaniddesavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Exposition of the Nines

960. Dasamassa avuttattā “sattesu uppattivaseneva kathitānī”ti vuttaṃ.

960. Because the tenth is not mentioned, it is said: 'They are spoken of only by way of arising among beings.'

963. Sukhavinicchayanti sevitabbāsevitabbasukhasanniṭṭhānanti attho. Ajjhattaṃ sukhanti sevitabbaṃ nekkhammasukhaṃ. Vinicchayāti dve vinicchayāti idaṃ –

963. 'Discernment of pleasure' (sukhavinicchaya) means the determination of what pleasure is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated. 'Internal pleasure' is the pleasure of renunciation, which is to be cultivated. 'Discernment' means the two kinds of discernment; this refers to what is said in the following verse:

“Sātaṃ [V 0.0231] asātanti yamāhu loke,

Tamūpanissāya pahoti chando;

Rūpesu disvā vibhavaṃ bhavañca,

Vinicchayaṃ kubbati jantu loke”ti. (su. ni. 873; mahāni. 102) –

“What they call pleasant and unpleasant in the world, relying on that, desire comes to be. Having seen the decline and existence of forms, a being in the world makes a discernment.”

Etassa niddese vuttaṃ.

This is explained in the Niddesa.

Idha vinicchayoti vuttoti imissā vibhaṅgapāḷiyā yo chandarāgassa paccayasabhāvena vinicchaya-saddena vutto, sakkapañhepi (dī. ni. 2.357) chandassa nidānabhāvena vitakka-saddena so eva āgatoti evaṃ vitakkassa vinicchayabhāvaṃ tasseva idha gahitatañca dasseti. Balavasanniṭṭhānanti balavatiyā taṇhāya ārammaṇassa niṭṭhapetvā gahaṇaṃ.

Here, what is called 'discernment' in this Vibhaṅga text—spoken of with the word 'discernment' as the conditional nature of desire and lust—is the very same thing that is mentioned in the Sakkapañha Sutta with the word 'thought' (vitakka) as the source of desire. Thus it is shown that thought has the nature of discernment and that this is what is meant here. 'Strong determination' means the grasping of an object, having established it through strong craving.

964. Satipi aññesañca saṅkhatabhāve ahanti asmīti ca sātisayā mānassa saṅkhatatāti katvā “saṅkhata”nti māno vutto. Seyyādivasena [M 0.0229] “ahamasmī”ti attano saṅkharaṇaṃ vā saṅkhataṃ. Ettha “bhavissantī”tiādikā pavatti taṇhādiṭṭhīnaṃ visesavatīti tāsampi iñjitādibhāvo vutto.

964. Although other things are also conditioned, conceit is called 'conditioned' because of the pre-eminent conditioned nature of the conceit that occurs as 'I am' and 'I exist.' Or, the 'conditioned' is the constructing of oneself as 'I am' in terms of being superior and so on. Here, the occurrence of such thoughts as 'I will be' is a special instance of craving and views, so their state as agitation and so on is also mentioned.

Navakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Nines is finished.

(10.) Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā

(10.) The Commentary on the Exposition of the Tens

970. Jālakkhipasaṃvidhānādikusalatāsaṅkappanaṃ upāyacintā, tassā micchābhāvapaṭicchādanabhāvena pavatto tadākāro moho upāyacintāvasena uppannoti daṭṭhabbo. Yathākate pana pāpe anādīnavadassanavasena pavattā saññā, saṅkappo vā paccavekkhaṇā, tassāpi micchābhāvapaṭicchādakaṃ tadākāraṃ, anādīnavadassanaṃ vā paccavekkhaṇākārena uppanno mohoti. Vimuttasaññitāti [V 0.0232] adhimānasampayuttaṃ, titthiyānaṃ vā attano diṭṭhiyā vimuttatāsañjānanaṃ. “Vimuttomhī”ti evaṃ pavatto akusalacittuppādo micchāvimuttīti keci vadanti. Phalaṃ viya vimuttanti gahite pana diṭṭhisampayuttacitte diṭṭhi micchāñāṇaṃ, samādhi ca micchāvimuttīti yuttaṃ siyā.

970. The thought that is skillful in arranging things such as the casting of nets is 'scheming' (upāyacintā). It should be understood that the delusion that proceeds in that form by way of concealing its wrong nature has arisen because of that scheming. Again, when an evil deed has been done, the perception or thought that proceeds by way of not seeing the danger is 'reflection' (paccavekkhaṇā). The delusion that conceals the wrong nature of this, having that form, or the not-seeing of danger that has arisen in the form of reflection, should be understood as delusion. 'The notion of being liberated' (vimuttasaññitā) is that which is associated with overestimation, or it is the notion held by adherents of other views that they are liberated through their own view. Some say that the unwholesome thought-arising that proceeds as 'I am liberated' is 'wrong liberation' (micchāvimutti). But when 'liberation' is taken as being like the 'fruit,' then in a mind associated with a view, the view is wrong knowledge and the concentration is wrong liberation; this would be appropriate.

Dasakaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Tens is finished.

Taṇhāvicaritaniddesavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Wanderings of Craving

973. Samūhagāhatoti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīnaṃ sādhāraṇaggahaṇatoti vadanti. “Itthaṃ evaṃ aññathā”ti pana visesaṃ akatvā gahaṇaṃ samūhagāhoti daṭṭhabbo. Aññaṃ ākāranti parasantānagataṃ ākāraṃ. Atthīti sadā saṃvijjatīti attho. Sīdatīti vinassati. Saṃsayaparivitakkavasenāti “kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ siyaṃ, na siya”nti evaṃ parivitakkavasena. Patthanākappanavasenāti “api nāma sādhu panāhaṃ siya”nti evaṃ patthanāya kappanavasena.

973. 'Collective grasping' (samūhagāha) is so called, they say, because it is a common grasping of craving, conceit, and views. It should be understood that 'collective grasping' is grasping without making a distinction such as 'in this way, thus, or otherwise.' 'Another mode' (aññaṃ ākāraṃ) means a mode belonging to another's mental continuity. 'It is' (atthi) means it always exists. 'It sinks' (sīdati) means it perishes. 'By way of doubt and pondering' (saṃsayaparivitakkavasena) refers to pondering such as, 'What if I were? What if I were not?' 'By way of aspiration and contriving' (patthanākappanavasena) refers to contriving with an aspiration such as, 'Oh, that I might be well!'

Suddhasīsāti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhīnaṃ sādhāraṇasīsā visesassa anissitattā “suddhasīsā”ti vuttā. Tattha diṭṭhisīsehi diṭṭhiyā taṇhā dassitā, sīsasīsamūlakehi [M 0.0230] mānadiṭṭhīhi sayameva cāti āha “evamete…pe… taṇhā vicaritadhammā veditabbā”ti. Diṭṭhimānesupi “taṇhāvicaritānī”ti vacanañca aññamaññaṃ vippayogīnaṃ diṭṭhimānānaṃ taṇhāya avippayogīnaṃ taṃmūlakattāva tappadhānatāya katanti veditabbaṃ.

They are called 'pure heads' because, being common heads for craving, conceit, and views, they are not dependent on any specific one. Therein, by the 'view-heads,' craving for views is shown; and by conceit and views themselves, which are rooted in the primary head, he says: 'Thus these... craving... should be understood as wandering phenomena.' And the statement that views and conceit are 'wanderings of craving' should be understood as having been made because, although views and conceit are mutually dissociated, they are not dissociated from craving, since they are rooted in it and have it as their principal factor.

974. Avakkarīti nipāto nānābhāve vattatīti anānākaraṇaṃ anavakkari, taṃ katvā, avakkari vā akatvā anavakkari katvāti evaṃ dassento āha “avinibbhogaṃ katvā”ti. “Anavakāriṃ karitvā”ti vā pāṭho, tattha avakiraṇaṃ vikkhepanaṃ samūhassa ekadesānaṃ vinibbhujjanaṃ avakāri, taṃ avakāriṃ vinibbhogaṃ akatvā, pañcapi khandhe samūhato ekatteneva gahetvā attato avinibbhujjitvā asmīti chandamānadiṭṭhiyo paṭilabhatīti [V 0.0233] attho. Asitabyābhaṅgitāyāti dāttena kājena cāti etena parikkhārena, asitabyābhaṅgīhi lavanavahanakiriyā vā “asitabyābhaṅgī”ti vuttā.

974. The particle 'avakkarī' functions in the sense of 'variousness.' Thus, 'not making various' is 'anavakkari.' Having done that, or not having done 'avakkari', is 'anavakkari'. Showing this, he said: 'having made it inseparable.' Alternatively, the reading is 'anavakāriṃ karitvā.' Therein, 'avakāri' means scattering, dispersing, the separating of parts of a whole. Not doing this 'avakāri'—that is, not separating—means taking the five aggregates collectively as a single thing, not separating them from self, and thus one acquires the desire, conceit, and views of 'I am.' 'Asitabyābhaṅgitāya' means with this equipment: a sickle and a carrying pole. Or the action of reaping and carrying with a sickle and carrying pole is called 'asitabyābhaṅgī'.

976. Avakāriṃ karitvāti rūpādīni attato vinibbhujjitvā iminā rūpena…pe… iminā viññāṇena asmīti chandaṃ paṭilabhatīti evaṃ sabbattha imināti etassa attato avinibbhuttena rūpādināti attho daṭṭhabbo. Attato hi avinibbhuttāni abahikatāni ahamicceva gahitāni rūpādīni upādāya upagantvā pavattā taṇhā “ajjhattikassa upādāyā”ti vuttā, attato ca vinibbhuttāni bahikatāni upagantvā pavattā “bāhirassa upādāyā”ti. Khaggena vā chattena vā ahaṃ niccoti abhimaṅgalasammatena khaggādinā mama vināso natthīti maññatīti attho. Ekekassāti idaṃ anādimhi anante ca saṃsāre ekekassa atītānāgatesu chattiṃsāyapi sambhavadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, ekekassa vā puggalassa yathālābhavasenāti idampi anissitataṇhāmānadiṭṭhiṃ katvā puthujjanassa addhāpaccuppanne kassaci sambhavadassanatthaṃ.

976. 'Having made a division' means that having separated form, etc., from the self, one acquires desire by thinking, 'I am by this form... by this consciousness.' In all such cases, 'by this' should be understood to mean 'by form, etc., which is not separated from the self.' For craving that proceeds by taking up and approaching form, etc., that are not separated from self, not externalized, and grasped as 'I,' is called 'clinging to the internal.' And craving that proceeds by approaching what is separated from self and externalized is called 'clinging to the external.' The meaning of 'I am eternal by means of a sword or an umbrella' is that one thinks, 'There is no destruction for me because of a sword, etc., which is considered auspicious.' 'For each one': this is said to show the possibility of this arising for each being in the past and future throughout the beginningless and endless saṃsāra, even in the thirty-six ways. Or, 'for each person according to what is obtained': this too is said to show the possibility of this arising in the present for some ordinary person, with regard to craving, conceit, and views that are not dependent on a specific object.

Taṇhāvicaritaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Wanderings of Craving is finished.

Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of Minor Topics is finished.

18. Dhammahadayavibhaṅgo

18. Analysis of the Heart of the Dhamma

1. Sabbasaṅgāhikavāravaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Section on All-Encompassing Inclusion

978. “Pañcakkhandhā”tiādinā [M 0.0231][V 0.0234] khandhādīnaṃ dhātusambhavapariyāpannapātubhāva bhūmantaratīsu dhātūsuuppādakadānādikusala kammatabbipākaabhiññeyyādiārammaṇadukadvayadiṭṭhādikusalattikāditikapañcakarūpalokiyadukadvayabhedabhinnānaṃ niravasesato saṅgahitattā dutiyavārādīnañca ettha anuppavesato sabbasāmaññena vutto paṭhamo sabbasaṅgāhikavāro nāma, dutiyo uppattānuppattidassanavāro nāmāti vuttaṃ. Tattha pana “kāmadhātuyā kati khandhā kati āyatanānī”tiādinā (vibha. 991) tesaṃ atthitā eva vuttā, kiriyāvisesassa appayogo “atthi bhavati saṃvijjatī”ti sāmaññakiriyāya viññeyyabhāvato, tenāyaṃ “sambhavāsambhavadassanavāro”ti vattuṃ yutto, catuttho ca upapattikkhaṇe uppattānuppattidassanavāroti tattha pātubhāvāpātubhāvavacanato.

978. Beginning with 'the five aggregates,' because of the complete inclusion, without remainder, of the aggregates and so forth—which are distinguished by their arising from elements, their inclusion and manifestation in various grounds and elements, productive wholesome kamma such as giving and its result, knowables, twofold pairs of objects, triplets such as views and the skillful, fivefold materiality, and worldly twofold pairs—and because the second section and so forth are not entered into here, the first section is generally called the 'All-Inclusive Section.' The second is called the 'Section on Seeing Arising and Non-Arising.' Therein, however, in the phrase 'In the sense-sphere realm, how many aggregates? How many sense bases?' and so on (Vibhaṅga 991), their existence alone is stated. The non-application of a specific action is to be understood by the general action 'there is, it becomes, it exists.' Therefore, this is rightly called the 'Section on Seeing Possibility and Impossibility,' and the fourth is called the 'Section on Seeing Arising and Non-Arising at the Moment of Rebirth,' because it speaks of manifestation and non-manifestation there.

979. Yathāpucchanti pucchānurūpaṃ avitathabyākaraṇaṃ parehi katampi sabbaññuvacanaṃ viññāya katattā sabbaññubyākaraṇameva nāma hoti, ko pana vādo sabbaññunā eva kateti adhippāyo.

979. Even a truthful answer given by others, corresponding to the questions asked, is called a statement of the Omniscient One because it is made with understanding of the Omniscient One's teaching. What then to speak of a statement made by the Omniscient One himself? This is the intention.

2. Uppattānuppattivāravaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Section on Arising and Non-Arising

991. Kāmadhātusambhūtānañcāti iddhiyā rūpadhātugatānaṃ kāmāvacarasattānañcāti attho. Ghānāyatanādīnaṃ abhāvenāti ettha yadi tadabhāvena gandhāyatanādīni āyatanādikiccaṃ na karonti[V 0.0235], asaññasattesu cakkhāyatanassa abhāvena rūpāyatanaṃ āyatanādikiccaṃ na kareyya. Tato “asaññasattānaṃ devānaṃ upapattikkhaṇe dvāyatanāni pātubhavantī”tiādivacanaṃ na vattabbaṃ siyā. Kāmāvacarādiokāsā tattha uppajjamānasattānaṃ, tattha pariyāpannadhammānaṃ vā adhiṭṭhānabhāvena “dhātū”ti vuccanti, tathā yesu kāmāvacarādisattanikāyesu kāmāvacarādisattā uppajjanti, tesaṃ sattānaṃ uppatti etthāti sattuppattīti vuccamānā te [M 0.0232] sattanikāyā ca, na panettha apariyāpannokāso apariyāpannasattanikāyo ca atthi, yo “dhātū”ti vucceyyāti imamatthaṃ dassento “okāsavasena vā sattuppattivasena vā apariyāpannadhātu nāma natthī”ti āha. Sattuppattivasenāti iminā vā okāsasattalokadvayaṃ saha gahetvā tādisāya apariyāpannadhātuyā abhāvaṃ dasseti, sattabhāvena vā uppatti sattuppatti, sattāvāsavasena taṃtaṃbhavavasena uppajjamānā upādinnakakkhandhā taṃtaṃpariyāpannānaṃ sadisādhiṭṭhānabhāvena dhātūti vuccantīti evaṃ apariyāpannadhātu natthīti attho.

991. 'Kāmadhātusambhūtānañca' means of beings born in the sense-sphere realm, and also of beings of the sense-sphere who have gone to the form-sphere realm by way of psychic power; that is the meaning. Regarding 'due to the absence of the nose sense base and so forth': if, due to their absence, the smell sense base and so forth do not perform the function of a sense base, then in the case of non-percipient beings, due to the absence of the eye sense base, the form sense base would not perform the function of a sense base. Therefore, the statement, 'For non-percipient devas at the moment of rebirth, two sense bases appear,' and so forth, could not be stated. Realms such as the sense-sphere are called 'elements' (dhātu) because they serve as the basis for those beings born there or for phenomena included therein. Similarly, those groups of beings, such as of the sense-sphere, wherein beings of the sense-sphere and so forth are born, are also called 'dhātu', being termed 'sattuppatti' (birth of beings) because 'the birth of those beings is herein'. There is no realm here, nor any group of beings, that is not included (apariyāpanna), which could be called a 'dhātu.' To show this meaning, he said: 'There is no dhātu that is not included, whether by way of realm or by way of the birth of beings.' Alternatively, by 'by way of the birth of beings' he indicates, taking together the two worlds of realm and beings, the absence of such an unincluded dhātu. Or, 'birth as beings' (sattuppatti) is the arising of appropriated aggregates by way of being a being, by way of the dwelling place of beings, by way of specific existences; and because they serve as a basis similar to those included in those specific realms, they are called 'dhātu.' Thus, the meaning is that there is no unincluded dhātu.

3. Pariyāpannāpariyāpannavāravaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Section on the Included and Unincluded

999. Bhavavasena okāsavasena ca paricchinnāti tattha aññattha ca uppajjamānā upādinnakakkhandhā taṃtaṃpariyāpannā sabbe daṭṭhabbā.

999. The appropriated aggregates that arise, limited by way of existence and by way of realm, here and elsewhere, are all to be seen as included in those respective categories.

6. Uppādakakammaāyuppamāṇavāro

6. The Section on Productive Kamma and the Measure of the Life Span

(1.) Uppādakakammavaṇṇanā

(1.) The Explanation of Productive Kamma

1021. Khandhādīnaṃ dhātusambhavādivasena pabhedaṃ vatvā ye sattā dhātuppabhedavanto, yañca tesaṃ uppādakakammaṃ, yo ca tassa vipāko, tesaṃ vasena pabhedaṃ dassetuṃ “tayo devā”tiādiko chaṭṭhavāro āraddho. Khandhādayo eva hi dhātuttayabhūtadevavasena dānādikammavasena taṃtaṃāyuppamāṇaparicchinnaupādinnakakkhandhavasena ca bhinnāti. Catudoṇaṃ ambaṇaṃ, chadoṇanti eke.

1021. Having explained the classification of the aggregates and so forth by way of their arising from elements and so on, the sixth section, beginning with 'three kinds of devas,' is commenced to show the classification by way of those beings who possess a diversity of elements, the productive kamma for them, and its result. For indeed, the aggregates and so forth are distinct by way of the devas who are the three elements, by way of kamma such as giving, and by way of the appropriated aggregates limited by their respective lifespans. An ambaṇa is four doṇas; some say six doṇas.

Uppādakakammavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of Productive Kamma is finished.

(2.) Āyuppamāṇavaṇṇanā

(2.) The Explanation of the Measure of the Life Span

1024. Tayopi [V 0.0236] janāti tayo janasamūhāti adhippāyo.

1024. 'Tayopi janā' means 'the three groups of people'; this is the intention.

1025. Ābhāti sobhanā pabhā.

1025. 'Ābhā' means beautiful radiance.

1026. Kañcanapiṇḍo viya sassirikā kañcanapiṇḍasassirikā. Tattha pana sobhanapabhāya kiṇṇā subhākiṇṇāti vattabbe ā-kārassa rassattaṃ [M 0.0233] antimaṇa-kārassa ha-kārañca katvā “subhakiṇhā”ti vuttā, atha pana subhena kiṇṇā subhakiṇṇā. Purimapadesupi parittaṃ subhaṃ etesanti parittasubhā, appamāṇaṃ subhaṃ etesanti appamāṇasubhāti subha-saddena samāso yojetabbo hoti.

1026. 'Kañcanapiṇḍasassirikā' means splendid like a lump of gold. However, where it should be said 'subhākiṇṇā' (filled with beautiful radiance), by shortening the initial 'ā' and changing the final 'ṇa' to 'ha', it is said 'subhakiṇhā.' Alternatively, 'subhakiṇṇā' means 'filled with beauty.' Also in the preceding terms, 'parittasubhā' means 'they have limited beauty,' and 'appamāṇasubhā' means 'they have immeasurable beauty'; thus, the compound should be formed with the word 'subha'.

1027. Ārammaṇamanasikārā pubbabhāgena kathitāti jhānakkhaṇe tato pacchā vā parittādikasiṇārammaṇabhāvanāya āvajjanena ca jhānassa ārammaṇamanasikāranānattatā na hoti, pubbabhāgabhāvanāya pana pubbabhāgāvajjanena ca hotīti attho. Pubbabhāgabhāvanāya vasena hi jhānaṃ parittapathavīkasiṇādīsu taṃtadārammaṇaṃ hoti, pubbabhāgena taṃtaṃkasiṇāvajjanena taṃtaṃmanasikāranti. Chandādayo pana appanākkhaṇepi vijjanti. Tattha paṇidhīti na taṇhāpatthanā, atha kho chandapatthanāva daṭṭhabbā. Adhimokkho nicchayo. Abhinīhāro cittappavattiyeva. Yadi pana bhavachandabhavapatthanādayo taṃtaṃbhavavisesaniyāmakā adhippetā. “Appanāyapi vaṭṭantī”ti etassa appanāya pavattāya tato pacchāpi vaṭṭantīti attho daṭṭhabbo. Saññāvirāgādīhi pana visesiyamānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ tathā tathā tattha pavatto manasikāro ca bhavavisesaniyāmako pubbabhāgova vaṭṭatīti “ārammaṇamanasikārā pubbabhāgena kathitā”ti vuttaṃ.

1027. 'Mental attention to the object is said to be in the preliminary part.' At the moment of jhāna, or after that, there is no variety in the mental attention to the object of jhāna by means of developing the object, such as the limited kasiṇa, or by adverting to it. However, the meaning is that there is variety due to preliminary development and preliminary adverting. For it is through preliminary development that jhāna takes the respective object, such as the limited earth-kasiṇa and so forth, and through preliminary adverting to that kasiṇa, there is that mental attention. But desire (chanda) and so forth are also present at the moment of absorption (appanā). There, 'aspiration' (paṇidhi) should not be seen as the aspiration of craving (taṇhā-patthanā), but rather as the aspiration of desire (chanda-patthanā). 'Decision' (adhimokkha) is certainty. 'Directing of the mind' (abhinīhāra) is simply the proceeding of the mind. If, however, the desire for existence (bhavachanda), aspiration for existence (bhavapatthanā), and so forth, are intended as the determiners of specific existences, then the meaning of 'they occur even in absorption' should be understood as 'they occur when absorption has arisen and continue even after that.' But the object, distinguished by dispassion towards perception (saññāvirāga) and so forth, and the mental attention directed accordingly, function as a determiner of specific existence only in the preliminary part. Hence, it is said, 'mental attention to the object is said to be in the preliminary part.'

Vipulā phalāti vipulasantasukhāyuvaṇṇādiphalā. Suṭṭhu passanti paññācakkhunā maṃsadibbacakkhūhi ca.

'Vipulā phalā' (abundant in fruits) means fruits such as abundant peace, happiness, long life, and beauty. They see well with the eye of wisdom, and with the fleshly eye and the divine eye.

1028. “Yāva na taṃ pāpakammaṃ byantī hotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.250) vacanato “kammameva [V 0.0237] pamāṇa”nti āha, abbudādiāyuppamāṇaparicchedo pana kammavaseneva katoti adhippāyo.

1028. From the statement, 'Until that evil action is exhausted' (MN 3.250), it is said that 'kamma alone is the measure.' The determination of lifespan, beginning with an abbuda and so forth, however, is done based on the power of kamma—this is the intended meaning.

Nilīyanokāsassa abhāvāti samānajātikena accharāgaṇena sabbadā parivāriyamānassa kāmaguṇākiṇṇassa tabbirahitaṭṭhānassa abhāvāti attho.

'Absence of a hiding place' means the absence of a place devoid of that, for one who is always surrounded by a host of similar celestial nymphs and crowded with sense pleasures—this is the meaning.

Kiṃ niyametīti kiṃ jhānaṃ upapattiṃ niyametīti attho. Nava brahmaloketi brahmapārisajjādayo navapi sodhetvā. Matthaketi vehapphalesūti [M 0.0234] attho. Seṭṭhabhavā nāmāti tato paraṃ agamanato uttamabhavāti adhippāyo. Teneva bhavasīsānīti gahitā. Imesu tīsu ṭhānesūti vehapphalādiṭṭhānāni eva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Vehapphalato pana purimesu navasu nibbattaanāgāmī arūpadhātuṃ upapajjatīti katvā “rūpadhātuyā cutassa arūpadhātuṃ upapajjantassa kassaci satta anusayā anusenti, kassaci pañca, kassaci tayo anusentī”ti (yama. 2.anusayayamaka.311) idaṃ vuttaṃ, na vehapphalādīsu upapannaṃ sandhāyāti ayamettha adhippāyo siyā.
