Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “navasu brahmalokesu nibbattaariyasāvakānaṃ tatrūpapattiyeva hoti, na heṭṭhūpapattī”ti, etena heṭṭhūpapatti eva nivāritā, na tesveva uparūpari vehapphale ca upapatti arūpadhātūpapatti ca. “Paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ nibbatto anāgāmī nava brahmaloke sodhetvā matthake ṭhito parinibbātī”ti idampi anupubbena ārohantaṃ sandhāya vuttanti na tena tassa matthakaṃ appattassa arūpadhātuṃ upapatti nivāritāti daṭṭhabbā.

'What determines it?' means 'what jhāna determines rebirth?' 'Nine Brahma worlds' means having purified the nine, beginning with the Brahma-pārisajjā. 'Matthake' means in the Vehapphala; this is the meaning. 'They are called the highest existences' (seṭṭhabhavā nāma) means they are the supreme existences because there is no going beyond them; this is the intention. Therefore, they are taken as the 'heads of existence' (bhavasīsāni). 'In these three places' is said with reference to the realms of Vehapphala and so forth. However, regarding the non-returner born in the nine realms preceding the Vehapphala, who is reborn in the formless realm, it is stated: 'For one who dies in the form realm and is reborn in the formless realm, some have seven latent tendencies, some five, and some three' (Yamaka 2.Anusaya-yamaka.311). This is said without referring to those born in the Vehapphala and other realms; this may be the intention here. But what is said, 'For noble disciples born in the nine Brahma worlds, rebirth occurs only there, not in lower realms'—by this, rebirth in lower realms is prevented, but not rebirth higher and higher within those same realms, nor in Vehapphala, nor in the formless realm. 'An anāgāmī born in the first jhāna realm, having purified the nine Brahma worlds, attains final nibbāna at the highest'—this too is said with reference to one ascending gradually; it should be understood that this does not prevent rebirth in the formless realm for one who has not reached that highest state.

Yo vā aññattha tattha vā maggaṃ bhāvetvā cavitvā tattha upapanno avikkhambhitarūparāgo ariyasāvako, taṃ sandhāya ayaṃ aṭṭhakathā vuttā. Teneva “navasu brahmalokesu nibbattaariyasāvakāna”nti, “paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ nibbatto anāgāmī”ti, “imesu tīsu ṭhānesu nibbattaanāgāmino”ti ca sabbattha nibbattaggahaṇaṃ kataṃ. Tassa pana yena tattha upapanno, tasmiṃ rūparāge vikkhambhite puna bhavābhilāso na bhavissatīti arūparāgupacchedo ca bhavissatiyeva. Yo pana puthujjano tattha nibbatto ariyamaggaṃ bhāvetvā arūpehi vikkhambhitarūparāgo uppanne magge nibbattabhavādīnavadassanavasena anivattitabhavābhilāso, tassa vasena yamakapāḷi pavattāti vā ayamattho adhippeto siyā.

Or, this commentary is spoken with reference to a noble disciple who, having developed the path elsewhere or there, passes away and is reborn there with lust for form unsubdued. Therefore, in the statements, 'noble disciples born in the nine Brahmā realms,' 'an anāgāmī born in the plane of the first jhāna,' and 'anāgāmins born in these three places,' the term 'born' is used throughout. For such a one, however, when that lust for form by which they were reborn there is subdued, there will be no further desire for existence, and the cutting off of lust for the formless will certainly occur. Or, this may be the intended meaning: the Yamaka passage proceeds with reference to an ordinary person who is reborn there and, having developed the noble path, has subdued lust for form by means of the formless attainments; when the path has arisen, by seeing the danger in the existence where they were born, their desire for existence does not return.

Āyuppamāṇavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the measure of life is concluded.

7. Abhiññeyyādivāravaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Section on What Should Be Fully Known, etc.

1030. “Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ [M 0.0235][V 0.0238] rūpaṃ, phusanalakkhaṇo phasso”tiādinā sāmaññavisesalakkhaṇapariggāhikā salakkhaṇapariggāhikā diṭṭhikaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyo ñātapariññā, tato paraṃ yāva anulomā tīraṇapariññā, udayabbayānupassanato paṭṭhāya yāva maggā pahānapariññā.

1030. 'Form has the characteristic of being afflicted; contact has the characteristic of impinging,' and so on—the purification of view and the purification by overcoming doubt, which grasp general, specific, and individual characteristics, are comprehension by knowing. Thereafter, up to conformity knowledge is comprehension by scrutinizing; and from the contemplation of rise and fall up to the path is comprehension by abandoning.

Tattha tatthāti khandhādīnaṃ tāva khandhavibhaṅgādīsu pañhapucchakavāre vattabbaṃ vuttaṃ, hetuādīnañca khandhādīsu antogadhattā tattha tattha pañhapucchakavāre vattabbaṃ vuttamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here and there—regarding the aggregates, what is to be said in the question-and-answer section in the Analysis of Aggregates, etc., has already been stated. And because the causes, etc., are included within the aggregates, what is to be said in the question-and-answer section here and there has already been stated—this should be understood.

Abhiññeyyādivāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on what should be fully known, etc., is concluded.

Dhammahadayavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Analysis of the Heart of the Dhamma is concluded.

Iti sammohavinodaniyā līnatthapadavaṇṇanā

Thus ends the explanation of the hidden meanings of words in the Dispeller of Delusion.

Vibhaṅga-mūlaṭīkā samattā.

The root subcommentary to the Vibhaṅga is complete.

Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Abhidhammapiṭake

In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.

Vibhaṅga-anuṭīkā

The Vibhaṅga Sub-subcommentary.

1. Khandhavibhaṅgo

1. The Analysis of the Aggregates

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Section on Discourses

Catusaccantogadhattā [M 0.0001][V 0.0001] catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ gāthāyaṃ “catusaccadaso”ti nippadesato saccāni gahitānīti nippadesato eva tadatthaṃ vibhāvento “cattāri saccānī”tiādimāha. Tattha samāhaṭānīti samānītāni, cittena ekato gahitānīti adhippāyo. “Samāhaṭānī”ti ca etena samāhāre ayaṃ samāsoti dasseti. Tenevassa katekattassa catusaccanti napuṃsakaniddeso [V 0.0002] “tivaṭṭa”ntiādīsu viya. Pattādipakkhepena hissa na itthiliṅgatā yathā pañcapattaṃ, catuyugaṃ, tibhuvananti, taṃ catusaccaṃ passi adakkhi, pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanābhisamayavasena paṭivijjhīti attho. Kasmā panettha anantāparimāṇesu anaññasādhāraṇesu mahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādīsu buddhaguṇesu saṃvijjamānesu sāvakehi, paccekabuddhehi ca sādhāraṇena catusaccadassanena bhagavantaṃ thometīti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “satipi sāvakāna”ntiādi. Tattha “anaññapubbakattā”ti iminā sāvakehi, “tattha cā”tiādinā paccekabuddhehi ca bhagavato catusaccadassanassa asādhāraṇataṃ, niratisayatañca dasseti. Parasantānesu pasāritabhāvena supākaṭattāti desanānubhāvena veneyyasantānesu catusaccadassanassa vitthāritabhāvena yāva devamanussesu suppakāsitattā. Nāthasaddaṃ loke [M 0.0002] yācanupatāpissariyāsīsāsu paṭhantīti tamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “nāthatīti nātho”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yasmā bhagavā catusaccadassanabhāveneva attano hitasukhāsīsāya kilesabyasanupatāpanassa, hitapaṭipattiyācanassa ca matthakaṃ patto, tasmā taṃ teneva pakāsitanti atthuddhāraṃ anāmasitvā paduddhāravasena nāthasaddassa atthaṃ dassento “veneyyānaṃ hitasukhaṃ āsīsatī”tiādimāha. “Catusaccadaso”ti vā iminā anaññasādhāraṇo bhagavato ñāṇānubhāvo pakāsitoti “nātho”ti iminā anaññasādhāraṇaṃ karuṇānubhāvaṃ vibhāvetuṃ “veneyyāna”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Paramena cittissariyena samannāgato bhagavā nāthoti vuccatīti yojanā. Tathā paramena cittissariyena samannāgato sabbasatte guṇehi īsatīti yojetabbaṃ. Cittissariyenāti ariyiddhiādinā citte vasībhāvena. Guṇehi īsatīti paramukkaṃsagatehi attano sīlādiguṇehi dhammena issariyaṃ vattetīti attho. Evaṃbhūto yasmā sabbābhibhū nāma hoti, tena vuttaṃ “abhibhavatī”ti. Tathā cāha “sadevake, bhikkhave, loke…pe… abhibhū anabhibhūto, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccatī”ti (a. ni. 4.23; dī. ni. 1.188). Duvidhenāpi issariyatthaṃ nāthasaddaṃ dasseti.

Because the four noble truths are included in the verse, and because the truths are grasped without specification in the verse by the term 'catusaccadaso' (seer of the four truths), he thus explains their meaning without specification by saying 'the four truths', etc. Herein, 'brought together' means gathered, the intention being that they are taken together by the mind. The term 'brought together' also indicates that this is a collective compound. For this reason, because it is a single collection, its designation 'catusaccaṃ' is in the neuter gender, just as in terms like 'tivaṭṭaṃ' (three rounds). Its gender is not feminine, as seen in examples like 'pañcapattaṃ' (five bowls), 'catuyugaṃ' (four yokes), and 'tibhuvananti' (three worlds). He saw that fourfold truth—he perceived it, penetrating it by way of full understanding, abandonment, realization, and development; this is the meaning. But why, when there are infinite and immeasurable qualities unique to the Buddha—such as great compassion, omniscience, and so on—does he praise the Blessed One here with the seeing of the four truths, which is common to disciples and paccekabuddhas? Considering this objection, he says, 'even though for disciples,' etc. Herein, by 'because he was the first to do it', he shows the uniqueness and unsurpassability of the Blessed One's seeing of the four truths compared to that of the disciples and paccekabuddhas. 'Because it is very evident through being extended in the mental continuities of others' means: because, through the power of his teaching, the seeing of the four truths was extended into the mental continuities of those to be trained and was thus well-proclaimed among gods and humans. The word 'nātha' (protector) is used in the world in the senses of asking, afflicting, sovereignty, and blessing; to show this meaning, it is said, 'he is a protector (nātha) because he protects (nāthati),' etc. Herein, because the Blessed One, precisely by seeing the four truths, has reached the pinnacle with respect to wishing for his own welfare and happiness, afflicting the calamity of defilements, and the request for the beneficial practice, it is therefore declared by that very means. Without referring to the extraction of the meaning, but by way of analyzing the term, he shows the meaning of the word 'nātha', saying: 'he wishes for the welfare and happiness of those capable of being taught,' etc. Alternatively, by 'Seer of the Four Truths' the Blessed One's unique power of knowledge is declared; thus, to explain his unique power of compassion by 'Protector', it is said 'for those capable of being taught,' etc. The Blessed One is called 'Protector' because he is endowed with supreme mastery of mind; this is the connection. Similarly, it should be construed that, being endowed with supreme mastery of mind, he rules over all beings with his virtues. 'By mastery of mind' means by mastery over the mind through noble psychic powers and so on. 'He rules with his virtues' means he exercises sovereignty through the Dhamma with his own virtues, such as morality, which have reached the highest excellence. Because one who is such is called 'the all-conqueror', it is said, 'he conquers'. And so he said: 'In this world with its devas, Bhikkhus... he is the conqueror, unconquered... therefore he is called the Tathāgata.' He shows the meaning of the word 'nātha' in two ways with respect to sovereignty.

Aṭṭhārasappabhedāya desanāya thomanamevāti yojanā. Samānagaṇanaguṇehīti samānagaṇanehi guṇehi karaṇabhūtehi. Yathāvuttena niratisayena catusaccadassanenāti sabbaññutaññāṇassa, dasabalesu vasībhāvassa ca padaṭṭhānabhūtena. Saccābhisambodhena hi abhinīhārānurūpaṃ rūpārūpadhammesu chattiṃsakoṭisatasahassamukhappavattena sātisayaṃ santatisamūhakiccārammaṇaghanappabhedena mahāvajirañāṇasaṅkhātena buddhāveṇikena sammasanena sambhūtena bhagavā sammāsambodhiyaṃ patiṭṭhitova [V 0.0003] kusalādibhedena, phassādibhedena ca dhamme vibhajanto cittuppādakaṇḍādivasena dhammasaṅgahaṃ catudhā desetuṃ samattho ahosi. Tathā atītaṃse appaṭihatañāṇatādibuddhadhammasamannāgato bhagavā atītādibhedato khandhādike vibhajitvā desetuṃ samattho ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ “yathāvuttena…pe… vibhaṅga”nti. “Sabbaññubhāsitattā”ti vatvā puna “asabbaññunā desetuṃ asakkuṇeyyataṃ dassento”ti etena dhammasaṅgaṇīvibhaṅgānaṃ [M 0.0003] anvayato byatirekato ca sammāsambuddhappaveditataññeva vibhāveti. Sammāsambuddhatādiguṇeti buddharatanassa sammāsambuddhatā, dhammasaṅgharatanānaṃ svākkhātatā, suppaṭipannatāti evamādiguṇe pakāseti.

The connection is that this is praise of the teaching with its eighteen distinctions. 'By qualities equal in enumeration' means by qualities, equal in number, that serve as the means. 'By the aforementioned unsurpassed seeing of the four truths' refers to that which is the foundation for the knowledge of omniscience and for mastery over the ten powers. For through the full awakening to the truths, the Blessed One, established in perfect enlightenment, was able to expound the Dhammasaṅgaṇī in four ways—such as by dividing phenomena into wholesome and unwholesome, or into contact and other categories, according to the divisions of the chapter on the arising of consciousness, etc.—by means of a comprehension unique to the Buddhas, known as the great adamantine knowledge, which arose in accordance with his aspiration and proceeded through thirty-six hundred thousand koṭis of methods concerning material and immaterial phenomena, with its exceedingly great distinctions of continuity, group, function, object, and mass. Likewise, endowed with the Buddha-qualities, such as unobstructed knowledge of the past, the Blessed One was capable of explaining the aggregates and other phenomena by classifying them into past, etc. Therefore, it is said: 'By the aforementioned... the Vibhaṅga.' Having stated, 'Because it was spoken by the Omniscient One,' and then showing the inability of a non-omniscient one to teach it, he thereby explains, both positively and negatively, that the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and the Vibhaṅga were indeed proclaimed only by the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'The qualities such as being a Perfectly Enlightened One' elucidates such qualities as the Buddha gem's quality of being a Perfectly Enlightened One, the Dhamma gem's quality of being well-proclaimed, and the Saṅgha gem's quality of being of good practice, and so forth.

Nanu ca “catusaccadaso”tiādinā bhagavatova guṇā vibhāvitāti? Saccaṃ, teneva dhammasaṅghānampi guṇā vibhāvitā honti tappabhavassa anaññathābhāvato, tadapadesena vā dhammo, tadādhāro ca saṅgho vuttova hotīti vuttaṃ “buddhādīnaṃ…pe… vibhāvetī”ti.

But is it not so that by 'the seer of the four truths,' and so on, the qualities of the Blessed One alone are delineated? True. By that very fact, the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are also delineated, because that which originates from him cannot be otherwise. Or, the Dhamma is spoken of by reference to him, and the Saṅgha as having him as its support; thus it is said: 'of the Buddha and so on... it delineates.'

Atītaṃseti atītakoṭṭhāse, pubbanteti attho. Appaṭihatanti nappaṭihataṃ, ñāṇassa paṭighāto nāma aññāṇaṃ, sabbampi vā kilesajātaṃ. Taṃ yasmā bhagavato saha vāsanāya pahīnaṃ, tasmāssa atītaṃse sabbatthakameva ñeyyāvaraṇappahānena ñāṇaṃ appaṭihatanti vuccati. Esa nayo sesesupi. Kiṃ panetāni pāṭiyekkaṃ visuṃ ñāṇāni, udāhu atītādīsu pavattanakañāṇāni eva? Tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇāni nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ bhagavato tīṇi ñāṇānevāti vadanti. Ekaṃyeva hutvā tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇaṃ nāma sabbaññutaññāṇameva. Sabbaṃ kāyakammanti yaṃ kiñci bhagavatā kattabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ. Ñāṇapubbaṅgamanti ñāṇapurecārikaṃ. Ñāṇānuparivattanti ñāṇassa anuparivattanakaṃ, sabbaṃ kāyapayogaṃ pavattento bhagavā ñāṇena paricchinditvā ñāṇasahitameva pavattetīti attho. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Chandassāti kattukamyatāya, mahākaruṇāsamāyogato sattānaṃ ekantahitesitāya hitakiriyāchandassāti attho. Dhammadesanāyāti dhammakathāya. Aparikkhayāparimeyyapaṭibhānatāya hi bhagavato karaṇasampattiyā ca dhammadesanā nirantaraṃ pavattiyamānāpi na kadācipi parikkhayaṃ gacchati, aññadatthu uparūpari vaḍḍhateva. Vīriyassāti parahitapaṭipattiyaṃ ussāhassa. Vimuttiyāti phalavimuttiyā. Ettha ca samādhiādīnaṃ ahāni taṃtaṃpaṭipakkhassa savāsanapahīnattā anaññasādhāraṇatāya veditabbā. Chandādīnaṃ pana mahākaruṇāsamāyogatopi. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

‘In the past’ (atītaṃse) means in the past portion (atītakoṭṭhāse), that is, the prior end. ‘Unobstructed’ (appaṭihataṃ) means not struck against; the obstruction to knowledge is ignorance, or the whole host of defilements. Since these have been abandoned by the Blessed One together with their latent tendencies, his knowledge regarding the past is therefore said to be unobstructed in every way through the removal of the hindrances to what is to be known. The same principle applies to the remaining cases. But are these separate, individual knowledges, or are they merely knowledges operating in the past, etc.? Some say that the unobstructed knowledges of the Blessed One regarding the three times are indeed three separate knowledges. Alternatively, being just one, the unobstructed knowledge regarding the three times is the knowledge of omniscience itself. ‘All bodily action’ (sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ) means whatever bodily action is to be performed by the Blessed One. ‘Preceded by knowledge’ (ñāṇapubbaṅgamaṃ) means having knowledge as its forerunner. ‘Following in accordance with knowledge’ (ñāṇānuparivattaṃ) means revolving after knowledge; the meaning is that the Blessed One, when engaging in any bodily exertion, determines it with knowledge and performs it accompanied by knowledge. The same principle applies to the remaining two terms. By ‘of will’ (chandassa) is meant of the desire to act; the meaning is the will to act for the welfare of beings, arising from great compassion and from the sole desire for their benefit. By ‘of teaching the Dhamma’ (dhammadesanāya) is meant of the discourse on the Dhamma. For due to the Blessed One’s inexhaustible and immeasurable eloquence and his perfect capability, his teaching of the Dhamma, though continuously ongoing, never diminishes; on the contrary, it only increases further. By ‘of energy’ (vīriyassa) is meant of the exertion in the practice for the welfare of others. By ‘of liberation’ (vimuttiyā) is meant of the liberation of fruition. Here, the non-decline of concentration, etc., should be understood as being due to the abandonment of their respective opposing factors along with their latent tendencies, and as being unparalleled. As for will, etc., it is also due to the association with great compassion. The rest is easily understood.

1. Te [M 0.0004][V 0.0004] eva dhammeti te eva kusalādike tikadukehi saṅgahite dhamme. Suttante khandhādivasena vutte khandhādivasena vibhajitunti yojanā. Nanu suttante paṭisambhidāvasena te na vuttāti? Yadipi sarūpato na vuttā, “jarāmaraṇe ñāṇaṃ, jarāmaraṇasamudaye ñāṇa”ntiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.33) pana hetuhetuphalādīsu ñāṇavibhāgassa vuttattā atthato vuttā eva honti, paṭisambhidāmagge (paṭi. ma. 2.30) vā paṭisambhidānaṃ āgatattā suttante paṭisambhidāvasenapi te dhammā vuttā eva. Tatthāti tasmiṃ suttante. Saṅkhepenāti samāsena. Uddesaniddesamatteneva hi suttante khandhādayo desitā, na paṭiniddesādināti saṅkhepena te tattha vuttāti vuttā. Tatthāti vā dhammasaṅgahe. Tatthāpi hi “tasmiṃ kho pana samaye cattāro khandhā hontī”tiādinā (dha. sa. 58) khandhādayo saṅkhepena vuttāti. Vibhajīyanti ettha, etena vā khandhādayoti vibhaṅgo, te eva pakirīyanti paṭṭhapīyanti ettha, etena vāti pakaraṇaṃ, vibhaṅgo ca so pakaraṇañcāti vibhaṅgappakaraṇaṃ. Ādisaddatthajotakenāti “iti vā, iti evarūpā naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā paṭivirato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.13) viya ādisaddassa atthadīpakena. Pakāratthajotakenāti “iti kho, bhikkhave, sappaṭibhayo bālo, appaṭibhayo paṇḍito”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.1) viya pakāratthavibhāvakena. “Ekadesena samudāyaṃ nidassetī”ti etena “rūpakkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho”ti ettha itisaddassa nidassanatthataṃ dasseti. Nidassanatthopi hi iti-saddo diṭṭho yathā “atthīti kho, kaccāna, ayameko anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.15; 3.90). Parisamāpanattho vā “tasmātiha me, bhikkhave, dhammadāyādā bhavatha, no āmisadāyādā. Atthi me tumhesu anukampā ‘kinti me sāvakā dhammadāyādā bhaveyyuṃ, no āmisadāyādā’ti” (ma. ni. 1.29) evamādīsu viya. Parisamāpanañhetaṃ suttantabhājanīyassa ekadesadassanena yadidaṃ “pañcakkhandhā rūpakkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho”ti tāva tadatthassa saṅgahitattā. Tatthāti vibhaṅgappakaraṇe. “Nibbānavajjāna”nti ettha yadi nibbānavajjānaṃ…pe… appakatarapadattā khandhānaṃ khandhavibhaṅgo ādimhi vutto, nanu saha nibbānena sabbadhammasaṅgāhakattā, sabbadhammasaṅgāhakehi ca āyatanādīhi khandhehi ca appakatarapadattā saccavibhaṅgo ādimhi vattabboti[M 0.0005]? Na, tatthāpi dukkhasaccavibhaṅge ekadesena khandhānaṃ eva vibhajitabbato. Yathāha “tattha katamaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ? Jātipi dukkhā…pe… saṃkhittena pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhā”ti (vibha. 190; dī. ni. 2.387; ma. ni. 1.120; 3.373). Idha pana anavasesatova khandhā [V 0.0005] vibhajīyantīti nibbānavajjānaṃ…pe… appakatarapadattā khandhānaṃ khandhavibhaṅgo ādimhi vutto.

1. ‘Those very phenomena’ (te eva dhamme) means those very phenomena included under the categories of wholesome and so forth, in the triads and dyads. The meaning is that when the aggregates and so on are mentioned in the discourses, they are to be analyzed in terms of the aggregates and so on. But are they not mentioned in the discourses in terms of the analytical knowledges? Even if not explicitly stated in their own form, they are indeed mentioned in meaning, as seen in phrases like ‘knowledge of aging-and-death, knowledge of the origin of aging-and-death’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.33), where the divisions of knowledge regarding cause, effect, and so on are stated. Alternatively, since the analytical knowledges are included in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.30), these phenomena are indeed mentioned in the discourses in terms of the analytical knowledges. ‘There’ (tattha) means in that discourse. ‘Briefly’ (saṅkhepena) means in summary. For in the discourses, the aggregates and so on are taught merely by way of brief statement and explanation, not by detailed analysis—thus, they are said to be stated there in brief. Or, ‘there’ (tattha) means in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. For there too, the aggregates and so on are stated briefly, as in: ‘At that time, there are four aggregates’ (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 58). ‘Vibhajīyanti’ (they are analyzed) means that here or by this the aggregates and so on are analyzed; this is the Vibhaṅga. ‘Te eva pakirīyanti paṭṭhapīyanti ettha’ (they are scattered and established here or by this) means this is the treatise (pakaraṇa). The Vibhaṅga and that treatise together form the Vibhaṅgappakaraṇa. ‘By the illumination of the meaning of the word ādi’ (ādisaddatthajotakena) means by the clarifier of the meaning of the word ādi, as in phrases like ‘or, refraining from such things as dancing, singing, music, and seeing shows’ (Dīgha Nikāya 1.13). ‘By the illumination of the meaning of the mode’ (pakāratthajotakena) means by the clarifier of the meaning of the mode, as in phrases like ‘thus, monks, the fool is fearful, the wise one is fearless’ (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.1). By ‘it indicates the whole by a part’ (ekadesena samudāyaṃ nidasseti) is shown the demonstrative function of the word ‘iti’ in phrases like ‘the aggregate of form… the aggregate of consciousness.’ For the word ‘iti’ is also seen to have a demonstrative meaning, as in ‘“It exists,” Kaccāna, this is one extreme’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.15; 3.90). Or, it has a concluding meaning, as in ‘Therefore, monks, be heirs in the Dhamma, not heirs in material things. I have compassion for you, thinking, “How may my disciples be heirs in the Dhamma, not heirs in material things?”’ (Majjhima Nikāya 1.29). For this is a conclusion by showing a part of the discourse’s division, namely, ‘the five aggregates: the aggregate of form… the aggregate of consciousness,’ since the meaning is thereby summarized. ‘There’ (tattha) means in the Vibhaṅgappakaraṇa. Regarding ‘excluding Nibbāna’ (nibbānavajjānaṃ): If the analysis of the aggregates is stated first due to the aggregates being fewer in words (appakatarapadattā) among those excluding Nibbāna, then, since the truth analysis encompasses all phenomena including Nibbāna, and since it is fewer in words than the sense bases, etc., and the aggregates, which also encompass all phenomena, should not the analysis of the truths be stated first? No, because even there, in the analysis of the truth of suffering, only part of the aggregates is analyzed, as stated: ‘And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering… in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering’ (Vibhaṅga 190; Dīgha Nikāya 2.387; Majjhima Nikāya 1.120; 3.373). Here, however, the aggregates are analyzed without omission—thus, due to the aggregates being fewer in words compared to those excluding Nibbāna, the analysis of the aggregates is stated first.

Apica rūpasammūḷhā arūpasammūḷhā ubhayasammūḷhāti tividhā bodhaneyyapuggalā, tathā saṃkhittarucino vitthārarucino nātisaṅkhepavitthārarucino, tikkhindriyā mudindriyā majjhimindriyāti ca. Tesu arūpasammūḷhānaṃ upakārāya khandhadesanā, rūpasammūḷhānaṃ āyatanadesanā, ubhayasammūḷhānaṃ dhātudesanā. Tathā saṃkhittarucīnaṃ khandhadesanā, nātisaṅkhepavitthārarucīnaṃ āyatanadesanā, vitthārarucīnaṃ dhātudesanā. Tikkhindriyānaṃ khandhadesanā, majjhimindriyānaṃ āyatanadesanā, mudindriyānaṃ dhātudesanāti iminā payojanena anukkamena ca khandhāyatanadhātuvibhaṅgānaṃ desanākkamova veditabbo. Taṃ panetaṃ khandhādittayaṃ pavattinivattitadubhayahetumukheneva ñāyamānaṃ yathābhūtāvabodhāya hoti, nāññathāti dassanatthaṃ saccavibhaṅgadesanā pavattā. So ca yathābhūtāvabodho visesato indriyasannissayenāti indriyavibhaṅgadesanā. Indriyānañca indaṭṭho taṃtaṃpaccayadhammabhūtānaṃ yathāsakaṃ paccayuppannesu paccayabhāvavisesenevāti paccayapaccayuppannavibhāgasandassanī paccayākāravibhaṅgadesanā. Paccayākārassa khandhādīnañca aviparītasabhāvāvabodho satipaṭṭhānādīsu sammāmanasikārenāti satipaṭṭhānasammappadhānaiddhipādabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgavibhaṅgadesanā. Svāyaṃ satipaṭṭhānādīsu sammāmanasikāro imāya paṭipattiyā hotīti jhānaappamaññāvibhaṅgadesanā, sā sammāpaṭipatti ettake sīle patiṭṭhitassa sambhavatīti sikkhāpadavibhaṅgadesanā, yathāvuttāya ca sammāpaṭipattiyā ime ānisaṃsāti paṭisambhidāñāṇavibhaṅgadesanā, te cime ñāṇavisesā imesu kilesesu pahīyantesu ca sambhavanti, nāññathāti kilesavibhaṅgadesanā, evaṃ [M 0.0006] vitthārato desite khandhādike saṅkhepatopi jānantassa atthasiddhi hoti evāti dassanatthaṃ pariyosāne dhammahadayavibhaṅgadesanā pavattāti evametesaṃ aṭṭhārasannaṃ mahāvibhaṅgānaṃ desanākkamakāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, there are three types of persons capable of being enlightened: those confused by form, those confused by the formless, and those confused by both. Likewise, there are those inclined to brevity, those inclined to detail, and those not excessively inclined to either brevity or detail; and those with keen faculties, dull faculties, and middling faculties. Among these, for the benefit of those confused by the formless, there is the teaching on the aggregates; for those confused by form, the teaching on the sense bases; for those confused by both, the teaching on the elements. Similarly, for those inclined to brevity, the teaching on the aggregates; for those not excessively inclined to brevity or detail, the teaching on the sense bases; for those inclined to detail, the teaching on the elements. For those with keen faculties, the teaching on the aggregates; for those with middling faculties, the teaching on the sense bases; for those with dull faculties, the teaching on the elements. Thus, by this purpose and sequence, the order of teaching the analysis of aggregates, sense bases, and elements should be understood. This triad of aggregates, etc., when understood through the causes of arising, ceasing, and both, leads to true understanding, not otherwise. To show this, the teaching on the analysis of the truths is presented. And that true understanding depends especially on the faculties—thus, the teaching on the analysis of faculties. And the controlling principle of the faculties (indaṭṭho) is precisely their distinct nature as conditions for their respective conditioned phenomena, which are themselves conditioning phenomena—thus, the teaching on the analysis of conditions (paccayākāravibhaṅgadesanā), showing the division of conditions and conditionally arisen phenomena (paccayapaccayuppannavibhāgasandassanī). The correct comprehension of the nature of conditions and the aggregates, etc., without distortion, comes through right attention in the foundations of mindfulness, etc.—thus, the teaching on the analysis of the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of psychic power, factors of enlightenment, and path factors. And this right attention in the foundations of mindfulness, etc., arises through this practice—thus, the teaching on the analysis of jhānas and the immeasurables. That right practice is possible for one established in just this much virtue—thus, the teaching on the analysis of training precepts. And through the rightly explained practice, these benefits arise—thus, the teaching on the analysis of the analytical knowledges. And these special knowledges arise when these defilements are abandoned, and not otherwise—thus, the teaching on the analysis of defilements. Thus, when the aggregates, etc., are explained in detail, even one who knows them in brief achieves the purpose. To show this, the teaching on the analysis of the heart of the Dhamma is presented at the conclusion. Thus, the reason for the sequence of teaching these eighteen great analyses should be understood in this way.

Rūpādīnanti rūpavedanāsaññāsaṅkhāraviññāṇānaṃ. Vedayitādisabhāvattābhāvāti yathākkamaṃ anubhavanasañjānanābhisaṅkharaṇādisabhāvattābhāvā. Na hi rūpaṃ vedayitādisabhāvaṃ, vedanādi vā ruppanādisabhāvaṃ. Yato rūpādīnaṃ vedanāsamavarodhanena “cattāro khandhā”tiādinā saṅkhipitvā khandhā 06 desetabbā siyuṃ. Ruppanādito aññassābhāvāti ruppanānubhavanādisabhāvato aññassa atītādike gahetvā rāsivasena vattabbassa saṃkhittassa sabhāvassa abhāvā. Na hi cetasikādibhāvo vedanādīnaṃ sabhāvo. Heṭṭhā gaṇanesūti pañcato heṭṭhā gaṇanesu. Aniṭṭhānanti apariyosānaṃ. Rūpādīsu hi katipaye, ekampi vā aggahetvā vuccamānā khandhavasena desanā anavasesasaṅkhatadhammasaṅgāhinī na sambhavati. Khandhassāti rāsaṭṭhassa khandhassa. Tenevāha “na hī”tiādi. Savibhāgadhammehīti sappabhedadhammehi.

"Rūpādīnanti" refers to form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. "Vedayitādisabhāvattābhāvāti" means, in order, the absence of the nature of experiencing, perceiving, constructing, etc. For form does not have the nature of experiencing, etc., nor do feeling, etc., have the nature of being afflicted, etc. For if form, etc., were included with feeling, and summarized by a term like 'the four aggregates,' then the aggregates would have to be taught in that reduced way. "Ruppanādito aññassābhāvāti" means the absence of another nature apart from being afflicted, experiencing, etc., when the past, etc., are taken and spoken of as a heap. For the state of being a mental factor, etc., is not the intrinsic nature of feeling, etc. "Heṭṭhā gaṇanesūti" means in counts less than five. "Aniṭṭhānanti" means incompleteness. For if some or even one among form, etc., is not included, the teaching about aggregates would not completely encompass all conditioned phenomena. "Khandhassāti" refers to the aggregate which has the characteristic of a heap. Therefore, it is said, "na hī"ti, etc. "Savibhāgadhammehīti" means with phenomena that have distinctions.

“Saddatthasahitaṃ khandhasaddassa visayaṃ dassetī”ti etena rāsisaddassa viya rāsaṭṭhe khandhasaddassa vācakabhāvena pavattiṃ dasseti pariyāyantarabhāvato. Guṇādīsu pana kevalaṃ tabbisayapayogabhāveneva pavatti, na vācakabhāvenāti āha “guṇe…pe… na saddattha”nti. Khandhasaddoti sīlādisadde sannidhāpito khandhasaddo. Tenevāha “sīlādiguṇavisiṭṭhaṃ rāsaṭṭhaṃ dīpetī”ti. Kecīti dhammasirittheraṃ sandhāya vadati. Etthāti “sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandho”ti (dī. ni. 3.355) ettha. Na kevalañca so eva, aṭṭhakathācariyehipi ettha guṇatthatā icchitā eva. Tathā hi aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ “sīlakkhandho samādhikkhandhotiādīsu guṇaṭṭhenā”ti (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 5) vuttaṃ. Nanu ca kevalopi khandhasaddo “tiṇṇaṃ kho, māṇava, khandhānaṃ vaṇṇavādī, na kho, āvuso visākha, tīhi khandhehi ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo saṅgahito”ti (ma. ni. 1.462) ca ādīsu sīlādivācako diṭṭhoti? Na, tatthāpi adhikārādivacchedakavasenevassa sīlādīsu pavattidassanato. Na khandhasaddo paññattisaddassa atthe vattatīti niruttivohārādisaddā [M 0.0007] viya paññattipariyāyo na hotīti attho. Dārukkhandhoti paññatti hotīti tassa khandhasaddassa paññattivisesappavattitaṃ dasseti. Viññāṇakkhandhoti khandhasaddoti “viññāṇaṃ viññāṇakkhandho”ti (yama. 1.khandhayamaka.32) ettha vutto khandhasaddo. Samudāye niruḷhoti atītādibhedabhinnassa paññāya abhisaṃyūhanena rāsikate viññāṇasamūhe niruḷho. Tāya eva ruḷhiyā pavattatīti tāya samudāye niruḷhatāya tadavayave ekasmimpi viññāṇe pavattatīti. Ettha ca ñāṇasampayutte niruḷho kosallasambhūtaṭṭhena kusalabhāvo viya ñāṇavippayutte viññāṇasamudāye niruḷho tadekadesepi ruḷhiyā pavattatīti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā kiñci nimittaṃ gahetvā satipi aññasmiṃ tannimittayutte kismiñcideva visaye sammutiyā cirakālatāvasena nimittavirahepi pavatti ruḷhi [V 0.0007] nāma, yathā mahiyaṃ setīti mahiṃso, gacchantīti gāvoti, evaṃ khandhasaddassāpi ruḷhibhāvo veditabbo.

"It shows the scope of the word 'khandha' as accompanied by its meaning." By this, it shows the functioning of the word 'khandha' as a designator in the sense of 'heap' (rāsaṭṭha), like the word 'rāsi,' because it is a synonym. But in the case of qualities, etc., it functions merely by being used in reference to those objects, not as a designator. Hence it is said, "in qualities... not the meaning of the word." The word 'khandha' (khandhasaddo) is the word 'khandha' placed alongside words like 'sīla,' etc. Therefore, it is said, "it illuminates a heap distinguished by qualities such as virtue." "Some" refers to the elder Dhammasiri. Here, in passages like "the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration" (Dī. Ni. 3.355), not only he but also the commentary teachers have desired that the meaning here pertains to qualities. For instance, in the Aṭṭhasālinī, it is said, "in 'the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration,' etc., the meaning is that of a quality" (Dha. Sa. Aṭṭha. 5). But is it not seen that even the word 'khandha' alone designates virtue, etc., in passages like, "O young man, one who praises the three aggregates," and "Friend Visākha, the noble eightfold path is not comprised of the three aggregates" (Ma. Ni. 1.462)? No, because even there, its usage in virtue, etc., is seen by way of distinguishing context and so on. The word 'khandha' does not function in the sense of a conventional term—it is not a synonym for a designation like terms of linguistic usage, etc. The phrase "a block of wood" (dārukkhandha) being a conventional term shows that the word 'khandha' functions as a particular kind of designation. The word 'khandha' in 'consciousness aggregate' is the word 'khandha' spoken of in the passage, "consciousness is the consciousness aggregate" (Yam. 1. Khandhayamaka. 32). "Established in a collection" means that it is established in the collection of consciousness, which, being divided into past, etc., is gathered into a mass by the synthesizing function of wisdom. It functions by that very established usage—thus, due to being established in a collection, it functions even in a single instance of consciousness as its component. Here, it should be understood that just as the state of skillfulness, being produced from skill, is established in what is associated with knowledge, so too, being established in the collection of consciousness dissociated from knowledge, it functions by established usage even in a single part of it. Alternatively, 'established usage' (ruḷhi) is when a word, having been based on some characteristic, comes to be used for a specific object by long-standing convention, even when other objects possess that characteristic, and even when that characteristic is absent. For example, 'mahiṃsa' (buffalo) from 'mahiyaṃ seti' (he lies on the ground), or 'gāvo' (cows) from 'gacchanti' (they go). In the same way, the fact that the word 'khandha' is an established usage should be understood.

Rāsito guṇatoti sabbattha bhummatthe vā nissakkavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Niyametvāti vavatthapetvā. Piṇḍaṭṭhoti saṅghātattho. Tasmāti yasmā pañceva khandhā vuttā, koṭṭhāsaṭṭhe ca khandhaṭṭhe nibbānassa vasena chaṭṭhenāpi khandhena bhavitabbaṃ, tasmā khandhaṭṭho nāma rāsaṭṭhoti yuttaṃ. “Yesaṃ vā atītādivasena bhedo atthī”tiādinā atītādivibhāgabhinnesu ruppanādisabhāvadhammesu visuṃ visuṃ koṭṭhāsabhāvena gayhamānesu tabbibhāgarahitassa ekassa nibbānassa rāsaṭṭhatā viya koṭṭhāsaṭṭhatāpi na sambhavatīti dasseti. Etena paññattiyāpi khandhesu aggahaṇe kāraṇaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

In 'Rāsito guṇato', the ablative case should be seen everywhere as being in the sense of the locative, or as a statement of removal. 'Niyametvā' means having determined, or defined. 'Piṇḍaṭṭho' refers to the meaning of a mass. Therefore, since only the five aggregates are mentioned, and if the meaning of 'aggregate' were that of 'division,' there would have to be a sixth aggregate by virtue of Nibbāna. Therefore, it is appropriate that the meaning of 'aggregate' is that of 'heap' (rāsaṭṭha). By the phrase 'Or of which there is a division by way of past, etc.' and so on, it shows that when phenomena with the nature of being afflicted, etc., which are divided by distinctions such as past, etc., are taken separately as distinct portions, for the one Nibbāna—which is devoid of such divisions—the meaning of 'portion' is not possible, just as the meaning of 'heap' is not. By this, it should be understood that the reason for not including concepts (paññatti) among the aggregates is also stated.

Kasmā panettha phassādike viya saṅkhārakkhandhe anavarodhetvā vedanāsaññā visuṃ khandhabhāvena gahitāti? Vivādamūlatādivisesadassanatthaṃ. Gahaṭṭhānañhi vivādakāraṇaṃ kāmajjhosānaṃ. Vuttañcetaṃ “puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāmādhikaraṇaṃ kāmānameva hetu mātāpi puttena vivadati, puttopi mātarā vivadatī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.168, 178). Pabbajitānaṃ diṭṭhābhiniveso. Vuttampi cetaṃ “ye diṭṭhimuggayha vivādayanti, ‘idameva [M 0.0008] sacca’nti (su. ni. 838; mahāni. 67) ca vādayantī”tiādi. Tesu kāmajjhosānaṃ vedanassādena hoti, diṭṭhābhiniveso saññāvipallāsena. Saññāvipallāsena hi cittavipallāso, cittavipallāsena diṭṭhimānataṇhāpapañcānaṃ vipallāsoti. Tathā vedanānugiddho vipallatthasañño ca saṃsarati. Vedanānugiddhassa hi vedanāpaccayā taṇhā siddhā hoti, tato ca taṇhāpaccayā upādānanti āvaṭṭati bhavacakkaṃ. Vipallatthasaññissa ca “saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā”ti (su. ni. 880) vacanato diṭṭhimānataṇhāpapañcānaṃ anupacchedato saṃsārassa anupacchedova. Iti vivādakāraṇānaṃ kāmajjhosānadiṭṭhābhinivesānaṃ kāraṇabhāvo saṃsārahetubhāvoti imassa vivādamūlatādivisesassa dassanatthaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhe anavarodhetvā vedanāsaññā visuṃ khandhabhāvena gahitāti veditabbaṃ.

Why, in this context, are feeling and perception separately taken as aggregates, without being included in the formations aggregate like contact, etc.? It is to show the distinctiveness of the root of disputes, etc. For the cause of dispute for householders is attachment to sensual pleasures. And it is said: 'Furthermore, monks, due to sensual desire, rooted in sensual desire, concerning sensual desire, a mother disputes with her son, a son disputes with his mother' (MN 1.168, 178). For those gone forth, it is adherence to views. And it is said: 'Those who cling to views and dispute, asserting, "This alone is true"' (Sn 838; Nidd I 67), etc. Among these, attachment to sensual pleasures arises from delight in feeling, while adherence to views arises from the distortion of perception. For distortion of perception leads to distortion of mind, and distortion of mind leads to distortion of views, conceit, craving, and proliferation. Thus, one obsessed with feeling and one with distorted perception wanders in saṃsāra. For one obsessed with feeling, craving arises conditioned by feeling, and from that craving, clinging arises—thus the cycle of existence revolves. For one with distorted perception, due to the statement 'Proliferation originates from perception' (Sn 880), as long as views, conceit, craving, and proliferation are not cut off, saṃsāra remains unbroken. Therefore, to show this distinctiveness of the root of disputes, etc.—namely, that attachment to sensual pleasures and adherence to views are the cause of disputes and the cause of saṃsāra—feeling and perception are separately taken as aggregates, without being included in the formations aggregate. This should be understood.

Okāsesūti [V 0.0008] vibhajanakiriyāya pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato atītādayo okāsāti vuttā. Itisaddenāti “upādāyarūpa”nti evaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaitisaddena. Nidassanatthenāti udāharaṇatthena. Sabboti sakalo ekādasasu okāsesu vibhatto vibhajananayo. Idañca vibhajananti “cattāro ca mahābhūtā…pe… upādāyarūpa”nti evaṃ vibhattaṃ idañca vibhajanaṃ. Oḷārikādīsūti oḷārikasukhumahīnapaṇītadūrasantikesu. Cakkhāyatanantiādivibhajanañcāti “cakkhāyatanaṃ…pe… phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ itthindriyaṃ…pe… kabaḷīkāro āhāro rūpā saddā gandhā rasā phoṭṭhabbāti evaṃ pavattaṃ vibhajanañca. Yathāsambhavanti yathārahaṃ. Ekādasasu okāsesu yaṃ yattha vibhajanaṃ yuttaṃ, taṃ tattha yojetabbaṃ. Evaṃ vedanākkhandhādīsupīti yathā rūpakkhandhe yathāsambhavaṃ ekādasasu okāsesu vibhajanaṃ yojetabbanti vuttaṃ, evaṃ vedanākkhandhādīsupi yathāsambhavaṃ ekādasasu okāsesu vibhajanaṃ yojetabbanti attho.

"Okāsesu" refers to the past and other occasions because they are the foundation for the occurrence of analysis. "Itisaddena" means 'by the word thus,' that is, by the word 'iti' stated in the commentary as 'upādāyarūpa.' "Nidassanatthenāti" means 'in the sense of an example.' "Sabbo" refers to the entire method of analysis divided into the eleven occasions. And this analysis—'the four great elements...upādāyarūpa'—is thus analyzed. "In the coarse, etc." refers to the coarse, subtle, inferior, superior, far, and near. "The eye base, etc." refers to the analysis beginning with the eye base: 'the eye base...the tangible base, the femininity faculty...edible food, forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles'—thus is the analysis presented. "Yathāsambhavanti" means 'as suitable.' In the eleven occasions, whatever analysis is fitting in each case should be applied there. Similarly, in the case of the feeling aggregate, etc.—just as it was said that the analysis should be applied appropriately across the eleven occasions in the case of the form aggregate, so too the meaning is that the analysis should be applied appropriately across the eleven occasions in the case of the feeling aggregate and others.

Tattha vedanākkhandho tāva purime okāsapañcake sukhādivedanāttikavasena vibhatto, itarasmiṃ kusalattikavedanāttikasamāpannadukasāsavadukavasena. Saññākkhandho pana purime okāsapañcake chaphassadvāravasena, itarasmiṃ oḷārikaduke paṭighasamphassadukavasena ceva yathāvuttakusalattikādivasena [M 0.0009] ca vibhatto. Sesesu kusalattikādivaseneva. Tathā saṅkhārakkhandho. Paṭighasamphassaduko panettha nattheva. Cetanāya eva cettha niddeso saṅkhārakkhandhadhammānaṃ cetanāppadhānabhāvadassanatthaṃ. Tathā hi sā “saṅkhārakkhandho”ti vuttā. Tatthāti tasmiṃ viññāṇakkhandhassa vibhajane paṭiniddese. Taṃ pana dvayanti manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātudvayaṃ. Yañhi sattaviññāṇadhātudesanāyaṃ “manodhātu, manoviññāṇadhātū”ti dvayaṃ desitaṃ, taṃ chaviññāṇakāyadesanāyaṃ “manoviññāṇa”ntveva vuccatīti.

Therein, the aggregate of feeling is first classified in the initial pentad of occasions by way of the triad of pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings. In the other, it is classified by way of the wholesome triad, the feeling triad, the dyad of attainment, and the dyad of taints. The aggregate of perception, however, is classified in the initial pentad of occasions by way of the six doors of contact. In the other, it is classified by way of the dyad of gross and subtle, the dyad of contact with resistance, and, as previously stated, by way of the wholesome triad and so forth. In the remaining occasions, it is classified only by way of the wholesome triad and so forth. Similarly, the aggregate of volitional formations is classified. However, the dyad of contact with resistance is not present here at all. Here, the exposition is of volition only to show that volition is the predominant factor among the phenomena of the aggregate of volitional formations. For thus it is called 'the aggregate of volitional formations.' 'Therein' means in that analysis and counter-exposition of the aggregate of consciousness. That twofold, however, refers to the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element. For that which was taught in the exposition of the seven consciousness-elements as 'mind-element and mind-consciousness-element,' in the exposition of the six consciousness-bodies is simply called 'mind-consciousness.'

Pāḷinayenāti khandhavibhaṅgapāḷinayena. Aññena pakārenāti dhammasaṅgahe, tadaṭṭhakathāyañca āgatena pakārantarena.

‘By the method of the Pāli text’ (Pāḷinayena) means by the method of the Pāli text of the Khandhavibhaṅga. ‘By another method’ (Aññena pakārena) means by another method as found in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and its commentary.

1. Rūpakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Exposition of the Aggregate of Form

2. “Kiñcī”ti padaṃ “ekacca”nti iminā samānatthanti āha “kiñcīti pakārantarabhedaṃ āmasitvā aniyamanidassana”nti. Ubhayenāti pakārabhedaṃ anāmasitvā āmasitvā [V 0.0009] ca aniyamadassanavasena pavattena “yaṃ kiñcī”ti padadvayena. Adhippetatthanti rūpaṃ. Aticcāti atikkamitvā. Pavattitoti pavattanato. Niyamanatthanti nivattanatthaṃ.

2. The word ‘kiñcī’ is equivalent in meaning to ‘ekacca’ (some), and it is said: ‘“Kiñcī,” having touched upon a variety of types, shows non-restriction.’ ‘By both’ (ubhayena) means by the two words ‘yaṃ kiñcī,’ which function in the way of showing non-restriction, both by not touching upon a variety of types and by touching upon them. ‘The intended meaning’ (adhippetattha) is form. ‘Aticca’ means having transgressed. ‘Pavattito’ means because of arising. ‘Niyamanatthaṃ’ means for the purpose of prevention.

“Kiñcā”ti ettha kiṃ-saddo pucchāyaṃ hetuatthadīpako, karaṇe cetaṃ paccattavacanaṃ, ca-saddo vacanālaṅkāroti āha “kena kāraṇena vadethā”ti. Dutiyavikappe pana vuttanayeneva kāraṇatthe pavattaṃ kiṃ-saddaṃ “vadethā”ti kiriyāpadasambandhanena upayogavasena pariṇāmetvā vadati “taṃ kāraṇaṃ vadethā”ti.

In the phrase ‘kiñcā,’ the word ‘kiṃ’ indicates a question and also reveals the meaning of cause. This is a singular form in the instrumental case. The word ‘ca’ is a particle for embellishment of speech. Thus, it is said: ‘For what reason would you speak?’ In the second alternative, however, following the method already stated, the word ‘kiṃ,’ which functions in the sense of cause, is transformed by its connection with the verb ‘vadethā’ (you would speak) through its functional relationship, and it is said: ‘Speak that reason.’

Purimasantānassa bhedanti purimasantānassa vināsaṃ, vināsāpadesena cettha santāne visadisuppādameva dasseti. Tenevāha “visadisasantānuppattidassanato”ti. Nanu ca arūpadhammānampi virodhipaccayasamavāye visadisuppatti atthīti? Saccaṃ atthi, sā pana na pākaṭatarā, pākaṭatarā ca idhādhippetā. Tenevāha “sītādisannipāte”ti. Tathā cāha bhagavā “sītenapi ruppati, uṇhenapi ruppatī”tiādi (saṃ. ni. 3.79). Idāni bheda-saddo ujukameva vikārāpattiṃ vadatīti dassento “bhedo cā”tiādimāha[M 0.0010]. Visadisarūpuppattiyeva, na uppannassa aññathābhāvoti adhippāyo. Tena kāpiliyaṃ pariṇāmavādaṃ paṭikkhipati. Yadi purimasantānato bhedo visadisuppatti ruppanaṃ, evaṃ sante lakkhaṇassa atippasaṅgo siyāti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “arūpakkhandhāna”ntiādi. Ettha sītādīhīti ādi-saddena yathā uṇhajighacchādayo saṅgayhanti, evaṃ āhārādīnampi saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Yenāti yena sītādīhi samāgamena. Tatthāti tesu rūpadhammesu. Āhārādikassa vā ṭhitippattassāti sambandho. Yathā rūpadhammānaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇe sītādīhi samāgamo hoti, evaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ aññehi samāgamo natthi atilahuparivattito, tasmā arūpadhammā rūpadhammānaṃ viya pākaṭassa vikārassa abhāvato “ruppantī”ti, “ruppanalakkhaṇā”ti ca na vuccantīti sambandho. “Ruppatī”ti padassa kattukammasādhanānaṃ vasena atthaṃ dassetuṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “kuppati ghaṭṭīyati pīḷīyati bhijjatī”ti vuttanti tadatthaṃ vivaranto “kuppatīti etenā”tiādimāha. Kopādikiriyāti kopasaṅghaṭṭanapīḷanakiriyā. Kopa-saddo cettha khobhapariyāyo veditabbo. Kattubhūto kammabhūto ca atthoti kattukammasādhanānaṃ vasena vuccamāno bhūtupādāyarūpasaṅkhāto attho. Kammakattutthena bhijjati-saddenāti yadā kammakattuttho ruppati-saddo, tadā bhijjati-saddopi tadattho eva veditabboti attho. Tattha yadā kammatthe “ruppatī”ti padaṃ, tadā “sītenā”tiādīsu kattuatthe [V 0.0010] karaṇavacanaṃ. Yadā pana “ruppatī”ti padaṃ kattuatthe kammakattuatthe vā, tadā hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Yaṃ pana ruppatī”tiādinā “kuppatī”tiādīnaṃ kattukammatthānampi atthavacanānaṃ vacane kāraṇaṃ dasseti. Yadipi attha-saddo “pīḷanaṭṭho”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.17; 2.8) sabhāvapariyāyopi hoti, “kenaṭṭhenā”ti panettha abhidheyyapariyāyo adhippetoti āha “kenaṭṭhenāti pucchāsabhāgavasena ruppanaṭṭhenā”ti, ruppanasaddābhidheyyabhāvenāti attho. Tenevāha “na kevalaṃ saddatthoyeva ruppana”nti. Tassa atthassāti tassa bhūtupādāyappabhedassa sabhāvadhammassa. Ruppanalakkhaṇañca nāmetaṃ aniccatādi viya kakkhaḷattādito aññanti na gahetabbaṃ. Paññattiviseso hi tanti, kakkhaḷattādīnaṃyeva pana arūpadhammavidhuro sabhāvavisesoti veditabbaṃ.

‘The breaking of the preceding continuity’ (purimasantānassa bheda) means the destruction of the preceding continuity. Here, by the term ‘destruction,’ it shows only the arising of a dissimilar continuity. Therefore, it is said: ‘Because it shows the arising of a dissimilar continuity.’ But is there not also the arising of dissimilarity in the case of immaterial phenomena when conflicting conditions come together? Indeed, there is, but that is not as evident, whereas here what is intended is more evident. Therefore, it is said: ‘In the case of the encounter with cold, and so forth.’ Thus, the Blessed One said: ‘One is afflicted by cold, one is afflicted by heat,’ and so forth (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.79). Now, to show that the word ‘breaking’ (bheda) straightforwardly refers to the occurrence of alteration, it is said: ‘Breaking, etc.’ The meaning is the arising of a dissimilar form, not the alteration of what has already arisen. By this, he rejects the transformation theory of the Kāpilas. If the breaking of the preceding continuity is the arising of a dissimilar form—affliction—then in that case, the characteristic would be overly extended. Considering this objection, he says: ‘For the immaterial aggregates,’ and so forth. Here, by ‘cold, etc.’ (sītādīhi), with the word ‘etc.’ (ādi-saddena), just as heat, hunger, and so forth, are included, so too should food, and so forth, be understood as included. ‘By which’ (yena) means by the encounter with cold, and so forth. ‘There’ (tattha) means in those material phenomena. Or, the connection is with ‘having reached stability in food, and so forth.’ Just as material phenomena encounter cold, and so forth, at the moment of stability, so too the immaterial aggregates do not encounter other factors due to their extremely rapid change. Therefore, immaterial phenomena, unlike material phenomena, do not have evident alteration, and thus are not said to be ‘afflicted’ or to have ‘the characteristic of affliction’—this is the connection. To explain the meaning of the word ‘ruppati’ (is afflicted) in terms of agent and object, the commentary says: ‘It is disturbed, struck, oppressed, broken.’ Expanding on that meaning, it says: ‘By “disturbed,” etc.’ ‘Actions of disturbance, etc.’ (kopādikiriyā) means actions of agitation, impact, and oppression. Here, the word ‘kopa’ should be understood as a synonym for agitation. ‘The meaning is both agent and object’ (kattubhūto kammabhūto ca attho) refers to the meaning, which is the state of primary and derived material phenomena, when spoken of in terms of agent and object. ‘By the word “bhijjati” (is broken) in the sense of action-agent’ means that when the word ‘ruppati’ is in the sense of action-agent, then the word ‘bhijjati’ should also be understood in the same sense. Here, when the word ‘ruppati’ is in the sense of object, then in phrases like ‘by cold,’ and so forth, the instrumental case refers to the agent. But when the word ‘ruppati’ is in the sense of agent or action-agent, then the instrumental case should be understood as referring to the cause. With ‘that which is afflicted,’ and so forth, he shows the cause for the use of words like ‘disturbed,’ and so forth, which express meanings in terms of both agent and object. Although the word ‘meaning’ (attha) can also refer to the nature of things in contexts like ‘the meaning of oppression,’ and so forth (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.17; 2.8), here the intended sense in ‘by what meaning?’ (kenaṭṭhena) is the meaning to be expressed. Therefore, he says: ‘“By what meaning?” means by the meaning of affliction, in the form of a question’—that is, by being what is expressed by the word ‘affliction.’ Therefore, he says: ‘Affliction is not merely the meaning of the word.’ ‘Of that meaning’ (tassa atthassa) means of that natural phenomenon, which is a division of primary and derived phenomena. And this characteristic of affliction should not be taken as something distinct from hardness and so forth, in the way that impermanence and so forth are distinct. For it is a special designation in the tradition. Rather, it should be understood as a particular nature of hardness and so forth themselves, a nature which is absent in immaterial phenomena.

Mucchāpattiyāti [M 0.0011] mucchāya mohassa āpajjanena. Kappasaṇṭhānaṃ udakanti kappasaṇṭhāpakamahāmeghavuṭṭhaṃ udakaṃ. Tathāti tappakāratāya khārabhāve sati udakena kappavuṭṭhānakāle viya pathavī vilīyeyya. Lokantariyasattānaṃ pana pāpakammabalena akhārepi khāre viya sarīrassa vilīyanā veditabbā. Tenevāti saussadanissayanirayassa vuttattā eva. Na hi avīcimhi pañcavidhabandhanādikammakāraṇaṃ karonti.

‘Falling into infatuation’ (mucchāpatti) means falling into delusion through infatuation. ‘The water of the world-cycle formation’ (kappasaṇṭhānaṃ udakaṃ) refers to the water from the great rain cloud that establishes the world-cycle. ‘Similarly’ (tathā) means that due to that condition, if there is a saline property, the earth would dissolve with water, as at the time of the world-cycle’s emergence. However, the dissolution of the bodies of beings in the Lokantarika hell, even in non-saline conditions, should be understood as being due to the power of their evil deeds, as if it were saline. ‘Therefore’ (teneva) means precisely because the Saussada hell has been mentioned. For in Avīci they do not perform actions such as the five kinds of bondage.

3. Pakaraṇappattaṃ rūpaṃ pakkhipitvā mātikā ṭhapitāti ānetvā sambandho. Mahābhūtu…pe… āpajjati tappakārabhāvena atītaṃse gaṇanaṃ gatanti vuttattāti adhippāyo. “Na hī”tiādinā dhammantaranivattanatthatā pakārantaranivattanatthatā ca bhūtupādāyagahaṇassa natthīti dasseti. Taṃdassaneti gaṇanantaradassane. Taṃsabhāvattāti bhūtupādāyasabhāvattā. “Na cā”tiādinā bhūtupādāyasabhāvo atītaṃsagaṇitatāya taṃsabhāvassapi aññathā gaṇitattā, ataṃsabhāvassa ca tathā gaṇitattā akāraṇanti dasseti. “Ajjhatta…pe… labbhatī”ti etena dutiyanaye na kevalaṃ yathāvuttova doso, atha kho abyāpitopi dosoti dasseti. Tadetaṃ pana akāraṇaṃ kāraṇabhāvasseva anadhippetattā. Na hettha bhūtupādāyarūpabhāvo atītaṃse gaṇanassa kāraṇanti adhippetaṃ, yato yathāvuttadosāpatti siyā.

3. ‘The material form that has come up for exposition, having been placed in the matrix’ is connected by bringing it in. ‘The great elements… and so forth… attain’ means that due to their being of such a nature, they are included in the reckoning of the past—this is the meaning because it has been stated thus. By ‘For it is not,’ and so forth, it is shown that the taking up of the primary elements and derived materiality does not have the purpose of excluding other phenomena or the purpose of excluding other types. ‘Showing that’ means showing another enumeration. ‘Due to its own nature’ means due to the nature of primary elements and derived materiality. By ‘Nor is it,’ and so forth, it is shown that the nature of primary elements and derived materiality is not a cause, because its own nature is counted differently by being included in the past, and that which is not of its own nature is also counted thus. With ‘Internal… and so forth… is obtained,’ it is shown that in the second method, there is not only the fault just mentioned, but also the fault of non-pervasiveness. But this is not a cause, because the state of being a cause is not intended at all. Here, the state of being primary elements and derived materiality is not intended as the cause for being counted in the past, for then the fault just mentioned would apply.

“Kintī”ti ettha “ki”nti pubbe yaṃ “rūpa”nti sāmaññato gahitaṃ, tassa sarūpapucchā. Iti-saddo nidassanattho, na kāraṇattho. Tenassa yaṃ rūpaṃ atītaṃ niruddhaṃ…pe… atītaṃsena [V 0.0011] saṅgahitaṃ atītakoṭṭhāse gaṇanaṃ gataṃ, taṃ kinti ce? “Cattāro ca…pe… rūpa”nti bhūtupādāyavibhāgadassanamukhena visesaṃ nidasseti. Yattakā hi idha visesā niddiṭṭhā cakkhāyatanādayo, tesamidaṃ nidassananti. Na cettha purimanayato aviseso. Tattha hi rūpassa bhūtupādāyatāmattasabhāvadassanatā vuttā. Tenāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “atītarūpampi bhūtāni cevā”tiādi. Idha pana bhūtupādāyena nidassanabhūtena rūpassa sabbavisesavibhāvanatā dassitā. Evañca katvā abyāpitadosopi cettha anokāsova, yaṃ rūpaṃ ajjhattaṃ…pe… upādinnaṃ, kinti? Cattāro ca…pe… rūpanti tadaññavisesanidassanassa adhippetattā. Tathā cāha “evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo”ti.

In the phrase ‘kinti,’ ‘kiṃ’ is a question about the specific nature of what was previously taken generally as ‘material form.’ The word ‘iti’ is for illustration, not for causation. Therefore, whatever material form is past, ceased… and so forth… included in the past category, counted in the past section—what kind is it? ‘The four… and so forth… material form’ shows the distinction through the explanation of the primary elements and derived materiality. Whatever distinctions are indicated here, such as the eye-base and so forth, this is an illustration of them. And there is a distinction here from the previous method. There, the nature of material form was stated as merely having the nature of primary elements and derived materiality. Therefore, the commentary says: ‘Past material form is also the primary elements,’ and so forth. Here, however, the primary elements and derived materiality are shown as illustrative, revealing all the various characteristics of material form. Having done so, the fault of non-pervasiveness also has no place here. Whatever material form is internal… and so forth… clung to—what kind is it? ‘The four… and so forth… material form’—this is intended to show other specific characteristics. And thus, it is said: ‘In this way, the meaning should be understood everywhere.’

Pariyāyadesanattāti [M 0.0012] sabhāvato pariyāyanaṃ parivattanaṃ pariyāyo, ujukaṃ appavattīti attho. Pariyāyena, pariyāyabhūtā vā desanā etthāti pariyāyadesanaṃ, suttantaṃ. Suttantañhi veneyyajjhāsayavasena desetabbadhamme lesato labbhamānabhāvakathanaṃ, na ujunippadesabhāvakathananti pariyāyadesanaṃ nāma. Teneva taṃ “yathānulomasāsana”nti vuccati. Abhidhammo pana desetabbadhamme ujunippadesakathananti nippariyāyadesanaṃ nāma, yato “yathādhammasāsana”nti vuccati. Nicchayena desoti vavatthānato kathanaṃ. Tathā bhaddekarattasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 3.272 ādayo) viya atītādibhāvo atītānāgatapaccuppannabhāvo addhāvasena idhāpi khandhavibhaṅge suttantabhājanīyattā niddisitabbo siyāti yojanā.

‘Because it is an indirect teaching’: ‘indirectness’ (pariyāya) is a turning, a changing from the natural way; the meaning is that it does not proceed directly. The teaching here is indirect or of the nature of indirectness—hence, it is called an indirect teaching, that is, the Suttanta. For the Suttanta is called an indirect teaching because it explains the nature of what should be taught by a hint, in dependence on the inclinations of those to be taught, not by stating the nature of the matter directly and in full. For this reason, it is also called ‘teaching that is compliant.’ The Abhidhamma, however, explains what should be taught by stating the nature of the matter directly and in full—hence, it is called a direct teaching, because it is called ‘teaching according to the ultimate realities.’ ‘Teaching with certainty’ means explaining through definitive determination. The connection is as follows: just as in the Bhaddekaratta Sutta and so forth, the state of being past, and so forth—that is, the past, future, and present states, in dependence on time—should be indicated here too in the Khandhavibhaṅga, because it is the Suttanta exposition.

Sannipatitanti samāgataṃ. Santānavasenāti pubbāparavasena. Pubbenāparassa samappamāṇatāya anūnaṃ anadhikaṃ, tato eva ekākāraṃ. Pavattikālavasena vā anūnaṃ anadhikaṃ, samānasabhāvatāya ekākāraṃ. Tena visabhāgautunā anantaritataṃ dasseti. Evaṃ āhārepīti ettha visabhāgāhārena anantarito anekavāraṃ anekadivasampi bhutto sabhāgekāhāraṃ nāma. “Tato pubbe visabhāgautuāhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ atītaṃ, pacchā anāgata”nti hi vuttanti. “Ekāhārasamuṭṭhāna”nti pana vuttattā ekasseva āhārassa yojanā yuttarūpāti apare. Pañcadvāravasenāti ettha pañcadvārāvajjanato paṭṭhāya yāva tadārammaṇaṃ, yāva javanaṃ, yāva vā voṭṭhabbanaṃ, tāva pavattā cittasantati ekavīthi. Ekajavanasamuṭṭhānanti ekajavanavārasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Ettha ca samayaṃ anāmasitvāva santativasena, santatiñca anāmasitvāva samayavasena atītādivibhāgo gahetabbo.

'Gathered together' means assembled. 'By way of continuity' means in sequence from earlier to later. Due to the equal measure of what precedes and follows, it is neither deficient nor excessive, and therefore of a single kind. Alternatively, by way of the duration of occurrence, it is neither deficient nor excessive, and of a single kind due to having the same intrinsic nature. Thereby, it shows that it is not interrupted by a dissimilar season. Similarly with regard to nutriment: here, what is called ‘nutriment of a single kind’ is that which is eaten many times over many days, uninterrupted by dissimilar nutriment. For it is said, 'Before that, what has arisen from dissimilar season and nutriment is past; afterward, it is future.' However, since it is said to be 'arising from a single nutriment,' others say that the application to a single nutriment is more fitting. 'By way of the five sense-doors'—here, from the five-door adverting up to registration, or up to impulsion, or even up to determining, the continuity of consciousness that occurs is one cognitive process. 'Arising from a single impulsion' means arising from a single round of impulsions. Here, without considering the moment, the division into past, etc., should be understood by way of continuity; and without considering continuity, it should be understood by way of the moment.

Tesanti [V 0.0012] hetupaccayānaṃ. Kalāpassāti rūpakalāpassa. Kammānantarādīti kammādi, anantarādīti paccekaṃ ādi-saddo yojetabbo. Tattha paṭhamena ādisaddena upanissayapaccayassa āhārādino ca dutiyena samanantarānantarūpanissayādino saṅgaho veditabbo. Cittuppādassa cettha kammānantarādipaccayavasena, itarassa kammādivaseneva janakabhāve yojanā daṭṭhabbā. Tathā cittuppādassa purejātavasena, itarassa pacchājātavasena, ubhayesampi sahajātavasena upatthambhanaṃ veditabbaṃ[M 0.0013]. Tenevāha “yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabba”nti. Uppādakkhaṇeti hetukiccakkhaṇe. Hetukiccaṃ nāma tassa tassa uppādetabbassa uppattikaraṇaṃ, tañca tasmiṃ khaṇe uppannaphalattā tato paraṃ kattabbābhāvato niṭṭhitañcāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Itaraṃ pana tīsupi khaṇesu paccayakiccaṃ daṭṭhabbanti yojanā.

'Of them' refers to the root-conditions. 'Of the group' refers to the material group. In ‘kammānantarādi,’ the word ‘ādi’ should be applied to each separately: ‘kamma, etc.’ and ‘contiguity, etc.’ Herein, by the first ‘ādi,’ the inclusion of the support condition, nutriment, etc., should be understood. By the second, the inclusion of contiguity, immediate contiguity, decisive support, etc., should be understood. Herein, the application of the generative function should be seen for the arising of consciousness by way of kamma, contiguity, etc., as conditions, and for the other (materiality) by way of kamma, etc., alone. Similarly, for the arising of consciousness, support should be understood as prenascent; for the other, as postnascent; and for both, as co-nascent support. Therefore, it is said: ‘It should be applied as is possible.’ ‘At the moment of arising’ refers to the moment of the function of the root-condition. The function of the root-condition is the production of what is to be produced, and since the effect arises in that moment, and there is nothing further to be done afterward, it is to be seen as complete. However, the function of the other conditions should be seen as occurring in all three moments; this is how the application should be understood.

6. Aniṭṭhanāmanivattanassāti aniṭṭhanāmanivattiyā akāraṇabhāvadassanena iṭṭhanāmalābhāpanassa akāraṇabhāvaṃ dasseti.

6. ‘Of the turning away from undesirable names’: By showing that it is not a cause for the turning away from undesirable names, it shows that it is not a cause for the obtaining of desirable names.

Devamanussasampattibhaveti sampattiyutte sampanne devamanussabhave. Samiddhasobhanatāti abhivuddhasobhanatā. Tato evāti sampattivirahato eva, asampannattā evāti attho. Tesaṃyeva hatthiādīnaṃ sukhassa hetubhāvaṃ na gacchanti sāraṇādivasena dukkhapaccayattā. Tesanti hatthirūpādīnaṃ. “Tassa tassevā”tiādinā yathāvuttamatthaṃ vivarati. Akusalena attanā katena nibbattaṃ dukkhassa paccayo hotīti yojanā. Tasmāti yasmā kammaṃ yasmiṃ santāne nibbattaṃ, tattheva sukhadukkhānaṃ paccayo hoti, na aññattha, tasmā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ panāti ekaccamatadassanaṃ. Tattha “aniṭṭhaṃ nāma natthī”ti yasmā paṭisedhadvayena kusalakammajassa iṭṭhabhāvo niyato, tasmā “kusalakammajameva iṭṭha”nti evaṃ aniyametvā “kusalakammajaṃ iṭṭhamevā”ti evamettha niyamo gahetabboti dassento “akusalakammajampī”tiādimāha. Kinti akusalakammajaṃ sobhanaṃ, yaṃ paresaṃ iṭṭhaṃ nāma siyā? Yadi duggatiyaṃ kesañci tiracchānānaṃ saṇṭhānādisampatti sugatiyaṃ sattānaṃ akusalanissandena virūparūpatā viya kusalanissandena, kathaṃ tassā akusalakammajatā. Atha pana yaṃ kesañci amanāpampi samānaṃ rūpaṃ manāpaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, evampi yathā kesañci tiracchānādīnaṃ kusalakammajaṃ manussādirūpaṃ amanāpato upaṭṭhahantampi kusalavipākasseva ārammaṇabhāvato atthato iṭṭhameva nāma hoti, evaṃ akusalakammajaṃ kesañci manāpaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhahantampi akusalavipākasseva ārammaṇabhāvato [V 0.0013] atthato aniṭṭhameva nāma hoti, evañcetaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Aññathā “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso, yaṃ kāyaduccaritassa iṭṭho kanto manāpo vipāko uppajjeyyā”tiādiaṭṭhānapāḷiyā (ma. ni. 3.131) virodho siyā. Tenevāha “kusalakammajassa panā”tiādi. Sabbesanti attano, paresañca[M 0.0014]. Iṭṭhassa abhāvo vattabboti yathā “kusalakammajaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ nāma natthī”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ kiñcāpi “akusalakammajaṃ iṭṭhaṃ nāma natthī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ na vuttaṃ, tena pana nayadassanena akusalakammajassa abhāvo vutto eva hotīti so saṃvaṇṇanāvasena niddhāretvā vattabboti adhippāyo. Etena kusalakammajameva iṭṭhanti purimapadāvadhāraṇassa gahetabbataṃ dasseti.

'Devamanussasampattibhave' means in the state of human and divine existence endowed with and accomplished in prosperity. 'Samiddhasobhanatā' means flourishing magnificence. 'Tato eva' means precisely due to the absence of prosperity, that is, due to being unaccomplished. Those very things—such as elephants—do not become causes of happiness through means like training, as they are causes of suffering. 'Tesaṃ' refers to forms such as those of elephants. The phrase 'tassa tasseva' and so on elaborates the meaning as stated. The connection is: what is produced by unwholesome actions done by oneself becomes a cause of suffering. 'Tasmā' (therefore): since kamma that arises in a particular continuum becomes the cause of happiness and suffering right there, and not elsewhere, for that reason. 'Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana' introduces a certain view. There, because the desirable nature of what is born of wholesome kamma is made definite by the double negation in a statement like 'there is nothing called undesirable,' therefore, to show that the rule here should be understood not as 'only what is born of wholesome kamma is desirable' but rather as 'what is born of wholesome kamma is indeed desirable,' it says 'akusalakammajampi,' etc. How can something born of unwholesome kamma be splendid, such that it might be considered desirable by others? If, for some animals in a woeful state, there is a perfection of form and so on, just as for beings in a happy state there is a distorted form from the after-effect of unwholesome kamma, how can that perfection of form be born of unwholesome kamma? Or else, it is said with reference to a form that, though displeasing to some, appears as pleasing to others. In this way, just as a human form, etc., born of wholesome kamma, though appearing displeasing to some animals and others, is in essence called desirable because it is an object of a wholesome resultant consciousness; so too, something born of unwholesome kamma, though appearing pleasing to some, is in essence called undesirable because it is an object of an unwholesome resultant consciousness. And this is how it should be accepted. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Pāli passage on impossible things: 'This is impossible, there is no chance, that a desirable, pleasing, agreeable result could arise from bodily misconduct,' etc. (MN 3.131). For that reason, it says 'kusalakammajassa pana,' etc. 'Sabbesaṃ' refers to oneself and to others. Regarding the statement 'The absence of the desirable should be stated': just as it was said, 'There is nothing called an undesirable result of wholesome kamma,' so too, although it is not stated in the commentary that 'there is nothing called a desirable result of unwholesome kamma,' by showing this method, the absence of the desirable for what is born of unwholesome kamma is indeed stated. The intention is that this should be determined and stated by way of explanation. By this, it shows that the emphasis on the first word in the phrase 'only what is born of wholesome kamma is desirable' is to be understood.

Idāni “hatthiādīnampī”tiādinā tamevatthaṃ vivarati. Kusalavipākassāti etthāpi kusalavipākasseva ārammaṇanti attho. Manussānanti ca nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Itaresampi ca akusalakammajaṃ akusalavipākasseva, kusalakammajañca kusalavipākasseva ārammaṇanti dassitovāyaṃ nayoti. Kasmā pana iṭṭhāniṭṭhamissite vatthumhi manāpatāva saṇṭhātīti āha “iṭṭhārammaṇena…pe… sakkā vattu”nti. Suṭṭhu vuttanti “iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ ekantato vipākeneva paricchijjatī”ti vadantehi iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇavavatthānaṃ sammadeva vuttaṃ. Taṃ anugantvāti vipākavasena iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇavavatthānaṃ anugantvā. Sabbatthāti sugatiduggatīsu, sabbesu vā ārammaṇesu.

Now, with 'even elephants, etc.,' he elucidates that very meaning. Regarding 'result of wholesome kamma,' here too, it means that the object is only the result of wholesome kamma. And 'humans' should be regarded merely as an illustration. For others as well, what is born of unwholesome kamma has as its object only the result of unwholesome kamma, and what is born of wholesome kamma has as its object only the result of wholesome kamma—this principle has been shown. But why does only pleasantness persist in an object mixed with pleasant and unpleasant? He says, 'with a pleasant object...it can be said.' 'Well said' means that by those who say, 'pleasant and unpleasant are definitively determined by the result alone,' the determination of pleasant and unpleasant objects is rightly stated. 'Following that' means, following the determination of pleasant and unpleasant objects in accordance with the result. 'In all cases' means in happy and unhappy destinations, or in all objects.

“Aniṭṭhā”ti vacaneneva tesaṃ iṭṭhatā nivattitāti āha “sadisatā ca rūpādibhāvoyevā”ti. Iṭṭhāneva rūpādīni kāmaguṇāti sutte vuttānīti mittapaṭipakkho amitto viya iṭṭhapaṭipakkhā aniṭṭhāti adhippetāti vuttaṃ “aniṭṭhāti…pe… vohāro viyā”ti. Sabbāni vāti ettha “piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa”nti (dī. ni. 2.400; ma. ni. 1.133; vibha. 203) vacanato kathaṃ aniṭṭhānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ kāmaguṇabhāvāpattīti ce? Tesampi vipallāsavasena taṇhāvatthubhāvato piyarūpabhāvassa adhippetattā. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ “cakkhuviññeyyāni rūpāni iṭṭhānī”tiādisuttapadaṃ (ma. ni. 1.166; 2.155; 3.57; saṃ. ni. 5.30) nīyatīti āha “atisayenā”tiādi.

By the very word 'unpleasant,' their pleasantness is negated; thus it is said, 'and similarity is simply the state of being forms, etc.' The pleasant forms, etc., are indeed the objects of sensual pleasure, as stated in the sutta. Just as an enemy is the opposite of a friend, the unpleasant is intended as the opposite of the pleasant. This is stated as, 'unpleasant...and so on...like a conventional expression.' And as for 'all,' here, if it is asked, 'how can forms, etc., which are unpleasant, become objects of sensual pleasure, given the statement "beloved and agreeable forms" (piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ)?' (The answer is:) Because, even for them, their nature as 'beloved' is intended due to their being a basis for craving through distortion (vipallāsa). If so, how is the sutta passage, 'forms cognizable by the eye are pleasant,' etc., to be interpreted? It is explained by saying, 'due to the exceeding,' etc.

Indriyabaddharūpavasena pāḷiyaṃ hīnadukaniddeso pavattoti dassetuṃ “dvīsupi hīnapaṇītapadesū”tiādimāha. Avayavayoge sāmivacanaṃ, na kattarīti adhippāyo. “Tesaṃ tesaṃ sattāna”nti [V 0.0014] indriyabaddharūpe niddiṭṭhe kasmā kammajavasena attho vutto, na catusantativasenāti āha “sattasantāna…pe… vutta”nti. Padhānattā hi kammajavasena atthaṃ vatvā sesesu “evaṃ utusamuṭṭhānādīsupī”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ atideso kato[M 0.0015]. “Tehi tehīti etasmiṃ atthe”ti iminā “tesaṃ tesa”nti kattari sāmivacanaṃ āsaṅkati. Tathā sati visaye vā sāmivacane laddhaguṇaṃ dasseti “na kammajavasenevā”tiādinā, kammajaggahaṇañcettha upalakkhaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

To explain that the exposition of the inferior pair in the Pāli text proceeds based on the form bound by faculties, it begins with the phrase, 'In both the inferior and superior sections,' etc. The expression 'sāmi-vacana' (possessive case) is in the context of parts, not the agent—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase, 'Of those various beings,' why, when the form bound by faculties is indicated, is the meaning conveyed through the mode of kamma-origin and not the fourfold continuity? It is stated, 'The continuity of beings... as explained.' Because of the prominence of kamma-origin, after stating the meaning by way of it, the commentary makes an extension to the others, such as 'similarly in the case of temperature-origin, etc.' By this phrase, 'By these, by these—in this meaning,' it raises the doubt that 'tesaṃ tesaṃ' (of those) is a possessive case in the sense of the agent. If that were so, to demonstrate the quality obtained in the object or in the possessive case, it states, 'Not merely by kamma-origin,' etc. Here, the mention of what is born of kamma should be seen as indicative of the other origins.

Mariyādābhūtanti uttamamariyādābhūtaṃ. Tenevāha “yassa yeva manāpā, tassa teva paramā”ti. Tesanti kāmaguṇānaṃ. Sabhāvatoti lakkhaṇato.

'Mariyādābhūtaṃ' (established as a limit) means established as the supreme limit. Therefore, it is said: 'What is agreeable to whom, that is supreme for them.' 'Tesaṃ' refers to the qualities of sensual pleasure. 'Sabhāvato' means by way of characteristic.

“Ekasmiṃyeva assādanakujjhanato”tiādinā “yasmā teyeva rūpādayo eko assādetī”tiādikaṃ suttantavivaraṇaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhabhāve hetubhāvena vuttanti dasseti. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhaggahaṇaṃ hotīti nibbāne viya aniṭṭhaggahaṇaṃ saññāvipallāsena aññesupi ārammaṇesu iṭṭhāniṭṭhābhiniveso hotīti adhippāyo.

With the phrase beginning 'From delighting and being vexed at the very same thing,' it shows that the explanation of the sutta, which begins 'because one person delights in those very forms, etc.,' states the cause for the state of being pleasant and unpleasant. The grasping of pleasant and unpleasant occurs; the meaning is that just as there is no grasping of the unpleasant in Nibbāna, so too, due to perceptual distortion, adherence to pleasant and unpleasant arises even in other objects.

Vibhāgo nāma asaṅkaro, vitthāro cāti “vibhatta”nti padassa “vavatthitaṃ, pakāsita”nti ca atthamāha. Aññesanti atiaḍḍhadaliddānaṃ. Idaṃ iṭṭhaṃ, aniṭṭhañca hotīti ettha ca-saddena aniṭṭhaṃ, iṭṭhañca hotīti ayampi attho vuttoti veditabbaṃ. Aniṭṭhaṃ iṭṭhanti iṭṭhassa “aniṭṭha”nti, aniṭṭhassa “iṭṭha”nti gahaṇe yathāsaṅkhyaṃ yojanā. Indriyavikārāpattiādināti ettha ādi-saddena pubbābhisaṅkhārādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Puretaraṃ pavattacittābhisaṅkhāravasenāpi hi vināva saññāvipallāsaṃ iṭṭhaṃ “aniṭṭha”nti, aniṭṭhañca “iṭṭha”nti gayhatīti.

'Vibhāgo' means non-confusion, and also expansion; thus, for the word 'vibhatta,' it gives the meanings 'distinct' and 'manifest.' 'Aññesaṃ' refers to the exceedingly rich and the exceedingly poor. Regarding 'This is pleasant, and unpleasant,' it should be understood that by the word 'ca' (and), the meaning 'this is unpleasant, and pleasant' is also stated. Regarding the grasping of the unpleasant as pleasant: the connection should be made respectively, in the taking of the pleasant as 'unpleasant' and the unpleasant as 'pleasant.' 'Through the occurrence of impairment of the faculties, etc.'—here, the word 'etc.' includes prior volitional formations, etc. For even without perceptual distortion, due to the force of prior mental volitional formations, the pleasant is apprehended as 'unpleasant,' and the unpleasant is apprehended as 'pleasant.'

Tena vipākenāti tena kusalākusalavipākena. Ārammaṇassa iṭṭhāniṭṭhatanti yattha taṃ uppajjati, tassa buddharūpādikassa gūthādikassa ca ārammaṇassa yathākkamaṃ iṭṭhataṃ aniṭṭhatañca nidasseti. Vijjamānepi saññāvipallāse ārammaṇena vipākaniyamadassananti iṭṭhārammaṇe kusalavipākova uppajjati, aniṭṭhārammaṇe akusalavipākovāti evaṃ ārammaṇena vipākaniyamadassanaṃ. Ārammaṇaniyamadassanatthanti yaṃ kusalavipākassa ārammaṇaṃ, taṃ iṭṭhaṃ nāma. Yaṃ akusalavipākassa ārammaṇaṃ, taṃ aniṭṭhaṃ nāmāti dassanatthaṃ. Ārammaṇena niyāmito hi vipāko attano upakārakassa ārammaṇassa niyāmako hotīti.

"By that result" means by that wholesome or unwholesome result. "As for the object being pleasant or unpleasant" shows, respectively, the pleasantness of an object such as the form of the Buddha, and the unpleasantness of an object such as excrement, wherever that result arises. "The demonstration of the determination of the result by the object, even when perceptual distortion exists" means that a wholesome result arises only with a pleasant object, and an unwholesome result arises only with an unpleasant object; thus it is a demonstration of the determination of the result by the object.
