"For the purpose of demonstrating the determination by the object" means for the purpose of showing that what is the object of a wholesome result is called pleasant, and what is the object of an unwholesome result is called unpleasant. For the result, being determined by the object, becomes the determiner of its own supporting object.

Dvārantare [M 0.0016][V 0.0015] dukkhassa paccayabhūtassa ārammaṇassa dvārantare sukhavipākuppādanato, dvārantare sukhassa paccayabhūtassa ārammaṇassa dvārantare dukkhavipākuppādanato vipākena ārammaṇaniyamadassanena vipākavasena iṭṭhāniṭṭhatā dassitāti yojanā.

Since an object that is a cause of suffering at one sense-door gives rise to a pleasant result at another, and an object that is a cause of happiness at one sense-door gives rise to an unpleasant result at another, the pleasantness and unpleasantness are shown by way of the result, through demonstrating the determination of the object by the result. This is the connection.

7. Duppariggahaṭṭhena kāraṇabhūtena lakkhaṇassa indriyādisabhāvassa duppaṭivijjhatā, evaṃ supariggahaṭṭhena lakkhaṇasuppaṭivijjhatā veditabbā. “Dūre”ti avuttassāti lakkhaṇato “dūre”ti akathitassa. Vuttampīti lakkhaṇato “dūre”ti vuttampi sukhumarūpaṃ.

7. Due to the reason of being difficult to grasp, the characteristic of the nature of the faculties and so on is difficult to penetrate; similarly, it should be understood that due to being easy to grasp, the characteristic is easy to penetrate. "'Far' means of that which is unstated"—that is, of that which is not spoken of as "far" with respect to its characteristic. "Even when stated"—that is, even a subtle form that is spoken of as "far" with respect to its characteristic.

“Bhindamāno”ti sambhindamānoti vuttaṃ hotīti āha “missakaṃ karonto”ti. Yasmā pana bhedanaṃ vibhāgakaraṇampi hoti, tasmā dutiyavikappe “bhindamāno”ti padassa “visuṃ karonto”ti atthamāha. Tatiyavikappe pana bhindamānoti vināsentoti attho. Tenāha “santikabhāvaṃ bhinditvā dūrabhāvaṃ, dūrabhāvañca bhinditvā santikabhāvaṃ karonto”ti. Na hi sakkā santikassa tabbhāvaṃ avināsetvā dūrabhāvaṃ kātuṃ, tathā itarassāpi. Santikabhāvakaraṇena na bhindati na vināseti, na ca okāsadūrato lakkhaṇato dūraṃ visuṃ karaṇena bhindati vibhāgaṃ karoti, nāpi okāsadūrena lakkhaṇato dūraṃ vomissakakaraṇena bhindati sambhindatīti yojanā. “Tidhā attho daṭṭhabbo”ti saṅkhepena vuttamatthaṃ “na hī”tiādinā vivarati. Visuṃ karoti, vomissakaṃ karotīti karoti-saddaṃ ānetvā sambandho. “Etthāpī”tiādinā yathā “okāsato dūrameva bhindatī”ti ettha okāsato dūrassa okāsato santikabhāvakaraṇaṃ adhippetanti vināsanaṃ bhedanaṃ, evaṃ “na lakkhaṇato dūraṃ bhindatī”ti etthāpi lakkhaṇato dūrassa lakkhaṇato santikabhāvākaraṇaṃ abhedanaṃ avināsananti imamatthaṃ dasseti. Vomissakakaraṇavibhāgakaraṇatthataṃ sandhāyāha “bhindamānoti ettha ca aññathā bhedanaṃ vutta”nti. Pacchimanaye vināsanatthameva sandhāya “bhedanaṃ idha ca aññathā vutta”nti avoca.

"'Bhindamāno' (breaking)" means "sambhindamāno" (mixing up); thus, he says, "making mixed." However, since "bhedana" (breaking) can also mean making a division, in the second alternative, he gives the meaning of the word "bhindamāno" as "making separate." In the third alternative, however, "bhindamāno" means destroying. Therefore, he says, "making distance by breaking nearness, and making nearness by breaking distance." For it is impossible to create distance without destroying the state of nearness, and likewise for the other. By making nearness, one does not break or destroy; nor does one break or make a division by separating what is distant in characteristic from what is distant in space; nor does one break or mix up by mixing what is distant in characteristic with what is distant in space—this is the connection. He elaborates with "For it is not..." and so on, the meaning briefly stated as "The meaning is to be seen in three ways." The connection is made by supplying the word "karoti" (makes) to get "makes separate" and "makes mixed." With "Here too..." and so on, he shows this meaning: just as here in the phrase "it breaks only what is distant in terms of space," the intended meaning of breaking is destruction, that is, the making spatially near of what is spatially distant; similarly, here in "it does not break what is distant in terms of characteristics," non-breaking means non-destruction, that is, the non-making near in terms of characteristics of what is distant in terms of characteristics. Referring to the meaning of making mixed and making a division, he says, "and here in 'bhindamāno', 'bhedana' is stated otherwise." In the last method, referring only to the meaning of destruction, he said, "and here 'bhedana' is stated otherwise."

Rūpakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Form is concluded.

2. Vedanākkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Feeling

8. Cakkhādayo [M 0.0017][V 0.0016] pasādāti oḷārikattabhāvapariyāpannā cakkhusotaghānajivhāpasādā, manomayattabhāvapariyāpannā cakkhusotappasādā ca. Kāyavohāraṃ arahantīti kāyantogadhattā kāyekadesattā ca kāyoti vattabbataṃ arahanti. Kāyoti hi attabhāvopi vuccati “sakkāyadiṭṭhī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.21; 3.155), karajakāyopi “so imamhā kāyā aññaṃ kāyaṃ abhinimminātī”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 3.14). Tabbatthukāti cakkhādinissitā kāyikāti pariyāyena vuttā, nippariyāyena pana cetasikāva. Yathāha “yaṃ tasmiṃ samaye tajjācakkhuviññāṇadhātusamphassajaṃ cetasikaṃ neva sātaṃ nāsātaṃ cetosamphassajaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedayita”ntiādi (dha. sa. 152). “Na hi cakkhādayo kāyappasādā hontī”ti iminā kāyapasādanissitā vedanā nippariyāyena kāyikāti dasseti. Kāyikacetasikādibhāvenāti ādi-saddena kusalākusalābyākatādibhāvā saṅgayhanti. Tenāti sukhādivedanekadesassa addhāsamayavasena atītādibhāvābhāvena. Keci panettha “heṭṭhā dassitanayattā pākaṭattā addhāvasena, ekamuhuttādipubbaṇhādīsu utuādinā rūpassa viya vedanāya vibhāgo na gayhatīti samayavasena ca atītādibhedo na dassito”ti vadanti. Santānavasena pavattānampi vedanānaṃ cittena samūhato gahetabbataṃ sandhāyāha “vedanāsamudāyo”ti. Tehīti addhāsamayavasena atītādibhāvehi. Etthāti etasmiṃ vibhaṅge. Teti “vedanekadesā”ti vuttā kāyikacetasikādibhāvena bhinnā sukhādivedanāvisesā. Yadi vedanekadesā ettha gahitā, khaṇaparicchinnāva te gahetabbā, na santatiparicchinnāti āha “ekasantatiyaṃ panā”tiādi. Tesūti sukhādibhedesu. Bhedoti viseso. Tassāti sukhādivisesassa. Yathā cettha, evaṃ “taṃsahitataduppādakā”ti etthāpi taṃ-saddena sukhādiviseso paccāmaṭṭhoti veditabbo. Santati paricchedikā bhavituṃ arahatīti sambandho. Santatikhaṇavaseneva paricchedo vutto, na addhāsamayavasenāti adhippāyo.

8. The eye and other faculties are sensitive matter (pasāda). The sensitive matter of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue are included in the state of being gross; and the sensitive matter of the eye and ear are included in the state of being mind-made. They are worthy of the designation 'body' (kāyavohāra) because, being included in the body and being a part of the body, they deserve to be called 'body'. For the word 'body' (kāya) can also refer to the individual existence (attabhāva), as in phrases like 'identity view' (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), or to the physical body (karajakāya), as in expressions like 'he creates another body from this body.' The phrase 'based on that' (tabbatthuka) means that feelings are called 'bodily' (kāyikā) in a figurative sense, as they rely on the eye and other faculties, but in a non-figurative sense, they are purely mental (cetasikā). As it is said: 'Whatever at that time is the mental, neither-pleasant-nor-unpleasant feeling born of contact with the eye-consciousness element, born of mental contact,' and so on. The statement 'for the eye and other faculties are not the sensitive matter of the body' indicates that feelings dependent on the sensitive matter of the body are, in a non-figurative sense, 'bodily' (kāyikā). By the phrase 'by way of being bodily or mental, etc.' (kāyikacetasikādibhāvena), states such as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate are included by the word 'etc.' 'By that' means due to the absence of past, etc., states for a portion of pleasant and other feelings by way of time-period and occasion. Some, however, argue here: 'Because the method explained below is evident, the distinction into past, etc., is not shown by way of time-period; and because the division of feeling is not grasped in terms of moments, mornings, etc., like the division of matter by seasons, etc., it is not shown by way of occasion.' The phrase 'aggregate of feelings' (vedanāsamudāyo) is said with reference to the fact that feelings occurring in a continuum are to be grasped collectively by the mind. The word 'by those' (tehi) refers to the states of being past, etc., by way of time-period and occasion. 'Here' (ettha) means in this analysis. The word 'those' (te) refers to the specific pleasant and other feelings, divided by being bodily or mental, etc., as mentioned in 'a portion of feelings.' If a portion of feelings is taken here, they should be understood as defined by the moment, not by continuity. Hence it is said: 'But in a single continuum...' 'Among them' (tesu) refers to the distinctions of pleasant, etc. 'Distinction' (bheda) means a specific kind. 'Of that' (tassā) means of that specific kind of pleasant feeling, etc. Just as here, so too in the phrase 'associated with that, arising from that' (taṃsahitataduppādakā), the word 'that' (taṃ) should be understood as referring back to the specific kind of pleasant feeling, etc. The connection is that a continuum is fit to be a basis for division. The division is stated only by way of continuity and moment, not by way of time-period and occasion—this is the intention.

“Pubbantāparantamajjhagatā”ti niṭṭhitahetukiccā aniṭṭhitapaccayakiccāti vuttā, taṃ pana atikkantahetupaccayakiccanti evaṃ vuttassa nayassa upalakkhaṇanti [M 0.0018] āha “pubbantāparantamajjhagatāti etena hetupaccayakiccavasena vuttanayaṃ dassetī”ti. Ettha kusalākusalakiriyavedanānaṃ [V 0.0017] rūpassa viya, vipākānaṃ viya ca ayaṃ nāma janakahetūti nippariyāyena na sakkā vattuṃ, pariyāyena pana anantarapaccayabhūto hetūti vattabbo.

"'Gone to the beginning, end, and middle'" refers to that whose function as a cause is completed and whose function as a condition is not completed. But that is an indicator of the method stated as 'having transcended the function of cause and condition'; thus he says: 'By this "gone to the beginning, end, and middle," he shows the method stated in terms of the function of cause and condition.' Here, concerning wholesome, unwholesome, and functional feelings, it is not possible to state non-figuratively, as with form and as with resultants, that 'this is the generative cause.' However, in a figurative sense, it should be stated that the immediately preceding condition is the cause.

11. Santāpanakiccanti pariḍahanakiccaṃ. Jātiādisaṅkaranti jātisabhāvapuggalalokiyalokuttarato saṅkaraṃ sambhedaṃ akatvā. Samānajātiyanti ekajātiyaṃ. Sukhato tajjātiyā adukkhamasukhā paṇītāti yojetabbāti sambandho. Samānabhedeti bhūmantarādisamānavibhāge. Upabrūhitānaṃ dhātūnanti uḷārarūpasamuṭṭhāpanena paṇītānaṃ rūpadhammānaṃ. Vibādhitānanti nippīḷitānaṃ milāpitānaṃ. Ubhayanti sukhādidvayaṃ. Ettha ca khobhanā, āluḷanā ca kāyikasukhassa vasena veditabbā. Abhisandanā jhānasukhassa. Madayanā kāmasukhassa. Tathā chādanā. Āsiñcanā sabbassa. Chādanā āsiñcanā vā sabbassa vasena veditabbā.

11. "The function of burning" means the function of scorching. "Confusion of birth, etc." means not making a confusion or mixing with respect to birth, nature, individuals, worldly, and supramundane. "Of the same kind" means of one kind. The connection is that the phrase 'from pleasure' should be construed with 'of that kind, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant is refined.' "Of the same division" refers to similar divisions such as different planes. "Of the nourished elements" means of the refined material phenomena enhanced by the production of superior form. "Oppressed" means pressed or withered. "Both" refers to the pair of pleasure, etc. And here, agitation and disturbance should be understood in terms of bodily pleasure. "Saturation" pertains to the pleasure of absorption. "Intoxication" pertains to sensual pleasure. Similarly, "covering." "Sprinkling" applies to all. "Covering" or "sprinkling" should be understood in terms of all.

Sabhāvādibhedena cāti sabhāvapuggalalokiyādibhedena ca. Ekantapaṇīte lokuttare hīnapaṇītānaṃ paṭipadānaṃ vasena hīnapaṇītatā. Ekantahīne akusale chandādivasena hīnapaṇītatā, oḷārikasukhumatā ca. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “yā oḷārikā, sā hīnā. Yā sukhumā, sā paṇītā”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 11). Akusalādīsu dosasahagatādiantarabhedavasena upādāyupādāya oḷārikasukhumatā taṃtaṃvāpanavasena vuccati, na kusalākusalādivasenāti āha “taṃtaṃvāpanavasena kathanepi parivattanaṃ natthī”ti. Dosussannatāyāti kilesādhikatāya. Tathāti dosussannatāya. Kathaṃ pana kusalesu dosussannatā? Upanissayavasena, kilesādhikehi santāne pavattamānā kusalā dhammā kilesehi sambādhappattiyā tiṇādīhi sambādhappattāni viya sassāni vipulaphalauḷāraphalā na hontīti. Tathāti mandadosatāya. Kusalānaṃ mandadosatāpi vuttanayānusārena veditabbā. Oḷārikasukhumanikantīti ettha antogadhavisesaṃ nikantiyā oḷārikasukhumatāsāmaññaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā hettha oḷārikasāmaññena oḷārikoḷārikataroḷārikatamā [M 0.0019] nikantiyo gayhanti, tathā sukhumasukhumatarasukhumatamā sukhumatāsāmaññena gayhantīti. Sukhumatamanikantivatthunti cettha yāva bhavaggaṃ vipassanāñāṇañca veditabbaṃ.

"And by distinctions of nature, etc." means and by distinctions of nature, person, worldly, etc. In the exclusively sublime supramundane, inferiority and sublimity are determined by way of the inferior and sublime paths. In the exclusively inferior unwholesome, inferiority and sublimity, and coarseness and subtlety, are determined by way of desire, etc. For it is stated in the commentary: "What is coarse is inferior; what is subtle is sublime." In the unwholesome, etc., by way of internal distinctions such as being accompanied by aversion, coarseness and subtlety are spoken of by way of their respective applications, taking them up one by one, not by way of wholesome, unwholesome, etc. Thus he says: "Even when speaking by way of their respective applications, there is no change." "By predominance of aversion" means by abundance of defilements. "Similarly" means by predominance of aversion. But how is there a predominance of aversion in wholesome states? By way of dependence: wholesome states that proceed in a continuity with abundant defilements, being oppressed by the defilements, like crops oppressed by weeds, do not yield abundant or excellent fruit. "Similarly" means by weak aversion. Weak aversion in wholesome states should also be understood according to the method stated. "Delight in the coarse and subtle": here the generality of the coarseness and subtlety of delight is stated, which includes the specific extremes. Just as here by the generality of 'coarse,' the delights that are coarse, coarser, and coarsest are included, so too by the generality of 'subtle,' the delights that are subtle, subtler, and subtlest are included. And here, as the object of the subtlest delight, should be understood all up to the peak of existence and also insight knowledge.

13. Yadi siyāti yadi asampayogo visaṃsaṭṭho siyā.

13. "If it were" means: if non-association were disjoined.

Santikato [V 0.0018] akusalatoti akusalabhāvena santikato lobhasahagatādiakusalavedayitato. Akusalāti dosasahagatādiakusalavedanā dūreti yathā uddharīyati. Tato dūrato kusalatoti tato akusalato dūrato kāmāvacarādikusalavedayitato kusalā kāmāvacarādikusalavedanā. “Na sakkā”ti vuttaṃ uddharituṃ asakkuṇeyyataṃ “tathā hi satī”tiādinā vivarati. Tasmāti yasmā dūrato santikuddharaṇaṃ vuttanayena santikato santikuddharaṇameva hoti, tathā sati atthaviseso na hoti, upādāyupādāya dūrasantikatā idha vuccati. Tasmā santikato santikuddharaṇañca na sakkā kātuṃ atthavisesābhāvato, anadhippetattā cāti adhippāyo.

"From the near, the unwholesome" means from what is near by nature of being unwholesome, that is, from unwholesome feeling associated with greed, etc. As for "unwholesome," it means that unwholesome feeling associated with aversion, etc., is extracted as "far." "From that far, the wholesome" means from what is far from that unwholesome state, that is, from wholesome feeling pertaining to the sense sphere, etc., wholesome feeling pertaining to the sense sphere, etc., is extracted. The impossibility of extracting, stated as "it is not possible," is explained by "for if that were so," etc. "Therefore" means: since extracting the near from the far would, in the way stated, be just extracting the near from the near, there would be no special meaning. Here, farness and nearness are spoken of by way of taking up one after another. Therefore, the meaning is that it is not possible to extract the near from the near, because there is no special meaning and because it is not intended.

Nanu ca atisayavacanicchāvasena attheva atthavisesoti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “dūradūrataratāya viya santikasantikataratāya ca anadhippetattā”ti. Yāti akusalavedanā. Tatoti kusalavedayitato. Idha vuttassa dūrassāti imasmiṃ vedanākkhandhavibhaṅge “akusalā vedanā kusalābyākatāhi vedanāhi dūre”tiādinā (vibha. 13) vuttassa dūrassa. Dūrato accantavisabhāgattāti yato yaṃ “dūre”ti vuttaṃ, tato accantavisadisattā tassa vasena dūre santikaṃ natthīti na sakkā dūrato santikaṃ uddharituṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – heṭṭhā yā vedanā yāya vedanāya dūreti vuttā, sā eva tassā kenacipi pariyāyena santiketi na uddharitabbāti. Santiketi vuttavedanaṃyeva sandhāya vadati. Bhinneti lobhasahagatādivasena vibhatte. Tatthevāti “santike”ti vuttaatthe eva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “akusalā vedanā akusalāya vedanāya santike”ti evaṃ vuttaakusalāya vedanāyameva lobhasahagatādivasena vibhattāya dūrabhāvopi labbhati. Evaṃ sesesupīti.

Keeping in mind the objection, "But is there not indeed a special meaning, by way of the desire for an exaggerated expression?," he said: "Because extreme farness and extreme nearness are not intended, as in 'far, farther' or 'near, nearer.'" "That which" refers to unwholesome feeling. "From that" means from wholesome feeling. "Of the 'far' spoken of here" refers to the 'far' spoken of in this Analysis of the Feeling Aggregate, beginning: "Unwholesome feeling is far from wholesome and indeterminate feelings," etc. "Far because of being utterly dissimilar" means: since that which is called "far" from something is utterly dissimilar to it, by virtue of that dissimilarity, "near" does not exist in relation to "far"; thus it is not possible to extract the near from the far. This is the meaning here: the feeling that was previously described as "far" from another feeling cannot in any way be extracted as "near" to it. He speaks with reference only to the feeling stated as "near." "Distinguished" means divided by way of being accompanied by greed, etc. "Therein itself" means in the very meaning stated as "near." This is what is meant: in the case of the unwholesome feeling spoken of thus, "unwholesome feeling is near to unwholesome feeling," even when this is divided by way of being accompanied by greed, etc., a state of farness is also found. The same applies to the rest.

Yadi [M 0.0020] santikato dūraṃ labbhati, yadaggena dūraṃ labbhati, tadaggena dūrato santikaṃ uddhariyeyyāti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “upādāyupādāya dūrato ca santikaṃ na sakkā uddharitu”ntiādi. Tassattho – yaṃ santikato dūraṃ labbhati, yadipi taṃ visabhāgaṭṭhena labbhati, tathāpi yaṃ tattha santikaṃ labbhati, taṃ sabhāgaṭṭheneva labbhatīti santikatova santikaṃ uddhaṭaṃ siyāti. Tasmāti yasmā visabhāgaṭṭhena dūratā, sabhāgaṭṭhena ca santikatā icchitā, tasmā. Lobhasahagatāya dosasahagatā visabhāgatāya dūre samānā kathaṃ santike bhaveyyāti adhippāyo. Nanu tāsaṃ akusalasabhāgatā labbhatevāti tattha uttaramāha “visabhāgatā”tiādi. Tattha bhedaṃ aggahetvā na pavattatīti bhedaṃ visesaṃ asadisataṃ gahetvā eva pavattati visabhāgatā. Dūratāyāti [V 0.0019] idhādhippetāya dūratāya sabhāgassa abyāpakattā dūrato santikuddharaṇaṃ na sakkā kātuṃ. Sati hi sabhāgabyāpakatte siyā santikatāti dūrato santikuddharaṇaṃ sakkā kātunti adhippāyo. “Na hī”tiādinā tamevatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ karoti. Sabhāgatāti sāmaññaṃ. Bhedanti visesaṃ. Antogadhaṃ katvāvāti abhibyāpetvāva. Visabhāgabyāpakattā santikatāyāti idhādhippetavisabhāgaṃ byāpetvā pavattanato heṭṭhā vuttasantikatāya santikato dūruddharaṇaṃ sakkā kātuṃ. Tamevatthaṃ “akusalatā hī”tiādinā pākaṭaṃ karoti.

"If distance is obtained from nearness, and by that principle distance is obtained, then by that same principle nearness should be extracted from distance"—having considered this objection, he says, "By taking one after another, nearness cannot be extracted from distance," and so on. The meaning is this: what is obtained as distance from nearness, even if it is obtained in the sense of dissimilarity, still, what is obtained there as nearness is obtained only in the sense of similarity. Therefore, nearness would be extracted from nearness itself. Thus, because distance is intended in the sense of dissimilarity and nearness in the sense of similarity, the intention is: how could those states associated with hatred, being dissimilar to those associated with greed, exist in nearness? But is not their commonality as unwholesome states indeed obtainable? In response to that, he says, "through dissimilarity," and so on. There, dissimilarity occurs only by grasping a distinction, a difference, an unlikeness; it does not occur without grasping a distinction. Regarding distance: because what is similar is not pervasive of the distance intended here, nearness cannot be extracted from distance. If what is similar were pervasive, then nearness could exist, and thus nearness could be extracted from distance—this is the intended meaning. With "For it is not..." and so on, he makes this very point clear. Similarity is generality. Distinction is particularity. "Having encompassed within" means having fully pervaded. Because nearness is pervasive of dissimilarity—since it proceeds by pervading the dissimilarity intended here—the extraction of distance from the nearness mentioned previously can be done. This very meaning is made clear by the statement, "For unwholesomeness..."

Vedanākkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the exposition of the aggregate of feeling is finished.

3. Saññākkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Perception

17. Tassāpīti saññāyapi. Tabbatthukattāti cakkhuvatthukattā. Paṭighaviññeyyoti yathāvuttapaṭighato vijānitabbo paṭighavasena gahetabbo. Uttarapadalopaṃ katvāti purimapade uttarapadalopaṃ katvā.

17. "Of that also" means of perception also. "Because it has that as its base" means because it has the eye as its base. "To be cognized through impact" means it should be known from impact as stated; it should be grasped by way of impact. "Having omitted the latter part of the word" means having omitted the latter part of the word in the former word.

Viññeyyabhāve, na uppattiyanti adhippāyo. Vacananti saddo, nāmanti attho. Vacanādhīnāti gahetabbataṃ pati saddādhīnā, nāmāyattagahaṇāti attho. Yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ nāmarūpaduke (dha. sa. mūlaṭī. 101-108) vuttameva. Adhivacanaṃ paññattipakāsakaṃ [M 0.0021] ñāpakaṃ etesaṃ atthīti adhivacanā yathā arisasoti. Tatojoti adhivacanasaṅkhātato arūpakkhandhato jāto. Arūpakkhandhapariyāpannattā phassepi yathāvutto attho sambhavatīti dassetuṃ “samphassoyeva vā”tiādimāha. Na kevalaṃ manodvārikaphasse eva, atha kho pañcadvārikaphassepi “viññeyyabhāve vacanaṃ adhikicca pavattā adhivacanā”tiādivuttappakāro attho sambhavati. Itīti tasmā. Tena pariyāyenāti manosamphassajapariyāyena. Tatojāpīti pañcadvārikaphassajātāpi. Aññappakārāsambhavatoti paṭighasamphassajapariyāyassa asambhavato. Āveṇikaṃ paṭighasamphassajatā. Pakārantaraṃ adhivacanasamphassajatā.

The intention is that it is in the state of being knowable, not in terms of arising. 'Vacana' means sound; 'nāma' means meaning. 'Dependent on speech' means that what is to be grasped is dependent on sound; the meaning is that grasping is dependent on name. Whatever is to be said here has already been stated in the dyad on name-and-form (Dhs. Mūlaṭī. 101-108). An expression is that which illuminates a concept and makes it known; because they have this, they are called expressions, as in 'arisa'. 'Born from that' means born from the formless aggregate designated as 'expression'. To show that, because it is included in the formless aggregates, the aforesaid meaning is also possible in the case of contact, he says, 'or indeed just contact,' and so on. Not only in the case of mind-door contact, but also in the case of five-door contact, the meaning of the aforesaid type, 'expressions are those that proceed with reference to speech in the state of being knowable,' is possible. 'Iti' means 'therefore'. 'By that method' means by the method of that which is born of mind-contact. 'Also born from that' means also born from five-door contact. 'Because another mode is impossible' means because the method of that which is born of resistance-contact is impossible. The state of being born from resistance-contact is unique. The state of being born from expression-contact is another mode.

Yadi [V 0.0020] evanti yadi pañcadvārikaphassehi uppannasaññā pariyāyato nippariyāyato ca “adhivacanasamphassajā”ti vuccanti, evaṃ cattāropi arūpino khandhā evaṃ vattuṃ yuttā. Evaṃ sante saññāva kasmā “adhivacanasamphassajā”ti vuttāti āha “tiṇṇaṃ khandhāna”ntiādi. Tattha tiṇṇaṃ khandhānanti vedanāsaṅkhāraviññāṇakkhandhānaṃ. Atthavasenāti “vacanaṃ adhikicca pavattā adhivacanā”tiādinā vuttaatthavasena anvatthatāvasena. Attano pattampi nāmanti “adhivacanasamphassajā”ti evaṃ attano anuppattampi nāmaṃ. Dhammābhilāpoti sabhāvanirutti. Pubbe catunnaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ sādhāraṇopi adhivacanasamphassajavohāro ruḷhivasena saññāya eva pavattoti vatvā idāni so tadaññārūpakkhandhasādhāraṇo saññāya nivesitoti dassetuṃ “atha vā”tiādimāha. Rajjitvā olokanādīsūti ettha ādi-saddena kujjhitvā olokanādi viya rajjitvā savanādipi saṅgayhatīti veditabbaṃ, tathāsotāvadhānādinopi rattatādivijānananimittatāsambhavato. Cakkhusamphassajāsaññāya pana pākaṭabhāvaṃ nidassanavasena dassetuṃ “olokanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇavisayasamāgame”tiādimāha.

If it is so, that is, if perceptions that have arisen from five-door contacts are called 'born of expression-contact' both figuratively and literally, then it is proper to speak of the four formless aggregates in the same way. This being the case, why is only perception said to be 'born of expression-contact'? He says, 'of the three aggregates,' and so on. Therein, 'of the three aggregates' refers to the aggregates of feeling, formations, and consciousness. 'By way of meaning' means by way of the meaning stated in 'expressions are those that proceed with reference to speech,' etc., that is, by way of etymological significance. 'A name that has come to it' means: thus, the name 'born of expression-contact' is a name that has not even come to it. 'Verbal expression of phenomena' means natural designation. Having first said that the term 'born of expression-contact', though common to the four formless aggregates, is applied by convention only to perception, he now says 'or else,' and so on, to show that it is assigned to perception as common to the other formless aggregates. In 'looking after being impassioned,' etc., here, by the word 'etc.' it should be understood that just as 'looking after being angry,' etc., so also 'listening after being impassioned,' etc., is included, because there is the possibility of a sign for recognizing passion, etc., even from attentiveness of the ear, etc. To show by way of example the evident nature of perception born of eye-contact, he says, 'looking is in the meeting of eye-consciousness with its object,' and so on.

Olokanassa apākaṭabhāve rattatādivijānanaṃ na hoti, pākaṭabhāve ca hotīti āha “pasādavatthukā evā”ti. “Aññaṃ cintenta”nti yaṃ pubbe tena kathitaṃ, kāyena vā pakāsitaṃ, tato aññaṃ kiñci atthaṃ cintentaṃ. Tenevāha “ñāta”nti.

When the looking is not evident, there is no recognition of passion, etc., but when it is evident, there is. Thus he says, 'based on the sensitive matter alone.' 'Thinking of something else' means thinking of some other meaning than what was previously said by him or indicated by body. For that reason he says, 'known'.

Saññākkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Aggregate of Perception is concluded.

4. Saṅkhārakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Analysis of the Aggregate of Formations

20. “Heṭṭhimakoṭiyāti [M 0.0022] etthā”ti idaṃ paṭhamaṃ “heṭṭhimakoṭiyā”ti vacanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tassa hi bhummavasena attho gahetabbo. Tenāha “tattha hi padhānaṃ dassita”nti. Heṭṭhimakoṭiyāva padhānaṃ dassitanti imamatthaṃ gahetvā “yadi eva”ntiādinā codeti. Itaro “heṭṭhimakoṭiyā padhānameva dassita”nti evamettha niyamo gahetabboti dassento “uparimakoṭigatabhāvenā”tiādinā taṃ pariharati. Padhānasseva dassanaṃ. Padhāne hi dassite appadhānampi [V 0.0021] atthato dassitameva hotīti. Tenāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “taṃsampayuttasaṅkhārā pana tāya gahitāya gahitāva hontī”ti. Yaṃ heṭṭhimakoṭiyaṃ labbhati, taṃ uparimakoṭiyampi labbhati evāti āha “heṭṭhimakoṭi hi sabbabyāpikā”ti. Dutiye karaṇaniddesataṃ dassetuṃ “āgatāti sambandho”ti āha. Āgamanakiriyā hi heṭṭhimakoṭiyā karaṇabhāvena tattha vuttāti. Yathā ca āgamanakiriyāya, evaṃ vacanakiriyāyapi heṭṭhimakoṭiyā karaṇabhāvo sambhavatīti dassetuṃ “purimepi vā”tiādimāha. “Ekūnapaññāsappabhede”ti idaṃ lokiyacittuppāde pāḷiāgatānaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhadhammānaṃ uparimakoṭiṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yevāpanakadhammehi saddhiṃ uparimakoṭiyā gayhamānāya “tepaññāsā”ti vattabbaṃ siyā, lokuttaracittuppādavasena pana “sattapaññāsā”ti.

20. The phrase 'here, at the lower limit' is said with reference to the first statement 'at the lower limit'. For its meaning should be taken in the sense of the locative. Therefore he says, 'for there the principal is shown.' Taking this meaning that 'the principal is shown only at the lower limit', he raises an objection with 'if so,' and so on. The other, showing that the rule 'only the principal is shown at the lower limit' should be understood here in this way, refutes it with 'by being in the upper limit,' and so on. It is a showing of the principal only. For when the principal is shown, the non-principal is also shown by implication. Therefore it is said in the commentary, 'but the formations associated with it are included when it is included.' What is obtained at the lower limit is also obtained at the upper limit. Thus he says, 'for the lower limit is all-pervasive.' To show the instrumental case in the second instance, he says, 'the connection is with "has come".' For the act of arriving is stated there by 'at the lower limit' functioning as an instrument. And to show that just as with the act of arriving, so too with the act of speaking, an instrumental function of 'at the lower limit' is possible, he says 'or even in the former,' and so on. 'In forty-nine kinds'—this is said with reference to the upper limit of the factors of the formations aggregate that have come down in the Pāli regarding mundane mind-arisings. When the upper limit is taken together with the yevāpanaka factors, it should be said 'fifty-three'; but in terms of supramundane mind-arisings, it is 'fifty-seven'.

Saṅkhārakkhandhaniddesavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of the Aggregate of Formations is concluded.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Miscellaneous Matters.

Samuggama-padassa tatvato pariyāyato ca atthaṃ dasseti “sañjātiyaṃ ādiuppattiya”nti. Bhedato pana samāyoge uggamananti. Tattha kena samāyoge, kuto, kathañca uggamananti vicāraṇāyaṃ āha “taṃtaṃpaccayasamāyoge”tiādi. Tatthevāti pañcavokārabhave eva. Tattha hi pañcakkhandhā paripuṇṇā samuggacchanti. Yathādhigatānaṃ adhigatappakārānaṃ, paṭisandhikānanti attho. Opapātikasamuggameneva cettha saṃsedajasamuggamopi gahitoti daṭṭhabbo pañcakkhandhapariyāpannānaṃ tadā uppajjanārahānaṃ [M 0.0023] uppajjanato. Tattha saṃsedajā uppajjitvā vaḍḍhanti, itare na vaḍḍhantīti idametesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ. Sukhumajātiyalomā eva kira keci eḷakā himavante vijjanti, tesaṃ lomaṃ sandhāya “jātimantaeḷakaloma”nti vuttaṃ atisukhumattā tesaṃ lomānaṃ. Keci pana “ajapākatikeḷakādīhi saṅkararahitānaṃ tesaṃ eḷakavisesānaṃ nibbatteḷakassa lomaṃ jātiuṇṇā, tampi taṅkhaṇanibbattassā”ti vadanti. Gabbhaṃ phāletvā gahitassāti apare. Evaṃsaṇṭhānanti jātiuṇṇaṃsuno paggharitvā agge ṭhitatelabindusaṇṭhānaṃ. Vaṇṇappaṭibhāgoti rūpapaṭicchanno saṇṭhānapaṭicchanno ca.

It explains the meaning of the term 'samuggama' both in its real sense and figuratively as 'in generation, in initial arising.' By way of analysis, however, it is 'emergence upon conjunction.' Therein, upon the inquiry 'upon conjunction with what, from where, and how is there emergence?', it is stated, 'upon conjunction with the respective conditions,' and so on. 'Therein' means specifically in the five-constituent existence. For there the five aggregates emerge completely. This means of those who have attained according to their attainment, that is, of those at rebirth-linking. Herein, it should be understood that by the emergence of the spontaneously born, the emergence of the moisture-born is also included, because of the arising of those things included in the five aggregates that are fit to arise at that time. Therein, the moisture-born arise and grow; the others do not grow. This is the difference between them. It is said that there are some goats in the Himalayas with fine, high-quality wool, and with reference to their wool, the term 'wool of a high-breed goat' is used due to the extreme fineness of their wool. Some, however, say that 'jāti-uṇṇā' (birth-wool) refers to the wool of a goat produced from a special breed of goats that is free from interbreeding with common goats, sheep, etc., and that too, of one produced at that very moment. Others say it is of one taken by splitting the womb. 'Of such a shape' means having the shape of a drop of oil that has trickled from a thread of birth-wool and stands at the tip. 'The counterpart of color' means that which is concealed by form and concealed by shape.

Santatimūlānīti [V 0.0022] tasmiṃ bhave rūpasantatiyā mūlabhūtāni. Anekindriyasamāhārabhāvatoti yathārahaṃ cakkhādianekindriyasaṅghātabhāvato. Padhānaṅganti uttamaṅgaṃ siro.

The roots of continuity: because they are the root of the continuity of form in that existence. The state of being a collection of multiple faculties: because it is a composite of various faculties, such as the eye and others, as appropriate. The principal limb: the foremost limb, the head.

Na tassa tassa khandhassa paripuṇṇataṃ, taṃtaṃkhandhekadesasseva vuttattāti adhippāyo. Kāmāvacarānanti kāmāvacarasattānaṃ. Parihīnāyatanassāti parihīnassa cakkhādiāyatanassa vasena. Tattha duggatiyaṃ andhassa cakkhudasakavasena, badhirassa sotadasakavasena, andhabadhirassa ubhayavasena santatisīsahāni veditabbā. Napuṃsakassa pana bhāvahāni vuttā eva. Tathā andhabadhirāghānakassa cakkhusotaghānavasena. Taṃ pana dhammahadayavibhaṅgapāḷiyā virujjhati. Taṃ parato āvi bhavissati. Rūpāvacarānaṃ pana cakkhusotavatthujīvitavasena cattāri santatisīsānīti itaresaṃ vasena santatisīsahāni veditabbā.

Not the completeness of each aggregate, but only a portion of each aggregate is intended. 'Kāmāvacarānaṃ' refers to beings in the sensuous sphere. 'Parihīnāyatanassa' means with regard to the decline of sense bases such as the eye. There, in a woeful state, the loss of the continuity-heading should be understood: for the blind, by way of the eye-decade; for the deaf, by way of the ear-decade; for the blind and deaf, by way of both. For the neuter, however, loss of the sex faculty has already been stated. Likewise, for one who is blind, deaf, and without the sense of smell, it is by way of the eye, ear, and nose. But that contradicts the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga Pāḷi. That will become clear later. For those in the form realm, however, there are four continuity-headings—namely, by way of the eye, ear, physical-base, and life faculty; for others, the loss of the continuity-heading should be understood accordingly.

Tesanti pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ. Vatthubhāvenāti vicāraṇāya adhiṭṭhānabhāvena. Paṭisandhiyaṃ uppannā pavattā pañcakkhandhāti paṭisandhikkhaṇe pavattikkhaṇe ca pañcakkhandhe dasseti. Bhummaniddesoti “pañcasu khandhesū”ti ayaṃ bhummaniddeso. Aññathāti niddhāraṇe anadhippete. “Bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇatthe”ti idaṃ visayādiatthānaṃ idhāsambhavato vuttaṃ. Ubhayanti rūpārūpaṃ. Rūpārūpasantatinti rūpasamuṭṭhāpakaṃ rūpasantatiṃ arūpasantatiñca. “Vatthu uppādakkhaṇe dubbalaṃ hotī”ti idaṃ na paṭisandhikkhaṇaṃ eva, nāpi vatthurūpaṃ eva sandhāya vuttanti dassento āha “sabbarūpānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe dubbalataṃ sandhāya vutta”nti. “Tadā hī”tiādi yathāvuttassa atthassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tattha tanti rūpaṃ. “Kammakkhittattā”ti idaṃ na kammajatāmattaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, atha kho kammajassa [M 0.0024] paṭhamuppattiyaṃ apatiṭṭhitataṃ sandhāyāti dassento “satipī”tiādimāha. Tato paranti tato paṭisandhito paraṃ. Sadisasantāne yathā patiṭṭhitaṃ, na tathā visadisasantāneti āha “samānasantatiya”nti.

Of them: of the five aggregates. As the basis: by way of being the foundation for investigation. The five aggregates arisen at rebirth-linking and occurring in the course of existence: this shows the five aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking and at moments of occurrence. The locative designation: this is the locative designation, 'in the five aggregates.' Otherwise: when specification is not intended. 'In the sense of the characteristic of a state': this is said because meanings such as 'object' are impossible here. Both: material and immaterial. The continuity of material and immaterial: the material continuity and the immaterial continuity that originates material form. 'At the moment of arising, the base is weak': this is not said referring only to the moment of rebirth-linking, nor only to the material base. To show this, it is said: 'It is said with reference to the weakness of all material phenomena at the moment of arising.' 'At that time,' etc.: this is a statement of the reason for the meaning as explained. There, 'that' refers to material form. 'Because it is impelled by kamma': this is not said referring only to what is produced by kamma, but rather to the instability of what is produced by kamma at its first arising. To show this, he says, 'even though there is,' etc. After that: after rebirth-linking. In a similar continuity, as it is established, but not so in a dissimilar continuity—thus it is said: 'in a similar continuity.'

Aṅgabhāvanti kāraṇabhāvaṃ. Tenevāha “sahāyabhāva”nti. Tesaṃ dhammānanti yehi saddhiṃ uppannaṃ, tesaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ cittacetasikadhammānaṃ. Tadāti ṭhitikkhaṇe bhaṅgakkhaṇe ca rūpuppādanameva natthi. Anantarādipaccayalābhena uppādakkhaṇe eva cittassa balavabhāvo, na itaratra. Tenāha “yadā ca rūpuppādanaṃ, tadā uppādakkhaṇe”ti.

As a component: as a causal state. Therefore, it is said: 'as companionship.' Of their phenomena: of those phenomena of consciousness and mental factors with which it arises at rebirth-linking. At that time: at the moment of duration and the moment of dissolution, there is no production of material phenomena at all. By obtaining conditions such as the contiguity condition, the strength of consciousness is only at the moment of arising, not at other times. Therefore, it is said: 'And when there is the production of material phenomena, then it is at the moment of arising.'

Yehākārehīti [V 0.0023] āhārindriyapaccayādiākārehi. Yathāsambhavaṃ paccayā hontīti phassādayo āhārādivasena yathārahaṃ paccayā honti. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭṭhāne “paṭisandhikkhaṇe vipākābyākatā āhārā sampayuttakānaṃ khandhānaṃ, kaṭattā ca rūpānaṃ āhārapaccayena paccayo”tiādi (paṭṭhā. 1.1.429).

In whatever modes: by modes such as nutriment, faculty, condition, etc. They are conditions according to possibility: contact and so forth become conditions appropriately by way of nutriment, etc. For this is said in the Paṭṭhāna: 'At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate nutriments are a condition for the associated aggregates, and for material phenomena produced by kamma, by way of the nutriment condition,' etc. (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.429).

Cuticittena saddhiṃ uppajjamānaṃ, cuticittena vā kāraṇabhūtena uppajjamānaṃ. Tato purimatarehi uppajjamānaṃ viyāti yathā cuticittato āsannehi purimatarehi uppajjamānaṃ rūpaṃ bhavantare na uppajjati, evaṃ cuticittena uppajjamānampi anupacchinnepi vaṭṭamūleti akāraṇaṃ vaṭṭamūlāvūpasamo cuticittassa rūpuppādaneti dasseti.

Arising together with the death-consciousness, or arising with the death-consciousness as its cause. Like that which arises from those immediately prior: just as material form arising from those immediately prior to the death-consciousness does not arise in another existence, so too that which arises with the death-consciousness does not. This shows that even when the root of the round of existence is not cut off, the non-cessation of the root of the round is not a cause for the death-consciousness's production of material form.

Arūpassāti āruppassa.

Of the immaterial: of the formless.

Utunāti paṭisandhicittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannena utunā. Samuṭṭhite rūpeti paṭisandhicittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe rūpe samuṭṭhite paṭisandhianantaraṃ paṭhamabhavaṅgacittaṃ rūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Uppādanirodhakkhaṇāti yathāvuttesu soḷasasu cittesu ādicittassa uppādakkhaṇo, soḷasamacittassa nirodhakkhaṇo cāti vadanti, rūpasseva pana uppādanirodhakkhaṇā veditabbā.

By temperature: by the temperature arising at the static moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness. When material form has arisen: when material form has arisen at the dissolution moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness, the first life-continuum consciousness immediately after rebirth-linking produces material form. The moments of arising and ceasing: they say that among the sixteen consciousnesses as stated, it is the arising-moment of the first consciousness and the ceasing-moment of the sixteenth consciousness. However, the moments of arising and ceasing should be understood as pertaining to material form itself.

Dharamānakkhaṇe evāti tassa utuno vijjamānakkhaṇe eva yadi gahitā, “soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukaṃ rūpa”nti vuttaṃ hoti soḷasaheva cittehi tassa dharamānatāya paricchinnattā. Uppādakkhaṇaṃ aggahetvāti utuno [M 0.0025] dharamānakkhaṇe uppādakkhaṇaṃ aggahetvā nirodhakkhaṇo atha gahito, “sattarasacittakkhaṇāyukaṃ rūpa”nti vuttaṃ hoti uppādakkhaṇasahitena ca ekassa cittakkhaṇassa gahitattā. “Adhikasoḷasacittakkhaṇāyuka”nti vuttaṃ hoti nirodhakkhaṇassa bahikatattā.

Only at the moment of duration: if it is taken only at the moment when that temperature exists, it is said to be 'material form with a lifespan of sixteen consciousness-moments,' because its duration is defined by just sixteen consciousnesses. Not apprehending the moment of arising: if, without apprehending the arising-moment of the temperature during its duration, the cessation-moment is then apprehended, it is said to be 'material form with a lifespan of seventeen consciousness-moments,' because one consciousness-moment is included along with the arising-moment. It is said to be 'material form with a lifespan of more than sixteen consciousness-moments' because the moment of cessation is excluded.

Evaṃ uppādanirodhakkhaṇesu gahitesu aggahitesu ca soḷasasattarasacittakkhaṇāyukatā, tato adhikacittakkhaṇāyukatā ca siyāti dassetvā idāni tattha ṭhitapakkhaṃ dassento “yasmā panā”tiādimāha. Tattha tassa dharamānakkhaṇe uppannesūti tassa utuno dharamānakkhaṇe uppannesu soḷasasu cittesu paṭisandhipi yasmā gahitā, tasmā utuno uppādakkhaṇo dharamānakkhaṇe gahitoti [V 0.0024] nirodhakkhaṇe aggahite “rūpe dharanteyeva soḷasa cittāni uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, taṃ pana sattarasamena cittena saddhiṃ nirujjhatī”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 26 pakiṇṇakakathā) evaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vakkhamānā adhikasoḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatā adhippetā. Gahite vā nirodhakkhaṇe soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatā adhippetāti sambandho. Ettha ca “adhikasoḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatā”ti idaṃ paṭisandhicittassa uppādakkhaṇo gahitoti katvā vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅgavaṇṇanāyaṃ “dve bhavaṅgāni, āvajjanaṃ, dassanaṃ, sampaṭicchanaṃ, santīraṇaṃ, voṭṭhabbanaṃ, pañca javanāni, dve tadārammaṇāni, ekaṃ cuticittanti pañcadasa cittakkhaṇā atītā honti, athāvasesaekacittakkhaṇāyuke”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 227), tathā tadārammaṇapariyosānāni, “ekaṃ cuticittaṃ, tadavasāne tasmiññeva ekacittakkhaṇaṭṭhitike ārammaṇe paṭisandhicittaṃ uppajjatī”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 227) ca vakkhati. Tasmā rūpassa soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatāyapi atthasiddhi hotiyeva. Tenāha “soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatā adhippetā”ti. Tathāpi uppajjitvā bhavaṅgacalanassa paccayo hoti, na uppajjamānamevāti sattarasacittakkhaṇāyukatā veditabbā.

Having thus shown that, with the moments of arising and cessation being either included or excluded, a lifespan of sixteen or seventeen consciousness-moments, or more, is possible, it now presents the established position by stating, 'But because...' Herein, 'when arisen at its moment of persistence' means that because the rebirth-linking consciousness is included among the sixteen consciousnesses that arise during the persistence moment of that temperature, therefore the arising moment of the temperature is included in the persistence moment. And when the cessation moment is not included, 'while material form persists, sixteen consciousnesses arise and cease, yet it ceases together with the seventeenth consciousness'—as will be stated in the commentary (Vibh-a. 26)—thus, the intended meaning here is a lifespan of more than sixteen consciousness-moments. Alternatively, if the moment of cessation is included, the intended meaning is a lifespan of sixteen consciousness-moments; this is the connection. Here, the phrase 'a lifespan of more than sixteen consciousness-moments' is stated considering that the moment of arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness is included. But because in the commentary on the Analysis of Dependent Origination it is said: 'Two life-continuum consciousnesses, adverting, seeing, receiving, investigating, determining, five impulsions, two registering consciousnesses, and one death-consciousness—fifteen consciousness-moments have passed; then, what remains has a lifespan of one consciousness-moment,' (Vibh-a. 227) and it will also state, 'one death-consciousness; at its conclusion, on the same object lasting for a single consciousness-moment, the rebirth-linking consciousness arises,' (Vibh-a. 227) therefore, the meaning is established even with a lifespan of sixteen consciousness-moments for material form. Hence it is said, 'a lifespan of sixteen consciousness-moments is intended.' Nevertheless, because it serves as a condition for the vibration of the life-continuum only after arising, not while arising, it should be understood as a lifespan of seventeen consciousness-moments.

Ojāya sabhāvasukhumatā upādārūpabhāvato. Ettha ca mātarā ajjhohaṭā ojā bāhirabbhañjanaṃ viya gabbhamallinā tasmiṃ santāne ojaṭṭhamakarūpuppattiyā paccayo hoti. Āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpapaveṇiyā ojāya viya sesatisantatiojāya rūpuppādananti udariye ojā rūpaṃ na samuṭṭhāpeti utusamuṭṭhānabhāvato, upādinnakaṭṭhāne eva pana samuṭṭhāpeti, rasaharaṇīhi gantvā kāyānusaṭanti veditabbaṃ.

Due to the subtle nature of nutritive essence, it is of the nature of derived materiality. Here, the nutritive essence absorbed by the mother, like an external ointment for the embryo, is a condition for the arising of the nutriment-octad in that continuum. Just as in the lineage of materiality originated by food, nutritive essence produces subsequent materiality, so the nutritive essence in the stomach does not generate materiality, because it is temperature-originated. However, it generates materiality only in the grasped locations, having gone via the nutrient-carrying vessels and pervading the body—this should be understood.

Cittañcevāti [M 0.0026] ettha ca-saddena paṭiyogīnaṃ kammameva samuccinoti, na cittena sampayuttadhammeti katvā āha “cittassa pubbaṅgamatāya vutta”nti. “Cittuppādaṃ gaṇhāti ‘cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotī’tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1) viya, na kammacetanaṃ viya ekadhammamevā”ti vutte “yathā cittasamuṭṭhānarūpassa hetuādayo cittasampayuttadhammāpi samuṭṭhāpakāva, evaṃ kammasamuṭṭhānarūpassa kammasampayuttāpī”ti codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā tassa parihāraṃ vattuṃ “kammasamuṭṭhānañcā”tiādimāha.

Here, in the phrase 'cittañceva,' the word 'ca' (and) includes only kamma as its correlate, not the mental states associated with the mind. Thus, it is said, 'It is stated because of the mind's precedence.' When it is said, 'It takes the arising of the mind, as in "the mind has arisen" (Dhs. 1), not like kamma-volition, which is a single phenomenon,' the objection is raised: 'Just as the causes and other mental states associated with the mind are also producers of mind-originated materiality, so too are the kamma-concomitant states [producers of kamma-originated materiality].' To state a resolution to this, it is stated: 'And kamma-originated...' and so on.

Rūpassāti rūpakkhaṇassa, rūpassa vā addhuno. Nayadassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ paṭisandhikkhaṇe eva [V 0.0025] rūpārūpadhammānaṃ ekakkhaṇe pātubhāvoti imassa atthassa anadhippetattā. Tenevāha “tato parampi rūpārūpānaṃ sahuppattisabbhāvato”ti. Yathā ca “paṭisandhikkhaṇe evā”ti niyamo na gahetabbo, evaṃ “ekakkhaṇe eva pātubhāvo”tipi niyamo na gahetabboti dassento “na paneta”ntiādimāha. Taṃdīpanatthamevāti asamānakālatādīpanatthameva, na sahuppādadīpanatthaṃ. Addhānaparicchedakathā hi ayanti.

'Rūpassa' refers to the moment of materiality, or the duration of materiality. It should be seen as merely a way of exposition, because the meaning that material and immaterial phenomena appear in a single moment only at the moment of rebirth-linking is not intended. Therefore, it is said, 'Beyond that, also due to the existence of the co-arising of material and immaterial phenomena.' Just as the restriction 'only at the moment of rebirth-linking' should not be taken, so too the restriction 'manifestation occurs only in a single moment' should not be taken, thus he says, 'But this is not so,' etc. The purpose of that is merely to clarify non-simultaneity, not to clarify co-arising. For this is a discourse defining duration.

Yadi evanti yathā phalapattāni, evaṃ rūpārūpadhammā yadi dandhalahuparivattino. Asamānaddhattāti atulyakālattā. Nicchiddesūti nibbivaresu. Tena nirantarappavattiṃ eva vibhāveti. Ayanti addhānaparicchedakathā. Cittajarūpādīnaṃ na tathā nirantarabhāvena pavatti, yathā kammajarūpānanti āha “kammajarūpappavattiṃ sandhāyā”ti. Kammajarūpānaṃ vā itaresaṃ mūlabhāvato padhānanti “kammajarūpappavattiṃ sandhāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Acittuppādakattā abyābajjhatāya nirodhasamāpattiyā nibbānapaṭibhāgatā veditabbā. Pade padaṃ akkamitvāti lakuṇḍakapādatāya attano akkantapadasamīpe padaṃ nikkhipitvā. Yo hi sīghapadavikkamo lakuṇḍakapādo, so idhādhippetoti āha “lahuṃ lahuṃ akkamitvāti attho”ti. Saheva nirujjhantīti rūpaṃ kammajamidhādhippetanti katvā vuttaṃ. Utujaṃ pana cutito uddhampi pavattati eva. Pubbe vuttanti “rūpassa sattarasacittakkhaṇā, arūpassa tato ekabhāgo”ti (vibha. mūlaṭī. 20 pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā) evaṃ vuttaṃ addhānappakāraṃ.

If it is so, just as fruits and leaves, so too are material and immaterial phenomena, if they are slow and quick in changing. 'Asamānaddhattā' means: due to being of unequal time. 'Nicchiddesu' means: in uninterrupted states. Thereby, it reveals only the uninterrupted continuity. This is the explanation of the division of time. The continuity of mind-originated materiality, etc., does not occur with such uninterruptedness as that of kamma-originated materiality; thus it is said, 'referring to the continuity of kamma-originated materiality.' Or, because kamma-originated materiality is primary, being the root of the others, thus it is said, 'referring to the continuity of kamma-originated materiality.' Due to the non-arising of consciousness, and due to its non-affliction, the attainment of cessation should be understood as resembling Nibbāna. 'Placing footstep by footstep' means: like a lame person, placing the foot near the spot where the previous foot was placed. For the lame person who walks swiftly is what is intended here; thus it is said, 'the meaning is stepping lightly, lightly.' 'It ceases together'; here, kamma-originated materiality is intended, hence it is stated. But temperature-originated materiality continues even beyond death. Previously stated: 'for materiality, seventeen mind-moments; for immateriality, one part thereof' (Vibhaṅga Mūlaṭīkā 20, Miscellaneous Explanation); thus was said regarding the manner of duration.

Ekuppādatoti samānuppādato. Samānattho hi ayaṃ eka-saddo. Eko daṭṭhabbākāroti eko ñātapariññāya passitabbākāro. Evañhi [M 0.0027] soḷasākārā siyuṃ, itarathā vīsati, tato adhikā vā ete ākārā bhaveyyuṃ. Tassāti pacchimakammajassa. Heṭṭhā soḷasaketi pariyosānasoḷasakassa anantarātītasoḷasake. Pacchimassāti tattha pacchimacittassa. Nānānirodhabhāvaṃ viya ekuppādabhāvampi pacchimakammajassa ṭhapane kāraṇaṃ anicchanto “yadi panā”ti sāsaṅkaṃ vadati. “Sabbampī”tiādinā tattha atippasaṅgaṃ dasseti. Vajjetabbaṃ nānuppādaṃ ekanirodhaṃ. Gahetabbaṃ ekuppādanānānirodhaṃ. Ubhayampi tadā natthi anuppajjanato. Tenevāha “kammajarūpassa anuppattito”ti. Tato pubbeti pacchimakammajarūpuppajjanato oraṃ. Aññassāti yassa cittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ, tato aññassa cittassa. Ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannassa ekuppādatā, bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannassa nānānirodhatā ca natthīti āha “ṭhitibhaṅgakkhaṇesu [V 0.0026] uppannarūpāni vajjetvā”ti. Tenāti rūpena. “Saṅkhalikassa viya sambandho”ti etena avicchinnasambandho idha “paveṇī”ti adhippetoti dasseti. Aññathāti vicchijjamānampi gahetvā “paveṇī”ti vuccamāne. Na hi rūpadhammānaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ viya anantarapaccayabhāvo atthīti rūpadhammānaṃ bhaṅgakkhaṇe uppannarūpadhamme aggahetvā “aṭṭhacattālīsā”ti vuttaṃ. Tesaṃ pana gahaṇe ekūnapaññāsāva siyāti āha “ekūnapaññāsakammajiyavacanaṃ kattabbaṃ siyā”ti.

'Ekuppādato' means from simultaneous arising. For this word 'eka' has the meaning of 'same.' 'Eko daṭṭhabbākāro' means one aspect to be seen, an aspect to be seen through knowing-comprehension. Thus, there would be sixteen aspects; otherwise, there would be twenty or even more of these aspects. 'Tassa' refers to the last kamma-originated. 'Heṭṭhā soḷasake' means: in the sixteen immediately preceding the final sixteen. 'Pacchimassa' refers to the last citta there. Not wishing to establish a reason for the last kamma-originated materiality to have the state of simultaneous arising, just as it has the state of diverse cessation, he speaks with doubt, saying 'yadi pana.' Through 'sabbampi,' he shows an absurd consequence there. One should reject non-simultaneous arising and single cessation. One should accept simultaneous arising and diverse cessation. Both are absent at that time because of non-arising. Therefore, he said, 'because kamma-originated materiality has not arisen.' 'Tato pubbe' means: before the arising of the last kamma-originated materiality. 'Aññassa' refers to a citta other than that citta at whose arising-moment it arose. The simultaneous arising of what arises at the moment of stability and the diverse cessation of what arises at the moment of dissolution do not exist, thus he says, 'excluding materiality arisen at the moments of stability and dissolution.' 'Tena' refers to that materiality. 'A connection like a chain' indicates that an unbroken connection is intended here as 'continuity.' Otherwise, if even interrupted things are included in what is called 'continuity.' Because there is no immediately preceding conditionality for material phenomena as there is for immaterial phenomena, without including material phenomena that arise at the moment of dissolution, it is said, 'forty-eight.' But if they were included, there would be forty-nine. Hence, it is stated, 'the statement "forty-nine kamma-originated" would have to be made.'

Sudīpanattāti sukhadīpanattā, nayadassanabhāvena vā suṭṭhu dīpanattā. Tenevāha “etena hi nayenā”tiādi. Tattha tanti rūpaṃ. Tenāti rūpena. Ubhayatthāti pacchimakammajarūpappavattiyaṃ, tato pubbe ca. Aññassāti ekassa cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe uppajjitvā tato aññassa cittassa. Tassāti rūpassa. Ettha ca pacchimakammajarūpappavattiyaṃ nirujjhanakanti vuttaṃ tato puretarappavattaṃ rūpaṃ veditabbaṃ. Catusantatikarūpenātiādi yathāvuttasaṅgahagamanadassanaṃ. Etthāti etasmiṃ nānuppādekanirodhatādīpane. Ṭhitikkhaṇeti arūpassa rūpassa ca ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannassa rūpassa ca arūpassa ca dassitattā. Adassitassāti yathā eva ettha, evaṃ tattha vibhajitvā adassitassa. Kasmā panettha pacchimakammajena dīpanāyaṃ samatiṃsakammajarūpaggahaṇaṃ katanti āha “samatiṃsa…pe… yojita”nti. Tato kammato jātā taṃkammajā, tesu. Saṅkharotīti saṅkhāro, jīvitañca taṃ saṅkhāro cāti jīvitasaṅkhāro, āyu. Jīvitena saṅkharīyantīti jīvitasaṅkhārā, usmādayo.

'Sudīpanattā' means: because of being easily explained, or because of being thoroughly explained by way of showing the method. Therefore, it is said, 'etena hi nayena' and so on. There, 'taṃ' refers to materiality. 'Tena' means: by that materiality. 'Ubhayattha' refers to: in the continuity of the last kamma-originated materiality, and before that. 'Aññassa' means: having arisen at the moment of stability of one citta, then [ceasing at the moment of stability] of another citta. 'Tassa' refers to that materiality. And here, what is said to cease in the continuity of the last kamma-originated materiality is to be understood as the materiality that arose earlier. 'Catusantatikarūpena' and so on is a showing of the inclusion according to what has been said. 'Ettha' refers to: in this clarification of non-simultaneous arising and single cessation. 'Ṭhitikkhaṇe' means: because both materiality arisen at the stability-moment of an immaterial phenomenon, and an immaterial phenomenon arisen at the stability-moment of a material phenomenon, have been shown. 'Adassitassa' means: of what is not shown by dividing it, just as here, so too there. But why, in this explanation by means of the last kamma-originated materiality, is the inclusion of thirty kamma-originated materialities made? It is said, 'samatiṃsa…pe… yojita' and so on. 'Tato kammato jātā taṃkammajā, tesu' means: born from that kamma, they are kamma-originated; among them. 'Saṅkharotīti saṅkhāro' means: that which conditions is a formation; and life is also a formation, thus 'jīvitasaṅkhāro' means life-force. 'Jīvitena saṅkharīyantīti jīvitasaṅkhārā' refers to: they are conditioned by life-force, these are life-formations, such as warmth and so on.

Aññassa [M 0.0028] uppādakkhaṇeti yassa cittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppannaṃ rūpaṃ aññassa tato sattarasamassa uppādakkhaṇe, ṭhitikkhaṇe uppannaṃ aññassa ṭhitikkhaṇeti sambandho. “Vuttanti adhippāyo”ti idaṃ pāḷiyā virujjhantampi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatabhāvadassanatthaṃ vuttanti ayamettha adhippāyoti attho. Kasmāti cittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ sandhāya pāḷi pavattā, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana kammajarūpanti sā tāya kena kāraṇena virujjhatīti āha “catu…pe… bhavitabbattā”ti, nipphannassāti adhippāyo. Tenāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “yo cāyaṃ cittasamuṭṭhānassa…pe… kammādisamuṭṭhānassāpi ayameva khaṇaniyamo”ti (vibha. aṭṭha. 26 pakiṇṇakakathā). Etehīti yathānīto yamakapāṭho, “kāyasaṅkhāro cittasamuṭṭhāno”tiādiko aṭṭhakathāpadesoti etehi[V 0.0027]. Natthiyeva ekuppādaekanirodhadīpanatoti adhippāyo. Tena hi vuttaṃ “yena cittena saddhiṃ uppajjati, tato paṭṭhāya sattarasamena saddhiṃ nirujjhatī”tiādi.

‘At the arising moment of another’ means: the materiality that arose at the arising moment of a certain consciousness ceases at the arising moment of another, the seventeenth from that; and what arose at the moment of stability ceases at the moment of stability of another—this is the connection. ‘The meaning is stated’—this is said to show that this is found in the commentary, even if it contradicts the Pāḷi; this is the intended meaning here. Why? The Pāḷi proceeds with reference to mind-originated materiality, but the commentary refers to kamma-originated materiality. So for what reason does the latter contradict the former? It is said, ‘Because of the four… it must be so,’ the meaning is ‘of what has been produced.’ Therefore, the commentary states, ‘And this same rule of moments that applies to mind-originated materiality… also applies to materiality originated by kamma and so on’ (Vibh. Aṭṭha. 26, Miscellaneous Discussion). ‘By these’ refers to the Yamaka passage as it is cited, and to these commentary passages such as ‘bodily formation is mind-originated,’ etc. The meaning is that there is no clarification of single arising and single cessation at all. Hence, it is said, ‘With whichever consciousness it arises, from that point onward, it ceases together with the seventeenth,’ and so on.

Puna “etehī”ti iminā ekuppādanānānirodhanānuppādaekanirodhadīpanavasena pavattā aṭṭhakathāpadesā gahitāti veditabbaṃ, ubhayatthāpi vā etehi ācariyehīti attho. Tatiyo bhāgo, tena adhikā soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatā tatiya…pe… yukatā vuttāti sambandho. Tatiya bhāgoti ca uppādaṭṭhitikkhaṇe upādāya bhaṅgakkhaṇo adhippeto. Yasmiṃ ekādasa cittakkhaṇā atītā, avasesapañcacittakkhaṇāyuke, yasmiṃ pañcadasa cittakkhaṇā atītā, avasesaekacittakkhaṇāyuke tasmiṃyeva ārammaṇeti yojetabbaṃ. Ubhayañcetaṃ yathākkamaṃ manodvāre pañcadvāre ca āpāthagataṃ veditabbaṃ. Na kho panevaṃ sakkā viññātuṃ ekacittakkhaṇātītaṃ ārammaṇaṃ sandhāya paṭiccasamuppādavibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 227) tathā vuttanti dassento “na hi sakkā”tiādimāha. Pañcadasāti atirekapañcadasa cittakkhaṇā atītāti sambandho. “Tasmā”tiādinā yattha khaṇekadesaṃ aggahitanti na sakkā vattuṃ, tameva dasseti. Evaṃ tāva na rūpaṃ sattarasacittakkhaṇāyukaṃ, nāpi tatiyabhāgādhikasoḷasacittakkhaṇāyukaṃ, atha kho soḷasacittakkhaṇāyukamevāti dassitaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, it should be understood that by the phrase 'by these,' the commentary passages that proceed by way of illustrating single arising and various cessations, or non-arising and single cessation, are taken. Alternatively, in both contexts, the meaning is 'by these teachers.' The third part: the connection is that by this, the duration of sixteen consciousness-moments, which is more than the third part, and so on, is stated. And by 'the third part,' the dissolution moment is intended, with reference to the arising and static moments. It should be construed that in that very same object, when eleven consciousness-moments have passed, it has a remaining duration of five consciousness-moments; and when fifteen consciousness-moments have passed, it has a remaining duration of one consciousness-moment. And both of these should be understood as having come into range in due order, at the mind-door and at the five sense-doors respectively. However, it is not possible to understand it thus. To show that it is stated thus in the commentary to the Vibhaṅga on Paṭiccasamuppāda (Vibh. Aṭṭha. 227) with reference to an object that has passed one consciousness-moment, he says, 'For it is not possible,' and so on. 'Fifteen' is connected as: more than fifteen consciousness-moments have passed. By 'Therefore,' and so on, it shows that very case where it is not possible to say that a fraction of a moment is not taken. Thus, it has been demonstrated that material form has neither a duration of seventeen consciousness-moments, nor a duration of sixteen consciousness-moments exceeding the third part, but rather, it has a duration of sixteen consciousness-moments alone.

Kasmā [M 0.0029] panettha rūpameva samānepi aniccasaṅkhatādibhāve cirāyukaṃ jātanti? Dandhaparivattibhāvato. Arūpadhammā hi sārammaṇā cittapubbaṅgamā, te yathābalaṃ attano ārammaṇavibhāvanavasena pavattantīti tadatthanipphattisamanantarameva nirujjhanato lahuparivattino. Tenāha bhagavā, “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmi evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ, yadidaṃ, bhikkhave, citta”nti (a. ni. 1.48). Rūpadhammā pana anārammaṇā, te ārammaṇavasena arūpadhammehi vibhāvetabbā. Sā ca nesaṃ vohārānuguṇā vibhāvetabbatā attano dandhaparivattitāya, tesañca lahuparivattitāya soḷasahi sattarasahi vā cittakkhaṇehi nippajjatīti rūpamevettha cirāyukaṃ jātaṃ. Kiñca – lahuviññāṇavisayasantatimattādhīnavuttitāya tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ, ārammaṇūpaladdhimattabhāvato viññāṇassa ca lahuparivattitā, dandhamahābhūtappaccayatāya pana rūpassa dandhaparivattitā. Nānādhātūsu tathāgatasseva yathābhūtañāṇaṃ, tena ca rūpameva purejātapaccayo vutto, pacchājātapaccayo ca tassevāti na ettha aniccasaṅkhatādibhāvasāmaññena [V 0.0028] rūpārūpaṃ samānāyukaṃ parikappetabbaṃ. Vuttanayena rūpameva cirāyukanti niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṃ.

Why here has material form alone become long-lived, even though it is similar in being impermanent, conditioned, and so on? Because of its slow-changing nature. For immaterial phenomena, being with an object and mind-led, proceed according to their strength by clarifying their objects, and thus, because they cease immediately upon the accomplishment of their purpose, they are rapidly changing. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Monks, I do not perceive even one other thing that changes as swiftly as the mind, namely, the mind' (A. Ni. 1.48). Material phenomena, however, are without an object; they must be made clear by immaterial phenomena by way of an object. And their being made clear, which is in accordance with conventional usage, is accomplished in sixteen or seventeen mind-moments due to their own slow-changing nature and the rapid-changing nature of those immaterial phenomena. Thus, material form alone has become long-lived here. Moreover, the rapid-changing nature of the three aggregates is due to their existence being dependent merely on a continuum of rapid consciousness-objects; and the rapid-changing nature of consciousness is due to its nature of merely apprehending objects; but the slow-changing nature of material form is due to its being conditioned by the slow-changing great elements. Only the Tathāgata has knowledge of things as they truly are in the various elements. And by that knowledge, material form alone is stated as the pre-nascent condition, and the post-nascent condition is also of that material form. Therefore, here, material and immaterial phenomena should not be conceived of as having equal lifespans based on their common characteristic of being impermanent, conditioned, and so on. By the stated method, it should be concluded that material form alone is long-lived.

Yathā ca rūpassa sattarasacittakkhaṇāyukatā, tatiyabhāgādhikasoḷasacittakkhaṇāyukatā vā na hoti, taṃ dassetvā yvāyaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇe rūpuppādo vutto, tattha ṭhitikkhaṇameva tāva cittassa ananujānanto “yo cettha…pe… vicāretabbo”ti vatvā yamake uppannauppajjamānavārādipāḷiṃ āharanto “cittayamake”tiādimāha. Tattha paripuṇṇavissajjaneti ubhayampi yamakapadaṃ ahāpetvā katavissajjane. Uppādakkhaṇe anāgatañcāti uppādakkhaṇe ca cittaṃ, anāgatañca cittaṃ na niruddhaṃ, nirujjhamānanti attho. Ṭhitikkhaṇābhāvaṃ cittassa dīpetīti uppannauppajjamānavārādīsu “ṭhitikkhaṇe”ti avacanaṃ cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇaṃ nāma natthīti imamatthaṃ dīpeti bodheti. Na hi yathādhammasāsane abhidhamme labbhamānassa avacane kāraṇaṃ dissatīti adhippāyo. Na kevalamabhidhamme avacanameva cittassa ṭhitikkhaṇābhāvajotakaṃ, apica kho [M 0.0030] suttantapāḷipīti dassento “suttesupī”tiādimāha. Tattha aññathattaṃ nāma pubbāparaviseso. Khaṇadvayasamaṅgiṃ ṭhitanti paccuppannassa ṭhitabhāvamāha. Aññathattaṃ pana santāneyeva veditabbaṃ.

And having shown how material form has neither a duration of seventeen mind-moments, nor a duration of sixteen mind-moments exceeding the third part, he then addresses the arising of material form at the mind's static moment, which is stated in the commentary. Not acknowledging the mind's static moment itself, and after having said 'whatever here... should be investigated,' he cites the Pāḷi from the Yamaka, beginning with the section on 'arisen and arising,' and says, 'in the Citta Yamaka,' and so on. Therein, 'in the complete answer' means in the answer given without omitting either term of the Yamaka. And 'at the moment of arising and the future' means that the mind at the moment of arising and the future mind have not ceased, but are in the process of ceasing. The non-mention of 'static moment' in the sections beginning with 'arisen and arising' reveals the absence of a static moment for the mind; it reveals and makes known this meaning: that there is no such thing as a static moment of the mind. For no reason is seen for not mentioning in the Abhidhamma something that is obtainable in accordance with the true teaching—this is the intention. Not only is the non-mention in the Abhidhamma an indicator of the mind's lack of a static moment, but also, showing that it is so in the Suttanta Pāḷi as well, he says, beginning with 'in the Suttas as well.' Therein, 'alteration' means the distinction between before and after. 'Stable, possessing two moments' refers to the stable nature of the present. However, alteration should be understood as occurring only in the continuum.

Ettha ca keci “yathābhūto dhammo uppajjati, kiṃ tathābhūtova bhijjati, udāhu aññathābhūto? Yadi tathābhūtova bhijjati, na jaratāya sambhavo. Atha aññathābhūto, añño eva soti sabbathāpi ṭhitikkhaṇassa abhāvoyevā”ti vadanti. Tattha ekadhammādhārabhāvepi uppādanirodhānaṃ aññova uppādakkhaṇo, añño nirodhakkhaṇo. Uppādāvatthañhi upādāya uppādakkhaṇo, nirodhāvatthaṃ upādāya nirodhakkhaṇo. Uppādāvatthāya ca bhinnā nirodhāvatthāti ekasmiṃyeva sabhāvadhamme yathā icchitabbā, aññathā aññova dhammo uppajjati, añño dhammo nirujjhatīti āpajjeyya, evaṃ nirodhāvatthāya viya nirodhābhimukhāvatthāyapi bhavitabbaṃ. Sā ṭhiti, jaratā cāti sampaṭicchitabbametaṃ. Yadi evaṃ kasmā pāḷiyaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇo na vuttoti? Vineyyajjhāsayānurodhena nayadassanavasena pāḷi gatāti veditabbā. Abhidhammadesanāpi hi kadāci vineyyajjhāsayānurodhena pavattati. Tathā hi rūpassa uppādo “upacayo, santatī”ti bhinditvā desito. Hetusampayuttadukādidesanā cettha nidassitabbā.

Here, some say: 'A phenomenon arises as it truly is. Does it disintegrate in that same true nature, or in a different nature? If it disintegrates in that same true nature, there is no possibility of aging. But if it disintegrates in a different nature, then it is indeed another thing—thus, there is no static moment at all.' In this regard, even with a single phenomenon as the basis, the moment of arising and the moment of cessation are distinct. The moment of arising is with reference to the state of arising, and the moment of cessation is with reference to the state of cessation. And it is to be accepted that in one and the same intrinsic phenomenon, the state of cessation is different from the state of arising; otherwise, it would follow that one phenomenon arises and another phenomenon ceases. Similarly, just as there is a state of cessation, there must also be a state facing cessation. This is stability and aging, and this should be accepted. If so, why is the static moment not mentioned in the Pāḷi? It should be understood that the Pāḷi proceeds in accordance with the disposition of those to be trained and by way of showing the method. Indeed, even the Abhidhamma teaching sometimes proceeds in accordance with the disposition of those to be trained. For example, the arising of material form is taught by dividing it into 'accumulation' and 'continuity.' The teaching of the dyads, such as that associated with roots, should be given as an example here.

“Yassa [V 0.0029] vā panā”tiādi pucchāvacanaṃ. Tassa “no”ti vissajjanaṃ. Samudayasaccaṃ nirujjhatīti cittuppādassa nirodhakkhaṇo vutto. Ayamettha adhippāyo – yadi cittassa bhaṅgakkhaṇe rūpaṃ uppajjeyya, taṃ dukkhasaccanti katvā “no”ti vattuṃ na sakkā, vuttañcetaṃ. Tasmā viññāyati “cittassa nirodhakkhaṇe rūpuppādo natthī”ti. Tayidamakāraṇaṃ. Arūpalokañhi sandhāya, cittasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ vā “no”ti sakkā vattunti. Ayañhi yamakadesanāya pakati, yadidaṃ yathāsambhavayojanā. Etena “na ca cittasamuṭṭhānarūpamevā”tiādivacanaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā paccāsattiñāyena yaṃ samudayasaccaṃ nirujjhati, tena yaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ uppādetabbaṃ cittacetasikatappaṭibaddharūpasaṅkhātaṃ, tassa tadā uppatti natthīti “no”ti vissajjanaṃ, na sabbassa.

“‘And to whom indeed,’ and so on, is the question. To that, the answer is ‘no.’ By ‘the truth of origination ceases’ is meant the moment of cessation of a mind-moment. The meaning here is this: if form were to arise at the moment of the mind's dissolution, it being the truth of suffering, it would be impossible to say ‘no,’ and yet this is said. Therefore, it is understood that ‘at the moment of the mind's cessation, there is no arising of form.’ This is not the reason. For it is possible to say ‘no’ with reference to the formless realm, or with reference to mind-originated form. This is indeed the nature of the Yamaka exposition, namely, construing according to what is possible. By this, statements such as ‘nor is it only mind-originated form’ should be seen as refuted. Or alternatively, by the principle of proximity, when that truth of origination ceases, that truth of suffering which is to be produced by it—namely, what is reckoned as form bound up with mind and mental factors—does not arise at that time. Hence, the answer is ‘no,’ but not in reference to all form.

Sahuppādekanirodhavacanatoti “yassa kāyasaṅkhāro nirujjhati, tassa cittasaṅkhāro nirujjhatīti? Āmantā”ti (yama. 2.saṅkhārayamaka.79) evaṃ sahuppādasahanirodhavacanato. Tena vacanenāti “yassa kāyasaṅkhāro”tiādivacanena. Aññarūpānanti [M 0.0031] kammautuāhārajarūpānaṃ. Sahuppādasahanirodhādikānanti etthāyaṃ yojanā – appaṭikkhittasahuppādasahanirodhaananuññātanānuppādanānānirodhaanivāritaabyākatabhāvānaṃ kammajādīnanti. Etenāti “yassa kusalā dhammā uppajjantī”tiādikena (yama. 3.dhammayamaka.163) pāṭhena, “na cittasamuṭṭhānarūpamevā”ti yuttivacanena ca. Yamakapāḷianussaraṇeti yathādassitacittayamakapāḷiyā yathārutavaseneva anussaraṇe vijjamāne. Bhijjamānatāti cittassa bhijjamānatā nāma nirujjhamānatā ṭhitiyā abhāvato. Sahāyabhāvaṃ nāpi gacchati nissayatthibhāvādinā paccayabhāvābhāvato. Uppādakkhaṇe eva hi anantarādipaccayalābhena cittassa balavatā. Evañca satīti evañca utunāpi bhavaṅgacittassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva rūpasamuṭṭhāpane sati. Taṃcittakkhaṇeti tassa cittassa khaṇe, khaṇadvayepīti attho. Tenevāti atilahuparivattibhāveneva. Atha vā tenevāti dandhaparivattikatāya rūpassa sakalaṃ ekacittakkhaṇaṃ uppajjamānabhāveneva. Tanti cittaṃ. Paṭisandhicittaṃ sampayuttadhammānaṃ viya sahajātarūpadhammānampi sahajātādipaccayena paccayo hotīti āha “paṭisandhito uddha”nti. Cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ cittaṃ sahajātādipaccayo hotiyevāti vuttaṃ “acittasamuṭṭhānāna”nti. Tadanantaranti yena cittena sahuppannaṃ, tassa cittassa anantaraṃ. Tanti rūpaṃ. Tadanantaraṃ cittanti sahuppannacittānantaraṃ cittaṃ. Yadi evanti yadi sakalaṃ cittakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ uppajjamānameva hoti, cittassa [V 0.0030] uppādakkhaṇe eva rūpassa uppādārambhoti āha “na, cittanirodhakkhaṇe rūpuppādārambhābhāvato”ti. Cittakkhaṇeti attanā sahuppannacittassa khaṇe. Tanti rūpaṃ. Rūpasamuṭṭhāpanapurejātapaccayakiccanti rūpasamuṭṭhāpanakiccañca purejātapaccayakiccañca. Ṭhitippattivisesālābhanti ṭhitippattiyā laddhabbo yo viseso, tassa alābhaṃ. Idaṃ vuttanti “yena sahuppajjati, taṃcittakkhaṇe rūpaṃ uppajjamānamevā”ti idaṃ pariyāyena vuttaṃ.

From the statement about simultaneous arising and single cessation—“For one whose bodily formation ceases, does the mental formation also cease? Yes.” (Yamaka 2, Saṅkhārayamaka, 79)—thus from the statement of simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation. “By that statement” means by the statement “for one whose bodily formation,” etc. “Other forms” means kamma-born, temperature-born, and nutriment-born material phenomena. Regarding “simultaneous arising, simultaneous cessation, etc.,” the construction here is this: of kamma-born phenomena, etc., which have unopposed simultaneous arising and cessation, unprohibited non-arising, non-different cessation, and an unrestricted indeterminate nature. By this—that is, by the text “for whom wholesome phenomena arise,” etc. (Yamaka 3, Dhammayamaka, 163), and by the reasoned statement “not merely mind-originated material phenomena.” “When there is recollection of the Yamaka text” means when there is recollection of the Yamaka text on consciousness as it was shown and as it was heard. “The breaking up of the consciousness” refers to the cessation of the consciousness due to the absence of a duration-moment. It does not attain the state of a companion because of the absence of conditions such as dependence, presence, and so on. Indeed, at the moment of arising, the consciousness is strong due to obtaining the contiguity condition, etc. “And when this is the case” means when material phenomena are produced by temperature at the very arising-moment of the life-continuum consciousness. “In that mind-moment” means in the moment of that consciousness, that is, in both moments. “By that” means due to its extremely rapid transformation. Alternatively, “by that” means due to the slow transformation of material phenomena, by the fact of its arising for an entire single mind-moment. “That” refers to the consciousness. The rebirth-linking consciousness, like its associated phenomena, is a condition for co-nascent material phenomena through the co-nascence condition, etc. Hence, he says, “from rebirth-linking onwards.” Because consciousness is indeed a co-nascence condition, etc., for mind-originated phenomena, it is said “for non-mind-originated phenomena.” “Immediately after that” means immediately after the consciousness with which it arose simultaneously. “That” refers to material phenomena. “The consciousness immediately after that” means the consciousness immediately after the simultaneously arisen consciousness. “If it is so” means: if form arises for an entire mind-moment, then the beginning of the arising of form is at the very arising-moment of the consciousness. To this, he says: “No, because there is no beginning of the arising of form at the cessation-moment of the consciousness.” “In the mind-moment” means in the moment of the consciousness that arose simultaneously with it. “That” refers to material phenomena. “The function of producing material phenomena and the pre-nascence condition” means the function of producing material phenomena and the function of the pre-nascence condition. “The absence of a distinctive attainment of duration” means the lack of gaining the distinction that should be obtained through the attainment of duration. “This is stated” means this—“the material phenomenon arises within the moment of that consciousness with which it arises simultaneously”—is stated by way of paraphrase.

Yaṃ yassa sambandhibhāvena vuttaṃ, taṃ dūre ṭhitampi tena sambandhanīyanti āha “tato paraṃ…pe… etena saha sambandho”ti. Tasmā “tato”ti ettha taṃsaddena cutiṃ paccāmasatīti vuttaṃ “cutito paranti attho”ti.

Whatever is said to be related to something, even if it stands far away, is to be connected with that. Thus he says: “Beyond that...pe...the connection is with this.” Therefore, concerning the word “tato” here, it is said that by the pronoun “taṃ” within it, it refers back to the death-consciousness; the meaning is ‘after the death-consciousness.’”

Natthīti [M 0.0032] katvāti yadipi yathā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ, tathā ekuppādekanirodhatā rūpānaṃ arūpehi, arūpānañca rūpehi natthi. Yathā ca amhehi vuttaṃ, tathā atthevāti adhippāyo.

Having considered it as “it does not exist”: The meaning is that although, as it is stated in the commentary, there is thus no simultaneous arising and single cessation of material phenomena with immaterial phenomena, nor of immaterial phenomena with material phenomena, it does exist in the way that has been stated by us.
