Catutthassa pakārassa vuccamānattā “tayo pakāre āhā”ti vuttaṃ.

Because the fourth aspect is being discussed, it is said, “He spoke of three aspects.”

“Tesaṃyeva rūpānaṃ kāyavikāro”tiādinā parinipphannānaṃ vikārādibhāvaṃ dassetvā “sabbaṃ parinipphannaṃ saṅkhatamevā”ti vadantena parinipphannatāpariyāyo dassito. Pubbantāparantaparicchinnoti pātubhāvaviddhaṃsabhāvaparicchinno, udayabbayaparicchinno vā. “Ayaṃ datto nāma hotū”tiādinā nāmakaraṇaṃ nāmaggahaṇaṃ. Samāpajjanaṃ nirodhasamāpattiyā samathavipassanānukkamena nāmakāyassa nirodhameva. Ādi-saddena sattakasiṇādipaññattiyā paññāpanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Nipphādiyamānoti sādhiyamāno.

By stating, “The alteration of the body among those very material forms,” etc., and having shown the nature of alteration and so on in what is fully formed, the aspect of being fully formed is indicated by the one who declares, “All that is fully formed is conditioned.” “Bounded by the past end and the future end” means bounded by the nature of appearance and destruction, or bounded by arising and passing away. “Let this be called ‘Datta’,” etc., is the making of a name, the taking up of a name. “Attainment” is precisely the cessation of the mentality-group by means of the sequence of tranquility and insight in the attainment of cessation. By the word “etc.,” he includes the designating of the concept of the seven kasinas and so on. “Being accomplished” means being brought to accomplishment.

Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discussions is concluded.

Kamādivinicchayakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discussion of the Determination of Sequence and so forth.

Uppattikkamādīsu [V 0.0031] desanākkamopi labbhatevāti “cattāro satipaṭṭhānātiādiko desanākkamovā”ti vuttaṃ. Anupubbukkaṃsatoti dānasīlakāmādīnavādidassananekkhammakathānaṃ anukkamena ukkaṭṭhabhāvato kathānaṃ anupubbukkaṃsatā vuttā. Tena ukkaṃsakkamo nāmāyaṃ visuṃ kamoti dasseti. Tathāpi dānādīnaṃ desanākkamāvarodhane kāraṇamāha “uppattiādivavatthānābhāvato”ti. Tattha ādi-saddena pahānapaṭipattibhūmikkame saṅgaṇhāti. “Cakkhuādīnampi visayabhūta”nti iminā pañcarūpindriyagocaratā adhippetāti āha “ekadesenā”tiādi. Ekadesenāti bāhiroḷārikāyatanehi. Etthāti “yaṃ vedayati, taṃ sañjānātī”ti etasmiṃ pade vuttanayena.

The sequence of teaching is indeed found in the order of arising, etc.—thus it is said: “The four foundations of mindfulness, etc., constitute a sequence of teaching.” “Gradual exaltation” refers to the progressive elevation of discussions, stated because of the sequential excellence of the talks on generosity, virtue, the dangers of sensual pleasures, and renunciation. By this, he shows that this, the sequence of exaltation, is a separate sequence. Nevertheless, he states the reason for including generosity and so on in the sequence of teaching: “Due to the absence of distinction in arising, etc.” Here, the term “etc.” includes the sequence of abandoning, the practice, and the stages. By “The eye, etc., also being objects,” it is intended that they are the domain of the five physical sense faculties, as stated: “in part,” etc. “In part” means through the external gross sense bases. “Here” refers to the method stated in the phrase, “What one feels, that one perceives.”

Taṃsabhāvatānivattanatthanti anāsavadhammasabhāvatānivattanatthaṃ. Anāsavā khandhesveva vuttāti attho sāsavānampi khandhesu vuttattā. Nanu ca anāsavadhammo khandhesu avuttopi atthīti? Saccaṃ atthi, khandhādhikāre khandhapariyāpannā eva anāsavā gayhantīti nāyaṃ doso.

“For the purpose of not reverting from that nature” means for the purpose of not reverting from the nature of taintless phenomena. The meaning is that the taintless are spoken of only as they are included in the aggregates, because the tainted are also spoken of in relation to the aggregates. But is it not so that a taintless phenomenon exists even though it is not spoken of in relation to the aggregates? True, it exists; but in the section on the aggregates, only those taintless phenomena that are included within the aggregates are to be taken. Thus, there is no fault here.

Yathā [M 0.0033] phassādayo visesato tadanuguṇavuttitāya saṅkhatābhisaṅkharaṇasabhāvāti saṅkhārakkhandhe samavaruddhā, na evaṃ vedanāsaññāviññāṇānīti rūpadhammā viya tāni visuṃ khandhabhāvena vuttāni. Etena phassādīnaṃ visuṃ khandhasaddavacanīyatābhāvo vuttoti veditabbo. Tena vuttaṃ “phusanādayo panā”tiādi. Itiādīnañca suttānanti ettha ādi-saddena “rūpe kho, bhikkhave, sati rūpaṃ upādāya rūpaṃ abhinivissa uppajjanti saṃyojanābhinivesavinibandhā. Vedanāya…pe… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe sati viññāṇaṃ upādāya viññāṇaṃ abhinivissa uppajjanti saṃyojanābhinivesavinibandhā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.158), tathā “ahaṃ rūpaṃ, mama rūpanti pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyī hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.1) ca evamādīnaṃ suttapadānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Etenāti attanā dassitasuttena. Vakkhamānasuttavasena cāti “rūpe kho, bhikkhave, satī”tiādikassa aṭṭhakathāyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 26 pakiṇṇakakathā) vakkhamānassa suttassa vasena. “Parittārammaṇādivasena na vattabbā”ti etena navattabbārammaṇāpi diṭṭhi khandhe eva nissāya uppajjati, pageva khandhārammaṇāti dasseti.

Just as contact and the like are specifically included in the aggregate of formations due to their nature as conditioned volitional formations that function accordingly, feeling, perception, and consciousness are not. Like material phenomena, these are stated as separate aggregates. Thus, it should be understood that contact and the like are not individually designated by the term 'aggregate.' Therefore, it is said, 'But contact and the rest...' and so on. Here, the word 'and so on' includes such suttas as: 'Bhikkhus, when there is form, by relying on form and fixating on form, bonds, fixations, and attachments arise. When there is feeling... perception... formations... consciousness, by relying on consciousness and fixating on consciousness, bonds, fixations, and attachments arise' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.158). Similarly, 'He holds the persistent view, "I am form, form is mine"' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.1), and other such sutta passages should be understood as included. 'By this' means by the sutta shown by oneself. 'And according to the sutta being explained' refers to the explanation in the commentary (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 26, Pakiṇṇakakathā) of the sutta beginning, 'Bhikkhus, when there is form...' The statement 'They should not be spoken of in terms of limited objects, etc.' indicates that even a view with an object that is not an aggregate arises in dependence on the aggregates, let alone one with an aggregate as its object.

Vedanākāraṇāyāti [V 0.0032] vedanāyātanāya. Chādāpanatoti rocāpanato. Bāhullenāti bahulabhāvena. Upādānakkhandhā hi bāhullappavattikā, na itare.

'For the reason of feeling' (vedanākāraṇāya) means 'for the base of feeling' (vedanāyātanāya). 'From making pleasant' (chādāpanato) means 'from making agreeable' (rocāpanato). 'Abundantly' (bāhullena) means 'by the state of being abundant' (bahulabhāvena). For the aggregates of clinging are of abundant occurrence, not the others.

Puṭaṃ katvāti ca chattasadisaṃ puṭaṃ bandhaṃ katvā. Vatthumhīti cakkhādivatthumhi. Vaṭṭagatavedanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sā hi idha daṭṭhabbabhāve ṭhitā. Ūnehīti vatthunā, kilesehi ca ūnehi.

'Having made a pouch' means having made a tied pouch like an umbrella. 'In the base' refers to the base of the eye, etc. It is said with reference to the feeling that has become part of the round of existence. For it stands here in a state to be understood. 'By the deficient' (ūnehi) means deficient in the base and in the defilements.

Māyāyāti indajālādimāyāya payogo māyāti adhippāyenāha “māyāya dassitaṃ rūpaṃ ‘māyā’ti āhā”ti. Vatthubhāvāditoti ādi-saddena ārammaṇasampayuttādike saṅgaṇhāti. Katthacīti rūpakkhandhādike. Koci visesoti asubhādikova.

'By illusion' (māyāya): with the intention that it is an illusion produced by a trick such as Indra's net, he said, 'The form shown by illusion is called "illusion".' 'From the state of being a physical basis, etc.': by the word 'etc.' he includes what is associated with an object, and so on. 'Where?' means in the aggregate of form, etc. 'What particular aspect?' means such as the foul, etc.

Tassāti ajjhattikarūpassa. Yassa kāmarāgappahānamukhena sabbarāgappahānaṃ sambhavati, taṃ sandhāyāha “kāmarāgamukhena vā sabbalobhappahānaṃ vadatī”ti. Yojetabbanti vedanāya chandarāgaṃ pajahanto tassā samudayabhūte [M 0.0034] phassepi chandarāgaṃ pajahatīti yojetabbanti. Pariññattayassa yojanā pākaṭā eva.

'Of that' refers to internal form. This is said with reference to that for which, through the abandoning of sensual desire, the abandoning of all desire occurs: 'Or, by way of sensual desire, the abandoning of all greed is spoken of.' 'Should be connected' means that in abandoning desire and lust for feeling, one abandons desire and lust even for contact, which is the ground of its arising—thus it should be connected. The connection of the threefold full understanding is indeed clear.

Tatoti dukkhuppādanasukhavināsanānaṃ adassanato. Bhindatīti vināseti. Tanti manosañcetanāhāraṃ ñātatīraṇapariññāhi pariggaṇhāti tīreti.

'From that' is because of not seeing the production of suffering and the destruction of pleasure. 'It destroys' means it annihilates. 'That' refers to mental volitional food; one comprehends and judges it by means of the full understanding of knowing and discerning.

Taṃ pajahantoti avijjaṃ pajahanto. Parāmaṭṭhanti parāmāsasaṅkhātāya diṭṭhiyā niccādivasena gahitaṃ. Viññāṇaṃ niccato passanto diṭṭhupādānaṃ upādiyatīti ayamattho “tadevidaṃ viññāṇaṃ sandhāvati saṃsarati, anañña”ntiādisuttapadehi (ma. ni. 1.396) dīpetabbo.

‘Abandoning that’ means abandoning ignorance. ‘Adhered to’ refers to what is grasped as permanent, etc., by the view known as adherence. The meaning that one who sees consciousness as permanent takes up the clinging to views should be illustrated by sutta passages like, 'This same consciousness runs on, wanders on, not another' (MN 1.396).

Kamādivinicchayakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the discourse on the analysis of sensual pleasures, etc., is concluded.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Suttanta Exposition is concluded.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition

34. Taṃ [V 0.0033] vatvāti taṃ bhūmivasena jānitabbataṃ “sabbāpi catubhūmikavedanā”tiādinā vatvā. Sampayuttato dassitatādīti ettha ādi-saddena hetujātibhūmiindriyavatthusamphassajabhedato dassitataṃ anavasesato saṅgaṇhāti.

34. 'Having stated that' means having stated what should be known by way of the planes—'All feeling is of the four planes,' etc. 'Shown as associated, etc.': here, the word 'etc.' inclusively encompasses, without omission, what is shown by way of the distinctions of root, class, plane, faculty, base, contact, and arising.

Yadipi taṃ-saddo pubbe vuttassa sāmaññato paṭiniddeso, tathāpi anantarameva paccāmasituṃ yutto itarattha asambhavatoti āha “aṭṭha…pe… yojanā”ti. “Aṭṭhavidhattābhāvato”ti iminā taṃ asambhavaṃ dasseti.

Although the word 'that' is a general reference to what was said before, it is still appropriate to refer back to it immediately, as another meaning is impossible—thus it is said, 'eight... yojanas.' By 'because of the absence of an eightfold nature,' he indicates that impossibility.

Pūraṇatthameva vutto, apubbatābhāvatoti attho.

It is stated merely for the sake of completion; the meaning is that there is an absence of novelty.

Gahaṇavaḍḍhanavasenāti gahaṇassa vaḍḍhanavasena. Gahaṇanti cettha kathanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, tassa vaḍḍhanaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne avuttassa kathanaṃ. Tenāha “pubbe gahitato aññassa gahaṇaṃ vaḍḍhana”nti, tato eva ca “purimagahite aññupacayavasenā”ti vuttaṃ. “Vaḍḍhanasaddo chedanattho”ti idaṃ yathā asivā “sivā”ti, diṭṭhañca “adiṭṭha”nti vuccati, evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nayanīharaṇanti nīyatīti nayo, desanā, tassa nīharaṇaṃ pavattanaṃ. Vaḍḍhanakanayoti [M 0.0035] yathāvuttavaḍḍhanakavasena pavatto desanānayo. Aññe bhedāti ekavidhacatubbidhādayo bhedā. Yadi avisiṭṭhā, kasmā vuttāti āha “tathāpī”tiādi. Tattha paññāppabhedajananatthanti dhammavisayāya pabhedagatāya paññāya vineyyānaṃ nibbattanatthaṃ, vijjāṭṭhānādivasena vineyyānaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidāya uppādanatthanti attho. Abhiññeyyadhammavibhāgatāya sammasanavārassa visayabhāvato vuttaṃ “ekekassa vārassa gahitassa niyyānamukhabhāvato”ti. Itarepi bhedā vuttāti duvidhatividhabhedānaṃ yaṃ nānattaṃ, tassa vasena itare bhedā anānattāpi yathāvuttakāraṇato vuttā. “Na kevala”ntiādinā bhedānaṃ aññamaññapekkhataṃ dassetvā “tasmā”tiādinā tesaṃ visiṭṭhataṃ dasseti.

'By means of increasing the grasp' means by means of the increase of grasping. Here, 'grasping' should be understood as a statement; and its increase, the statement in various places of what was not previously stated. Hence it is said, 'The grasping of something other than what was previously grasped is an increase,' and for that very reason it was said, 'by means of accumulating another on what was previously grasped.' 'The word "increase" has the meaning of cutting'—this should be understood just as the inauspicious is called 'auspicious,' or how 'seen' is called 'unseen.' 'Drawing out the method' means: what is led is a method, that is, the teaching; its drawing out is its presentation. 'The method of increasing' refers to the method of teaching presented by way of the increase as described. 'Other divisions' refer to divisions such as the singlefold, fourfold, etc. If they are not distinct, why are they mentioned? It is said, 'yet even so,' etc. Here, 'for the purpose of generating distinctions in wisdom' means for the sake of producing for those to be trained a wisdom that has entered into distinctions regarding the domain of phenomena; that is, for producing for those to be trained the analytical knowledge of phenomena by way of the bases of knowledge, etc. It is said, 'because each section, when grasped, serves as a door to liberation,' due to its being the object of the section on comprehension regarding the classification of phenomena to be directly known. 'Other divisions are also mentioned' means that by means of the diversity of the twofold and threefold divisions, other divisions, though not diverse, are mentioned for the reasons stated. With 'Not only,' etc., he shows the interdependence of the divisions; and with 'therefore,' etc., he indicates their distinctiveness.

Yathā dukamūlakādīsu bhedā gaṇanānupubbiyā pavattā pabhedantarāpekkhā, na evamete. Ete pana sattavidhādibhedā pabhedantaranirapekkhā kevalaṃ bahuvidhabhāvasāmaññeneva vuttāti dasseti “aññappabhedanirapekkhā”tiādinā. Dukatikapadatthānaṃ yathārahaṃ apekkhitabbāpekkhakabhāvena vuttattā [V 0.0034] yathā duke ṭhapetvā vuttā tikā tattha pakkhittā nāma jātā, evaṃ tikadukapadatthānaṃ apekkhitabbāpekkhakabhāvena vuttattā duke vatvā vuttesupi tikesu te pakkhittā nāma hontīti āha “parato…pe… yojitattā”ti.

Just as in the dyads, etc., the divisions proceed in sequence according to enumeration, dependent on further distinctions, these are not like that. However, these sevenfold and other divisions are stated merely by way of the commonality of their manifold nature, without depending on further distinctions—this is shown by the phrase 'independent of other distinctions,' etc. Because the meanings of the terms of the dyads and triads are stated with appropriate relevance in terms of what is to be considered and what considers, just as when the triads are stated after setting aside the dyads, they are said to be 'included,' so too, because the meanings of the terms of the triads and dyads are stated with appropriate relevance in terms of what is to be considered and what considers, even when the triads are stated after the dyads, they are said to be 'included'—this is said by the phrase 'since they are connected subsequently,' etc.

Samānavīthiyanti ekavīthiyaṃ. Cakkhusaṅghaṭṭanāyāti cakkhurūpapaṭighātena. Soti cakkhurūpapaṭighāto. Taduppādikāti tassa cakkhusamphassassa uppādikā. Sāti āvajjanavedanā. Nanu ca vedanāpaccayo phasso vutto, na phassapaccayā vedanāti? Na, vedanāsīsena cittuppādassa gahitattāti. Tappayojanattāti cakkhusamphassapayojanattā. Payojayatīti payojanaṃ, phalaṃ.

'In the same process' means in a single process. 'By the striking of the eye' means by the impact of the eye and form. 'That' refers to the impact of the eye and form. 'Producer of that' means producer of that eye-contact. 'That' refers to the feeling of adverting. But is it not said that contact is conditioned by feeling, not that feeling is conditioned by contact? No, because the arising of consciousness is taken with feeling as its head. 'Because of its purpose' means because of the purpose of eye-contact. 'It directs' (payojayati) means purpose, result.

Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarānaṃ vipākānanti adhippāyo. Te hi idha aggahitā. Tenevāha “tesaṃ sayameva manodvārabhūtattā”tiādi. Tatoti bhavaṅgato. Cakkhusamphassapaccayādikusalādīnanti ettha purimena ādi-saddena “sotasamphassapaccayā”ti evamādayo saṅgahitā, dutiyena akusalādayo. “Kāmāvacaraaṭṭhakusalacittavasenā”tiādinā kusalābyākatānampi kāmāvacarānaṃyeva yojitattā vuttaṃ “samānavīthiyaṃ labbhamānatā [M 0.0036] aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttā”ti. Vedanāpītisanidassanattikavajjānaṃ ekūnavīsatiyā tikānaṃ vasena ekūnavīsaticatuvīsatikā. Yadi asamānavīthiyampi kusalādīnaṃ labbhamānatā yojetabbā, atha kasmā samānavīthiyaṃyeva yojitāti āha “aṭṭhakathāyaṃ panā”tiādi. Tenevāti asamānavīthiyaṃ appaṭikkhittattāyeva.

The meaning is the resultants of the form-sphere and the formless-sphere, for they are not included here. Therefore, it is said, 'Because they themselves are the mind-door,' and so on. That is, from the life-continuum. Regarding 'dependent on eye-contact, etc., wholesome, etc.,' here, by the first 'etc.' are included 'dependent on ear-contact,' and so on; by the second, the unwholesome and others. By the phrase 'by means of the eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense-sphere,' and so on, since even the wholesome and indeterminate are connected only with those of the sense-sphere, it is said, 'The obtainability in the same cognitive process is stated in the commentary.' Excluding the triads of feeling, joy, and visibility, by way of nineteen triads, there are nineteen sets of twenty-four. If the obtainability of the wholesome, etc., is to be connected even in a different cognitive process, then why is it connected only in the same cognitive process? To this, it is said, 'But in the commentary,' and so on. Therefore, it is precisely because it is not rejected in a different cognitive process.

Cittasambandhoti cittena sambandho cittasambandhaṃ katvā cittasīsena vedanāya kathanaṃ. Tikabhūmivasenāti kusalattikāditikavasena, kāmāvacarādibhūmivasena ca. Dvāratikavasenāti cakkhādiuppattidvāravasena, kusalattikāditikavasena ca. Yattha katthacīti dīpetabbassa atthassa visesābhāvato sattavidhabhedādīsu yattha katthaci. Na ca dvāraṃ anāmaṭṭhanti yojanā. Tena sattavidhabhedato tiṃsavidhabhede visesaṃ dasseti. Yadipi ubhayattha bhūmiyo āgatā, rūpāvacarādibhūmiāmasanena pana asamānavīthiyaṃ labbhamānatā dassitāti āha “atibyattā ca ettha samānāsamānavīthīsu labbhamānatā”ti. Sukhadīpanāni honti dvārabhūmiāmasanamukhena vedanākkhandhassa vibhattattā. Na bhūmiyo apekkhitvā ṭhapitāti kathetabbabhāvena bhūmiyo apekkhitvā [V 0.0035] na ṭhapitā, bhūmivibhāgena na kathitāti attho. Apekkhitabbarahitāti dvārabhūmīnaṃ aggahitattā ākaṅkhitabbadvārādivisesarahitā.

'Connection with mind' means a connection with the mind; having made a connection with the mind, it is an explanation of feeling with mind as the head. 'By way of triads and planes' means by way of the triads such as the wholesome triad, and by way of the planes such as the sense-sphere. 'By way of doors and triads' means by way of the doors of arising such as the eye, and by way of the triads such as the wholesome triad. 'Wherever' means wherever among the sevenfold divisions, etc., because there is no distinction in the meaning to be explained. The construction is: 'And the door is not untouched.' Thereby, it shows the distinction in the thirtyfold division from the sevenfold division. Although planes are mentioned in both, by touching upon the planes such as the form-sphere, the obtainability in a different cognitive process is shown. Hence it is said, 'And here, the obtainability in similar and dissimilar cognitive processes is very evident.' They are clear expositions because the feeling aggregate is analyzed by way of referring to the doors and planes. 'The planes are not established in consideration of them' means that the planes are not established in consideration of them as a topic to be discussed; the meaning is that it is not explained by way of a division of planes. 'Devoid of what is to be considered' means that because the doors and planes are not included, it is devoid of the particularities to be expected, such as the doors.

“Upanissayakoṭiyā”ti ettha nippariyāyato pariyāyato ca upanissayakoṭidassanamukhena idhādhippetaupanissayakoṭiṃ dassetuṃ “saddhaṃ upanissāyā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha upanissayānanti vedanāya upanissayabhūtānaṃ. Dassananti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, disvā vā gahaṇaṃ. Upanissayantabhāvenāti lāmakūpanissayabhāvena. Yadi ghāyanādīni upanissayo bhaveyyuṃ, pakatūpanissayāneva siyuṃ. Pakatūpanissayo ca nānāvīthiyaṃyevāti tadalābhavacanaṃ idha nānāvīthijotakanti dasseti “ghānādidvāresū”tiādinā. Kasiṇaparikammādīnanti kasiṇaparikammasamāpattinibbattanavipassanāvaḍḍhanādīnaṃ. Tadalābhoti upanissayālābho, so ca ghāyanādīhi paresaṃ paṭipattiyā jānituṃ asakkuṇeyyattā. Antimabhavikabodhisattādīnaṃ savanena vinā taṃphusanaṃ siyā mūlūpanissayoti “yebhuyyenā”ti vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'in the category of strong dependence,' here, to show the intended category of strong dependence by way of showing the category of strong dependence both directly and indirectly, 'having depended on faith,' and so on, is said. Therein, 'of strong dependencies' means of those that have become a strong dependence for feeling. 'Seeing' means eye-consciousness, or grasping after having seen. 'By the nature of being a dependence' means by the nature of being an inferior strong dependence. If smelling, etc., were a strong dependence, they would be only natural strong dependencies. And since natural strong dependence occurs only in different cognitive processes, the statement of its non-attainment here indicates different cognitive processes, as shown by 'in the nose-door, etc.,' and so on. 'Of the preparatory work on kasiṇas, etc.' means of the preparatory work on kasiṇas, the attainment, the production of insight, the development of insight, etc. 'Its non-attainment' means the non-attainment of strong dependence, and that is because of the inability to know the practice of others through smelling, etc. For beings like the Bodhisatta in his final existence, its attainment without hearing could be a root strong dependence; therefore, 'for the most part' is said.

Sampannajjhāsayoti [M 0.0037] vivaṭṭūpanissayasampattiyā sampannajjhāsayo. Tenāti “evaṃ cakkhuviññāṇa”nti vacanena. Tadupanissayanti tato paraṃ uppannakasiṇarūpadassanādīnaṃ upanissayabhūtaṃ.

'One with a perfected inclination' means one with a perfected inclination due to the attainment of the strong dependence for liberation. 'By that' means by the statement 'thus eye-consciousness.' 'Its strong dependence' means that which has become a strong dependence for the subsequently arisen seeing of kasiṇa-forms, etc.

Thāmagamanaṃ nāma kāmarāgādīnaṃyeva āveṇiko sabhāvoti āha “appahīnakāmarāgādikassa vā”ti. “Rāgo uppanno”tiādinā iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇe rāgapaṭighānaṃ uppattivicāraṇāva vuttā, na nesaṃ kiccavisesoti kiccavisesena vutte dassento “asamapekkhanāyā”tiādimāha. Pavattā vedanāti attho. Pakārantarenāti cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppannakilesānaṃ samatikkamanasaṅkhātena pakārantarena. Tathā bhāvanāvasenāti ettha tathā-saddena cakkhusamphassassa catubhūmikavedanāya upanissayabhāvo eva pakārantarena kathitoti imamevatthaṃ ākaḍḍhati. Bhāvanāyevettha pakārantaraṃ.

'Becoming strong' is the inherent nature unique to sensual desire, etc.; thus he says, 'or of one whose sensual desire, etc., is not abandoned.' By 'lust has arisen,' etc., only the investigation of the arising of lust and aversion towards agreeable and disagreeable objects is stated, not their specific function. Showing that it is stated with a specific function, he says 'by not considering,' etc. The meaning is 'feeling that has occurred.' 'By another mode' means by another mode designated as the overcoming of defilements that have arisen conditioned by eye-contact. Regarding 'similarly, by way of development,' here the word 'similarly' refers to this very meaning: that the state of eye-contact being a strong dependence for feeling of the four planes has itself been described by another mode. Here, development itself is the other mode.

Sabbaṃ sammasanaṃ bhāvanāti veditabbā, na nīvaraṇappahānapariññāva.

All contemplation should be understood as development, not just the abandoning or full understanding of the hindrances.

Aññamaññassa cāti phoṭṭhabbamahābhūtesu itarītarassa, āpodhātuyā ca vasena.

'And of one another' refers to the mutual relationship of each other among the tangible great elements, and also by way of the water element.

Tesanti [V 0.0036] jātiādīnaṃ, kammatthe cetaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Sahajātassa manosamphassassa balavapaccayabhāvaṃ dassetīti sambandho. Tassa vā dassanassāti tassa vā jātiādike bhayato dassanavasena pavattassa kāmāvacarañāṇassa.

'Of them' means of birth, etc., and this is a genitive case in the sense of the object. The connection is that it shows the state of being a strong condition of simultaneously arisen mind-contact. Or 'of that seeing' refers to the sense-sphere knowledge that has occurred by way of seeing with fear regarding birth, etc.

Tadeva attano phalasseva phalabhāvenāti “manosamphasso”ti phassassa kāraṇabhāvena yaṃ vuttaṃ, tadeva viññāṇaṃ attano phalassa phalabhāvena vuttassa phassassa “cakkhusamphassaja”ntiādinā phalabhāvena vattuṃ na yuttaṃ. “Manosamphasso”tiādinā labbhamānopi viññāṇaṃ paṭicca phassassa paccayabhāvo hetuphalasaṅkarapariharaṇatthaṃ na vuttoti vatvā yadipi phasso viññāṇassa paccayo hoti, na pana phassassa viya viññāṇaṃ so tassa visesapaccayo hotīti viññāṇassa cakkhusamphassajāditā na vuttāti dassetuṃ “yasmā vā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'that very thing being a fruit in the same way as its own fruit': it is not appropriate to call that very consciousness—which was referred to as 'mind-contact' because contact is its cause—'born of eye-contact,' etc., in the sense of being the fruit of contact. Having said that, although the fact that contact is a condition dependent on consciousness is obtainable from 'mind-contact,' etc., it is not stated in order to avoid the confusion of cause and effect. And to show that although contact is a condition for consciousness, consciousness is not a specific condition for it in the way that contact is, and therefore the 'born of eye-contact,' etc., nature of consciousness is not stated, 'or because,' etc., is said.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition is concluded.

3. Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Section of Questions

150. Taṃ [M 0.0038] taṃ samudāyanti taṃ taṃ cittuppādasaṅkhātadhammasamudāyaṃ, anavasesarūpadhammasamudāyañca. Yathāsambhavanti copanaṃ patto saṃvaro chaṭṭhadvāre, itaro chasupīti evaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ. Tatoti abhijjhādomanassādito. Yathāyoganti yo saṃvaritabbo, tadanurūpaṃ.

150. 'That and that aggregate' means that and that aggregate of phenomena designated as a mind-moment, and the aggregate of material phenomena without remainder. 'As is possible' means: restraint pertaining to transgression is at the sixth door, the other in all six; thus, 'as is possible.' 'From that' means from covetousness, displeasure, etc. 'According to what is suitable' means in accordance with that which should be restrained.

Katthacīti te eva parivaṭṭe sāmaññena vadati. Katthacīti vā tesu parivaṭṭesu kismiñcipi padese. Kiñcipi appakampi. Ekova paricchedo, na āyatanavibhaṅgādīsu viya nānāti adhippāyo.

'Somewhere': he speaks generally of those very cycles. Or 'somewhere' means in any place whatsoever within those cycles. Anything at all, even a little. The meaning is: there is only one division, not various ones as in the Analysis of the Sense Bases, etc.

Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Section of Questions is concluded.

Khandhavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Analysis of the Aggregates is concluded.

2. Āyatanavibhaṅgo

2. The Analysis of the Sense Bases

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta Exposition

154. Asādhāraṇatoti [M 0.0039][V 0.0037] āveṇikato. Taṃ nesaṃ asādhāraṇabhāvaṃ vipakkhavasena patiṭṭhāpetuṃ sādhāraṇaṃ udāharaṇavasena dasseti “āyatanasaddattho viyā”ti. Atha vā cakkhādiattho eva cakkhādisaddavisesito āyatanatthoti taṃ tādisaṃ āyatanatthaṃ sandhāyāha “āyatanasaddattho viya asādhāraṇato”ti.

154. 'Because of being uncommon' means because of being exclusive. To establish their uncommon nature by way of its opposite, he shows what is common by way of an example: 'like the meaning of the word āyatana.' Alternatively, the meaning of 'eye,' etc., itself is the meaning of 'āyatana' specified by the word 'eye,' etc. Referring to such a meaning of āyatana, he says, 'like the meaning of the word āyatana, because of being uncommon.'

Yadi visayassādanattho cakkhu-saddo, sotādīnampi ayaṃ samaññā siyāti atippasaṅgaṃ pariharanto “satipī”tiādimāha. Dutiye atthavikappe cakkhatīti viññāṇādhiṭṭhitaṃ samavisamaṃ ācikkhati, ācikkhantaṃ viya, vibhāventaṃ viya vā hotīti attho. Rūpamiva cakkhuviññeyyaṃ viya saviggahamiva sabimbakaṃ viya vaṇṇavācako rūpa-saddo adhippetoti āha “vitthāraṇaṃ vā rūpasaddassa attho”ti.

If the term 'eye' were for the meaning of enjoying objects, then this designation would apply to the ear and so forth as well. Avoiding this over-extension, he says, 'even though there is,' and so on. In the second interpretation of the meaning, 'cakkhati' (it sees) means that, being established by consciousness, it indicates what is equal or unequal; or it is as if pointing out, or as if distinguishing—this is the meaning. The word 'rūpa', which denotes color, is intended as if it were form, as if cognizable by eye-consciousness, as if embodied, as if possessing an image; therefore, he says, 'Or, the meaning of the word rūpa is expansion.'

Vacanamevāti saviññattikasaddameva. Gamīyatīti upanīyati. Ajjhoharaṇassa rasaggahaṇamūlatāvacanena rasassa paramparāya jīvitahetutaṃ dasseti. Rasanimittañhi rasaggahaṇaṃ, rasaggahaṇanimittaṃ ajjhoharaṇaṃ, taṃnimittaṃ jīvitanti. Rasaggahaṇamūlatā ca ajjhoharaṇassa yebhuyyato veditabbā. Dissati apadissati etena phalanti deso, hetūti āha “uppattidesoti uppattikāraṇa”nti. Tathāti cakkhāyatanādippakārena. Manogocarabhūtāti manaso eva gocarabhūtā. Sāmaññalakkhaṇenevāti anubhavanādivisesalakkhaṇaṃ aggahetvā dhammabhāvasaṅkhātasādhāraṇalakkhaṇeneva[V 0.0038]. Ekāyatanattaṃ upanetvā vuttā dvādasa ekasabhāvattā bhinditvā vacane payojanābhāvā. Dvārālambanavibhāgadassanatthā hi āyatanadesanāti.

'Vacanaṃ eva' (only speech) means only sound that conveys intimation. 'Gamīyati' (is gone to) means it is brought near. By stating that the basis of swallowing is the grasping of taste, it shows that taste is the sequential cause of life. For the condition for grasping taste is taste; the condition for swallowing is the grasping of taste; and the condition for life is that. And it should be understood that the grasping of taste is for the most part the basis of swallowing. That by which a result appears or disappears is a place and a cause; therefore, he says, 'the place of arising is the cause of arising.' 'Tathā' (thus) refers to the manner of the eye-base and so forth. 'Manogocarabhūtā' (being the domain of the mind) means being the domain of the mind alone. 'Sāmaññalakkhaṇeneva' (only by the general characteristic) means without grasping the specific characteristics such as experiencing, but only with the common characteristic designated as the state of phenomena. The twelve are stated by reducing them to a single base, because, due to their single nature, there is no purpose in speaking of them separately. For the teaching of the bases is for the purpose of showing the division of doors and objects.

Pubbantatoti purimabhāgato pākabhāvato. Pākabhāvo hi sabhāvadhammānaṃ pubbanto, viddhaṃsābhāvo aparanto.

'Pubbanto' (the prior end) means from the prior part, from the state of maturing. For the state of maturing is indeed the prior end of phenomena with their own nature, and the state of dissolution is the latter end.

Nivāsaṭṭhānādīsu āyatana-saddo na āyatanatthādīsu viya padatthavivaraṇamukhena pavatto, atha kho tasmiṃ tasmiṃ devagharādike niruḷhatāya evamatthoti āha “ruḷhivasena āyatanasaddassatthaṃ vattu”nti. Manoti dvārabhūtamano[M 0.0040]. Nissayabhāvoti ettha nissayasadiso nissayo, sadisatā ca phalassa tappaṭibaddhavuttitāya daṭṭhabbā. Vacanīyattho bhāvattho.

In the context of dwelling places and the like, the word 'āyatana' is not employed by way of explaining the word's meaning, as it is in 'āyatanattha' and so on; but rather, it has such a meaning due to its established usage in reference to various divine abodes and the like. Therefore, he says, 'to state the meaning of the word āyatana according to conventional usage.' 'Mano' (mind) means the mind that has become a door. 'Nissayabhāvo' (the state of being a support): here, the support is like a support, and the similarity should be understood from the fact that the occurrence of the result is bound to it. The meaning to be stated is that of the abstract noun.

Tāvatvatoti tattakato. Ūnacodanāti dvādasato ūnāni kasmā na vuttānīti codanā. Yadi cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ asādhāraṇaṃ dhammajātaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ, evaṃ sante cakkhādīnampi dhammāyatanabhāvo siyāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “satipī”tiādi. Dvārārammaṇabhāvehīti na ārammaṇabhāveneva asādhāraṇaṃ, atha kho dvārārammaṇabhāvehi asādhāraṇaṃ sambhavatīti vacanaseso.

'Tāvatvatā' (by that much) means by that measure. 'Ūnacodanā' (the objection of deficiency) means the objection as to why fewer than twelve were not stated. 'If the unique class of phenomena such as eye-consciousness and so forth is the base of phenomena, then, this being the case, even the eye and so forth would have the nature of a base of phenomena'—referring to this objection, he says, 'even though there is,' and so on. 'By the states of being door and object' means it is not unique merely by the state of being an object, but rather that uniqueness is possible by the states of being door and object—this is the remainder of the statement.

Yebhuyyasahuppattiādīhīti yebhuyyena cakkhāyatanādīni kassaci kadāci ekato uppajjanti. “Kāmadhātuyā upapattikkhaṇe kassaci ekādasāyatanāni uppajjantī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Tasmā āyatanānaṃ uppattikkamo tāva na yujjati, na pahānakkamo kusalābyākatānaṃ appahātabbato, na paṭipattikkamo akusalānaṃ, ekaccaabyākatānañca appaṭipajjanīyato, na bhūmikkamo aḍḍhekādasannaṃ āyatanānaṃ ekantakāmāvacarattā, itaresaṃ catubhūmipariyāpannattā, ekaccassa lokuttarabhāvato ca. Evaṃ uppattikkamādiayuttiyojanā veditabbā. Yesu vijjamānesu attabhāvassa paññāpanā, te “mayhaṃ cakkhu”ntiādinā adhikasinehavatthubhūtā cakkhādayo yathā ajjhattikatāya, evaṃ dassanādikiccakaraindriyatā ca padhānāti āha “ajjhattikabhāvena, visayibhāvena cā”ti. Ghānādikkamenāti ghānaṃ jivhā kāyoti iminā kamena.

'By way of mostly simultaneous arising, and so on' means that for the most part, the eye-base and so on arise together for someone at some time. For it has been said, 'At the moment of rebirth in the desire realm, eleven bases arise for someone.' Therefore, an order of arising of the bases is not appropriate; nor is an order of abandoning, since wholesome and indeterminate states are not to be abandoned; nor is an order of practice, since unwholesome states and some indeterminate states are not to be practiced; nor is an order of planes, since ten and a half bases are exclusively of the desire realm, while the others pertain to the four planes, and one is supramundane. Thus, the application of the inappropriateness of the order of arising, and so on, should be understood. Those in the presence of which there is the designation of personality, namely, the eye and so on, which are objects of excessive attachment expressed as 'my eye,' and so on, are principal both due to being internal and as faculties performing the function of seeing and so on. Thus, he says, 'by way of being internal and by way of being a subject.' 'By the order of nose and so on' means by this order: nose, tongue, body.

Paccuppannārammaṇattā vā cakkhādīni paṭhamaṃ vuttāni, mano pana kiñci paccuppannārammaṇaṃ[V 0.0039], kiñci yāvanavattabbārammaṇanti pacchā vuttaṃ. Paccuppannārammaṇesupi upādārūpārammaṇāni cattāri paṭhamaṃ vuttāni, tato bhūtarūpārammaṇaṃ. Upādārūpārammaṇesupi dūratare dūre, sīghataraṃ sīghañca ārammaṇasampaṭicchanadīpanatthaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ desanākkamo. Cakkhusotadvayañhi dūragocaranti paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ. Tatrāpi cakkhu dūrataragocaranti sabbapaṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ. Passantopi hi dūratare nadisotaṃ na tassa saddaṃ suṇāti. Ghānajivhāsupi ghānaṃ sīghataravuttīti [M 0.0041] paṭhamaṃ vuttaṃ. Purato ṭhapitamattassa hi bhojanassa gandho gayhatīti. Yathāṭhānaṃ vā tesaṃ desanākkamo. Imasmiñhi sarīre sabbupari cakkhussa adhiṭṭhānaṃ, tassa adho sotassa, tassa adho ghānassa, tassa adho jivhāya, tathā kāyassa yebhuyyena, mano pana arūpībhāvato sabbapacchā vutto. Taṃtaṃgocarattā tassa tassānantaraṃ bāhirāyatanāni vuttānīti vuttovāyamatthoti evampi imesaṃ kamo veditabbo.

Alternatively, the eye and so on are mentioned first because they have present objects. The mind, however, is mentioned later because some of its objects are present, while others extend as far as can be spoken of. Even among those with present objects, the four with derived material objects are mentioned first, then the one with a primary material object. Even among those with derived material objects, the teaching order of the eye and so on is for the purpose of illustrating the reception of objects that are more distant and distant, and quicker and quick. For the pair of eye and ear are mentioned first because they have a distant range. And among them, the eye is mentioned first of all because it has a more distant range. For even when seeing a more distant river-stream, one does not hear its sound. Among the nose and tongue, the nose is mentioned first because it operates more quickly. For the smell of food is apprehended as soon as it is placed in front. Alternatively, their teaching order is according to their location. For in this body, the physical basis of the eye is at the very top, below it that of the ear, below that that of the nose, below that that of the tongue, and for the most part so for the body. The mind, however, being formless, is mentioned last of all. The external bases are mentioned immediately after each corresponding internal base because they are their respective objects; this meaning has also been stated. Thus, their order should also be understood in this way.

Tatoti hadayavatthubhedato. Yañhi hadayavatthuṃ nissāya ekaṃ manoviññāṇaṃ pavattati, na tadeva nissāya aññaṃ pavattati. Niddesavasenāti saṅkhepavitthāraniddesavasena. Yojetabbaṃ “kusalasamuṭṭhānaṃ kusalasamuṭṭhānassa sabhāga”ntiādinā.

'Tato' (from that) means from the difference of the heart-base. For when one mind-consciousness proceeds depending on a certain heart-base, another does not proceed depending on that very same one. 'By way of exposition' means by way of brief and detailed exposition. It should be connected thus: 'That which is of wholesome origin is homogeneous with that which is of wholesome origin,' and so on.

Sabhāvoti visayivisayabhāvo, tadabhinibbattiyañca yogyatā. Kāraṇasamatthatāti kāraṇabhūtā samatthatā paccayabhāvo. Dvārādibhāvoti dvārārammaṇe dvāravuttibhāvo. Imasmiṃ attheti anantaraṃ vuttaatthe. Yasmāti yāya dhammatāya yena dvārādibhāvena kāraṇabhūtena. Sambhavanavisesananti kiriyāya parāmasanamāha. Yaṃ sambhavanaṃ, dhammatāvesāti attho. Rittakānevāti dhuvādibhāvarittakāneva. Visamādīsu ajjhāsayo etesanti visamādiajjhāsayāni, visamādiajjhāsayāni viya hontīti visamādiajjhāsayāni, cakkhādīni. Visamabhāva…pe… vanabhāvehīti visamabhāvādisannissitaahiādisadisupādinnadhammehi cakkhādīhi, vanasannissitamakkaṭasadisena cittena ca abhiramitattā. Vanabhāvoti hi vanajjhāsayoti attho.

'Sabhāvo' (own-nature) is the state of being object and subject, and the suitability for its production. 'Kāraṇasamatthatā' (capability of a cause) is the capacity that has become a cause, the state of being a condition. 'Dvārādibhāvo' (the state of being a door, etc.) is the state of functioning as a door with respect to a door and an object. 'Imasmiṃ atthe' (in this sense) refers to the meaning stated immediately before. 'Yasmā' (because) means by which principle, by which state of being a door, etc., that is causal. 'Sambhavanavisesana' (the modifier 'producing') refers to the consideration of the action. 'That which is production' means it is the principle itself. 'Rittakāneva' (empty indeed) means empty of the state of permanence and so on. 'Visamādiajjhāsayāni' means 'they have an inclination towards the uneven, etc.,' or 'they are like inclinations towards the uneven, etc.'; this refers to the eye and so on. The phrase 'by the state of unevenness... up to the state of a forest' means because of delighting in the clung-to phenomena, such as the eye and so on, which are similar to snakes and the like that depend on states of unevenness and so on, and in the mind, which is similar to a monkey that depends on a forest. For 'vanabhāvo' (the state of a forest) means 'inclination towards a forest'.

Purimantavivittatāti pubbabhāgaviraho. Uppādato purimakoṭṭhāso hi idha purimanto. Aparanteti aparabhāge, bhaṅgato uddhanti attho. Udayabbayaparicchinno hi sabhāvadhammo. Yaṃ sandhāya [V 0.0040] vuttaṃ “anidhānagatā bhaggā, puñjo natthi anāgate”ti (mahāni. 10). Sadā abhāvoti na sadā abhāvapatiṭṭhāpanaṃ sabbakālampi natthīti, atha kho udayabbayaparicchinnattā sadābhāvapaṭikkhepoti āha “aniccalakkhaṇa”nti. Sabhāvavijahananti bhaṅgappattimāha[M 0.0042]. Viparivattanaṃ uppādajarāvatthāhi santānaṃ vinā na vikārāpattīti āha “santānavikārāpatti vā”ti.

The absence of the prior end (purimantavivittatā) means the absence of the prior part. Here, the prior end refers to the initial portion from the point of arising. The latter end (aparante) means the subsequent portion, that is, after dissolution. For an intrinsic phenomenon is defined by arising and passing away. This is what is meant by the statement: 'They are gone without a foundation, destroyed; there is no heap in the future' (Mahāni. 10). 'Always non-existent' (sadā abhāvo) does not mean establishing non-existence at all times—that it does not exist at any time—but rather, because of being defined by arising and passing away, it is a rejection of eternal existence. Hence, it is said: 'the characteristic of impermanence.' Abandoning intrinsic nature (sabhāvavijahana) refers to the attainment of dissolution. Transformation (viparivattana) means that without continuity, there is no undergoing alteration by the states of arising and aging. Thus, it is said: 'or undergoing alteration of continuity'.

Jātidhammatādīhīti jātijarābyādhimaraṇādisabhāvatāhi. Aniṭṭhatāti na iṭṭhatā, dukkhatāti attho. Purimaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇanti “paṭipīḷanaṭṭhenā”ti pubbe sāmaññato vuttaṃ dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ. Paccayavasena dukkhanākārena pavattamānānaṃ sabhāvadhammānaṃ dukkhanaṃ puggalasseva vasena dukkhamatāti āha “puggalassa pīḷanato dukkhama”nti. Dukkhavacananti “dukkha”nti satthu vacanaṃ.

'By nature of birth, etc.' (jātidhammatādīhi) means by the intrinsic nature of birth, aging, sickness, death, and so forth. 'Undesirability' (aniṭṭhatā) means not being desirable; the meaning is suffering. 'The former general characteristic' (purimaṃ sāmaññalakkhaṇaṃ) refers to the characteristic of suffering previously stated in general terms as 'by way of oppression.' The suffering of intrinsic phenomena, which occur in the mode of suffering due to conditions, is considered suffering only in terms of the individual. Thus, he says: 'It is suffering because of the oppression of the individual.' 'The word 'suffering'' (dukkhavacanaṃ) refers to the Teacher's statement 'suffering'.

“Natthi etassa vasavattako”ti iminā natthi etassa attāti anattāti imamatthaṃ dasseti, “nāpi idaṃ vasavattaka”nti iminā pana na attāti anattāti. Attanoti niyakajjhattaṃ sandhāya vadati. Parasminti tato aññasmiṃ. Parassa ca attanīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Taṃ etassa natthīti taṃ yathāvuttaparaparikappitaṃ vasavattakaṃ etassa cakkhādino natthi, etena catukoṭikasuññatāya saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. “Suññaṃ taṃ tena vasavattanākārenā”ti iminā ubhayathāpi avasavattanaṭṭhe dassitabbe tattha tāva ekaṃ dassetuṃ “parassā”tiādiṃ vatvā puna “atha vā”tiādinā itaraṃ dasseti. Sāmi eva sāmiko, na sāmiko assāmikoti evaṃ atthe gayhamāne “assāmikato”ti padassa suññavisesanatāya payojanaṃ natthi. Kāmakāriyanti yathākāmakaraṇīyaṃ. Avasavattanatthaṃ visesetvā dasseti samāsadvayatthasaṅgahato.

'There is no controller of this' (natthi etassa vasavattako) shows the meaning 'there is no self in this, hence it is non-self.' But 'nor is this controllable' (nāpi idaṃ vasavattakaṃ) indicates 'not self, therefore non-self.' 'Of oneself' (attano) refers to one's own inner being. 'In another' (parasmiṃ) means in someone different from that. And regarding 'of another and in oneself' (parassa ca attani), the same method applies. That, the previously described controller imagined by others, does not exist in this, that is, in the eye, etc.; by this, its inclusion in the fourfold emptiness should be understood. By 'empty is that of such controlling power' (suññaṃ taṃ tena vasavattanākārenā), when the meaning of non-control is to be shown in both ways, to explain one aspect, it states 'of another,' etc., and then, with 'or,' it explains the other. An owner is indeed a master; one who is not a master is without a master. If the meaning is taken thus, the word 'without a master' (assāmikato) serves no purpose as a qualifier of emptiness. 'Subject to one's will' (kāmakāriyaṃ) means doing as one wishes. It shows the meaning of non-control by specifying it, due to the inclusion of the meaning of the two compounds.

Sasantāne dhammānaṃ visadisuppatti idha bhāvasaṅkantigamanaṃ nāmāti āha “santatiyaṃ bhāvantaruppattiyevā”ti. Tathā visadisuppattiyaṃ purimākāravigamo pakatibhāvavijahananti āha “santatiyā yathāpavattākāravijahana”nti. Bhavatīti vā bhāvo, avatthāviseso, tassa saṅkamanaṃ bhāvasaṅkanti. Sabhāvadhammo hi uppādakkhaṇaṃ ṭhitikkhaṇañca patvā bhijjatīti uppādāvatthāya jarāvatthaṃ, tato bhaṅgāvatthaṃ saṅkamatīti vuccati. Tathā saṅkamato ca attalābhakkhaṇato uddhaṃ jarāmaraṇehi taṃsabhāvapariccāgo pakatibhāvavijahananti khaṇavasena cetaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Pubbāparavasenāti [V 0.0041] ca khaṇānaṃ pubbāparavasenāti attho sambhavati. Ekatthattāti [M 0.0043] samānādhikaraṇattā, na pana visesanavisesitabbabhāvānaṃ ekattā. “Cakkhuṃ anicca”nti vutte “aniccaṃ cakkhu”ntipi vuttameva hotīti “yaṃ cakkhu, taṃ aniccaṃ, yaṃ aniccaṃ, taṃ cakkhu”nti āpannamevāti āha “aniccānaṃ sesadhammānampi cakkhubhāvo āpajjatī”ti.

In one's own continuity, the arising of dissimilar phenomena is here called 'transition of existence.' Thus, it is said: 'It is merely the arising of a different state in the continuity.' Similarly, in the arising of dissimilar states, the disappearance of the previous form is called 'the abandoning of the natural state.' Thus, it is said: 'The abandoning of the form as it proceeded in the continuity.' Or 'existence' (bhāva) means 'that which becomes,' a particular state; its transition is 'transition of existence' (bhāvasaṅkanti). For an intrinsic phenomenon, having reached the moment of arising and the moment of stability, breaks up—thus, from the state of arising, it is said to transition to the state of decay, and from there to the state of dissolution. Likewise, as it is transitioning, the relinquishment of its intrinsic nature through aging and death after the moment of gaining existence is 'the abandoning of the natural state.' This should be related to moments. And 'by way of earlier and later' means by way of the earlier and later of moments; this meaning is possible. 'Because of being in one thing' (ekatthattā) means because they share the same substratum, but not because there is a unity of the state of being a qualifier and that which is qualified. When it is said, 'The eye is impermanent,' it is as good as saying, 'The impermanent is the eye.' Thus, 'What is the eye, that is impermanent; what is impermanent, that is the eye'—this is inevitably the case. Therefore, it is said: 'The state of being the eye would also apply to the other impermanent phenomena'.

Tehi ca aniccadukkhalakkhaṇehi ca anattalakkhaṇameva visesena dassitaṃ “yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.15, 45, 76, 85; 2.4.1, 2; paṭi. ma. 2.10) viya. Dosalakkhaṇākāranidassanatthoti dosassa lakkhitabbākāranidassanattho. Evaṃ dukkhenāti evaṃ nānappakārena akkhirogādidukkhena ābādhatāya. Anattalakkhaṇadīpakānanti anattatāpaññāpanassa jotakānaṃ upāyabhūtānaṃ. Na hi ghaṭabhedakaṇṭakavedhādivasena labbhamānā aniccadukkhatā sattānaṃ ekantato anattatādhigamahetū honti. Paccayapaṭibaddhatāabhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanādivasena pana labbhamānā honti. Tathā hi cakkhādīni kammādimahābhūtādipaccayapaṭibaddhavuttīni, tato eva ahutvā sambhavanti, hutvā paṭiventīti aniccāni, abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷitattā dukkhāni, evaṃbhūtāni ca avasavattanato anattakānīti pariggahe ṭhitehi samupacitañāṇasambhārehi passituṃ sakkā.

And by those characteristics of impermanence and suffering, the characteristic of non-self is especially shown, as in passages such as: 'What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.15, 45, 76, 85; 2.4.1, 2; Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.10). 'For the purpose of showing the characteristic mode of fault' (dosalakkhaṇākāranidassanattho) means for the purpose of showing the mode to be characterized as a fault. 'Thus, through suffering' (evaṃ dukkhena) means thus through being afflicted in various ways, such as by eye disease and the like. 'The illuminators of the characteristic of non-self' (anattalakkhaṇadīpakānaṃ) refers to the means that illuminate the manifestation of non-self. For impermanence and suffering, obtained through things like the breaking of pots and the piercing of thorns, are not by themselves causes for beings to fully realize non-self. Rather, they are obtained through being bound to conditions, through constant oppression, and the like. Indeed, the eye and other faculties, whose occurrences are bound to conditions such as kamma, the great elements, and so forth, arise having not been before and, having been, cease—thus, they are impermanent. Being constantly oppressed, they are suffering. And being of such a nature, due to their uncontrollability, they are non-self. For those established in comprehension, with accumulated stores of knowledge, it is possible to see this.

Kathaṃ panetesaṃ hutvā abhāvo jānitabboti? Khaṇe khaṇe aññathattadassanato. Taṃ kathaṃ ñāyatīti? Yuttito. Kā panettha yuttīti? Visesaggahaṇaṃ. Yadi cakkhādīnaṃ khaṇe khaṇe aññathattaṃ na siyā, bahipaccayabhede yadidaṃ pacchā visesaggahaṇaṃ, taṃ na siyā. Yassa hi tādisaṃ khaṇe khaṇe aññathattaṃ natthi, tassa asati bahipaccayavisese kathaṃ pacchā visesaggahaṇaṃ bhaveyya, bhavati ca visesaggahaṇaṃ. Tasmā atthi nesaṃ khaṇe khaṇe aññathattaṃ yaṃ saṇikaṃ saṇikaṃ vaḍḍhentaṃ pacchā pākaṭataraṃ jāyatīti. Tathā hi sarīrassa tāva ānāpānānaṃ anavatthānato parissamato ca visesaggahaṇaṃ. Anavatthitā hi assāsapassāsā vātā vārena vārena pavattanato. Yadi hi assasite vā passassite vā sarīrassa koci pacchā viseso na siyā, na nesaṃ [M 0.0044] koci bhedo siyā, diṭṭho ca so. Tasmā assasitaṃ sarīraṃ aññathā hontaṃ kamena tādisaṃ avatthaṃ pāpuṇāti. Yā passāsassa paccayo hoti, passasite ca puna tatheva assāsassa paccayo hotīti ānāpānānaṃ anavatthānatopi sarīrassa visesaggahaṇaṃ [V 0.0042] aññathattasiddhi. Tathā parissamopi asati visese pacchā sarīrassa na siyā, yenāyaṃ iriyāpathantarādīni sevanena parissamavinodanaṃ karoti.

How then is their having come into being and then ceasing to be known? By seeing their moment-to-moment otherness. How is this known? By reasoning. And what is the reasoning here? The perception of distinctions. If there were no moment-to-moment otherness in the eye and so on, then the later perception of distinctions—which arises when external conditions differ—would not occur. For something that lacks such moment-to-moment otherness, how could there later be a perception of distinctions when there is no specific external condition? Yet such perception of distinctions does occur. Therefore, there is indeed moment-to-moment otherness in them, which, increasing little by little, gradually becomes more evident. For example, in the case of the body, the perception of distinctions arises from the instability of in-and-out breaths and from exertion. The in-and-out breaths are unstable because the winds occur in turn. If after inhaling or exhaling there were no subsequent distinction in the body, there would be no difference between them; but such a difference is seen. Therefore, the body, having inhaled, becomes otherwise and gradually reaches such a state that it becomes a condition for exhaling; and having exhaled, again in the same way, it becomes a condition for inhaling. Thus, from the instability of in-and-out breaths, the body’s perception of distinctions and the establishment of otherness are proven. Similarly, if there were no distinction, there would be no subsequent exertion in the body, by which one relieves fatigue by resorting to changes in posture and so on.

Atha vā rūpādibhedatopi visesaggahaṇaṃ. Rūpagandharasaphassādīnañhi visesena yo sarīre anindriyabaddhesu ca khīrūdakavatthapupphaphalosadhidhaññādīnaṃ pacchā viseso gayhati, so asati bahipaccayavisese nesaṃ jarādiavatthāsu vaṇṇabalādibhedo, rasavīriyavipākānubhāvabhedo ca khaṇe khaṇe aññathattaṃ vinā kathamupalabbheyya. Yaṃ pana taṃ dhammatārūpaṃ silādi, tattha kathanti? Tassāpi sītuṇhasamphassabhedato attheva visesaggahaṇaṃ. Taṃ khaṇe khaṇe aññathattaṃ vinā na yujjatīti. Sati ca rūpādibhede siddhova taṃnissayamahābhūtabhedopi. Na hi nissayamahābhūtabhedena vinā nissitabhedo sambhavatīti. Evaṃ tāva rūpadhammānaṃ visesaggahaṇato khaṇe khaṇe aññathattaṃ, tato ca hutvā abhāvasiddhi.

Alternatively, the grasping of distinctions also arises from the diversity of forms and so on. For indeed, specific characteristics of form, odor, taste, touch, etc., whether in the body (not bound by the faculties) or in external things like milk, water, cloth, flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, grains, etc., are grasped afterward as distinctions. Without a distinction in external conditions, how could differences in color, strength, etc., in their successive stages of aging and so on, or differences in taste, potency, result, and influence, be perceived without moment-to-moment otherness? But how is it in regard to that natural form like stone and so on? There also, the grasping of distinctions certainly exists due to differences in cold and hot contact. Without moment-to-moment otherness, that would not be fitting. And with distinctions in form, etc., established, the diversity of the supporting great elements dependent on them is also established. For without diversity in the supporting great elements, the diversity of what is dependent cannot occur. Thus, from the grasping of distinctions in material phenomena, moment-to-moment otherness is established, and from that, the establishment of their having come into being and then ceased to be.

Arūpadhammānaṃ pana ārammaṇādibhedena visesaggahaṇaṃ. Yattha yattha hi ārammaṇe arūpadhammā uppajjanti, tattha tattheva te bhijjanti, na aññaṃ saṅkamanti, ārammaṇadhammā ca yathāsakaṃ khaṇato uddhaṃ na tiṭṭhantīti. Svāyamattho padīpādiudāharaṇena veditabbo. Aññe eva hi khaṇe khaṇe rūpādayo padīpajālāya, tathā khīradhārādīsu patantīsu, vāyumhi ca paharante samphassāni. Yathā cetesaṃ khaṇe khaṇe aññathattaṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana cittacetasikānaṃ. Kiñca saddabhedato, saddavisesatopi tannimittānaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ khaṇe khaṇe aññathattaṃ, tato visesaggahaṇaṃ. Paguṇañhi ganthaṃ sīghaṃ parivattentassa cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ saddānaṃ [M 0.0045] bhedo diṭṭho. Na hi kāraṇabhedena vinā phalabhedo atthi. Yathā taṃ vāditasaddānaṃ, evaṃ ārammaṇabhedena arūpadhammānaṃ visesaggahaṇaṃ. Teneva nesaṃ khaṇe khaṇe aññathattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Jātibhūmisampayuttadhammabhedena visesaggahaṇepi eseva nayo. Evaṃ rūpārūpadhammānaṃ visesaggahaṇato khaṇe khaṇe aññathattasiddhi. Yato hutvā abhāvato cakkhādīni aniccānīti siddhāni, aniccattā eva abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanato dukkhāni, tato ca avasavattanato anattakāni. Tenāha bhagavā “yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.15, 45, 76, 85; 2.4.1, 2; paṭi. ma. 2.10).

As for immaterial phenomena, their distinctions are grasped through differences in their objects and so on. For wherever immaterial phenomena arise in relation to an object, there they also cease, without shifting elsewhere. And objective phenomena do not persist beyond their own moment. This meaning should be understood by means of examples such as a lamp. For in each successive moment, forms and other phenomena—like the flame of a lamp, falling streams of milk, or contacts in the blowing wind—are different. Since these change moment by moment, what need be said of mental and associated phenomena? Furthermore, due to the differentiation of sounds and distinctions among sounds, the mental and associated phenomena that take them as their objects also change moment by moment; hence, distinctions are grasped. For one skilled in swiftly reciting a text, the variation in sounds produced by the mind is evident. Indeed, there is no variation in effect without a variation in cause. Just as with the sounds of musical instruments, so too is the grasping of distinctions in immaterial phenomena due to differences in objects. Thus, their moment-to-moment alteration is to be understood. The same method applies to grasping distinctions based on differences in birth, plane, and associated phenomena. In this way, through grasping the distinctions of material and immaterial phenomena, their moment-to-moment alteration is established. Since they are subject to ceasing after arising, the eye and so on are proven to be impermanent. Because of this impermanence, they are suffering due to constant oppression. And because they are not subject to control, they are non-self. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "What is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is non-self" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.15, 45, 76, 85; 2.4.1, 2; Paṭisambhidāmagga 2.10).

Nirantaraṃ [V 0.0043] pavattamānassāti abhiṇhasaddatthaṃ visesetvā vadati. Dhātumattatāyāti dhātumattabhāvena. Samūhatoti sasambhāracakkhādipiṇḍato. “Cakkhādīna”nti idaṃ “samūhato”ti padaṃ apekkhitvā sambandhe sāmivacanaṃ, “vinibbhujana”nti padaṃ apekkhitvā kammattheti veditabbaṃ. Cattāripi ghanānīti santatisamūhakiccārammaṇaghanāni. Pavattarūpādiggahaṇatoti ruppanādivasena pavattañca taṃ rūpādiggahaṇañcāti pavattarūpādiggahaṇaṃ, tatoti yojetabbaṃ. Aniccādiggahaṇassa sabbhāvāti rūpavedanādiñāṇato bhinnassa aniccādiñāṇassa labbhamānattā. Tena satipi rūpādiatthānaṃ aniccādibhāve ruppanādibhāvato aniccādibhāvassa bhedamāha. Idāni tameva bhedaṃ ñātatīraṇapariññāvisayatāya pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ “na hī”tiādimāha. Nātidhāvitunti idha lakkhaṇalakkhaṇavantā bhinnā vuttā. Tattha lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāya khandhārammaṇatāvacanena abhinnāti aññamaññavirodhāpādanena atidhāvituṃ na yuttaṃ. Kasmāti ce? Vuttaṃ “te panākārā”tiādi. Adhippāyopi cettha lakkhaṇānaṃ rūpādiākāramattatāvibhāvananti daṭṭhabbo. “Aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti hi saṅkhāre sabhāvato sallakkhentoyeva lakkhaṇāni ca sallakkhetīti. Yathā aniccādito aniccatādīnaṃ vuttanayena bhedo, evaṃ aniccatādīnampi satipi lakkhaṇabhāvasāmaññe nānāñāṇagocaratāya, nānāpaṭipakkhatāya, nānindriyādhikatāya ca vimokkhamukhattayabhūtānaṃ aññamaññabhedoti dassento “aniccanti ca gaṇhanto”tiādimāha. Taṃ suviññeyyameva.

The phrase 'continually occurring' is said to specify the meaning of 'constant' (abhiṇha). 'By the state of being mere elements' means by being mere elements. 'From a mass' refers to the eye and so forth as a collection with its components. The phrase 'of the eye and so on' (cakkhādīnaṃ) should be understood as a genitive case in relation to the word 'from a mass' (samūhato), and as an accusative case in relation to the word 'disintegration' (vinibbhujanaṃ). 'The four compacts' refer to the compacts of continuity, mass, function, and object. 'From the grasping of form, etc., that has arisen' is to be construed as the grasping of form, etc., which has arisen in the sense of being afflicted and so on; thus, it should be connected to 'that' (tato). 'The existence of the grasping of impermanence, etc.' is because the knowledge of impermanence, etc., which is distinct from the knowledge of form, feeling, etc., is obtainable. Therefore, even though things such as form have the nature of impermanence, etc., it speaks of a difference between their state of being afflicted, etc., and their state of impermanence, etc. Now, to make that very distinction clear in terms of the scope of knowledge, judgment, and full understanding, it is said: 'For not...' and so on. 'Not to be overextended' means that here, the characteristic and what possesses the characteristic are spoken of as distinct. In that case, since insight takes characteristics as its object, it is not proper to overextend by causing a mutual contradiction, saying that the aggregates are not different as its object. Why? It is stated: 'But those aspects...' etc. Here, the intention should also be seen as the distinguishing of characteristics as mere aspects of form, etc. For indeed, when one discerns formations as inherently impermanent, suffering, and non-self, one also discerns their characteristics. Just as there is a distinction between impermanence, etc., and the state of impermanence, etc., as explained, so too, regarding the states of impermanence, etc., even though they share the commonality of being characteristics, he shows that there is a mutual distinction among them as the three gateways to liberation, due to their being the domain of different knowledges, having different opposing factors, and having different dominant faculties, by saying: 'When one grasps "impermanent"...' etc. This is very easy to understand.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Suttanta Division is concluded.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. Exposition of the Abhidhamma Division

155. Paccayayugaḷavasenāti [M 0.0046] ajjhattikabāhirapaccayadvayavasena. Ajjhattikabāhiravasena abbokāratoti ajjhattikavasena ceva bāhiravasena ca asaṅkarato.

155. 'By way of a pair of conditions' means by way of the two conditions, internal and external. 'By way of internal and external, unmixed' means without confusion between the internal and external.

167. Visaṅkhāraninnassāti nibbānapoṇassa. Vinimuttasaṅkhārassāti samucchedapaṭipassaddhivimuttīhi samukhena, tappaṭibaddhachandarāgappahānena ca suṭṭhu vinimuttasaṅkhārassa paramassāsabhāvena, gatibhāvena ca patiṭṭhānabhūte. “Nibbānaṃ arahato gatī”ti (paṭi. 339) hi [V 0.0044] vuttaṃ. Ṭhitibhāvenāti ca pāṭho. Taṃsacchikaraṇābhāveti tassa nibbānassa sacchikaraṇābhāve. Nītoti pāpito, pakāsitoti attho.

167. 'Visaṅkhāraninnassa' means inclined towards the unconditioned, that is, Nibbāna. 'Vinimuttasaṅkhārassa' means that for one who is well-liberated from formations—by means of liberation through cutting off and pacification, and by the abandonment of desire and lust connected with them—Nibbāna is the foundation, having the nature of ultimate solace and being a destination. For it is said, 'Nibbāna is the destination of the Arahant' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.339). There is also a reading as 'Ṭhitibhāvena,' meaning by the state of stability. 'Taṃsacchikaraṇābhāve' refers to the absence of the realization of that Nibbāna. 'Nīto' means led, that is, made clear.

Cuṇṇitanti bheditaṃ. Tvameva kiṃ na jānāsīti kiṃ tvaṃ na jānāsiyevāti attho. “Kiṃ tvaṃ ekaṃ nānaṃ jānāsi, kiṃ tvaṃ na jānāsi evā”ti evaṃ vikkhepaṃ karontaṃ paravādiṃ “nanu ñāte”tiādinā sakavādī nibandhati. Vibhajitvāti “rāgādīnaṃ khīṇante uppannattā”ti bhāvatthaṃ vibhajitvā. Rāgādīnaṃ khayā na hontīti yojanā. Sasabhāvatā ca nibbānassa āpannā hotīti sambandho.

'Cuṇṇitaṃ' means broken or crushed. 'Tvameva kiṃ na jānāsi?' means 'Do you yourself not know?' The meaning is, 'Do you indeed not know?' When the opponent creates confusion by saying, 'Do you know one as many? Or do you not know at all?' the proponent counters with 'nanu ñāte' and so forth, establishing his own position. 'Vibhajitvā' means analyzing, stating the meaning, 'Because of their arising when lust, etc., are destroyed.' The construction is: 'They are not the destruction of lust, etc.' The connection is that Nibbāna's own nature is attained.

Nibbānārammaṇakaraṇena kāraṇabhūtena. Hetuatthe hi idaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Kilesakkhayamattataṃ vā nibbānassa icchato kilesakkhayena bhavitabbanti yojanā.

By making Nibbāna the object, which is the cause. For this instrumental case is in the sense of cause. Or, for one who desires Nibbāna to be merely the destruction of defilements, the construction is that it must come to be by the destruction of defilements.

Evaṃ kilesakkhayamatte nibbāne khepetabbā kilesā bahuvidhā nānappakārā, maggo ca odhiso kilese khepeti. Svāyaṃ “katamaṃ kilesakkhayaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā katame kilese khepetī”ti purimapucchādvayameva vadati. Tadevāti yaṃ “avijjātaṇhānaṃ kiñci ekadesamattampī”ti vuttaṃ, tadeva.

Thus, when Nibbāna is merely the destruction of defilements, the defilements to be eradicated are of various kinds and diverse, and the path eradicates the defilements specifically. This simply states the previous two questions: 'Having made which destruction of defilements the object, which defilements does Nibbāna eradicate?' 'That same' refers to what was said: 'Even some mere portion of ignorance and craving.'

Ettha ca yāyaṃ “kilesakkhayova nibbāna”nti nibbānassa abhāvatācodanā, tatrāyaṃ āgamato yuttito cassa bhāvābhāvavibhāvanā. Tañhi bhagavatā –

Here, regarding the statement 'Nibbāna is merely the destruction of defilements,' which is an accusation of the non-existence of Nibbāna, this is the demonstration of its existence and non-existence based on scripture and reasoning. For that has been said by the Blessed One—

“Atthi, bhikkhave, ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhata”nti (udā. 73; itivu. 43).

'Monks, there is the unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned' (Udāna 8.3).

“Atthi[M 0.0047], bhikkhave, tadāyatanaṃ, yattha neva pathavī na āpo na tejo na vāyo”ti (udā. 71) –

'Monks, there is that dimension where there is neither earth, nor water, nor fire, nor air' (Udāna 8.1)—

Ca ādinā, tathā –

and so on, and likewise—

“Gambhīro [V 0.0045] duddaso duranubodho santo paṇīto atakkāvacaro nipuṇo paṇḍitavedanīyo”ti (ma. ni. 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7-8) –

‘Deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise’ (MN 2.337; SN 1.172; Mahāvagga 7–8)—

“Asaṅkhatañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi asaṅkhatagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ, anataṃ, anāsavaṃ, saccaṃ, pāraṃ, nipuṇaṃ, sududdasaṃ, ajajjaraṃ, dhuvaṃ, apalokitaṃ, anidassanaṃ, nippapañcaṃ, santaṃ, amataṃ, paṇītaṃ, sivaṃ, khemaṃ, taṇhākkhayaṃ, acchariyaṃ, abbhutaṃ, anītikaṃ, anītikadhammaṃ, nibbānaṃ, abyābajjhaṃ, virāgaṃ, suddhiṃ, muttiṃ, anālayaṃ, dīpaṃ, leṇaṃ, tāṇaṃ, saraṇaṃ, parāyaṇañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi parāyaṇagāminiñca paṭipada”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.377) –

‘I will teach you the unconditioned, monks, and the path leading to the unconditioned: the endless, the taintless, the truth, the further shore, the subtle, the very hard to see, the undecaying, the stable, the imperishable, the unseen, the unproliferated, the peaceful, the deathless, the sublime, the auspicious, the secure, the destruction of craving, the amazing, the wondrous, the unafflicted, the unafflicted state, Nibbāna, the unoppressed, dispassion, purity, freedom, the unattached, the island, the shelter, the protection, the refuge, and the final resort. And I will teach you the final resort, monks, and the path leading to the final resort’ (SN 4.377)—

Evamādīhi ca suttapadehi “appaccayā dhammā, asaṅkhatā dhammā (dha. sa. dukamātikā 7), sabbañca rūpaṃ asaṅkhatā ca dhātū”tiādīhi (dha. sa. 1192, 1198, 1200) abhidhammapadesehi ca paramatthabhāveneva desitaṃ. Na hi sabhāvavirahitassa abhāvamattassa gambhīrāsaṅkhatādibhāvo abyākatadhammādibhāvo ca yutto, vutto ca so. Tasmā na abhāvamattaṃ nibbānaṃ.

And by such sutta passages as these, and by Abhidhamma passages such as ‘causeless phenomena, unconditioned phenomena’ (Dhs. Duka-mātikā 7), and ‘all form and the unconditioned element,’ etc. (Dhs. 1192, 1198, 1200), it is taught as an ultimate reality. For what is devoid of intrinsic nature, a mere absence, cannot properly be described as profound, unconditioned, etc., nor as an indeterminate phenomenon, yet it is so described. Therefore, Nibbāna is not a mere absence.

Api cāyaṃ abhāvavādī evaṃ pucchitabbo – yadi kilesābhāvo nibbānaṃ, svāyamabhāvo eko vā siyā aneko vā? Yadi eko, ekeneva maggena kato sacchikato ca hotīti uparimānaṃ maggānaṃ niratthakatā āpajjati. Na hi ekaṃ anekehi kammappavattehi sādhetabbaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. Atha siyā ekova so kilesābhāvo, na pana maggehi kātabbo, atha kho sacchikātabboti. Evaṃ sati suṭṭhutaraṃ maggassa niratthakatā āpajjati kilesānaṃ appahānato. Akaronto ca maggo kilesābhāvaṃ tassa sacchikiriyāya [M 0.0048] kamatthaṃ sādheyya, atha maggānaṃ saṃyojanattayappahānādipaṭiniyatakiccatāya pahāyakavibhāgena kilesābhāvabhedo, evaṃ sati vinā sabhāvabhedaṃ bahubhāvo natthīti bahubhāvatāpadesenassa sasabhāvatā āpannā. Athāpi siyā “yesaṃ abhāvo, tesaṃ bahubhāvena bahubhāvopacāro”ti, evaṃ sati yesaṃ abhāvo, tesaṃ sabhāvatāya sasabhāvopacāropi siyā. Tathā tesaṃ kilesasaṅkhatāditāya kilesasaṅkhatādibhāvā ca siyuṃ, na cetaṃ yuttanti na tesaṃ bahubhāvopacāro yutto. Ekabhāvopi [V 0.0046] cassa asabhāvatāya eva vattuṃ na sakkāti ce? Na, abhāvasāmaññato, abhāvasāmaññena abhedasamaññāya ekattaniddeso. Sati ca ekatte pubbe vuttadosānativatti.

Moreover, this advocate of non-existence should be asked thus: If the non-existence of defilements is Nibbāna, is this non-existence one or many? If one, then since it is accomplished and realized by a single path, the higher paths would become useless. For it is not seen that one thing is to be accomplished by many acts of practice. But if that non-existence of defilements were one, and not to be brought about by the paths, but rather to be realized, then in that case, the uselessness of the path would be even more evident, as the defilements would not be abandoned. And if the path does not bring about this non-existence, for what purpose would it serve in its realization? If, however, the non-existence of defilements is divided by way of abandoning, due to the specific functions of the paths in abandoning the three fetters, etc., then without a difference in intrinsic nature, there is no plurality—thus, by the designation of plurality, it would be admitted to have intrinsic nature. Or if it were said, ‘the designation of plurality is a figure of speech based on the plurality of those things whose non-existence it is,’ then in that case, because of the intrinsic nature of those things, there would also be a figurative designation of its having intrinsic nature. And thus, because those things are defilements, conditioned, and so on, this non-existence would also have the nature of being a defilement, conditioned, and so on; and this is not reasonable, so the figurative designation of its plurality is not reasonable. If it is said: ‘But cannot its singularity also be spoken of as being without intrinsic nature?’ No, because of the generality of non-existence; the description of unity is by the generality of non-existence, by the generality of non-difference. And if there is unity, the previously stated faults are not overcome.

Bahubhāve ca sasabhāvatā siddhā. Yadipi siyā yathā bahubhāvo sasabhāvataṃ, evaṃ sāmaññena sasabhāvatā bahubhāvaṃ na byabhicareyyāti sasabhāvapakkhepi nibbānassa bahubhāvo āpajjatīti? Taṃ na, kasmā? Tathā sāmaññābhedato. Na hi evaṃ vattuṃ labbhā yathā kharabhāvo sasabhāvataṃ na byabhicarati, evaṃ sasabhāvatāpi kharabhāvaṃ na byabhicareyyāti. Evañhi sati tadaññasabbadhammābhāvappasaṅgo siyā, tasmā bahubhāvo sasabhāvatāpekkho, na sasabhāvatā bahubhāvāpekkhāti na sasabhāvassa nibbānassa bahubhāvāpatti. “Ekañhi saccaṃ na dutīyamatthi (su. ni. 890; mahāni. 119), ekā niṭṭhā na puthuniṭṭhā”tiādivacanato.

And in the case of plurality, having intrinsic nature is established. Even if it were that just as plurality does not deviate from having intrinsic nature, so too, generally, having intrinsic nature should not deviate from plurality, then would plurality also apply to Nibbāna, even on the side of it having intrinsic nature? That is not so. Why? Because of the non-difference of generality in that way. For it cannot be said that just as hardness does not deviate from having intrinsic nature, so too having intrinsic nature should not deviate from hardness. If this were the case, it would imply the absence of all other phenomena. Therefore, plurality is dependent on having intrinsic nature, but having intrinsic nature is not dependent on plurality. Hence, plurality cannot be attributed to Nibbāna, which has its own intrinsic nature. ‘For there is one truth, there is no second; one consummation, not many consummations,’ and so on, as stated in the texts.

Api cettha kilesābhāvo nāma rāgādīnaṃ samucchedo accantappahānaṃ anuppādanirodho. Tassa ca ekatte ekeneva maggena sādhetabbatā kiccavisesābhāvatoti dassanādimaggavibhāgo na siyā. Icchito ca so odhisova kilesānaṃ pahātabbattā. So ca maggavibhāgo saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ nātitikkhatikkhatikkhataratikkhatamabhāvena ekasmimpi samucchedappahānayogyabhāve [M 0.0049] sacchikiriyāvisesena hotīti nibbānassa sasabhāvatāyayeva yutto. Abhāvo pana kilesānaṃ maggena kātabbo siyā “mā maggassa niratthakatā ahosī”ti, na sacchikātabbo. Ko hi tassa sabhāvo, yo tena sacchikariyeyya. So ca kilesābhāvo ekeneva maggena sādhetabbo siyā, na catūhi “mā catubhāvanibbānatāpatti, nibbānavisesāpatti ca ahosī”ti. Tato dassanādimaggavibhāgo na siyāti sabbaṃ āvattati.

Furthermore, here, the absence of defilements means the eradication, final abandonment, and non-arising-cessation of lust and other defilements. If this were one, because it would have to be accomplished by a single path due to the absence of specific functions, there would be no division into paths such as the path of seeing, etc. And that division is desired, precisely as the limit for abandoning defilements. And that division of the path occurs through a special realization, even with the same suitability for eradication and abandonment, due to the faculties of faith, etc., being not very keen, keen, keener, and keenest; and this is fitting precisely because of Nibbāna’s having intrinsic nature. The absence of defilements, however, would have to be brought about by the path—lest the path be meaningless—but not realized. For what intrinsic nature does it have that could be realized? And that absence of defilements would have to be accomplished by a single path, not by four, lest there be the consequence of a fourfold Nibbāna and of distinctions in Nibbāna. Therefore, there would be no division into paths like the path of seeing, etc. Thus, everything reverts to the original problem.

Yadi ca abhāvo bhāvassa siyāti tassa bhāvadhammatā icchitā, evaṃ sati yathā saṅkhatadhammassa tassa jarāmaraṇādīnaṃ viya saṅkhatadhammatāpi āpannā, evaṃ bahūnaṃ kilesānaṃ dhammassa tassa bahubhāvādippasaṅgopi dunnivāroti ataṃsabhāvassa asaṅkhatassekassa sasabhāvassa nibbānabhāvo veditabbo.

And if absence were to belong to existence, its nature as an existent would be accepted. In that case, just as for a conditioned phenomenon, a conditioned nature like aging and death is entailed, so too for a phenomenon of many defilements, the implication of multiplicity and so on would be hard to avoid. Therefore, the state of Nibbāna should be understood as not having the nature of those things, as unconditioned, as singular, and as having its own intrinsic nature.

Yadi [V 0.0047] evaṃ kasmā “rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.315, 330) vuttanti? Khayena adhigantabbattā. Khayo hi ariyamaggo. Yathāha “khaye ñāṇaṃ, anuppāde ñāṇa”nti (dha. sa. dukamātikā 142). Tena rāgādikkhayapariyāyena ariyamaggena adhigantabbato “paramatthaṃ gambhīraṃ nipuṇaṃ duddasaṃ duranubodhaṃ nibbānaṃ rāgādikkhayo”ti vuttaṃ. Rāgādippahānamukhena vā tathā pattabbato, yathā aññatthāpi vuttaṃ “madanimmaddano pipāsavinayo”tiādi (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90).

If so, why is it said, ‘The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion’ (SN 4.315, 330)? Because it is to be attained by way of destruction. For destruction is the Noble Path. As it is said, ‘Knowledge in destruction, knowledge in non-arising’ (Dhs. Dukamātikā 142). Therefore, because it is to be attained by the Noble Path, which is a synonym for the destruction of lust, etc., it is said, ‘Nibbāna, which is ultimate, profound, subtle, hard to see, hard to understand, is the destruction of lust, etc.’ Or because it is attainable in that way through the gateway of the abandonment of lust, etc., as it is said elsewhere, ‘The crushing of conceit, the removal of thirst,’ and so on (AN 4.34; Itiv 90).

Apica yathā pariññeyyatāya sauttarānaṃ kāmānaṃ rūpānañca paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ tabbidhurasabhāvaṃ nissaraṇaṃ paññāyati, evaṃ sasabhāvānaṃ sabbesampi saṅkhatadhammānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtena tabbidhurasabhāvena nissaraṇena bhavitabbaṃ. Yañca tannissaraṇaṃ, sā asaṅkhatā dhātu. Kiñca bhiyyo – saṅkhatadhammārammaṇaṃ vipassanāñāṇaṃ api anulomañāṇaṃ kilese tadaṅgavasena pajahati, na samucchedavasena [M 0.0050] pajahituṃ sakkoti. Tathā sammutisaccārammaṇaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīsu ñāṇaṃ vikkhambhanavaseneva kilese pajahati, na samucchedavasena. Iti saṅkhatadhammārammaṇassa, sammutisaccārammaṇassa ca ñāṇassa kilesānaṃ samucchedappahāne asamatthabhāvato tesaṃ samucchedappahānakarassa ariyamaggañāṇassa tadubhayaviparītasabhāvena ārammaṇena bhavitabbaṃ, sā asaṅkhatā dhātu. Tathā “atthi, bhikkhave, ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhata”nti (udā. 73; itivu. 43) idaṃ nibbānassa paramatthato atthibhāvajotakaṃ vacanaṃ aviparītatthaṃ bhagavatā bhāsitattā. Yañhi bhagavatā bhāsitaṃ, taṃ aviparītatthaṃ yathā taṃ “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā, sabbe dhammā anattā”ti (dha. pa. 277-279; theragā. 676-678; netti. 5), tathā nibbāna-saddo katthaci visaye yathābhūtaparamatthavisayo upacāravuttisabbhāvato seyyathāpi sīha-saddo. Atha vā attheva paramatthato asaṅkhatā dhātu itaratabbiparītavimuttisabhāvattā seyyathāpi “pathavīdhātu vedanā cā”ti evamādīhi nayehi yuttitopi asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā paramatthato atthibhāvo veditabbo.

Furthermore, just as the escape from the sensual and form realms, which are to be fully understood and have a superior state beyond them, is discerned as being opposed to them and having a nature far removed from them, so too must there be an escape from all conditioned phenomena, which have their own intrinsic nature, with a nature opposed to them and far removed from them. And that escape is the unconditioned element. Moreover, insight knowledge that takes conditioned phenomena as its object, and even conformity knowledge, abandons defilements by way of substitution; it is not able to abandon them by way of eradication.
