Similarly, knowledge in the first jhāna and so on, which takes conventional truth as its object, abandons defilements only by way of suppression, not by way of eradication. Thus, because knowledge that takes conditioned phenomena or conventional truth as its object is incapable of eradicating defilements, the noble path knowledge, which accomplishes their eradication, must have an object with a nature opposite to both—that is the unconditioned element. Likewise, the statement, 'There is, monks, the unborn, the unbecome, the unmade, the unconditioned' (Udā. 73; Itivu. 43), is a declaration that illuminates the existence of Nibbāna in an ultimate sense, spoken by the Blessed One with non-perverted meaning. For whatever is spoken by the Blessed One has a non-perverted meaning, just as 'All formations are impermanent, all formations are suffering, all phenomena are not-self' (Dhp. 277-279; Thag. 676-678; Netti. 5). Similarly, the term 'Nibbāna' in some contexts refers to the ultimate reality as it truly is, due to the existence of figurative usage, just like the term 'lion.' Or, the unconditioned element truly exists in an ultimate sense because its nature is liberation, the opposite of the other. Thus, from reasoning as well, by such methods as 'the earth element and feeling,' and so on, the existence of the unconditioned element in an ultimate sense should be understood.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Abhidhamma Division is concluded.

3. Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā

3. Exposition of the Interrogation

168. Kiñcīti [V 0.0048] kiñci ārammaṇaṃ. Ālambanatoti ārammaṇakaraṇato.

168. Kiñci means any object. Ālambanato means because of making it an object.

Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Interrogation is concluded.

Āyatanavibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Analysis of the Bases is concluded.

3. Dhātuvibhaṅgo

3. The Analysis of Elements

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. Exposition of the Sutta Division

172. Abhidhamme [M 0.0051][V 0.0049] ca āgatāti imasmiṃ dhātuvibhaṅge abhidhammabhājanīyapañhapucchakesu, nikkhepakaṇḍadhammahadayavibhaṅgādīsu ca desanāruḷhā. Yathā pana suttante abhidhamme ca āgatā khandhādayo suttante desitaniyāmena khandhavibhaṅgādīsu suttantabhājanīyavasena vibhattā, evamidhāpi cakkhudhātādayo suttantabhājanīyavasena vibhajitabbā siyuṃ. Tattha khandhādīnaṃ sabbasaṅgāhako abhidhammadesanāvisiṭṭho suttante āgato añño desetabbākāro natthīti te rūpakkhandhādivaseneva suttantabhājanīye desitā, dhātūnaṃ pana so atthīti te tiṇṇaṃ dhātuchakkānaṃ vasena idha desitāti dassento āha “suttantesveva…pe… vibhattanti veditabba”nti. Tenāha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sabbā dhātuyo chahi chahi dhātūhi saṅkhipitvā”ti.

172. 'And as found in the Abhidhamma' means that in this Analysis of Elements, the teaching is established in the Abhidhamma Division, in the Interrogation, and in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa, Dhammahadayavibhaṅga, and so on. Just as the aggregates and other teachings found in the Suttas and the Abhidhamma are analyzed in the Khandhavibhaṅga and others by way of the Sutta Division, in accordance with the method taught in the Suttas, so too here the eye-element and others should be analyzed by way of the Sutta Division. In that regard, since there is no other mode of teaching found in the Suttas that is comprehensive of all aggregates, etc., and is distinctive of the Abhidhamma exposition, they are taught in the Sutta Division by way of the aggregate of form and so on. But since there is such a method for the elements, they are taught here by way of the three hexads of elements. To show this, it is said: 'In the Suttas themselves... it should be understood as analyzed.' Therefore, it is said in the commentary: 'All the elements are summarized by six elements each.'

Kathaṃ pana chasu chasu dhātūsu aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ samavarodhoti? Sabhāvanissayadvārārammaṇasampayogasāmaññato. Tattha paṭhamachakke tāva pathavītejovāyodhātuyo sabhāvato phoṭṭhabbadhātu. Āpodhātuākāsadhātuyo dhammadhātuekadeso. Viññāṇadhātu sattaviññāṇadhātuyo. Catudhātuggahaṇena cettha tadāyattavuttikā nissayāpadesena, viññāṇadhātuyā dvārārammaṇabhāvena vā avasiṭṭhā rūpadhātuyo samavaruddhā, viññāṇadhātuggahaṇena taṃsampayogato dhammadhātuekadesoti evaṃ sabbadhātusamavarodho daṭṭhabbo. Dutiye chapi dhātuyo sabhāvato, dhammāyatanekadeso, taṃsampayogato sattaviññāṇadhātuyo, yathārahaṃ tesaṃ nissayadvārārammaṇabhāvato avasiṭṭhadhātuyo samavaruddhā. Tatiyachakkepi eseva nayo. Evamettha chasu chasu dhātūsu aṭṭhārasannaṃ dhātūnaṃ samavarodho daṭṭhabbo. Tena vuttaṃ “sabbā dhātuyo chahi chahi dhātūhi saṅkhipitvā”ti.

But how is the inclusion of the eighteen elements in sets of six elements accomplished? By way of intrinsic nature, support, door, object, association, and generality. In the first hexad, the earth, fire, and air elements are, by intrinsic nature, the tangible element. The water element and the space element are a portion of the mental-object element. The consciousness element is the seven consciousness elements. Here, by the inclusion of the four great elements, those that function dependent on them are included by way of support, or the remaining material elements are included by way of being the door and object for the consciousness element. By the inclusion of the consciousness element, a portion of the mental-object element is included due to its association with it. Thus, the inclusion of all elements should be seen. In the second hexad, the six elements are included by intrinsic nature; a portion of the mental-object base is included; the seven consciousness elements are included by association with that; and the remaining elements are included by way of being their support, door, and object, as appropriate. The same method applies to the third hexad. Thus, the inclusion of the eighteen elements in these sets of six elements should be seen. Therefore, it was said: 'All the elements are summarized by six elements each.'

Suññoti [V 0.0050] attasuñño, tena sasabhāvatāya ca idha dhātuvohāroti āha “suññe sabhāvamatte niruḷho dhātusaddo”ti. Taṃtaṃbhūtavivittatā rūpapariyantova ākāsoti yehi vivitto, yesañca [M 0.0052] paricchedo, tehi asamphuṭṭhatā tesaṃ byāpakabhāve sati na hotīti āha “catūhi mahābhūtehi abyāpitabhāvo”ti. Paricchinnavuttīni hi bhūtānīti.

'Empty' means empty of self. And because of that, and because of its own nature, the term 'element' is used here; thus it is said: 'The word "element" is established in mere nature that is empty.' Space is that which is distinct from the respective elements and is bounded by form. Since it is separate from them and is their boundary, if they were pervasive, there would be no non-contact with them. Therefore, it is said: 'It is the state of not being pervaded by the four great elements.' For the great elements function within limits.

173. Avayavavinimutto samudāyo nāma koci natthīti purimatthaṃ asambhāvento “dve eva vā”tiādinā samudāyena vinā dutiyatthamāha. Paccattaṃ attani jātatanti pāṭipuggalikataṃ.

173. Not considering the former meaning, that there is no so-called aggregate separate from its components, he states the second meaning with 'or only two,' etc., without the aggregate. 'Born individually in oneself' means individualized.

Pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāsoti vā lomādiitarakoṭṭhāsehi asammisso visuṃ eko pathavīkoṭṭhāsoti attho.

'A particular portion' means a single, separate portion of the earth element, unmixed with other portions such as hair of the head, etc.

Payoganti bhāvanāpayogaṃ. Vīriyanti bhāvanānipphādakaṃ ussāhaṃ. Āyūhananti tādisaṃ cetanaṃ.

'Application' means the application of development. 'Energy' means the effort that accomplishes development. 'Exertion' means such volition.

Dhātupaṭikkūlavaṇṇamanasikārānanti dhātumanasikārapaṭikkūlamanasikāravaṇṇamanasikārānaṃ. Abyāpāratāyāti “ahametaṃ nipphādemi, mama esā nipphādanā”ti cetanārahitatāya. Karontīti ābhogapaccavekkhaṇāni uppādenti.

'Of the reflections on elements, repulsiveness, and color' means of the reflection on elements, the reflection on repulsiveness, and the reflection on color. 'By non-activity' means by being devoid of the volition, 'I produce this, this is my production.' 'They do' means they generate advertence and reviewing.

Lakkhaṇavasenāti sabhāvavasena. So pana yasmā pathavīdhātuyā kakkhaḷakharatā hotīti āha “kakkhaḷaṃ kharigatantiādivacanaṃ sandhāya vutta”nti.

'By way of characteristic' means by way of intrinsic nature. And since the intrinsic nature of the earth element is hardness and roughness, it is said, referring to the statement, 'Hardness, roughness, etc.'

Vekantakaṃ nāma sabbalohacchedanasamatthaṃ lohaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ vikantati chindatīti vikantaṃ, vikantameva vekantakanti vuccati. Lohasadisanti lohākāraṃ lohamalaṃ viya ghanasahitaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati. Tāpetvā tāḷitaṃ pana chinnaṃ chinnaṃ hutvā visarati, mudu maṭṭhaṃ kammaniyaṃ vā na hoti, tena “lohavijātī”ti vuccatīti. Tiputambādīhīti tiputambe missetvā kataṃ kaṃsalohaṃ, sīsatambe missetvā kataṃ vaṭṭalohaṃ, jasadatambe missetvā kataṃ ārakūṭaṃ[V 0.0051]. Yaṃ pana kevalaṃ jasadadhātuviniggataṃ, yaṃ “pittala”ntipi vadanti, taṃ idha nādhippetaṃ, yathāvuttamissakameva pana gahetvā “kittima”nti vuttaṃ.

The term 'vekantaka' refers to a metal capable of cutting all other metals. Indeed, it cuts and severs, thus it is 'cutting' (vikanta), and 'vikanta' itself is termed 'vekantaka.' 'It resembles metal' means it has the appearance of metal, remaining dense like metal dross. However, when heated and struck, it shatters into pieces and disperses; it does not become soft, smooth, or workable. Therefore, it is called 'a different kind of metal.' 'With tin and copper, etc.' refers to bronze made by mixing tin and copper, vaṭṭaloha made by mixing lead and copper, and bell metal made by mixing zinc and copper. But that which is produced purely from zinc ore—which some also call 'brass'—is not intended here. Only the aforementioned mixture is taken and called 'artificial.'

Nidassanamattanti muttānaṃ jātito anekabhedattā vuttaṃ. Tathā hi hatthikumbhaṃ varāhadāṭhaṃ bhujaṅgasīsaṃ valāhakūṭaṃ veṇupabbaṃ macchasiro saṅkho sippīti [M 0.0053] aṭṭha muttāyoniyo. Tattha hatthikumbhajā pītavaṇṇā pabhāhīnā. Varāhadāṭhajā varāhadāṭhavaṇṇāva. Bhujaṅgasīsajā nīlādivaṇṇā suvisuddhā, vaṭṭalā ca. Valāhakajā bhāsurā dubbibhāgarūpā rattibhāge andhakāraṃ vidhamantā tiṭṭhanti, devūpabhogā eva honti. Veṇupabbajā kāraphalasamānavaṇṇā, na bhāsurā, te ca veḷavo amanussagocare eva padese jāyanti. Macchasīsajā pāṭhīnapiṭṭhisamānavaṇṇā, vaṭṭalā, laghavo ca honti pabhāvihīnā, te ca macchā samuddamajjheyeva jāyanti. Saṅkhajā saṅkhoracchavivaṇṇā, kolappamāṇāpi honti pabhāvihīnāva. Sippijā pana pabhāvisesayuttāva honti nānāsaṇṭhānā. Evaṃ jātito aṭṭhavidhāsu muttāsu yā macchasaṅkhasippijā, tā sāmuddikā. Bhujaṅgajāpi kāci sāmuddikāti vadanti, itarā asāmuddikā. Tena vuttaṃ “sāmuddikamuttāti nidassanamattametaṃ, sabbāpi pana muttā muttā evā”ti. Bahulato vā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ etaṃ vuttaṃ “muttāti sāmuddikamuttā”ti. Bahulañhi loke sāmuddikāva muttā dissanti. Tatthāpi sippijāva, itarā kadāci kācīti.

The phrase 'merely illustrative' is said because pearls are of many kinds by origin. Indeed, there are eight sources of pearls: the elephant's frontal globes, the boar's tusk, the serpent's head, the cloud's peak, the bamboo joint, the fish's head, the conch, and the oyster. Among these, those born from an elephant's frontal globes are yellow in color and lack radiance. Those from a boar's tusk are of the same color as a boar's tusk. Those from a serpent's head have colors like blue, etc., are very pure, and are round. Those from clouds are radiant, of indistinct form, and dispel darkness at night; they are only for the enjoyment of deities. Those from bamboo joints are of the same color as a kāra fruit, are not radiant, and those bamboos grow only in places frequented by non-humans. Those from a fish's head are of the same color as a pāṭhīna fish's back, are round, light, and lack radiance; these fish are born only in the middle of the ocean. Those from conchs are of the same color as a conch shell, can be the size of a jujube fruit, and also lack radiance. Those from oysters, however, possess special radiance and come in various shapes. Thus, among the eight kinds of pearls by origin, those from fish, conchs, and oysters are marine. Some say even those from serpents are marine, while the others are non-marine. Therefore, it is said, 'marine pearls are merely illustrative, but all pearls are indeed pearls.' Or, for the most part, the commentary states, 'pearls mean marine pearls,' for mostly, marine pearls are seen in the world. Among them, those from oysters are most common, while others are found only occasionally.

174. Idha natthi niyamo kevalaṃ dravabhāvasseva adhippetattā.

174. Here, there is no fixed rule, since only the liquid state is intended.

175. Nisitabhāvenāti santāpanādivasappavattena tikhiṇabhāvena. Usmākārañhi nisānaṃ idha nisitabhāvo. Pākatikoti sābhāviko kāyusmāti adhippeto. Sadāti sabbakālaṃ yāva jīvitindriyaṃ pavattati. Petaggi nijjhāmataṇhikapetaggi. Idhāti bāhiratejodhātukathāyaṃ.

175. 'By sharpness' means by sharpness due to the activity of burning, etc. For the nature of heat is sharpness here. 'Natural' means inherent, referring to bodily heat. 'Always' means at all times, as long as the life faculty lasts. 'Ghost-fire' is the ghost-fire of those consumed by craving. 'Here' means in the discussion of the external fire element.

176. Vāyanaṃ bījanaṃ, taṃ pana thāmasā pavattīti āha “savegagamanavasenā”ti. Samudīraṇaṃ allaparisosanaṃ, bhūtasaṅghātassa desantaruppattihetubhāvo vā.

176. 'Vāyana' means blowing, and it occurs forcefully; hence it is said, 'by way of forceful movement.' 'Samudīraṇa' means the drying up of moisture, or being the cause for the arising of the aggregate of elements in another place.

177. Bhitticchiddādivasena labbhamānaṃ ajaṭākāsaṃ nissāyeva paricchedākāsassa parikammakaraṇanti āha “ajaṭākāsassa ca kathitata”nti.

177. The preparation of delimited space is effected only by relying on unobstructed space obtainable through cracks in walls, etc.; hence it is said, 'and because unobstructed space has been spoken of.'

179. Sukhadukkhaphoṭṭhabbasamuṭṭhāpanapaccayabhāvenāti [V 0.0052] iṭṭhāniṭṭhaphoṭṭhabbānaṃ nibbattakabhūtena paccayabhāvena. Kassa pana so paccayabhāvoti āha “sarīraṭṭhakautussā”ti[M 0.0054]. Paccayabhāvenāti ca hetumhi karaṇavacanaṃ. Tena hi kāraṇabhūtena sukhadukkhaphoṭṭhabbānaṃ yathāvuttasamatthatā hotīti. “Tathevā”ti iminā “yathābalaṃ sarīrekadesasakalasarīra”nti idaṃ anukaḍḍhati. Evanti attano phalūpacārasiddhena pharaṇappakārena. Etesanti sukhādīnaṃ. “Oḷārikappavatti eva vā pharaṇa”nti iminā nirupacāraṃ etesaṃ pharaṇaṭṭhaṃ dasseti. Ubhayavatoti sukhadukkhavato, somanassadomanassavato ca, pharaṇāpharaṇaṭṭhānavato vā.

179. 'By being the condition for the arising of pleasant and unpleasant tactile sensations' means by being the productive cause of agreeable and disagreeable tactile sensations. But of what is that the causal condition? It is said, 'of the heat abiding in the body.' And 'by being the condition' is an instrumental case in the sense of cause. Therefore, by being the cause, the ability to produce pleasant and unpleasant tactile sensations as described is established. 'Just so'—this draws in 'according to strength, part of the body or the whole body.' 'Thus' means by the manner of pervasion that achieves its own result by way of figurative expression. 'These' refers to pleasant sensations, etc. By 'or just gross occurrence is pervasion,' he shows the meaning of pervasion without figurative expression. 'Possessing both' means possessing pleasure and pain, and joy and displeasure, or possessing the state of pervasion and non-pervasion.

181. Ettha vuttaṃ saṅkappanti etasmiṃ “saṅkappo kāmo”tiādike (mahāni. 1; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 8) niddesapadese vuttaṃ saṅkappaṃ. Tattha hi kilesakāmova “saṅkapparāgo purisassa kāmo”tiādīsu (a. ni. 6.63; kathā. 513) viya. Vatthukāmassa tathā tathā saṅkappanato parikappanato “saṅkappo”ti vutto, na vitakkoti ayamettha attho vutto. Ṭīkāyaṃ pana vitakkavasena atthaṃ dassetuṃ “sopi hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tatrāpi purimo evattho adhippetoti ce, sampiṇḍanattho pi-saddo niratthako siyā, “kilesasanthavasambhavato”ti ca na vattabbaṃ siyā, parato ca “byāpādavacanena byāpādavitakkaṃ dassetī”ti vakkhati. Kilesakāmo vibhatto kilesasampayuttattāti adhippāyo. Kāmapaṭibaddhāti ettha kāma-saddena vatthukāmāpi saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbā.

181. The 'intention' (saṅkappa) mentioned here refers to the 'intention' spoken of in the exposition passage beginning 'intention is sensual desire' (saṅkappo kāmo), etc. (Mahāni. 1; Cūḷani. Ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 8). There, it is indeed defilement-sensual desire, as in 'intention-lust is a person’s sensual desire' (saṅkapparāgo purisassa kāmo), etc. (A. Ni. 6.63; Kathā. 513). Object-sensual desire is called 'intention' because it is conceived and considered in various ways, not because it is 'thought' (vitakka)—this is the meaning stated here. However, in the subcommentary, to explain the meaning in terms of thought, 'that too' (sopi hi) etc. is said. If even there the former meaning is intended, then the particle 'pi', which has an inclusive meaning, would be meaningless, and 'because it arises from association with defilements' should not have been said. Later, it will be explained, 'by the word 'ill will,' it indicates the thought of ill will.' The intention is that defilement-sensual desire is distinguished because it is associated with defilements. In 'bound to desire,' it should be understood that object-sensual desire is also included by the word 'desire'.

182. Ubhayattha uppannoti sattesu, saṅkhāresūti ubhayattha uppanno, sattākāro, saṅkhārākāroti vā ārammaṇassa ubhayākāraggahaṇavasena uppanno. Kammapathaviseso, kammapathavināsako ca kammapathabhedoti dassetuṃ “abhijjhāsaṃyogenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tathā vihiṃsāya vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ dassetīti yojanā. Vihiṃsāyāti ca vihiṃsāvacanenāti attho. Yathāsambhavaṃ pāṇātipātādivasenāti ādi-saddena adinnādānamusāvādapesuññapharusavācāsamphappalāpe saṅgaṇhāti. Sabba…pe… saṅgāhakehi kāmanekkhammadhātūhi. Dve dveti byāpādavihiṃsādhātuyo, abyāpādaavihiṃsādhātuyo ca. “Etthāti panā”tiādinā saṃkilesavodānānaṃ saṅkarabhāvassa aniṭṭhāpajjanassa ca dassanena purimaṃyeva atthaṃ byatirekamukhena sampādeti.

182. 'Arisen in both places' means arisen in both beings and formations; or, arisen as the aspect of beings and the aspect of formations; or, arisen by grasping the object in its dual aspects. To show the distinction, the destroyer, and the division of the course of action, it is said, 'by the connection with covetousness,' etc. Similarly, the connection is that it shows the thought of harming through harming. And 'through harming' means by the expression 'harming.' 'As appropriate, in the manner of killing living beings, etc.'—the word 'etc.' includes taking what is not given, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. All... (the rest is omitted by 'pe') ...with the encompassing elements, namely, the elements of sensual desire and renunciation. 'Two and two' means the elements of ill will and harming, and the elements of non-ill will and non-harming. By 'But here,' etc., by showing the mingling of defilement and purification and the arising of the undesirable, it establishes the preceding meaning through the method of contrast.

Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Suttanta Division is concluded.

2. Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

2. Exposition of the Abhidhamma Division

183. Āveṇikattho [M 0.0055][V 0.0053] atisayattho ca visesasaddo hotīti tadubhayaṃ dassetuṃ “puggalantarāsādhāraṇaṃ, nīlādisabbarūpasādhāraṇañcā”ti vuttaṃ. Asādhāraṇakāraṇenāpi hi niddeso hoti yathā “bherisaddo, yavaṅkuro”ti. Atisayakāraṇenapi yathā “atītānāgatapaccuppannānaṃ kammasamādānānaṃ ṭhānaso hetuso vipākaṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (kathā. 355; paṭi. ma. 2.44). Dhātuattho evāti “dhātu”iti imassa dhātusaddasseva attho. Dhātuvacanīyo hi attho upasaggena jotīyati.

183. The word 'visesa' (distinct) signifies both uniqueness (āveṇika) and superiority (atisaya). To show both, it is said, 'not shared by another individual, and shared by all forms like blue, etc.' For exposition also occurs due to the cause of being unshared, as in 'the sound of a drum, a barley sprout.' And due to the cause of superiority, as in 'he understands, as it actually is, the result of past, future, and present courses of action in terms of place and cause.' 'Simply the meaning of the element' means the meaning of the word 'dhātu' itself. For the meaning expressed by a root is illuminated by a prefix.

Purimena asadiso vidhānadhāraṇatthānaṃ pākaṭo bhedoti. Visabhāgalakkhaṇā visadisasabhāvā avayavā bhāgā, tesu.

A clear distinction, dissimilar to the preceding, regarding the modes of arrangement and sustentation. Among them, the dissimilar parts are the divisions with dissimilar characteristics and dissimilar natures.

Yathāsambhavanti kiriyāmanodhātu upanissayakoṭiyā, vipākamanodhātu vipākamanoviññāṇassa anantarādināpi, itarassa sabbāpi upanissayakoṭiyāva. Dhammadhātu pana vedanādikā sahajātā sahajātādinā, asahajātā anantarādinā, upanissayena ārammaṇādinā ca manoviññāṇassa paccayoti evaṃ manodhātudhammadhātūnaṃ manoviññāṇassa hetubhāvo yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbo. Dvārabhūtamanopi sutte “manodhātū”ti vuccatīti āha “dvārabhūtamanovasena vā”ti. Tassā manodhātuyā manoviññāṇassa hetubhāvo yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabboti sambandho.

'As appropriate'—the functional mind-element is a condition through the support condition category; the resultant mind-element is a condition for resultant mind-consciousness through the immediately contiguous condition, etc.; all the rest are solely through the support condition category. But the dhamma-element—co-nascent, such as feeling, etc.—is a condition through the co-nascence condition, etc.; non-co-nascent is a condition through the immediately contiguous condition, etc.; and it is a condition for mind-consciousness through the support condition, object condition, etc. Thus, the causal relation of the mind-element and the dhamma-element to mind-consciousness should be connected as appropriate. The mind that serves as a door is also called 'mind-element' in the sutta—thus it is said, 'or in terms of mind serving as a door.' The causal relation of that mind-element to mind-consciousness should be connected as appropriate—this is the connection.

Purimanayenāti visesanaṃ dutiyanayassa hīnattikavaseneva vibhattattā. Nānādhātūnañca cakkhudhātuādīnanti sambandho.

'By the previous method' is a qualification of the second method, because it is classified only by way of the inferior triad. And the connection is with the various elements, such as the eye-element, etc.

Na hi dve manoviññāṇadhātuyo santi aṭṭhārasadhātuvibhāgadassaneti adhippāyo. Khandhāyatanadhātindriyānaṃyeva vasena saṅkhepādivibhāgadassanaṃ tesaṃ bahulaṃ pariññeyyadhammasaṅgaṇhanato. Saccadesanā pana atisaṃkhittabhāvatoyevettha bahikatā.

For there are not two mind-consciousness elements; the intention is to show the division into eighteen elements. The brief and detailed divisions are seen mainly in terms of aggregates, sense bases, elements, and faculties, because they encompass numerous phenomena to be fully understood. However, the exposition of the truths is excluded here because of its extremely condensed nature.

Nijjīvassātiādi visesato sattasuññatādīpanatthā dhātudesanāti katvā vuttaṃ. Purimanayo aññesampi kamavuttīnaṃ dhātūnaṃ sambhavatīti adhippāyena [M 0.0056][V 0.0054] vuttoti “manodhātuyeva vā”tiādinā dutiyanayo vutto. Tattha avijjamānepi purecarānucarabhāveti purecarānucarābhisandhiyā abhāvepi kevalaṃ anantarapubbakālaanantarāparakālatāya manodhātu purecarānucarā viya daṭṭhabbāti vuttā.

The phrase 'devoid of life,' etc., was stated by way of teaching the elements, specifically to illustrate the emptiness of beings and other such points. The previous method applies to other elements as well, as they arise in sequence; hence, the second method is stated with 'or just the mind-element,' etc., with this intention. There, even though there is no actual relationship of preceding or following, that is, even in the absence of an intention of preceding or following, the mind-element is said to be like a preceding and following element merely due to its being immediately prior and immediately subsequent in time.

“Aññaṃ aggahetvā pavattituṃ asamatthatāyā”ti etena viññāṇassa ekantasārammaṇatādassanena “ārammaṇena vinā sayameva nīlādiābhāsaṃ cittaṃ pavattatī”ti evaṃ pavattitaṃ viññāṇavādaṃ paṭisedheti.

The phrase 'incapable of occurring without grasping another' demonstrates that consciousness is invariably object-dependent, thereby refuting the doctrine of consciousness that asserts, 'Without an object, the mind itself manifests appearances such as blue, etc.'

184. Ekanānāsantānagatānanti ekasantānagatānaṃ abhinnasantānagatānaṃ dvārānaṃ, nānāsantānagatānaṃ bhinnasantānagatānaṃ ārammaṇānanti yojanā. Ekanānājātikattāti cakkhādiekekajātikattā dvārānaṃ, nīlādianekajātikattā ārammaṇānaṃ.

184. 'Belonging to a single or multiple continua' means belonging to a single continuum—unseparated continua—for the doors, and belonging to multiple continua—separated continua—for the objects. This is the interpretation. 'Because of being of single or multiple kinds' means that the doors are of a single kind, like the eye, etc., while the objects are of multiple kinds, like blue, etc.

Cakkhādi ekampi viññāṇassa paccayo hoti, rūpādi pana anekameva saṃhatanti imassa vā atthavisesassa dassanatthaṃ cakkhurūpādīsu vacanabhedo kato. Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ cakkhādi ekampi viññāṇassa paccayo hoti, rūpādi pana anekamevāti? Paccayabhāvavisesato. Cakkhu hi cakkhuviññāṇassa nissayapurejātaindriyavippayuttapaccayehi paccayo hontaṃ atthibhāveneva hoti tasmiṃ sati tassa bhāvato, asati abhāvato, yato taṃ atthiavigatapaccayehissa paccayo hotīti vuccatīti. Taṃnissayatā cassa na ekadesena allīyanavasena icchitabbā arūpabhāvato, atha kho garurājādīsu sissarājapurisādīnaṃ viya tappaṭibaddhavuttitāya. Itare ca paccayā tena tena visesena veditabbā. Svāyaṃ paccayabhāvo na ekasmiṃ na sambhavatīti ekampi cakkhu cakkhuviññāṇassa paccayo hotīti dassetuṃ pāḷiyaṃ “cakkhuñca paṭiccā”ti ekavacananiddeso kato.

The eye, etc., is each a condition for consciousness, whereas forms, etc., are only many and combined. To show this distinction in meaning, the differentiation in grammatical number is made regarding the eye, forms, etc. But what is the reason that the eye, etc., is each a condition for consciousness, whereas forms, etc., are only many? It is due to the difference in the nature of the conditionality. The eye, for instance, is a condition for eye-consciousness through the conditions of dependence, pre-nascence, faculty, and dissociation, simply by its existence—since when it exists, eye-consciousness arises, and when it does not exist, it does not arise. Therefore, it is called a condition by its existence and non-disappearance. Its dependence should not be understood as clinging in part due to its immaterial nature, but rather like the dependence of disciples or attendants on a great king, etc., in terms of their function being bound to it. Other conditions should be understood according to their specific characteristics. Since this nature of conditionality is not impossible for a single entity, to show that even a single eye is a condition for eye-consciousness, the Pāli text uses the singular form: 'dependent on the eye.'

Rūpaṃ pana yadipi cakkhu viya purejātaatthiavigatapaccayehi paccayo hoti puretaraṃ uppannaṃ hutvā vijjamānakkhaṇeyeva upakārakattā, tathāpi anekameva saṃhataṃ hutvā paccayo hoti ārammaṇabhāvato. Yañhi paccayadhammaṃ sabhāvabhūtaṃ, parikappitākāramattaṃ [M 0.0057] vā [V 0.0055] viññāṇaṃ vibhāventaṃ pavattati, tadaññesañca satipi paccayabhāve so tassa sārammaṇasabhāvato yaṃ kiñci anālambitvā pavattituṃ asamatthassa olubbha pavattikāraṇatāya ālambanīyato ārammaṇaṃ nāma. Tassa yasmā yathā yathā sabhāvūpaladdhi viññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayalābho, tasmā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ rūpaṃ ārabbha pavattamānaṃ tassa sabhāvaṃ vibhāventameva pavattati. Sā cassa indriyādhīnavuttikassa ārammaṇasabhāvūpaladdhi na ekadvikalāpagatavaṇṇavaseneva hoti, nāpi katipayakalāpavaṇṇavasena, atha kho ābhogānurūpaṃ āpāthagatavaṇṇavasenāti anekameva rūpaṃ saṃhaccakāritāya viññāṇassa paccayo hotīti dassento bhagavā “rūpe cā”ti bahuvacanena niddisi.

Moreover, although form, like the eye, serves as a condition through pre-nascence, existence, and non-disappearance, being arisen earlier and helpful precisely at the moment of its existence, still, it functions as a condition only in aggregation by way of being an object. For, that which is a condition-phenomenon, whether it be of its own intrinsic nature or merely a conceptualized appearance, when consciousness arises manifesting it, then, even with the presence of other conditions, it is due to its object-nature that it is called an object, since consciousness, incapable of arising without relying on something, depends for its arising on that which is fit to be relied upon. Since the acquisition of the object-condition by consciousness is in accordance with the perception of the object's nature, eye-consciousness, arising in dependence on form, arises only by manifesting that nature. And this apprehension of the object's nature, for a consciousness whose activity is dependent on the sense faculty, does not occur through just one or two particles of color, nor through a few groups of particles of color, but rather through a range of colors that come within the scope of attention. Thus, to show that form serves as a condition for consciousness by its collective action, the Blessed One indicated this with the plural, 'and forms.'

Yaṃ pana “rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā, taṃsampayuttakānañca dhammānaṃ ārammaṇapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.1) vuttaṃ, taṃ kathanti? Tampi yādisaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa ārammaṇapaccayo, tādisameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kīdisaṃ pana tanti? Samuditanti pākaṭoyamattho. Evañca katvā yadeke vadanti “āyatanasallakkhaṇavasena cakkhuviññāṇādayo sallakkhaṇārammaṇā, na dabyasallakkhaṇavasenā”ti, taṃ yuttameva hoti. Na cettha samudāyārammaṇatā āsaṅkitabbā samudāyābhogasseva abhāvato, samuditā pana vaṇṇadhammā ārammaṇapaccayā honti. Kathaṃ pana paccekaṃ asamatthā samuditā ārammaṇā honti, na hi paccekaṃ daṭṭhuṃ asakkontā andhā samuditā passantīti? Nayidamekantikaṃ visuṃ asamatthānaṃ sivikāvahanādīsu samatthatāya dassanato. Kesādīnañca yasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhitānaṃ paccekaṃ vaṇṇaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkā, tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne samuditānaṃ taṃ gahetuṃ sakkāti bhiyyopi tesaṃ saṃhaccakāritā paribyattā. Etena kiṃ cakkhuviññāṇassa paramāṇurūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, udāhu taṃsamudāyotiādikā codanā [M 0.0058] paṭikkhittā veditabbā. “Sotañca paṭicca sadde cā”tiādīsupi ayameva nayo.

Regarding what is said, "The form base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element and its associated states by way of the object condition" (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.1), how is that to be understood? That too refers to the kind of form base that serves as an object condition for eye-consciousness. What kind is it then? It is the aggregated form; this meaning is evident. And having established this, when some say, "Eye-consciousness and so forth take their object by way of the characteristic of the base, not by way of the characteristic of the individual substance," that is indeed correct. Here, the notion of a collective object should not be suspected, since there is no engagement with a collective entity. However, aggregated visible forms do serve as an object condition. But how can they, individually incapable, become objects when aggregated? For blind people, being unable to see individually, do not see when aggregated. This is not an absolute rule, for it is seen that even those who cannot lift things individually can do so when combined, as in the case of carrying a palanquin. And further, regarding hairs and the like: in the place where individual colors cannot be discerned, their aggregated form can be discerned—this demonstrates their combined action even more clearly. Through this, any objection—whether eye-consciousness takes an atomic form as its object or the aggregate thereof, and so on—should be understood as refuted. The same principle applies to passages like, "Dependent on the ear and sounds," etc.

Evampi [V 0.0056] attho labbhatīti “manodhātuyāpī”ti pi-saddena na kevalaṃ javanapariyosānā manoviññāṇadhātuyeva sampiṇḍīyati, atha kho tadārammaṇabhavaṅgasaṅkhātāpi sampiṇḍīyatīti evampi attho labbhati, sambhavatīti attho. Evaṃ satīti evaṃ aññamanodhātuppavattiyā oraṃ pavattacittānaṃ manoviññāṇadhātutādassane sati. Satipi manaso sambhūtabhāve manodhātuyā manoviññāṇadhātubhāvappasaṅgo na hotiyeva taṃsabhāvasseva manoviññāṇadhātubhāvena niddiṭṭhattā. Idāni tamevatthaṃ “pañcaviññāṇadhātumanodhātū”tiādinā pākaṭataraṃ karoti. Tabbidhurasabhāvenāti pañcaviññāṇadhātūhi visadisasabhāvena. Uppattiṭṭhānena cāti manodhātukiriyamanoviññāṇadhātuādīhi paricchinnena uppajjanaṭṭhānena ca. Idāni ekattaggahaṇaṃ vināpi yathāvuttassa atthassa sambhavaṃ dassetuṃ “anupanītepī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sāmaññavasenāti sadisatāvasena. Tassāti bhavaṅgānantaraṃ uppannacittassa. Amanoviññāṇadhātubhāvāsiddhitoti manodhātubhāvāsiddhito. Na hi “manoviññāṇadhātuyāpi uppajjitvā niruddhasamanantaraṃ uppajjati cittaṃ…pe… tajjā manoviññāṇadhātū”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ bhavaṅgānantaraṃ uppannacittassa manodhātubhāvaṃ sādheti. Siddhe hi manodhātubhāve taṃ tassa nivattakaṃ siyāti adhippāyo. Manoviññāṇadhātuyā pana uppannassa cittassa manoviññāṇadhātubhāvadīpakaṃ vacanaṃ tādisāya manodhātuyāpi manoviññāṇadhātubhāvameva dīpeyyāti kathaṃ tassā nivattakaṃ siyāti āha “na hi yaṃ codīyati, tadeva parihārāya hotī”ti.

Thus, this meaning is also obtained: by the word 'pi' in 'even in the case of the mind-element', not only is the mind-consciousness-element culminating in javana included, but also what is designated as registering consciousness and life-continuum is included. Thus, this meaning is obtained, that is, it is possible. 'When this is so' means: when the nature of the mind-consciousness-element is demonstrated for the cittas that arise prior to the arising of another mind-element. Even when the state of the mind has arisen, there is no occasion for the mind-element to become the mind-consciousness-element, because that very nature has been pointed out as the mind-consciousness-element. Now, to make this meaning clearer, he states, 'the five sense-consciousness-elements and the mind-element,' and so on. 'Of a different nature from those' means of a nature dissimilar to the five sense-consciousness-elements. 'And by the place of arising' means by the place of arising which is defined by the mind-element, the functional mind-consciousness-element, and so on. Now, to show the possibility of the aforesaid meaning even without taking them as one, it is said, 'even without being brought near,' and so on. Herein, 'by way of generality' means by way of similarity. 'Of that' means of the citta that arises immediately after the life-continuum. 'Because its state of not being the mind-consciousness-element is not established' means because its state as the mind-element is not established. For the statement, 'Even in the case of the mind-consciousness-element, a citta arises immediately after one has arisen and ceased... that mind-consciousness-element born of it,' does not establish the nature as mind-element for the citta arising immediately after the life-continuum. For if its nature as mind-element were established, that would be its negator; this is the intention. But a statement indicating the nature as mind-consciousness-element for a citta that has arisen from the mind-consciousness-element would indicate only the nature as mind-consciousness-element even for such a mind-element—how could that be its negator? Thus, it is said: 'For that which is challenged cannot itself be the refutation.'

Yadi evaṃ pañcadvārāvajjanassa manoviññāṇadhātubhāvāpatti evāti codanaṃ manasi katvā āha “manodhātuyāpī”tiādi. Pañcaviññāṇehi manodhātūhi ca visiṭṭho sabhāvo pañcaviññāṇa…pe… sabhāvo, tassa vasena. Cutipaṭisandhibhavaṅgānanti tadārammaṇampi bhavaṅgantogadhaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Javanāvasānānīti vā javanārammaṇattā tadārammaṇampi gahitaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenevāha “chadvārikacittehi vā”tiādi.

Having kept in mind the objection, 'If so, the five-door-adverting consciousness would become a mind-consciousness-element,' he said, 'Even by the mind-element,' and so on. By way of its nature, which is distinct from the five consciousnesses and the mind-elements, the nature of the five consciousnesses... and so on. Regarding 'death, rebirth-linking, and life-continuum,' this is said having included registering consciousness within the life-continuum. Or, in the phrase 'at the end of the javanas,' it should be understood that registering consciousness is also included, because it has the javana as its object. Therefore, he said, 'Or by the six-door cittas,' and so on.

Visuṃ kātuṃ yuttanti āvajjanampi yadipi rūpādivisayaṃ hoti, javanaṃ viya ārammaṇarasānubhavanaṃ pana na hotīti edise ṭhāne visuṃ kātabbameva. Mano [M 0.0059] cāti ca-saddo “manañca paṭiccā”tiādīsu viya na sampiṇḍanattho, atha kho byatirekattho daṭṭhabbo.

'It is fitting to distinguish' means: although adverting also has form and so on as its object, there is no experiencing of the object’s flavour as in the javana-process. Therefore, in such a case, it should definitely be distinguished. And in 'the mind and,' the word 'ca' should be seen not as having a collective meaning, as in 'depending on the mind and,' and so on, but rather as having a disjunctive meaning.

Abhidhammabhājanīyavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Abhidhamma Exposition is concluded.

3. Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Section of Questions

Heṭṭhā [V 0.0057] vuttanayattāti dhammadhātumanoviññāṇadhātūnaṃ “pañcapaṇṇāsa kāmāvacaradhamme ārabbha rajjantassā”tiādinā (vibha. aṭṭha. 150; 168) parittārammaṇādibhāve dassiyamāne “cittuppādarūpavasena taṃ taṃ samudāyaṃ ekekaṃ dhammaṃ katvā”tiādinā (vibha. mūlaṭī. 150) tadatthassa khandhavibhaṅgavaṇṇanādīsu vuttanayattā.

'Because of the method stated previously' means: because, while the state of the dhamma-element and the mind-consciousness-element as having limited objects and so forth is being shown by the passage beginning, 'of one who lusts concerning the fifty-five sense-sphere dhammas...' (Vibhaṅga Aṭṭhakathā 150; 168), the method for its meaning has been stated in the Commentary on the Analysis of Aggregates and so on, with the passage beginning, 'having made each and every collection into a single dhamma by way of the arising of consciousness and matter...' (Vibhaṅga Mūlaṭīkā 150).

Pañhapucchakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section of Questions is concluded.

Dhātuvibhaṅgavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Analysis of Elements is concluded.

4. Saccavibhaṅgo

4. The Analysis of the Truths

1. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta Exposition

Uddesavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Summary

189. Saccavinimuttaṃ [M 0.0060][V 0.0058] natthi pavattinivattitadubhayahetusandassanavasena pavattanato. Saccesu kamatīti saccesu visayabhūtesu pavattati. Desetabbatthavisayā hi desanāti. Etesu kamatīti etesu ariyasaccesu pariññādikiccasādhanavasena pavattati. “Sīlasamādhipaññāsaṅkhāta”nti vuttaṃ atthasabhāvaṃ kamanakiriyāya kattubhāvena gahitanti pākaṭataraṃ katvā dassetuṃ “kiṃ kamatī”ti pucchati. Tabbohārenāti tadupacārena. Etena nippariyāyena atthasabhāvaṃ sāsanaṃ, pariyāyena vacanasabhāvanti dasseti.

189. There is nothing apart from the truths, because it proceeds by way of showing the causes of both that which has come to be and that which ceases. 'It proceeds in the truths' means it functions with the truths as its object. For the teaching has as its object that which is to be taught. 'It proceeds in these' means it functions concerning these noble truths by way of accomplishing tasks such as full understanding and so forth. To show more clearly that the essential nature of the meaning, which is called 'morality, concentration, and wisdom,' is taken as the agent of the action of proceeding, the question 'What proceeds?' is asked. 'By that expression' means by that figurative usage. By this, it is shown that the teaching is, in a direct sense, the nature of the meaning, and in an indirect sense, the nature of speech.

Taṃsabhāvāti dukkhādisabhāvā. Amusāsabhāvāti bādhanādibhāvena bhūtasabhāvā. Aññākārarahitāti abādhanādiākāravivittā. Dvidhāti dukkhadukkhatātannimittatāhi. Rāgādikilesapariḷāho kilesadāho. Santānassa avipphārikatākaraṇaṃ puggalahiṃsanaṃ. Attano eva tikhiṇabhāvoti saṅkhatadhammassa attano sabhāveneva rujāvahatikkhabhāvo. Sarasenevāti sabhāveneva. Sampiṇḍakassa samudayassa, kilesasantāparahitassa maggassa, avipariṇāmassa nirodhassa dassanena yathāsaṅkhyaṃ dukkhassa saṅkhatasantāpavipariṇāmaṭṭhā āvi bhavantīti āha “itare yathākkamaṃ samudayamagganirodhadassanehi āvibhavanākārā”ti. Byāpetvāti bhavādīsu nānārammaṇesu ca visaṭā hutvā. Anekatthattā dhātūnaṃ “ūhanaṃ rāsikaraṇa”nti vatvā puna tadatthaṃ vivarati “dukkhanibbattana”nti. Ekavokārabhavepi hi rāsibhūtameva dukkhaṃ nibbattati anekadhammasamūhato[V 0.0059], pageva catupañcavokārabhavesu. Ettha ca byāpanatthaṃ ākāraṃ, tassa ca ya-kārāgamaṃ katvā sampiṇḍanatthaṃ āyūhananti padaṃ veditabbaṃ. Nidadātīti dukkhassa ekantakāraṇattā taṃ nidassentaṃ viya janetīti dassento “idaṃ taṃ dukkha”ntiādimāha. Dukkha…pe… āvi bhavati rogadassanena viya roganidānaṃ. Saṃyoga…pe… dassanehīti saṃyogaṭṭho visaṃyogasabhāvassa nirodhassa, palibodhaṭṭho niyyānasabhāvassa maggassa dassanena āvi bhavatīti attho. Teti saṃyogapalibodhaṭṭhā.

'Its nature' means the nature of suffering and so forth. 'The nature of not being false' means the nature of being real by way of affliction and so forth. 'Devoid of other characteristics' means free from the characteristics of non-affliction and so forth. 'Twofold' means by way of the suffering of pain and its cause. The torment of defilements such as greed is the burning of defilements. Making the continuity not spread out is harming a person. 'Its own sharp nature' means the sharp nature of a conditioned phenomenon that brings pain by its own nature. 'By its own essence' means by its own nature. Through the seeing of the origin which gathers, the path which is free from the torment of defilements, and the cessation which is unchanging, the meanings of suffering—as conditioned, as torment, and as change—become manifest respectively. Thus it is said: 'The others are modes of becoming evident in sequence through the seeing of arising, the path, and cessation.' 'Having pervaded' means having spread among various objects such as states of existence and so forth. Because of the multiple meanings of the term 'dhātu', having stated 'piling up and heaping,' he further explains its meaning as 'producing suffering.' For even in a single-constituent existence, suffering is produced as a heap from a collection of many phenomena, let alone in four- or five-constituent existences. Here, the word 'āyūhana' should be understood as meaning 'gathering,' with the prefix 'ā' having the meaning of 'pervading' and with the insertion of the letter 'ya'. 'It lays down': showing that because it is the exclusive cause of suffering, it generates it as if pointing it out, he says, 'This is that suffering,' and so forth. Suffering... becomes manifest, just as the cause of a disease becomes manifest through seeing the disease. 'Bondage... through seeing': the meaning is that the aspect of connection becomes manifest through seeing cessation, which has the nature of disconnection, and the aspect of obstruction becomes manifest through seeing the path, which has the nature of leading out. These are the aspects of connection and obstruction.

Etthāti [M 0.0061] etasmiṃ ārammaṇabhūte sati. Samudayato viveko vivekaṭṭho. Nirodho ca taṇhākkhayabhāvato samudayato vivitto, tasmā avivekabhūtassa samudayassa dassanena nirodhassa vivekaṭṭho āvi bhavati, nibbānādhigamahetubhūtassāpi maggassa sappaccayatāya saṅkhatabhāvaṃ passato appaccayassa nirodhassa asaṅkhataṭṭho āvi bhavati, tathā maraṇadhammatāya dukkhaṃ vinassantaṃ passato amaraṇadhammassa nirodhassa amataṭṭho āvi bhavatīti imamatthaṃ dasseti “vivekā”tiādinā. Itare samudayanirodhadukkhadassanehīti ettha samudayadassanena “nāyaṃ hetu nibbānādhigamāya, ayaṃ pana hetū”ti hetuṭṭho āvi bhavati. Tathā paramagambhīrassa nipuṇatarassa duddasassa nirodhassa dassanena dassanaṭṭho sukhumarūpadassanena cakkhuno viya, dukkhadassanena pana anekarogāturakapaṇajanadassanena issarajanassa uḷārabhāvo viya maggassa ādhipateyyaṭṭho āvi bhavati.

'Here' means when this has become the object. 'Seclusion from arising' is the meaning of seclusion. And cessation is secluded from arising because it is the destruction of craving; therefore, by seeing arising, which is non-secluded, the meaning of seclusion regarding cessation becomes evident. And by seeing the path, which is a cause for the attainment of Nibbāna, as conditioned due to its having a condition, the unconditioned meaning of cessation, which is without a condition, becomes evident. Similarly, by seeing suffering as perishing due to its nature of being subject to death, the deathless meaning of cessation, which is not subject to death, becomes evident. This meaning is shown by 'from seclusion,' and so forth. As for the others, through the seeing of arising, cessation, and suffering: herein, by seeing arising, the meaning of cause becomes evident, thus: 'This is not the cause for attaining Nibbāna, but this is the cause.' Likewise, by seeing cessation, which is exceedingly deep, very subtle, and difficult to see, the meaning of vision becomes evident, like that of the eye seeing a subtle form. And by seeing suffering, the meaning of dominance of the path becomes evident, like the magnificence of a lordly person upon seeing many people who are afflicted by disease and wretched.

Te panete hetuṭṭhādike sarūpato dassetuṃ “tattha palibodhupacchedavasenā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha palibodhupacchedavasenāti samudayappahānavasena. “Maggādhipatino dhammā”ti vacanatoti yasmā satipi jhānādīnaṃ ārammaṇādhipatibhāve “jhānādhipatino dhammā”ti evamādi na vuttaṃ, “maggādhipatino dhammā” icceva pana vuttaṃ. Tasmā sātisayo maggaṅgadhammānaṃ ārammaṇādhipatibhāvo. Tenāha “visesato vā ārammaṇādhipatibhūtā maggaṅgadhammā hontī”ti. So tesaṃ ākāroti yo maggaṅgānaṃ garuṃ katvā paccavekkhaṇavasena pavattadhammānaṃ ārammaṇādhipatipaccayatāsaṅkhāto ākāro, so maggassa ādhipateyyaṭṭho. Purimo pana ādhipateyyaṭṭho sahajātādhipativasena vutto. Abhisametabbaṭṭhoti yathāvuttapīḷanādiatthameva paṭivijjhitabbatāya ekajjhaṃ katvā vadati. Tena abhisamayasaddaṃ kammatthaṃ dasseti. Abhisamayassāti ñāṇassa. Pavattiākāroti parijānanādivisesākāro. So hi maggakkhaṇe asammohato [V 0.0060] siddho, pacchā paccavekkhaṇādinā pākaṭo hoti. Ākāropi ñāṇena araṇīyato atthoti vuccatīti katvā tatiyanayo dassito. Pīḷanādinā dassito visayavibhāgenapi visayivibhāgo hoti yathā “rūpasaññā, saddasaññā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.57).

Now, to show these meanings of cause and so forth in their own nature, it is said, 'Herein, by way of cutting off obstructions,' and so forth. Herein, 'by way of cutting off obstructions' means by way of abandoning arising. Because of the statement, 'phenomena that have the path as dominant': since, even though there is the state of dominant object for jhāna and so forth, it is not said, 'phenomena that have jhāna as dominant,' and so forth, but it is only said, 'phenomena that have the path as dominant,' therefore, the state of dominant object for the phenomena that are path factors is preeminent. Hence, it is said, 'Or, specifically, the phenomena that are path factors become dominant objects.' That is their mode: the mode designated as the condition of dominant object for phenomena that proceed by way of reviewing, having given weight to the path factors—that is the meaning of dominance for the path. The former meaning of dominance, however, was stated by way of co-nascent dominance. 'The meaning of what is to be fully understood': he speaks of the very meaning of affliction and so forth, as stated, by unifying it for the purpose of its being penetrated. Thereby, he shows that the word 'full understanding' has a passive sense. 'Of full understanding' means of knowledge. 'The mode of its proceeding' means the specific mode of full understanding and so forth. For that is accomplished at the moment of the path through non-delusion, and it becomes manifest afterward through reviewing and so forth. And because the mode is also called the meaning, since it is to be attained by knowledge, the third method is shown. Through the division of the object, shown by affliction and so forth, there is also a division of the subject, as in 'perception of form, perception of sound' (SN 3.57).

Kucchitaṃ [M 0.0062] khanti garahitaṃ hutvā asāraṃ. “Samāgamo”tiādinā anvayato byatirekato ca saṃ-saddassa saṃyogatthajotakattamāha. “Uppannaṃ udita”ntiādīsu kevalassa panna-saddassa, ita-saddassa ca payoge uppattiatthassa anupalabbhanato, u-saddassa ca payoge upalabbhanato so uppattiatthaṃ dīpetīti āha “evaṃ uppannaṃ uditanti etthāpī”ti. Visuṃ payujjamānāti āgama-ita-padehi vinā payujjamānā. Sadhātukanti antonītena dhātunā sadhātukaṃ. Teneva te “upasaggā”ti ca vuttā.

It is called 'despised,' meaning that, being censured, it is worthless. Beginning with 'conjunction,' he states, by way of positive and negative concomitance, that the syllable 'saṃ' indicates the meaning of combination. In such cases as 'arisen' (uppannaṃ) and 'risen' (uditaṃ), because the meaning of arising is not found when the mere words 'panna' and 'ita' are used, but is found when the syllable 'u' is used, he says that it indicates the meaning of arising, thus: 'So it is also here in "arisen" and "risen".' 'Being used separately' means being used without the stems to which they are attached. 'With a root' means with an internal root. For that very reason, they are also called 'prefixes' (upasaggā).

Dukkhavivekabhāvanti dukkhavivittataṃ. Nivattiyāti nibbānassa. Nivattetvāti anuppādasaddena visesanavasena nivattetvā. Nirodhapaccayatā nirodhassa maggassa ārammaṇapaccayatā. Puggalasacchikiriyādhammabhāvehīti puggaladhammabhāvena sacchikaraṇadhammabhāvena ca. Phalanti ariyaphalaṃ. Tassāti niṭṭhānabhūtāya phalasaṅkhātāya dukkhanirodhappattiyā abhisamayabhūtāya dukkhanirodhappattiyā paṭipadatā daṭṭhabbā.

'The state of seclusion from suffering' means separation from suffering. 'From cessation' means of Nibbāna. 'Having turned back' means having turned back by way of specification with the word 'non-arising.' 'The state of being a condition for cessation' means the state of the path being an object-condition for cessation. 'By way of the natures of a person and a phenomenon to be realized' means by way of the nature of a person and by way of the nature of a phenomenon to be realized. 'The fruit' means the noble fruit. 'Of that': the quality of being the path should be understood as being for the attainment of the cessation of suffering, which has become the culmination, designated as the fruit, and which has become the realization.

Paṭivijjhanakāle nippariyāyena buddhādisamaññāti āha “paṭividdhakāle pavatta”nti. Tato evāti tena pakāsitattā eva.

At the time of penetration, it is the designation 'Buddha' and so forth in the primary sense; hence it is said, 'that which occurs at the time of penetration.' 'From that very thing' means because it is revealed by that very thing.

Tannimittabhāvoti jātiādi viya adhiṭṭhānabhāvena dukkhassa kāraṇabhāvo, na samudayasaccaṃ viya pabhavabhāvena. Udayabbayapīḷitabhāvo saṅkhāradukkhatā. Pavattanamevāti pavatti eva. Kiccaṃ rasoti rasassa kiccatthataṃ dasseti. Pavattinivattīsūti niddhāraṇe bhummaṃ. Avikāratā vikārābhāvo niccatā.

'The state of being its cause' means the state of being a cause for suffering by way of being a foundation, like birth and so forth, not by way of being a source, like the truth of origin. The state of being afflicted by arising and passing away is the suffering of formations. 'Just proceeding' means simply proceeding. 'Function is taste' shows that the meaning of taste is function. 'In proceeding and ceasing' is the locative of specification. 'Unalterability' means the absence of alteration, which is permanence.

Marīcimāyāattānanti marīciyā māyāya attano ca ariyañāṇassāti ariyānaṃ ñāṇassa. Tena ariyānaṃ maggañāṇānusārena pavattanakañāṇampi saṅgahitaṃ hoti. Tenāha “avitathagāhakassā”tiādi[V 0.0061]. Tesanti paṭivedhapaccavekkhaṇañāṇānaṃ. Tattha paṭivedhañāṇassa paṭivijjhitabbatā gocarabhāvo, itarassa ārammaṇabhāvo. Paṭivijjhitabbatā, ārammaṇabhāvo vā paṭivedhañāṇassa gocarabhāvo, itarassa ārammaṇabhāvova.

'Mirage, illusion, and self' is an expansion: of mirage, of illusion, and of self. 'Of noble knowledge' means of the knowledge of the noble ones. By this, the knowledge that proceeds in accordance with the path-knowledge of the noble ones is also included. Therefore, it is said, 'for one who grasps without falsehood,' and so forth. 'Of those' means of the knowledges of penetration and reviewing. Herein, for the knowledge of penetration, its domain is what is to be penetrated; for the other, it is the state of being an object. The state of being what is to be penetrated, or the state of being an object, is the domain for the knowledge of penetration, while for the other, it is only the state of being an object.

Bādhakappabhavabhāvenāti bādhakassa uppādakabhāvena visuṃ gahitattā na taṇhā bādhakabhāvena gahitā pavattipavattihetūnaṃ asaṅkaravasena bodhanato. Evañca katvā abhidhammabhājanīyepi ayamatthavaṇṇanā yujjateva[M 0.0063]. Yadipi evaṃ “dukkhameva bādhaka”nti niyamānupapatti, samudayabhāvappasaṅgo cāti codanaṃ sandhāyāha “jātiādīnaṃ viya vā”tiādi. Bādhakattassa bādhakatte ca niyamoti āha “dvidhāpi bādhakatthāvadhāraṇenā”ti. Yathā hi bādhakattassa dukkhe niyatatā, evaṃ dukkhassa ca bādhakatte niyatatāti. Suttantabhājanīye taṇhāya eva samudayabhāvassa dassitattā taṇhāvasena niyamaṃ dassento “na taṇhāya vinā”tiādimāha. Suttantabhājanīyavaṇṇanā hesāti. “Kusalehi vinā”tiādinā dukkhahetutāya taṇhāya padhānabhāvamāha. Tathā hi sā kammavicittatāya hetubhāvaṃ gacchantī visesena kammassa sahakārikāraṇaṃ hotīti. Dvidhāpi niyamenāti maggova niyyānaṃ, niyyānameva ca maggoti dvippakārena niyamena.

'By the nature of being a source of affliction' means: because it is taken separately as the producer of affliction, craving is not taken as affliction, since this clarifies without confusion the causes of proceeding and the proceeding itself. And having done so, this explanation of the meaning is indeed appropriate also in the Abhidhamma analysis. Even so, with reference to the objection that the rule 'only suffering is affliction' would be improper and that there would be the unwanted consequence of it being the origin, he says, 'or like birth, etc.' And the rule is that what is afflicting has the nature of affliction; he says, 'by the determination of the meaning of affliction in both ways.' For just as the nature of affliction is fixed in suffering, so too is suffering fixed in the nature of affliction. In the Suttanta analysis, since the state of being the origin is shown for craving itself, he shows the rule in terms of craving, saying, 'not without craving,' and so forth. For this is the explanation of the Suttanta analysis. By 'without wholesome states,' and so forth, he states the primary nature of craving as a cause of suffering. For indeed, it, becoming a cause through the diversity of kamma, is specifically a cooperative cause for kamma. 'By the rule in both ways' means by the twofold rule that the path is the escape, and the escape is the path.

Vacīsaccaṃ saccavācā, taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā cāti āha “viratisacceti musāvādaviratiya”nti. Keci pana “viratisaccaṃ samādānaviratī”ti vadanti, tesampi na samādānamattaṃ viratisaccaṃ, atha kho samādānāvisaṃvādanaṃ. Taṃ pana paṭiññāsaccattā musāvādaviratiyeva hoti. Tenāha “na hi aññaviratīsu saccasaddo niruḷho”ti. Satipi dukkhasamudayāvabodhe yāvadeva nirodhamaggādhigamatthā paññābhāvanāti pacchimadvayasseva saccatthaṃ sātisayaṃ, tadadhigamassa ca avivādahetukaṃ sutte vibhāvitaṃ dassento “tassa panā”tiādimāha.

Truthful speech is true speech, and the volition that gives rise to it—thus he says, 'the truth of abstinence is abstinence from false speech.' Some, however, say, 'the truth of abstinence is abstinence by undertaking.' For them too, the truth of abstinence is not merely the undertaking, but rather not being inconsistent with the undertaking. That, however, being a truth of promise, is indeed abstinence from false speech. Therefore, it is said, 'For the word “truth” is not established in other abstinences.' Even with the understanding of suffering and its origin, since the cultivation of wisdom is for the purpose of attaining cessation and the path, the meaning of truth for the last two is pre-eminent. And showing that its attainment is a cause for non-dispute, as explained in the Sutta, he says, 'But for that...' and so on.

Ṭhānaṃ natthīti attano vādapatiṭṭhāpanakāraṇaṃ natthīti attho. Attabhāvapaṭilābheneva sattānaṃ jātiādīnaṃ patti sammukhībhāvo ca jāyatīti āha “sampattatā, paccakkhatā ca paṭhamatā”ti. Bhagavato desanākkameneva vā paṭhamāditā daṭṭhabbā.

'There is no ground' means there is no cause for establishing one's own doctrine. With the acquisition of individual existence alone, the attainment of birth and so on for beings, and their direct manifestation, come to be. Thus, he said, 'Attainment, direct experience, and primacy.' Alternatively, primacy should be understood according to the order of the Blessed One's teaching.

Parijananādīhīti [V 0.0062] pariññāppahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāhi, nissakkavacanañcetaṃ aññasaddapekkhāya. Dhammañāṇakiccanti sabhāvadhammāvabodhakiccaṃ. Pariññeyyādīni etapparamānevāti ito paraṃ neyyaṃ natthīti dasseti.

'Through full understanding, etc.' means through full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development. This is a term of exclusion with respect to other words. 'The function of knowledge of the Dhamma' is the function of understanding the inherent nature of phenomena. 'Things to be fully understood, etc., are limited to this' shows that there is nothing further to be understood beyond this.

Dukkhādīnaṃ ariyasaccabhāvassa anurūpaṃ yuttaṃ, ācariyaparamparāgataṃ vā savanaṃ anussavo. Sutānusārena, aññathā vā kakkhaḷaphusanādianiccādisabhāvasāmaññākārapariggaṇhanaṃ ākāraparivitakko. Yathāvitakkitākārassa diṭṭhisaṅkhātāya dassanabhūtāya paññāya nijjhānakkhamanaṃ rocanaṃ diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti[M 0.0064]. Ādicco viya pabhāya nirodhaṃ phusati sacchikaroti kilesandhakāraṃ viddhaṃseti. Cattāripi saccāni passatīti vuttaṃ “yo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ passatī”tiādinā.

Hearing that is appropriate and fitting to the nature of the Noble Truths, beginning with suffering, or that is transmitted through the lineage of teachers, is 'anussava' (repeated hearing/tradition). Contemplation of aspects is the grasping of the general characteristic mode of impermanence, etc., in accordance with what has been heard, or otherwise, through harsh contact and so on. The approval and acceptance of the aspect thus contemplated, through the wisdom which is of the nature of seeing and is known as view, is the acquiescence in view. Like the sun with its radiance, it touches and realizes cessation and dispels the darkness of defilements. That one sees all four truths is said in the passage beginning, 'Monks, one who sees suffering...'

Kālantaradassananti nānābhisamayaṃ vadati. Ekadassinoti ekasaccadassino. Na yojetabbā siyāti yojanāyañca sabbadassanaṃ dassanantaraparamanti dassanānuparamo āpajjeyya, saccānañca nānābhisamaye dukkhadassanādīhi paṭhamamaggādippaheyyānaṃ saṃyojanattayādīnaṃ ekadesappahānaṃ āpajjati. Tathā ca sati ekadesasotāpattimaggaṭṭhatā, tadanantarañca pattabbena phalena ekadesasotāpannatā ca āpajjati, tasmā na saccānaṃ nānābhisamayo yutto. Yathā ca nānābhisamayo na yutto, evaṃ ārammaṇābhisamayopi. Yadi hi ārammaṇakaraṇena catusaccābhisamayo icchito, na maggo sayameva attānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karotīti aparipuṇṇo saccābhisamayo siyā. Aññena maggena maggo ālambīyatīti paripuṇṇovāti ce? Evaṃ sati yena maggena maggo ālambito, sopi aññena, sopi aññenāti anavaṭṭhānaṃ siyā, tasmā na ārammaṇapaṭivedhato catusaccābhisamayo yutto, vuttanayeneva pana yutto. Kiñca paricchinditabbaṃ samucchinditabbañca ālambitvā paricchedasamucchedabhāvanā maggañāṇassa na yuttā tato anissaṭabhāvato, sabbasaṅkhatavinissaṭaṃ nibbānameva pana ārammaṇatā yuttā. Ahetukadiṭṭhi akiriyadiṭṭhiggahaṇena gahitā hetubyāpārova paramatthato kiriyāti katvā.

'Seeing at different times' means realizing the truths separately. 'Of one who sees one' means of one who sees one truth. It should not be connected, for if connected, complete seeing, being subsequent to another seeing, would lead to a cessation of seeing; and in the separate realization of the truths, through seeing suffering, etc., the partial abandonment of the three fetters, etc., which are to be abandoned by the first path, etc., would result. Thus, there would be a partial state of being on the path of stream-entry, and immediately afterwards, due to the fruit to be attained, a partial state of being a stream-enterer. Therefore, separate realization of the truths is not appropriate. Just as separate realization is not fitting, so too is realization by way of an object. For if the realization of the four truths is desired by making them an object, the path itself does not make itself an object—thus, the realization of the truths would be incomplete. If it is said that another path takes the path as its object, and so it is complete, then the path by which a path is taken as an object would itself be taken as an object by another, and that one by another, leading to an infinite regress. Therefore, the realization of the four truths through penetration by way of an object is not appropriate, but it is fitting in the way stated. Furthermore, for path-knowledge, the development of defining and uprooting by taking as an object that which is to be defined and uprooted is not appropriate, because of not having escaped from it. However, Nibbāna alone, which is entirely free from all conditioned things, is a fitting object. The view of no-cause is included under the view of no-action, on the grounds that the activity of a cause is, in the ultimate sense, action.

Pavattetīti sajjati, pavattiyā vā hetu hoti. Nivattetīti saṃharati palayaṃ gameti, palokatādivasena vā mokkhahetu hoti. Padhānatoti pakatito, yaṃ “abyatta”ntipi vuccati.

'Causes to continue' means it clings, or it is the cause of continuity. 'Causes to cease' means it gathers in, brings to destruction, or is the cause of liberation through states like vanishing, etc. 'From the Pradhāna' means from the original state, which is also called 'unmanifest.'

“Kālo [V 0.0063] karoti bhūtāni, kālo saṃharatī pajā;

Kālo sutte jāgarati, kālo hi duratikkamo”ti. –

'Time creates beings, time destroys creatures; Time is awake among the sleeping, for time is hard to overcome.'

Evaṃvādā kālavādino. “Kaṇṭakassa tikhiṇatā, kapiṭṭhaphalādīnaṃ parimaṇḍalatā, migapakkhisarīsapādīnaṃ vicittabhāvoti evamādayo kena kāritā? Sabhāveneva siddhā, evaṃ sabbampi, na ettha kassaci kāmakāro”ti evaṃvādā sabhāvavādino. “Loko niyato acchejjasuttāvutābhejjamaṇisadiso[M 0.0065], na ettha kassaci purisakāro”ti evaṃpavattavādā niyativādino, –

Those who speak thus are the proponents of time. 'The sharpness of a thorn, the roundness of fruits like the wood-apple, the diverse nature of animals, birds, and reptiles—by whom are these made? They are established by their own nature alone. Thus is everything; here, no one has any power of will,' thus speak the proponents of own-nature. 'The world is fixed, like an unbreakable gem strung on an unbreakable thread; here, no one has any human agency,' thus declare the proponents of determinism.

“Yadicchāya pavattanti, yadicchāya nivattare;

Yadicchāya sukhadukkhaṃ, tasmā yadicchatī pajā”ti. –

'By chance they proceed, by chance they turn back; by chance there is pleasure and pain; therefore, people desire.'

Evaṃpavattavādā yadicchāvādisaṅkhātā adhiccasamuppattivādino ca ettha sabhāvavāde eva antogadhāti daṭṭhabbā. Aṇūhi loko pavattatīti ājīvakavādaṃ sandhāyāha. So hi akāraṇapariggaho. Kaṇādavādo pana issaricchāvasena aṇūnaṃ saṃyogaviyogato lokassa pavattinivattiṃ vadati. Padhānassa appavattīti mahatādibhāvena apariṇāmo, anabhibyatti vā. “Ahamañño, pakati aññā”ti evaṃ pavattapakatipurisantarajānanena attasukhadukkhamohesu avibhāgaggahaṇe nivattite kira vuttanayena padhānaṃ nappavattati, so vimokkhoti kāpilā. Evamādīti ādi-saddena mahābrahmuno samīpatā, saṃyogoti evamādīnampi saṅgaho veditabbo.

Those whose doctrine proceeds thus, the proponents of chance, also known as the adherents of fortuitous origination, should be understood as included here within the doctrine of own-nature. 'The world proceeds from atoms'—this is said with reference to the doctrine of the Ājīvikas, for that is the acceptance of non-cause. The doctrine of Kaṇāda, however, states that the origination and cessation of the world occur through the combination and separation of atoms by the will of Īśvara. 'The non-proceeding of the Pradhāna' means its non-transformation by way of the Mahat, etc., or its non-manifestation. 'I am different, Nature is different'—thus, when the grasping of non-distinction in one's own happiness, suffering, and delusion is ceased through the knowledge of the distinction between Puruṣa and Prakṛti that proceeds thus, the Pradhāna indeed does not proceed; that is liberation, according to the Kāpilas. By 'and so on,' the inclusion of such things as proximity to Mahā Brahmā and combination should also be understood.

Ekattāti ekabhāvato ekopi vutto. Tayoti kiccavibhāgena. Tānīti sammāvācādisīlāni. Chandassa saddahanānukūlāpi chandanavasena pavatti hotīti saddhindriyasaddhābalehi saddhiṃ chandiddhipādo vutto. Tādise kāle upekkhānimittānubrūhanena upakārā samādhissa samavāhitāvasena tādisakiccāva upekkhā veditabbā.

'As one' means it is also called one from being of a single nature. 'As three' means by division of function. 'Those' refers to the virtues such as right speech. Because the arising of desire is also conducive to belief and occurs through the influence of desire, the basis of spiritual power that is desire is mentioned together with the faculty of faith and the power of faith. At such a time, equanimity should be understood as having that very function, being an aid to concentration through the cultivation of the sign of equanimity, due to its bringing about balance.

Vighātakattāti saṃharaṇīyavasena vihantabhāvato.

'Because of being destructive' means due to its nature of destroying, in the sense of being something to be removed.

Ariyasaccadvayanti samudayamaggasaccadvayaṃ. Tenevāti yathāvuttadukkhādisaddānaṃ pariññeyyādivācakattā [V 0.0064] eva. Ādipadasaṅgahoti “dukkhaṃ, na ariyasacca”nti iminā catukke ādipade saṅgaho. Tadapekkhanti ariyasaccasaddāpekkhaṃ dukkhasaddaṃ. Catutthapadasaṅgahoti “neva dukkhaṃ, na ariyasacca”nti iminā padena saṅgaho. Avasesakilesādayoti taṇhāvajjakilesā avasesākusalā, sāsavāni kusalamūlāni, sāsavā ca kusaladhammā. Te hi abhidhammabhājanīye samudayabhāvena vuttā, na ariyasaccabhāvenāti āha “samudayo, na ariyasacca”nti. Aññāni maggaṅgānīti phalasammādiṭṭhiādayo. Iminā nayenāti etthāyaṃ yojanā – atthi [M 0.0066] samudayo, na ariyasaccaṃ, atthi ariyasaccaṃ, na samudayo, atthi samudayo ceva ariyasaccañca, atthi neva samudayo, na ariyasaccaṃ. Tattha paṭhamapadaṃ vuttatthaṃ. Nirodho ariyasaccaṃ, na samudayo, taṇhā samudayo ceva ariyasaccañca, maggasampayuttā dhammā sāmaññaphalāni ca yassa pahānāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati, tadabhāvato neva samudayo, na ariyasaccaṃ. Itarasaccadvayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ tassa tassa pabhāvakaṭṭhena siyā samudayo, na pana yassa pahānāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathatthena. Itaracatukkadvayepi ādipadaṃ vuttatthameva. Sesesu samudayo ariyasaccaṃ, na nirodho, asaṅkhatadhātu nirodho ceva ariyasaccañca, maggasampayuttā dhammā, sāmaññaphalāni ca yassa sacchikiriyāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathatthena neva nirodho, na ariyasaccaṃ. Itarasaccadvayaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, nirodhadhammatāya siyā nirodho, na pana yassa sacchikiriyāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathatthena. Tathā nirodho ariyasaccaṃ, na maggo, ariyamaggo maggo ceva ariyasaccañca, maggasampayuttā dhammā, sāmaññaphalāni ca yassa bhāvanāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathatthena neva maggo, na ariyasaccaṃ. Itarasaccadvayaṃ siyā maggo upapattimaggabhāvato, na pana yassa bhāvanāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati tathatthena.

The two noble truths are the two truths of origin and path. Thus, because the terms such as 'suffering' as stated denote what is to be fully understood, etc. The inclusion of the initial phrase means the inclusion of the initial phrase in the tetrad, such as 'suffering, not a noble truth.' 'Tadapekkhanti' means the word 'suffering' is dependent on the word 'noble truth.' The inclusion of the fourth phrase means the inclusion by this phrase, such as 'neither suffering nor a noble truth.' The remaining defilements, etc., are the defilements apart from craving, the remaining unwholesome states, the wholesome roots with taints, and wholesome states with taints. For these are stated in the Abhidhamma classification as the nature of origin, not as the nature of a noble truth; hence it is said, 'origin, not a noble truth.' The other path factors are right view associated with fruition, etc. By this method, the following explanation applies: there is origin, but not a noble truth; there is a noble truth, but not origin; there is both origin and a noble truth; there is neither origin nor a noble truth. Here, the first phrase has the meaning already stated. Cessation is a noble truth, but not origin. Craving is both origin and a noble truth. The states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship are neither origin nor a noble truth, because they are not that for the abandonment of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. The other two truths are noble truths; they might be origin due to their generative nature, but not in the sense of that for the abandonment of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. Similarly, in the other two tetrads, the initial phrase has the meaning already stated. In the remaining cases, origin is a noble truth, but not cessation. The unconditioned element is both cessation and a noble truth. The states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship are neither cessation nor a noble truth in the sense of that for the realization of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. The other two truths are noble truths; they might be cessation due to their nature of cessation, but not in the sense of that for the realization of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. Likewise, cessation is a noble truth, but not the path. The noble path is both path and a noble truth. The states associated with the path and the fruits of recluseship are neither path nor a noble truth in the sense of that for the development of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. The other two truths might be a path due to their nature as a path to rebirth, but not in the sense of that for the development of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.

Santanti samānaṃ. Evaṃ itaresupīti kātabbāpi kiriyā kārakarahitā kevalaṃ attano paccayehi tāya pavattamānāya paccayasāmaggī kiriyaṃ karotīti vohāramattaṃ hoti. Nibbutigamakesupi eseva nayo.

'Santanti' means 'equal' or 'the same.' Thus, in the case of others too, even actions to be done, being without a doer and simply proceeding by their own conditions, it is merely a conventional way of speaking to say that an assemblage of conditions performs the action. The same principle applies also to those headed for Nibbāna.

Sāsavatā asubhatā kilesāsucipaggharaṇato. Dukkhādīnanti dukkhasamudayamaggānaṃ. Samudayādibhāvoti dukkhassa samudayamaggabhāvo, samudayassa maggadukkhabhāvo, maggassa dukkhasamudayabhāvo ca, na pana nirodhabhāvo dukkhādīnanti sambandho. Aññamaññasamaṅgitāti dukkhādīnaṃ [V 0.0065] itarītarasabhāvayogo. Taṇhāyāti ādhāre bhummaṃ. Punabbhavassāti punabhavasaṅkhātassa āyatidukkhassa. Pakativādīnanti kāpilānaṃ. Vikārāti mahatādayo byattā. Vibhāvatoti abhibyattito, pariṇāmato vā pubbe. Paṭippalīnā cāti pacchā pakatiyaṃ palayaṃ gatā vesammaṃ muñcitvā sattādisamabhāvena anto samoruddhā. Tenāha “pakatibhāveneva tiṭṭhantī”ti. Pakatibhāvenevāti abyattabhāveneva[M 0.0067]. Samudayabhāvenāti taṇhāsaṅkhātapabhavabhāvena. Aññathā taṃsampayuttaavijjādīnampi samudayabhāvo labbhatevāti. Avibhattehīti vesammavirahena pakatibhāvaṃ gatehi. “Vikārehī”ti sāmaññato vutte “mahantā”tiādinā sarūpato dasseti. Tattha mahantoti mahābuddhi. Tañhi kāpilā “mahāajjhāsayo”ti ca voharanti. Rūpatammattādayo pañca tammattā, ahaṃkāro cāti cha avisesā. Cakkhu sotaṃ ghānaṃ jivhā kāyo vācā pāṇi pādo pāyu upatthaṃ manoti ekādasindriyāni. Pathavī āpo tejo vāyo ākāsanti pañca bhūtavisesā, tehi. “Pakatibhāveneva ṭhitehī”ti iminā “avibhattehī”ti padassa atthaṃ vadati. Sagabbhāti sabījā asuññatā. Tantūsūti suttesu samavāyikāraṇabhūtesu. Tathā kapālesu. Tividhañhi te kāraṇaṃ vadanti upādānakāraṇaṃ nimittakāraṇaṃ samavāyikāraṇanti. Tattha turivemasalākādayo upādānakāraṇaṃ. Tantavāyo nimittakāraṇaṃ. Tantavo samavāyikāraṇanti. Dvīsu aṇūsūti pathavībhūtesu vā āpotejovāyobhūtesu vā dvīsu paramāṇūsu. Idhabuddhivohārajanakoti “idha tantūsu paṭo, idha kapālesu ghaṭo, idha bīraṇesu ghaṭo”tiādinā nayena hetuphalānaṃ sambandhabhūtena sattānaṃ idhabuddhivohārā jāyanti. So govisāṇānaṃ viya avisuṃ sahasiddhānaṃ sambandho samavāyo. Khāṇusenānaṃ viya pana visuṃsiddhānaṃ sambandho saṃyogo. Tīsu aṇūsu tiaṇukaṃ phalaṃ samavetaṃ ekībhūtamiva sambandhanti yojanā. “Samaveta”nti etassa “ekībhūtamiva sambandha”nti idaṃ atthavivaraṇaṃ. Mahāparimāṇanti mahantaparimāṇaṃ mahāpathavīādikaṃ ekaṃ phalaṃ, yaṃ te “kāriyaṃ drabya”nti vadanti. Yehi kāraṇehi āraddhaṃ kāriyadrabyaṃ, tadantogadhāni eva tāni kāraṇāni maññantīti āha “attano antogadhehi kāraṇehī”ti. Sati samavāye hetumhi phalaṃ samavetanti phale hetu siyā, taṃ natthīti dassento āha “samavāyābhāvā phale hetu natthīti hetusuññaṃ phala”nti.

It is impure due to its taints, because defilements and impurities ooze forth. 'Dukkhādīnaṃ' refers to suffering, origin, and path. The nature of origin, etc., means the nature of origin and path in relation to suffering; the nature of path and suffering in relation to origin; and the nature of suffering and origin in relation to the path; but the connection does not apply to the nature of cessation in relation to suffering, etc. Mutual association means the combination of suffering, etc., with each other's nature. 'Taṇhāya' is in the locative case, indicating a basis. 'Punabbhavassa' refers to future suffering, designated as renewed existence. The proponents of inherent nature are the Kapilas. 'Vikārā' are the manifest evolutes, such as the great principle. 'Vibhāvato' means from manifestation, or from transformation previously. And 'reverting' means later, having reverted to the primordial nature, abandoning diversity, and being inwardly constrained with an equality of being, etc. Hence it is said, 'They remain in their primordial nature.' 'Pakatibhāveneva' means in the unmanifest nature. The nature of origin is the nature of arising designated as craving. Otherwise, the nature of origin would also be obtained for ignorance, etc., associated with it. 'Avibhattehi' means having gone to the primordial state through the absence of diversity. When 'transformations' is stated generally, 'the great principle,' etc., show their specific forms. There, 'the great principle' means the great intellect. For the Kapilas also call it 'the great disposition.' The five subtle elements—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—along with ego, these six are undifferentiated. The eleven faculties are eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, speech, hand, foot, anus, genitals, and mind. The five specific elements are earth, water, fire, air, and space. 'They remain in their primordial nature' explains the meaning of the word 'undifferentiated.' 'Sagabbhā' means containing seed, not empty. 'Tantūsu' refers to threads, which are the co-inherent causes. Similarly, in pot-shards. For they speak of three kinds of causes: the material cause, the instrumental cause, and the co-inherent cause. Among these, the spindles, shuttles, etc., are the material causes. The weaver is the instrumental cause. The threads are the co-inherent causes. 'In two atoms' means in two ultimate atoms, either of the earth element or of the water, fire, and air elements. The generation of conventional understanding here means that beings generate conventional understanding, such as 'here is the cloth in the threads, here is the pot in the pot-shards, here is the pot in the reeds,' etc., by way of the connection between cause and effect. This connection, like that between a cow and its horns, is of co-arisen and inseparable things, which is co-inherence. But the connection, like that between a stump and an army, is of separately established things, which is conjunction. The explanation is that in three atoms, the triad atom, the result, is co-inherent, connected as if it has become one. This 'connected as if it has become one' is the explanation of the meaning of 'co-inherent.' 'The great measure' is a single great result, such as the great earth, etc., which they call 'the effect substance.' They consider those causes by which the effect substance is produced as included within it. Hence it is said, 'with causes included within itself.' If there were co-inherence, the effect would be co-inherent in the cause, which would mean the cause is in the effect; but that is not the case. Therefore, showing this, he says, 'Due to the absence of co-inherence, there is no cause in the effect; thus, a result is empty of a cause.'

Āhārabhedeti kabaḷīkārādiāhāravisese. Tappaccayadhammabhedeti ajjhoharaṇīyavatthusaḷāyatanaavijjāabhisaṅkhārasaṅkhāte tesaṃ paccayabhūtadhammavisese, ojaṭṭhamakarūpavedanāpaṭisandhiviññāṇanāmarūpasaṅkhāte [V 0.0066] vā tannibbattadhammavisese, te paccayā etesaṃ dhammavisesānanti tappaccayadhammabhedā[M 0.0068]. Rūpādiārammaṇavasena vāti yojanā. Yānadvayavasenāti samathavipassanāyānadvayavasena. Kiñcāpi maggakkhaṇe samathavipassanā yuganaddhāva, yathā pana suññatādisamaññā, evaṃ samathavipassanāsamaññāpi āgamanato maggassa siyunti āha “āgamanavasena vutto”ti. Yassa vā paññindriyaṃ adhikaṃ, tassa maggo vipassanā, itarassa samathoti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

The division of nutriment refers to the different types of nutriment, such as edible morsels, etc. The division of phenomena dependent on that refers to the distinct phenomena that serve as conditions for them, such as ingestible objects, the six sense bases, ignorance, and volitional formations; or to the distinct phenomena produced by them, such as the material octad with nutritive essence as the eighth, feeling, rebirth-linking consciousness, and name-and-form. Those are the conditions for these distinct phenomena; hence, 'the division of phenomena dependent on that.' Alternatively, the explanation is in terms of objects such as forms, etc. By means of the two vehicles refers to the two vehicles of serenity and insight.
